case_title: Aquarius H2O Dynamics Private Limited vs. M/s Riddhi Siddhi Metals
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Aquarius H2O Dynamics Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and Respondent is M/s Riddhi Siddhi Metals (Operational Creditor)[cite: 39]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Supply of industrial goods and services by operational creditor under commercial invoices[cite: 39]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational creditor claimed Rs. 1,16,40,233/- (principal of Rs. 1.01 crore plus unilaterally added interest of Rs. 15,19,753/-)[cite: 39]. Corporate debtor had made payments totaling Rs. 11 lakhs between October 2023 and January 2024[cite: 39]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Payments of Rs. 11 lakhs made between 11.10.2023 and 31.01.2024[cite: 39]; Section 8 demand notice issued on 19.03.2024[cite: 39]; NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-I admitted Section 9 ex-parte on 29.11.2024[cite: 39]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements proving credit of Rs. 9.50 lakhs (from sister concern Shreeji Equipment), Rs. 2.50 lakhs (Simon Patel), and Rs. 1 lakh (Rameshbhai Patel), contrasting with incomplete creditor ledger accounts[cite: 39]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad admitted the Section 9 petition ex-parte after closing debtor's right to reply[cite: 39]. Corporate debtor appealed under Section 61 asserting threshold suppression[cite: 39].
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 application was maintainable when deduction of suppressed part payments made prior to the Section 8 demand notice reduced the actionable operational debt below the mandatory Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 crore[cite: 39].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An operational creditor cannot artificially manufacture the Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1 crore by suppressing part-payments and unilaterally adding uncontracted interest; when valid part-payments reduce the principal operational debt below Rs. 1 crore, a Section 9 application is non-maintainable[cite: 39]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4 mandates a strict default threshold of Rs. 1 crore for triggering CIRP, which must be genuine and legally due on the date of demand[cite: 39]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Direct banking credit entries showing receipt of funds by the operational creditor rebut discrepancies in creditor-maintained ledgers[cite: 39]. Unilateral inclusion of interest without contractual backing cannot be accepted to satisfy pecuniary thresholds[cite: 39]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since legitimate payments reduced the operational debt below Rs. 1 crore, the ex-parte admission was legally flawed and unsustainable[cite: 39].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 39 of 2025 is allowed; the NCLT order dated 29.11.2024 is set aside, and the Corporate Debtor is freed from CIRP, leaving the creditor liberty to pursue civil recovery remedies[cite: 39].
summary: Aquarius H2O Dynamics appealed against an ex-parte NCLT Ahmedabad order admitting a Section 9 CIRP petition filed by Riddhi Siddhi Metals for an alleged debt of Rs. 1.16 crores[cite: 39]. The appellant demonstrated that it had paid Rs. 11 lakhs prior to the demand notice, which was credited to the creditor's bank account but suppressed in its debtor ledger, and that Rs. 15 lakhs of interest was unilaterally claimed without contractual agreement[cite: 39]. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that deducting the proven payments and uncontracted interest brought the actual operational default below the mandatory Rs. 1 crore threshold under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 39]. The appeal was allowed, the CIRP admission was quashed, and the corporate debtor was restored to independent functioning[cite: 39].

case_title: Nagri Farm Tea Co. Ltd. vs. Ram Ratan Modi (RP of Duncans Industries Ltd.) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Nagri Farm Tea Co. Ltd. (entity possessing Marybong Tea Estate), Respondent No. 1 is Ram Ratan Modi (RP of Duncans Industries Ltd.), and Respondent No. 2 is Uniglobal Papers Pvt. Ltd. (SRA)[cite: 40]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Long-term tea garden leases in West Bengal granted to corporate debtor Duncans Industries Ltd.; Marybong Tea Estate was possessed by appellant under MoUs dated 01.01.2004 and 05.07.2013[cite: 40]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not applicable as this is a plan approval and lease renewal challenge[cite: 40]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 05.03.2020; NCLAT held on 02.08.2024 that expired leases were not debtor assets; NCLT Kolkata approved the resolution plan on 18.10.2024, prompting this appeal[cite: 40]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tea estate lease records, bilateral MoUs, Tea Board reports, and paragraph 18 and clause 9.2.1 of the approved resolution plan[cite: 40]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata approved the resolution plan in IA (IB) No. 237/(KB)/2022 and permitted the SRA to take steps for lease renewal of expired tea estates with the lessor[cite: 40]. Appellant challenged paragraph 18 regarding Marybong Tea Estate[cite: 40].
legal_issues: Whether NCLT's direction granting liberty to the Successful Resolution Applicant to apply for or pursue lease renewals with the State Government for expired tea estates prejudices possessory rights of third-party operators[cite: 40].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan granting the successful resolution applicant liberty to apply for statutory renewals of expired corporate debtor leases does not prejudice third-party occupiers where the order clarifies that it does not adjudicate the merits of lease renewals, which remain exclusively within the governmental lessor's domain[cite: 40]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 confers on the resolution applicant the standing of the corporate debtor to prosecute pending renewal applications before competent authorities[cite: 40]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Restricting tribunal directions to a simple procedural liberty to apply prevents interference with existing third-party possessory claims pending governmental decision[cite: 40]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Since the Adjudicating Authority expressed no opinion on the grant or refusal of lease renewals, the challenge to the approval order is baseless[cite: 40].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2291 of 2024 is dismissed, with the clarification that the Adjudicating Authority expressed no opinion on the merits of renewal applications[cite: 40].
summary: Nagri Farm Tea Co. Ltd. challenged an NCLT Kolkata order approving the resolution plan for Duncans Industries Ltd., specifically targeting directions permitting the Successful Resolution Applicant to apply for lease renewals regarding the Marybong Tea Estate, which the appellant possessed under MoUs[cite: 40]. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that the SRA is entitled to step into the corporate debtor's shoes to pursue renewal applications[cite: 40]. Clarifying that the NCLT's directions merely granted liberty to apply without opining on the merits of the renewal, which remains strictly within the discretion of the State Government, the Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal[cite: 40].

case_title: Mr. K.S. Chowdry vs. Mummaneni Vazra Laxmi, Liquidator, Ravi Cranes & Movers
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. K.S. Chowdry, a suspended director and prospective resolution applicant of the Corporate Debtor; the Respondent is Mummaneni Vazra Laxmi, the Liquidator/Resolution Professional of the Corporate Debtor, M/s. Ravi Cranes and Movers Limited (which also acted as Corporate Guarantor for M/s. RCM Infrastructure Ltd); Indian Overseas Bank was the initiating Financial Creditor; and M/s. Maximus ARC Limited was the assignee of debt from Union Bank of India. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities were availed by the Corporate Debtor from Indian Overseas Bank, leading to insolvency proceedings; additionally, M/s. Maximus ARC Limited acquired loan portfolios and security interests originally held by Union Bank of India under an Assignment Deed dated 19.08.2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Following loan defaults, CIRP was triggered against the Corporate Debtor under Section 7 on 26.09.2022; specific quantified figures of total default are not detailed in the order beyond the failure of the CIRP process and subsequent liquidation initiation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against the Principal Borrower (M/s. RCM Infrastructure Ltd) was initiated on 03.01.2019; CIRP against the Corporate Debtor was initiated on 26.09.2022; the 21st CoC meeting resolved to liquidate the Corporate Debtor on 08.04.2024; an assignment deed was executed in favour of Maximus ARC on 19.08.2024; the Appellant communicated interest to submit a plan on 24.08.2024; orders were reserved on the liquidation application IA(IBC)(liq)/14/2024 on 02.09.2024; and an intervention application IA No. 34/2024 was filed by Maximus ARC on 05.09.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The minutes of the 21st CoC meeting dated 08.04.2024 demonstrated a unanimous 100% voting share resolution favoring liquidation after 20 earlier failed meetings; records showed the Appellant failed to cooperate or submit a resolution plan during the active CIRP; and Maximus ARC's application was filed post reservation of orders without formally praying for leave to intervene. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Resolution Professional filed IA(IBC)(liq)/14/2024 under Section 33(2) before the NCLT Hyderabad, which ordered the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor while holding Maximus ARC's intervention application IA No. 34/2024 unsustainable as the 100% liquidation vote had already concluded prior to reservation of orders.
legal_issues: Whether, when corporate insolvency resolution proceedings have reached the stage of Section 33(2) of the IBC following a unanimous CoC decision to liquidate, the subsequent pendency of an Interlocutory Application seeking intervention by an assignee of debt to explore alternative resolution avenues creates an impediment to passing an order of liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A subsequent intervention application by a debt assignee seeking to defer liquidation or consider belated resolution proposals cannot impede or stall the adjudicating authority from passing a liquidation order under Section 33(2) when the statutory majority of the Committee of Creditors has already decisively and validly voted to liquidate prior to the application. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) mandates that once the Committee of Creditors resolves to liquidate the Corporate Debtor with not less than the statutory voting threshold before plan approval and intimates the authority, the Adjudicating Authority is required to pass a liquidation order under Section 33(1), which cannot be held hostage by post-decision assignments or belated applications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict adherence to the record of statutory voting within CoC meetings and procedural timeliness; an intervention application filed after orders on the liquidation application have already been reserved, supported only by speculative proposals from non-cooperating suspended directors, lacks bona fides and legal viability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The unanimous decision of the CoC to liquidate having been validly exercised after exhaustively exploring resolution over extended periods, neither the debt assignment to Maximus ARC nor the pendency of its IA No. 34/2024 creates any legal barrier to the liquidation of the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 47/2025 is dismissed, affirming the liquidation order passed by the Adjudicating Authority against the Corporate Debtor.
summary: Mr. K.S. Chowdry, suspended director of Corporate Debtor M/s. Ravi Cranes and Movers Limited, appealed against the NCLT's liquidation order passed under Section 33(2) of the IBC. After 20 unsuccessful CoC meetings, the CoC had voted with 100% consensus in its 21st meeting to liquidate the company. Following reservation of orders on the liquidation application, an assignee of debt (Maximus ARC) filed an intervention application seeking to keep liquidation in abeyance to consider a belated resolution proposal from the Appellant. The NCLAT held that the commercial decision of the CoC to liquidate validly taken under Section 33(2) cannot be stalled by subsequent debt assignments or intervention applications filed after reservation of orders, and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Hiren Anand Agarwal & Ors. vs. National Company Law Tribunal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Hiren Anand Agarwal & Ors., who are members of the suspended board of directors of the Corporate Debtor; the Respondent is the National Company Law Tribunal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An underlying corporate insolvency resolution proceeding was initiated via company petition C.P. No. (IB)/760(MB)2021 before the NCLT Mumbai Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics are not detailed, as the lis strictly pertains to an administrative transfer order regarding the pending company petition. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The President of the NCLT issued an administrative transfer order transferring the petition to Court No. 1, which was formally communicated by the Registrar via letter dated 13.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The administrative communication dated 13.02.2025 issued under Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules, 2016, and record of previous proceedings in Court No. IV where hearings had taken place and an earlier transfer request had been rejected on 02.02.2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The President of the NCLT exercised administrative powers to reassign and transfer C.P. No. (IB)/760(MB)2021 from Court No. IV to Court No. 1, which the Appellants directly challenged before the NCLAT on the ground that reasons for the transfer were not recorded or disclosed.
legal_issues: Whether the President of the NCLT, acting as master of the roster under Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules, 2016, is legally required to assign and communicate reasons to parties when transferring a case from one Bench/Court to another, and whether such an administrative transfer prejudicially affects the rights of a suspended director so as to warrant appellate interference.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An administrative order transferring a case between benches passed by the head of a tribunal as master of the roster does not determine substantive rights or inflict civil consequences; hence, recording and communicating reasons to the litigants is not a prerequisite unless the transfer causes demonstrated prejudice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 vests broad administrative discretion in the President to transfer cases when circumstances so warrant (such as bench reconstitutions, member transfers, and roster adjustments), without imposing an obligation to record justiciable reasons for the litigants. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The requirement to record reasons laid down in administrative law jurisprudence (e.g., Kranti Associates) applies strictly to administrative actions that entail civil consequences or prejudicially affect the legal rights of parties; mere reallocation of a forum does not meet this threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transfer of C.P. No. (IB)/760(MB)2021 to Court No. 1 by the President was a valid exercise of administrative power as master of the roster that caused no legal prejudice to the suspended directors, justifying no appellate interference.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 555 of 2025 along with I.A. No. 2112 of 2025 is dismissed.
summary: Appellants, suspended directors of the Corporate Debtor, challenged the administrative order dated 13.02.2025 issued by the President of NCLT transferring C.P. No. (IB)/760(MB)2021 from Court No. IV to Court No. 1. The Appellants contended that reasons must be recorded and communicated for an administrative transfer under Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Kranti Associates. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the President is the master of the roster with administrative authority to assign and reallocate cases to meet administrative exigencies, and that routine transfer between benches causes no civil consequences or legal prejudice requiring disclosure of reasons.

case_title: Mr. Rajesh Bhatia & Mr. Ashwani Kumar Bhatia vs. Canara Bank & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 143/2024 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 150/2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mr. Rajesh Bhatia and Mr. Ashwani Kumar Bhatia, Managing Directors and Personal Guarantors of the Corporate Debtor, M/s. ARS Energy Private Limited; Respondent No. 1 is Canara Bank, lead bank of the consortium of financial creditors; Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Ramachandran Subramanian, the appointed Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor availed financial credit facilities aggregating to a sanctioned limit of Rs. 397.64 crores from a consortium led by Canara Bank, secured by Personal Guarantee Deeds executed by the Appellants on 29.06.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding dues stood at Rs. 305.22 crores as on 29.09.2023; the loan account was declared a Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 29.08.2022; default claimed under the personal guarantee invocation notice was Rs. 93.46 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee executed on 29.06.2017; NPA classification on 29.08.2022; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 20.09.2023; Section 95(4) demand notice issued on 30.11.2023; Section 13(4) SARFAESI possession notice issued on 02.12.2023; Section 95 petitions filed thereafter. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Personal Guarantee Deeds dated 29.06.2017; SARFAESI notices under Section 13(2) and Section 13(4); statutory demand notices under Section 95(4) dated 30.11.2023 for Rs. 93.46 crores; SA No. 2/2024 pending before the DRT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed CP(IB)/57(CHE)/2024 and CP(IB)/58(CHE)/2024 under Section 95(1) before NCLT Chennai; NCLT passed impugned orders on 19.03.2024 and 20.03.2024 appointing Respondent No. 2 as Resolution Professional under Section 97 with directions to examine the applications and submit a report under Section 99.
legal_issues: Whether the appointment of a Resolution Professional under Section 97 of the IBC in a petition filed under Section 95(1) constitutes an adjudicatory proceeding causing legal prejudice that confers a right of challenge upon the Personal Guarantor prior to the Section 100 stage.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In personal insolvency resolution proceedings, actions and procedures from Section 95 up to Section 99—including the appointment of a Resolution Professional under Section 97—are non-adjudicatory and facilitative, creating no legal injury or cause of action for the debtor/guarantor to maintain an appeal prior to formal admission or rejection under Section 100. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 97 read with Section 99 designates the Resolution Professional as a facilitator tasked with collation of information and submission of a recommendation report; the Personal Guarantor has no statutory audience or entitlement to challenge the appointment mechanism at this preliminary threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Reliance on the binding ratio of the Supreme Court in Dilip B Jiwrajka v. Union of India, affirming that the absence of judicial determination between Sections 95 and 100 shields the appointment of a Resolution Professional from intermediate judicial review, provided all substantive defenses remain available under Section 99 and Section 100. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because all rights and objections of the Personal Guarantors remain preserved for consideration at the stage of reporting under Section 99 and admission/rejection under Section 100, the Appellants are not aggrieved persons entitled to challenge the Section 97 appointment order.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 143/2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 150/2024 are dismissed; connected Interlocutory Applications are closed.
summary: Appellants, Personal Guarantors of M/s. ARS Energy Private Limited, challenged orders of NCLT Chennai appointing a Resolution Professional under Section 97 of the IBC in Section 95(1) insolvency proceedings initiated by Canara Bank for dues amounting to Rs. 93.46 crores. The Appellants contended that the appointment mechanism violated Section 97(3) and (4). Dismissing both appeals, the NCLAT applied the Supreme Court ruling in Dilip B Jiwrajka v. Union of India, holding that steps between Sections 95 and 99 are administrative and facilitative without adjudicatory determination of rights. Since guarantors can raise all objections before the NCLT upon submission of the Section 99 report, the challenge was premature.

case_title: Mr. Sadananda Maiya P & Ors. vs. Karnataka Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mr. Sadananda Maiya P, Mr. Sudarshan Maiya, and Mrs. Sunanda Maiya, who are Personal Guarantors; Respondent No. 1 is Karnataka Bank Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Balakrishnan Venkatachalam, appointed Interim Resolution Professional/Resolution Professional[cite: 7, 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities were extended by Respondent No. 1 to the principal borrower/company for which the Appellants executed personal guarantees[cite: 7, 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Defaults occurred leading Respondent No. 1 to initiate insolvency resolution processes under Section 95 of the IBC against the personal guarantors; specific default and debt amounts are not detailed in the text of the order[cite: 7, 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Respondent No. 1 filed applications under Section 95 of the IBC, leading to interim moratoria under Section 96, followed by the NCLT Bengaluru passing appointment orders on 28.01.2025[cite: 7, 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Financial Creditor submitted Part IV of Form C proposing the name of the Resolution Professional along with the written consent and affidavit/undertaking confirming no disciplinary proceedings were pending against him[cite: 7, 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 initiated insolvency petitions C.P. (IB) No. 06/BB/2025, C.P. (IB) No. 05/BB/2025, and C.P. (IB) No. 04/BB/2025 before the NCLT Bengaluru[cite: 7, 10]; the Adjudicating Authority passed impugned orders on 28.01.2025 appointing Respondent No. 2 as the RP under Section 97[cite: 7, 10]; Appellants appealed under Section 61 contending the NCLT was bound to direct the IBBI to nominate an RP under Section 97(3) instead of accepting the creditor's proposed RP[cite: 7, 10].
legal_issues: Whether a Personal Guarantor has an actionable cause of action under Section 61 of the IBC to maintain an appeal challenging the appointment of a Resolution Professional under Section 97 prior to the submission of the Section 99 report and the adjudication of admission/rejection under Section 100[cite: 7, 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Steps and orders passed by the Adjudicating Authority between Section 95 and Section 99 of the IBC—including the facilitative appointment of a Resolution Professional under Section 97—are purely procedural and administrative without determining substantive rights; thus, a debtor/guarantor has no cause of action to file an appeal prior to judicial determination under Section 100[cite: 7, 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 97 is merely an enabling procedural mechanism designed to appoint a facilitator for collating relevant facts and evidence[cite: 7, 10]; it does not involve judicial adjudication of rights, and the appointment cannot be questioned under Section 61 as an aggrieved person until the Section 100 stage is reached[cite: 7, 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict application of the Supreme Court's ruling in Dilip B. Jiwrajka v. Union of India, establishing that absent an adjudicatory function or final determination of legal rights affecting the parties, procedural irregularities prior to the Section 99 recommendation report cannot give rise to appellate interference[cite: 7, 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Personal Guarantors suffer no legal prejudice at the Section 97 appointment stage because all substantive objections and rights remain reserved and can be raised before the Adjudicating Authority at the stage of Section 100 consideration[cite: 7, 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 180, 181, and 182 of 2025 are dismissed without prejudice to the Appellants' rights to raise objections regarding the RP's appointment at the Section 100 stage[cite: 7, 10]. Pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 7, 10].
summary: Appellants, Personal Guarantors against whom Karnataka Bank Ltd. filed Section 95 applications, appealed against NCLT Bengaluru orders dated 28.01.2025 appointing the Resolution Professional proposed by the Financial Creditor[cite: 7, 10]. The Appellants contended that the Tribunal was statutorily mandated under Section 97(3) to direct the IBBI to nominate an RP rather than accepting the creditor's nominee[cite: 7, 10]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT applied the Supreme Court decision in Dilip B. Jiwrajka v. Union of India, holding that proceedings between Sections 95 and 99 are administrative and facilitative without any adjudicatory determination[cite: 7, 10]. The personal guarantors suffered no prejudice, and their rights to object remain fully reserved at the Section 100 admission/rejection stage[cite: 7, 10].

case_title: Ajay Singal vs. Ranjan Chakraborti & Anr. (with connected appeal)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant in CA 1285/2024 is Ajay Singal, Director of Corporate Debtor M/s GRJ Distributors & Developers Private Limited; the Appellants in CA 1472/2024 are flat buyers (Varsha Gupta & Ors.); Respondent No. 1 is Ranjan Chakraborti (IRP); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Bajrang Fire Protection (Operational Creditor)[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Three purchase orders were issued by the Corporate Debtor to the Operational Creditor as a turnkey contractor for the supply and installation of ventilation, fire alarm, and fire-fighting systems in the 'Avalon Rangoli, Dharuhera' residential project in Rewari, Haryana[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed was Rs. 1,24,16,610/- against several RA bills raised between 15.01.2016 and 07.11.2017; the last invoice was dated 07.11.2017 and last part-payment by the Corporate Debtor occurred on 26.07.2017[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purchase orders issued on 04.09.2015, 13.01.2017, and 01.03.2017; Section 8 demand notice was issued on 05.02.2024; Section 9 petition was filed on 22.02.2024[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Operational Creditor produced bank statements of FY 2016-17 and RA Bills; to counter the plea of limitation, letters dated 16.04.2018 (admitting outstanding dues of Rs. 82.40L, Rs. 19.87L, and Rs. 7.94L), 03.01.2019 (acknowledging Rs. 1,10,21,553/-), and 22.12.2021 (acknowledging debt and requesting time due to real estate recession) were placed on record[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed (IB)-144(ND)/2024 under Section 9; NCLT New Delhi Court-III admitted the application on 10.05.2024, restricting the CIRP to the 'Avalon Rangoli, Dharuhera' project and appointing Mr. Sanjeet Kumar Sharma as IRP; the Corporate Debtor's director appealed on ground of limitation, while homebuyers appealed alleging collusive CIRP to defeat Consumer Commission refund decrees[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether the Section 9 application was barred by limitation under the IBC when the last invoice was raised in 2017, and whether subsequent written letters acknowledging liability and seeking extensions to pay constitute a valid acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to extend the limitation period[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A plea of limitation touches upon the jurisdiction of the Adjudicating Authority and may be raised for the first time in appeal, whereupon written acknowledgements of liability executed prior to the expiry of the prescriptive period operate under Section 18 of the Limitation Act to restart the limitation clock afresh[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to applications filed under Section 9 of the IBC; successive written communications expressing commitments to settle outstanding liabilities extend the limitation period of 3 years from the date of each respective acknowledgement[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted written letters issued by the Corporate Debtor acknowledging specific outstanding liabilities and citing liquidity crunches suffice as evidence of acknowledgement of debt; introduction of such evidence in appeal is permissible when limitation is challenged for the first time in appellate proceedings[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor having acknowledged the debt in writing on 16.04.2018, 03.01.2019, and finally on 22.12.2021, the Section 9 petition filed on 22.02.2024 was well within the three-year limitation period running from the last acknowledgement[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1285 of 2024 is dismissed[cite: 8]. Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1472 of 2024 is disposed of with directions to the Resolution Professional to process the flat buyers' refund claims in accordance with law[cite: 8]. No order as to costs[cite: 8].
summary: Ajay Singal, director of Corporate Debtor M/s GRJ Distributors & Developers Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT's admission order under Section 9 of the IBC, arguing for the first time that the operational claim for work executed up to 2017 was time-barred[cite: 8]. Flat buyers also challenged the admission, alleging collusion to frustrate Consumer Commission execution orders[cite: 8]. The NCLAT held that written letters issued by the Corporate Debtor on 16.04.2018, 03.01.2019, and 22.12.2021 constituted valid acknowledgements of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 8]. Since the petition was filed on 22.02.2024, within three years of the December 2021 letter, it was within limitation[cite: 8]. The appeals were dismissed/disposed of, directing the RP to process allottees' claims[cite: 8].

case_title: Subh Laxmi Investment Advisory Pvt. Ltd. vs. Committee of Creditors of Sintex Plastics Technology Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Subh Laxmi Investment Advisory Pvt. Ltd., an Unsuccessful Prospective Resolution Applicant (PRA); Respondent No. 1 is the Committee of Creditors of Sintex Plastics Technology Ltd. (consisting solely of RBL Bank Ltd with 100% voting share); Respondent No. 2 is the erstwhile RP (Nimai Gautam Shah); Respondent No. 3 is the Liquidator (CA Bimal Ashok Desai); Respondents No. 4 to 7 are the successful auction purchasers[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor M/s Sintex Plastics Technology Ltd. under Section 7 on 21.02.2023 on a petition filed by Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 9] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default metrics of the underlying Section 7 petition are not indicated; in the CIRP, the Appellant submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 4 Crores, subsequently revised via addenda up to Rs. 8 Crores, against the subsequent liquidation going concern auction sale price realized at Rs. 20.63 Crores[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 21.02.2023; Form G published on 14.08.2023; Appellant submitted initial plan on 17.10.2023 and final plan on 02.12.2023; CoC e-voting concluded on 26.03.2024; CIRP period expired on 30.03.2024; RP filed liquidation application IA No. 09 of 2024 under Section 33(1); NCLT ordered liquidation on 03.05.2024[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Voting records showed RBL Bank (sole CoC member) abstained from voting on all three submitted resolution plans; written email consent was given by the CoC on 27.03.2024 approving the filing of the liquidation application and nomination of the liquidator; liquidation e-auction conducted on 21.06.2024 yielded Rs. 20.63 Crores from Respondents 4–7 with sale certificate issued on 25.07.2024[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following expiration of the maximum CIRP period without an approved resolution plan, the RP filed IA No. 09 of 2024 under Section 33(1); NCLT Ahmedabad allowed the application on 03.05.2024 ordering liquidation; the Appellant appealed under Section 61 contending that the CoC's abstention did not amount to rejection and liquidation could not be filed without formal approval under Section 33(2)[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether the abstention of a sole CoC member from voting on resolution plans constitutes a valid exercise of commercial wisdom, and whether the Resolution Professional is duty-bound under Section 33(1) of the IBC to file for liquidation upon the expiry of the CIRP period without needing a separate 66% resolution under Section 33(2)[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The decision of a Committee of Creditors to abstain from voting on a resolution plan constitutes a non-justiciable exercise of its commercial wisdom, and when the statutory CIRP period expires without an approved plan, the Adjudicating Authority is statutorily mandated to order liquidation under Section 33(1)[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(1) operates mandatorily where no resolution plan is received or approved prior to the expiry of the maximum CIRP period; the requirement of a 66% CoC resolution under Section 33(2) applies only when the CoC decides to liquidate the Corporate Debtor during the pendency of the CIRP, not when the statutory period has already expired[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under CIRP Regulations, members are entitled to vote in favour, against, or abstain; abstention resulting in non-approval of a plan is an exercise of commercial wisdom that cannot be questioned by an unsuccessful resolution applicant[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CIRP having expired on 30.03.2024 without any plan obtaining affirmative approval, the RP correctly applied for liquidation under Section 33(1) with the CoC's written consent, and the liquidation order suffers from no legal infirmity[cite: 9].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1104 of 2024 is dismissed without any order as to costs[cite: 9]. Pending interlocutory applications are closed[cite: 9].
summary: Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant Subh Laxmi Investment Advisory Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order directing the liquidation of Sintex Plastics Technology Ltd. under Section 33(1) of the IBC[cite: 9]. The Appellant contended that the sole CoC member's (RBL Bank) abstention from e-voting did not equate to a rejection of its plan, and that the RP could not apply for liquidation absent a formal CoC resolution under Section 33(2)[cite: 9]. The NCLAT held that abstention reflects the CoC's non-justiciable commercial wisdom[cite: 9]. Because the statutory CIRP period had expired on 30.03.2024 without any approved plan, the RP was statutorily mandated to seek liquidation under Section 33(1)[cite: 9]. The appeal was dismissed, noting the corporate debtor had already been sold as a going concern at auction for Rs. 20.63 Crores[cite: 9].

case_title: Brihanmumbai Electric Supply and Transport Undertaking vs. Mr. Ashok Kumar Golecha, Liquidator for Spark Green Energy (Satara) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Brihanmumbai Electric Supply and Transport Undertaking ('BEST'), a government undertaking claiming status as a Secured Financial Creditor; the Respondent is Mr. Ashok Kumar Golecha, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Spark Green Energy (Satara) Ltd.[cite: 11] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: An Investment Agreement dated 23.12.2008 and Energy Purchase Agreement dated 01.10.2009 were executed where the Appellant provided an interest-free deposit of Rs. 30 Crores to develop a 25 MW biomass power project at Lonand MIDC, Satara, with delayed commissioning compensated by discounted energy tariffs[cite: 11]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The Appellant submitted a claim of Rs. 156,23,71,177/- (comprising Rs. 30 Crores principal and Rs. 126.23 Crores interest); the Liquidator admitted only Rs. 30 Crores as an unsecured claim and rejected the interest component of Rs. 126.23 Crores[cite: 11]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Corporate Debtor was ordered into liquidation on 28.07.2023; Appellant submitted Form-D claim on 24.08.2023; the Liquidator rejected the interest claim and classified Appellant as unsecured; NCLT upheld the decision on 25.10.2024[cite: 11]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Investment Agreement (Clause 3.3(a)(iv)) specifically categorized the Rs. 30 Crores advance as an 'Interest Free Deposit' and stipulated that a second charge on fixed assets would be given after project lenders created a first charge[cite: 11]; no charge was ever registered with the ROC under Section 77 of the Companies Act, nor entered in any Information Utility or CERSAI records[cite: 11]; and an earlier MERC regulatory ruling had declined interest[cite: 11]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant challenged the Liquidator's classification and interest rejection before NCLT Mumbai Bench-II in C.P. (IB) No. 4260/MB/2018; the Adjudicating Authority dismissed the application on 25.10.2024; Appellant appealed under Section 61 of the IBC[cite: 11].
legal_issues: Whether an interest-free deposit containing delayed-compensation clauses through discounted tariffs entitles the creditor to interest under the IBC, and whether a creditor can be classified as a Secured Financial Creditor in liquidation proceedings when no charge document was executed and no charge was registered under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 or Regulation 21 of the Liquidation Process Regulations[cite: 11].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A liquidator and the adjudicating authority exercising summary insolvency jurisdiction must strictly enforce express contractual terms and cannot read interest provisions into an agreement expressly designated as interest-free; furthermore, a claimant cannot be treated as a secured creditor in the absence of a charge document and registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013 and Regulation 21 of the Liquidation Process Regulations[cite: 11]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 77(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, read with Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, no charge created by a company can be taken into account by a Liquidator unless duly proved by Information Utility records, an ROC certificate of registration of charge, or CERSAI registration[cite: 11]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict document verification; in the absence of any executed charge document or statutory proof of registration, a plea of an equitable or 'floating charge' cannot create security interest under Section 3(31) of the IBC[cite: 11]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The underlying agreement expressly established an interest-free deposit without any interest entitlement, and because no charge was ever created or registered with the ROC, the Liquidator rightly admitted only the principal sum of Rs. 30 Crores as an unsecured financial debt[cite: 11].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 281 of 2025 is dismissed without costs, affirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 11].
summary: BEST appealed the NCLT Mumbai order affirming the Liquidator's decision admitting its claim against Spark Green Energy (Satara) Ltd. for only Rs. 30 Crores as an unsecured financial creditor, while rejecting an interest claim of Rs. 126.23 Crores[cite: 11]. BEST argued that delayed-commissioning compensation under its Investment Agreement implied interest and that failure to register the agreed second charge was the debtor's fault[cite: 11]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that summary jurisdiction does not permit rewriting contracts to award interest on explicitly interest-free deposits[cite: 11]. Moreover, pursuant to Section 77(3) of the Companies Act and Regulation 21 of the Liquidation Process Regulations, a liquidator cannot recognize a security interest without an executed charge document and proof of registration[cite: 11].

case_title: Deccan Advanced Sciences Private Limited vs. Escientia Biopharma Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 43/2025 & Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 44/2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Deccan Advanced Sciences Private Limited; the Respondents include Escientia Biopharma Private Limited (EBPL, Respondent No. 1), individual shareholders/directors Yadagiri Reddy Pendri & Ors. (Respondents No. 2 to 8, 10 to 13), Deccan Fine Chemicals (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 9), and a court-appointed Administrator (Devaki Vasudeva Rao)[cite: 13, 15]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying dispute involves an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241 of the Companies Act, 2013 regarding the affairs, governance, shareholding buy-out options, and management control of Escientia Advanced Sciences Private Limited (EASPL) and Escientia Biopharma Private Limited (EBPL)[cite: 13, 15]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an IBC debt-default recovery action; the dispute centers on internal company management, appointment of an Administrator, valuation of equity shares, and mutual buyout directives between rival shareholder groups[cite: 13, 15]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The principal docket order was pronounced and uploaded by NCLT Hyderabad on 07.03.2025 (deferring enforcement till 18.03.2025); a suo motu rectification order was passed on 10.03.2025; the detailed main judgment was uploaded on 11.03.2025; the Appellant e-filed an appeal (CA No. 39/2025) against the 07.03.2025 order on 14.03.2025; the Administrator filed a rectification memorandum on 20.03.2025; and NCLT passed the second rectification order on 25.03.2025[cite: 13, 15]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Court records demonstrated that the suo motu order of 10.03.2025 altered the entity designations from EASPL to EBPL without prior notice to the parties[cite: 13, 15]; the Administrator's subsequent memorandum dated 20.03.2025 sought extensive substantive modifications across numerous pages/clauses expanding directives to encompass both EASPL and EBPL; and copies of the memorandum were never served upon the Appellant prior to the 25.03.2025 order[cite: 13, 15]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP No. 44/241/HDB/2023, NCLT Hyderabad issued an interim docket order on 07.03.2025, subsequently modified suo motu under Rule 154 on 10.03.2025, and further modified on the Administrator's memo on 25.03.2025[cite: 13, 15]; the Appellant filed Company Appeals (AT) (CH) Nos. 43 & 44 of 2025 challenging both modification orders on grounds of natural justice violations and statutory bar under Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 13, 15].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT can exercise rectification powers under Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to introduce extensive corrections without prior notice to affected parties, and whether the first proviso to Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013 completely bars the NCLT from entertaining a rectification application once an appeal has already been preferred against the principal order[cite: 13, 15].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The power of rectification is strictly circumscribed to correcting accidental slips or arithmetical/clerical errors and cannot be exercised to alter substantive rights ex parte without issuing notice to affected parties; moreover, the moment an appeal is preferred against an order, the statutory jurisdiction of the lower tribunal to amend or rectify that order is completely ousted[cite: 13, 15]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the first proviso to Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, no amendment or rectification shall be made in respect of any order against which an appeal has been preferred under the Act, creating an absolute jurisdictional bar once an appeal is filed[cite: 13, 15]; furthermore, Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 cannot override the statutory prohibition or dispense with the fundamental requirements of audi alteram partem[cite: 13, 15]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of procedural filing stamps and service records establishing that the appeal was filed on 14.03.2025 prior to the Administrator's application of 20.03.2025, and absence of notice/service to affected parties vitiated the proceedings on grounds of natural justice[cite: 13, 15]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The orders dated 10.03.2025 and 25.03.2025 were invalid as they effected substantive alterations without giving the Appellant notice or opportunity of hearing, and the order of 25.03.2025 was directly barred by the first proviso to Section 420(2) due to the prior filing of the appeal[cite: 13, 15].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 43/2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 44/2025 are allowed, and the impugned orders dated 10.03.2025 and 25.03.2025 passed by NCLT Hyderabad are quashed, without preventing Respondents from filing a fresh application under Rule 154 subject to law[cite: 13, 15]. All connected Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 13, 15].
summary: Appellant Deccan Advanced Sciences Private Limited challenged two rectification orders passed by NCLT Hyderabad under Rule 154 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 which substantially modified a primary order dated 07.03.2025 in an oppression/mismanagement proceeding[cite: 13, 15]. The initial modification on 10.03.2025 was made suo motu without hearing the Appellant, while the second on 25.03.2025 was passed on an unserved memorandum filed by the Administrator after the Appellant had already lodged an appeal before the NCLAT on 14.03.2025[cite: 13, 15]. The NCLAT quashed both rectification orders, holding that substantive alterations made ex parte violate audi alteram partem, and that pursuant to the first proviso to Section 420(2) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal loses jurisdiction to rectify or amend an order once an appeal against it has been preferred[cite: 13, 15].

case_title: Mr. Harsha Vardhan Reddy vs. Merit Inn Southern Star Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Harsha Vardhan Reddy; Respondent No. 1 is Merit Inn Southern Star Private Limited; Respondents No. 2 & 3 are Mr. M.R. Sarangapani Reddy and the legal representative of Mrs. Saalini Sarangapani; Respondents No. 4 to 11 are professionals, directors, and entities including TCS Ltd.[cite: 16] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying litigation involves company petition TCP/110/2016 (originally CP/107/2012) concerning allegations of oppression and mismanagement in the affairs and shareholdings of Merit Inn Southern Star Private Limited under the Companies Act, 1956[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an IBC debt default; the issue strictly concerns an inordinate limitation delay in challenging a final company petition judgment[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Impugned Order by NCLT Chennai was delivered on 27.09.2017; limitation of 45+45 days expired on 26.12.2017; Appellant claimed knowledge of the order on 06.08.2024; application for certified copy was filed on 25.10.2024; certified copy was received on 30.10.2024; appeal was e-filed on 08.01.2025 (amounting to 2659 days of delay)[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Court records showed the Appellant had appeared in the company petition prior to its dismissal in default on 31.08.2016 and subsequent restoration on 17.10.2016; Appellant waited 80 days after claimed knowledge on 06.08.2024 to apply for a certified copy on 25.10.2024; the condonation application IA No. 604/2025 pleaded a delay of only 25 days by computing limitation from the receipt of the certified copy[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Challenging the NCLT Chennai order dated 27.09.2017, the Appellant e-filed an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 along with IA No. 604/2025 seeking condonation of delay, which was opposed by the Respondents on grounds of lack of statutory jurisdiction to condone delay beyond 90 days[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether the Appellate Tribunal has statutory jurisdiction under the proviso to Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 to condone an inordinate delay of 2659 days in filing an appeal where the litigant failed to apply for a certified copy within the prescribed limitation period and attempts to compute limitation from the date of subsequent knowledge and receipt of the certified copy[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The maximum period for which the Appellate Tribunal can condone delay under the proviso to Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 is strictly 45 days beyond the initial 45-day limitation period (total 90 days); any delay beyond this statutory cap is fatal and cannot be condoned under the guise of subsequent knowledge or delayed receipt of a certified copy when the copy was not applied for with due diligence within the limitation period[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421(3) and its proviso constitute a self-contained and mandatory statutory limitation scheme; the phrase 'from the date on which a copy of the order is made available' does not permit an active litigant who participated in the proceedings to remain indolent for years and claim computation of limitation afresh from the date of belated knowledge[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Due diligence test; an appearing party is under an affirmative legal obligation to monitor proceedings, and where the application for a certified copy is itself preferred 80 days after admitted knowledge and years past the order, Section 12 exclusion of the Limitation Act cannot revive an extinguished right of appeal[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The actual delay in filing the appeal was 2659 days from the date of the impugned order (27.09.2017), far exceeding the outer statutory limit of 90 days prescribed by Section 421(3), leaving the Tribunal with no jurisdiction to condone the delay[cite: 16].
operative_order: Interlocutory Application IA No. 604/2025 for condonation of delay is rejected; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 55/2025 and all other pending Interlocutory Applications are dismissed[cite: 16].
summary: Appellant Harsha Vardhan Reddy challenged an order of NCLT Chennai passed on 27.09.2017 under Sections 397/398 of the Companies Act, 1956, e-filing the appeal only on 08.01.2025 along with an application for condonation of delay[cite: 16]. The Appellant claimed he had learned of the order only on 06.08.2024 and alleged a delay of merely 25 days from the date of receiving the certified copy[cite: 16]. Rejecting the application, the NCLAT held that the Appellant had participated in the original proceedings and had a duty to monitor the case[cite: 16]. Because the application for a certified copy was filed 80 days after knowledge and years after the judgment, the actual delay was 2659 days[cite: 16]. Since the proviso to Section 421(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 strictly limits condonable delay to a maximum of 45 days beyond the initial 45-day period, the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to condone the delay and dismissed the appeal[cite: 16].

case_title: Mr. Sandeep Jain & Mr. Bijender Jain vs. IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mr. Sandeep Jain (Ex-Director of Principal Borrower, Shree Vardhman Buildprop Pvt. Ltd.) and Mr. Bijender Jain (Ex-Director of Corporate Guarantor, DSS Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited (Debenture Trustee for Kautilya Finance); Respondent No. 2 is M/s Ducturus Resolution Professional Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 17] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Principal Borrower executed a Debenture Subscription Agreement on 14.06.2016 with debenture holders for Rs. 35 Crores to develop an affordable housing project ('Shree Vardhman Mantra', Sector 67, Gurgaon), secured by a corporate guarantee from DSS Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. and an Escrow Agreement dated 18.07.2016; subsequently, a second Debenture Trust Deed (DTD) was executed on 02.02.2021 restructuring dues and disbursing an additional Rs. 15 Crores[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 57,87,76,971/- as on 31.03.2023 claimed against the Principal Borrower, and guarantee invocation demand of Rs. 60,07,19,783/- plus future interest claimed against the Corporate Guarantor; no payments of principal or interest were made between 2016 and 2023[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: First DTD on 14.06.2016; default notices issued on 05.08.2019 and 18.11.2020; second DTD executed on 02.02.2021 with first revised due date on 31.03.2021; Section 138 NI Act notice issued on 20.01.2023; demand notice to principal borrower on 16.06.2023; guarantee invocation notice on 06.07.2023; Section 7 petitions filed on 21.07.2023 and 02.08.2024[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Dishonoured post-dated cheques issued by the Corporate Debtor; replies to Section 138 notices admitting liability towards debenture holders; executed first and second Debenture Trust Deeds[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 filed C.P. (IB) No. 445/2023 against the Corporate Debtor and C.P. (IB) No. 446/2023 against the Corporate Guarantor; NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-IV admitted both petitions on 29.04.2024 and 07.05.2024 respectively; Appellants challenged admission arguing the lender controlled escrow cash flows and project viability made CIRP inappropriate[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is required to evaluate the commercial feasibility or financial viability of a housing project before admitting a Section 7 petition, or whether admission is mandatory once the twin criteria of debt and default under Section 3(12) and Section 7(5) are established, notwithstanding lender oversight of escrow accounts[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied of the existence of a financial debt and an occurrence of default under Section 7(5) of the IBC, it has no statutory discretion to examine project viability, feasibility, or external financial arrangements, and admission of CIRP must mandatorily follow[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Default under Section 3(12) of the IBC means non-payment of debt when whole or any part or instalment has become due and payable; under Section 7(5), upon establishing default, the tribunal has no discretion to refuse admission on extraneous grounds such as pending permissions, zero periods, or escrow operations[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Application of binding Supreme Court precedents in Innoventive Industries, E.S. Krishnamurthy, and M. Suresh Kumar Reddy, holding that evidence of unpaid matured debentures and dishonoured cheques conclusively proves default, and the corporate debtor's obligation is not diminished by lender participation in project escrow accounts[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Principal Borrower and Corporate Guarantor having defaulted on debenture obligations without paying principal or interest for over five years, admission under Section 7 was lawful and unavoidable[cite: 17].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1026 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1055 of 2024 are dismissed, affirming the admission orders of the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 17].
summary: Suspended directors of Shree Vardhman Buildprop Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) and DSS Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor) appealed NCLT New Delhi orders admitting them into CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC on applications by debenture trustee IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited for defaults exceeding Rs. 57 Crores[cite: 17]. Appellants argued that the debenture trustee controlled escrow accounts, most residential units were sold, and given 12 months, revenues from unsold units would clear the debt[cite: 17]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, relying on Supreme Court rulings in Innoventive Industries and M. Suresh Kumar Reddy, affirming that lender oversight of project accounts does not absolve the debtor's payment liability, and once debt and default are established under Section 7(5), admission of CIRP is mandatory[cite: 17].

case_title: Mr. Jugal Kishore Saraff vs. CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mr. Jugal Kishore Saraff, Suspended Director of Corporate Guarantors Machine Works (International) Limited and Motijug Agencies Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (assignee of Allahabad Bank/Indian Bank); Principal Borrower is M/s Ural India Ltd. (UIL)[cite: 18]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Principal Borrower availed financial credit facilities from Allahabad Bank, secured by Guarantee Deeds executed by the Corporate Guarantors on 12.10.2010 and 28.06.2012; the debt was subsequently assigned to CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 18] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal Borrower account declared NPA on 12.07.2014; demand notice under Section 13(2) claimed outstanding dues of Rs. 28,29,36,894.28 as of 31.07.2014 plus future interest[cite: 18]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantees executed on 12.10.2010 and 28.06.2012; NPA declared on 12.07.2014; Section 13(2) notice issued to borrower and guarantors on 31.07.2014; Section 13(4) notice on 24.08.2015; DRT recovery application filed on 29.03.2017; Section 7 petition against principal borrower filed on 13.08.2018 (liquidation ordered on 15.01.2021); Section 7 petitions against guarantors filed in July 2022[cite: 18]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 13(2) notice dated 31.07.2014 demanding Rs. 28,29,36,894.28; Corporate Debtor's reply affidavit in CP (IB) 91/2022 admitting that guarantee was invoked on 31.07.2014; audited balance sheets of the Principal Borrower for FYs 2014-15, 2016-17, and 2018-19 reflecting debt acknowledgement; and written One Time Settlement (OTS) proposals dated 17.07.2020 and 06.09.2020[cite: 18]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed Section 7 applications CP (IB) No. 200/KB/2022 and CP (IB) No. 91/KB/2022 against the Corporate Guarantors; NCLT Kolkata Court No. II admitted both applications on 08.01.2025; Appellant appealed contending the guarantee was never formally invoked as per Clause 12 of the Guarantee Deed and that claims were barred by limitation[cite: 18].
legal_issues: Whether a statutory demand notice under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act constitutes valid invocation of a corporate guarantee, and whether continuous balance sheet acknowledgements and OTS proposals by the principal borrower extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 for initiating Section 7 CIRP against corporate guarantors[cite: 18].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A comprehensive demand notice issued under Section 13(2) of the SARFAESI Act calling upon corporate guarantors to discharge outstanding liabilities operates as a valid legal invocation of the guarantee, and subsequent acknowledgements of debt in audited balance sheets and OTS proposals extend the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act to maintain a Section 7 petition against the guarantors[cite: 18]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963 applies to corporate insolvency proceedings against guarantors; under the rule established in Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union of India, an acknowledgement of debt by the principal borrower in its balance sheets and settlement proposals effectively extends the limitation against the corporate guarantor whose liability is co-extensive[cite: 18]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Pleadings and admissions on affidavit bind the party; where the corporate debtor's reply expressly acknowledges that guarantee invocation occurred on 31.07.2014, it cannot later argue non-invocation[cite: 18]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The guarantee was effectively invoked on 31.07.2014, and the Section 7 application filed in 2022 was well within limitation by virtue of successive balance sheet acknowledgements (2014-15, 2016-17, 2018-19) and OTS proposals submitted in 2020[cite: 18].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 211 and 374 of 2025 are dismissed, upholding the Section 7 admission orders passed by NCLT Kolkata[cite: 18].
summary: Suspended director Jugal Kishore Saraff challenged the NCLT Kolkata order admitting Section 7 applications against corporate guarantors Machine Works (International) Ltd. and Motijug Agencies Ltd. filed by assignee CFM Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. for defaults of Rs. 28.29 Crores[cite: 18]. The Appellant contended that guarantee invocation under the Guarantee Deed never occurred and that the 2022 filings were time-barred since default occurred in 2014[cite: 18]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that the Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice dated 31.07.2014 constituted valid invocation, as admitted in the debtor's own reply[cite: 18]. Applying the Supreme Court's ruling in Laxmi Pat Surana v. Union of India, the Tribunal held that successive balance sheet acknowledgements and OTS proposals from 2014 to 2020 validly renewed the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, making the petitions timely[cite: 18].

case_title: Mr. Iqbal Jumabhoy & Mr. Hussain Somjee vs. Shri Manoj Kumar Anand & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Mr. Iqbal Jumabhoy and Mr. Hussain Somjee, Personal Guarantors to the Corporate Debtor, M/s Raffles Residency Private Limited; Respondent No. 1 is Shri Manoj Kumar Anand, Resolution Professional; Respondent No. 2 is Assets Care and Reconstruction Enterprise Limited (ACRE), assignee of the financial debt[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan agreement executed on 21.03.2018 between Indiabulls Housing Finance Limited (IHFL) and Raffles Residency Private Limited, for which the Appellants executed personal guarantees; the debt was assigned to IBARCL on 30.09.2020 and subsequently to Respondent No. 2 (ACRE) on 26.04.2021[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details stem from the loan facility and guarantee invocation; specific financial numbers are not detailed in the text beyond the demand notices and the fact that a subsequent settlement agreement dated 01.02.2022 was terminated on 16.06.2022 due to event of default[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan agreement executed on 21.03.2018; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice on 14.02.2020; Rule 7(1) Form B demand notice on 20.02.2020; DRT recovery applications filed on 12.08.2020; settlement agreement dated 01.02.2022 terminated on 16.06.2022; revival notice on 12.07.2022; Section 95 petitions filed in 2023; RP report under Section 99 submitted in 2024; Section 100 admission orders passed on 06.11.2024[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Over 25 opportunities via email, phone, and WhatsApp were given by the RP to the guarantors to provide information; NCLT granted repeated extensions to file objections to the Section 99 report on 29.04.2024 and 14.06.2024; right to file reply was forfeited on 28.06.2024 due to continuous failure to submit responses[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 2 filed CP (IB) Nos. 15/BB/2023 & 14/BB/2023 under Section 95 before NCLT Bengaluru; RP filed IA Nos. 447/2024 & 445/2024 submitting Section 99 reports recommending admission; NCLT Bengaluru admitted both petitions under Section 100 on 06.11.2024; Appellants appealed claiming denial of personal hearing and violation of natural justice principles[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT violated principles of natural justice and the legal standards laid down in Dilip B. Jiwrajka v. Union of India when passing Section 100 admission orders against Personal Guarantors after forfeiting their right to file written objections following multiple unavailed opportunities[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Natural justice in personal insolvency proceedings requires providing a fair and reasonable opportunity to the guarantor to submit objections against the Resolution Professional's Section 99 report; where a guarantor is afforded repeated opportunities over extended periods and persistently fails to submit a reply, the forfeiture of the right to reply and subsequent adjudication under Section 100 violates neither natural justice nor the Dilip B. Jiwrajka principles[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 99 envisions a facilitative, non-adjudicatory role for the Resolution Professional in collating facts, while the adjudicatory function resides strictly under Section 100 where the NCLT must observe natural justice; however, natural justice is not an inflexible doctrine that permits endless delays contrary to strict statutory IBC timelines[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Daily order sheets demonstrating that the Resolution Professional and the Adjudicating Authority granted over two months and multiple explicit extensions to reply before forfeiting the right, establishing full procedural compliance[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Personal Guarantors having failed to participate or file objections despite ample opportunities, the Adjudicating Authority committed no procedural error in admitting the Section 95 applications under Section 100 based on the recommendatory report[cite: 14].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 29 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 34 of 2025 are dismissed; all pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 14].
summary: Appellants Iqbal Jumabhoy and Hussain Somjee, Personal Guarantors to Raffles Residency Pvt. Ltd., appealed NCLT Bengaluru orders admitting Section 95 petitions filed by assignee ACRE under Section 100 of the IBC[cite: 14]. Appellants contended they were denied effective hearing and that their rights were violated under the Supreme Court's Dilip B. Jiwrajka ruling because orders were passed after forfeiting their right to reply to the RP's Section 99 recommendatory report[cite: 14]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that the daily order sheets clearly proved the Appellants were provided more than 25 communications by the RP and over two months by the NCLT across multiple hearings to submit objections, which they neglected to do[cite: 14]. Because strict timelines govern the IBC and adequate opportunity was extended, no breach of natural justice occurred[cite: 14].

case_title: Sashi Kanta Jha & Anr. vs. Devi Prasad & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Sashi Kanta Jha (suspended director of the Corporate Debtor) and Acme Consultant Private Limited; Respondent No. 1 is Devi Prasad (an individual workman/Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Deepak Kumar Agarwal (IRP/RP); Respondent No. 3 is Geo Jute Limited (formerly Juggilal Kamlapat Jute Mills Company Limited / JK Jute Mills, Corporate Debtor)[cite: 21]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment and provision of services by the workman Devi Prasad to the Corporate Debtor mill, which had been closed since March 2014 and previously registered under SICA before BIFR[cite: 21]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 claimed unpaid dues of Rs. 5,24,132/-; core established default was based on an unpaid Assistant Labour Commissioner gratuity award dated 26.02.2014 for Rs. 70,700/- plus 8% interest per annum totaling Rs. 1,23,725/-, which exceeded the pre-amendment Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1.0 Lakh[cite: 21]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Labour Commissioner award passed on 26.02.2014; BIFR abated on 25.11.2016; Delhi High Court order in WP(C) 440/2017 disposed on 06.12.2017 granting liberty to workers to approach NCLT; Section 8 demand notice in Form 3 issued by R-1 on 29.05.2018; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 280(ALD)/2018 filed thereafter in 2018[cite: 21]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Final adjudicated gratuity award dated 26.02.2014 from the Assistant Labour Commissioner never challenged by the Corporate Debtor; Corporate Debtor's interim application enclosing a Demand Draft of Rs. 1,30,830/- acknowledging liability; earlier civil suits (Suit No. 500/2017 filed on 19.05.2017 and Suit No. 2506/2017 filed on 15.12.2017) filed by the debtor seeking injunction against workers[cite: 21]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench admitted Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 280(ALD)/2018 on 19.01.2024 holding the gratuity claim to be an operational debt and finding no pre-existing dispute or limitation bar; the suspended director appealed contending res judicata due to dismissal of an earlier trade union petition and pre-existing civil suit disputes[cite: 21].
legal_issues: Whether crystallized gratuity dues awarded by a competent Labour Authority constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC, whether civil suits filed after agreeing before a High Court that workmen can approach NCLT constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute, and whether an earlier dismissal of a Section 9 petition filed by a trade union solely on the procedural ground of prematurity operates as res judicata against an individual workman's petition[cite: 21].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory gratuity dues payable under an uncontested award of a competent labour authority fall within the definition of operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC as claims arising from employment, and opportunistic civil suits filed to forestall insolvency proceedings do not constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute; moreover, procedural dismissal of a prior representative petition for prematurity does not bar subsequent individual claims under the doctrine of res judicata[cite: 21]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) defines operational debt to encompass claims in respect of employment, interpreted in harmony with Section 326 of the Companies Act, 2013, which expressly includes gratuity and welfare dues in workmen dues[cite: 21]; Section 8 and 9 preclude admission only when a genuine dispute pre-dates the statutory demand notice, excluding moonshine or bad-faith suits[cite: 21]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unappealed decretal order/award of the Labour Commissioner conclusively establishes legally crystallized debt and default[cite: 21]; procedural dismissal of an earlier petition without adjudication on the merits fails to satisfy the elements of res judicata[cite: 21]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had an uncontroverted liability exceeding the statutory threshold arising from employment services; neither the frivolous civil suits nor the earlier dismissal of the trade union's appeal on premature filing barred the Section 9 application[cite: 21].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 214 of 2024 is dismissed; interim stay order vacated, with the period from 02.02.2024 to the date of order excluded from the CIRP timeline; parties to bear their own costs[cite: 21].
summary: A suspended director of Geo Jute Limited (formerly JK Jute Mills) appealed against the NCLT Allahabad Bench order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by workman Devi Prasad for recovery of unpaid gratuity awarded by the Assistant Labour Commissioner in 2014[cite: 21]. The Appellant argued that gratuity does not constitute operational debt, that pending civil suits demonstrated a pre-existing dispute, and that an earlier dismissed trade union petition operated as res judicata[cite: 21]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that gratuity dues arising out of employment are operational debts under Section 5(21)[cite: 21]. The Tribunal further held that post-facto civil suits constituted a moonshine defense and that the prior petition's dismissal for premature filing did not decide the merits to trigger res judicata[cite: 21].

case_title: Sarla Performance Fibres Ltd. vs. Mr. Vivek Murlidhar Dabhade, Liquidator of Desimran Cartons (P) Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sarla Performance Fibres Ltd. (Licensee/claimant); Respondent is Mr. Vivek Murlidhar Dabhade, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor M/s Desimran Cartons Private Limited[cite: 22]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor entered into a 12-year Leave and License Agreement dated 07.06.2019 letting out factory land (1,000 sq. meters) and two-floor building at Village Amli, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, for a monthly license fee of Rs. 5,000/- for the first 5 years (and Rs. 7,000/- thereafter) after entering into an alleged agreement of sale dated 16.04.2019, receiving Rs. 60 Lakhs refundable deposit and Rs. 55 Lakhs advance[cite: 22]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Jalgaon Janta Sahakari Bank had an existing mortgage on the asset and initiated Section 7 CIRP on 08.05.2019; during liquidation, the premises were successfully auctioned on an 'as is where is' basis for Rs. 4.21 Crores; Appellant claimed Rs. 1,15,00,000/-[cite: 22]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed by the Bank on 08.05.2019; Leave and License Agreement executed on 07.06.2019; CIRP commenced and liquidation ordered on 28.03.2022; Liquidator issued vacation notice on 18.05.2022 and filed disclaimer application IA No. 2012/2022; auction conducted pursuant to public notice dated 21.01.2023[cite: 22]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Leave and License Agreement executed for an uncommercial token rent of Rs. 5,000/- per month without secured creditor consent; Appellant subsequently offered to pay Rs. 2,25,000/- per month upon notice from Liquidator, establishing that the contractual rate was grossly unprofitable and burdensome to the liquidation estate[cite: 22]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 2012/2022 under Section 45 and Regulation 10 to disclaim the agreement; Appellant filed IA 672/2023 challenging auction and IA 2897/2023 challenging claim rejection; NCLT Mumbai Bench-III allowed disclaimer under Regulation 10, directed Appellant to vacate in 30 days, dismissed IA 672/2023, and directed liquidator to reconsider Appellant's Rs. 1.15 Crore monetary claim; Appellant appealed challenging the validity of Regulation 10 and citing divergence between tribunal members[cite: 22].
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 10 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 empowering a liquidator to disclaim onerous property and unprofitable contracts is ultra vires the IBC, and whether the Leave and License Agreement dated 07.06.2019 was an unprofitable/onerous contract subject to disclaimer[cite: 22].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Regulation 10 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, authorizing the disclaimer of onerous property and unprofitable contracts, is intra vires the IBC, as it is framed in valid exercise of statutory rule-making powers under Section 240(2)(y) read with Sections 34(2), 35(1)(d), and 35(1)(o) of the Code; furthermore, uncommercial long-term leases executed at nominal rent post-insolvency filing are unprofitable contracts subject to disclaimer[cite: 22]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(1)(o) read with Section 3(32) and Section 240(2)(y) empowers the IBBI to specify functions of the liquidator by regulation, including the power of disclaimer modeled after Section 535 of the Companies Act, 1956, to preserve and maximize asset value; this power operates independently of avoidance provisions in Sections 43 to 51[cite: 22]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison of contractual consideration against market value; leasing valuable industrial property for a nominal sum of Rs. 5,000/- per month compared to an admitted subsequent willingness to pay Rs. 2,25,000/- per month demonstrates that the contract is burdensome, unprofitable, and not in good faith[cite: 22]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Both adjudicating members concurred that the agreement was an unprofitable/onerous contract under Regulation 10; hence the Liquidator was legally justified in disclaiming the agreement and requiring vacant possession[cite: 22].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 379, 380, and 381 of 2025 are dismissed, affirming the NCLT's common order[cite: 22].
summary: Appellant Sarla Performance Fibres Ltd. appealed an NCLT Mumbai order allowing the Liquidator of Desimran Cartons Pvt. Ltd. to disclaim a 12-year Leave and License Agreement dated 07.06.2019 under Regulation 10 of the Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016 and ordering the Appellant to vacate[cite: 22]. The Appellant argued that Regulation 10 was ultra vires the IBC because the Code only permits avoidance under Sections 43 to 51, and that there was divergence between the Technical and Judicial Members[cite: 22]. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that Regulation 10 is fully authorized by Sections 34, 35(1)(o), and 240(2)(y) of the IBC to facilitate asset maximization[cite: 22]. The Tribunal affirmed that leasing prime industrial land for Rs. 5,000/- per month was undeniably an unprofitable contract properly disclaimed by the liquidator[cite: 22].

case_title: Manjeera Majestic Commercial Owners Association vs. Manjeera Retail Holdings Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Manjeera Majestic Commercial Owners Association (a registered society of commercial unit buyers); Respondent No. 1 is Manjeera Retail Holdings Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Developer); Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Birendra Kumar Agarwal (Resolution Professional)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development of commercial building 'Manjeera Majestic Commercial' at Kukatpally, Rangareddy District on land acquired from Telangana Housing Board; 199 commercial units out of 206 were allotted to buyers under agreements for sale, but registered conveyance deeds were never executed[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted claims in Form F totaling multiple crores, including Corpus Fund of Rs. 1,75,83,503/-, property tax reimbursement of Rs. 4,47,161/-, Building Management System costs of Rs. 50,00,000/- (later claimed as Rs. 63,09,500/-), basement parking staff reimbursement of Rs. 10,09,106/-, exhaust pipes costs of Rs. 1,84,080/-, and permanent accommodation costs of Rs. 2,00,00,000/-; RP admitted only Rs. 1,23,31,078/- towards the Corpus Fund based on company ledgers and rejected all other claims[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 18.07.2023; Form A public announcement on 19.07.2023; Form F claims submitted by Appellant on 09.09.2023; RP communicated partial admission on 22.01.2024[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unregistered agreements for sale dated 05.08.2010; no registered sale deed conferring ownership or title for any unit or association office space was produced; no tax receipts proving local municipal tax payment were tendered; no contractual documents proving the Corporate Debtor agreed to reimburse management expenses or office costs were produced[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 625/2024 under Section 60(5) seeking admission of all rejected Form F claims and execution of registered sale deeds, and IA 16/2024 seeking intervention in the approval of the resolution plan; NCLT Hyderabad dismissed IA No. 625/2024 and disposed of IA 16/2024 as infructuous on 04.10.2024; Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether unadmitted monetary demands and demands for specific performance (execution of registered sale deeds) founded upon an unregistered agreement for sale can be admitted as operational or financial 'debt' under Section 3(11) of the IBC during CIRP, and whether the evidentiary bar under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908 applies[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1.
