ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Monetary claims and reliefs seeking execution of conveyance deeds founded upon an unregistered agreement for sale cannot be admitted as legally enforceable debt in CIRP, as unregistered instruments cannot create or transfer title or be received in evidence under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908, nor can the summary jurisdiction under the IBC be substituted for a civil suit for specific performance[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: For a claim to qualify as a 'debt' under Section 3(11) of the IBC, there must exist a crystallized and legally enforceable liability due from the Corporate Debtor supported by admissible proof under CIRP Regulations 7 and 9; an unregistered agreement for sale fails to create an interest in immovable property under Section 54 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 and is inadmissible under Section 49 of the Registration Act[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The burden of proving the existence and admissibility of debt lies squarely upon the claimant submitting Form F under Section 18(b) and Regulation 7; unverified unilateral demands and unliquidated expenditures without contractual privity or admission by the debtor do not constitute proved claims[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP and NCLT correctly admitted only the verified ledger-backed Corpus Fund amount of Rs. 1,23,31,078/- and rightly rejected all remaining claims, as the Appellant held neither registered title nor any enforceable contractual right against the Corporate Debtor[cite: 23].
operative_order: Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 406/2024 is dismissed[cite: 23].
summary: Appellant Manjeera Majestic Commercial Owners Association challenged an NCLT Hyderabad order upholding the Resolution Professional's rejection of various claims filed in Form F (including property tax reimbursements, building management systems, office costs, and a prayer for execution of registered sale deeds) against Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 23] The RP had admitted only Rs. 1.23 Crores towards the Corpus Fund[cite: 23]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Appellant's claims were based on an unregistered agreement for sale which cannot transfer title or be admitted in evidence under Section 49 of the Registration Act, 1908[cite: 23]. The Tribunal held that insolvency proceedings cannot be used as a vehicle to seek specific performance of conveyance or recover unadmitted, unsubstantiated demands[cite: 23].

case_title: Mrs. Ritu Khanna vs. Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Mrs. Ritu Khanna (third party, non-litigant spouse); Respondent No. 1 is Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited; Respondent No. 9 is Col. Ashish Khanna (Retd., Appellant's husband and former Secretary/CEO of the Club); Union of India was the original petitioner; other respondents include former directors and legal counsels[cite: 24]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management dispute arising from a petition filed by the Union of India under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 alleging mismanagement and oppression in the affairs of Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-IBC corporate litigation; NCLT imposed a cost of Rs. 50,000/- on Col. Ashish Khanna by order dated 15.12.2023 for filing frivolous recall applications[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 71/ND/2020 instituted by UOI; interim order passed by single member judicial on 24.04.2020; Col. Khanna filed recall application CA 440/PB/2022, dismissed on 15.12.2023; Col. Khanna's subsequent recall CA 49/2024 dismissed on 14.03.2024 and his appeal dismissed on limitation on 21.10.2024; Appellant filed CA 90/PB/2024 on 03.04.2024; NCLT dismissed it on 10.09.2024[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate record showing Appellant Mrs. Ritu Khanna was neither a shareholder, member, nor party to the Section 241/242 proceedings; multiple prior recall applications raising identical jurisdictional grounds had already been filed by her husband Col. Ashish Khanna and dismissed on the merits[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CA 90/PB/2024 before NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi seeking recall of the order dated 15.12.2023 and striking off of the Rs. 50,000/- cost imposed on her husband; NCLT rejected the application on 10.09.2024 holding she lacked locus standi as a complete stranger to the litigation; Appellant appealed invoking Section 44 of the Evidence Act and Order 1 Rule 8A CPC[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether a non-party stranger to a Section 241/242 proceeding has locus standi under Section 44 of the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 or Order 1 Rule 8A CPC to maintain an application for recall of an order passed against their spouse on grounds of alleged lack of jurisdiction or coram non judice[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A stranger to a company law proceeding possesses no locus standi to file an application for recall of an order passed by the tribunal, and the evidentiary provisions of Section 44 of the Evidence Act cannot be weaponized by third parties to bypass the doctrine of locus standi and reopen concluded proceedings against an adverse party[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 44 of the Evidence Act, 1872 is a rule of evidence allowing 'any party to a suit or other proceeding' to impeach judgments introduced as evidence in subsequent proceedings on grounds of fraud or lack of competence, but does not confer locus on strangers to intervene and seek recall within the very same proceeding[cite: 24]; Order 1 Rule 8A CPC is merely an enabling discretion for the court in public interest and confers no right on non-parties to seek recall[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict threshold scrutiny of locus standi; an individual who is neither an applicant, respondent, necessary party, nor proper party in a company petition cannot sustain an application on the sole ground of marital relation or sharing a joint bank account affected by costs[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had no legal standing or locus standi in CP 71/ND/2020, and the NCLT committed no error in rejecting the recall application as unmaintainable[cite: 24].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 59 of 2025 is dismissed[cite: 24].
summary: Appellant Mrs. Ritu Khanna appealed an NCLT Principal Bench order rejecting her application (CA 90/PB/2024) seeking recall of an order dated 15.12.2023 passed in a Section 241/242 proceeding against Delhi Gymkhana Club Limited, which had imposed a cost of Rs. 50,000/- on her husband, Col. Ashish Khanna[cite: 24]. Her husband had previously filed recall applications on identical grounds that were dismissed[cite: 24]. The Appellant argued she had standing under Section 44 of the Evidence Act and Order 1 Rule 8A CPC because the order was allegedly passed coram non judice and the costs impacted their joint account[cite: 24]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a stranger to a proceeding has no locus standi to seek recall and that Section 44 cannot be used by non-parties to subvert locus rules[cite: 24].

case_title: Suresh Atlani vs. Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Suresh Atlani, Personal Guarantor of the Corporate Debtor, Geekay Colonizers and Builders Limited; the original Financial Creditor was Dewan Housing Finance Ltd. (DHFL), succeeded by Piramal Capital and Housing Finance Limited, and subsequently assigned to Respondent Omkara Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.; Ms. Sneh Maheshwari was appointed as the Resolution Professional (RP)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: DHFL sanctioned a project loan of Rs. 94 Crore to the Corporate Debtor, out of which Rs. 69 Crore was disbursed, secured by a personal guarantee executed by the Appellant[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The loan account was declared NPA on 01.01.2016; total default claimed in Part III of the Section 95 petition was Rs. 103,25,42,189/-[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Entire facility recalled on 15.06.2016; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 21.10.2016; partial payment made under OTS submitted on 13.03.2018; DHFL acquired by Piramal on 30.09.2021; Rule 7(1) demand notice issued on 13.07.2022; Section 95 petition filed on 31.10.2022; debt assigned to Omkara on 10.01.2023; RP appointed on 16.01.2024 and communicated on 02.02.2024; RP filed Section 99 report on 02.02.2024 and amended supplementary report on 14.02.2024; both reports taken on record by NCLT on 05.03.2024; Section 100 admission order passed on 20.12.2024[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, guarantee deeds, recall notices, Rule 7(1) statutory demand notice dated 13.07.2022, and the Resolution Professional's recommendation reports dated 02.02.2024 and 14.02.2024 incorporating information received from the financial creditor[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent filed C.P. (IB)-10/CB/2023 under Section 95(1); NCLT Cuttack Bench admitted the petition under Section 100 on 20.12.2024; Appellant challenged the admission on the ground that the RP's Section 99 report was filed beyond the statutory 10-day period without leave or condonation of delay, rendering it invalid[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether the 10-day timeline prescribed under Section 99(1) of the IBC for the Resolution Professional to submit a recommendatory report is mandatory or directory, and whether an amended or supplementary report submitted beyond 10 days can be taken on record and relied upon by the Adjudicating Authority to admit a Section 95 application under Section 100[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory timelines governing the submission of facilitative reports by court-appointed professionals, where no statutory invalidation or consequence of non-compliance is prescribed, are directory in nature rather than mandatory, and reasonable procedural delays in submitting such reports do not vitiate the adjudication process or render the report inadmissible[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 99(1) must be read harmoniously with Section 99(4), (5), and (6), which allow the Resolution Professional to seek information within seven days and re-examine facts; the 10-day period is not a period of limitation for which a Section 5 Limitation Act application is required, but an administrative guideline enabling early resolution[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The Adjudicating Authority has full jurisdiction to evaluate and accept supplementary reports filed on affidavit to incorporate necessary creditor responses, provided the delay is reasonably explained and causes no prejudice[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The initial report and the supplementary report were validly taken on record by the NCLT on 05.03.2024, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no legal error in relying upon them to pass the Section 100 admission order against the Personal Guarantor[cite: 26].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 200 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT's admission order dated 20.12.2024[cite: 26].
summary: Appellant Suresh Atlani, Personal Guarantor of Geekay Colonizers and Builders Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Cuttack Bench order admitting a Section 95(1) IBC insolvency petition filed by assignee Omkara Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. for a default of Rs. 103.25 Crores[cite: 26]. The Appellant contended that the Resolution Professional submitted the Section 99 report beyond the 10-day period specified in Section 99(1) without seeking condonation of delay, rendering the report void[cite: 26]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the 10-day timeframe under Section 99(1) is directory and not a statute of limitation[cite: 26]. The RP acts as an officer of the court in a facilitative role, and the NCLT possesses the jurisdiction to accept reasonable delays and supplementary reports[cite: 26].

case_title: Busy Bee Airways Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Dinkar T Venkatasubramanian, Liquidator, Go Airlines (India) Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Busy Bee Airways Pvt. Ltd. (Prospective Resolution Applicant), Bhartiya Kamgar Sena Mumbai (Trade Union), and Capt. Arjun Dhawan & 24 employees; Respondent No. 1 is Dinkar T Venkatasubramanian (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Go Airlines (India) Ltd.); other Respondents are CoC members (Central Bank of India, Bank of India, IDBI Bank)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor operated low-cost airline 'GoAir'/'GoFirst' for 17 years; due to grounded aircraft and defective engines supplied by Pratt & Whitney (subject to SIAC arbitration), operations halted, leading to a voluntary Section 10 filing[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor had admitted claims of approximately Rs. 3,600 Crores; defaulted on vendors and aircraft lessors; 34% of aircraft grounded in 2022[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 10 application allowed by NCLT on 10.05.2023; Form-G published on 10.07.2023; Delhi High Court directed DGCA to deregister lessors' aircraft on 26.04.2024; RP notified Busy Bee of non-compliance on 09.07.2024; 37th CoC meeting held on 23.07.2024; e-voting from 24.07.2024 to 31.07.2024 passed liquidation resolution with 100% majority; NCLT allowed liquidation IA(Liq.) 33/ND/2024 on 20.01.2025[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of 37th CoC meeting showing only two non-compliant resolution plans were received; Appellant withdrew and requested EMD refund; all leased aircraft deregistered and exported; airport slots revoked; airport premises demanded back; and non-binding commercial proposal submitted by Appellant post-liquidation[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA(Liq.) 33/ND/2024 under Section 33(2) before NCLT New Delhi Court V; NCLT ordered liquidation on 20.01.2025; Appellants challenged the liquidation order arguing the airline held valuable intangible assets and ought to have been preserved and sold as a going concern[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether the CoC's commercial decision to liquidate the Corporate Debtor under Section 33(2) with 100% voting share, after finding no compliant resolution plans and considering that all aircraft were deregistered and operations suspended, is arbitrary or open to judicial review, and whether the Liquidator is mandatorily bound to sell the company only as a going concern[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 33(2) of the IBC, the Committee of Creditors possesses the absolute and wide statutory discretion, in exercise of its commercial wisdom, to resolve to liquidate the corporate debtor at any time before plan confirmation, and such decision is not subject to judicial interference unless arbitrary or unconstitutional[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 33(2) mandates that upon intimation of a liquidation decision approved by not less than 66% voting share, the Adjudicating Authority shall pass a liquidation order; Regulation 39C provides the CoC discretion to recommend going-concern sale, but does not mandate going-concern sale where assets are depleted and operations are non-existent[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of business realities on record; complete loss of commercial fleet through court-ordered deregistration, revocation of flight slots, and absence of operational revenue substantiate the objective reasonableness of the CoC's liquidation vote[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CIRP having run for over 14 months without any compliant plan, the CoC validly exercised its commercial wisdom to order liquidation, while reserving liberty to consider suo motu compromise/arrangement schemes under Regulation 2B and Section 230 of the Companies Act[cite: 27].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 124, 175 & 244 of 2025 are dismissed, subject to liberty for the Appellant or eligible applicants to submit a scheme for compromise/arrangement under Regulation 2B[cite: 27].
summary: Appellants, including Prospective Resolution Applicant Busy Bee Airways and employees of Go Airlines (India) Ltd. (GoFirst), challenged the NCLT New Delhi order ordering liquidation of the airline under Section 33(2) of the IBC[cite: 27]. The Appellants argued that the airline held valuable assets like its Air Operating Certificate and arbitration claims, and should have been preserved and sold as a going concern[cite: 27]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that the CIRP lasted over 14 months without yielding any compliant resolution plan, and the CoC exercised its paramount commercial wisdom by a 100% vote to liquidate after all aircraft were deregistered and airport slots revoked[cite: 27]. The Tribunal clarified that interested parties remain free to submit compromise/arrangement schemes under Section 230 of the Companies Act within statutory timelines[cite: 27].

case_title: Mr. Somangsu Biswas vs. The Calcutta Cricket & Football Club & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Somangsu Biswas, a General Committee member of Respondent No. 1; Respondent No. 1 is The Calcutta Cricket & Football Club (a Section 8 company without share capital, comprising ~1,850 members); Respondents No. 16 to 19 are petitioning members of the General Committee; other respondents are General Committee members and office bearers[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate governance and internal administration of a historic Section 8 non-profit sports club; Respondents No. 16 to 19 filed CP No. 287/KB/2023 alleging oppression, illegal AGM, and financial mismanagement[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an IBC debt default; non-share capital company where statutory filing threshold under Section 244(1)(b) is one-fifth (20%) of total membership (~370 members), whereas the 4 petitioners constituted 0.002% of total membership[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: AGM held on 11.09.2023; 90 members issued joint complaint on 22.08.2023; CP No. 287/KB/2023 along with waiver application IA (CA) No. 183/KB/2023 filed in 2023; NCLT heard advance-noticed parties and reserved orders on 17.10.2023; impugned waiver order pronounced on 17.01.2024[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Detailed allegations of unauthorized convening of AGM on 11.09.2023, exclusion of committee members, violation of Calcutta High Court order dated 17.05.2023, embezzlement and siphoning of club funds by respondent No. 14, and supporting representations signed by 90 club members[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP No. 287/KB/2023, NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed waiver IA No. 183/KB/2023 under the proviso to Section 244(1) on 17.01.2024, holding that addressing governance issues in a premier heritage sports institution serves the public interest; Appellant appealed under the Companies Act contending lack of exceptional circumstances and denial of natural justice[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT judiciously exercised its discretionary power under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant waiver of the 20% membership threshold to 4 members of a Section 8 company, and whether the presence of serious allegations of financial mismanagement and wide public interest in a historic sports institution constitutes an 'exceptional circumstance' under the Cyrus Investments framework[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appellate tribunal will not substitute its own discretion for the discretion exercised by the court of first instance in granting statutory waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, unless the exercise of discretion is proven to be arbitrary, capricious, perverse, or in violation of settled legal principles[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 244(1) confers open-ended judicial discretion upon the Tribunal to waive numerical thresholds in genuine cases where allegations pertain to oppression and mismanagement; the criteria outlined in Cyrus Investments are non-exhaustive and do not require deciding the petition's merits at the threshold waiver stage[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prima facie evaluation of pleadings; where the petition details specific allegations of financial misappropriation, disputed elections, and lack of prior adjudication, coupled with broad member support (90 members) and public interest in a Section 8 company, exceptional circumstances justifying waiver are established[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT properly satisfied itself that the petition was not frivolous and raised substantial governance concerns in a public-interest sports institution; hence the waiver order was lawful and did not warrant appellate interference[cite: 28].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 56 of 2024 is dismissed; connected pending applications are closed; no order as to costs[cite: 28].
summary: Appellant Somangsu Biswas challenged an NCLT Kolkata order allowing an application under the proviso to Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, granting waiver of the 20% membership threshold to 4 members of The Calcutta Cricket & Football Club (a Section 8 non-share capital company with ~1,850 members) to maintain an oppression and mismanagement petition[cite: 28]. The Appellant contended that 4 members (0.002%) could not be granted waiver without demonstrating exceptional circumstances under Cyrus Investments[cite: 28]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that appellate courts will not interfere with discretionary orders unless arbitrary or perverse[cite: 28]. The Tribunal affirmed that serious allegations of fund embezzlement, disputed AGMs, and independent complaints by 90 members regarding a premier public sports institution fully justified the grant of waiver[cite: 28].

case_title: Shitanshu Bipin Vora vs. Shree Hari Yarns Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Shitanshu Bipin Vora, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Exclusive Linen Fabrics Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Shree Hari Yarns Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Rajan Garg (Interim Resolution Professional)[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent No. 1 supplied yarn under 18 invoices to the Corporate Debtor between 09.03.2021 and 13.04.2021, containing a boilerplate term: 'interest will be charged on delayed payment @ 18%'[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 claimed a total operational default of Rs. 1,29,08,449/-, comprising a principal sum of Rs. 88,16,301/- and interest of Rs. 40,92,148/-; the principal amount falls below the statutory threshold of Rs. 1 Crore under Section 4 of the IBC[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices raised March–April 2021; payment made on 02.06.2021; Section 8 demand notice issued on 18.09.2023; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 1133/MB/2023 filed in 2023; NCLT reserved orders on 06.08.2024, listed for clarification on 30.08.2024, accepted additional affidavit on 03.09.2024, and admitted CIRP on 05.09.2024[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The 18 invoices contained a vague clause stating interest at 18% without mentioning whether it was per annum, per month, or the applicable credit period; no formal written agreement existed for interest payment; Corporate Debtor had raised contemporaneous quality shortfall disputes and received cash discounts; Appellant deposited the entire principal amount of Rs. 88,16,301/- before NCLAT pursuant to an interim order dated 12.12.2024[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 9 application on 05.09.2024, holding that unpaid interest could be combined with principal to meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold; Appellant appealed under Section 61 contending that interest was never agreed upon and excluded from the definition of operational debt[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether an interest component arising out of a vague, unilateral clause in commercial invoices can be clubbed with the principal operational debt to cross the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 of the IBC in the absence of an explicit contract or consensus ad idem between the parties[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Unlike 'financial debt' under Section 5(8), the definition of 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC does not inherently include interest; consequently, interest cannot be claimed or clubbed to satisfy the Section 4 pecuniary threshold unless there is an explicit, unambiguous contractual agreement between the parties providing for interest on delayed payments[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) deliberately omits interest from operational debt, whereas Section 5(8) expressly includes interest; a unilateral, non-specific invoice clause stating 'interest @ 18%' without specifying the period or grace period cannot be interpreted or rewritten by the Adjudicating Authority to mean '18% per annum'[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unilateral invoices bearing vague interest terms, contested by contemporaneous quality disputes and credit discounts, fail to prove an agreed liability; past isolated deductions or payments do not establish a binding contract to pay delayed interest[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Excluding the unsubstantiated interest claim of Rs. 40,92,148/-, the principal debt of Rs. 88,16,301/- fell below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4, rendering the Section 9 application non-maintainable[cite: 29].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2204 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned admission order dated 05.09.2024 is set aside, releasing the Corporate Debtor from CIRP; the deposited principal amount of Rs. 88,16,301/- is directed to be released to Respondent No. 1, with liberty granted to pursue appropriate remedies for remaining claims in accordance with law[cite: 29].
summary: Appellant Shitanshu Bipin Vora, suspended director of Exclusive Linen Fabrics Pvt. Ltd., challenged the NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 9 application filed by Shree Hari Yarns Pvt. Ltd. for a total default of Rs. 1.29 Crores[cite: 29]. The claimed sum included Rs. 88.16 Lakhs principal and Rs. 40.92 Lakhs interest based on a boilerplate invoice clause stating 'interest @ 18%'[cite: 29]. Setting aside the admission order, the NCLAT held that operational debt under Section 5(21) does not automatically include interest, and courts cannot rewrite vague invoice terms in the absence of an express written contract[cite: 29]. Because the principal operational debt was below the mandatory Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4, the petition was non-maintainable[cite: 29]. The Appellant having deposited the full principal amount, the Corporate Debtor was released from CIRP[cite: 29].

case_title: Shailendra Agarwal vs. Asit Upadhyaya & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Shailendra Agarwal, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s NHA Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. (formerly Nikhil Home Associates); Respondents No. 1 to 22 are individual homebuyers/allottees (Financial Creditors in a class); Respondent No. 23 is the Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 24 is Pramod Kumar Sharma (IRP)[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor launched a 5-tower residential housing project named 'Nikhil Park Royale' at Shamsabad, Agra under a Tripartite Agreement dated 20.09.2011 with the landowner and marketing entity; allottees entered into Builder-Buyer Agreements promising possession within 36 months plus 6 months grace[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default date in Part IV was 10.12.2015 based on failure to deliver possession; 22 homebuyers holding 34 units claimed total outstanding unpaid dues exceeding Rs. 1 Crore; project comprises 247 total units[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Tripartite agreement executed on 20.09.2011; construction commenced on 10.06.2012; promised possession default occurred on 10.12.2015; project registered with UPRERA on 31.10.2017 with revised completion date 10.06.2019; UPRERA refund orders passed on 13.10.2020 and 18.06.2022; Corporate Debtor converted from partnership to private company on 06.08.2022; UPRERA cancelled project registration on 24.12.2022; balance sheet acknowledgment as of 30.06.2022; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 11/ALD/2024 filed on 12.01.2024; admitted on 31.01.2025[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder-Buyer Agreements; orders and Recovery Certificates issued by UPRERA; balance sheet/statement of affairs of the Corporate Debtor as on 30.06.2022 filed on the MCA portal acknowledging outstanding customer advance deposits without qualification[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Homebuyers filed CP (IB) No. 11/ALD/2024 under Section 7; Corporate Debtor filed IA No. 250/2024 seeking dismissal under Section 65 on grounds of limitation, speculative investor status, and lack of threshold; NCLT Allahabad Bench dismissed IA No. 250/2024 and admitted the Section 7 petition on 31.01.2025; Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether the failure of a real estate developer to deliver possession constitutes a continuing default under Section 22 of the Limitation Act, 1963, whether balance sheet entries filed on the MCA portal extend limitation under Section 18, and whether allottees who obtained RERA Recovery Certificates continue to be Financial Creditors in a class to satisfy the threshold under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Failure to deliver possession of real estate units constitutes a continuing breach and recurring cause of action under Section 22 of the Limitation Act, and unreserved entries in audited financial statements operate as an acknowledgement of debt under Section 18; further, allottees who obtain recovery certificates or decrees retain their character as financial creditors in a class to satisfy the Section 7(1) numerical threshold[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Homebuyers who secure RERA recovery certificates remain financial creditors within Section 5(8)(f) as governed by the Supreme Court ruling in Vishal Chelani v. Debashis Nanda, overruling contrary precedents; under Section 369 of the Companies Act, conversion of a partnership firm into a company maintains the continuity of pre-existing liabilities[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Balance sheet verification; entries showing outstanding allottee deposits without qualifying caveats provide unequivocal acknowledgement of liability extending limitation[cite: 30]; allegations of fraudulent filing under Section 65 require strict documentary proof, which the corporate debtor failed to establish[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The petitioning 22 homebuyers holding 34 units satisfied the statutory threshold (over 10% of 247 units), the claim was fully within limitation via Section 22 continuing wrong, Supreme Court COVID exclusions, and balance sheet acknowledgement, rendering admission under Section 7 lawful[cite: 30].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 327 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the NCLT Allahabad admission order dated 31.01.2025; CIRP to continue; all pending IAs disposed of; no orders as to costs[cite: 30].
summary: Suspended director Shailendra Agarwal appealed an NCLT Allahabad order admitting Corporate Debtor M/s NHA Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. into CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC on a petition filed by 22 homebuyers holding 34 units out of 247 total units in the 'Nikhil Park Royale' project[cite: 30]. The Appellant argued that the 2024 petition was time-barred since default occurred in 2015, that RERA decree holders were speculative investors, and that the statutory 10% threshold was not met[cite: 30]. Dismissing the appeal, the NCLAT held that failure to hand over possession is a continuing default under Section 22 of the Limitation Act, and unreserved balance sheet entries dated 30.06.2022 extended limitation under Section 18[cite: 30]. Applying Vishal Chelani v. Debashis Nanda, the Tribunal affirmed that RERA decree-holders retain allottee status as financial creditors, fulfilling the Section 7(1) threshold[cite: 30].

case_title: EPC Constructions India Limited vs. M/s Matix Fertilisers and Chemicals Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is EPC Constructions India Limited (formerly Essar Projects (India) Ltd.), represented through its Liquidator Abhijit Guhathakurta; the Respondent is M/s Matix Fertilisers and Chemicals Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties entered into EPC and related contracts in 2009-2010 for setting up a fertilizer complex in West Bengal[cite: 31]; upon request by Respondent to convert outstanding contract receivables into subordinated debt/equity, Appellant agreed, and pursuant to board/shareholder resolutions in July-August 2015, converted Rs. 250 Crores of receivables into 25,00,00,000 8% Cumulative Redeemable Preference Shares (CRPS) of Rs. 10/- each redeemable at par at the end of 3 years[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed was Rs. 310 Crores (comprising Rs. 250 Crores principal/nominal value plus Rs. 60 Crores cumulative dividend at 8% p.a.); the alleged date of default was 26.08.2018 upon the maturity/redemption date[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board approval and CRPS allotment took place on 30.07.2015 and 26.08.2015; CIRP was initiated against Appellant on 20.04.2018; Appellant demanded redemption on 20.08.2018/28.08.2018; Respondent replied on 24.08.2018 seeking set-off against its counterclaims; Section 7 application CP (IB) No. 156/KB/2022 was filed by Appellant's liquidator on 25.04.2022 and dismissed by NCLT on 29.08.2023[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: EPC agreements, Board resolutions dated 30.07.2015 and 14.08.2015, allotment letter dated 26.08.2015, audited balance sheets of Respondent where CRPS were reclassified from equity to financial liability under Ind AS 109, and letters exchanged in August 2018[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Liquidator of Appellant filed CP (IB) No. 156/KB/2022 under Section 7 before NCLT Kolkata Bench-II, which rejected the petition on 29.08.2023 holding that preference shares are share capital and cannot be redeemed under Section 55 of the Companies Act absent profits/distributable reserves, hence no financial debt or default was established[cite: 31]; Appellant appealed under Section 61[cite: 31].
legal_issues: Whether Cumulative Redeemable Preference Shares (CRPS) allotted in lieu of trade receivables constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, and whether a preference shareholder can maintain a Section 7 petition as a financial creditor when the issuing company has not generated profits or fresh equity proceeds to permit lawful redemption under Section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a pre-existing commercial debt is converted into share capital/preference shares, the debt is extinguished and converted into equity/capital, which does not constitute a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC; a preference shareholder remains a shareholder rather than a financial creditor, and failure to redeem preference shares in the absence of distributable profits or fresh share proceeds does not constitute a default under the Code[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Terms not defined in the IBC derive meaning from the Companies Act, 2013 pursuant to Section 3(37) of the Code[cite: 31]; Section 43 classifies preference shares as part of share capital, and Section 55(2) strictly prohibits redemption of preference shares except out of company profits available for dividend or proceeds of a fresh issue of shares[cite: 31]; accounting reclassifications under Ind AS 109 in financial statements do not alter the substantive legal character of capital into debt[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of the transaction documents under Section 91 of the Evidence Act; the contractual instruments established a subscription and allotment of preference share capital rather than a loan facility or debt instrument, and in the absence of distributable profits, no legal obligation to pay matured[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor having earned no profits and issued no fresh shares for redemption, no redemption was legally permissible under Section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013, meaning no debt was due or in default to sustain a Section 7 application[cite: 31].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1424 of 2023 is dismissed, affirming the order of the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 31].
summary: Appellant EPC Constructions India Limited (through its liquidator) appealed the dismissal of its Section 7 IBC application against Matix Fertilisers and Chemicals Limited seeking recovery of Rs. 310 Crores based on unredeemed 8% Cumulative Redeemable Preference Shares (CRPS) issued in lieu of EPC contract receivables[cite: 31]. The Appellant argued that the transaction had the commercial effect of borrowing under Section 5(8)(f) and was classified as a financial liability under Ind AS[cite: 31]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that conversion of debt into capital extinguishes the creditor-debtor relationship[cite: 31]. Because Section 55 of the Companies Act, 2013 bars redemption of preference shares absent company profits or fresh share issue proceeds, no debt was legally payable, and no actionable default occurred under Section 7[cite: 31].

case_title: Bank of Baroda & Ors. vs. Formation Textile LLC & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants/Respondents across connected appeals include Bank of Baroda (Lead Creditor/CoC), Charu Desai (erstwhile RP of Corporate Debtor Mandhana Industries Limited / GB Global Limited), Formation Textile LLC (defaulting former SRA), and various Interim Trade Creditors (Vishal Dyes & Chemicals, Anglomonto Resource, Gimatex Industries)[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor under Section 7 on 29.09.2017; Formation submitted a Resolution Plan offering Rs. 460 Crores approved by NCLT on 30.11.2018; interim control was handed over to Formation on 31.01.2019, during which Formation incurred operational trade debts for raw materials but failed to make upfront infusions or implement the plan[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Formation deposited Rs. 5 Crores EMD, furnished Rs. 50 Crores Performance Bank Guarantee (PBG), and deposited Rs. 38.82 Crores towards equity (totaling Rs. 93.82 Crores infused), but failed to pay Rs. 226 Crores upfront considerations and Rs. 160 Crores ECB infusion[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]; Interim Trade Creditors remained unpaid to the extent of Rs. 20.9 Crores[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Plan approved on 30.11.2018; handover on 31.01.2019; default in upfront payments; control restored back to CoC/RP on 05.12.2019; CoC invoked PBG on 10.12.2019; fresh CIRP initiated on 05.02.2020; DLH's resolution plan approved on 19.05.2021 ordering Rs. 42.99 Crores (equity deposit plus interest) to remain in fixed deposit; NCLT passed impugned order on 06.07.2023 ordering full refund of Rs. 93.82 Crores to Formation and dismissing Interim Trade Creditors' applications[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Process Memorandum March 2018 (Clauses 14.2, 14.6, 14.8, 15.4); minutes of CoC meetings; emails confirming default; order dated 19.05.2021 reserving Rs. 42.99 Crores fixed deposit; and admissions of Rs. 20.9 Crores operational liability incurred during Formation's management[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I allowed Formation's IA No. 443/2021 directing refund of Rs. 93.82 Crores, dismissed Bank of Baroda's compensation IA No. 1847/2021, and rejected Interim Trade Creditors' applications (IA Nos. 1785/2021, 1986/2021, 1052/2022); all affected parties appealed to the NCLAT[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35].
legal_issues: Whether a Committee of Creditors is entitled to forfeit the EMD and invoke the Performance Bank Guarantee of an SRA who fails to implement an approved Resolution Plan in terms of the Process Memorandum, whether PBG/EMD can be adjusted against equity infusion, whether non-disclosure of a Transaction Audit Report renders plan performance voidable, and whether Interim Trade Creditors who supplied goods while the defaulting SRA was in management are entitled to payment from the SRA's unallotted equity funds held in fixed deposit[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved Resolution Plan statutorily binds the SRA under Section 31(1), and the SRA cannot avoid implementation or escape consequences by alleging data asymmetry; the CoC has full contractual and legal authority under the Process Memorandum to forfeit the PBG and EMD upon default; furthermore, unallotted equity funds deposited by the defaulting SRA must first satisfy legitimate trade liabilities incurred during its management before any residual refund can be issued[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29 and Regulation 36(2) of CIRP Regulations do not mandate incorporating internal Transaction Audit Reports into the Information Memorandum, and resolution applicants are bound by their 'as is where is' due diligence covenants; Clause 14.8 of the Process Memorandum prohibits setting off or treating PBG as consideration or equity infusion; and Section 42(6) of the Companies Act has no application to equity obligations under an IBC resolution plan[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict enforcement of Process Memorandum terms and the Supreme Court rulings in Ebix Singapore and State Bank of India v. Consortium of Murari Lal Jalan, establishing that performance securities are distinct from consideration and subject to absolute forfeiture on non-implementation[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC lawfully forfeited the Rs. 50 Crores PBG and Rs. 5 Crores EMD[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]; from the remaining Rs. 38.82 Crores equity money (held as Rs. 42.99 Crores with accrued interest), Interim Trade Creditors must be paid their Rs. 20.9 Crores dues with interest, and only the balance Rs. 22.09 Crores with interest is refundable to Formation[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins.) Nos. 983 and 1026 of 2023 are allowed, setting aside the full refund order and limiting Formation's refund to Rs. 22.09 Crores with accrued interest[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]; Appeals Nos. 984 and 1027 of 2023 are dismissed[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]; Appeal No. 1163 of 2023 is dismissed[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]; and Appeals Nos. 1098, 1099, 1100, 1101, 1236, and 1237 of 2023 are allowed, directing CoC to pay Rs. 20.9 Crores plus interest to the Interim Trade Creditors from the fixed deposit within 30 days[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. Parties to bear their own costs[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35].
summary: Multiple appeals arose from the NCLT Mumbai order directing Bank of Baroda/CoC to refund Rs. 93.82 Crores (comprising EMD, PBG, and equity deposit) to defaulting SRA Formation Textile LLC, while rejecting claims of Interim Trade Creditors who supplied goods while Formation managed the Corporate Debtor[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. The NCLAT set aside the full refund, holding that the CoC was entirely justified under the Process Memorandum and Supreme Court precedents (Ebix Singapore, Murari Lal Jalan) in forfeiting the Rs. 50 Crores PBG and Rs. 5 Crores EMD due to Formation's failure to implement the plan[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35]. The Tribunal held that the remaining Rs. 42.99 Crores equity fixed deposit must first be utilized to discharge the Rs. 20.9 Crores dues of Interim Trade Creditors with interest, with only the residual Rs. 22.09 Crores refunded to Formation[cite: 32, 33, 34, 35].

case_title: Shirish Vinod Shah (HUF) & Ors. vs. Bharti Telecom Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 273 to 280, 336 to 340 and 354 of 2019
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are 35 minority public shareholders (holding approx. 0.11% of equity); Respondent No. 1 is Bharti Telecom Limited (BTL, an unlisted Core Investment Company holding 50.10% in listed subsidiary Bharti Airtel Limited - BAL); Respondents No. 2 & 3 are RoC and Regional Director (MCA)[cite: 36, 37]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: BTL was delisted in 1999–2000; the Promoter Group (Bharti Group and SingTel Group) held 98.91% equity, while 4,942 public minority shareholders held 1.09% (2,84,57,840 shares)[cite: 36, 37]; on 19.06.2018, BTL's Board approved a Scheme of Reduction of Share Capital under Section 66(1)(b)(ii) to cancel and extinguish all 1.09% minority shares[cite: 36, 37]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an IBC debt default; the capital reduction offered minority shareholders an exit consideration of Rs. 163.25 plus Rs. 33.55 Dividend Distribution Tax (totaling Rs. 196.80 per share), reducing equity capital by Rs. 28,45,78,400/-[cite: 36, 37]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board meeting held on 19.06.2018; Notice with Explanatory Statement issued on 19.06.2018; Special Resolution approved via postal ballot/e-voting on 26.07.2018 (99.90% overall approval and 76.35% of minority voting in favour); petition filed before NCLT on 02.08.2018; NCLT approved scheme on 27.09.2019[cite: 36, 37]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation report by Ernst & Young Merchant Banking Services Pvt. Ltd. dated 19.06.2018 valuing BTL shares at Rs. 196.80 applying an Adjusted Net Asset Method and a 25% Discount for Lack of Marketability (DLOM)[cite: 36, 37]; Fairness Opinion from SPA Capital Advisors dated 19.06.2018[cite: 36, 37]; 100% creditor NOCs and RoC/RD no-objection report[cite: 36, 37]; confirmatory independent valuation reports by ICICI Securities and SBI Caps Securities submitted to the Special Court (TORTS Act) upholding the E&Y valuation[cite: 36, 37]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench approved the capital reduction petition CP (IB) No. 167/Chd/Hry/2018 under Section 66 on 27.09.2019[cite: 36, 37]; Appellants filed 14 connected appeals under Section 421 contending selective reduction is discriminatory, valuation was depressed compared to a prior Rs. 310 SingTel preferential issue, and DLOM was impermissible[cite: 36, 37].
legal_issues: Whether a company can carry out a selective capital reduction under Section 66(1)(b)(ii) of the Companies Act, 2013 to extinguish minority shares against their will upon payment of fair value, whether applying a 25% Discount for Lack of Marketability (DLOM) instead of a Control Premium is legally justifiable for unlisted investment company shares, and whether making valuation reports available for physical inspection complies with Section 102(3)[cite: 36, 37].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Capital reduction under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 is a domestic commercial matter governed by majority corporate democracy, permitting selective reduction and extinguishment of a class of shares against cash compensation, provided the scheme is fair, not unconscionable, supported by overwhelming majority votes, and pays fair market value determined by expert valuers[cite: 36, 37]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66(1) empowers a company to reduce share capital 'in any manner' via special resolution, which encompasses selective cancellation of minority shares; minority shareholders have no statutory veto or vested right to perpetuity of shareholding[cite: 36, 37]; under Section 102(3), offering inspection of valuation documents at registered offices satisfies statutory disclosure requirements for capital reduction without needing physical enclosure of reports[cite: 36, 37]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Judicial restraint in expert share valuation; courts and tribunals will not interfere with valuation methodologies (including the application of DLOM for unlisted illiquid shares) unless ex-facie unreasonable or fraudulent, as reaffirmed in Cadbury India, Miheer H. Mafatlal, and Hindustan Lever[cite: 36, 37]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: With 99.90% overall approval and 76.35% voting approval among minority shareholders, proper creditor consent, independent valuation backed by merchant banker fairness opinion and Special Court confirmation, the capital reduction scheme was lawful and fair[cite: 36, 37].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) Nos. 273 to 280, 336 to 340 and 354 of 2019 are dismissed without costs; all pending Interlocutory Applications are closed[cite: 36, 37].
summary: 35 minority public shareholders challenged the NCLT Chandigarh Bench order approving a Scheme of Capital Reduction under Section 66 of the Companies Act, 2013 for Bharti Telecom Limited (BTL)[cite: 36, 37]. The scheme cancelled 1.09% public shareholding against a cash payout of Rs. 196.80 per share determined by Ernst & Young using an Adjusted Net Asset Method with a 25% Discount for Lack of Marketability (DLOM)[cite: 36, 37]. The Appellants contended that selective reduction forcefully squeezed out minority holders, DLOM was unjustified, and valuation should match a prior preferential allotment to SingTel at Rs. 310[cite: 36, 37]. The NCLAT dismissed all 14 appeals, holding that Section 66 allows selective capital reduction in any manner when approved by special resolution (passed here by 99.90%)[cite: 36, 37]. Relying on Cadbury India and Reckitt Benckiser, the Tribunal held that minority holders have no vested right to remain shareholders and courts cannot substitute their views for expert valuations that are neither perverse nor illegal[cite: 36, 37].

case_title: Sashi Kanta Jha & Anr. vs. Devi Prasad & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Sashi Kanta Jha (suspended director of the Corporate Debtor) and Acme Consultant Private Limited; Respondent No. 1 is Devi Prasad (an individual workman/Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Deepak Kumar Agarwal (IRP/RP); Respondent No. 3 is Geo Jute Limited (formerly Juggilal Kamlapath Jute Mills Company Limited / JK Jute Mills, Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment and provision of services by the workman Devi Prasad to the Corporate Debtor mill, which had been closed since March 2014 and was previously registered under SICA before the BIFR. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 claimed unpaid dues of Rs. 5,24,132/-; the core default was established on an unpaid Assistant Labour Commissioner gratuity award dated 26.02.2014 for Rs. 70,700/- plus 8% interest per annum totaling Rs. 1,23,725/-, exceeding the pre-amendment Section 4 threshold of Rs. 1.0 Lakh. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Labour Commissioner award passed on 26.02.2014; BIFR abated on 25.11.2016; Delhi High Court order in WP(C) 440/2017 disposed of on 06.12.2017 granting liberty to workers to approach NCLT; Section 8 demand notice in Form 3 issued by R-1 on 29.05.2018; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 280(ALD)/2018 filed thereafter in 2018. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Final adjudicated gratuity award dated 26.02.2014 from the Assistant Labour Commissioner never challenged by the Corporate Debtor; Corporate Debtor's interim application enclosing a Demand Draft of Rs. 1,30,830/- acknowledging liability; earlier civil suits (Suit No. 500/2017 filed on 19.05.2017 and Suit No. 2506/2017 filed on 15.12.2017) filed by the debtor seeking an injunction against workers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench admitted Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 280(ALD)/2018 on 19.01.2024 holding the gratuity claim to be an operational debt and finding no pre-existing dispute or limitation bar; the suspended director appealed contending res judicata due to dismissal of an earlier trade union petition and pre-existing civil suit disputes.
legal_issues: Whether crystallized gratuity dues awarded by a competent Labour Authority constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC, whether civil suits filed after agreeing before a High Court that workmen can approach NCLT constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute, and whether an earlier dismissal of a Section 9 petition filed by a trade union solely on the procedural ground of prematurity operates as res judicata against an individual workman's petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory gratuity dues payable under an uncontested award of a competent labour authority fall within the definition of operational debt under Section 5(21) of the IBC as claims arising from employment, and opportunistic civil suits filed to forestall insolvency proceedings do not constitute a genuine pre-existing dispute; moreover, procedural dismissal of a prior representative petition for prematurity does not bar subsequent individual claims under the doctrine of res judicata. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(21) defines operational debt to encompass claims in respect of employment, interpreted in harmony with Section 326 of the Companies Act, 2013, which expressly includes gratuity and welfare dues in workmen dues; Sections 8 and 9 preclude admission only when a genuine dispute pre-dates the statutory demand notice, excluding moonshine or bad-faith suits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An unappealed decretal order/award of the Labour Commissioner conclusively establishes legally crystallized debt and default; procedural dismissal of an earlier petition without adjudication on the merits fails to satisfy the elements of res judicata. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor had an uncontroverted liability exceeding the statutory threshold arising from employment services; neither the frivolous civil suits nor the earlier dismissal of the trade union's appeal on premature filing barred the Section 9 application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 214 of 2024 is dismissed; interim stay order vacated, with the period from 02.02.2024 to the date of order excluded from the CIRP timeline; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: A suspended director of Geo Jute Limited (formerly JK Jute Mills) appealed against the NCLT Allahabad Bench order admitting a Section 9 IBC application filed by workman Devi Prasad for recovery of unpaid gratuity awarded by the Assistant Labour Commissioner in 2014. The Appellant argued that gratuity does not constitute operational debt, that pending civil suits demonstrated a pre-existing dispute, and that an earlier dismissed trade union petition operated as res judicata. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that gratuity dues arising out of employment are operational debts under Section 5(21). The Tribunal further held that post-facto civil suits constituted a moonshine defense and that the prior petition's dismissal for premature filing did not decide the merits to trigger res judicata.

case_title: Sarla Performance Fibres Ltd. vs. Mr. Vivek Murlidhar Dabhade, Liquidator of Desimran Cartons (P) Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Sarla Performance Fibres Ltd. (Licensee/claimant); Respondent is Mr. Vivek Murlidhar Dabhade, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor M/s Desimran Cartons Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor entered into a 12-year Leave and License Agreement dated 07.06.2019 letting out factory land (1,000 sq. meters) and two-floor building at Village Amli, Dadra and Nagar Haveli, for a monthly license fee of Rs. 5,000/- for the first 5 years (and Rs. 7,000/- thereafter) after entering into an alleged agreement of sale dated 16.04.2019, receiving Rs. 60 Lakhs refundable deposit and Rs. 55 Lakhs advance. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Jalgaon Janta Sahakari Bank had an existing mortgage on the asset and initiated Section 7 CIRP on 08.05.2019; during liquidation, the premises were successfully auctioned on an 'as is where is' basis for Rs. 4.21 Crores; Appellant claimed Rs. 1,15,00,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed by the Bank on 08.05.2019; Leave and License Agreement executed on 07.06.2019; CIRP commenced and liquidation ordered on 28.03.2022; Liquidator issued vacation notice on 18.05.2022 and filed disclaimer application IA No. 2012/2022; auction conducted pursuant to public notice dated 21.01.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The Leave and License Agreement executed for an uncommercial token rent of Rs. 5,000/- per month without secured creditor consent; Appellant subsequently offered to pay Rs. 2,25,000/- per month upon notice from Liquidator, establishing that the contractual rate was grossly unprofitable and burdensome to the liquidation estate. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 2012/2022 under Section 45 and Regulation 10 to disclaim the agreement; Appellant filed IA 672/2023 challenging auction and IA 2897/2023 challenging claim rejection; NCLT Mumbai Bench-III allowed disclaimer under Regulation 10, directed Appellant to vacate in 30 days, dismissed IA 672/2023, and directed liquidator to reconsider Appellant's Rs. 1.15 Crore monetary claim; Appellant appealed challenging the validity of Regulation 10 and citing divergence between tribunal members.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 10 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 empowering a liquidator to disclaim onerous property and unprofitable contracts is ultra vires the IBC, and whether the Leave and License Agreement dated 07.06.2019 was an unprofitable/onerous contract subject to disclaimer.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Regulation 10 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, authorizing the disclaimer of onerous property and unprofitable contracts, is intra vires the IBC, as it is framed in valid exercise of statutory rule-making powers under Section 240(2)(y) read with Sections 34(2), 35(1)(d), and 35(1)(o) of the Code; furthermore, uncommercial long-term leases executed at nominal rent post-insolvency filing are unprofitable contracts subject to disclaimer. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 35(1)(o) read with Section 3(32) and Section 240(2)(y) empowers the IBBI to specify functions of the liquidator by regulation, including the power of disclaimer modeled after Section 535 of the Companies Act, 1956, to preserve and maximize asset value; this power operates independently of avoidance provisions in Sections 43 to 51. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Comparison of contractual consideration against market value; leasing valuable industrial property for a nominal sum of Rs. 5,000/- per month compared to an admitted subsequent willingness to pay Rs. 2,25,000/- per month demonstrates that the contract is burdensome, unprofitable, and not in good faith. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Both adjudicating members concurred that the agreement was an unprofitable/onerous contract under Regulation 10; hence the Liquidator was legally justified in disclaiming the agreement and requiring vacant possession.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 379, 380, and 381 of 2025 are dismissed, affirming the NCLT's common order.
summary: Appellant Sarla Performance Fibres Ltd. appealed an NCLT Mumbai order allowing the Liquidator of Desimran Cartons Pvt. Ltd. to disclaim a 12-year Leave and License Agreement dated 07.06.2019 under Regulation 10 of the Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016 and ordering the Appellant to vacate. The Appellant argued that Regulation 10 was ultra vires the IBC because the Code only permits avoidance under Sections 43 to 51, and that there was divergence between the Technical and Judicial Members. Dismissing the appeals, the NCLAT held that Regulation 10 is fully authorized by Sections 34, 35(1)(o), and 240(2)(y) of the IBC to facilitate asset maximization. The Tribunal affirmed that leasing prime industrial land for Rs. 5,000/- per month was undeniably an unprofitable contract properly disclaimed by the liquidator.

case_title: Avni Jain & Ors. vs. Manoj Kulshrestha, IRP for Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are 8 individual unit purchasers (Avni Jain, Paritosh Jain, Sangeeta Jain, Akshat Jain, Divyansh Jain, Sarita Jain, Meenu Jain, Niharika Jain), all relatives of Adesh Jain, a long-time tax consultant of the Corporate Debtor; the Respondent is Manoj Kulshrestha, Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) for Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor was developing a group housing real estate project named 'RG Luxury Homes' at Plot No. GH-07A, Sector 16B, Greater Noida (UP); Appellants claimed allotment of residential units (e.g., Unit No. E-2401 to Avni Jain for total consideration of Rs. 46,80,000/-) via Allotment-cum-Builder Buyer Agreements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP was triggered against the Corporate Debtor by homebuyers on 19.09.2019; Appellants claimed allotments with token booking amounts of Rs. 50,000/- per unit, with the balance due on offer of possession, but no payment was made on or prior to the date of allotment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Application for allotment submitted on 20.08.2019; CIRP initiated and moratorium imposed on 19.09.2019; allotment letters issued by suspended management on 19.09.2019; reverse CIRP ordered on 05.02.2020; token booking cheques (Rs. 50,000/-) encashed between 07.12.2019 and 20.01.2020; IRP issued cancellation notices received on 10.09.2022; cancelled units re-allotted to third-party homebuyers on 16.01.2023; IBBI dismissed complaint against IRP on 11.04.2023; NCLT dismissed Appellants' IAs on 20.09.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Allotment applications requiring mandatory 10% payment prior to allotment letter issuance and payment into designated UP RERA Karnataka Bank accounts; receipts and ledger entries showing token payments of Rs. 50,000/- made via cheques dated December 2019 deposited into non-RERA accounts several months after CIRP commencement; absence of any contemporaneous proof of consideration on 19.09.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed IA Nos. 4572, 4573, 4574, 4575, 4576, 4629, 4659, and 4518 of 2023 before NCLT New Delhi Court VI challenging the IRP's cancellation of their allotments; NCLT dismissed all applications on 20.09.2024 holding the allotments void ab initio due to Section 14 moratorium and non-payment; Appellants appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether unit allotments executed by the suspended management of a Corporate Debtor on the exact date of CIRP commencement without consideration and without IRP consent are void ab initio under Section 14(1) of the IBC, and whether an IRP has administrative authority to treat such paper allotments as non-est without filing an avoidance application under Section 45.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Upon commencement of CIRP and imposition of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, the powers of the board of directors stand suspended, and any alienation, encumbrance, or allotment of corporate debtor assets by the suspended management without consideration or the approval of the resolution professional is void ab initio and non-est in law. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) strictly prohibits transferring, encumbering, alienating, or disposing of any assets of the corporate debtor post-moratorium; Section 45 governs undervalued transactions executed during the statutory look-back period prior to CIRP and has no application to transactions executed after or on the day CIRP commences, which are void due to complete absence of managerial authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Scrutiny of banking and transaction records; where allotment terms require prior deposit into designated statutory RERA escrow accounts and no payment is remitted until months after insolvency commencement, subsequent payments made into unauthorized accounts cannot retrospectively validate void paper transactions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The purported allotments having been executed post-moratorium without payment and without IRP consent, the IRP acted within his statutory duties to protect the corporate debtor's estate by cancelling the void allotments and re-allotting the units to genuine homebuyers.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 2288, 2289, 2290, 2293, 2294, 2295, 2296 & 2297 of 2024 are dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants appealed against an NCLT New Delhi common order rejecting their applications challenging the IRP's cancellation of residential unit allotments in the 'RG Luxury Homes' project of Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 38, 39, 40] The Appellants claimed allotments dated 19.09.2019, the very day CIRP commenced and the Section 14 moratorium came into force[cite: 38, 39, 40]. The IRP cancelled the allotments after discovering they were issued without receiving booking amounts or IRP approval, and token payments of Rs. 50,000/- were deposited only months later into non-designated bank accounts[cite: 38, 39, 40]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that the suspended management had no authority to alienate assets once CIRP commenced[cite: 38, 39, 40]. The paper allotments were void ab initio under Section 14, and the IRP acted within his administrative mandate to protect corporate debtor assets without needing to invoke Section 45[cite: 38, 39, 40].

case_title: Avni Jain vs. Manoj Kulshrestha, IRP for Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Avni Jain (Appellant, allottee/homebuyer related to Adesh Jain, long-time tax consultant of the Corporate Debtor); Manoj Kulshrestha (Respondent, Interim Resolution Professional); Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP/reverse CIRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported allotment of Unit No. E-2401 in residential project 'RG Luxury Homes', Greater Noida, under an Allotment-cum-Builder Buyer Agreement dated 19.09.2019 following an application dated 20.08.2019 for a total sale consideration of Rs. 46,80,000. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a petition on debt default; issue arose from cancellation of real estate allotment where the booking token amount of Rs. 50,000 was paid only on 18.12.2019 rather than upon booking, and remainder consideration was never remitted prior to cancellation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated and Section 14 moratorium imposed by NCLT on 19.09.2019; reverse CIRP ordered on 05.02.2020; IRP issued cancellation notice received on 10.09.2022; Appellant replied on 14.10.2022; unit re-allotted to a third party on 16.01.2023; IBBI complaint dismissed on 11.04.2023; IAs filed before NCLT in August 2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement Clause 12 requiring 10% payment before allotment; Clause 2.1 prescribing mandatory deposit into UP RERA account with Karnataka Bank Ltd.; Cheque No. 784711 dated 16.12.2019 encashed into a non-designated bank account on 18.12.2019; absence of contemporaneous payment receipts dated 19.09.2019 or earlier. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 4572 of 2023 under Section 60(5) IBC before NCLT Court VI New Delhi seeking quashing of unit cancellation; NCLT dismissed all applications on 20.09.2024 holding the allotment void due to moratorium under Section 14(1) and failure to deposit in the designated RERA account.
legal_issues: Whether the Interim Resolution Professional has the administrative authority to treat an allotment of corporate debtor assets made on the date of CIRP initiation without payment as non-est and void without filing an application under Section 45 for undervalued transactions; and whether an allotment executed on the date of CIRP initiation without requisite upfront consideration violates the Section 14 moratorium.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An allotment of corporate debtor property executed by suspended management on or after the date CIRP is initiated, without prior consideration paid into designated accounts, is non-est and void ab initio by operation of the statutory moratorium under Section 14, enabling the IRP to administratively disregard it to preserve assets without invoking avoidance proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 45 applies strictly to transactions executed during the look-back period under Section 46 (one year for unrelated parties, two years for related parties) prior to the commencement of CIRP, and cannot apply to transactions entered into on or after the CIRP admission date. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented failure to tender consideration into the mandatory contractually stipulated and statutory RERA bank account prior to CIRP initiation conclusively demonstrates the allotment was a paper transaction lacking enforceable legal existence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The management lost authority to encumber or transfer assets on 19.09.2019 upon CIRP initiation; hence, the post-dated payment in December 2019 into an unauthorised account cannot validate a void transaction, and the IRP acted within his statutory remit in cancelling the allotment.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal held that the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the applications; found no merit in the appeals; dismissed all connected appeals; and made no order as to costs.
summary: Avni Jain and other appellants challenged the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing their applications against the IRP's cancellation of unit allotments in the Corporate Debtor's project 'RG Luxury Homes'. The appellants claimed allotments dated 19.09.2019, the very day CIRP commenced against the Corporate Debtor. The IRP cancelled the allotments as unauthorized, void ab initio, and contrary to Section 14 moratorium, noting that the Rs. 50,000 booking token was paid months later in December 2019 into an unapproved bank account. NCLAT held that Section 45 was inapplicable because the transaction occurred on the date of CIRP rather than within the prior look-back period. Confirming the allotment was non-est, NCLAT dismissed the appeals.
