case_title: Niharika Jain vs. Manoj Kulshrestha, IRP for Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Niharika Jain (Appellant, allottee/homebuyer related to Adesh Jain, long-time tax consultant of the Corporate Debtor); Manoj Kulshrestha (Respondent, Interim Resolution Professional); Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP/reverse CIRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claimed allotment of residential unit in project 'RG Luxury Homes' executed by the Corporate Debtor under Allotment-cum-Builder Buyer Agreement dated 19.09.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a petition on debt default; dispute concerned invalidation of allotment due to non-payment of booking sum at the time of allotment, with staggered payments tendered between December 2019 and January 2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated and Section 14 moratorium imposed by NCLT on 19.09.2019; reverse CIRP ordered on 05.02.2020; IRP cancelled allotment in September 2022; IA No. 4576 of 2023 filed in August 2023 before NCLT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Obligation under clause 2.1 to deposit all consideration into UP RERA account with Karnataka Bank Ltd.; payments tendered into an unauthorized account between December 2019 and January 2020 long after CIRP admission; no evidence of consideration prior to 19.09.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 4576 of 2023 before NCLT Court VI New Delhi challenging unit cancellation; NCLT rejected the application on 20.09.2024 on grounds of moratorium breach and payment default.
legal_issues: Whether an allotment made on the date of CIRP initiation without consideration paid into the statutory account is void ab initio under Section 14 moratorium; and whether the IRP is required to seek avoidance under Section 45 when ignoring unauthorized post-CIRP dispositions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An allotment of corporate debtor property executed by suspended management on or after the date CIRP is initiated, without prior consideration paid into designated accounts, is non-est and void ab initio by operation of the statutory moratorium under Section 14, enabling the IRP to administratively disregard it to preserve assets without invoking avoidance proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 45 applies strictly to transactions executed during the look-back period under Section 46 prior to the commencement of CIRP, and does not apply to transactions entered into on or after the CIRP admission date. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Staggered subsequent payments into non-designated accounts cannot cure or validate a void transaction executed without consideration when management powers stood suspended. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The management lost authority to transfer assets on 19.09.2019 upon CIRP initiation; the IRP acted properly within his administrative authority to disregard the void allotment and re-allot the unit.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal held that the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the application; found no merit in the appeal; dismissed the appeal; and made no order as to costs.
summary: Niharika Jain appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dismissing IA No. 4576 of 2023, wherein she challenged the IRP's cancellation of her flat allotment in Rajesh Projects (India) Pvt. Ltd.'s project 'RG Luxury Homes'. The allotment was claimed under an agreement dated 19.09.2019, the date CIRP commenced and moratorium came into effect, with payments deposited into a non-designated bank account months later. The NCLAT upheld the dismissal, ruling that transactions on the date of CIRP cannot fall under Section 45 avoidance but are non-est and void under Section 14 moratorium. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak vs. Suraksha Realty Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak (Appellant, Resolution Professional); Suraksha Realty Ltd. and Sheth Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Respondents/Financial Creditors); Arrow Engineering Ltd. and Central Bank of India (Financial Creditors/CoC members); Golden Tobacco Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) dated 26.12.2009 under which Corporate Debtor granted joint development rights over Vile Parle property (31,128 sq. mtrs.) to Suraksha Realty Ltd. and Sheth Developers Pvt. Ltd. for Rs. 542.70 Crores, against which developers advanced Rs. 132 Crores (Rs. 66 Crores each); title deeds deposited with Kanga & Co. Advocates as Escrow Agent via joint letter dated 26.12.2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Advance of Rs. 132 Crores was refundable with 18% interest per annum under Clause 9.1 upon Corporate Debtor's failure to execute formal Joint Development Agreement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor under Section 7 on 07.06.2022; claims submitted in Form C on 20.06.2022 and rejected by IRP on 26.06.2022; NCLT order dated 16.03.2023 classified respondents as Financial Creditors; RP decision on 20.03.2023 admitted principal of Rs. 66 Crores each but rejected 18% interest and secured status; NCLT passed impugned order on 13.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supreme Court judgment dated 12.05.2016 in Civil Appeal No. 5038 of 2016 holding the MoU void as violative of the BIFR Rehabilitation Scheme; escrow letter dated 26.12.2009 lacking express intent to create mortgage; Corporate Debtor balance sheets for FY 2011-12 to 2013-14 admitting refundable advances; pleadings in Section 9 Arbitration Petition No. 667 of 2012 acknowledging refund liability with interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court II in IA Nos. 357 & 358 of 2023 allowed 18% interest, affirmed unsecured status, arbitrarily restricted Arrow Engineering's claim from Rs. 265 Crores to Rs. 40.75 Crores, stigmatized Central Bank's claim as inflated, directed discharge/replacement of RP Dr. Pathak with Sanjay Borad, and ordered a KPMG forensic audit.
legal_issues: Whether deposit of title deeds with an escrow agent pursuant to an unregistered MoU constitutes a valid mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; whether an interest-bearing refundable advance under an MoU later declared void retains the status of a financial debt bearing 18% interest; and whether the Adjudicating Authority can replace an RP, reduce admitted creditor claims, and order a forensic audit in violation of natural justice and statutory procedure under Section 27 IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) requires a clear contemporaneous intention to create a security interest in favor of the creditor; depositing title deeds with a third-party escrow agent to await execution of an agreement does not constitute a mortgage, and any written document embodying such bargain requires compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC encompasses advances having commercial effect of borrowing; even if underlying commercial agreements are declared void, money disbursed with time value of money acknowledged by the debtor remains an enforceable financial debt along with the contractually agreed interest. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Natural justice strictly requires that claims formally verified and admitted by the RP cannot be unilaterally reduced or characterized as inflated by the Adjudicating Authority without impleading and affording the affected creditors an opportunity to be heard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Replacement of the RP was legally untenable as statutory procedures under Section 27 were bypassed and founded upon unproven, adverse findings; direction for KPMG forensic audit was unwarranted and set aside; the RP Dr. Pathak is reinstated and Suraksha/Sheth are confirmed as unsecured Financial Creditors entitled to 18% interest.
operative_order: Company Appeals 1017 and 1018 of 2024 allowed, setting aside the replacement of RP Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak and terminating appointment of Sanjay Borad; Company Appeal 1096 of 2024 allowed, quashing restriction of Arrow Engineering's claim to Rs. 40.75 Crores; Company Appeals 1060 and 1061 of 2024 partly allowed, expunging observations on inflated claims of Central Bank of India; KPMG forensic audit set aside; Company Appeals 1309 and 1310 of 2024 dismissed, upholding denial of secured creditor status; CIRP extended to 17.10.2025; parties to appear before NCLT on 17.06.2025 for pending IA Nos. 703 and 697 of 2023.
summary: NCLAT disposed of a batch of appeals challenging the NCLT Ahmedabad order in the CIRP of Golden Tobacco Ltd. NCLT had granted Suraksha Realty and Sheth Developers 18% interest on Rs. 132 Crores advance while denying them secured status, replaced RP Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak, curtailed Arrow Engineering's claim, censured Central Bank of India, and ordered a forensic audit. NCLAT upheld the 18% interest as valid financial debt and affirmed that deposit of title deeds with an escrow agent did not create a valid mortgage under Section 58(f) of TPA. However, NCLAT set aside the replacement of the RP, the claim reductions made without hearing creditors, and the KPMG forensic audit, reinstating the RP.

case_title: Arrow Engineering Ltd. vs. Suraksha Realty Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Arrow Engineering Ltd. (Appellant, initiating Financial Creditor holding 98% voting share in initial CoC); Suraksha Realty Ltd. and Sheth Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Respondents/Financial Creditors); Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak (Erstwhile RP); Golden Tobacco Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Arrow Engineering initiated Section 7 proceedings; Suraksha Realty and Sheth Developers claimed status under MoU dated 26.12.2009 for Vile Parle land development for Rs. 542.70 Crores with Rs. 132 Crores advanced and title deeds deposited with an escrow agent. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Arrow Engineering's admitted claim was Rs. 265,97,10,569; Suraksha and Sheth claimed Rs. 132 Crores principal plus 18% per annum interest from 15.03.2011. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 admission ordered on 07.06.2022; Arrow's claim admitted on 17.06.2022; Arrow's impleadment application IA No. 1058/2023 rejected by NCLT on 22.03.2024; impugned NCLT order passed on 13.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order dated 22.03.2024 expressly finding no collusion between RP and Arrow Engineering and declaring Arrow not a necessary party to IA No. 357/2023; pending substantive challenges to Arrow's claim in IA No. 703/2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Adjudicating Authority NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 357/2023 sua sponte restricted Arrow Engineering's admitted claim from Rs. 265.97 Crores to Rs. 40.75 Crores pending KPMG audit, despite having previously denied Arrow impleadment and hearing in that application.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority could curtail an admitted financial creditor's claim from Rs. 265.97 Crores to Rs. 40.75 Crores in an interlocutory proceeding to which the creditor was denied impleadment, in blatant breach of principles of natural justice.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order adversely impacting the substantive legal rights or quantum of claim of a creditor passed without providing notice and an adequate opportunity of hearing is void for violation of natural justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The summary jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC cannot be exercised to determine or prune admitted claims behind a party's back when dedicated applications challenging such claims are pending adjudication. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Having formally rejected Arrow Engineering's impleadment application on the premise that no reliefs were claimed against it, the Tribunal cannot subsequently adjudicate against Arrow's admitted claim in that very proceeding. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The reduction of Arrow Engineering's claim was unsustainable and passed in violation of procedural due process; merits of the quantum must be resolved strictly in pending IA No. 703 of 2023.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1096 of 2024 allowed; directive in the impugned order restricting Arrow Engineering's claim to Rs. 40.75 Crores set aside; NCLT directed to adjudicate pending IA No. 703 of 2023 and IA No. 697 of 2023 within 60 days from 17.06.2025 on merits without being influenced by observations in the impugned order.
summary: Arrow Engineering Ltd., a major financial creditor in the CIRP of Golden Tobacco Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order which pruned its admitted claim from Rs. 265.97 Crores to Rs. 40.75 Crores. NCLT had previously rejected Arrow's application for impleadment in IA No. 357 of 2023 holding it had no locus standi, yet proceeded to reduce its claim in that proceeding. NCLAT set aside the reduction of Arrow's claim, holding it was an egregious violation of principles of natural justice, and directed that objections regarding Arrow's claim be heard independently in the pending IA No. 703 of 2023.

case_title: Sheth Developers Ltd. vs. AVM Resolution Professional LLP (Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sheth Developers Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor); Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak / AVM Resolution Professional LLP (Respondent, RP); Golden Tobacco Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: MoU dated 26.12.2009 for joint development of Vile Parle land measuring 31,128 sq. mtrs. for Rs. 542.70 Crores; Appellant advanced Rs. 66 Crores; original conveyance title deeds deposited with M/s Kanga & Co. as escrow agent under letter dated 26.12.2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim of Rs. 66 Crores with 18% per annum interest from 15.03.2011; Appellant claimed total debt of Rs. 424,63,62,138 jointly with Suraksha Realty Ltd. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 07.06.2022; claim in Form C filed on 21.06.2022; RP rejected security interest on 20.03.2023; NCLT denied secured creditor status on 13.05.2024 in IA No. 358/2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint letter dated 26.12.2009 instructing escrow agent to hold title deeds pending formal Joint Development Agreement execution; absence of mortgage registration under Section 125 of Companies Act, 1956 or Section 17 Registration Act; Supreme Court judgment dated 12.05.2016 holding that MoU entered in violation of BIFR scheme lost legal force and conferred no rights. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 358/2023 held that deposit of title deeds with escrow agent did not create an equitable mortgage or valid registered charge, denying Appellant status as a Secured Financial Creditor.
legal_issues: Whether the deposit of title deeds with an escrow agent pursuant to an unregistered memorandum of understanding creates a valid mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, entitling the claimant to status as a Secured Financial Creditor under the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The essential ingredient of a mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act is the delivery of documents to the creditor or its agent with the express intention to create a security thereon; delivery to an escrow agent pending contract performance excludes the legal implication of mortgage creation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Where parties reduce terms of deposit into writing that forms an integral part of the bargain regarding security, the document is compulsorily registrable under Section 17 of the Registration Act, failing which no valid charge or security interest arises. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The escrow letter and MoU demonstrated that custody was contingent upon future execution of a joint development agreement, disproving any contemporaneous intent by the debtor to transfer a property interest by way of security. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Supreme Court's declaration that the MoU was void and devoid of legal force precluded any accrual of security rights; the Adjudicating Authority properly classified the Appellant as an unsecured Financial Creditor.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1310 of 2024 dismissed; findings of the Adjudicating Authority in order dated 13.05.2024 denying secured creditor status upheld; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: Sheth Developers Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order rejecting its prayer to be classified as a Secured Financial Creditor of Corporate Debtor Golden Tobacco Ltd. The Appellant claimed a security interest over Vile Parle land on the basis of title deeds deposited with an escrow agent under an MoU dated 26.12.2009. The NCLAT held that deposit of title deeds with an escrow agent lacks the requisite legal intention to create a mortgage under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, and that the unregistered arrangement could not create an enforceable charge, especially after the Supreme Court declared the MoU void. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak vs. Suraksha Realty Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak (Appellant, Resolution Professional); Suraksha Realty Ltd. and Sheth Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Respondents/Financial Creditors); Arrow Engineering Ltd. and Central Bank of India (Financial Creditors/CoC members); Golden Tobacco Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) dated 26.12.2009 under which Corporate Debtor granted joint development rights over Vile Parle property (31,128 sq. mtrs.) to Suraksha Realty Ltd. and Sheth Developers Pvt. Ltd. for Rs. 542.70 Crores, against which developers advanced Rs. 132 Crores (Rs. 66 Crores each); title deeds deposited with Kanga & Co. Advocates as Escrow Agent via joint letter dated 26.12.2009. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Advance of Rs. 132 Crores was refundable with 18% interest per annum under Clause 9.1 upon Corporate Debtor's failure to execute formal Joint Development Agreement. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor under Section 7 on 07.06.2022; claims submitted in Form C on 20.06.2022 and rejected by IRP on 26.06.2022; NCLT order dated 16.03.2023 classified respondents as Financial Creditors; RP decision on 20.03.2023 admitted principal of Rs. 66 Crores each but rejected 18% interest and secured status; NCLT passed impugned order on 13.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supreme Court judgment dated 12.05.2016 in Civil Appeal No. 5038 of 2016 holding the MoU void as violative of the BIFR Rehabilitation Scheme; escrow letter dated 26.12.2009 lacking express intent to create mortgage; Corporate Debtor balance sheets for FY 2011-12 to 2013-14 admitting refundable advances; pleadings in Section 9 Arbitration Petition No. 667 of 2012 acknowledging refund liability with interest. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court II in IA Nos. 357 & 358 of 2023 allowed 18% interest, affirmed unsecured status, arbitrarily restricted Arrow Engineering's claim from Rs. 265 Crores to Rs. 40.75 Crores, stigmatized Central Bank's claim as inflated, directed discharge/replacement of RP Dr. Pathak with Sanjay Borad, and ordered a KPMG forensic audit.
legal_issues: Whether deposit of title deeds with an escrow agent pursuant to an unregistered MoU constitutes a valid mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; whether an interest-bearing refundable advance under an MoU later declared void retains the status of a financial debt bearing 18% interest; and whether the Adjudicating Authority can replace an RP, reduce admitted creditor claims, and order a forensic audit in violation of natural justice and statutory procedure under Section 27 IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A mortgage by deposit of title deeds under Section 58(f) requires a clear contemporaneous intention to create a security interest in favor of the creditor; depositing title deeds with a third-party escrow agent to await execution of an agreement does not constitute a mortgage, and any written document embodying such bargain requires compulsory registration under Section 17 of the Registration Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC encompasses advances having commercial effect of borrowing; even if underlying commercial agreements are declared void, money disbursed with time value of money acknowledged by the debtor remains an enforceable financial debt along with the contractually agreed interest. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Natural justice strictly requires that claims formally verified and admitted by the RP cannot be unilaterally reduced or characterized as inflated by the Adjudicating Authority without impleading and affording the affected creditors an opportunity to be heard. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Replacement of the RP was legally untenable as statutory procedures under Section 27 were bypassed and founded upon unproven, adverse findings; direction for KPMG forensic audit was unwarranted and set aside; the RP Dr. Pathak is reinstated and Suraksha/Sheth are confirmed as unsecured Financial Creditors entitled to 18% interest.
operative_order: Company Appeals 1017 and 1018 of 2024 allowed, setting aside the replacement of RP Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak and terminating appointment of Sanjay Borad; Company Appeal 1096 of 2024 allowed, quashing restriction of Arrow Engineering's claim to Rs. 40.75 Crores; Company Appeals 1060 and 1061 of 2024 partly allowed, expunging observations on inflated claims of Central Bank of India; KPMG forensic audit set aside; Company Appeals 1309 and 1310 of 2024 dismissed, upholding denial of secured creditor status; CIRP extended to 17.10.2025; parties to appear before NCLT on 17.06.2025 for pending IA Nos. 703 and 697 of 2023.
summary: NCLAT disposed of a batch of appeals challenging the NCLT Ahmedabad order in the CIRP of Golden Tobacco Ltd. NCLT had granted Suraksha Realty and Sheth Developers 18% interest on Rs. 132 Crores advance while denying them secured status, replaced RP Dr. Vichitra Narayan Pathak, curtailed Arrow Engineering's claim, censured Central Bank of India, and ordered a forensic audit. NCLAT upheld the 18% interest as valid financial debt and affirmed that deposit of title deeds with an escrow agent did not create a valid mortgage under Section 58(f) of TPA. However, NCLAT set aside the replacement of the RP, the claim reductions made without hearing creditors, and the KPMG forensic audit, reinstating the RP.

case_title: Jayshree Agnihotri vs. Nirmal Kumar Jain & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jayshree Agnihotri (Appellant, 50% shareholder/Agnihotri group); Nirmal Kumar Jain and 9 other home-buyers/allottees (Respondents No. 1 to 10, Financial Creditors in a class); Ashok Kumar Jain (Jain group/suspended management); Pushp Ratna Realty Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development of a real estate township project 'Lush by Pushp Ratna' at Khajrana, Indore, across 2,01,858 sq. ft. of land owned by the Agnihotri group under an MoU dated 14.09.2009 with the Jain group/Corporate Debtor; out of 140 units, 77 were booked, with the 10 home-buyers issued allotment letters between 28.03.2014 and 15.11.2016 requiring construction and possession handover within 30 months. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose upon the expiry of 30 months from the respective allotment letters (default dates ranging from 28.09.2016 to 15.05.2019) due to total failure to construct/deliver the units, involving unpaid claims exceeding the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Original Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 83/MP/2023 was withdrawn with liberty; fresh Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 26(MP)2024 filed on 22.05.2024; Appellant filed settlement IA No. 386/2024 on 23.09.2024; NCLT admitted Section 7 and rejected IA No. 386/2024 on 16.10.2024; CoC rejected Appellant's settlement proposal in 2nd meeting on 03.12.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited balance sheet for FY 2019-20 (Note 2.7) showing 'Advances from Customers against Flat Bookings' of Rs. 3,87,14,432 as current liabilities; balance confirmation letters dated 09.11.2021 issued by Corporate Debtor admitting delivery delay and promising interest compensation; physical site inspection indicating only 30-40% progress on 3 out of 9 towers with stalled construction since 2014-15. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench Court No. 1 admitted CP (IB) No. 26(MP)2024 under Section 7 on 16.10.2024 and dismissed Appellant's IA No. 386/2024, holding the application within limitation and debt/default established.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 7 petition filed by allottees in a real estate project was barred by limitation; whether inter se shareholder disputes or allegations of collusion between allottees and management render the petition a collusive proxy litigation under Section 65; and whether an Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can force home-buyers/CoC to accept an ex-promoter's unilateral settlement proposal outside Section 12A.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Entries in audited balance sheets coupled with balance confirmation letters constitute a valid acknowledgment of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, resetting the limitation period; allottees who have paid considerations and suffered prolonged project delays are entitled to initiate CIRP notwithstanding ongoing inter se governance disputes between shareholder factions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Once a CoC is constituted, any termination or withdrawal of CIRP based on settlement must strictly follow the statutory framework of Section 12A and cannot be foisted upon the CoC or allottees unilaterally. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of mutual settlement discussions and arbitral disputes between shareholder groups does not establish collusion between creditors and the debtor, particularly where the debtor's books clearly reflect received advances as current liabilities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The home-buyers satisfied the threshold criteria and established genuine debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 Crore, and their commercial decision in the CoC to reject the promoter's buy-out/settlement proposal was neither arbitrary nor irrational, justifying admission of the CIRP.
operative_order: All three connected appeals (Company Appeal Nos. 2112, 2113, and 2335 of 2024) are dismissed; the interim stay order is vacated; the CIRP of the Corporate Debtor shall proceed in accordance with the IBC; no order as to costs.
summary: Jayshree Agnihotri (50% shareholder) and Ashok Kumar Jain (suspended management) appealed the NCLT Indore order admitting a Section 7 CIRP application filed by 10 home-buyers of 'Lush by Pushp Ratna' and rejecting Agnihotri's IA No. 386/2024 offering to pay off allottees. Appellants alleged the petition was time-barred, collusive, and malicious. NCLAT held that the debt was kept alive within limitation through Note 2.7 of the 2019-20 audited balance sheet and confirmation letters dated 09.11.2021. NCLAT further ruled that inter se disputes between shareholder factions cannot prejudice allottees' statutory rights under Section 7, nor can allottees be compelled to accept settlement proposals outside Section 12A. The appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Shrinathji Spintex Pvt. Ltd. vs. Shantilal Parbatbhai Lakkad & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shrinathji Spintex Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Operational Creditor); Shantilal Parbatbhai Lakkad (Respondent No. 1, alleged Personal Guarantor); State Bank of India (Respondent No. 2, Secured Financial Creditor/Intervenor); Rajendra Jain (Respondent No. 3, Resolution Professional); Sunrise Ginning Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Oral agreement between April and July 2015 for supply of cotton bales worth Rs. 3,44,98,716 by Appellant to the Corporate Debtor (both related family-run businesses). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Invoices unpaid; debt claimed under a subsequent Consent Decree dated 05.03.2020 totaling Rs. 5,77,85,361 (including interest); demand notice issued on 10.11.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor admitted to CIRP and Section 14 moratorium imposed on 20.11.2019 (quashed on 12.03.2020); Special Civil Suit No. 02 of 2020 filed before Principal Civil Judge Rajkot on 02.01.2020; Consent Decree passed on 05.03.2020; Demand Notice Form B issued on 10.11.2022; Section 95 application CP (IB) No. 26/AHM/2023 filed on 13.12.2022; RP appointed on 01.02.2023 and submitted Section 99 report on 22.02.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent Decree dated 05.03.2020 signed by suspended directors during moratorium promising repayment 'as soon as possible' and purporting to hypothecate properties previously mortgaged to SBI in 2011/2013; no independent written deed of guarantee executed; no prior notice invoking personal guarantee produced. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench on 31.07.2024 dismissed the Section 95 petition holding that no valid written guarantee existed, the petition was a fraudulent attempt to execute a civil compromise, imposed Rs. 1 Lakh penalty each on Appellant and RP, and referred the RP to IBBI.
legal_issues: Whether a civil court consent decree recording a joint promise to repay 'as soon as possible' constitutes a valid contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Indian Contract Act and Section 5(22) of the IBC; whether invocation of a personal guarantee is a mandatory prerequisite for initiating Section 95 insolvency proceedings; and whether a consent decree obtained during a Section 14 moratorium through suppression of CIRP is void ab initio for fraud.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Contract Act requires a clear, unequivocal assumption of secondary liability triggered upon default of the principal debtor; an open-ended consent decree promising payment 'as soon as possible' without defining secondary liability cannot constitute a contract of guarantee for personal insolvency under Section 95 IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Rule 3(e) of the Personal Guarantor Rules, 2019, read with Section 95 of the IBC, formal invocation of the guarantee is a sine qua non before a guarantor can be said to have committed default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Instituting a civil suit and procuring a consent decree against a corporate debtor during the subsistence of a Section 14 moratorium without disclosing CIRP proceedings vitiates the compromise decree by fraud, rendering it void ab initio and incapable of sustaining insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The consent decree was void, unenforceable, and did not constitute an invoked personal guarantee; the RP committed gross negligence in recommending admission without scrutinizing the validity of the decree and moratorium violation, justifying the dismissal, penalty, and reference to IBBI.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1694, 1837, and 1838 of 2024 are dismissed; adverse remarks, penalty of Rs. 1 Lakh on the RP, and reference to IBBI upheld; all pending IAs closed with no order as to costs.
summary: Shrinathji Spintex Pvt. Ltd. and Resolution Professional Rajendra Jain appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing Section 95 applications against personal guarantors of Sunrise Ginning Pvt. Ltd., imposing a Rs. 1 Lakh penalty on the RP, and referring him to IBBI. The creditor relied on a civil court consent decree dated 05.03.2020 to establish an oral personal guarantee and default date. NCLAT held that the consent decree did not satisfy the legal requirements of a contract of guarantee under Section 126 of the Contract Act or Section 5(22) of the IBC. Furthermore, the decree was obtained during a Section 14 moratorium without disclosing CIRP, rendering it void ab initio for fraud, and the guarantee was never formally invoked. All appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Bhupesh Gupta, Ex-Liquidator, Supreme Tex Mart Limited vs. Ravinder Kumar Goel, Liquidator
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhupesh Gupta (Appellant, Ex-Liquidator); Ravinder Kumar Goel (Respondent, Successor Liquidator); Supreme Tex Mart Limited (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant served as Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor from 08.08.2018 to 31.10.2019 (1 year and 84 days) and operated the Corporate Debtor as a going concern until 31.03.2019, generating operational sales turnover of Rs. 78,47,31,778 alongside government recoveries (GST refunds and insurance claims). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute concerns computation of Liquidator's remuneration where CoC did not fix fees under Regulation 4; Appellant claimed fees of Rs. 1,88,02,261 based on total turnover/recoveries, having earlier drawn Rs. 31.09 Lakhs without CoC approval. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted to CIRP on 29.09.2017; liquidation ordered on 08.08.2018; Appellant replaced on health grounds on 01.11.2019; IBBI issued disciplinary order on 21.04.2020 directing refund of Rs. 31.09 Lakhs; Appellant filed IA No. 893/2020 on 18.11.2020; NCLT dismissed IA on 28.09.2022; NCLAT remanded matter on 11.03.2024; NCLT passed fresh dismissal order on 04.03.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Only fixed asset sold during Appellant's tenure was a Toyota car realizing Rs. 2,60,000; total operational purchases and direct/indirect expenses incurred during going concern operations totaled Rs. 1,32,64,70,965.02 (inclusive of Rs. 98.24 Crores purchases and Rs. 7.52 Crores audit-determined costs), far exceeding total receipts. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench in remand proceedings dismissed IA No. 893/2020 on 04.03.2025, finding that gross liquidation costs (Rs. 132.64 Crores) exceeded sales realization (Rs. 78.47 Crores), leaving zero net realization for fee computation under Regulation 4(3).
legal_issues: Whether operational revenue generated while running a Corporate Debtor as a going concern constitutes 'amount realised' under Regulation 4(3) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016; whether all operational expenses incurred during going concern operations constitute 'liquidation cost' under Regulation 2(1)(ea) to be deducted from gross receipts; and whether an ex-liquidator is entitled to fee compensation on quantum meruit when operational expenditures exceed operational realizations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Regulation 4(3) of the Liquidation Regulations, where fees are not fixed by the CoC, the liquidator is entitled to remuneration computed strictly as a percentage of the amount realized 'net of other liquidation costs'; if total liquidation costs incurred to generate revenue exceed the gross realization, net realization is nil and no fee is payable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 2(1)(ea)(v) and Section 53(1)(a) mandate that costs incurred in carrying on the business as a going concern are liquidation costs payable in priority, and must be deducted in full from realization to determine 'amount realised net of other liquidation costs' under Regulation 4. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following the striking down of Clauses 2.1 and 2.5 of the IBBI Circular dated 28.09.2023 by the Bombay High Court in Amit Gupta, fee calculation cannot be claimed on gross turnover or liquid assets without offsetting full operational expenses. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because verified liquidation costs of Rs. 132.64 Crores significantly exceeded sales realizations of Rs. 78.47 Crores, no net realization remained; statutory regulations leave no room for awarding fees on a quantum meruit basis.
operative_order: The Appellate Tribunal held that nothing is payable to the Appellant as Liquidator's fee under Regulation 4 read with Regulation 2(1)(ea) and Section 5(16) IBC; the appeal is dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary: Ex-Liquidator Bhupesh Gupta appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order denying him liquidation fees for his 14-month tenure managing Supreme Tex Mart Ltd. as a going concern. While Appellant claimed fees of Rs. 1.88 Crores based on operational sales of Rs. 78.47 Crores, the successor liquidator demonstrated that going-concern operational expenditures exceeded Rs. 132.64 Crores. NCLAT held that under Regulation 4(3) read with Regulation 2(1)(ea), liquidator remuneration is strictly payable on the 'amount realised net of other liquidation costs'. Since expenses incurred to preserve and run the business as a going concern formed part of liquidation costs and exceeded total turnover, net realization was nil. NCLAT rejected the plea for quantum meruit compensation and dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Rajendra Jain vs. Hemantbhai Parbatbhai Lakkad & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajendra Jain (Appellant, Resolution Professional); Hemantbhai Parbatbhai Lakkad (Respondent No. 1, alleged Personal Guarantor); Shrinathji Spintex Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 2/Creditor); State Bank of India (Respondent No. 3, Secured Financial Creditor/Intervenor); Sunrise Ginning Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Oral contract for cotton bales supply by Shrinathji Spintex to Sunrise Ginning in 2015; unpaid invoices totaling Rs. 3,44,98,716 settled via Consent Decree dated 05.03.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed upon passing of Consent Decree on 05.03.2020 for Rs. 5,77,85,361; demand notice served on 10.11.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted to CIRP on 20.11.2019; civil suit filed on 02.01.2020 during moratorium; consent decree passed on 05.03.2020; Section 95 petition CP (IB) No. 25/AHM/2023 filed against Respondent No. 1; Appellant appointed RP under Section 97(5) on 01.02.2023 and submitted Section 99 report on 22.02.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent decree executed during moratorium by suspended management without IRP or civil court being apprised of CIRP; lack of separate deed of guarantee or guarantee invocation letter; hypothecated properties were already mortgaged to SBI. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed CP (IB) No. 25/AHM/2023 on 31.07.2024, imposed Rs. 1 Lakh penalty on RP, and referred him to IBBI for dereliction of duty and recommending admission without verifying facts.
legal_issues: Whether a Resolution Professional can be penalized and referred to the IBBI under Section 99 of the IBC for submitting a report recommending personal insolvency based on an uninvoked consent decree obtained during a corporate debtor's Section 14 moratorium.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A Resolution Professional acting under Section 99 has a statutory duty of due diligence to examine the legal validity and enforceability of documents forming the basis of default; recommending insolvency on the basis of a fraudulent compromise decree obtained in violation of a statutory moratorium constitutes actionable professional negligence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 99(4) empowers the RP to seek requisite facts and verify whether an enforceable contract of guarantee exists and has been duly invoked prior to recommending admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the RP possesses actual knowledge of the corporate debtor's prior CIRP and moratorium dates, recommending admission on a consent decree executed during that exact moratorium period demonstrates failure of due diligence or bad faith. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the Section 95 petition, imposing a Rs. 1 Lakh penalty on the RP, and referring his conduct to the IBBI.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1838 of 2024 dismissed; penalty of Rs. 1 Lakh and direction referring the RP to IBBI affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Resolution Professional Rajendra Jain appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order in CP (IB) No. 25/AHM/2023, which dismissed a Section 95 petition against personal guarantor Hemantbhai Parbatbhai Lakkad, slapped a Rs. 1 Lakh penalty on the RP, and referred him to IBBI. The RP had recommended personal insolvency based on a civil consent decree obtained during the Corporate Debtor's CIRP moratorium without guarantee invocation. NCLAT upheld the findings, ruling that the RP failed to perform his statutory duty under Section 99 by blindly relying on a collusive decree that violated Section 14. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Bhavik Bhimjyani vs. Uday Vinodchandra Shah & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bhavik Bhimjyani (Appellant, 60% shareholder/Ex-Director of Corporate Debtor); Uday Vinodchandra Shah (Respondent No. 1, Liquidator); Leisure Enterprises LLP (Respondent No. 2, private purchaser and related party promoted by Anand Jain); Urban Infrastructure Trustees Ltd. - UITL (40% shareholder and sole financial creditor of CD, subsidiary of Jai Corp Ltd. promoted by Anand Jain); Neelkanth Township & Construction Pvt. Ltd. - NTCPL (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor owns an undivided prime land parcel of 80.6 acres in Alibaug (30 acres directly held by NTCPL and 50.6 acres held via 100% subsidiary Urban Rupi Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. - URIPL); proposed private sale of land and 100% equity shares in URIPL to Leisure Enterprises LLP for Rs. 58.51 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: NTCPL admitted under Section 7 on 21.04.2017 for Rs. 51 Crores claim; liquidation ordered on 03.09.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD ordered into liquidation on 03.09.2018; 1st and 2nd public auctions in July/December 2019 failed; 3rd and 4th auctions held in March 2021 failed; Leisure Enterprises submitted private offer on 10.06.2021; Liquidator conditionally confirmed private sale on 02.07.2021 and filed IA No. 1577/2021 on 09.07.2021; NCLT approved private sale on 05.12.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Government valuation by Collector Raigad dated 20.10.2021 assessed the land/shares at Rs. 70,31,40,400; independent expert valuations (Colliers) and 2018 resolution plan indicated values from Rs. 67 Crores to Rs. 103 Crores; multiple alternative higher offers placed before NCLT ranging between Rs. 72.54 Crores and Rs. 95 Crores; Liquidator issued confirmation of sale and accepted 10% EMD before seeking NCLT approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 1577/2021 approved the private sale to Leisure Enterprises LLP on 05.12.2023 at Rs. 58.51 Crores and dismissed Appellant's intervention and auction applications (IA Nos. 2117/2021, 1617/2022, 4212/2023).
legal_issues: Whether the liquidator can execute a private sale of corporate debtor assets to a related party under Regulation 33 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 without obtaining prior permission from the Adjudicating Authority before negotiating and confirming the sale; and whether an undervalued private sale can be approved where statutory auction norms were bypassed and higher competing offers were on record.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Regulation 33(1) mandates public auction as the normal mode of liquidation sale; private sale under Regulation 33(2) is an exception, and the proviso strictly mandates that prior permission of the Adjudicating Authority must be obtained before entering into, negotiating, or confirming a private sale to a related party. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Seeking ex-post facto approval after conditionally accepting consideration and issuing confirmation letters reduces the statutory requirement of 'prior permission' to an empty formality and violates Regulation 33(2) and (3). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Conducting rapid back-to-back auctions during the Covid pandemic with limited newspaper publicity and selling property at Rs. 58.51 Crores when official Ready Reckoner rates stood at Rs. 70.31 Crores conclusively proves undervaluation and procedural compromise. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The private sale to Leisure Enterprises LLP violated Regulation 33 and compromised value maximization; the approval order must be quashed, the private sale set aside, and an independent Liquidator appointed to conduct a de novo liquidation process.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 23 of 2024 allowed; Impugned Order dated 05.12.2023 approving private sale to Leisure Enterprises LLP set aside; NCLT directed to appoint a new Liquidator within 15 days; new Liquidator to restart the liquidation process afresh via public auction or private sale strictly as per law; connected appeals disposed of with no order as to costs.
summary: Bhavik Bhimjyani, 60% shareholder of Neelkanth Township & Construction Pvt. Ltd. (in liquidation), appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order approving the private sale of an 80.6-acre Alibaug land parcel and subsidiary shares to Leisure Enterprises LLP (a related party entity linked to Anand Jain and creditor UITL) for Rs. 58.51 Crores. NCLAT held that the private sale flagrantly violated Regulation 33 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 because the Liquidator confirmed the sale and accepted earnest money before seeking prior permission from the NCLT. Furthermore, the land was sold at an undervalued price compared to the Collector's valuation of Rs. 70.31 Crores, and public auction norms were compromised during the Covid period. NCLAT set aside the private sale and ordered the appointment of a new Liquidator to re-conduct the process afresh.

case_title: Mudraksh Investfin Pvt. Ltd. vs. Gursev Singh
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mudraksh Investfin Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Financial Creditor); Gursev Singh (Respondent/Personal Guarantor); Mica Industries Limited (Principal Borrower/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan of Rs. 10 Lakhs advanced by the Appellant to the Principal Borrower on 01.02.2023, which was secured by a personal guarantee provided by the Respondent on 08.02.2023. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on loan repayment; Financial Creditor invoked the personal guarantee on 15.10.2023 for an underlying debt of Rs. 10 Lakhs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan advanced on 01.02.2023; guarantee executed on 08.02.2023; personal guarantee invoked on 15.10.2023; Section 95 application CP IB No. 422/2024 filed before NCLT; NCLT dismissed the application on 14.11.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 02.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement dated 01.02.2023; personal guarantee agreement dated 08.02.2023; guarantee invocation letter dated 15.10.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed CP IB No. 422/2024 (Old No. IB-422/ND/2024) under Section 95(1) of the IBC before NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-II) seeking initiation of CIRP against the Personal Guarantor; NCLT rejected the application on 14.11.2024 holding that the debt did not meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold; Appellant challenged the rejection in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 9 of 2025.
legal_issues: What is the minimum debt threshold required for filing an application under Section 95(1) of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 by a financial creditor against a personal guarantor of a corporate debtor before the National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT)—whether it is Rs. 1 Crore as provided under Section 4 for corporate debtors or Rs. 1,000 as provided under Section 78 for individuals?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When an insolvency resolution process against a personal guarantor of a corporate debtor is instituted before the NCLT pursuant to Section 60, the applicable minimum debt threshold is the Rs. 1 Crore limit prescribed under Section 4 of the IBC, and not the Rs. 1,000 limit prescribed under Section 78 for ordinary individual debtor proceedings before the Debt Recovery Tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60 integrates the insolvency proceedings of a corporate debtor and its personal guarantor before a common forum (NCLT); personal guarantors are treated as a separate species of individuals due to their intimate corporate connection, making the corporate-debtor threshold applicable to their NCLT proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an application under Section 95 against a personal guarantor is filed before the NCLT for an amount below Rs. 1 Crore (in this case Rs. 10 Lakhs), the application fails to satisfy the jurisdictional threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the Section 95 application for failing to meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold, as permitting personal insolvency proceedings before the NCLT for nominal amounts like Rs. 1,000 would overwhelm the forum and frustrate the statutory framework.
operative_order: The appeal filed by the financial creditor is dismissed, and the parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: Mudraksh Investfin Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order rejecting its Section 95 application against Gursev Singh, the personal guarantor of Mica Industries Limited, for a debt of Rs. 10 Lakhs. The NCLT had dismissed the petition for failing to meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold. NCLAT upheld the dismissal, ruling that although Section 78 prescribes a threshold of Rs. 1,000 for general individuals under Part III, applications filed against personal guarantors of corporate debtors before the NCLT under Section 60 are subject to the Rs. 1 Crore threshold applicable to corporate matters. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Saurabh Jhunjhunwala vs. Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Saurabh Jhunjhunwala (Appellant, suspended director of Corporate Debtor); Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Private Limited (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor/Assignee); Allahabad Bank (Original Lender); Fairdeal Supplies Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial facilities of Rs. 34.50 Crores sanctioned by Allahabad Bank in 2010 to purchase a property at Coimbatore via High Court auction; account classified as NPA on 30.09.2011; debt assigned to Pegasus by registered assignment deed dated 27.09.2013 for Rs. 350 Crores aggregate consideration. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed in Section 7 application amounting to Rs. 1,45,74,89,265 as on 04.08.2022, based on default dating back to NPA on 30.09.2011. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan sanctioned on 05.03.2010; NPA declared on 30.09.2011; debt assigned on 27.09.2013; Section 7 application filed on 18.08.2022; NCLT admitted Section 7 on 19.03.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 01.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered assignment deed dated 27.09.2013; Corporate Debtor balance sheets for FY 2013-14 through 2019-20 acknowledging indebtedness; NeSL record of default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted Section 7 application on 19.03.2024 in CP (IB) No. 308/KB/2022; Appellant challenged the admission before NCLAT, offering during appeal to deposit the principal amount of Rs. 22,02,51,721.
legal_issues: Whether an assignment agreement registered outside the State of Tamil Nadu is void under Section 28(b) of the Registration Act (as amended in Tamil Nadu) in respect of underlying immovable property situated in Coimbatore; whether Section 7 application was barred by limitation given continuous balance sheet acknowledgments; and whether depositing the principal sum during appeal extinguishes the debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 28(b) of the Registration Act as amended in Tamil Nadu, an assignment deed executed and registered outside Tamil Nadu in respect of immovable property situated within Tamil Nadu is void solely qua that specific immovable property, but the assignment of the underlying intangible financial debt remains severable and valid. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Continuous acknowledgment of debt in the corporate debtor's balance sheets constitutes a valid acknowledgement under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, extending limitation even if the assignee's name is not explicitly named in the balance sheet entries. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Financial debt and default being established through loan records, balance sheets, and NeSL filings, unilateral deposit of principal during appeal does not discharge statutory interest or invalidate CIRP admission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The assignment deed was void only regarding the Coimbatore immovable property mortgage (which was severable), the debt was alive within limitation, and the Section 7 admission order was legally sound.
operative_order: NCLAT upheld the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 19.03.2024 admitting Section 7; interim orders vacated; period from 08.04.2024 till date excluded from CIRP; deposited principal to be refunded to Appellant with interest; assignment agreement held void only qua the Coimbatore land mortgage.
summary: Saurabh Jhunjhunwala, suspended director of Fairdeal Supplies Limited, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order admitting a Section 7 application filed by Pegasus Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. The Appellant argued that the assignment deed was void under Section 28(b) of the Registration Act (Tamil Nadu Amendment) because it assigned a Coimbatore property mortgage without registration in Tamil Nadu, and that the claim was time-barred. NCLAT held that while the assignment was void qua the Coimbatore immovable property mortgage, that portion was severable, leaving the financial debt assignment valid. NCLAT also confirmed that balance sheet acknowledgments kept the debt within limitation. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. M/s L.R. Builders Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Appellant/Financial Creditor); M/s L.R. Builders Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent/Corporate Guarantor); M/s P.P. Jewellers (Delhi) (Principal Borrower). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan of Rs. 60 Crores sanctioned by e-SBBJ on 31.12.2011 and working capital facility of Rs. 40 Crores sanctioned by SBI on 23.02.2012 to P.P. Jewellers (Delhi), secured by separate corporate guarantees executed by L.R. Builders Pvt. Ltd. on the respective dates. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by principal borrower leading to NPA classification by SBI on 31.12.2015 and e-SBBJ on 31.03.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan sanctioned in 2011/2012; NPA declared in December 2015/March 2016; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 612/2022 filed on 13.06.2022; NCLT dismissed Section 7 and allowed Respondent's Section 65 application on 07.10.2024; borrower completed final OTS payment by 28.11.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 23.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Executed loan agreements, corporate guarantees, revival letters dated 31.10.2014 and 03.02.2015, balance confirmation dated 21.01.2016, and emails from Respondent dated 13.09.2021 and 15.09.2021 acknowledging liability. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench (Court-III) on 07.10.2024 dismissed SBI's Section 7 petition and allowed Respondent's IA No. 4749/2022 under Section 65 of IBC, imposing severe adverse findings of fraud, collusion, and malicious intent against SBI; SBI appealed to NCLAT seeking expungement of Section 65 adverse remarks.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in invoking Section 65 of the IBC to dismiss a financial creditor's Section 7 petition and record adverse findings of fraud and malicious intent against a public sector bank without valid evidentiary support.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 65 of the IBC can only be invoked when insolvency proceedings are initiated with demonstrable fraudulent or malicious intent for an extraneous purpose; routine banking decisions, commercial disputes, or pending civil/DRT recovery proceedings do not constitute fraudulent initiation under Section 65. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A corporate guarantee executed in continuous terms remains enforceable independently of loan renewals, and subsequent debt settlements via OTS do not render prior bona fide insolvency filings malicious ab initio. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Recording findings of fraud and collusion against a nationalized bank based on misread bank entries and quashed criminal proceedings (where Delhi High Court quashed the FIR and cleared bank officials) is perverse and legally unsustainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed grave error by passing unsubstantiated adverse remarks and finding malice under Section 65, warranting complete expungement of those observations.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 2205 of 2024 allowed; impugned order dated 07.10.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi in IA No. 4749/2022 in CP (IB) No. 612/2022 set aside; all adverse findings and remarks against SBI expunged; no order as to costs.
summary: State Bank of India appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated 07.10.2024, which dismissed SBI's Section 7 petition against corporate guarantor L.R. Builders Pvt. Ltd. and allowed the guarantor's Section 65 application, recording harsh adverse findings of fraud, collusion, and malicious intent against the Bank. Although the underlying loan was settled via OTS during appellate proceedings, SBI pursued the appeal solely to expunge the adverse remarks. NCLAT held that the NCLT's findings of malice and fraud were perverse, unsupported by evidence, and ignored the Delhi High Court's judgment quashing a related FIR against bank officials. NCLAT set aside the Section 65 order and expunged all adverse remarks against SBI.

case_title: Hari Vitthal Mission vs. Ravi Sethia & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Hari Vitthal Mission (Appellant/Financial Creditor); Ravi Sethia (Respondent No. 1, Resolution Professional); J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. and Axis Bank Ltd. (Respondents No. 2 and 3, Committee of Creditors); Consortium of Nishkala Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. & Ujin Pharma Chem (Respondent No. 4, Successful Resolution Applicant); Suasth Healthcare Foundation (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against Suasth Healthcare Foundation on 31.08.2021 under Section 10 of the IBC on its own application; Appellant filed a claim of Rs. 62,16,33,563/- and was admitted as an unsecured financial creditor, but subsequently declared a 'related party' by the RP on 11.01.2022 (upheld by NCLT on 23.09.2022 and NCLAT on 05.11.2024). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not an application on debt default, but an appeal challenging the approval of a Resolution Plan allocating 'NIL' payment to the unsecured financial creditor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 31.08.2021; Resolution Plan approved by CoC in 15th meeting on 21.09.2022; NCLT initially remitted the plan back on 28.08.2023; CoC reaffirmed distribution on 07.09.2023; NCLT approved the plan on 18.12.2023; CoC subsequently allocated Rs. 10 Lakhs to Appellant on 26.12.2023 (disbursed in July 2024); NCLAT appeal decided on 14.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Official List of Financial Creditors; CoC meeting minutes; approved Resolution Plan offering Rs. 180 Crores total (allocating Rs. 157 Crores to secured creditors with first charge, Rs. 12 Crores to secured creditors with residual charge, Rs. 73 Lakhs to employees/workmen, and Rs. 27 Lakhs to other operational creditors). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench vide order dated 18.12.2023 approved the Resolution Plan submitted by Respondent No. 4 while leaving it to the CoC's commercial wisdom to allocate a reasonable amount to the Appellant; CoC allocated Rs. 10 Lakhs; Appellant challenged the approval order via Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 04 & 05 of 2024.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan can allocate 'NIL' or nominal payment to an unsecured financial creditor who is classified as a related party, without violating Section 30(2) or Section 53 of the IBC; and whether the commercial wisdom of the CoC regarding distribution among various classes and sub-classes of creditors is open to judicial interference.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The distribution of plan value and determination of payments to different classes or sub-classes of creditors falls squarely within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors (CoC), provided the plan complies with the mandatory requirements of Section 30(2) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) mandates that dissenting financial creditors and operational creditors receive no less than their liquidation value under Section 53; where the total liquidation value is insufficient to fully satisfy secured creditors, the liquidation value and mandatory entitlement of an unsecured financial creditor is 'NIL'. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Differentiation in payment between secured and unsecured financial creditors or related versus unrelated parties based on security interest and commercial viability does not constitute unlawful discrimination under the Code. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The allocation of 'NIL' initial value (subsequently supplemented by Rs. 10 Lakhs in the CoC's commercial wisdom) to the Appellant as an unsecured financial creditor did not violate Section 30(2) or Section 53 of the Code, and the CoC's commercial wisdom in approving the plan cannot be interfered with.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) Nos. 04 & 05 of 2024 are dismissed; the impugned order dated 18.12.2023 approving the Resolution Plan is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Hari Vitthal Mission, an unsecured financial creditor and related party of Suasth Healthcare Foundation, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order approving the Resolution Plan submitted by Nishkala Healthcare and Ujin Pharma Chem. The Appellant argued that allocating 'NIL' value to it while paying operational creditors violated Section 30(2) and Section 53 of the IBC. NCLAT held that since liquidation value was insufficient to cover secured creditors, the Appellant's liquidation entitlement was 'NIL', making the plan compliant with Section 30(2). Furthermore, distribution is a matter of CoC commercial wisdom. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Shankar Mukherjee & Anr. vs. Ravi Sethia & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shankar Mukherjee and Badri Kumar Tulsyan (Appellants, Suspended Board of Directors/Promoters of the Corporate Debtor); Ravi Sethia (Respondent No. 1, Resolution Professional); J.C. Flowers Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. and Axis Bank Ltd. (Respondents No. 2 and 3, Committee of Creditors); Consortium of Nishkala Healthcare Pvt. Ltd. & Ujin Pharma Chem (Respondent No. 4, Successful Resolution Applicant); Suasth Healthcare Foundation (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against Suasth Healthcare Foundation on 31.08.2021 under Section 10 on application of the Corporate Debtor itself; Resolution Plan submitted by Respondent No. 4 approved by CoC with 100% voting share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default or insolvency admission appeal, but an appeal by suspended directors challenging the NCLT order approving the Resolution Plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 31.08.2021; Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 06.10.2022; NCLT remitted plan back on 28.08.2023; CoC reaffirmed plan on 07.09.2023; NCLT approved plan on 18.12.2023; NCLAT appeal decided on 14.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan allocating Rs. 180 Crores total, providing Rs. 73 Lakhs to employees/workmen against admitted claims of Rs. 1.53 Crores and 'NIL' to unsecured financial creditors; liquidation value of Corporate Debtor assessed at Rs. 294 Crores against secured debt exceeding Rs. 628 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench approved the Resolution Plan on 18.12.2023 in I.A. (IB) No. 1733/KB/2023; suspended directors filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 01 of 2024 challenging the approval order.
legal_issues: Whether suspended directors (ex-promoters) have the locus standi to challenge the approval of a resolution plan by the CoC and Adjudicating Authority; and whether a resolution plan allocating partial payments to employees and 'NIL' to unsecured financial creditors violates Section 30(2) or Section 53 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Suspended members of the Board of Directors/ex-promoters lack the locus standi to challenge the commercial wisdom of the CoC and the approval of a resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority under Section 31 of the IBC unless their own direct legal rights or shares are prejudiced. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Allocation of funds to operational creditors (employees/workmen) complying with the minimum statutory liquidation value requirement and the non-discriminatory treatment of unsecured financial creditors based on CoC commercial wisdom does not violate Section 30(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where liquidation value is insufficient to cover secured debt, operational creditors and unsecured creditors receive allocations determined strictly by the commercial wisdom of the CoC, and ex-promoters cannot espouse grievances on behalf of uncomplaining employees. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants lacked locus standi as suspended directors to challenge the plan approval, and the distribution mechanism within the approved Resolution Plan was fully compliant with the provisions of the IBC.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 01 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 18.12.2023 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Shankar Mukherjee and Badri Kumar Tulsyan, suspended directors of Suasth Healthcare Foundation, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order approving the Resolution Plan for the Corporate Debtor. They argued that the plan under-allocated funds to employees, improperly granted discretion to the SRA, and assigned 'NIL' value to unsecured financial creditors. NCLAT held that suspended board members lack the locus standi to challenge a CoC-approved resolution plan. Furthermore, the distribution mechanism aligned with the liquidation value and the CoC's commercial wisdom. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Kavindra Kumar & Ors. vs. Desein Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kavindra Kumar and 11 other individual employees/workmen (Appellants/Operational Creditors); Desein Private Limited (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants appointed as employees/workmen between 1979 and 2018; Company failed to disburse monthly salaries, allowances, and dues post June 2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in salary payments resulting in a joint operational debt claimed at Rs. 2,89,73,950/- across all 12 applicants, with individual dues for each applicant falling below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default occurred post June 2018; joint demand notice under Section 8 issued on 11.03.2022; reply sent by company on 23.03.2022; Section 9 application filed in 2022; NCLT dismissed Section 9 application on 14.07.2023; NCLAT appeal decided on 01.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint demand notice dated 11.03.2022 detailing individual unpaid salary claims (e.g., Kavindra Kumar claimed Rs. 35,26,000/-); company reply raising pre-existing disputes and non-maintainability of joint notices/applications. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational creditors filed joint Section 9 application before NCLT New Delhi (Court-IV) in C.P. (IB) No. 423(ND)/2022; NCLT rejected the application on 14.07.2023 holding that each joint applicant individually failed to meet the Rs. 1 Crore threshold under Section 4 of the IBC; Appellants challenged the dismissal in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1272 of 2023.
legal_issues: Whether multiple individual operational creditors (employees/workmen) can club their individual operational debts in a joint Section 9 application to cross the minimum default threshold of Rs. 1 Crore prescribed under Section 4 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Multiple individual operational creditors cannot club their separate individual debts into a single joint application under Section 9 of the IBC for the purpose of meeting the Rs. 1 Crore minimum default threshold mandated under Section 4. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While Section 7 explicitly permits joint filings by financial creditors, Sections 8 and 9 of the IBC contemplate independent default demands and applications by individual operational creditors; the note in Form 5 permitting joint filing by a representative (such as a trade union) relates to a single collective entity and does not permit aggregation of distinct individual claims. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where each individual employee's claim is below the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold (e.g., Rs. 35.26 Lakhs), the joint application is not maintainable under Section 9. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly applied the binding precedent in Sadashiv Nomaya Nayak v. Gammon Engineers & Contractors Pvt. Ltd. in holding that individual operational creditors cannot aggregate their claims to satisfy the threshold requirement.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1272 of 2023 is dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 14.07.2023 rejecting the Section 9 application; no order as to costs.
summary: Kavindra Kumar and 11 other employees appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order rejecting their joint Section 9 application against Desein Private Limited for unpaid salaries totaling Rs. 2.89 Crores, because each individual's claim was below the Rs. 1 Crore threshold. The Appellants argued that the note in Form 5 permitted joint applications and aggregation of claims for workmen/employees. NCLAT held, relying on Sadashiv Nomaya Nayak, that individual operational creditors cannot aggregate their separate claims to meet the Rs. 1 Crore statutory threshold under Section 4. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP vs. Union of India & Ors. (along with connected appeals)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP, Manu Kochhar, Udayan Sen, Rajesh Kotian, Kalpesh Mehta, Milind Patel (Appellants, erstwhile Auditors, Directors, and Key Managerial Personnel of IL&FS/IFIN); Union of India, Ministry of Corporate Affairs (Respondent No. 1). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Investigation of IL&FS and its subsidiaries (including IFIN) directed to the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) on 30.09.2018; Union of India filed Company Petition No. 3638 of 2018 under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default or insolvency matter; corporate governance and fraud investigation proceedings under Sections 241-242 and 339 of the Companies Act. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. 3638 of 2018 filed on 01.10.2018; SFIO submitted interim reports; MA No. 2696 of 2019 for amendment allowed on 25.11.2019; NCLT heard matters on 20.02.2024 and granted time to serve amended petition; amended petition incorporating new prayer (e) served on 21.02.2024; NCLT passed impugned order rejecting appellants' objections on 22.07.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 15.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original petition prayer 22(c) and amendment application MA No. 2696/2019 prayers (C) and (D) seeking general leave to 'supplement/enlarge/amend/modify' scope of reliefs via separate applications/documents; newly introduced prayer clause (e) in February 2024 seeking specific declarations and recovery under Section 339 of the Companies Act against specified respondents. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CA No. 60 of 2024 and other applications before NCLT Mumbai Bench-I challenging the insertion of prayer clause (e) without a formal amendment application or leave of the Tribunal; NCLT dismissed the applications on 22.07.2024, holding prayer (e) fell within the purview of prayer (C)/(D) allowed on 25.11.2019.
legal_issues: Whether a petitioner in a company petition under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act can suo moto incorporate substantial new substantive prayers (such as under Section 339) into the petition without filing a specific amendment application and obtaining explicit leave of the Adjudicating Authority, merely on the strength of a general enabling clause granted years prior.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A pleading once filed forms part of the court record and cannot be altered, modified, substituted, or expanded to include new substantive reliefs without a formal amendment application setting out specific proposed changes and obtaining the explicit leave of the tribunal. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: General enabling prayers or past omnibus orders permitting a party to 'supplement or modify the scope of reliefs by filing documents or applications' cannot be construed as a blanket authorization to unilaterally insert new substantive prayers without due process or a proper application. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Introducing a substantive prayer invoking Section 339 to hold specific respondents liable for fraudulent conduct without a targeted amendment application violates Rule 155 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and principles of natural justice. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in holding that prayer clause (e) was covered automatically by past enabling orders; pleadings cannot be amended without a formal application and judicial leave, rendering the incorporation of clause (e) unsustainable.
operative_order: All connected appeals allowed; impugned orders dated 22.07.2024 and 29.07.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I set aside; CA No. 60 of 2024 and corresponding applications allowed; Union of India directed to strike off and delete prayer clause (e) from CP No. 3638 of 2018, with liberty to file a fresh and proper amendment application in accordance with law; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: Appellants, including Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP and former directors/auditors of IL&FS/IFIN, appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order rejecting their applications to strike out a newly added prayer clause (e) in Company Petition No. 3638 of 2018. The Union of India had unilaterally inserted prayer (e) invoking Section 339 of the Companies Act, claiming it was authorized by an earlier 2019 omnibus order allowing it to modify the scope of relief. NCLAT held that pleadings cannot be unilaterally altered or appended with substantive reliefs without filing a formal amendment application and obtaining explicit judicial leave under Rule 155 of the NCLT Rules. The NCLAT set aside the impugned order, ordered the deletion of prayer clause (e), and granted liberty to the Union of India to move a proper amendment application.

case_title: Ashok Kriplani vs. Konduru Prasanth Raju & Anr.
appeal_number: Contempt Case (AT) No. 8 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 34 of 2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ashok Kriplani (Petitioner/Applicant, erstwhile IRP); Konduru Prasanth Raju (Respondent No. 1, Resolution Professional); Authorized Representative of Dreamz Infra India Ltd. (Respondent No. 2); Dreamz Infra India Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP commenced against Dreamz Infra India Ltd. on 20.08.2019; applicant Kriplani appointed as IRP; replaced by Respondent No. 1 as RP in 2nd CoC meeting on 19.11.2019; NCLT Bengaluru on 17.12.2019 offered post of IRP to Applicant at Rs. 6.75 Lakhs/month; NCLAT vide order dated 13.01.2021 set aside the appointment order while protecting past actions and fees earned in terms of the impugned order. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default case, but a contempt petition alleging wilful disobedience of NCLAT's protection order regarding CIRP fees and costs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 20.08.2019; NCLAT order passed on 13.01.2021; CoC in 11th meeting rejected former and current RP's CIRP expenses; CoC in 14th/15th meetings voted with 98% share to withdraw CIRP under Section 12A; RP filed IA No. 546/2024 for withdrawal on 10.07.2024; Contempt case filed in 2025 and decided on 02.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLAT order dated 13.01.2021 protecting CIRP fees/costs paid or payable; CoC meeting minutes recording 100% rejection of CIRP expenses for both former and current RPs; Form FA dated 28.06.2024 submitted by CoC for withdrawal under Section 12A with request to waive bank guarantee due to lack of funds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Erstwhile IRP Ashok Kriplani filed Contempt Case (AT) No. 8 of 2025 alleging that filing an IA for withdrawal of CIRP under Section 12A without providing for his unpaid fees (assessed at Rs. 1.48 Crores + interest) violated NCLAT's protective order dated 13.01.2021.
legal_issues: Whether filing an application for withdrawal of CIRP under Section 12A of the IBC pursuant to a 98% majority vote of the Committee of Creditors (CoC), where the CoC has rejected CIRP expenses due to lack of funds, constitutes wilful disobedience or civil contempt of an appellate order protecting a former resolution professional's fees and costs.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Civil contempt requires proof beyond reasonable doubt of wilful and deliberate disobedience of a court order; the extraordinary power of contempt cannot be invoked to compel execution of a decree or coerce payment when an alternative statutory remedy exists or when compliance is rendered impossible due to compelling circumstances. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A read with Regulation 30A of the CIRP Regulations empowers the CoC with a 90% majority to seek withdrawal of CIRP, and the Resolution Professional is under a statutory obligation to file such an application on behalf of the applicant/CoC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where individual homebuyers comprising the CoC are of modest financial background and have rejected past CIRP costs due to lack of corpus or liquid assets, filing a mandatory Section 12A withdrawal application does not constitute contumacious conduct or wilful breach of a fee-protection order. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The RP acted in accordance with his statutory duties upon receiving a 98% CoC mandate to withdraw the CIRP, and the failure of the CoC to fund costs does not amount to civil contempt by the respondents.
operative_order: Contempt Case (AT) No. 8 of 2025 is dismissed; no order as to costs.
summary: Ashok Kriplani, erstwhile IRP of Dreamz Infra India Ltd., filed a contempt petition against RP Konduru Prasanth Raju and the Authorized Representative, alleging that filing an application to withdraw the CIRP under Section 12A without securing his unpaid fees violated NCLAT's protection order dated 13.01.2021. NCLAT held that filing a Section 12A withdrawal application backed by a 98% CoC vote is a statutory duty of the RP, and since the home-buyers on the CoC lacked funds and unanimously rejected past expenses, there was no wilful disobedience or contumacious conduct. The contempt petition was dismissed.

case_title: Vashisth Builders and Engineers Limited and Vashisth Estates Limited (in Consortium) vs. Trishul Dream Homes Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 732 of 2025 (along with Nos. 680 and 681 of 2025)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vashisth Builders and Engineers Limited and Vashisth Estates Limited (Consortium, Successful Resolution Applicant); Jalesh Kumar Grover (Resolution Professional); Committee of Creditors of Trishul Dream Homes Limited through Authorised Representative Rahul Verma; Trishul Dream Homes Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Trishul Dream Homes Ltd. commenced on 16.06.2023; public announcement made on 18.06.2023; Expression of Interest published on 12.09.2023; Resolution Plan submitted by the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) approved by the CoC with a 91.55% voting share on 28.02.2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default or insolvency admission appeal, but an appeal challenging the rejection of a plan approval application by the Adjudicating Authority. 4.
