STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 16.06.2023; SRA plan approved by CoC on 28.02.2024; plan approval application I.A. (Plan) 05/CHD/2024 filed on 11.03.2024; Adjudicating Authority dismissed plan approval on 23.04.2025; NCLAT appeals decided on 20.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Plan dated 19.02.2024 along with addendum dated 26.02.2024; compliance affidavit filed by the Resolution Professional on 04.11.2024; valuation reports by IBBI-registered valuers showing fair value and liquidation value. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench-II vide order dated 23.04.2025 dismissed I.A. (Plan) 05/CHD/2024 seeking approval of the SRA's Resolution Plan, raising issues regarding valuation discrepancies, balance sheet claim reconciliations, Regulation 6A compliance, PUFE transaction proceeds allocation, and CIRP cost adjustments; CoC, RP, and SRA jointly filed appeals against the rejection.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can reject a Resolution Plan approved by the CoC with a 91.55% majority based on valuation discrepancies, unfiled claims mentioned in balance sheets, alleged non-compliance with Regulation 6A, and commercial terms regarding CIRP cost increases and PUFE recoveries, in the absence of any violation of Section 30(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) in approving a resolution plan is paramount and non-justiciable; the Adjudicating Authority can only review a resolution plan for compliance with Section 30(2) of the IBC and cannot enter into qualitative analysis of asset valuation, claim reconciliations, or commercial terms. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 38(2)(d) of the CIRP Regulations expressly permits a resolution plan to provide for the manner in which avoidance/PUFE proceedings are pursued and how proceeds therefrom are distributed, making clauses allocating such proceeds to the SRA legally permissible. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where no objections to the asset valuation reports prepared by IBBI-registered valuers are raised by any stakeholder during CIRP, the Adjudicating Authority cannot independently re-evaluate balance sheet assets or question valuation figures to reject the plan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in substituting its own wisdom for that of the CoC and raising unsustainable objections regarding valuation and compliance, as the Resolution Plan met all requirements under Section 30(2) and was validly approved by a 91.55% majority.
operative_order: Company Appeals (Ins. Nos. 732, 680, and 681 of 2025) are allowed; impugned order dated 23.04.2025 is set aside; I.A. (Plan) 05/CHD/2024 is allowed, and the Resolution Plan submitted by the SRA is approved; Adjudicating Authority to pass consequential orders within 60 days.
summary: The CoC, Resolution Professional, and Successful Resolution Applicant (Vashisth Consortium) jointly appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order rejecting the approval of the Resolution Plan for Trishul Dream Homes Ltd. The NCLT had rejected the plan based on perceived valuation discrepancies, unfiled balance sheet claims, Regulation 6A notice issues, and provisions allocating PUFE recoveries to the SRA. NCLAT held that none of these reasons constituted a violation of Section 30(2) of the IBC and that the Adjudicating Authority impermissibly interfered with the commercial wisdom of the CoC. The appeals were allowed, and the Resolution Plan was approved.

case_title: M/s Rajputana Constructions Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s Rajasthan Land Holdings Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 853 of 2023 (along with No. 785 of 2023)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajputana Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant/Operational Creditor); Anuradha Gupta (Appellant/Erstwhile Resolution Professional); Rajasthan Land Holdings Limited - RLHL (Corporate Debtor); IL&FS Transportation Networks Limited - ITNL (Financial Creditor/Intervenor); Hi-Line Buildcon India Pvt. Ltd. & S. Bhandari & Co. (Operational Creditors/CoC members). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate debtor RLHL admitted into CIRP on 24.09.2019 under Section 9 on application of Rajputana Constructions Pvt. Ltd. for an operational debt of Rs. 23,97,086/-; ITNL filed a claim of Rs. 181 Crores treated as a related-party financial debt and excluded from CoC, leading to extensive litigation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on operational debt of Rs. 23,97,086/- owed to Rajputana Constructions Pvt. Ltd. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 24.09.2019; CoC constituted on 24.10.2019; RP fee fixed at Rs. 1 Lakh/month (enhanced to Rs. 2 Lakhs/month on 20.03.2020); CIRP stayed by NCLT from 05.08.2020 to 16.03.2021; NCLT capped RP fee to Rs. 1 Lakh/month on 11.11.2021; NCLT terminated CIRP on 20.04.2023; NCLAT appeal decided on 16.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate debtor bank account balance of Rs. 3.68 Crores at admission increasing to approximately Rs. 7 Crores during CIRP; total admitted CoC claims of Rs. 26,76,962/- against available cash far exceeding operational dues; seventh CoC meeting minutes dated 01.02.2023 showing CoC refusal to accept settlement/repayment offered by ITNL. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Jaipur Bench vide order dated 20.04.2023 terminated the CIRP in IA No. 100/JPR/2020 and CP No. (IB)-44/9/JPR/2019, holding that continued CIRP was an abuse of process since corporate debtor had ample funds to pay off the meagre CoC claims, and reduced the RP's remuneration to Rs. 50,000/- per month; Operational Creditor and RP filed Company Appeal Nos. 853 and 785 of 2023.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority is justified in terminating the CIRP of a corporate debtor under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules and Section 60(5) of the IBC where the corporate debtor possesses sufficient liquidity to pay off 100% of the admitted CoC claims, but the CoC members stubbornly refuse to accept payment and prolong proceedings for oblique motives; and whether an RP's fees can be reduced for charging fees during a judicial stay period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent powers under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules and Section 60(5) of the IBC to terminate CIRP proceedings and prevent abuse of process when members of a CoC refuse to accept full settlement of their admitted claims and drag out insolvency proceedings for extraneous, oblique motives despite the corporate debtor having ample liquidity. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A Resolution Professional cannot charge or claim professional fees for the duration during which the CIRP is stayed by a judicial order, as no active insolvency resolution duties can be performed during a stay. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where available cash balances in the corporate debtor's account (approx. Rs. 7 Crores) vastly exceed the total admitted CoC claims (Rs. 26.76 Lakhs) and the CoC arbitrarily rejects 100% repayment to continue billing excessive CIRP costs, the insolvency process stands vitiated by bad faith and abuse of process. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly terminated the malicious CIRP and reduced the RP's remuneration to Rs. 50,000 per month, disallowing fees charged during the stay period.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 853 and 785 of 2023 are dismissed; the impugned order dated 20.04.2023 terminating the CIRP and adjusting RP remuneration is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Rajputana Constructions (Operational Creditor) and Anuradha Gupta (erstwhile RP) appealed against the NCLT Jaipur order terminating the CIRP of Rajasthan Land Holdings Ltd. and reducing the RP's fees. NCLT had terminated the process upon discovering that while the corporate debtor had over Rs. 7 Crores in cash—more than enough to pay off the CoC's admitted claims of Rs. 26.76 Lakhs—the CoC members stubbornly refused to accept repayment in order to keep the CIRP alive. NCLAT held that continuing CIRP under such circumstances constituted an abuse of process, affirmed the termination, and upheld the reduction of the RP's remuneration for charging fees during a judicial stay period. Both appeals were dismissed.

case_title: Max Publicity & Communication Pvt. Ltd. vs. Enviro Home Solutions Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Max Publicity & Communication Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant, arrayed as Respondent in company petition); Enviro Home Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent, Operational Creditor); Veda / Suumaya (third-party entities involved in CSR transactions). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 9 operational debt application filed by Enviro Home Solutions Pvt. Ltd. against Max Publicity & Communication Pvt. Ltd., alleging debt and default arising from transactions and CSR obligations involving Veda. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Section 9 application filed for operational debt; sales transactions of Rs. 387,67,30,440/- and Rs. 14,45,53,775/- reversed by the Corporate Debtor on 31.03.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP No. (IB) 303/MB/C-III/2022 filed by Operational Creditor; NCLT Mumbai dismissed Section 9 application on 21.01.2025 while issuing observations and forwarding copies to investigative authorities; NCLAT appeal decided on 15.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Letter of Intent dated 11.08.2021; Purchase Order dated 13.08.2021 confirming receipt of goods and invoices; sales reversal entries dated 31.03.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-III vide order dated 21.01.2025 dismissed the Section 9 application (para 67), but in paragraphs 63-66 made observations regarding a potential CSR scam and directed the Registry to forward copies of the order to the MCA, RoC Mumbai, Income Tax, and GST authorities; Appellant challenged paragraphs 53 to 66 in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 456 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority, while dismissing an application under Section 9 of the IBC, has the jurisdiction to make sweeping observations regarding fraud and forward copies of the order to statutory authorities (such as SFIO, EOW, Income Tax, RoC) for investigation without following the statutory procedure prescribed under Section 213 of the Companies Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While dismissing an application under Section 9 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority lacks jurisdiction to issue direct mandates or orders for criminal or investigative bodies (such as SFIO or EOW) to investigate a corporate debtor without adhering to the procedural safeguards and opportunity of hearing mandated under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Forwarding copies of an order to regulatory authorities for taking appropriate steps under applicable statutes is permissible, but such transmission cannot be construed as a binding direction or order for investigation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Observations regarding potential malpractices or fraud made in a summary proceeding where the main petition is dismissed cannot serve as a substitute for a formal, procedurally sound inquiry. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned directions did not amount to a formal order of investigation under Section 213; however, references to EOW and SFIO in paragraph 65 were unwarranted and are accordingly deleted, while the transmission of copies under paragraph 66 is upheld as a mere forwarding of records.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 456 of 2025 is disposed of; observations and directions in paragraphs 65 and 66 are clarified not to constitute a binding direction for investigation; references to EOW and SFIO in paragraph 65 are deleted; forwarding of copies under paragraph 66 is upheld without fettering the discretion of statutory authorities.
summary: Max Publicity & Communication Pvt. Ltd. appealed against portions of an NCLT Mumbai order dated 21.01.2025 which dismissed an operational debt application under Section 9 but made strong observations regarding a Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) fraud and forwarded the order to various authorities including SFIO, EOW, Income Tax, and RoC. NCLAT clarified that the NCLT's order did not constitute a formal direction for investigation under Section 213 of the Companies Act. However, NCLAT deleted references to EOW and SFIO from paragraph 65, while upholding the mere forwarding of order copies to regulatory bodies. The appeal was disposed of accordingly.

case_title: Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. ASC Insolvency Services LLP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Appellant, Dissenting Financial Creditor with 18.69% vote share); OCL Iron and Steel Limited (Respondent No. 2, Successful Resolution Applicant); National Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. - NARCL (Respondent No. 3, Financial Creditor with 73.36% vote share); International Finance Corporation - IFC (Respondent No. 4, Financial Creditor with 7.95% vote share); Gateway Investment Management Services Limited (Respondent No. 5, Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant); Helios Photo Voltaic Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor Helios Photo Voltaic Ltd. admitted into CIRP on 11.01.2024; CoC issued RFRP for resolution plans; Challenge Process conducted on 29.07.2024 where Gateway offered NPV of Rs. 101.05 Crores and OCL offered NPV of Rs. 99.05 Crores; CoC approved OCL's Resolution Plan on 12.09.2024 with 73.38% vote share; Gateway subsequently made a revised email offer of Rs. 120 Crores on 07.10.2024, which CoC rejected. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default or insolvency admission dispute, but an appeal challenging the NCLT order approving a Resolution Plan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 11.01.2024; Challenge Process held on 29.07.2024; CoC approved OCL's plan on 12.09.2024; NCLT approved OCL's plan on 22.01.2025 in IA No. 52 of 2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 15.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor balance sheets as on 31.03.2023 and 31.03.2024 showing asset value of Rs. 70.76 Crores and turnover of Rs. 13.72 Crores; MCA Notification dated 07.03.2024 exempting combinations where assets are under Rs. 450 Crores or turnover under Rs. 1,250 Crores; Resolution Plan dividing debt into sustainable and unsustainable portions, assigning unsustainable debt to the SRA. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench New Delhi vide order dated 22.01.2025 approved OCL's Resolution Plan in IA No. 52 of 2024 and rejected Gateway's application in IA No. 5176 of 2024; Alchemist ARC (dissenting financial creditor) appealed the plan approval in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 179 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan providing for a composite scheme of merger/demerger requires prior CCI approval under Section 5 of the Competition Act despite MCA de minimis exemption notifications; whether an Asset Reconstruction Company (ARC) can assign its debt to a non-ARC successful resolution applicant under the SARFAESI Act and RBI Master Directions; and whether assignment of an external commercial borrowing (ECB) debt from IFC requires RBI approval prior to plan approval.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5 of the Competition Act read with the MCA exemption Notification dated 07.03.2024, mergers or amalgamations where the acquired enterprise's assets are under Rs. 450 Crores or turnover is under Rs. 1,250 Crores are exempt from prior CCI combination approval. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 9(1)(e) of the SARFAESI Act and RBI Master Directions (ARCs) 2024 empower ARCs to effect 'settlement of dues', which encompasses classifying debt into sustainable and unsustainable portions and assigning unsustainable debt to a resolution applicant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where corporate balance sheets confirm the target enterprise's asset value is Rs. 70.76 Crores (well below the Rs. 450 Crore threshold), Section 5 of the Competition Act is inapplicable, and prior CCI approval is not required. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Resolution Plan complied with all applicable statutory frameworks, including SARFAESI, RBI guidelines, and Competition Act exemptions, and the CoC's commercial wisdom in approving the plan with 73.38% vote share was unassailable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 179 of 2025 is dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 22.01.2025 approving the Resolution Plan is upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: Alchemist Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd., a dissenting financial creditor (18.69% vote share), appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench order approving the Resolution Plan submitted by OCL Iron and Steel Limited for Helios Photo Voltaic Ltd. The Appellant argued that the plan violated Section 5 of the Competition Act for lacking prior CCI approval, contravened SARFAESI and RBI directions by assigning ARC debt to a non-ARC, and improperly dealt with foreign debt and third-party lease land. NCLAT held that the target's asset value (Rs. 70.76 Crores) fell below the MCA exemption threshold of Rs. 450 Crores, negating the need for prior CCI approval, and that debt assignment under SARFAESI settlement measures was legally permissible. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Gateway Investment Management Services Limited vs. Ravi Sethia & Ors. (and connected appeals)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gateway Investment Management Services Limited (Appellant/Unsuccessful Resolution Applicant); Ravi Sethia (Resolution Professional); OCL Iron and Steel Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant); Helios Photo Voltaic Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Helios Photo Voltaic Ltd.; Challenge Process conducted on 29.07.2024 where Gateway offered NPV of Rs. 101.05 Crores and OCL offered NPV of Rs. 99.05 Crores; final resolution plans submitted by 05.08.2024; CoC approved OCL's plan on 12.09.2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default case, but an appeal challenging the rejection of an unsolicited post-voting revised financial offer submitted by an unsuccessful resolution applicant. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Challenge Process held on 29.07.2024; final plans submitted by 05.08.2024; voting concluded on 07.09.2024; CoC approved OCL's plan on 12.09.2024; Gateway sent email modifying payment terms on 05.09.2024 and submitted a revised offer of Rs. 120 Crores on 07.10.2024; CoC rejected revised offer on 14.10.2024; NCLT rejected Gateway's IA No. 5176 of 2024 on 22.01.2025; NCLAT appeal decided on 15.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Challenge Process Document barring modification of financial bids post-bidding; evaluation matrix scoring where OCL scored 51 marks and Gateway scored 48 marks; CoC meeting minutes dated 14.10.2024 resolving to adhere to RFRP terms and reject post-approval revisions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Gateway Investment Management Services Limited filed IA No. 5176 of 2024 before NCLT Principal Bench seeking consideration of its revised Rs. 120 Crore offer submitted post-voting; NCLT dismissed the application and approved OCL's plan on 22.01.2025; Gateway appealed in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 148 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors (CoC) is bound to consider an unsolicited, enhanced financial offer submitted by an unsuccessful resolution applicant after the conclusion of the challenge process, voting, and formal approval of another resolution plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a challenge process is concluded, final plans are submitted, voting is completed, and a resolution plan is formally approved by the CoC in its commercial wisdom, an unsuccessful resolution applicant has no vested right to have an unsolicited, post-voting enhanced financial offer considered. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Upholding the sanctity of the Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP) and Challenge Process Document is essential to maintain certainty, finality, and discipline in time-bound CIRP proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Permitting belated, post-approval bidding wars would indefinitely protract the insolvency process, undermine competitive bidding rules, and violate the commercial wisdom of the CoC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC acted lawfully and in accordance with process guidelines by rejecting the unsolicited, post-approval revised offer, and the Adjudicating Authority correctly dismissed the unsuccessful applicant's application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 148 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 22.01.2025 rejecting IA No. 5176 of 2024; no order as to costs.
summary: Gateway Investment Management Services Limited, an unsuccessful resolution applicant, appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench order rejecting its application to consider a revised, enhanced offer of Rs. 120 Crores submitted after voting and CoC approval of OCL Iron and Steel Limited's plan. NCLAT held that allowing post-approval, unsolicited bids would destroy the finality and discipline of the CIRP bidding process, and the CoC acted within its commercial wisdom in rejecting the belated offer. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Vinod Singh vs. Chandra Prakash Jain & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 800 of 2025 (with No. 801 of 2025)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vinod Singh (Appellant, Managing Director / Director of Corporate Debtor); Chandra Prakash Jain (Respondent No. 1, Erstwhile Voluntary Liquidator); Transmissions International Holding GmbH (Respondent No. 2, Majority Shareholder); Arun Gupta (Respondent No. 6, Newly Appointed Voluntary Liquidator); Transmissions International India Private Limited - TIIPL (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Voluntary liquidation of TIIPL approved by board resolution on 22.02.2024 and EGM on 21.03.2024 appointing Umesh Ved as first liquidator; Rs. 134.99 crores repatriated to majority shareholder on 31.05.2024; shareholders replaced first liquidator with Chandra Prakash Jain on 18.09.2024; Chandra Prakash Jain filed IA No. 1834/2024 on 03.12.2024 seeking return of repatriated funds; board and EGM on 28.02.2025 and 17.03.2025 respectively resolved to replace Chandra Prakash Jain and appoint Arun Gupta (Respondent No. 6) as the new liquidator. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default or insolvency resolution process, but a voluntary liquidation dispute concerning the replacement of a voluntary liquidator under Section 59 of the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Voluntary liquidation initiated on 22.02.2024; Respondent No. 1 appointed on 18.09.2024; removal resolution passed on 28.02.2025 and EGM on 17.03.2025; Respondent No. 1 filed removal challenge application IA No. 450/2025 on 21.03.2025; NCLT passed status quo order on 28.03.2025; order reserved on 02.04.2025 and de-reserved on 29.04.2025; NCLAT appeal filed on 12.05.2025 and decided on 30.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Board resolution dated 28.02.2025 and EGM resolution dated 17.03.2025 replacing Respondent No. 1 for lack of transparency and misconduct; email notice to Respondent No. 1 on 19.03.2025 relieving him of duties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-II on 28.03.2025 directed status quo regarding the liquidator in IA No. 450/2025, and subsequently on 29.04.2025 de-reserved its final judgment due to purported procedural defects in foreign shareholder authorizations and vakalatnamas; Appellant filed Company Appeal Nos. 800 and 801 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the directors and shareholders of a corporate debtor undergoing voluntary liquidation under Section 59 of the IBC possess the unfettered statutory right to replace a voluntary liquidator without requiring prior approval or judicial intervention from the Adjudicating Authority; and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in issuing a status quo order and subsequently de-reserving a reserved judgment on procedural technicalities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 59 of the IBC read with Regulation 5 of the IBBI (Voluntary Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2017, the corporate debtor's directors and shareholders possess the autonomous statutory right to replace a voluntary liquidator 'wherever required' by passing a resolution, without needing the approval or permission of the Adjudicating Authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Voluntary liquidation under Chapter V of the IBC operates on a solvent, self-contained mechanism distinct from court-appointed liquidation under Chapter III, leaving no scope for the Adjudicating Authority to force a liquidator upon unwilling shareholders via a status quo order. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a corporate debtor follows the due procedure to replace a voluntary liquidator due to lack of transparency, the removal is complete upon passing the requisite resolutions, and a status quo order preventing the new liquidator from taking charge is legally unsustainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by issuing a status quo order continuing an unseated voluntary liquidator, and the new liquidator (Respondent No. 6) is entitled to take over the liquidation process.
operative_order: Company Appeal No. 800 of 2025 is allowed, and the status quo order dated 28.03.2025 is vacated; Respondent No. 6 is authorized to proceed with the voluntary liquidation, and Respondent No. 1 is directed to hand over all records under Regulation 41(4); Company Appeal No. 801 of 2025 is disposed of directing the Adjudicating Authority to hear the removal application on its merits on 09.06.2025; no costs.
summary: Vinod Singh, Managing Director of Transmissions International India Pvt. Ltd., appealed against two NCLT Ahmedabad orders (dated 28.03.2025 and 29.04.2025) which maintained status quo regarding voluntary liquidator Chandra Prakash Jain after the company had validly replaced him with Arun Gupta (Respondent No. 6) via board and EGM resolutions. NCLAT held that under Section 59 of the IBC and Regulation 5 of the Voluntary Liquidation Regulations, shareholders have the absolute right to replace a voluntary liquidator without judicial approval, making the NCLT's status quo order illegal. The appeal against the status quo order was allowed, and the new liquidator was permitted to take charge.

case_title: State Tax Officer vs. Premraj Ramratan Laddha & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Tax Officer, Gujarat (Appellant); Premraj Ramratan Laddha (Respondent No. 1, Resolution Professional); Suryadeep Alloys Steel Casting Pvt. Ltd. (Resolution Applicant/Respondent No. 3); Twenty First Century Castings Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Section 9 application filed by M/s Harsh Foundry Fluxes & Alloys against Twenty First Century Castings Pvt. Ltd. admitted on 16.01.2020; statutory tax dues accrued under the Gujarat Value Added Tax (GVAT) Act, 2003 and Central Sales Tax (CST) Act for Assessment Years 2009-11 and 2014-16 totaling Rs. 11,70,47,801/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid statutory tax dues of Rs. 11,70,47,801/- owed to the State Tax Department, with assessment appeals rejected by the GVAT Tribunal in 2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 16.01.2020; CoC approved resolution plan on 28.08.2020; RP filed plan approval application IA No. 591/2020; NCLT approved resolution plan on 09.12.2020; NCLAT appeal decided on 16.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Claim filed by State Tax Officer in Form B on 06.07.2020 admitted provisionally by RP; resolution plan allocated 'NIL' payment to the State Tax Department while admitting its claim of Rs. 11,70,47,801/-; total proposed resolution plan value was Rs. 4,00,05,000/- against total admitted claims of Rs. 37,95,64,751/-. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench approved the resolution plan on 09.12.2020; State Tax Officer filed Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 720 of 2021 challenging the plan approval for failing to provide any payment to the State despite its status as a secured creditor under Section 48 of the GVAT Act.
legal_issues: Whether statutory tax dues owed to a State Government create a first charge on the property of the dealer by operation of law under Section 48 of the GVAT Act, thereby making the State Tax Department a secured creditor entitled to priority distribution under Section 53 of the IBC in accordance with the Supreme Court's ruling in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Limited.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 48 of the Gujarat Value Added Tax Act, 2003, statutory tax dues constitute a first charge on the property of the dealer by operation of law, making the State a secured creditor within the meaning of Section 3(30) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 53 of the IBC is not contrary to Section 48 of the GVAT Act; debts owed to a secured creditor (including the State under GVAT) rank equally under Section 53(1)(b)(ii), and a resolution plan that completely ignores statutory charges and allocates 'NIL' to the State must be rejected under Section 30(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a resolution plan ignores statutory demands payable to a State Government and fails to provide proportional reduction or fair treatment, the Adjudicating Authority is bound to reject the resolution plan pursuant to the binding precedent of Rainbow Papers. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in approving a resolution plan that allocated zero payment to the State Tax Department while treating it as an operational creditor, ignoring its status as a secured creditor under Section 48 of the GVAT Act.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 720 of 2021 is allowed; the impugned order dated 09.12.2020 approving the resolution plan is set aside; the matter is remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority; parties to appear before the Tribunal on 30.05.2025.
summary: The State Tax Officer of Gujarat appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 09.12.2020 approving the resolution plan for Twenty First Century Castings Pvt. Ltd. The plan had admitted the State's tax claim of Rs. 11.70 Crores but allocated 'NIL' payment, treating it as an operational creditor. Relying on the Supreme Court's judgment in State Tax Officer v. Rainbow Papers Limited, NCLAT held that Section 48 of the GVAT Act creates a first charge on the property by operation of law, making the State a secured creditor entitled to equal priority under Section 53 of the IBC. The appeal was allowed, the plan approval was set aside, and the matter was remanded back.

case_title: Mr. Sunil Gutte vs. Mr. Avil Menezes & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sunil Gutte (Appellant, Promoter and Suspended Director); Avil Menezes (Respondent No. 1, Liquidator of M/s. Sunil Hitech Engineers Ltd.); DPRS Infra Developers Pvt. Ltd., Rayon Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., Navneesh Traders Pvt. Ltd., Shreehari Associates Pvt. Ltd. (Respondents No. 2 to 5, Vendors/Service Providers); Harshavardhan Kaushik (Respondent No. 6, Chief Financial Officer); Sunil Hitech Engineers Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP under Section 7 on 07.09.2018 (pronounced on 07.09.2018, delivered/uploaded on 10.09.2018 specifying moratorium from 10.09.2018); suspended management made unauthorized payments totaling Rs. 11.01 Crores from HDFC Bank account of the Corporate Debtor to vendors (Respondents No. 2 to 5) post-commencement across two phases (10.09.2018 to 14.09.2018 and 27.09.2018 to 10.10.2018). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default or insolvency admission appeal, but an appeal challenging an NCLT order setting aside post-commencement unauthorized payments made in breach of moratorium. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 07.09.2018 (moratorium effective from 10.09.2018); IRP sent take-over notice on 14.09.2018; RP appointed on 27.11.2018; RP issued notice regarding unauthorized payments on 29.03.2019; RP filed M.A. No. 1833 of 2019 in 2019; NCLT allowed M.A. No. 1833 of 2019 on 04.02.2025; NCLAT appeal decided on 30.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Nine RTGS transfers made between 10.09.2018 and 14.09.2018 totaling Rs. 7.03 Crores; three cheque encashments post-moratorium totaling Rs. 3.98 Crores (cheques dated 06.09.2018 and 08.09.2018 encashed after 10.09.2018); email clarification from IRP confirming no authorization was given for payments from HDFC account. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I vide order dated 04.02.2025 allowed M.A. No. 1833 of 2019 filed by the RP, setting aside the payments of Rs. 11.01 Crores, holding the promoter and officers jointly and severally liable to refund the amount to the corporate debtor, and recommending IBBI action under Section 74(1); suspended director appealed in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 515 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether payments made by the suspended management of a corporate debtor to vendors after the commencement of CIRP and declaration of moratorium—without the authorization of the IRP—violate Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC; and whether such unauthorized payments are liable to be refunded to the corporate debtor's asset pool.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a CIRP application is admitted and a moratorium is declared under Section 14 of the IBC, the suspended management is strictly prohibited from transferring, disposing of, or utilizing corporate debtor funds unilaterally, and any post-commencement payments made without IRP authorization violate the statutory moratorium. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1)(b) prohibits any transfer or disposal of corporate debtor assets during moratorium to preserve the asset pool for efficient resolution; notions of commercial necessity or ordinary course of business cannot override express statutory prohibitions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Post-commencement RTGS transfers executed during moratorium and pre-dated cheques encashed after the effective moratorium date without IRP consent are void and illegal, obligating the recipients and suspended directors to refund the sums jointly and severally. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly held that the payments totaling Rs. 11.01 Crores made post-commencement and post-moratorium without IRP authorization were illegal, and rightly ordered their refund to the corporate debtor.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 515 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 04.02.2025 in M.A. No. 1833 of 2019; liberty granted to Respondents No. 2 to 5 to file their claims before the RP/Liquidator in accordance with law; no costs.
summary: Sunil Gutte, promoter and suspended director of Sunil Hitech Engineers Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 04.02.2025 which set aside payments of Rs. 11.01 Crores made to four vendors between 10.09.2018 and 10.10.2018 (post-commencement of CIRP and moratorium) without IRP authorization, holding the promoter and officers jointly and severally liable to refund the money. NCLAT held that post-commencement payments made without IRP approval flagrantly violate Section 14(1)(b) of the IBC, regardless of whether the vendors had pre-existing contracts or routine invoices. The appeal was dismissed, with liberty to vendors to file claims before the liquidator.

case_title: Wakai Hospitality Private Limited vs. Harish Kant Kaushik (Liquidator) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Wakai Hospitality Private Limited (Appellant/Licensee); Palak Desai / Harish Kant Kaushik (Respondent No. 1, Liquidator of Rajmal Lakhichand Jewelers Private Limited); ASREC India Limited (Respondent No. 2, Asset Reconstruction Company / assignee of Jalgaon People's Co-op Bank Ltd.); Rajmal Lakhichand Jewelers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Leave and License Agreement (LLA) dated 14.07.2022 granted by Corporate Debtor to Appellant for commercial premises ('Mangal Sandesh Building', Khar, Mumbai) for 5 years at Rs. 7,50,000/- monthly fee with a 3-year lock-in; mortgage over the subject property created in favour of Jalgaon People's Co-op Bank Ltd. on 15.01.2015 (pre-dating the LLA by 7 years), debt subsequently assigned to ASREC India Limited on 26.03.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by Appellant in paying monthly license fees from the commencement of the LLA (13.09.2022 onwards), accumulating arrears of Rs. 1,14,84,348/- (inclusive of 18% interest up to 24.10.2023). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mortgage created on 15.01.2015; LLA executed on 14.07.2022; licence commencement on 12.07.2022 (fit-out period ended 13.09.2022); Section 7 petition admitted and CIRP initiated on 09.02.2023; Liquidator issued demand notice on 12.07.2023 and legal notice terminating LLA on 02.09.2023; Liquidator filed IA No. 5065/2023 on 26.10.2023; NCLT allowed IA on 29.02.2024; NCLAT interim stay granted on 15.03.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 28.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clause 5 of LLA restricting fit-out extensions strictly to pandemic lockdowns; unauthenticated communications from a suspended board member agreeing to rent adjustments; ASREC India Limited notice of non-relinquishment of security under Section 52 dated 11.07.2024 following liquidation order dated 11.06.2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV vide order dated 29.02.2024 allowed IA No. 5065(MB) of 2023 filed by the Liquidator, directing the Appellant to vacate the licensed premises and pay arrears of rent of Rs. 1.14 Crores; Appellant challenged the order in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 524 of 2024, obtaining a conditional stay on 15.03.2024 requiring 50% deposit and monthly use/occupation charges.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 18(f) and Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to entertain an application by a liquidator/resolution professional seeking eviction of a licensee and recovery of outstanding license fees under a Leave and License Agreement; and whether Section 14 or general principles bar a liquidator from terminating a license agreement for non-payment during CIRP/liquidation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority and NCLAT possess residuary and summary jurisdiction under the IBC to adjudicate upon the termination of commercial contracts and direct third-party licensees in possession of corporate debtor assets to hand over vacant possession to the resolution professional or liquidator under Section 18(f). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 of the IBC protects the corporate debtor from actions against it, but does not grant immunity or moratorium protection to third-party licensees who are in material breach of their contractual obligations (such as non-payment of rent/license fees). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a licensee fails to pay license fees from the inception of an agreement and unauthenticated side-correspondence with suspended directors contradicts express terms of the Leave and License Agreement (which limits fit-out extensions strictly to pandemic lockdowns), the licensee's retention of the property is unlawful. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted well within its jurisdiction in ordering the eviction of the defaulting licensee and recovery of arrears, especially given that the mortgagee ARC held a prior overriding charge created 7 years before the license agreement.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 524 of 2024 is dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 29.02.2024 in IA No. 5065(MB) of 2023; no order as to costs.
summary: Wakai Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 29.02.2024 directing it to vacate a licensed commercial property ('Mangal Sandesh Building', Khar, Mumbai) belonging to Corporate Debtor Rajmal Lakhichand Jewelers Pvt. Ltd. and pay Rs. 1.14 Crores in license fee arrears. The Appellant argued that the NCLT lacked jurisdiction over license disputes (which should go to the Small Causes Court) and that rent was adjustable against fit-out expenses. NCLAT held that the NCLT has summary jurisdiction under Section 18(f) to take custody of corporate debtor assets, that moratorium under Section 14 does not protect defaulting licensees, and that the mortgagee ARC (ASREC India Limited) held a prior charge pre-dating the license agreement by 7 years. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Amit Somani vs. National Financial Reporting Authority
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amit Somani (Appellant, Engagement Quality Control Reviewer / EQCR); National Financial Reporting Authority - NFRA (Respondent); M/s BSR & Associates LLP (Statutory Auditor); Aravind Maiya (Engagement Partner / EP); M/s Coffee Day Enterprises Ltd. - CDEL (Audited Company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory audit of Coffee Day Enterprises Ltd. (CDEL) for the financial year 2018-19 conducted by BSR & Associates LLP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default or insolvency matter, but a professional misconduct and regulatory penalty matter under Section 132(4) of the Companies Act, 2013. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Audit conducted for FY 2018-19; Show Cause Notice issued by NFRA on 17.01.2024; Appellant replied on 29.03.2024; personal hearing held on 31.05.2024; written submissions filed on 14.06.2024; NFRA passed penalty and debarment order on 19.08.2024; Appeal e-filed on 18.09.2024; defects notified by NCLAT registry on 20.09.2024 and subsequently on multiple dates; final refiling completed on 21.02.2025 with a refiling delay of 147 days. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Defect sheets issued by NCLAT registry on 16.10.2024, 21.11.2024, 02.12.2024, 10.12.2024, 19.12.2024, 06.01.2025, and 16.01.2025 listing 14 distinct procedural and technical defects (such as unsigned papers, missing pre-deposit of 10% penalty amounting to Rs. 2.5 Lakhs, defective bookmarking, pagination, and landscape formatting); out of 14 defects, only 1 defect was cured on 22.10.2024 while 13 defects remained uncured continuously until January 2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NFRA vide Order No. 020/2024 dated 19.08.2024 found Appellant guilty of professional misconduct under Clause 7, Part I of the Second Schedule of the Chartered Accountants Act, 1949, imposing a 5-year debarment and a monetary penalty of INR 25,00,000; Appellant filed Company Appeal (AT) No. 54 of 2025 along with IA No. 1337 of 2025 for condonation of a 147-day refiling delay.
legal_issues: Whether an appellant who fails to cure notified registry defects within the stipulated 7-day period under Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 and allows a prolonged, unexplained refiling delay of 147 days while leaving core defects uncured is entitled to condonation of delay under Rule 26 read with larger bench rulings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016, a party must cure notified registry defects within 7 days; while a refiling delay exceeding the limitation period can theoretically be condoned for sufficient cause under the V.R. Ashok Rao 5-member bench precedent, the applicant must provide convincing, day-to-day justification and demonstrate bona fide diligence rather than casual, callous, or prolonged negligence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 26 does not prescribe an absolute statutory bar or limitation period for refiling, but condonation requires rigorous proof of sufficient cause and genuine attempts to rectify defects. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an appellant e-files an appeal within time but permits 14 months or 147 days of refiling delay by repeatedly resubmitting papers without curing 13 out of 14 fundamental defects (including pre-deposit, signatures, and pagination) despite multiple registry notices, the explanation is deemed unsatisfactory. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant's total negligence and failure to offer any valid cause for the 147-day refiling delay disentitle him to discretionary relief under Rule 26, rendering the appeal legally unconstituted.
operative_order: IA No. 1337 of 2025 for condonation of refiling delay is dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) No. 54 of 2025 is dismissed as legally not constituted without examining the merits of the case; no costs.
summary: Amit Somani, Engagement Quality Control Reviewer (EQCR) for the audit of Coffee Day Enterprises Ltd., appealed against an NFRA order dated 19.08.2024 imposing a 5-year debarment and a Rs. 25 Lakh penalty for professional misconduct under the Chartered Accountants Act. Although the appeal was e-filed within time, the Appellant took 147 days to refile after rectifying registry defects, repeatedly resubmitting papers with 13 out of 14 fundamental defects left uncured. NCLAT held that the Appellant failed to provide sufficient cause or explanation for the gross negligence and delay under Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules. The delay condonation application was rejected, and the appeal was dismissed without entering into the merits.

case_title: Jalesh Kumar Grover (RP of Trishul Dream Homes Ltd.) vs. Vashisth Builders and Engineers Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 681 of 2025 (along with Nos. 732 and 680 of 2025)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Jalesh Kumar Grover (Appellant, Resolution Professional of Trishul Dream Homes Ltd.); Vashisth Builders and Engineers Limited and Vashisth Estates Limited (Consortium, Successful Resolution Applicant); Committee of Creditors of Trishul Dream Homes Limited through Authorised Representative Rahul Verma (CoC); Trishul Dream Homes Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Trishul Dream Homes Ltd. commenced on 16.06.2023; Expression of Interest published on 12.09.2023; Resolution Plan submitted by the Vashisth Consortium approved by the CoC with a 91.55% voting share on 28.02.2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default or insolvency admission case, but an appeal by the Resolution Professional challenging the rejection of a resolution plan approval application. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 16.06.2023; plan approved by CoC on 28.02.2024; plan approval application I.A. (Plan) 05/CHD/2024 filed on 11.03.2024; Adjudicating Authority dismissed plan approval on 23.04.2025; NCLAT appeals decided on 20.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Resolution Plan dated 19.02.2024 and addendum dated 26.02.2024; compliance affidavit filed by the Resolution Professional on 04.11.2024 detailing communication with 174 unrepresented homebuyers; valuation reports by IBBI-registered valuers. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench-II vide order dated 23.04.2025 dismissed I.A. (Plan) 05/CHD/2024 seeking approval of the Resolution Plan, citing valuation discrepancies, balance sheet reconciliation issues, Regulation 6A compliance lapses, PUFE proceeds allocation, and CIRP cost adjustment clauses; Resolution Professional filed Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 681 of 2025 (alongside parallel appeals by the CoC and SRA).
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority can reject a Resolution Plan approved by a 91.55% majority of the CoC based on technical objections regarding balance sheet reconciliations, individual homebuyer communications, valuation figures, and commercial mechanisms for managing CIRP cost increases.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is paramount and immune from judicial interference unless the plan explicitly violates Section 30(2) of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 6A proviso establishes that where direct communication with individual creditors is impracticable, public announcement under Regulation 6 is deemed sufficient communication. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the Resolution Professional files a detailed compliance affidavit demonstrating that individual letters were dispatched to unrepresented creditors and that balance sheet reconciliations and valuation reports were duly conducted by registered valuers, the Adjudicating Authority cannot reject the plan on surmises. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed material error by substituting its own subjective evaluation for the commercial wisdom of the CoC and ignoring compliance affidavits submitted by the Resolution Professional.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 681 of 2025 (together with Nos. 732 and 680 of 2025) is allowed; the impugned order dated 23.04.2025 is set aside; the Resolution Plan submitted by the SRA is approved; Adjudicating Authority to pass consequential approval orders within 60 days.
summary: Jalesh Kumar Grover, Resolution Professional of Trishul Dream Homes Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order rejecting the approval of the CoC-approved Resolution Plan. The NCLT had cited valuation variances, balance sheet reconciliation issues, Regulation 6A non-compliance, and plan terms regarding CIRP cost adjustments as grounds for rejection. NCLAT held that the RP had filed comprehensive compliance affidavits addressing all queries, that valuation reports by registered valuers cannot be second-guessed without stakeholder objection, and that CoC commercial wisdom cannot be overridden. The appeal was allowed, and the Resolution Plan was approved.

case_title: M/s SNJ Synthetics Limited vs. M/s PepsiCo India Holdings Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: M/s SNJ Synthetics Limited (Appellant/Operational Creditor, MSME); M/s PepsiCo India Holdings Private Limited (Respondent/Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Long-standing business relationship formalised through a Supply Agreement dated 09.10.2018 under which the Operational Creditor supplied PET preforms and thermoplastics; transactions maintained through reconciled open accounts. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed at Rs. 1,96,80,953/- as on 28.02.2021 (comprising Rs. 91,63,886/- principal and Rs. 1,05,17,067/- interest at 24% p.a.); principal revised to Rs. 77,37,886/- post-reconciliation during proceedings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 served on 13.03.2021; Section 9 petition filed thereafter; NCLT directed principal payment on 02.01.2023; Respondent paid reconciled principal of Rs. 77,37,886/- on 10.02.2023; NCLT dismissed Section 9 petition on 02.01.2025; NCLAT appeal decided on 07.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supply Agreement dated 09.10.2018 containing payment terms (Schedule D) with no provision for interest on delayed payments; invoices containing a unilateral stipulation of 24% p.a. interest; proof of principal payment of Rs. 77,37,886/- made on 10.02.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench-I vide order dated 02.01.2025 dismissed the Section 9 application in C.P. (IB) No. 157/CHD/HRY/2021, holding that CIRP could not be initiated or maintained solely for a contested interest component once the undisputed principal amount had been fully paid; Operational Creditor appealed in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 386 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether an operational creditor can maintain an application under Section 9 of the IBC solely for the recovery of a disputed interest component when the entire principal amount of the operational debt has been paid off during the pendency of proceedings; and whether unilateral interest clauses in invoices can create an enforceable operational debt in the absence of a contractual interest provision in the principal agreement.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the principal operational debt is fully paid off prior to the admission of a Section 9 application, a petition cannot be maintained or pursued solely for the realization of a contested interest component. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unilaterally generated invoices containing interest stipulations cannot override or rewrite the express terms of a bi-partite written supply agreement that does not provide for interest on delayed payments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a supply agreement lacks any interest clause and past dealings show no history of interest payments, claiming interest via unilateral invoices constitutes a disputed claim that cannot be resolved through the summary jurisdiction of the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly dismissed the Section 9 petition since the principal operational debt had been fully satisfied, and pursuing insolvency proceedings solely for disputed interest amounts constitutes an abuse of the IBC process.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 386 of 2025 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 02.01.2025 is affirmed; no costs.
summary: SNJ Synthetics Limited, an MSME operational creditor, appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order dismissing its Section 9 application against PepsiCo India Holdings Pvt. Ltd. PepsiCo had paid the reconciled principal amount of Rs. 77.37 Lakhs during proceedings, leaving only a disputed interest claim of Rs. 1.05 Crores at 24% p.a. NCLAT held that because the Supply Agreement contained no interest provision and the invoices were unilateral, no enforceable contractual debt for interest existed. Furthermore, pursuing an insolvency petition solely for a contested interest amount after full principal repayment violates the principles of the IBC. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Shankar Kashid vs. Intec Capital Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shankar Kashid (Appellant, suspended director of Shivani Flexipack Limited); Intec Capital Limited (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor/NBFC); Shivani Flexipack Limited (Respondent No. 2, Corporate Debtor); Polygraph Printing Technologies Limited (Respondent No. 4, Machine Manufacturer/Vendor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility of Rs. 1,66,40,134 sanctioned by Intec Capital Limited to Shivani Flexipack Limited vide Loan Agreement dated 18.01.2012 to finance lamination/printing machinery purchases from Polygraph Printing Technologies Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of monthly installments under the loan agreement; Arbitral Award passed on 21.02.2018 directing payment of Rs. 1,42,95,144 along with 12% interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan agreement executed on 18.01.2012; loan recall notice issued on 28.11.2012; Arbitral Award passed on 21.02.2018; Section 34 challenge dismissed by Delhi High Court on 01.04.2019; SLP dismissed by Supreme Court on 17.09.2018; Section 7 application CP (IB)-641(MB)/C-III/2022 filed thereafter; NCLT admitted Section 7 on 28.11.2023; NCLAT appeal decided on 02.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreement dated 18.01.2012; disbursement instructions dated 18.01.2012; Arbitral Award dated 21.02.2018; Delhi High Court order dated 01.04.2019 upholding the award. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench (Court-III) vide order dated 28.11.2023 admitted the Section 7 application filed by Intec Capital Limited and initiated CIRP against Shivani Flexipack Limited; suspended director Shankar Kashid appealed in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 62 of 2024.
legal_issues: Whether a crystallized financial debt arising from a binding arbitral award that has attained finality constitutes a valid financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, justifying the admission of a Section 7 application despite underlying commercial or contractual disputes between the corporate debtor and a third-party machinery supplier.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unpaid arbitral award that has attained finality crystallizes a liability that qualifies as a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC, and default in its payment entitles the award holder to initiate CIRP under Section 7. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority is strictly required to ascertain only the existence of a financial debt and occurrence of a default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Third-party contractual disputes between the corporate debtor and a machinery supplier regarding delivery or specifications cannot constitute a valid defense to scuttle insolvency proceedings when debt and default to the financial creditor are proven. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted the Section 7 application based on the final arbitral award and established default, and the appeal lacks merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 62 of 2024 is dismissed, and the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 28.11.2023 admitting Section 7 is affirmed; no costs.
summary: Shankar Kashid, suspended director of Shivani Flexipack Limited, appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order admitting a Section 7 application filed by Intec Capital Limited. The financial creditor had initiated insolvency based on a final arbitral award dated 21.02.2018 for Rs. 1.42 Crores following default on a machinery loan agreement. The Appellant argued that the financial creditor prematurely disbursed funds to the machinery supplier (Polygraph Printing Technologies) and that machinery was never delivered due to a gutka ban. NCLAT held that third-party supplier disputes cannot obscure an undisputed, finalized financial debt and default, and that the arbitral award validly constituted a financial debt under Section 5(8). The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Mr. Abhinav Bhatnagar vs. Bank of Baroda & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Abhinav Bhatnagar (Appellant, Shareholder and Erstwhile Management of Extol Industries Ltd.); Bank of Baroda (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor); Ms. Teena Saraswat Pandey (Respondent No. 2, Resolution Professional); Extol Industries Limited (Respondent No. 3, Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Term loan of Rs. 12.72 Crores and Cash Credit Limit of Rs. 15 Crores sanctioned to Extol Industries Ltd. by Bank of Baroda in 2011, subsequently restructured and renewed on 26.06.2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Account classified as Non-Performing Asset (NPA) on 31.03.2016; default persisting continuously. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan sanctioned in 2011; restructured on 26.06.2013; No Due Certificate allegedly issued on 16.01.2016; NPA declared on 31.03.2016; recall notice issued on 28.04.2016; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 18/MP/2024 filed in 2024; NCLT admitted Section 7 on 24.03.2025; NCLAT appeal decided on 30.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Cryptic No Due Certificate dated 16.01.2016; Bank recall notice dated 28.04.2016 detailing overdues; certified statement of accounts under Bankers Books Evidence Act; continuous recording of long-term borrowings in corporate balance sheets from FY 2015-16 to FY 2022-23 (specifically acknowledging Bank of Baroda debt in FY 2022-23 balance sheet). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Special Bench at Indore vide order dated 24.03.2025 admitted CP (IB) No. 18/MP/2024 under Section 7 and dismissed Appellant's IA No. 98/MP/2025 seeking re-hearing; Appellant appealed in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 615 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition is maintainable and within limitation when based on an NPA classification date of 31.03.2016, where the corporate debtor's balance sheets continuously acknowledge long-term borrowings and defaults qua the financial creditor; and whether an informal, cryptic 'No Due Certificate' dated 16.01.2016 can override audited financial statements and bank records demonstrating default.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Continuous recording of debt and default in the corporate debtor's audited balance sheets constitutes a valid acknowledgement of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, effectively extending the limitation period for initiating Section 7 proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A cryptic 'No Due Certificate' lacking account numbers, transaction details, and verified repayments cannot outweigh certified bank statements and balance sheet disclosures demonstrating subsisting default. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where certified statements of account and balance sheet entries from FY 2015-16 to FY 2022-23 establish an ongoing debt and default to the financial creditor, the Section 7 petition is well within limitation and legally sound. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly admitted the Section 7 application upon finding clear evidence of financial debt and continuous default, and the appeal lacks merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 615 of 2025 is dismissed, and the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 24.03.2025 admitting Section 7 is affirmed; no costs.
summary: Mr. Abhinav Bhatnagar, former management of Extol Industries Ltd., appealed against the NCLT Indore Special Bench order admitting a Section 7 application filed by Bank of Baroda. The Appellant argued that the account was incorrectly classified as NPA on 31.03.2016 in violation of RBI guidelines, especially given an alleged 'No Due Certificate' issued on 16.01.2016, and that the petition was time-barred. NCLAT held that the cryptic No Due Certificate lacked credibility, whereas certified bank statements and continuous acknowledgments of debt in the corporate debtor's balance sheets from FY 2015-16 to FY 2022-23 firmly established subsisting debt and default within limitation. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: GST & Central Excise Angul Division, Rourkela GST Commissionerate vs. Shri Dinesh Sood & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is GST & Central Excise Angul Division, Rourkela GST Commissionerate (Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Dinesh Sood (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Bindals Sponge Industries Ltd.); Respondent No. 3 is Kalinga Allied Industries India Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying statutory liability arose from unpaid statutory central excise and service tax dues of the Corporate Debtor under the Central Excise Act, 1944 and Finance Act, 1994. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed statutory operational debt of Rs. 24,26,89,882/- submitted in Form-B to the Interim Resolution Professional/RP. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP of Corporate Debtor was initiated on 11.05.2018 upon a Section 7 IBC application by Oriental Bank of Commerce; Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 12.11.2019; Appellant filed objections on 05.12.2019; on 19.04.2024 (24th CoC meeting), plan was modified enhancing payment to State GST Department Odisha from 2.71% to 29.61% under Rainbow Papers, while Appellant remained at 2.71% (later 2.69%); Appellant filed IA No. 2537/2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-B claim submissions, 24th CoC meeting minutes dated 19.04.2024 modifying plan allocations for State GST Department, Odisha, and resolution plan provisions allocating 2.71% to Central Excise/Service tax dues. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 2537/2024 before NCLT New Delhi Bench V seeking direction to modify the plan and treat Appellant as a secured creditor under the Rainbow Papers doctrine; NCLT dismissed the IA on 21.01.2025 holding Section 11E of Central Excise Act is not pari materia with Section 48 of Gujarat VAT Act.
legal_issues: Whether statutory central excise and service tax dues under Section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944 create a first charge by operation of law making the tax authority a secured creditor under the IBC on parity with the Rainbow Papers ruling, and whether paying a lower percentage to the Central Excise Department compared to the State GST Department violates Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory government dues do not automatically acquire secured creditor status under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code unless the governing statute explicitly creates an unconditional first charge by operation of law without subordinating itself to insolvency legislation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944 contains an express non-obstante carve-out ('save as otherwise provided in... the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016'), which distinguishes it fundamentally from Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act, 2003 and Section 55 of the Odisha VAT Act, 2004; therefore, IBC provisions override the first charge under Section 11E. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To claim the status of a secured creditor under Section 3(30) read with Section 53 of the IBC, the creditor must establish an operative security interest created by contract or by an overriding statutory charge that is not legislatively subordinated to the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The ruling in Rainbow Papers cannot be extended to claims under Section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944; hence the Appellant remains an unsecured operational creditor, and differential treatment vis-a-vis secured statutory creditors (like State VAT/GST) does not violate Section 30(2)(b) or the equitable treatment principle under Essar Steel.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 21.01.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority (NCLT Court V, New Delhi) rejecting IA No. 2537 of 2024 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 495 of 2025 is dismissed without costs.
summary: The Appellant (GST & Central Excise Angul Division) appealed against an NCLT order rejecting its application to be treated as a secured creditor under the Corporate Debtor's resolution plan pursuant to the Supreme Court's Rainbow Papers judgment[cite: 6]. The Appellant contended that its excise and service tax claim of Rs. 24.26 crores was entitled to equal percentage distribution as the State GST Department, Odisha (29.61% instead of 2.71%)[cite: 6]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 11E of the Central Excise Act contains an express saving clause subordinating its first charge to the IBC, unlike Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act[cite: 6]. Thus, the Appellant cannot be treated as a secured creditor[cite: 6].

case_title: Ajay Agarwal vs. State Bank of India SAM Branch & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 291/2025 (with Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 292, 293 & 294/2025)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Ajay Agarwal, Ashok Agarwal, Ankit Agarwal, and Anitha Agarwal are the Appellants (Personal Guarantors); State Bank of India SAM Branch is Respondent No. 1 (Financial Creditor); T.R. Ravichandran is Respondent No. 2 (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying credit/loan facilities granted by State Bank of India SAM Branch to the principal borrower for which the Appellants executed personal guarantees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default occurred upon failure to discharge personal guarantee obligations; State Bank of India instituted personal insolvency proceedings under Section 95 of the IBC against each guarantor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor initiated Section 95 applications; the Adjudicating Authority passed impugned orders on 30.01.2025 (uploaded on 31.01.2025); appeals were e-filed on 15.03.2025 with an application to condone 14 days of delay in filing and 1 day in re-filing. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Applications filed under Section 95 of the IBC, records of guarantee invocations, and procedural directives issued under Section 97(6) of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Division Bench-I, Chennai, vide common/respective orders dated 30.01.2025, directed the Resolution Professional under Section 97(6) to examine the Section 95 applications and recommend acceptance or rejection within 10 days under Section 99(1); Appellants appealed against these directions before NCLAT Chennai under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal lies under Section 61 of the IBC against an order of the Adjudicating Authority directing the Resolution Professional under Section 97(6) to examine an application filed under Section 95 and submit a recommendatory report under Section 99(1), prior to the stage of judicial determination under Section 100.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim order merely directing a Resolution Professional to examine an application and submit a recommendatory report does not determine or adjudicate substantive rights of parties and is not appealable under insolvency appellate provisions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Relying on the Supreme Court ruling in Dilip B. Jiwrajka v. Union of India, the bench interpreted the statutory scheme spanning Section 95 to Section 99 of the IBC as purely facilitative and non-adjudicatory; no judicial determination or adjudication of a 'lis' occurs until the Adjudicating Authority decides whether to accept or reject the application under Section 100. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The existence of an appealable grievance requires an effective judicial determination affecting legal rights of the parties, which cannot be founded on a recommendatory report or a preliminary direction issued under Section 97. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the impugned order only directed compliance under Section 97(6) and Section 99(1) without deciding jurisdictional facts or merits, no appeal is maintainable, without prejudice to the Appellants' right to contest the merits under Section 100.
operative_order: Delay of 14 days in filing and 1 day in re-filing condoned; interim stay applications dismissed as infructuous; the Company Appeals are dismissed as not maintainable, without prejudice to the Appellants' right to contest the matters on merits at the stage of Section 100 of the IBC.
summary: The Appellants, personal guarantors against whom State Bank of India filed insolvency petitions under Section 95 of the IBC, challenged NCLT Chennai's orders directing the Resolution Professional under Section 97(6) to examine the petitions and submit a recommendatory report under Section 99(1)[cite: 1]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that, as established in the Supreme Court judgment in Dilip B. Jiwrajka, proceedings between Sections 95 and 99 are purely facilitative and involve no judicial adjudication of rights[cite: 1]. Judicial determination occurs only under Section 100[cite: 1]. Consequently, an order issuing directions under Section 97(6) is not appealable, and all four company appeals were dismissed as not maintainable[cite: 1].

case_title: Gagan Chhabra vs. SMS Vishwa JV
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Gagan Chhabra (Appellant, Advocate/Operational Creditor); SMS Vishwa JV (Respondent, alleged Corporate Debtor, unincorporated Joint Venture between SMS Paryavaran Ltd., Vishwa Infrastructures & Services Pvt. Ltd., and GSJ Envo Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Legal representation provided by Appellant to SMS Vishwa JV in arbitration proceedings against Thane Municipal Corporation, followed by an MoU dated 09.06.2018 for settlement of professional fees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational debt of Rs. 2,49,00,000/- based on unpaid invoices and MoU dated 09.06.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Joint venture formed on 20.08.2008; Section 7 CIRP against member Vishwa Infrastructures admitted on 31.08.2018 (liquidation closed 01.07.2022); Section 7 CIRP against member SMS Paryavaran admitted on 03.01.2020; Appellant's Form-C claim of Rs. 2.49 crores rejected by RP on 26.09.2020 while Form-B claim of Rs. 13,07,060 admitted; Demand notice issued on 12.06.2023; Reply issued on 11.07.2023; Section 9 petition filed on 18.07.2023; NCLT rejected petition on 14.05.2024; NCLAT decided appeal on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Joint Venture Agreement dated 20.08.2008; MoU dated 09.06.2018; fee invoices; Section 8 Demand Notice dated 12.06.2023; Reply dated 11.07.2023 pleading unincorporated status; Appellant's maintainability affidavit dated 26.10.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-IV dismissed CP (IB) No. 538/ND/2023 on 14.05.2024 holding that claims based on an MoU do not constitute operational debt; Appellant challenged the rejection before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an application for initiation of corporate insolvency resolution process under Section 9 of the IBC is legally maintainable against an unincorporated Joint Venture that does not constitute a corporate person under Section 3(7) and Section 3(8) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Proceedings under Section 9 of the IBC can only be initiated and maintained against an incorporated legal entity that qualifies as a 'corporate debtor' possessing limited liability under Section 3(7) and 3(8). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(8) restricts the term 'corporate debtor' to a 'corporate person' who owes a debt, while Section 3(7) exhaustively defines 'corporate person' as a company under the Companies Act, an LLP, or an entity incorporated with limited liability under any prevailing statute; an unincorporated joint venture falls outside this definition. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admission by the creditor that the respondent is an unincorporated joint venture formed via a joint venture agreement without independent limited-liability incorporation conclusively establishes that the entity cannot be sued as a corporate debtor under the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 application was non-maintainable ab initio because SMS Vishwa JV is not a corporate person, warranting dismissal of the petition on the threshold ground of maintainability.
operative_order: The objection to maintainability raised by the Respondent is sustained; the order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing the Section 9 petition is affirmed on maintainability grounds; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1749 of 2024 is dismissed; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: The Appellant, an advocate who represented an unincorporated joint venture (SMS Vishwa JV) in arbitration proceedings, filed a Section 9 petition to recover unpaid legal fees of Rs. 2.49 crores under an MoU[cite: 2]. NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected the application[cite: 2]. On appeal, NCLAT held that under Section 3(7) and Section 3(8) of the IBC, corporate insolvency proceedings can strictly be maintained only against an incorporated 'corporate person'[cite: 2]. Since the Respondent is an unincorporated joint venture formed solely by agreement among three companies, the Section 9 petition was legally non-maintainable[cite: 2]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 2].

case_title: Shri Shakti Bhushan & Ors. vs. M/s Titan Industries Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 50/2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 55/2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Shakti Bhushan, Shri Bhushan Kumar Bagga, and Smt. Veena Bhushan (Appellants, Shareholders/Plaintiffs); M/s Titan Industries Ltd. (Respondent No. 1, Company); M/s TSR Darashaw Ltd. (Respondent No. 2, Registrar and Transfer Agent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Suit No. 365 of 2012 (renumbered as TP No. 301 of 2017) filed under Section 108 of the Companies Act, 1956 for mandatory and permanent injunctions regarding registration and transfer of 400 shares (Folio No. TW/P0026051, Certificate No. 13430), bonus shares, and dividends. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure of Respondents to implement NCLT decree dated 28.02.2019 directing registration of shares and payment of dividend and bonus benefits within one month, carrying default interest at 18% per annum. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Final decree passed on 28.02.2019; Contempt Petition No. 154/BB/2019 filed on 09.05.2019; NCLT dismissed contempt petition for default on 30.08.2019; Restoration Application (CA No. 16/2021) and Delay Condonation Application (CA No. 16A/2021 for 374 days) filed on 11.12.2020; NCLT dismissed both applications on 28.05.2024; NCLAT decided appeals on 20.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Medical records proving acute illnesses of Appellants 1 and 2 (including Acute Coronary Syndrome of 75-year-old Appellant No. 2); Registry defect notes dated 10.06.2019 and 14.06.2019; affidavit explaining delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed Contempt Petition No. 154/BB/2019 for want of prosecution on 30.08.2019 due to non-curing of defects and absence of appearance; NCLT later dismissed restoration and condonation applications on 28.05.2024; Appellants preferred appeals under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a contempt petition filed under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 can be dismissed for default/want of prosecution on procedural defect grounds, and whether an Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing to condone a 374-day delay in filing for its restoration supported by medical certificates.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Contempt proceedings are essentially an inquiry between the judicial forum and the contemnor to vindicate the administration of justice; hence, they should not be dismissed for default on curable procedural defects, and subsequent compliance does not bar examination of deliberate past non-compliance. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, the applicant acts as an informer; dismissing a contempt application for default prior to curing procedural defects is impermissible because the cause has not fully matured for dismissal on the merits of prosecution. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Uncontroverted medical records demonstrating chronic illness and hospitalization of elderly litigants establish sufficient cause under the Limitation Act read with Section 433 of the Companies Act, 2013. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the contempt petition for default and refusing to condone the 374 days of delay, as alleged compliance is a question to be examined upon hearing the restored contempt petition on its merits.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (CH) Nos. 50 and 55 of 2024 are allowed; impugned orders dated 28.05.2024 are quashed; dismissal order dated 30.08.2019 is recalled; Contempt Petition No. 154/BB/2019 is restored to original number to be decided on its merits.
summary: Appellants filed a contempt petition under Section 425 of the Companies Act, 2013 after Titan Industries Ltd. failed to comply with an order dated 28.02.2019 directing registration of 400 shares and payment of dividend and bonus shares[cite: 3]. NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the contempt petition for default on 30.08.2019 due to defect non-rectification, and later dismissed applications seeking restoration and condonation of 374 days delay[cite: 3]. NCLAT Chennai Bench held that contempt proceedings protect the dignity of the court and should not be dismissed for want of prosecution on technical defects[cite: 3]. Relying on uncontroverted medical evidence, NCLAT condoned the delay, set aside the dismissal orders, and restored the contempt petition[cite: 3].

case_title: Bank of Baroda & Anr. vs. The Regional Provident Fund Commissioner & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bank of Baroda SAM Branch and Bank of India (Appellants, Secured Financial Creditors); Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, EPFO Madurai (Respondent No. 1, Statutory Creditor); Ms. Rajalakshmi Varadarajan (Respondent No. 2, Liquidator of M/s Supreme Coated Board Mills Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory liability of the Corporate Debtor towards unpaid Provident Fund, Insurance Fund contributions, administrative charges, damages, and interest for the period October 2014 to October 2018 under the EPF & MP Act, 1952. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 filed a total claim of Rs. 3,98,92,397/- in Form-C (Section 6/6A/6C contributions: Rs. 1,44,77,852/-; Section 14B damages: Rs. 1,44,77,852/-; Section 7Q interest: Rs. 1,09,36,693/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 30.09.2019; liquidation order passed on 07.02.2023; Form-C claim submitted on 01.03.2023; Liquidator issued partial rejection admitting only Rs. 82,13,064/- on 14.03.2023; Section 7A assessment order passed on 30.03.2023; RPFC filed IA No. 1020/CHE/2023 on 13.06.2023; NCLT allowed claim on 12.01.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 04.06.2025. 5.
