FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 7A assessment order dated 30.03.2023; ESIC wage records; correspondence between Liquidator and RPFC dated 14.03.2023, 05.04.2023, 11.04.2023, and 16.05.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator admitted Rs. 82,13,064/- and rejected the balance; NCLT Chennai Bench allowed RPFC's application under Section 42 read with Section 60(5) on 12.01.2024, setting aside the partial rejection and directing full admission of Rs. 3,98,92,397/-; Financial Creditors appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether penal damages under Section 14B and interest under Section 7Q of the EPF & MP Act, 1952 form part of 'any amount due from an employer' under Section 11(2) having first charge priority over secured creditors, and whether finalizing a Section 7A assessment during the liquidation period violates the moratorium under Section 33(5) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory provident fund dues along with interest and penal damages assessed under the EPF & MP Act, 1952 constitute an overriding statutory charge under Section 11(2) that must be satisfied in full outside the liquidation waterfall under Section 53 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Harmoniously reading Section 11(2) with Sections 7A, 7Q, and 14B of the EPF & MP Act and following the Supreme Court's ruling in Maharashtra State Cooperative Bank, the phrase 'any amount due from an employer' encompasses contributions, damages, and interest; the liquidation moratorium under Section 33(5) does not bar quantification of pre-CIRP defaults where the Liquidator participated in the assessment proceedings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a statutory authority passes an assessment order pursuant to hearings attended by the Liquidator and no statutory appeal is preferred, the Liquidator cannot unilaterally reassess or reduce the claim. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The full claim of Rs. 3,98,92,397/- including Section 14B damages and Section 7Q interest is payable as statutory dues under Section 11(2), and the NCLT committed no error in directing its full admission.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 81 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 12.01.2024 is affirmed.
summary: Appellants (consortium of financial creditors) appealed against an NCLT Chennai order directing the Liquidator of M/s Supreme Coated Board Mills Pvt. Ltd. to admit the entire Rs. 3.98 crore claim filed by the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner, Madurai[cite: 4]. The Liquidator had admitted only Rs. 82.13 lakhs, contending that damages and interest under Sections 14B and 7Q were determined during the liquidation period based on ESIC data[cite: 4]. NCLAT held that, under Supreme Court precedent, 'any amount due from an employer' under Section 11(2) of the EPF & MP Act includes contributions, interest, and damages[cite: 4]. As the dues pertained to pre-CIRP defaults and the Liquidator did not appeal the assessment order, the full claim was properly admitted[cite: 4].

case_title: Mr. Tumkur Vajram Shetty Jayawanth & Anr. vs. M/s. Agile Labs Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Tumkur Vajram Shetty Jayawanth and Ms. U. Lakshmi (Appellants, Shareholders holding 15.67% share capital); M/s Agile Labs Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1, Company); M.S. Sabarish and 14 other shareholders/investors (Respondents 2 to 16). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two rights issues undertaken on 10.11.2015 and 27.01.2017 to raise expansion capital under Section 62(1)(a) of the Companies Act, 2013, followed by transfers of shares by certain shareholders to Geetham Shares and Securities Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 14). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate oppression/mismanagement petition alleging wrongful dilution of shareholding and reduction to minority status via rights issues of 2,83,814 shares and 6,33,750 shares. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appellants resigned as directors on 19.05.2012 (Form 32 filed 23.03.2013); Rights offer issued on 12.10.2015; Appellants objected on 27.10.2015 and 31.10.2015; Board approved rights issues on 10.11.2015 and 27.01.2017; CP No. 599/BB/2018 filed in 2018; NCLT dismissed petition on 31.12.2018; NCLAT decided appeal on 23.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Articles 3, 4, and 5 of the Articles of Association; Letters of Offer for rights issues; Board Resolutions approving allotments; Shareholders' Agreement dated 15.10.2007; and company reply letters dated 02.11.2015. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed CP No. 599/BB/2018 under Sections 241, 242, and 59 before NCLT Bengaluru seeking annulment of the 2015 and 2017 rights issues, cancellation of share transfers, and an interim injunction against removal as promoter; NCLT dismissed the petition on 31.12.2018 as premature and non-oppressive; Appellants appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a bona fide decision by the board and majority shareholders to increase authorized capital and offer rights shares proportionately to all existing members under Section 62(1)(a) constitutes oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Increasing authorized share capital and issuing rights shares in compliance with statutory provisions and the Articles of Association for business expansion cannot be characterized as oppressive or fraudulent merely because an existing shareholder chooses not to subscribe and suffers dilution. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act require proof of harsh, burdensome, and wrongful conduct prejudicial to the company or its shareholders; an exercise of corporate power to raise funds under Section 62(1)(a) does not meet this threshold when all members receive equal participation rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the company proves that rights offers met all conditions in the Articles of Association and shares were offered proportionately to the complainants, allegations of oppression are unsubstantiated. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The rights issues of 2015 and 2017 complied with the Articles of Association and the Companies Act, 2013, and the Adjudicating Authority properly dismissed the petition as premature and devoid of credible merit.
operative_order: TA (AT) No. 28/2022 (Company Appeal (AT) No. 44/2019) is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Bengaluru dated 31.12.2018 is affirmed without costs.
summary: Appellants, holding 15.67% share capital in M/s Agile Labs Pvt. Ltd., filed a petition under Sections 241, 242, and 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 seeking to set aside rights issues conducted in 2015 and 2017 and cancel associated share transfers, alleging that the transactions diluted their stake and constituted oppression and mismanagement[cite: 5]. NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the petition[cite: 5]. On appeal, NCLAT Chennai Bench affirmed the dismissal, holding that increasing share capital for bona fide business purposes in accordance with the Articles of Association and Section 62(1)(a) cannot be termed oppressive when proportionate offers were extended to all shareholders[cite: 5]. The appeal was dismissed[cite: 5].

case_title: GST & Central Excise Angul Division, Rourkela GST Commissionerate vs. Shri Dinesh Sood & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: GST & Central Excise Angul Division, Rourkela GST Commissionerate (Appellant, Operational Creditor); Dinesh Sood (Respondent No. 1, Resolution Professional of M/s Bindals Sponge Industries Ltd.); Kalinga Allied Industries India Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 3, Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory claims arising from unpaid central excise and service tax dues under the Central Excise Act, 1944 and Finance Act, 1994. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational statutory debt of Rs. 24,26,89,882/- claimed in Form-B and admitted by the Resolution Professional. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 11.05.2018 under Section 7; CoC approved Resolution Plan on 12.11.2019 providing 2.71% payout to Appellant; Appellant objected on 05.12.2019; CoC modified plan in 24th meeting on 19.04.2024 increasing State GST Odisha payout to 29.61% under Rainbow Papers while retaining Appellant at 2.71%; Appellant filed IA No. 2537/2024; NCLT rejected IA on 21.01.2025; NCLAT decided appeal on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-B claim submission; 24th CoC meeting minutes dated 19.04.2024; Resolution Plan allocations showing 29.61% for State GST and 2.71% for Appellant; Central Excise Act Section 11E statutory text. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 2537 of 2024 before NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-V seeking to be treated as a secured creditor and given parity with State GST under Rainbow Papers; NCLT dismissed the IA on 21.01.2025; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether statutory dues under Section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944 create a first charge by operation of law rendering the tax department a secured creditor under the IBC on parity with Rainbow Papers, and whether differential allocation between Central Excise and State GST violates Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory government dues do not automatically acquire secured creditor status under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code unless the governing statute creates an unconditional first charge by operation of law without subordinating itself to the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Unlike Section 48 of the Gujarat VAT Act or Section 55 of the Odisha VAT Act, Section 11E of the Central Excise Act, 1944 contains an express non-obstante exception ('save as otherwise provided in... the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016'), which explicitly subordinates its first charge to the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To be categorized as a secured creditor under Section 3(30) and Section 53 of the IBC, a statutory creditor must demonstrate a valid security interest that is not legislatively subordinated to insolvency proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Rainbow Papers is inapplicable to Central Excise dues under Section 11E; the Appellant remains an unsecured operational creditor, and differential treatment vis-a-vis secured statutory creditors is permissible under CoC of Essar Steel.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 495 of 2025 is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT New Delhi Bench dated 21.01.2025 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant (GST & Central Excise Angul Division) challenged an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting its application to be treated as a secured creditor under the Corporate Debtor's resolution plan pursuant to Rainbow Papers[cite: 6]. Appellant contended its Rs. 24.26 crore excise claim should receive the same 29.61% distribution allocated to State GST Odisha rather than 2.71%[cite: 6]. NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 11E of the Central Excise Act contains an express exception subordinating its first charge to the IBC, unlike State VAT statutes[cite: 6]. Consequently, Central Excise dues remain unsecured operational debt[cite: 6].

case_title: Government of Tamil Nadu, Commercial Tax & Registration Dept. vs. Nithiyanantham Ramachandran & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Government of Tamil Nadu Commercial Tax & Registration Dept., rep by Assistant Commissioner (ST), Sriperumbudur Assessment Circle (Appellant, Statutory Operational/Secured Creditor); Nithiyanantham Ramachandran (Respondent No. 1, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor M/s Chowel India Pvt. Ltd.); Sub-Registrar, Sriperumbudur (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP on 05.05.2020 on a Section 9 application; liquidation ordered on 29.11.2021; Appellant created an encumbrance/attachment over the Corporate Debtor's land (4.41 acres) and building (66,728.30 sq. ft.) in Survey No. 449, Mannur Village, Sriperumbudur, to recover unpaid GST/tax dues under the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1864. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory tax dues totaling Rs. 85,42,436/- claimed by the Appellant via Form C submitted to the Liquidator. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 05.05.2020; liquidation ordered on 29.11.2021; Liquidator requested lifting of attachment on 19.01.2022; Appellant refused on 03.02.2022; Liquidator filed IA No. 445/CHE/2022 on 04.04.2022; NCLT directed removal of attachment on 11.01.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Encumbrance Certificate reflecting attachment; Form C claim filed by the State for Rs. 85,42,436/-; Liquidator's requisition letter dated 19.01.2022 and Appellant's rejection letter dated 03.02.2022; absence of Form 5 District Gazette publication and Form 7 notice under the 1864 Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench allowed Liquidator's IA No. 445/CHE/2022 on 11.01.2024 directing Appellant to lift its property attachment within two weeks to permit liquidation sale; Appellant challenged the direction before NCLAT Chennai under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a State Commercial Tax Department can continue an attachment over corporate debtor assets under the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1864 during liquidation when it has submitted its claim to the Liquidator, or whether the attachment must be lifted to allow the liquidator to sell the assets in accordance with the overriding mandate of Section 238 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory authority that lodges its claim before a liquidator cannot simultaneously maintain an attachment over the corporate debtor's assets under local recovery laws, as liquidation proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code override inconsistent state attachment laws by virtue of Section 238. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC has overriding effect over the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1864; lifting the attachment facilitates asset liquidation and settlement of claims (including the tax department's priority or security claim as settled under law), which fulfills rather than prejudices the object of recovery. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Once a claimant submits Form C to participate in liquidation distribution, retaining a separate statutory attachment disrupts the collective statutory liquidation framework. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly directed the removal of the attachment over the property to enable an orderly e-auction sale by the Liquidator.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 446 of 2024 is dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 11.01.2024 directing removal of attachment is upheld.
summary: The Commercial Tax Department of Tamil Nadu appealed against an NCLT Chennai order directing it to remove an attachment over the land and building of the Corporate Debtor (M/s Chowel India Pvt. Ltd.) levied under the Tamil Nadu Revenue Recovery Act, 1864 for tax dues of Rs. 85.42 lakhs[cite: 7]. The Appellant argued that it held the status of a secured creditor under Rainbow Papers and was entitled to retain its encumbrance[cite: 7]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that because the department had submitted its claim in Form C to the Liquidator, lifting the attachment to enable a liquidation sale via e-auction was necessary under Section 238 of the IBC and did not prejudice the adjudication of its claim priority[cite: 7].

case_title: Dr. Thoyajakshi Bai Sakranaik vs. Patanjali Hospitals Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Dr. Thoyajakshi Bai Sakranaik (Appellant, Director/Shareholder); Patanjali Hospitals Private Limited (Respondent No. 1, Company); Dr. Sathyanarayana Rao Mukunda Rao Kodaganur and Smt. Latha Mukunda Rao (Respondents 2 and 3, Directors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Governance and management dispute concerning the affairs of Patanjali Hospitals Pvt. Ltd., contractual obligations of the Appellant as a whole-time medical professional, and convening of an Extraordinary General Meeting (EGM) to remove the Appellant from directorship. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Interlocutory corporate governance dispute; forensic audit revealed cash collection of Rs. 1,38,52,270/- from patients between 01.01.2021 and 31.03.2023, of which only Rs. 56,05,900/- was remitted to the hospital cash counter, leaving Rs. 82,46,370/- allegedly retained and misappropriated by the Appellant. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution to appoint forensic auditor passed on 22.04.2024; Board meeting notice issued on 29.04.2025 proposing EGM on 23.05.2025; Company Petition No. 127/BB/2023 heard on interim relief; NCLT Bengaluru rejected interim stay on 01.05.2025; NCLAT decided appeal on 06.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic Audit Report by M/s Yedida and Associates based on the hospital patient register; service contract restricting private outside medical practice; undisclosed concurrent litigations between the parties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed an interlocutory application in CP No. 127/BB/2023 under Sections 241-242 before NCLT Bengaluru seeking an interim stay on holding the EGM scheduled for 23.05.2025 to consider her removal; NCLT declined interim relief on 01.05.2025 citing breach of employment contract, unclean hands, and prima facie diversion of hospital funds; Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in exercising judicial discretion by declining to grant an interim injunction to keep in abeyance an EGM called for the removal of a director under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, where prima facie evidence of financial misappropriation and suppression of material litigations existed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The grant or refusal of an interim injunction in proceedings under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 is an equitable, discretionary remedy requiring the applicant to establish a prima facie case, balance of convenience, and clean hands. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Removal of a director via an EGM convened in accordance with statutory procedures cannot be enjoined where the petitioner has engaged in conduct detrimental to company interests in violation of fiduciary duties under Section 166 of the Companies Act, 2013. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an independent audit report based on primary hospital registers demonstrates retention of substantial cash receipts and the applicant suppresses parallel litigation between the parties, the applicant is disentitled to discretionary equitable relief. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority did not commit any legal error in refusing to stall the EGM, leaving substantive allegations of oppression and mismanagement to be adjudicated upon exchange of complete pleadings.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 65 of 2025 is rejected; the interlocutory order of NCLT Bengaluru dated 01.05.2025 declining an interim stay on the EGM is affirmed.
summary: The Appellant, a director of Patanjali Hospitals Pvt. Ltd., appealed an interlocutory order of NCLT Bengaluru refusing to stay an EGM convened to remove her from directorship in a pending Section 241-242 petition[cite: 9]. The NCLT declined the injunction after finding that an audit report showed Rs. 82.46 lakhs of hospital collections were retained by the Appellant, that she engaged in unauthorized outside practice, and that she suppressed pending litigations[cite: 9]. The NCLAT affirmed the order, holding that interim relief is discretionary and equitable[cite: 9]. Because the Appellant failed to approach the court with clean hands and breached her service duties, the refusal of interim relief was justified[cite: 9].

case_title: JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. vs. Mr. Venkatachalam & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: JM Financial Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (Appellant, Financial Creditor acting as trustee of Rail December 2024 Trust); Mr. Venkatachalam (Respondent, Resolution Professional of Raigarh Champa Rail Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.); M/s Medha Servo Drives Pvt. Ltd. (Existing H1 Resolution Applicant); JSW Energy Ltd. (Prospective Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Raigarh Champa Rail Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. commenced on 01.01.2021; resolution plan of Medha Servo Drives approved by CoC with 100% vote and submitted for NCLT approval; CoC subsequently resolved on 23.10.2024 with 78.59% majority to withdraw plan approval and undertake challenge mechanism; CoC later on 13.03.2025 resolved with 78.59% majority to issue fresh Form G to invite new EoIs while retaining existing applicants. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Value maximization dispute in CIRP; proposal to fix existing highest bid by Medha as the baseline reserve price for fresh bidding. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 01.01.2021; First Form G issued 24.08.2021; fresh Form G issued 11.04.2024; CoC approved Medha's plan on 04.06.2024; plan approval reserved on 10.07.2024; CoC resolved to withdraw plan approval on 23.10.2024; NCLT allowed withdrawal on 25.10.2024; RP's limited reopening IA No. 388/2025 dismissed on 06.03.2025; 44th CoC meeting held on 13.03.2025 resolving to issue fresh Form G; RP filed IA No. 608/2025 on 28.03.2025; NCLT rejected IA on 03.04.2025; NCLAT decided appeal on 19.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of the 43rd and 44th CoC meetings approving issuance of fresh Form G by 78.59% voting share; Challenge Mechanism framework under Regulation 39(1A); bid records showing Medha's approved offer. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed RP's IA (IBC)/608/2025 on 03.04.2025 holding that issuing fresh Form G was an indirect attempt to admit JSW Energy after prior rejections; Appellant (CoC member) appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Committee of Creditors, in exercise of its commercial wisdom aimed at asset value maximization, has the jurisdiction and power under the IBC and CIRP Regulations to issue a fresh Form G and invite fresh Expressions of Interest from the public even after a resolution plan had previously been approved and withdrawn for challenge mechanism proceedings.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is paramount, and the CoC possesses the inherent statutory prerogative to reissue Form G to invite fresh expressions of interest and intensify competition in pursuit of value maximization for the corporate debtor, provided strict CIRP timelines are preserved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 36A and Regulation 39(1A) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations, 2016 do not impose an absolute statutory bar preventing the CoC from cancelling, modifying, or reissuing an invitation for EoI or RFRP; the commercial wisdom of a requisite majority (Section 30(4)) retains supremacy to negotiate or restart bidding. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the CoC passes a resolution with a 78.59% majority to issue a fresh open Form G (without favoring any single entity), retains existing applicants, and preserves the highest bid as the reserve price, the action is transparent, non-discriminatory, and aligned with the primary objective of value maximization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in restricting the commercial wisdom of the CoC and refusing permission to issue fresh Form G.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 230 of 2025 is allowed; impugned order dated 03.04.2025 is quashed; IA (IBC)/608/2025 is allowed permitting the Resolution Professional to issue fresh Form G to invite fresh EoIs subject to adhering to time-bound CIRP completion.
summary: JM Financial ARC appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order which rejected the Resolution Professional's application (IA No. 608/2025) seeking permission to issue a fresh Form G to invite new Expressions of Interest for Raigarh Champa Rail Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 10] The CoC had voted with a 78.59% majority to reissue Form G using the previous highest bidder's offer as a reserve price to maximize asset value[cite: 10]. NCLT viewed this as an attempt to introduce an ineligible bidder (JSW Energy)[cite: 10]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench reversed the decision, holding that the commercial wisdom of the CoC to re-publish Form G and maximize value cannot be curtailed, provided CIRP timelines are respected[cite: 10].

case_title: Anitha Agarwal vs. State Bank of India SAM Branch & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 294/2025 (with Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 291, 292 & 293/2025)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anitha Agarwal, Ajay Agarwal, Ashok Agarwal, and Ankit Agarwal (Appellants, Personal Guarantors); State Bank of India SAM Branch (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor); T.R. Ravichandran (Respondent No. 2, Interim Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate loan and credit facilities granted to the principal borrower by SBI SAM Branch, for which the Appellants executed personal guarantees. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of credit facilities by the principal corporate borrower; SBI filed personal insolvency petitions against the guarantors under Section 95 of the IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial Creditor filed Section 95 petitions; NCLT Chennai Division Bench-I passed impugned orders on 30.01.2025 (uploaded 31.01.2025); appeals e-filed on 15.03.2025 accompanied by delay condonation applications (14 days in filing, 1 day in re-filing); NCLAT decided appeals on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Section 95 petition records, personal guarantee deeds, and NCLT order directing procedural examination under Section 97(6) of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai vide order dated 30.01.2025 directed the Resolution Professional to examine the Section 95 petition under Section 97(6) and submit a recommendation under Section 99(1) within 10 days; Appellant challenged the direction before NCLAT Chennai under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is maintainable against a preliminary procedural order of the Adjudicating Authority directing the Resolution Professional to examine a Section 95 application and submit a recommendatory report under Section 99(1) prior to judicial determination under Section 100.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A preliminary direction to a Resolution Professional under personal insolvency provisions to collate facts and formulate a recommendatory report does not adjudicate any substantive right or lis and is non-appealable. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In accordance with the Supreme Court decision in Dilip B. Jiwrajka v. Union of India, the functions performed by the Resolution Professional between Section 95 and Section 99 are strictly facilitative; adjudicatory determination takes place solely before the Adjudicating Authority at the Section 100 stage. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: An appeal under Section 61 requires an order determining substantive rights or causing legal prejudice; an order merely initiating a recommendatory inquiry does not satisfy this threshold. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The appeal against the Section 97(6) direction is premature and non-maintainable, without prejudice to the guarantor's right to contest the proceedings on merits under Section 100.
operative_order: Delay condoned; interim stay application dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 294 of 2025 is dismissed as not maintainable, reserving the Appellant's right to contest on merits under Section 100 of the IBC.
summary: The Appellant, a personal guarantor to a corporate debtor, appealed against an NCLT Chennai order directing the Resolution Professional under Section 97(6) of the IBC to examine State Bank of India's personal insolvency petition and submit a report under Section 99(1)[cite: 11]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that, pursuant to the Supreme Court ruling in Dilip B. Jiwrajka, proceedings between Sections 95 and 99 are purely facilitative and do not involve judicial determination of substantive rights[cite: 11]. Adjudication occurs only under Section 100[cite: 11]. Consequently, an order directing procedural examination under Section 97(6) is not appealable under Section 61, and the appeal was dismissed[cite: 11].

case_title: Swaminarayan Diamonds Pvt. Ltd. vs. Canara Bank
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Swaminarayan Diamonds Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant, Corporate Debtor); Canara Bank (Respondent, Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities extended by Canara Bank to Swaminarayan Diamonds Pvt. Ltd., which subsequently defaulted in debt service obligations. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor account declared NPA on 06.07.2024; date of default originally stated in Form No. 1 was 05.04.2024 (calculated as 90 days prior to NPA), later amended to 10.04.2024 as the actual first default date, with both dates falling comfortably within the period of limitation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 06.07.2024; Section 7 petition filed by Canara Bank; NCLT Mumbai passed impugned order on 28.05.2025 granting liberty to amend Form No. 1 and granting 7 days to Corporate Debtor to reply; NCLAT appeal decided on 23.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original statutory Form No. 1 specifying default date as 05.04.2024; proposed amended Form No. 1 correcting default date to 10.04.2024; loan account statements and NPA classification records. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-VI on 28.05.2025 permitted Canara Bank to amend Form No. 1 to correct the date of default, granting Swaminarayan Diamonds 7 days to file a reply to the amended Form; Corporate Debtor appealed to NCLAT contending that allowing amendment without a formal application took away a valuable defense.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 7 of the IBC to permit a financial creditor to amend statutory Form No. 1 to rectify/clarify the date of default prior to the admission order, and whether such an amendment prejudices the corporate debtor when both dates fall within limitation and an opportunity to file a reply is granted.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Pleadings and statutory forms in a Section 7 IBC application may be amended or supplemented with additional documents at any stage prior to the final order of admission or rejection, provided the amendment is clarificatory and does not manipulate limitation or prejudice accrued statutory rights. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: As held by the Supreme Court in Dena Bank v. C. Shivakumar Reddy, an application under Section 7 in Form 1 cannot be equated with a plaint in a civil suit and is not governed by strict technical rules of pleading; the proviso to Section 7(5)(b) expressly enables rectification of defects. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the correction of the default date from 05.04.2024 to 10.04.2024 is clarificatory, remains within limitation, does not circumvent Section 10A, and the debtor is given full opportunity to file a reply, no legal prejudice or loss of a vested defense is caused. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error or illegality in granting liberty to file an amended Form No. 1 with right of reply to the debtor, as the amendment assists in the proper determination of default.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 885 of 2025 is dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 28.05.2025 is upheld, and the NCLT is requested to proceed with the Section 7 application.
summary: The Corporate Debtor (Swaminarayan Diamonds Pvt. Ltd.) challenged an NCLT Mumbai order granting Canara Bank liberty to amend its Section 7 Form No. 1 to correct the date of default from 05.04.2024 to 10.04.2024, with seven days given to the debtor to file a reply[cite: 12]. The Appellant argued that permitting the change without a formal amendment application deprived it of a valid defense[cite: 12]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under the Supreme Court's ruling in Dena Bank, Section 7 petitions are not regular civil suits and amendments/additional documents can be permitted anytime prior to admission, provided they do not manipulate limitation[cite: 12]. Since both dates were well within limitation, no prejudice was caused[cite: 12].

case_title: Comandur Parthasarathy vs. Lalit Kumar Dangi & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Comandur Parthasarathy (Appellant, Personal Guarantor); Lalit Kumar Dangi (Respondent No. 1, Resolution Professional); Shinhan Bank (Respondent No. 2, Financial Creditor); M/s Karvy Data Management Services Limited (Respondent No. 3, Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal insolvency proceedings initiated under Section 95 of the IBC by Shinhan Bank against the Appellant in his capacity as personal guarantor to credit facilities availed by Karvy Data Management Services Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial facilities; Shinhan Bank initiated Section 95 proceedings against the Personal Guarantor in CP (IB) No. 111/95/HDB/2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RP issued notice under Section 99(4) on 21.06.2024 providing only 2 days to reply; RP prepared report on 26.06.2024; Appellant requested petition copies on 29.06.2024; RP supplied copies on 03.07.2024; RP filed Section 99 report on 14.08.2024 (prior reference date 23.07.2024); NCLT passed impugned order on 21.10.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 19.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP's requisition notice dated 21.06.2024 granting only 2 days to submit information; reminder letter dated 03.07.2024; internal report preparation notes dated 26.06.2024; Section 99 recommendation report submitted to NCLT. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench in IA No. 1987/2024 in CP (IB) No. 111/95/HDB/2024 rejected Appellant's objections on 21.10.2024, holding that under Surendra B. Jiwrajka the personal guarantor had no vested right to contest at the Section 99 stage; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the statutory 7-day period prescribed under Section 99(5) of the IBC is mandatory upon the Resolution Professional once discretion is exercised to call for information under Section 99(4), and whether curtailing this period to 2 days violates natural justice and vitiates the subsequent Section 99 recommendation report.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the power of a Resolution Professional to call for information under personal insolvency provisions is discretionary, once that discretion is exercised by issuing a requisition notice, the statutory timeline allowing the recipient a full seven days to reply becomes strictly mandatory. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Reading Section 99(4) conjunctively with Section 99(5) of the IBC, the word 'may' applies only to the initial discretion to seek information; once a notice is issued, Section 99(5) mandates giving 7 full days, and a unilateral truncated notice cannot be validated by subsequent reminder letters or post-decisional opportunities. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the record establishes that the RP gave only 2 days to submit information and finalized his report before issuing any reminder, the procedural safeguard enacted under Section 99(5) stands directly breached. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in applying the non-adjudicatory principle of Surendra B. Jiwrajka to override the express statutory command of Section 99(5); the impugned order cannot be sustained and the guarantor must be afforded 7 days to furnish information.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 429 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 21.10.2024 is quashed; the matter is remitted back to the Adjudicating Authority to decide afresh after granting the Appellant 7 days to submit information under Section 99(5) of the IBC; pending IAs closed.
summary: The Appellant, personal guarantor to Karvy Data Management Services Ltd., challenged an NCLT Hyderabad order which rejected his application seeking an opportunity to respond to the Resolution Professional's Section 99 inquiries[cite: 13]. The RP had issued a notice under Section 99(4) giving only 2 days to respond instead of the statutory 7 days under Section 99(5), and proceeded to finalize the recommendation report[cite: 13]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that while calling for information is discretionary, adhering to the 7-day period under Section 99(5) becomes mandatory once notice is issued[cite: 13]. The NCLAT set aside the impugned order and remitted the matter to grant the Appellant 7 days to furnish information[cite: 13].

case_title: Shri Chand Narain Kuchroo vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shri Chand Narain Kuchroo (Appellant, Personal Guarantor); State Bank of India (Respondent No. 1, Financial Creditor/Consortium Lead Bank); Manish Agarwal (Respondent No. 2, Resolution Professional); M/s K K Milk Fresh India Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit Facility Agreement dated 19.11.2013 executed by consortium of banks led by SBI to the Corporate Debtor, secured by Deed of Personal Guarantee executed by the Appellant on 22.11.2013 (and Supplemental Deed dated 16.09.2015) for Rs. 172 crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor declared NPA on 28.09.2016; Demand Notice issued under Section 13(2) of SARFAESI on 01.09.2017 claiming debt of Rs. 110,16,95,531/-; Legal Demand Notice issued on 10.10.2017 claiming Rs. 1,11,89,59,417/-; SBI's admitted claim in CIRP was Rs. 144,34,78,998/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted to CIRP on 24.09.2019; SBI issued Form-B demand notice under Rule 7(1) on 28.10.2020; Section 95 petition filed in 2021; RP appointed on 20.04.2021/07.09.2022; NCLT struck off right to file reply on 17.04.2024; NCLT heard oral submissions on 08.05.2024 and admitted petition on 04.06.2024; NCLAT appeal decided on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Speed post receipts and tracking reports dated 08.09.2017 and 11.09.2017 delivering notice under Section 13(2) at Gurgaon and Aligarh addresses; Form-B notice delivered on 09.11.2020; orders dated 21.12.2023, 16.01.2024, 01.03.2024, and 17.04.2024 showing multiple opportunities granted to file reply. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Allahabad Bench in CP (IB) No. 52/ALD/2022 admitted SBI's Section 95 petition on 04.06.2024 after closing Appellant's right to file reply due to repeated defaults; Appellant appealed under Section 61 alleging non-service of guarantee invocation notice.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 95 application was vitiated by alleged non-service of notice invoking the personal guarantee or demand notice under Rule 7(1), and whether a personal guarantor can raise factual pleas of non-service for the first time in appeal after having failed to file a written reply before the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Factual defenses regarding non-service of pre-insolvency notices cannot be raised for the first time before an appellate tribunal when the appellant neglected multiple opportunities to raise them before the trial authority and uncontroverted postal tracking records establish valid service. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Service of demand notice in Form-B under Rule 7(1) and invocation of guarantee are procedural pre-requisites under Section 95; however, proof of dispatch and delivery via registered/speed post to verified addresses satisfies the statutory evidentiary standard. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unrebutted postal receipts and tracking reports establishing successful physical delivery of notice to the debtor's addresses fully discharge the creditor's burden of proving service. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Postal evidence established valid service of guarantee invocation and statutory demand notices, and the Adjudicating Authority properly admitted the Section 95 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1466 of 2024 is dismissed; interim stay vacated; Adjudicating Authority order dated 04.06.2024 is upheld; no order as to costs.
summary: The Appellant, personal guarantor to M/s K K Milk Fresh India Ltd., appealed against an NCLT Allahabad order admitting SBI's Section 95 petition and initiating personal insolvency resolution against him[cite: 14]. The Appellant contended that the notice invoking the personal guarantee and the Form-B demand notice were never served[cite: 14]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that postal receipts and speed post tracking reports produced on record conclusively proved delivery to the Appellant's verified addresses[cite: 14]. Furthermore, the Appellant had neglected repeated opportunities to file a reply before the NCLT and could not raise new factual pleas on appeal[cite: 14].

case_title: Fintags Technologies Private Limited & Ors. vs. Dominic Savio & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Fintags Technologies Private Limited (Appellant No. 1, Company); Mr. Santhosh Wilson and Ms. Sabnam Mehra (Appellants 2 and 3, Directors/Transferor); Mr. Dominic Savio (Respondent No. 1, Shareholder/Transferee); Ms. Shanthi Balamurugan, RoC Chennai, MCA (Respondents 2, 3, and 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Transfer of shares in Fintags Technologies Pvt. Ltd. from Appellant No. 3 to Respondent No. 1 for agreed consideration of Rs. 50,000/- executed via Securities Transfer Form (Form SH-4). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Refusal/delay by company management to register transfer of shares and update the register of members pursuant to executed transfer forms and received payment. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP(CA)/34(CHE)2025 instituted before NCLT Chennai; payment deposited on 31.03.2025; NCLT passed order on 25.04.2025 directing compliance by 07.05.2025; NCLAT appeal decided on 13.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Duly signed Share Transfer Form (SH-4) by Appellant No. 3; bank deposit proof dated 31.03.2025 (Annexure 5, Page 206) reflecting transfer of Rs. 50,000/- into Appellant No. 1's bank account; email correspondence dated 22.03.2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench in CP(CA)/34(CHE)2025 passed an order on 25.04.2025 recording consent and directing Appellants to effect share transfer within one week; Appellants appealed under Section 421 alleging consideration was never paid.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 is maintainable against a consent order directing the registration of a share transfer, where the appellant challenges the underlying consideration without establishing that the consent was vitiated by fraud.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: No appeal lies against an order passed with the consent of parties unless the appellant establishes by cogent evidence that the recorded consent was vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, or lack of authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013 does not permit a consenting litigant to renege on an agreed direction regarding share transfer under Section 59 where the record shows mutual assent before the Adjudicating Authority. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented banking evidence proving receipt of agreed consideration into the company's account, combined with an executed Form SH-4, disproves assertions of non-payment. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority was in substance a consent order based on established payment and signed transfer instruments, rendering the appeal devoid of merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 79 of 2025 is dismissed; the impugned order of NCLT Chennai dated 25.04.2025 is affirmed.
summary: Appellants appealed against an NCLT Chennai order directing them to register a transfer of shares in favor of Respondent No. 1 within one week and report compliance[cite: 15]. The Appellants claimed that the agreed transfer consideration of Rs. 50,000/- had never been paid[cite: 15]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that banking records on file established that the consideration was duly deposited into the company's account and supported by a signed Form SH-4[cite: 15]. Furthermore, because the NCLT order was passed with the consent of the parties and no fraud was shown, the appeal was untenable and dismissed[cite: 15].

case_title: Sanjeevani Krishna Kamlakar vs. Birendra Kumar Agarwal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sanjeevani Krishna Kamlakar (Applicant/Appellant, non-party to original lis); Birendra Kumar Agarwal (Respondent No. 1, Resolution Professional/Liquidator). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Corporate Debtor where RP filed IA No. 381 of 2025 seeking a 180-day extension from 19.10.2024 to complete CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory timeline lapse leading to termination of CIRP and initiation of liquidation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT rejected CIRP extension and ordered liquidation on 05.03.2025; Appellant claimed knowledge of order on 15.03.2025; appeal e-filed on 28.04.2025 (total 54 days elapsed); delay condonation application IA No. 2928 of 2025 heard and decided on 02.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: E-filing receipt dated 28.04.2025; certified copy endorsement of order dated 05.03.2025; affidavit supporting condonation application claiming 14 days delay from date of knowledge. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed IA No. 381 of 2025 on 05.03.2025 and ordered liquidation of Corporate Debtor; Appellant filed appeal along with IA No. 2928 of 2025 seeking condonation of 14 days delay counted from date of knowledge (15.03.2025).
legal_issues: Whether limitation for filing an appeal under Section 61(2) of the IBC runs from the date of the pronouncement/passing of the order or from the date of knowledge of an aggrieved person, and whether delay beyond the 15-day condonable window can be condoned.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 61(2) of the IBC, the statutory limitation period of 30 days begins strictly on the date the order is passed, not from the date of knowledge; any delay exceeding the discretionary 15-day grace period is incurable and cannot be condoned by any court. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Following the Supreme Court ruling in V. Nagarajan v. SKS Ispat and Power Ltd., the scheme of the IBC mandates that limitation is calculated from the date of order pronouncement; the principle in National Spot Exchange Ltd. v. Anil Kohli establishes that delay beyond the 15-day proviso cannot be condoned even under Article 142. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Counting from 06.03.2025, filing on 28.04.2025 consumed 54 days (30 days statutory period + 15 days grace period + 9 days beyond condonable threshold), rendering the delay legally incurable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay exceeded the maximum period condonable under Section 61(2) of the IBC, requiring dismissal of both the application and the appeal.
operative_order: IA No. 2928 of 2025 seeking condonation of delay is dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 764 of 2025 is dismissed as barred by limitation.
summary: The Appellant challenged an NCLT order dated 05.03.2025 rejecting a CIRP extension application and ordering liquidation[cite: 16]. The appeal was e-filed on 28.04.2025 with an application seeking condonation of delay, arguing that limitation should run from 15.03.2025 when the Appellant first acquired knowledge of the order[cite: 16]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the application and appeal, holding that under the Supreme Court's ruling in V. Nagarajan, limitation begins from the date of the order, not knowledge[cite: 16]. As 54 days had elapsed, the delay exceeded the statutory 30-day period plus the 15-day grace period under Section 61(2), leaving the court without jurisdiction to condone it[cite: 16].

case_title: Employees Provident Fund Organisation, Nashik vs. Girish Siriram Juneja & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Employees Provident Fund Organisation, Nashik (Appellant, Statutory Creditor); Girish Siriram Juneja (Respondent No. 1, Liquidator); Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation process of Corporate Debtor commenced on 13.04.2023; statutory claims for default in provident fund contributions, damages under Section 14B, and interest under Section 7Q of the EPF & MP Act, 1952. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Initial timely claim under Section 7A filed for Rs. 2,48,13,087/- (admitted for Rs. 2,41,20,619/-); revised claim for Rs. 7,33,82,101/- under Sections 7Q and 14B based on orders dated 23.10.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation commenced on 13.04.2023; initial claim filed on 28.04.2023; revised claim based on orders dated 23.10.2023 filed on 28.10.2023; Liquidator rejected revised claim on 02.01.2024; NCLT Mumbai dismissed IA No. 4943/2024 on 07.03.2025; NCLAT appeal decided on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form C claim submissions dated 28.04.2023; assessment orders under Sections 7Q and 14B dated 23.10.2023; rejection email from Liquidator dated 02.01.2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator rejected the revised claim of Rs. 7.33 crores as time-barred and arising post-liquidation; NCLT Mumbai rejected EPFO's IA No. 4943/2024 on 07.03.2025 holding the claim inadmissible and noting that no Section 42 appeal was filed; EPFO appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether claims for penal damages under Section 14B and interest under Section 7Q of the EPF & MP Act, 1952 arising from assessment orders passed after the liquidation commencement date can be entertained by a Liquidator under the IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Only debts and claims in existence as on the liquidation commencement date are admissible in the liquidation process; claims created or finalized by orders rendered post-liquidation commencement cannot be entertained by the liquidator. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, the cut-off date for crystallizing claims against the corporate debtor is the liquidation commencement date; an EPFO revised claim founded on statutory orders passed months after the liquidation date cannot relate back to displace liquidation timelines. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Orders under Section 7Q and 14B passed on 23.10.2023 definitively established that the liability was determined subsequent to the liquidation commencement date of 13.04.2023. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the application seeking admission of the revised post-liquidation claim.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 693 of 2025 and IA No. 2676 of 2025 are dismissed; the order of NCLT Mumbai dated 07.03.2025 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: The Employees Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO), Nashik appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting its application to direct the Liquidator to admit a revised claim of Rs. 7.33 crores under Sections 7Q and 14B of the EPF & MP Act, 1952[cite: 17]. While EPFO's initial Section 7A claim had been admitted, the revised damages and interest claims arose from orders passed on 23.10.2023, well after the liquidation commencement date of 13.04.2023[cite: 17]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that under the IBBI Liquidation Regulations, only claims in existence as of the liquidation commencement date are admissible[cite: 17].

case_title: Mr. Sridhar Somashekar & Anr. vs. M/s Vinyas Constructions Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Sridhar Somashekar and Mr. Ramesh S (Appellants, Director and Shareholders); M/s Vinyas Constructions Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1, Company); Sreenivasa Garudanahalli Thimmappagowda, Nagaraja Venkatappa Reddy, and Anand Gowda (Respondents 2, 3, and 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Company petition under Sections 241-242 read with Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 challenging illegal board resolutions and statutory filings for oppression and mismanagement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Not a debt default; petition sought declarations that Board Resolutions dated 28.09.2018 and 29.09.2016, alongside Form DIR-12 filings dated 02.10.2018 and 14.10.2018, were illegal and void. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP/34/BB/2019 filed in 2019; NCLT passed impugned order on 23.08.2024 disposing of the petition sine-die pending criminal trial; NCLAT appeal decided on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Impugned Board resolutions, Registrar of Companies DIR-12 filings, and records of parallel criminal proceedings pending before a Magistrate Court regarding identical allegations. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru Bench on 23.08.2024 disposed of CP/34/BB/2019 relying on the service jurisprudence precedent Capt. M. Paul Anthony v. Bharat Gold Mines Ltd., holding that because criminal proceedings were pending regarding the same charges, the company petition must be kept in abeyance with liberty to re-approach; Appellants appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether a company petition alleging oppression and mismanagement under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 can be stayed or kept in abeyance sine-die solely due to the pendency of a parallel criminal proceeding involving similar allegations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of criminal proceedings does not warrant keeping civil company law proceedings in abeyance; civil remedies adjudicating inter-se rights of shareholders must be decided independently since the purpose, standard of proof, and evidentiary rules differ from criminal trials. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 provide statutory remedies to adjudicate prejudice and mismanagement in corporate affairs; applying service law doctrines (such as Capt. M. Paul Anthony) to stall statutory corporate oppression remedies constitutes an abuse of the judicial process. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Standards of evidence in criminal trials (proof beyond reasonable doubt to impose penalties) cannot be imported into or used as a justification to stall summary civil adjudications governed by preponderance of probabilities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in staying the company petition until the conclusion of criminal proceedings; the petition must be decided expeditiously on its own merits without awaiting criminal trial findings.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 09 of 2025 is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Bengaluru dated 23.08.2024 is quashed; CP/34/BB/2019 is remitted back to NCLT Bengaluru to be decided on its own merits without awaiting the criminal proceedings.
summary: Appellants appealed an NCLT Bengaluru order disposing of their oppression and mismanagement petition (CP/34/BB/2019) with liberty to re-approach after the conclusion of parallel criminal proceedings, relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in Capt. M. Paul Anthony[cite: 18]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench set aside the order, ruling that service jurisprudence regarding simultaneous disciplinary and criminal proceedings does not apply to company petitions[cite: 18]. Stalling civil adjudication of shareholder rights due to criminal complaints creates abuse of process[cite: 18]. The matter was remitted back to NCLT for adjudication on merits[cite: 18].

case_title: Koneru Gandhi vs. M/s NRI Power & Infra Corporation Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Koneru Gandhi (Appellant, Respondent No. 2 in Company Petition); M/s NRI Power & Infra Corporation Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent No. 1, Company); Indira Devi (Respondent No. 2, Petitioner in Company Petition); Respondents 3 to 9 (other shareholders/directors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Rectification of the register of members and corporate governance dispute initiated by Respondent No. 2 under Section 59 of the Companies Act, 2013 in CP No. 46/59/HDB/2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory dispute regarding limitation; Appellant asserted that the cause of action expired on 28.11.2021 and argued the petition was barred by limitation. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Cause of action accrued such that the ordinary 3-year limitation period expired on 28.11.2021 (within the COVID-19 exclusion period of 15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022); Company Petition filed on 08.09.2022; NCLT Hyderabad passed composite order on 21.08.2024 holding petition within limitation; NCLAT decided appeal on 16.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Supreme Court Suo Motu Writ Petition (Civil) No. 3/2020 extension orders; corporate filings; chronological computation of the 625 days balance limitation period remaining as of 15.03.2020. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench vide common order dated 21.08.2024 held that CP No. 46/59/HDB/2022 was within limitation by applying the Supreme Court's COVID-19 exclusion directives, but dismissed the petition on other grounds; Appellant appealed under Section 421 challenging solely the adverse finding that the petition was not barred by limitation.
legal_issues: Whether the computation of limitation for a company petition whose limitation period expired during the COVID-19 exclusion window (15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022) is entitled to the exclusion of the entire balance period surviving as on 15.03.2020 with effect from 01.03.2022 pursuant to the Supreme Court ruling in Arif Azim Co. Ltd. v. Aptech Ltd.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a period of limitation expires during the statutorily excluded pandemic window between 15.03.2020 and 28.02.2022, the actual balance period of limitation remaining as on 15.03.2020 becomes available to the litigant starting from 01.03.2022. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: In accordance with the Supreme Court ruling in Arif Azim Company Limited v. Aptech Limited interpreting the Suo Motu Cognizance orders, the extension is not restricted to a flat 90-day grace period from 01.03.2022 if a larger unexpired balance of limitation remained available as on 15.03.2020. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The remaining limitation of 625 days existing on 15.03.2020 extended the deadline from 01.03.2022 to 25.11.2023, establishing conclusively that the company petition instituted on 08.09.2022 was well within time. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in determining that the company petition was not barred by limitation, rendering the appeal devoid of merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 79 of 2024 is dismissed; the finding of the Adjudicating Authority holding CP No. 46/59/HDB/2022 to be within limitation is affirmed; all pending interlocutory applications closed.
summary: The Appellant challenged a finding in an NCLT Hyderabad order dated 21.08.2024 holding that a Section 59 company petition filed by Respondent No. 2 on 08.09.2022 was not barred by limitation[cite: 21]. The Appellant argued that under the Supreme Court's COVID-19 extension orders, the limitation period expired on 30.05.2022 (90 days from 01.03.2022)[cite: 21]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that pursuant to the Supreme Court's decision in Arif Azim Co. Ltd. v. Aptech Ltd., the balance period of 625 days remaining as on 15.03.2020 became available from 01.03.2022, extending limitation up to 25.11.2023[cite: 21]. Hence, the petition was timely[cite: 21].

case_title: Mr. Jangam Gopi vs. D.S.R.K. Saibaba & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Jangam Gopi (Appellant, Ex-Director and Promoter of M/s GJS Infratech Pvt. Ltd.); D.S.R.K Saibaba (Respondent No. 1, Interim Resolution Professional); Canara Bank (Respondent No. 2, Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities availed by the Corporate Debtor (M/s GJS Infratech Pvt. Ltd.) from Canara Bank, leading to insolvency proceedings under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in repayment of financial facilities resulting in CIRP admission under Section 7 of the IBC in CP No. 257/7/HDB/2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Hyderabad Bench ordered service by paper publication on 05.01.2024; affidavit of service perused on 09.02.2024; NCLT set the Corporate Debtor ex-parte on 23.02.2024; CIRP admission order passed; NCLAT appeal decided on 16.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Affidavit of service proving paper publication under Order V Rule 20 CPC; track record of postal returns; records establishing Appellant's participation in parallel DRT proceedings and settlement discussions. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad ordered substituted service by paper publication after postal notices returned undelivered, and set the Corporate Debtor ex-parte on 23.02.2024; NCLT admitted Section 7 application; Appellant appealed under Section 61 asserting violation of Rule 208(1) of Indian Postal Rules, 1933.
legal_issues: Whether an order setting a corporate debtor ex-parte and admitting a Section 7 IBC application is vitiated for lack of natural justice when service was completed via paper publication under Order V Rule 20 of the CPC, notwithstanding non-compliance with the 7-day retention period under Rule 208(1) of the Indian Postal Rules, 1933.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where service of notice by substituted mode via paper publication is duly ordered and verified by an affidavit of service under Order V Rule 20 of the CPC, there is an unrebutted deeming presumption of valid service that cures prior postal non-delivery defects. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 208(1) of the Indian Postal Rules, 1933 applies to returned physical postal articles and cannot override the statutory deeming presumption of complete service arising from newspaper publication under Order V Rule 20(2) of the CPC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Participation in parallel DRT litigation and ongoing debt settlement discussions establishes constructive and actual knowledge of insolvency proceedings, preventing a promoter from claiming ignorance of Section 7 proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Service of notice was validly effected by publication, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in proceeding ex-parte and admitting the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 111 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned admission order passed in CP No. 257/7/HDB/2023 is affirmed.
summary: The Appellant, promoter of M/s GJS Infratech Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order admitting a Section 7 IBC petition filed by Canara Bank[cite: 22]. The Appellant argued that he was set ex-parte without proper service because the post office failed to retain the registered notice for seven days as required by Rule 208(1) of the Indian Postal Rules, 1933[cite: 22]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that the NCLT had validly ordered substituted service through paper publication under Order V Rule 20 CPC[cite: 22]. This created a legal presumption of valid service, especially since the Appellant was actively aware of the dispute through ongoing DRT proceedings[cite: 22].

case_title: Medekar Intisar Mohamed vs. K. Muruganandan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Medekar Intisar Mohamed (Appellant, Erstwhile Director of Corporate Debtor); K. Muruganandan (Respondent, Liquidator of Samaara Leathers Private Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation proceedings of Samaara Leathers Pvt. Ltd.; Liquidator initiated an application under Section 66 of the IBC alleging fraudulent trading and underreported transactions during FY 2017-18 and 2018-19. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Avoidance/fraud claim seeking disgorgement/repayment of Rs. 27,07,470/- to the liquidation estate (comprising Rs. 20,44,411/- in underreported ledger balances and Rs. 6,63,059/- in missing cash balances) based on a forensic audit report. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT Chennai passed impugned order on 06.03.2025 (uploaded on 10.03.2025); appeal e-filed on 23.04.2025 (44 days from uploading, 14 days delay condoned under Section 61(2)); NCLAT decided appeal on 23.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic audit report; statutory auditor's affidavit confirming changes in opening and closing balances; Corporate Debtor's disputed ledger accounts for FY 2017-18 and 2018-19. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IA(IBC)/1592(CHE)/2022 in CP/141/IB/2019 under Section 66, NCLT Chennai on 06.03.2025 directed the Appellant to file an affidavit confirming the accuracy of ledger transactions within two weeks; Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 61 of the IBC is maintainable against a purely interlocutory procedural direction of the Adjudicating Authority directing an erstwhile director to file an affidavit confirming the accuracy of ledger transactions in a pending Section 66 avoidance proceeding.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A purely procedural fact-finding direction issued by the Adjudicating Authority to verify the sanctity of accounts does not determine substantive rights or liabilities and is not appealable under Section 61 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 of the IBC provides an appellate remedy against orders deciding substantive rights; a direction to place an explanatory affidavit on record in a Section 66 proceeding is an incidental case-management order that does not prejudice legal rights. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Requiring a former director to confirm ledger entries in light of conflicting forensic audit reports and auditor affidavits is a routine evidentiary directive, and the filed affidavit remains subject to independent evaluation on merits by the tribunal. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order is purely procedural and preliminary; hence the Appellate Tribunal declines to interfere on merits, affirming the direction without prejudice to the trial before NCLT.
operative_order: Delay of 14 days condoned; Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 275 of 2025 is dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 06.03.2025; pending IAs closed.
summary: The Appellant, erstwhile director of Samaara Leathers Pvt. Ltd., appealed an NCLT Chennai order directing him to file an affidavit confirming the accuracy of ledger entries for FY 2017-18 and FY 2018-19 in a pending Section 66 fraud application seeking recovery of Rs. 27.07 lakhs[cite: 24]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the direction was a purely procedural, fact-finding order aimed at ascertaining account accuracy amidst conflicting forensic audit findings[cite: 24]. Because the order did not determine any substantive rights or liabilities under Section 66, the appeal was dismissed without interfering with the ongoing trial[cite: 24].

case_title: Indian Bank, SAMB Chennai vs. Mr. K.R. Tirumuruhan
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Indian Bank, Stressed Assets Management Branch (Appellant, Financial Creditor); Mr. K.R. Tirumuruhan (Respondent, Personal Guarantor); IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited (Prior Petitioning Financial Creditor in CP(IB) No. 785/2020). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underlying credit facilities availed by the corporate borrower from Indian Bank and other financial creditors, secured by personal guarantee executed by the Respondent. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by the principal corporate borrower and the Personal Guarantor in repayment of financial facilities; Indian Bank filed personal insolvency proceedings under Section 95 in CP(IB)/80/2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Prior Section 95 petition filed against the personal guarantor by IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited in CP(IB) No. 785/2020 triggering interim moratorium under Section 96; Indian Bank filed subsequent Section 95 application in CP(IB)/80/2024; NCLT Chennai dismissed it as infructuous on 06.01.2025; NCLAT decided appeal on 04.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Filings in CP(IB) No. 785/2020; order sheets of NCLT Chennai in CP(IB)/80/2024; coordinate NCLAT judgment dated 30.04.2025 in Comp App (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 121/2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench on 06.01.2025 dismissed Indian Bank's Section 95 application as infructuous with liberty to refile later because a prior Section 95 application against the same personal guarantor was already pending; Indian Bank appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a subsequent application under Section 95 of the IBC can be entertained against a personal guarantor when an earlier Section 95 application by another financial creditor is already pending and an interim moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC is in operation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 96 of the IBC, the filing of an application under Section 95 immediately triggers an interim moratorium in respect of all debts of the debtor, creating a statutory bar that precludes the entertainment or initiation of subsequent personal insolvency applications against the same personal guarantor during its subsistence. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 96 operates as a comprehensive statutory stay on any legal action or proceeding in respect of any debt of the personal guarantor; following the coordinate bench decision in Indian Bank v. T. Prabhakar, subsequent Section 95 petitions are rendered non-maintainable while an earlier petition is sub judice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where court records confirm that a prior Section 95 proceeding against the personal guarantor is pending before the Adjudicating Authority, the statutory moratorium under Section 96 applies automatically as a matter of law. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the subsequent Section 95 application as infructuous with liberty to refile upon culmination of the earlier proceedings.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 150 of 2025 is dismissed; NCLT Chennai requested to expedite the pending Section 95 proceedings.
summary: Indian Bank appealed against an NCLT Chennai order dismissing its Section 95 application against personal guarantor K.R. Tirumuruhan as infructuous, with liberty to file afresh[cite: 28]. The dismissal was premised on the fact that an earlier Section 95 application filed by IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. was already pending against the same guarantor[cite: 28]. Following its own coordinate bench precedent in Indian Bank v. T. Prabhakar, the NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the statutory interim moratorium under Section 96 of the IBC bars any subsequent Section 95 petition against the debtor while a prior petition is pending[cite: 28]. The appeal was dismissed with a request to the NCLT to expedite the pending insolvency proceedings[cite: 28].

case_title: Satyabrat Behera vs. Ashok Agarwal & Anr. (along with connected appeals)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Satyabrat Behera, Proprietor of Satya Logistics (Appellant, Financial Creditor); Ashok Agarwal, Ajay Agarwal, Ankit Agarwal, and Anita Agarwal (Respondent No. 1 in respective appeals, Personal Guarantors to M/s Ankit Ispat Pvt. Ltd.); Mrs. Anjali Nirav Choksi (Respondent No. 2, Resolution Professional); State Bank of India, Central Bank of India, Federal Bank (Intervening Non-Party Banks). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal guarantees executed by the Respondents in favor of Satya Logistics for credit facilities availed by Corporate Debtor M/s Ankit Ispat Private Limited, leading to petitions under Section 95 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on financial debt obligations leading to initiation of personal insolvency proceedings in CP(IB) Nos. 230, 231, 232, and 233 of 2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Ms. Anjali Nirav Choksi appointed IRP on 16.12.2024; Section 99 report taken on record; NCLT heard final arguments and reserved orders on 19.02.2025; matter listed for order delivery on 21.03.2025; NCLT dismissed petitions on 21.03.2025 based on an unnotified mention by non-parties; NCLAT appeals decided on 26.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order sheet dated 19.02.2025 recording reservation of orders; order dated 30.01.2025 in IBA No. 702/2020 before Division Bench-I Chennai; absence of any formal application or advance notice regarding the mention made before Division Bench-II. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Arguments in CP(IB) Nos. 230, 231, 232, and 233/2024 concluded before NCLT Chennai Bench-II and orders reserved on 19.02.2025; on the date fixed for pronouncement (21.03.2025), non-party banks mentioned that separate insolvency petitions were pending against the same guarantors before Bench-I; Bench-II dismissed the petitions without hearing the Appellant; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority committed grave procedural impropriety and violated the principles of natural justice (audi alteram partem) by dismissing reserved Section 95 petitions on the date fixed for pronouncement based on an oral mention by non-party financial institutions without affording the petitioning creditor prior notice or an opportunity of hearing.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once judicial proceedings are concluded and orders are reserved for pronouncement, an adjudicatory forum cannot dismiss the petitions based on fresh facts introduced via an oral mention by a non-party without providing formal notice and a full hearing to the affected litigant. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Summary proceedings under Section 95 to Section 100 of the IBC remain governed by fundamental principles of natural justice and judicial propriety; dismissing a creditor's petition on unverified external statements without reopening the case properly violates audi alteram partem. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Entertaining unverified, unnotified factual representations from entities not arrayed as parties to the company petition when the case is listed solely for judgment pronouncement constitutes fatal procedural unfairness. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The dismissal orders dated 21.03.2025 were rendered in direct breach of natural justice and judicial discipline, necessitating their quashing and remand for fresh hearing.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 271, 272, 273, and 274 of 2025 are allowed; impugned orders dated 21.03.2025 are quashed; matters remitted back to NCLT Bench-II Chennai to redecide afresh after giving both parties an opportunity to be heard; pending IAs closed.
summary: The Appellant (Financial Creditor) appealed against common orders of NCLT Chennai Bench-II dismissing four Section 95 personal insolvency petitions against personal guarantors of M/s Ankit Ispat Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 29] The NCLT had reserved orders on 19.02.2025, but on the date scheduled for pronouncement (21.03.2025), dismissed the petitions based on an oral mention by counsel for external banks (SBI, Central Bank of India, Federal Bank) asserting that separate petitions were pending before Bench-I[cite: 29]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench set aside the dismissals, holding that entertaining submissions from non-parties on the date of order delivery without prior notice or hearing to the Appellant violated natural justice and judicial propriety[cite: 29]. The matters were remanded for fresh adjudication[cite: 29].

case_title: Vinod Khattar vs. Narendra Kumar Sharma RP, Indirapuram Habitat Centre (P) Ltd. (along with connected appeals)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 130 of 2024 (with Nos. 131, 132 & 133 of 2024)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Vinod Khattar, Veena Khattar, Sarthak Khattar, and Subhash Khattar (Appellants, Real Estate Unit Buyers); Narendra Kumar Sharma (Respondent, Resolution Professional of M/s Indirapuram Habitat Centre Private Limited); Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of commercial units and residential studio apartments ('Club Suites' Nos. 1109, 1407, 923, 907, 911, and C-77 to C-87) in the project Indirapuram Habitat Centre, Ghaziabad, under Space Buyers Agreements / Builder Buyer Agreements. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants paid 100% consideration (e.g., Rs. 35,70,000/- each for Club Suites 1109 and 1407 via RTGS) and received assured returns until June 2018; filed Form-CA claims totaling Rs. 65,68,800/- each for recognition as financial creditors in a class (allottees). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 22.08.2019; claims filed in Form CA on 06.09.2019; RP admitted claims as collateral/unsecured financial creditors rather than allottees; NCLT directed RP to reconsider on 22.08.2022; RP rejected allottee status on 22.09.2022 citing CRM omissions; NCLT dismissed IAs on 21.11.2023; NCLAT decided appeals on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder Buyer Agreements dated 15.11.2013 and 06.05.2016; RTGS bank payment receipts showing full consideration; TDS deduction certificates on assured returns; possession offer letters; conflicting corporate debtor CRM software data and alleged surrender records dated 12.12.2016. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP refused to treat Appellants as financial creditors in a class because CRM software did not show their names and units were re-allotted to third parties; NCLT New Delhi Bench-II dismissed Appellants' IAs (Nos. 1377, 1375, 1376, 1385 of 2023) on 21.11.2023 solely by referencing an order in an unrelated matter (IA No. 5177/2022); Appellants appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional and Adjudicating Authority can reject real estate buyers' claims to be categorized as financial creditors in a class (allottees) solely based on omissions in the corporate debtor's CRM software records, without evaluating individual executed Builder Buyer Agreements, proven RTGS payment receipts, and newly alleged unproven surrender claims.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a claimant produces executed allotment contracts, builder-buyer agreements, and undisputed proof of full banking consideration paid to the corporate debtor, the Resolution Professional cannot summarily discard their status as allottees merely because the corporate debtor's internal software or CRM databases failed to capture their allotments or recorded third-party re-allotments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 and Section 21(6A)(b) of the IBC require the Resolution Professional to collate and determine claims based on comprehensive evidence including underlying contracts and banking transactions, rather than relying exclusively on potentially compromised or incomplete company records. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Dismissing multiple claims on individual contracts via a blanket reference to an unrelated interlocutory order, without examining the specific proof of payment and without adjudicating belated assertions of cancellation/surrender, constitutes a failure of judicial scrutiny. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the applications without individualized assessment; the applications must be revived for proper evaluation of executed agreements, payment proofs, and surrender claims.
operative_order: Appeals are partly allowed; the impugned order of NCLT New Delhi dated 21.11.2023 in IA Nos. 1377, 1375, 1376, and 1385 of 2023 is set aside; the applications are revived and remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority for fresh individualized consideration with liberty to file additional affidavits within two weeks; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: The Appellants, purchasers who paid 100% consideration for units in Indirapuram Habitat Centre under Builder Buyer Agreements, appealed an NCLT New Delhi order rejecting their applications to be recognized as financial creditors in a class (allottees)[cite: 30]. The RP had classified them as unsecured creditors/collateral on grounds that the corporate debtor's CRM software lacked their allotment records and showed the units allotted to third parties, while NCLT dismissed their pleas solely relying on an unrelated case order[cite: 30]. The NCLAT Principal Bench set aside the dismissal, holding that valid contracts and unrefuted banking receipts cannot be discarded merely due to CRM omissions[cite: 30].
