The applications were remanded for fresh individualized determination[cite: 30].

case_title: Anil Kumar & Ors. vs. Majinder Singh Sandhu & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Anil Kumar & Ors. (Appellants, arrayed as Respondents No. 7, 10, and 11 in lower court application); Majinder Singh Sandhu & Ors. (Respondents, Applicants in IA No. 3143 of 2022); Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) proceedings wherein Respondents filed IA No. 3143 of 2022 seeking directions for the constitution/reconstitution of the Committee of Creditors (CoC). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Procedural dispute regarding the closure of the right to file a reply affidavit to IA No. 3143 of 2022 after closure of oral arguments. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Arguments in IA No. 3143/2022 heard and closed on 02.05.2025 with directions to submit written submissions within 10 days; compliance checked on 19.05.2025 where closure of arguments was reiterated; Appellants filed IA No. 2398 of 2025 under Rules 11 and 15 of NCLT Rules, 2016 to place reply on record; NCLT dismissed the IA on 21.05.2025; NCLAT appeal decided on 02.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Daily order sheets dated 02.05.2025, 15.05.2023, 19.05.2025, and 21.05.2025; court record showing representation by counsel on 15.05.2023 without any correction application filed under Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak principles. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench rejected Appellants' IA No. 2398 of 2025 on 21.05.2025, refusing permission to file a belated reply affidavit after arguments in IA No. 3143/2022 had already been formally closed on 02.05.2025; Appellants appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a party to an interlocutory proceeding before the NCLT can be permitted to file a reply affidavit under Rules 11 and 15 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 after oral arguments have been concluded and the case is reserved for written submissions and orders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Pleadings cannot be permitted to be filed after the formal conclusion and closure of oral arguments, as permitting indiscriminate post-hearing filings creates unending procedural delays and defeats orderly trial conclusion. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Judicial records are conclusive as to proceedings transacted before a court pursuant to the Supreme Court ruling in State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak; a litigant claiming an inaccurate recording of appearance must apply to that court for rectification rather than challenging it collaterally on appeal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an order sheet conclusively records the closure of arguments on a specific date and no application for rectification of the record is preferred, an application seeking leave to tender fresh responsive pleadings is impermissible. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted in accordance with procedural discipline in rejecting the application to introduce a reply affidavit after hearing of the main application had concluded.
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Ins) Nos. 833 and 834 of 2025 are dismissed; the impugned orders of NCLT New Delhi dated 09.05.2025 and 21.05.2025 are affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Appellants appealed against NCLT New Delhi orders rejecting their application (IA No. 2398 of 2025) seeking leave to file a reply affidavit to IA No. 3143 of 2022 concerning CoC constitution[cite: 40]. The NCLT had closed oral arguments on 02.05.2025 and permitted only written submissions[cite: 40]. Appellants claimed they were unrepresented and could not file written submissions without an on-record reply[cite: 40]. The NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that judicial records are conclusive under the Supreme Court's Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak doctrine[cite: 40]. Furthermore, allowing litigants to tender replies after oral arguments have closed would cause indefinite delay in proceedings[cite: 40].

case_title: Mr. Nagarajan vs. Mohalingam Suresh Kumar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Nagarajan (Appellant, Technical Assistant/Workman); Mohalingam Suresh Kumar (Respondent, Liquidator of M/s Easun Reyrolle Ltd.); M/s Easun Reyrolle Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Employment and service dues claimed by the Appellant against the Corporate Debtor, encompassing balance gratuity, workmen salary, COVID-period salary, and privilege leave encashment. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidator partially rejected Appellant's submitted claim on 06.05.2022; Appellant filed Section 42 appeal seeking admission of full service dues and entitlements. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP on 05.05.2020; liquidation ordered on 17.02.2022; Liquidator partially rejected claim on 06.05.2022; Appellant filed IA No. 1982/CHE/2023 (appeal under Section 42) along with IA No. 1989/CHE/2023 (application to condone delay); NCLT dismissed applications on 01.12.2023; NCLAT appeal decided on 10.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's partial rejection communication dated 06.05.2022; service records, gratuity calculations, and leave encashment records; delay condonation application IA No. 1989/2023 setting out grounds for delay. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai Bench in IBA/1045 & 1169/2019 dismissed IA No. 1982/2023 and IA No. 1989/2023 on 01.12.2023 without examining or recording any findings or reasons on the delay condonation application or the merits of the rejected claims; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether an order of the Adjudicating Authority dismissing an appeal under Section 42 of the IBC along with an application for condonation of delay without providing any reasons, findings, or independent analysis on either the delay or the merits of the claim reflects non-application of mind and is liable to be set aside.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicatory body exercising judicial or quasi-judicial functions must provide reasoned findings when dismissing statutory applications; an unreasoned summary rejection that fails to consider a condonation of delay application or substantive grounds of claim constitutes patent non-application of mind. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 42 of the IBC provides an important appellate safeguard against liquidator decisions; the Adjudicating Authority is under a legal obligation to examine whether delay in preferring the appeal was excusable and whether the rejection of workmen dues was justified on facts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The total absence of reasoning or evaluation of the explanation tendered in the delay condonation application in the impugned order renders the judicial disposal unsustainable in law. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order dated 01.12.2023 suffered from total non-application of mind, warranting that it be quashed and remitted to the NCLT for fresh consideration on merits and limitation.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 67 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order of NCLT Chennai dated 01.12.2023 in IA Nos. 1982/2023 and 1989/2023 is quashed; matters remitted back to NCLT Chennai to redecide on merits and delay after hearing parties.
summary: The Appellant, an employee of M/s Easun Reyrolle Ltd. (in liquidation), appealed an NCLT Chennai order dismissing his Section 42 application and delay condonation application concerning rejected service dues, gratuity, and salary[cite: 41]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench held that the NCLT order contained no findings, analysis, or reasons regarding the delay or the merits of the claim, demonstrating patent non-application of mind[cite: 41]. The impugned order was quashed and the matter was remanded to NCLT Chennai for fresh adjudication[cite: 41].

case_title: Joint Commissioner of Commercial Taxes & GST vs. Smt. Anuradha Bisani
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Joint Commissioner of Commercial Taxes & GST, Cuttack-1 East, Odisha (Appellant, Statutory Creditor); Smt. Anuradha Bisani (Respondent, Liquidator of M/s Lanco Infratech Ltd.); M/s Lanco Infratech Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory tax assessments under the Odisha VAT Act, OET Act, and CST (Odisha) Rules for Assessment Years 2011-12 to 2016-17 against the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory tax dues and penalties totaling Rs. 740,20,84,616/- claimed against the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 07.08.2017; liquidation ordered on 27.08.2018; public announcement in Form A published on 29.08.2018 fixing claim deadline as 26.09.2018; Appellant submitted Form B on 02.09.2020 and revised Form C on 06.10.2020; Liquidator rejected claim on 24.11.2020; Appellant filed defective Section 42 appeal on 16.12.2020 (beyond 14 days) and left defects uncured for over 2.5 years; filed fresh Section 42 application (IA No. 1459/2023) on 16.07.2023; NCLT rejected application on 05.04.2024; NCLAT decided appeal on 30.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator rejection email dated 24.11.2020; Form A notice dated 29.08.2018; Form C claim filed after a two-year delay; records confirming approval of sale of the Corporate Debtor's assets as a going concern to the successful acquirer. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator rejected the belated tax claim on 24.11.2020; NCLT Hyderabad Bench on 05.04.2024 dismissed IA (IBC) No. 1459/2023 holding the Section 42 appeal barred by limitation and unmaintainable after the Corporate Debtor had already been sold as a going concern; Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a statutory tax authority can maintain a belated claim and appeal under Section 42 of the IBC filed years beyond the 14-day statutory limitation window, particularly after the liquidation sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern has attained finality.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory claims submitted years after the liquidation claim cut-off date cannot be entertained once the sale of the corporate debtor as a going concern has attained finality and rights have vested in the acquirer. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 42 of the IBC strictly prescribes a 14-day period to appeal a liquidator's decision; a litigant whose initial appeal is abandoned due to uncured defects cannot institute a second appeal years later to bypass limitation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Regulation 16 of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations (pre-2019 amendment), the claimant bears the burden of establishing substantiated proof of claim within the gazetted timelines, failing which belated statutory claims cannot disrupt settled liquidation transfers. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 42 application filed on 16.07.2023 against the rejection of 24.11.2020 was barred by limitation and extinguished upon the completion of the going-concern sale, rendering the appeal devoid of merit.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 296 of 2024 is dismissed; the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 05.04.2024 is affirmed.
summary: The Commercial Tax Department of Odisha appealed against an NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing its application under Section 42 of the IBC to admit a tax claim of Rs. 740.20 crores against M/s Lanco Infratech Ltd. (in liquidation)[cite: 50]. The claim was originally submitted two years past the public announcement deadline and rejected by the Liquidator on 24.11.2020[cite: 50]. The Appellant filed an initial defective appeal that remained unrectified for over two years before filing a second Section 42 application on 16.07.2023[cite: 50]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeal, holding that the application was heavily barred by limitation under Section 42 and could not be entertained after the Corporate Debtor had already been sold as a going concern[cite: 50].

case_title: Mr. Naseer Ahmed vs. Ravindra Beleyur & Ors. (along with connected appeals)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Mr. Naseer Ahmed, Mrs. Nuzhat Aisha Naseer, and Mr. Awaiz Ahmed (Appellants, Personal Guarantors); Ravindra Beleyur (Respondent, Resolution Professional); State Bank of India (Financial Creditor); M/s Scotts Garments Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal guarantees executed by the Appellants in favor of State Bank of India to secure credit facilities advanced to the Corporate Debtor, M/s Scotts Garments Limited. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in debt repayment leading to admission of personal insolvency applications under Section 95(1) of the IBC against the guarantors on 07.06.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 95 applications admitted on 07.06.2022; Respondent appointed RP on 23.06.2022; last date for claims under Section 102 was 20.08.2022; statutory 21-day timeline to submit repayment plan report under Section 106 expired on 20.08.2022; RP sought information from guarantors and granted extensions up to 19.08.2022; RP submitted Section 106 report on 15.09.2022 with a delay of 26 days; NCLT condoned delay on 11.12.2024; NCLAT appeals decided on 03.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence between RP and guarantors dated 04.07.2022, 26.07.2022, and 04.08.2022 granting extensions of time; statement of objections filed by Personal Guarantor on 21.02.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Resolution Professional filed IA Nos. 8/2023, 7/2023, and 6/2023 before NCLT Bengaluru Bench seeking to place the Section 106 report and list of creditors on record and condone 26 days delay in filing; NCLT allowed the applications on 11.12.2024; Appellants appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in condoning a 26-day delay by the Resolution Professional in submitting the repayment plan report under Section 106 of the IBC when the delay was occasioned by the personal guarantor's own failure to provide the repayment plan and financial disclosures.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory timelines for submitting reports on repayment plans under personal insolvency provisions are directory and facilitative; a minor delay caused by the guarantor's default in furnishing records is condonable to enable substantive adjudication. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 106 of the IBC does not impose a mandatory consequence of nullity or forfeiture for submitting a repayment plan report beyond 21 days; the provision is designed to facilitate the resolution process and cause no procedural prejudice to the debtor. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where contemporaneous email records show that the RP repeatedly extended deadlines at the guarantor's request and the guarantor failed to tender the repayment plan, no lack of bona fides can be attributed to the RP. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority properly exercised discretion in condoning the 26 days delay and taking the Section 106 report on record, causing no legal prejudice to the Appellants.
operative_order: Leave to appeal applications allowed; Company Appeals (AT) (CH) (Ins) Nos. 231, 233, and 235 of 2025 are dismissed; the impugned orders of NCLT Bengaluru dated 11.12.2024 are affirmed without costs.
summary: Appellants (personal guarantors of M/s Scotts Garments Ltd.) appealed against NCLT Bengaluru orders condoning a 26-day delay by the Resolution Professional in submitting the repayment plan report under Section 106 of the IBC and taking the report on record[cite: 51]. Appellants contended the delay lacked sufficient cause and violated statutory timelines[cite: 51]. The NCLAT Chennai Bench dismissed the appeals, holding that Section 106 timelines are directory and that the delay resulted directly from the guarantors' failure to submit the repayment plan despite extensions granted by the RP[cite: 51]. Condoning the 26-day delay expedited the process without causing procedural prejudice[cite: 51].

case_title: G. Yoganand vs. M/s. Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant G. Yoganand is the Personal Guarantor/Applicant; Respondent M/s Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. is the Financial Creditor/Lender Trustee. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Underpinning financial credit facilities where recovery proceedings were initiated against the guarantor, involving an Assignment Agreement dated 04.03.2021 executed in Mumbai and brought to the State of Telangana. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in the context of insolvency proceedings initiated against the personal guarantor under Section 95; exact quantum and default date are not specified in the order. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The disputed Assignment Agreement was executed on 04.03.2021; insolvency petition CP (IB)/359/95/HDB/2022 was instituted in 2022; interim application IA (IBC)/2208/2024 was rejected by NCLT on 11.03.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The core instrument produced was the Assignment Agreement dated 04.03.2021, which the Appellant alleged was insufficiently stamped under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 as applicable to Telangana, alongside Writ Petition No. 29803/2024 pending before the High Court of Telangana for impounding the deed. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB)/359/95/HDB/2022, the Appellant filed IA (IBC)/2208/2024 before NCLT Hyderabad to declare the Assignment Agreement null and void; NCLT dismissed the application on 11.03.2025, against which the Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT or NCLAT can adjudicate upon the validity and sufficiency of stamp duty of an Assignment Agreement when the identical primary subject matter is pending adjudication in a prior writ petition before the High Court.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A subordinate statutory tribunal cannot traverse upon or preempt the jurisdiction of a constitutional High Court when the principal subject matter and relief sought are pending adjudication before the High Court, to avoid contradictory findings across judicial forums. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60/61 IBC jurisdiction does not extend to usurping constitutional writ proceedings under Article 226 where the party has elected not to exhaust the High Court forum regarding statutory impounding under the Indian Stamp Act. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Doctrine of comity of courts and avoidance of conflicting judicial determinations where the primary relief is pending determination before a higher constitutional court. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Appellant's writ petition regarding stamp sufficiency remains pending before the High Court of Telangana, the appellate tribunal declined to entertain the appeal against the NCLT order, dismissing it without prejudice.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 266/2025 stands dismissed without prejudice to the pending adjudication in Writ Petition No. 29803/2024 before the Hon'ble High Court of Telangana.
summary: The Appellant challenged the NCLT Hyderabad's dismissal of IA (IBC)/2208/2024, wherein he had sought to declare an Assignment Agreement dated 04.03.2021 null and void for being insufficiently stamped under the Indian Stamp Act, 1899. The NCLAT observed that the Appellant had already instituted Writ Petition No. 29803/2024 before the High Court of Telangana seeking the identical principal relief of impounding and declaring the instrument insufficiently stamped. Holding that neither the NCLT nor the NCLAT can traverse upon the jurisdiction of the High Court or risk contradictory judicial findings, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal without prejudicing the High Court's upcoming adjudication.

case_title: Anil Kumar & Ors. vs. Majinder Singh Sandhu & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Anil Kumar and other stakeholders/respondents; Respondents No. 1 to 10 are applicant creditors/stakeholders in IA No. 3143 of 2022 along with the Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process proceedings involving an interlocutory application filed for the re-constitution of the Committee of Creditors (CoC). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default details and debt quantum are ancillary as the dispute arose out of CoC reconstitution procedures under IA No. 3143 of 2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Hearing on IA No. 3143/2022 took place on 02.05.2025 where arguments were closed; matter listed for compliance on 19.05.2025; Appellants moved IA 2398/2025 on 21.05.2025 seeking to file a reply affidavit. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Record of proceedings dated 15.05.2023 recording advocate appearance for Respondents 5, 7, 10, and 11, and NCLT daily orders of 02.05.2025 and 19.05.2025 recording that arguments had been fully concluded and only written submissions were permitted. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed IA 2398/2025 on 21.05.2025 refusing permission to file a reply after closure of arguments, directing Registry to explain how it accepted the reply; Appellants appealed this dismissal.
legal_issues: Whether a party can be permitted to introduce a substantive reply affidavit under Rule 11 and Rule 15 of NCLT Rules, 2016 after the adjudicating authority has formally closed oral arguments and reserved liberty only for written submissions.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The judicial record of a court is conclusive and presumed correct unless an application for correction is moved before the very same court; litigants cannot introduce fresh pleadings once oral arguments are concluded, as procedural finality precludes perpetual filing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inherent powers under Rule 11 read with Rule 15 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 cannot be invoked to subvert procedural timelines by filing replies after the closure of arguments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The evidentiary presumption established in State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak (1982 AIR 1249) that court records are sacrosanct and cannot be contradicted by appellate assertions absent a formal rectification application before the original forum. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants failed to seek correction of earlier appearance records and could not reopen pleadings after oral arguments had ended; the dismissal of the interlocutory application by NCLT was upheld.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 833 & 834 of 2025 is dismissed.
summary: The Appellants challenged NCLT New Delhi's orders dated 09.05.2025 and 21.05.2025 rejecting IA 2398/2025, which sought permission under Rule 11 read with Rule 15 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 to file a reply affidavit to IA No. 3143/2022 (concerning CoC reconstitution) after oral arguments were formally closed on 02.05.2025. The Appellants contended they could not file written submissions without an on-record reply and disputed their recorded appearance. The NCLAT, applying the Supreme Court's ruling in State of Maharashtra v. Ramdas Shrinivas Nayak, held that judicial records are sacrosanct unless rectified by the same bench and that permitting pleadings after argument closure would defeat expeditious adjudication. The appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Girish Siriram Juneja, RP, Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd. & Anr. vs. Soneko Marketing Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Girish Siriram Juneja (Resolution Professional/Appellant); Committee of Creditors of Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd. (CoC/Appellant); Soneko Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor holding 0.20% admitted debt/Respondent No. 1); Independent Sugar Corporation Ltd. [INSCO] (Resolution Applicant/Respondent No. 3); AGI Greenpac Pvt. Ltd. (Erstwhile Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) of Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd. involving submission and approval of resolution plans. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted debt metrics of the Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP; Respondent No. 1 holds an operational claim representing 0.20% of total admitted debt. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 21.10.2021; CoC approved AGI Greenpac's plan on 27.10.2022; NCLT approved plan on 28.04.2023; Supreme Court set aside AGI's plan on 29.01.2025 for lack of CCI approval and directed reconsideration; IBBI issued show cause notice suspending RP's Authorisation for Assignment (AFA) on 30.01.2025; CoC approved INSCO's plan on 04.02.2025; Respondent No. 1 filed Intervention Petition No. 5/2025 on 07.03.2025 seeking RP removal; Supreme Court dismissed review petitions on 16.05.2025 directing CIRP completion in 6 weeks; NCLT split order passed on 30.04.2025, Third Member opinion rendered on 10.06.2025, and final NCLT order passed on 13.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: IBBI show-cause notice dated 30.01.2025 initiating disciplinary proceedings under Section 219; Delhi High Court order in WP (C) No. 3065/2025 recording IBBI's statement that AFA suspension does not debar existing assignments; CoC resolution approving INSCO plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In IVN.P. No. 5/KB/2025, the NCLT Kolkata Bench split on 30.04.2025 (Judicial Member ordering RP replacement under Part III/Bye-Law 23A; Technical Member finding lack of locus and infructuous prayers); Third Member on 10.06.2025 affirmed locus to intervene but did not rule on merits/replacement; NCLT on 13.06.2025 disposed of the application citing a non-existent majority on Point (iii) to replace RP; RP and CoC appealed.
legal_issues: Whether suspension of Authorisation for Assignment (AFA) under Bye-Law 23A of the IBBI Model Bye-Laws automatically debars a Resolution Professional from continuing with pending/existing assignments or merely restricts accepting fresh assignments; and whether the NCLT's final order of 13.06.2025 ordering replacement of the RP on a purported majority view was legally sustainable when the Third Member never concurred on that issue.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim statutory suspension of a professional licence/authorisation pending enquiry prohibits the assumption of new mandates but does not automatically invalidate ongoing, pre-existing statutory assignments in the absence of explicit statutory mandate or formal removal by the competent body. Further, an order disposing of an application on a purported majority opinion is void if the referral bench never concurred on that specific point of difference. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Bye-Law 23A read alongside Regulation 7A of the IBBI (Insolvency Professionals) Regulations, 2016 and Regulation 13(6) of the IBBI (Inspection and Investigation) Regulations, 2017 shows that suspension of AFA operates prospectively against accepting fresh assignments; it does not debar an IP from discharging ongoing, pre-existing obligations. Sections 97 and 98 of IBC apply exclusively to Part III (individuals/partnerships) and cannot be invoked to replace an RP in a corporate insolvency under Part II. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Standard of quorum and majority rule under Section 419(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, requiring demonstrable concordance of views among members on points of difference referred. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: There was no majority decision on the replacement of the RP, and Bye-Law 23A does not bar the RP from continuing with the present assignment; consequently, the replacement direction is quashed and NCLT is directed to hear the plan approval application.
operative_order: Appeals are partly allowed; the impugned order dated 13.06.2025 directing IBBI to replace Resolution Professional Girish Siriram Juneja is set aside; the NCLT is directed to forthwith hear and decide the Resolution Plan approval application pursuant to the Supreme Court's directions dated 16.05.2025.
summary: The NCLAT set aside the NCLT Kolkata Bench's order directing the replacement of Resolution Professional Girish Siriram Juneja in the CIRP of Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd. The NCLT had disposed of an operational creditor's intervention petition based on a purported majority opinion after the RP's Authorisation for Assignment (AFA) was suspended by IBBI under Bye-Law 23A. The NCLAT held that the Third Member had only affirmed the applicant's locus to intervene and had expressed no opinion on replacing the RP, rendering the claimed majority non-existent. On the substantive legal question, the Tribunal ruled that suspension under Bye-Law 23A only debars an IP from accepting fresh assignments and does not disqualify them from concluding pending assignments.

case_title: Myotic Trading Private Limited vs. Deepak Maini, RP of Amzen Transportation Industries Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Myotic Trading Pvt. Ltd. (Lead Member of Consortium/Appellant); Fortune Global Solutions Pte. Ltd. (Withdrawing Consortium Partner/Respondent No. 7); Amzen Transportation Industries Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Deepak Maini (Resolution Professional/Respondent No. 1); Cosmic CRF Ltd. (Rival Prospective Resolution Applicant/Respondent No. 3); Prudent ARC Ltd. and UCO Bank (CoC Members/Respondents No. 4 & 5). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of resolution plans under Form-G dated 20.04.2024 for CIRP of Amzen Transportation Industries Ltd. requiring a minimum tangible net worth of Rs. 100 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate debtor admitted into CIRP on 04.05.2022 under CP(IB)3/ND/2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Form-G issued on 20.04.2024; Myotic-Fortune consortium submitted EOI on 06.05.2024 and Resolution Plan on 02.07.2024; CoC declared Cosmic CRF ineligible under Section 29A on 19.10.2024; NCLT remanded Cosmic CRF's eligibility to CoC on 09.01.2025; Fortune revoked PoA and withdrew from consortium on 06.03.2025 and 07.03.2025; CoC reversed stance and declared Cosmic CRF eligible on 06.03.2025; Myotic filed IA 1240/2025 on 10.03.2025; ED issued Provisional Attachment Order against CD on 25.03.2025; Myotic filed IA 2548/2025 on 27.05.2025; NCLT dismissed both applications on locus on 28.05.2025 and 29.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audit reports by AHSK & Co. and Priyanka Sharma & Associates (PSA) finding Cosmic CRF ineligible under Section 29A(a),(c),(h),(j); conflicting legal opinion of Senior Advocate; Fortune's formal revocation emails/affidavit; financial statements establishing Myotic's individual net worth at Rs. 43.21 Crores vs. required Rs. 100 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi dismissed IA 1240/2025 (challenging Cosmic's eligibility) and IA 2548/2025 (seeking CoC reconstitution and RP replacement) on 28.05.2025 and 29.05.2025 solely for lack of locus due to Fortune's withdrawal; Myotic appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a lead consortium member whose partner has withdrawn retains locus standi to participate or challenge rival bids as a Prospective Resolution Applicant when its individual net worth falls below the RFRP threshold; whether the CoC and RP can declare a resolution applicant eligible under Section 29A solely on a single legal opinion while discarding multiple expert forensic audit reports; and whether an application raising serious governance lapses and related-party presence in the CoC can be dismissed on locus without a speaking order.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant who fails to satisfy the mandatory threshold qualifications of an RFRP upon the exit of a consortium partner cannot assert rights as a Prospective Resolution Applicant. However, Section 29A compliance is an absolute statutory bar going to the root of the process that the RP, CoC, and Tribunal must enforce strictly, irrespective of adversary standing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A is mandatory and cannot be overridden by the commercial wisdom of the CoC or bypassed relying merely on a selective legal opinion when comprehensive expert audit reports demonstrate ineligibility. An 'irrevocable' Power of Attorney not coupled with interest does not prevent a joint venture partner from exiting. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantive scrutiny of Section 29A disqualification based on unrefuted corporate linkages and slump sales involving connected parties; non-speaking summary dismissals of applications challenging statutory integrity are legally unsustainable. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Myotic lacked standing as a solitary PRA, but Cosmic CRF was demonstrably ineligible under Section 29A based on on-record forensic findings; the CIRP was vitiated and must restart with a fresh Form-G, while IA 2548/2025 must be reheard on merits.
operative_order: Both appeals are partly allowed; NCLT's finding that Myotic lacked locus as a PRA is affirmed, but Cosmic CRF Ltd. is declared ineligible under Section 29A and its clearance is set aside; CIRP is directed to proceed afresh from the stage of issuing a new Form-G; order in IA 2548/2025 is set aside and remitted to NCLT for de novo consideration on merits.
summary: In the CIRP of Amzen Transportation Industries Ltd., Myotic Trading challenged NCLT New Delhi's summary dismissal of its applications challenging rival bidder Cosmic CRF's Section 29A eligibility and seeking reconstitution of the CoC. The NCLT had held that Myotic lost its locus standi because its consortium partner Fortune had withdrawn, dropping Myotic's individual net worth below the mandatory Rs. 100 Crore threshold. The NCLAT affirmed that Myotic lacked locus as an individual PRA but held that Section 29A compliance is non-negotiable. Finding that the CoC arbitrarily declared Cosmic CRF eligible based on a lone legal opinion while ignoring prior expert reports establishing disqualification, the Appellate Tribunal declared Cosmic CRF ineligible, quashed the bidding process, directed the issuance of a fresh Form-G, and remitted the CoC reconstitution application for decision on merits.

case_title: ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Interlocutory Application Nos. 254/2023, 6020/2023 in CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 1038/2020 & IA Nos. 705/2022, 6019/2023, 217/2025 in CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 1043/2020
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are ArcelorMittal India Pvt. Ltd. and ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel India Ltd. (AMNSIL/Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 is SREI Infrastructure Finance Ltd. (SIFL/Financial Creditor); Applicants seeking impleadment/intervention are SREI Multiple Asset Investment Trust (SMAIT/pre-CIRP shareholder of OSPIL), Vir Jai Khosla (shareholder in SIFL), Gujarat Operational Creditors Association & Sayam Shares & Securities (P) Ltd. (erstwhile Operational Creditors/assignees of Essar Steel), and Muhammad Ali Sheikh (foreign shareholder of parent company AMSA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation of approved Resolution Plans of Essar Steel India Ltd. and Odisha Slurry Pipeline Infrastructure Ltd. (OSPIL), and payment of Right to Use (RTU) charges of slurry pipeline. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute concerns NCLT's direction to AMNSIL to pay Rs. 1300 Crores to OSPIL as CIRP costs for usage of slurry pipeline. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Essar Steel CIRP resolution approved by Supreme Court on 15.11.2019; OSPIL resolution plan approved by NCLT on 02.03.2020 and affirmed by NCLAT on 18.01.2022; SIFL filed IA 245/2020 before NCLT Ahmedabad resulting in impugned order dated 10.11.2020; interim stay granted by NCLAT on 04.12.2020; various third-party impleadment applications filed between 2022 and 2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved resolution plans extinguishing pre-CIRP shareholding and operational claims; prior NCLAT judgment dated 18.01.2022 rejecting SMAIT's claim for equity payment; share purchase records showing Muhammad Ali Sheikh bought 85 shares in parent company in June 2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad allowed SIFL's IA 245/2020 on 10.11.2020 directing AMNSIL to pay Rs. 1300 Crores to OSPIL; AMNSIL appealed; multiple third parties filed interlocutory applications seeking impleadment or intervention to attack the resolution plans and claim entitlement to the Rs. 1300 Crores payout.
legal_issues: Whether third parties whose pre-CIRP rights and claims were extinguished upon final approval and implementation of resolution plans possess any direct, legally enforceable interest under Order 1 Rule 10 CPC to be impleaded in an appeal concerning post-CIRP cost adjudication; and whether a shareholder or stranger can claim an independent right of intervention under Order 1 Rule 8A CPC to address questions of law.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A party seeking impleadment must establish a direct and subsisting legal interest in the subject matter of the lis as distinguished from a commercial or collateral interest; once a resolution plan is approved and implemented, all pre-CIRP claims and shareholding stand extinguished, denuding erstwhile stakeholders of any locus standi to reopen concluded issues. Further, Order 1 Rule 8A CPC is an enabling discretion for the court to seek assistance and confers no substantive right on third-party intervenors to thrust legal submissions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) of the IBC, as expounded in Ghanshyam Mishra, creates a complete clean slate extinguishing all pre-CIRP claims not included in the plan; Section 424 of the Companies Act, 2013 guides tribunal procedure by principles of natural justice and principles analogous to Order 1 Rule 10 CPC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The two-fold test of a necessary/proper party: (i) whether relief is claimed directly against the party, and (ii) whether an effective order can be rendered in their absence without altering the character of the litigation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: All applicants are total strangers whose pre-CIRP claims were fully extinguished, and their applications represent a vexatious attempt to expand the litigation and relitigate settled issues; hence, all impleadment and intervention applications must be rejected.
operative_order: Interlocutory Application Nos. 705/2022, 254/2023, 217/2025, 6019/2023, and 6020/2023 are dismissed/rejected; the main company appeals are directed to be listed for final hearing.
summary: In appeals preferred by ArcelorMittal Nippon Steel India Ltd. against NCLT Ahmedabad's order directing payment of Rs. 1300 Crores to OSPIL as slurry pipeline RTU charges, multiple third parties (including an erstwhile shareholder of OSPIL, a shareholder of lender SIFL, an association of erstwhile operational creditors of Essar Steel, and a minority shareholder of ArcelorMittal SA) filed applications seeking impleadment or intervention under Order 1 Rule 10 and Order 1 Rule 8A CPC to claim shares in the payout and challenge past CIRP approvals. The NCLAT rejected all applications, holding that approval of the resolution plans extinguished all pre-CIRP claims and rights under Section 31 IBC. The applicants lacked direct legal interest, and Order 1 Rule 8A CPC is merely an enabling judicial power that gives strangers no right to intervene.

case_title: Mr. Anil Kohli, RP for Dunar Foods Ltd. vs. Directorate of Enforcement & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mr. Anil Kohli, Resolution Professional (and subsequent Monitoring Professional) of Dunar Foods Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Directorate of Enforcement (ED); Respondent No. 2 is Shri Amit Gupta (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by Dunar Foods Ltd. from a consortium led by State Bank of India (SBI), Canara Bank, and Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 758,73,62,546/- at the time of filing Section 7 petition, leading to NPA classification on 26.08.2014 and SARFAESI demand notice for Rs. 795,60,25,675.16. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated and Section 14 moratorium imposed on 22.12.2017; ED issued Provisional Attachment Order (PAO No. 12/2017) attaching properties worth Rs. 177,33,94,800/- on 26.12.2017; RP filed MA 129/2018 on 16.02.2018 seeking quashing of PAO; NCLT dismissed MA on 21.05.2018; PMLA Adjudicating Authority confirmed attachment on 11.06.2018; NCLT approved Resolution Plan on 26.11.2019 (rectified on 27.01.2020). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: ECIR No. ECIR/14/MZO/2013/PD AGRO/1733 registered by ED tracing proceeds of crime from associate entity M/s PD Agroprocessors Pvt. Ltd. into Dunar Foods Ltd.; PAO dated 26.12.2017; confirmation order under Section 8(3) PMLA dated 11.06.2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench vide order dated 21.05.2018 in MA 129/2018 held that PMLA attachment is not barred by Section 14 moratorium and that NCLT has no jurisdiction to direct ED to release attached properties; RP appealed.
legal_issues: Whether provisional attachment of assets under Section 5(1) of the PMLA violates the statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC; whether Section 238 of the IBC overrides the provisions of the PMLA regarding proceeds of crime; and whether the NCLT/NCLAT has jurisdiction under Section 60(5) to review or quash attachment orders confirmed under the PMLA.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Insolvency and anti-money laundering enactments operate in distinct statutory spheres; properties identified as proceeds of crime under criminal penal statutes do not constitute unencumbered commercial assets of the corporate debtor available for resolution. Insolvency tribunals lack jurisdiction under public law to review, stay, or quash attachment orders passed and confirmed by competent authorities under the PMLA. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 IBC bars suits and debt execution actions to preserve lawful corporate assets; it does not impede penal actions under the PMLA against tainted properties. Section 238 overrides laws only where there is irreconcilable conflict in the same legislative field. Section 32A immunity operates prospectively only after resolution plan approval and management transfer, and does not retrospectively invalidate prior attachments. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Public law jurisdictional bar; under Embassy Property Developments and Kalyani Transco, statutory bodies exercising penal/public law powers under the PMLA cannot have their orders reviewed by NCLT/NCLAT under Section 60(5) or Section 61 IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The attachment of tainted assets by ED does not violate Section 14 moratorium, IBC does not override PMLA regarding proceeds of crime, and NCLAT has no jurisdiction to interfere with confirmed PMLA attachments; the appropriate remedy lies before the PMLA Appellate Tribunal under Section 26 PMLA.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 389 of 2018 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 21.05.2018 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in MA No. 129 of 2018 is affirmed; all pending IAs are closed without costs.
summary: The Resolution Professional of Dunar Foods Ltd. challenged NCLT Mumbai's order refusing to direct the Directorate of Enforcement (ED) to release assets valued at Rs. 177.33 Crores provisionally attached under the PMLA four days after CIRP admission. The RP argued that the attachment violated the Section 14 moratorium and was overridden by Section 238 IBC. Applying Supreme Court precedents in Embassy Property Developments and Kalyani Transco v. Bhushan Power & Steel, the NCLAT held that the IBC and PMLA operate in separate domains and that tainted proceeds of crime do not form part of the resolution estate. It affirmed that Section 14 does not bar PMLA attachments, Section 238 does not override criminal forfeiture, and company law tribunals lack jurisdiction under public law to interfere with confirmed PMLA attachment orders.

case_title: Bizloan Private Limited vs. Mr. Amit Chandrashekhar Poddar, Liquidator for Autocop (India) Private Limited
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 210 of 2024 & I.A. No. 718 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Bizloan Private Limited (Financial Creditor claiming secured status); Respondent is Mr. Amit Chandrashekhar Poddar, Liquidator of Corporate Debtor M/s Autocop (India) Private Limited. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities in the form of Sales Bill Discounting (SBD) and Purchase Bill Discounting (PBD) aggregating to Rs. 1 Crore provided by Appellant to the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding claim of Rs. 1 Crore admitted in full by the Resolution Professional/Liquidator. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 16.03.2022; public announcement Form-A on 24.03.2022; Appellant filed Form C on 04.04.2022; Corporate Debtor ordered into liquidation on 19.05.2023; Liquidator classified Appellant as an unsecured creditor; Appellant filed IA No. 2620/2023 before NCLT Mumbai seeking classification as a Secured Financial Creditor. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Certificate/proof of charge registration over assets of the Corporate Debtor registered with the Central Registry of Securitisation Asset Reconstruction and Security Interest of India (CERSAI); absence of Form CHG-1 charge certificate issued by the Registrar of Companies (RoC) under Section 77(1) of the Companies Act, 2013; legal opinion dated 06.02.2023 obtained by RP confirming secured status. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-II dismissed IA No. 2620/2023 vide order dated 19.12.2023, upholding the Liquidator's decision that registration under Section 77 of the Companies Act is mandatory to claim secured creditor status in liquidation; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a financial creditor who has registered its security interest with CERSAI under Section 20 of the SARFAESI Act, but failed to register the charge with the Registrar of Companies (RoC) under Section 77 of the Companies Act, 2013, can be treated as a Secured Financial Creditor in liquidation proceedings under Section 52 of the IBC read with Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In corporate liquidation proceedings governed by the IBC, proof of a security interest is not restricted exclusively to registration with the Registrar of Companies; valid registration with CERSAI or an Information Utility independently establishes the status of a secured creditor under the specific insolvency regulations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 52(3) of the IBC enables proof of security interest by records of an information utility or by means specified by the Board. Under Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, clauses (a), (b), and (c) are disjunctive (separated by 'or'), creating three independent alternative modes of proof, including clause (c) (registration with CERSAI). By virtue of Section 238 of the IBC and the principle lex posterior derogat priori, Section 52(3) read with Regulation 21 prevails over Section 77(3) of the Companies Act, 2013 in the sphere of insolvency and liquidation. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Disjunctive statutory evidentiary criteria; production of valid CERSAI registration records is legally sufficient to establish security interest before a liquidator without requiring an RoC charge certificate. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant proved the existence of its charge through CERSAI registration and was entitled to be classified as a Secured Financial Creditor under Section 52 of the IBC.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 210 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 19.12.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-II in IA No. 2620/2023 is set aside, and IA No. 2620/2023 is restored; the Appellant is held to be a Secured Financial Creditor; parties directed to appear before NCLT on 14.07.2025.
summary: Bizloan Private Limited challenged the NCLT Mumbai Bench's order upholding the Liquidator's classification of the Appellant as an unsecured creditor of Autocop (India) Pvt. Ltd. The Liquidator argued that under Section 77(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, no charge could be recognized without registration with the RoC. The NCLAT reversed the decision and allowed the appeal, ruling that Section 52(3) of the IBC read with Regulation 21 of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 provides three alternative modes for proving security interest, using the disjunctive word 'or'. The Tribunal held that CERSAI registration is sufficient under Regulation 21(c) to prove secured status, and that the IBC framework overrides Section 77(3) of the Companies Act by virtue of the non-obstante clause in Section 238.

case_title: Axis Bank Ltd. vs. Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Axis Bank Ltd. (Escrow Bank and Financial Creditor of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Asset Reconstruction Company (India) Ltd. [ARCIL] (Financial Creditor/Applicant in IA 126/2024); Siti Networks Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor; Rohit Ramesh Mehra is the Resolution Professional; other lenders are Aditya Birla Finance Ltd., IDBI Bank Ltd., IndusInd Bank Ltd., and RBL Bank Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Consortium lending and escrow account mechanism maintained by Corporate Debtor with Axis Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 148,82,90,236/- by Siti Networks Ltd. leading to admission into CIRP on 22.02.2023; Axis Bank swept and distributed Rs. 143.15 Crores during the stay period. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application admitted on 22.02.2023; interim stay granted on 07.03.2023 in CA (AT) (Ins) No. 274/2023; withdrawals made by Axis Bank between 31.03.2023 and 05.06.2023; appeal dismissed on 10.08.2023 upholding CIRP admission; Supreme Court dismissed Civil Appeal No. 5340/2023 on 01.09.2023; ARCIL filed IA 126/2024 on 16.12.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Escrow account statements establishing debit of Rs. 143.15 Crores (including direct retention of Rs. 70.63 Crores by Axis Bank and transfers to other lenders); Joint Lenders' Meeting minutes dated 25.04.2023 and 04.05.2023 recording objections to unilateral set-off. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-III allowed ARCIL's IA 126/2024 on 01.10.2024 ordering Axis Bank and consortium lenders to reverse and remit Rs. 143.15 Crores back to the Corporate Debtor's account; Axis Bank appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the interim stay of a CIRP admission order suspends the Section 14 moratorium and entitles an escrow bank to exercise contractual banker's lien and set-off; whether an application seeking refund of appropriated amounts is barred by res judicata or issue estoppel following dismissal of the appeal; and whether the doctrine of restitution requires the bank to refund all monies swept during the operation of the interim stay upon dismissal of the appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interim stay order holds the operation of the impugned order in abeyance but does not quash it or wipe it out of existence. Upon final dismissal of the substantive appeal, the interim order merges and dissolves, and any party that appropriated benefits or altered the debtor's estate under cover of the stay order is bound by the doctrine of restitution (actus curiae neminem gravabit) to disgorge the proceeds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Admission under Section 7 IBC initiates proceedings in rem and fixes the Insolvency Commencement Date permanently under Section 5(12); an interim stay does not lift the statutory moratorium or permit preferential individual recoveries in violation of the collective distribution scheme of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Section 11 CPC doctrine of res judicata requires a conscious, conclusive adjudication on merits; mere summary closure of interim applications upon dismissal of the parent appeal does not constitute a decision on merits. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Axis Bank took a calculated risk in unilaterally appropriating Rs. 143.15 Crores while the admission order was stayed; upon dismissal of the appeal on 10.08.2023, Axis Bank became strictly liable under the doctrine of restitution to refund the entire amount to the Corporate Debtor.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1975 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 01.10.2024 in IA 126/2024 is affirmed, and Axis Bank is directed to remit the appropriated amounts back to the Corporate Debtor's CIRP account forthwith along with accrued interest; all pending IAs closed.
summary: Axis Bank appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order in IA 126/2024 directing it and other consortium lenders to refund Rs. 143.15 Crores swept from Siti Networks Ltd.'s escrow account during an interim stay of the CIRP admission order. Axis Bank argued that the stay suspended the Section 14 moratorium, restoring its contractual set-off rights, and that the closure of earlier applications by the NCLAT barred ARCIL's claim under res judicata. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that a stay order merely holds an order in abeyance without erasing the in rem insolvency status. Once the appeal against admission was dismissed, the doctrine of restitution applied, obligating Axis Bank to return all appropriated funds to the Corporate Debtor.

case_title: Moneywise Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. vs. Arunava Sikdar, RP of M/s Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Moneywise Financial Services Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor/NBFC); Respondent Arunava Sikdar, Resolution Professional of M/s Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/alleged Corporate Guarantor); Indirapuram Habitat Centre Pvt. Ltd. [IHCPL] (Principal Borrower/group company). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan facility of Rs. 10 Crores sanctioned under Term Sheet dated 07.04.2016 and Master Loan Agreement (MLA) dated 22.04.2016 extended to IHCPL, wherein the Corporate Debtor allegedly stood as corporate guarantor under Clause 28 of the MLA and executed a cross-collateralization Joint Declaration dated 27.12.2017. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding claim of Rs. 14,59,89,580/- (principal + accrued interest) claimed by the Appellant under the guarantee. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against IHCPL initiated on 22.08.2019 where Appellant lodged an admitted claim of Rs. 14,45,22,111/- on 07.09.2019; CIRP against Corporate Debtor Dream Procon commenced on 06.09.2019; last date for claims was 29.10.2019; Appellant filed Form C for another loan on 25.10.2019; Appellant filed belated Form C for the guarantee claim on 20.10.2020 (delay of 388 days); RP rejected claim on 13.11.2020; Appellant filed IA 767/2021 on 27.01.2021; CoC approved Resolution Plan with 90.66% majority on 07.05.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Master Loan Agreement dated 22.04.2016 containing Clause 28; Joint Declaration dated 27.12.2017; complete absence of any standalone executed Deed of Guarantee dated 22.04.2016, absence of Board Resolution from the Corporate Debtor authorizing the guarantee, and no record of guarantee invocation notice issued prior to the ICD (06.09.2019). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench dismissed Appellant's IA No. 767 of 2021 on 05.12.2023 holding that no direct disbursal was made to the Corporate Debtor and the claim did not qualify under Section 5(8); Appellant appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a clause in a composite tripartite loan agreement constitutes a valid and enforceable corporate guarantee giving rise to a financial debt under Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC in the absence of a standalone deed, board resolution, and pre-CIRP invocation; whether a financial claim filed with a 388-day delay after the claims deadline and post-approval of a resolution plan by the CoC is barred by limitation; and whether a creditor can pursue an identical unadjusted claim against both the principal borrower and the corporate guarantor without an adjustment mechanism.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An enforceable corporate guarantee under insolvency law cannot be inferred casually and must be evidenced by demonstrable corporate authority and executed instruments; an uninvoked contingent guarantee does not crystallize into an enforceable financial debt on the insolvency commencement date. Furthermore, stale claims submitted after an inordinate, unexplained delay and following approval of a resolution plan by the CoC cannot be admitted, as doing so violates statutory time discipline and prejudices third-party rights. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(i) encompasses guarantee liabilities, but the existence of a binding legal commitment must be proven; Clause 28 of an MLA requiring first demand invocation cannot be treated as a mature financial debt when no invocation occurred prior to the Section 14 statutory cutoff. Regulation 12(2) of the CIRP Regulations read with Section 12 IBC mandates strict adherence to procedural milestones, barring open-ended admissions. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict documentation test; failure to produce the alleged Deed of Guarantee referenced in Form C, lack of a board resolution under the Companies Act, and absence of invocation notices prove non-existence of a crystallized debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor never executed an authorized, enforceable guarantee; the guarantee was never invoked; the claim was submitted 388 days late after CoC plan approval; and filing an identical unadjusted claim constituted impermissible duplication/double-dipping.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 310 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 05.12.2023 passed by NCLT New Delhi in IA No. 767 of 2021 is affirmed; all pending IAs are closed without costs.
summary: Moneywise Financial Services appealed the NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of its application seeking admission of a Rs. 14.59 Crore claim as a financial debt against Corporate Debtor Dream Procon Pvt. Ltd., based on an alleged corporate guarantee in Clause 28 of a Master Loan Agreement executed for credit facilities extended to group entity IHCPL. The NCLAT affirmed the rejection on three grounds: first, the Appellant failed to produce any formal deed of guarantee or board resolution and never invoked the guarantee before CIRP commencement; second, the claim was lodged 388 days after the claims deadline and after the CoC had already approved a resolution plan; and third, the Appellant had already secured admission of the full claim in IHCPL's CIRP without proposing any adjustment mechanism, amounting to impermissible duplication.

case_title: Unified Titanium Common Association vs. Earth Iconic Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. Through Liquidator
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 250 of 2025 & I.A. No. 959 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Unified Titanium Common Association (UTCA), a Section 8 association of homebuyers/allottees in the Earth Titanium Project; Respondent is Earth Iconic Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in Liquidation) represented by Liquidator Harish Chander Manchanda. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of real estate units in the 'Earth Titanium Project' and submission of a Scheme of Compromise during liquidation proceedings. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dues arising under CIRP initiated under Section 7 and subsequent liquidation order dated 10.01.2020; delay in filing the present appeal was 117 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation commenced on 10.01.2020; Appellant filed IA No. 3698/2024 challenging rejection of compromise scheme; NCLT passed interim adjournment order on 02.08.2024; 30-day appeal limitation ended on 01.09.2024 and 15-day condonable period expired on 16.09.2024; Appellant had filed CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 1877/2024 challenging earlier daily orders on 02.08.2024, but on online refiling on 23.09.2024 substituted the challenge with order dated 02.08.2024; NCLAT dismissed CA 1877/2024 on 26.11.2024 with liberty to challenge 02.08.2024 order in accordance with law; present appeal filed on 27.12.2024 with IA 959/2025 for condoning 117 days delay. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Online filing logs showing substitution/replacement of impugned orders during defect refiling on 23.09.2024 without tribunal leave; orders dated 29.07.2024, 30.07.2024, and 02.08.2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Challenging NCLT New Delhi Court-V's order dated 02.08.2024 in IA 3698/2024, Appellant filed the appeal after 117 days delay, seeking benefit of Section 14 of the Limitation Act for the time spent prosecuting the previous defective appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLAT has the jurisdiction under Section 61(2) proviso of the IBC to condone a delay beyond the maximum extendable period of 15 days by invoking Section 14 of the Limitation Act, where the appellant engaged in unauthorized substitution of the impugned order during defect refiling in an earlier dismissed appeal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The appellate jurisdiction under the IBC is strictly circumscribed by statute; the Appellate Tribunal has no power to condone delay beyond the 15-day period stipulated in the proviso to Section 61(2) on equitable considerations or under Section 14 of the Limitation Act where the litigant failed to prosecute the prior proceedings with due diligence and good faith. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61(2) of the IBC prescribes a 30-day limitation period extendable by no more than 15 days upon showing sufficient cause. The limitation clock begins running from the date of pronouncement. Section 14 of the Limitation Act requires bona fide prosecution in good faith under Section 2(h); surreptitiously substituting an impugned order at the refiling stage after limitation has expired defeats good faith and disentitles the party from time exclusion. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The five-fold test for Section 14 Limitation Act under Consolidated Engineering Enterprises; an act lacking due care, attention, and procedural transparency cannot satisfy the statutory definition of good faith. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay of 117 days exceeds the statutory condonation threshold of 15 days under Section 61(2) of the IBC, and the benefit of Section 14 is unavailable due to reckless conduct; the appeal is barred by limitation.
operative_order: Interlocutory Application No. 959 of 2025 (condonation of delay) is dismissed; consequently, Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 250 of 2025 is dismissed as barred by limitation without any order as to costs.
summary: The Unified Titanium Common Association appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 02.08.2024 in the liquidation of Earth Iconic Infrastructures Pvt. Ltd. with a delay of 117 days, seeking exclusion of time under Section 14 of the Limitation Act on the ground that it had been prosecuting an earlier appeal with liberty granted. The NCLAT held that the earlier appeal had been manipulated by replacing the challenged orders at the refiling stage on 23.09.2024 after the 45-day statutory window had already expired, which negated due diligence and good faith under Section 2(h) of the Limitation Act. Reaffirming the Supreme Court's mandate in Tata Steel Ltd. v. Raj Kumar Banerjee, the Tribunal held that Section 61(2) IBC limits delay condonation strictly to 15 days, leaving the NCLAT with no jurisdiction to condone 117 days.

case_title: Girish Siriram Juneja, RP, Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd. & Anr. vs. Soneko Marketing Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Girish Siriram Juneja (Resolution Professional/Appellant); Committee of Creditors of Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd. (CoC/Appellant); Soneko Marketing Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor holding 0.20% admitted debt/Respondent No. 1); Independent Sugar Corporation Ltd. [INSCO] (Resolution Applicant/Respondent No. 3); AGI Greenpac Pvt. Ltd. (Original SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd. involving submission and consideration of resolution plans. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admitted debt metrics of Corporate Debtor; Respondent No. 1 holds an operational claim comprising 0.20% of total admitted claims. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 21.10.2021; CoC approved AGI Greenpac plan on 27.10.2022; NCLT approved plan on 28.04.2023; Supreme Court set aside plan on 29.01.2025 for lack of prior CCI approval; IBBI issued show-cause notice suspending RP's AFA on 30.01.2025; CoC approved INSCO plan on 04.02.2025; Respondent No. 1 filed IVN.P. No. 5/2025 on 07.03.2025; Supreme Court dismissed review on 16.05.2025 directing plan consideration within two weeks and CIRP completion within six weeks; NCLT split on 30.04.2025; Third Member opinion delivered on 10.06.2025; NCLT final order passed on 13.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: IBBI show cause notice dated 30.01.2025 suspending AFA; Delhi High Court order in WP (C) No. 3065/2025 noting IBBI's clarification; CoC resolution affirming approval of INSCO's resolution plan. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench split on 30.04.2025 in IVN.P. 5/2025; Third Member on 10.06.2025 answered referred questions on locus in affirmative while declining to rule on merits of RP replacement; NCLT on 13.06.2025 erroneously treated Point (iii) as decided by majority and directed IBBI to replace RP; RP and CoC appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the suspension of an Insolvency Professional's Authorisation for Assignment (AFA) under Bye-Law 23A of the IBBI Model Bye-Laws debars the professional from continuing with ongoing assignments or only prevents taking new assignments; and whether an order replacing the RP can stand when there was no majority decision among tribunal members on that point.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order premised on a purported majority determination is legally invalid if no actual concordance exists on the point of difference referred to the third member. Further, an interim administrative suspension of professional authorization pending disciplinary investigation operates prospectively against undertaking fresh engagements and does not automatically terminate ongoing statutory roles. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Harmonious construction of Bye-Law 23A of Model Bye-Laws alongside Regulation 7A of the IBBI (Insolvency Professionals) Regulations, 2016 and Regulation 13(6) of the IBBI (Inspection and Investigation) Regulations, 2017 establishes that suspension of AFA prohibits accepting new assignments but does not disable the IP from discharging pre-existing statutory obligations. Part III provisions (Sections 97 and 98) cannot be applied to corporate insolvency under Part II. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Section 419(3) Companies Act requirement of genuine majority concordance on referred points; the Third Member explicitly abstained from adjudicating the merits of RP replacement under prayer (b)/Point (iii). 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: No majority existed to order RP replacement, and AFA suspension under Bye-Law 23A does not bar completion of pending CIRP assignments; NCLT's direction to replace the RP is quashed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 890, 891, 892, and 911-913 of 2025 are partly allowed; the NCLT order dated 13.06.2025 directing IBBI to replace Resolution Professional Girish Siriram Juneja is set aside, and NCLT is directed to hear and decide the resolution plan approval application forthwith.
summary: Resolution Professional Girish Siriram Juneja and the CoC of Hindusthan National Glass & Industries Ltd. appealed against NCLT Kolkata's order directing IBBI to replace the RP following the suspension of his Authorisation for Assignment (AFA) under Bye-Law 23A. The NCLT had disposed of an operational creditor's intervention application citing a majority view. The NCLAT held that the Third Member had only affirmed the applicant's locus to intervene and had expressly refrained from ruling on the merits of RP replacement, meaning no majority existed. Interpreting Bye-Law 23A alongside Regulation 7A of the IP Regulations and Regulation 13(6) of the Inspection Regulations, the Tribunal ruled that AFA suspension bars only fresh assignments and does not disqualify an RP from concluding existing CIRP proceedings.

case_title: Hari Om Dixit vs. Ajit Srivastava & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Hari Om Dixit, Suspended Director of M/s Gayatri Hospitality and Realcon Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent Nos. 1 to 106 are allottees/homebuyers in the 'Gayatri Aura' project acting as Financial Creditors in a class; Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority is the lessor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allotment of residential units/flats in the real estate project 'Gayatri Aura' situated at Plot No. GH-11, Sector-1, Greater Noida (West), UP, under Builder Buyer Agreements providing a 40-month construction timeline. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed by 8 original applicants on 11.01.2019 amounting to an aggregate principal disbursement of Rs. 1,03,55,225/- plus interest at 24% p.a. due to non-delivery of possession from 2015 to 2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application CP(IB)/288(PB)/2019 filed on 11.01.2019 by 8 allottees; IBC Amendment Ordinance came into force on 28.12.2019 (enacted as Act 1 of 2020) introducing the 100-allottee or 10% threshold; Supreme Court upheld amendments on 19.01.2021 in Manish Kumar v. Union of India; Applicants filed IA 4163/2021 on 15.07.2021 to add 52 allottees; subsequent IAs filed on 07.07.2022 (IA 3422/2022) and 03.01.2023 (IA 499/2023); State Government granted zero period on 02.08.2023; NCLT admitted Section 7 application on 04.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder Buyer Agreements, UP RERA extension notifications, State Government zero-period order dated 02.08.2023, Advocate Commissioner's e-voting report dated September 2023, and filing dates of impleadment applications establishing that modification was sought 6 months after the Supreme Court's judgment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Principal Bench allowed the impleadment applications, held that the threshold of 100 allottees was satisfied, and admitted Section 7 CIRP vide order dated 04.03.2024; Suspended Director appealed against admission, and an allottee appealed against the appointment of the RP.
legal_issues: Whether a pre-amendment Section 7 application filed by fewer than 100 homebuyers is deemed to have been withdrawn by operation of law under the third proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC if the applicants fail to modify the application to meet the statutory threshold within 30 days of the amendment or within 30 days of the Supreme Court's judgment upholding the amendment.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a statute creates a mandatory condition precedent coupled with an express deeming fiction of withdrawal upon non-compliance within a prescribed timeframe, failure to comply strictly with the timeline results in automatic statutory withdrawal of the petition by operation of law without requiring a judicial order. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The third proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC mandates that pending, unadmitted Section 7 applications filed by real estate allottees must be modified within 30 days to comply with the threshold requirement of 100 allottees or 10% of allottees under the first or second proviso; failure to do so attracts the mandatory statutory consequence that 'the application shall be deemed to be withdrawn before its admission.' 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict statutory compliance; the date of enactment (28.12.2019) and the Supreme Court's verdict in Manish Kumar (19.01.2021) triggered the 30-day window, whereas the modification application (IA 4163/2021) was filed only on 15.07.2021, far beyond the permissible limit. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the application was not modified within 30 days, it stood deemed to have been withdrawn; the Adjudicating Authority had no jurisdiction to entertain subsequent impleadment applications or admit the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 513 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 04.03.2024 admitting Section 7 application CP(IB)/288(PB)/2019 is set aside, and the petition is held to be deemed withdrawn under the third proviso to Section 7(1) IBC; the Appellant is held bound to honour its settlement proposal to refund with SBI FD interest within 60 days or revive cancelled allotments; Company Appeal No. 1053 of 2024 is disposed of as infructuous.
summary: The Suspended Director of Gayatri Hospitality and Realcon Ltd. appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order admitting a Section 7 CIRP petition initiated by homebuyers in the Gayatri Aura project. The Section 7 application was originally filed on 11.01.2019 by only 8 allottees. Following the IBC (Amendment) Act, 2020 introducing the threshold of 100 allottees or 10%, the third proviso required pending applications to be modified within 30 days, failing which they were deemed withdrawn. The Supreme Court upheld this provision in Manish Kumar on 19.01.2021, but the applicants filed their first impleadment application to add 52 allottees only on 15.07.2021. The NCLAT held that the petition stood deemed to be withdrawn by operation of law upon expiry of the 30-day period, rendering the NCLT's admission order ultra vires, and set aside the CIRP while binding the promoter to its refund and unit-restoration settlement proposal.

case_title: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Limited vs. Takshashila Heights India Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. (EARCL/Assignee Financial Creditor), acting as Trustee of EARC Trust SC 444; Original Lender is ECL Finance Ltd.; Respondent is Takshashila Heights India Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Real Estate Developer); Intervenors include SBICAP Ventures Ltd. and The Elegna Co-operative Housing and Commercial Society Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two term loan facilities sanctioned on 19.07.2018 totalling Rs. 70 Crores (Rs. 40 Crores under TL-I and Rs. 30 Crores under TL-II) disbursed on 26.07.2018 and 26.09.2018, secured by hypothecation, personal guarantees, and registered mortgage, assigned to Appellant on 09.05.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding financial debt of Rs. 93,54,87,965/- as on 31.01.2024; account classified as NPA on 30.12.2021 after last payment on 30.09.2021; NeSL record of default authenticated. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30.12.2021; assignment executed on 09.05.2022; loan recall and guarantee invocation issued on 31.05.2022; DRT OA filed on 19.07.2022; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice on 21.07.2022; Restructuring Letter executed on 23.05.2023 for Rs. 55 Crores payable in 8 instalments; CD defaulted on second instalment on 30.09.2023 paying only Rs. 86 Lakhs out of Rs. 3 Crores; Appellant revoked restructuring on 29.12.2023; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 104(AHM)/2024 filed on 20.02.2024; NCLT dismissed petition on 06.11.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, hypothecation deeds, NeSL default authentication certificate, Restructuring Letter dated 23.05.2023, revocation notice dated 29.12.2023, correspondence confirming partial payment and default. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed Section 7 petition on 06.11.2024, holding that parallel DRT and SARFAESI actions showed a recovery intent rather than resolution, that the debtor was a going concern, and exercising discretion under Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd. to reject admission; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the discretion to reject a Section 7 petition under the doctrine of Vidarbha Industries on the grounds that the Corporate Debtor is a solvent going concern and the financial creditor is pursuing parallel recovery proceedings under SARFAESI and DRT, once the existence of debt and default is established and admitted.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied that a financial debt exists and a default has occurred, there is virtually no discretion left under Section 7(5)(a) of the IBC to refuse admission. The pendency of parallel recovery proceedings under the SARFAESI Act, DRT, or Negotiable Instruments Act does not bar the initiation of CIRP, nor does it establish fraudulent or malicious intent under Section 65 of the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) mandates admission upon satisfaction of debt and default; the ruling in Vidarbha Industries Power Ltd. v. Axis Bank Ltd. was rendered on its own peculiar facts and does not dilute the binding principles established in Innoventive Industries Ltd. v. ICICI Bank and M. Suresh Kumar Reddy v. Canara Bank. A company's status as an ongoing business or real estate developer does not confer immunity against CIRP when debt and default are undisputed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective default verification; admission of debt and default in pleadings coupled with NeSL authentication conclusively satisfies the statutory trigger for admission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt of Rs. 93.54 Crores and default were admitted on record; parallel recovery efforts do not constitute an abuse of process; the Adjudicating Authority committed a grave error in refusing admission based on Vidarbha Industries.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2261 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 06.11.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench is set aside; the Section 7 application is admitted; and NCLT is directed to pass consequential operational orders within 30 days.
summary: Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company Ltd. appealed the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench's dismissal of its Section 7 petition filed against real estate developer Takshashila Heights India Pvt. Ltd. for an admitted default of Rs. 93.54 Crores arising from term loan facilities. Relying on the Supreme Court's decision in Vidarbha Industries, the NCLT had rejected admission on grounds that the debtor was a viable going concern and that the creditor's simultaneous SARFAESI and DRT proceedings indicated a motive of debt recovery rather than resolution. The NCLAT reversed the decision and directed admission, ruling that under the binding precedents of Innoventive Industries and M. Suresh Kumar Reddy, satisfaction of debt and default leaves no discretion to refuse admission. The Tribunal reaffirmed that the IBC overrides other recovery laws and parallel recovery actions do not bar CIRP initiation.

case_title: Gaurav Katiyar, RP / Committee of Creditors of Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Nisus Finance and Investment Managers LLP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Gaurav Katiyar is the Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd.; Appellant Committee of Creditors (CoC) comprises homebuyers and financial creditors; Appellant Consortium of DS Infraheights Pvt. Ltd. & Anand Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA); Respondent No. 1 Nisus Finance & Investment Managers LLP and Respondent No. 2 Beacon Trusteeship Ltd. are Financial Creditors; Respondents No. 3 & 4 are Tulsiani Constructions & Developers Pvt. Ltd. and Mahesh Kumar Tulsiani. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission and consideration of resolution plans under Form-G for real estate projects of the Corporate Debtor, requiring a minimum project delivery experience of 10,00,000 sq. ft. super area and proof of Rs. 20 Crores committed funds at the EOI stage. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Insolvency proceedings initiated under Section 7 default in CP No. (IB) 1348(ND)/2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 08.01.2020; fresh Form-G issued on 10.05.2023; SRA included in final PRA list on 08.06.2023; CoC approved SRA's plan on 27.05.2023 with 70.18% majority; RP filed approval application IA No. 4466/2023 on 22.08.2023; Nisus filed objections in IA No. 5238/2023; NCLT passed impugned order on 02.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: UP RERA filings showing 'Luv Nest' was developed by Shreehari Realtech Pvt. Ltd. rather than the SRA; LDA RTI replies dated 19.08.2023 and 01.09.2023 showing rejection and non-issuance of completion certificate for 'Urban Woods'; HDFC Bank letter dated 19.08.2023 confirming its Rs. 20 Crore letter was neither a sanction nor proof of available funds. 6.
