PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-III vide order dated 02.05.2024 allowed IA No. 5238/2023, rejected the resolution plan for non-compliance and misrepresentation of eligibility credentials under Regulation 39(1)(c), and directed the RP to issue a fresh Form-G; RP, CoC, and SRA appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Prospective Resolution Applicant who relies on credentials of a third party and an uncertified real estate project lacking completion certificates meets the mandatory eligibility criteria of delivering 10 lakh sq. ft. super area, and whether a conditional bank letter constitutes proof of Rs. 20 Crores committed funds under Regulation 39(1)(c) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors cannot validate or approve a resolution plan submitted by a resolution applicant who fails to satisfy objective, threshold eligibility criteria or who provides false declarations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1)(c) of the IBBI (CIRP) Regulations, 2016 read with Section 30(2) requires every statement in a resolution plan to be true and correct; discovery of false or unsubstantiated information renders the applicant ineligible to continue. A conditional indicative letter from a bank does not constitute 'proof of available committed funds' under the RFRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict verification of project completion certificates; claims of 'deemed completion' under Section 15A of the UP Urban Planning and Development Act fail where the development authority has issued formal objections and reconfirmed non-issuance via RTI communications. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA failed to substantiate the mandatory 10 lakh sq. ft. delivery threshold and proof of committed funds; the resolution plan was rightly rejected by the Adjudicating Authority.
operative_order: All Company Appeals arising out of the common impugned order dated 02.05.2024 are dismissed; the rejection of the resolution plan and direction to issue fresh Form-G are affirmed; all pending IAs are closed without costs.
summary: The Resolution Professional, Committee of Creditors, and Successful Resolution Applicant (Consortium of DS Infraheights and Anand Buildtech) challenged the NCLT New Delhi's rejection of the CoC-approved resolution plan for Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. Financial creditor Nisus Finance objected to the plan, contending that the SRA was ineligible under the RFRP criteria. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that the SRA made false representations regarding its experience by wrongly counting the 'Luv Nest' project (developed by another entity) and the 'Urban Woods' project (which lacked completion/occupancy certificates from LDA). Furthermore, HDFC Bank's letter was not a valid proof of Rs. 20 Crores committed funds. Upholding the NCLT order, the Tribunal held that CoC commercial wisdom cannot override statutory non-compliance under Regulation 39(1)(c).

case_title: Consortium of DS Infraheights Pvt. Ltd. & Anand Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. vs. Nisus Finance and Investment Infratech Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Consortium of DS Infraheights Pvt. Ltd. & Anand Buildtech Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Nisus Finance and Investment Infratech Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Gaurav Katiyar (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 3 is Committee of Creditors of Corporate Debtor Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of Expression of Interest and Resolution Plan for revival of Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. under EOI stipulations requiring delivery of 10 lakh sq. ft. super area and Rs. 20 Crores committed funds. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP initiated under Section 7 against Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. in CP No. (IB) 1348(ND)/2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 08.01.2020; Form-G published on 10.05.2023; Appellant submitted resolution plan approved by CoC with 70.18% vote on 27.05.2023; RP filed IA 4466/2023 for plan approval; Nisus filed IA 5238/2023 objecting to SRA eligibility; NCLT allowed IA 5238/2023 and rejected plan on 02.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RERA records showing 'Luv Nest' project was registered under Shreehari Realtech Pvt. Ltd.; LDA communication dated 01.09.2023 stating completion certificate for 'Urban Woods' was withheld due to unresolved defects; HDFC clarification dated 19.08.2023 confirming the funding letter was conditional and not a sanction. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III rejected the SRA's resolution plan on 02.05.2024 and directed issuance of fresh Form-G; the SRA preferred this statutory appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the SRA consortium met the eligibility criteria regarding past project delivery of 10 lakh sq. ft. and financial capability of Rs. 20 Crores committed funds, and whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by rejecting the CoC-approved plan.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant who fails to satisfy objective qualification parameters laid down in an Expression of Interest cannot seek protection under the umbrella of the Committee of Creditors' commercial wisdom. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 39(1)(c) of the IBBI CIRP Regulations invalidates the participation of any resolution applicant whose submitted records are found to be inaccurate or false. A plea of 'deemed completion' under local development laws cannot be sustained when statutory authorities have formally documented subsisting objections and refused certification. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented verification standard; official communications from statutory planning authorities and lending institutions override self-serving certificates and uncommitted comfort letters. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: After excluding the unauthorized Luv Nest project and incomplete Urban Woods project, the SRA's delivered area fell below 10 lakh sq. ft., and its conditional HDFC letter failed the committed funds test; the rejection of the resolution plan was lawful.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 969 & 970 of 2024 are dismissed; the impugned order dated 02.05.2024 rejecting the resolution plan and directing a fresh Form-G is upheld; all pending IAs closed.
summary: The Successful Resolution Applicant consortium (DS Infraheights and Anand Buildtech) challenged NCLT New Delhi's order rejecting its resolution plan for Earthcon Universal Infratech Pvt. Ltd. in an application filed by financial creditor Nisus Finance. The NCLT found the SRA ineligible for failing the 10 lakh sq. ft. completed project threshold and the Rs. 20 Crore committed funds requirement. The NCLAT affirmed the dismissal, finding that the SRA improperly claimed credentials from the Luv Nest project (owned by a separate entity) and the Urban Woods project (which lacked completion certificates from LDA). Additionally, HDFC Bank's conditional letter did not establish committed funds. The Tribunal reiterated that commercial wisdom cannot cure basic statutory and regulatory ineligibility under Regulation 39(1)(c).

case_title: Gaurav Katiyar, RP of Earthcon Universal Infra Tech Pvt. Ltd. vs. Nisus Finance And Investment Managers LLP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Gaurav Katiyar, Resolution Professional of Earthcon Universal Infra Tech Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Nisus Finance and Investment Managers LLP (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Beacon Trusteeship Ltd.; Respondents No. 3 & 4 are Tulsiani Constructions & Developers Pvt. Ltd. and Mahesh Kumar Tulsiani. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution Professional conducted CIRP and invited resolution plans for the Corporate Debtor, recommending the plan of DS Infraheights-Anand Buildtech consortium to the CoC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default forming the basis of CIRP admission under Section 7 in CP No. (IB) 1348(ND)/2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 08.01.2020; Form-G published on 10.05.2023; Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 27.05.2023; RP filed IA 4466/2023 for plan approval on 22.08.2023; Nisus filed IA 5238/2023 challenging SRA's eligibility; NCLT rejected the plan and directed a fresh Form-G on 02.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Chartered accountant certificates, UP RERA disclosures showing Luv Nest was executed by Shreehari Realtech Pvt. Ltd., LDA letters confirming Urban Woods lacked CC/OC, and HDFC Bank's clarification that its letter did not represent sanctioned or deployable funds. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT New Delhi Bench-III rejected the RP's application for plan approval (IA 4466/2023) and allowed IA 5238/2023 on 02.05.2024 due to material misstatements in SRA eligibility; the RP appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional complied with statutory due diligence obligations in verifying the technical and financial eligibility credentials of the Prospective Resolution Applicant before placing the plan before the CoC, and whether the plan was rightly rejected under Section 30(2) of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Resolution Professional is statutorily obligated to verify that resolution applicants strictly satisfy all eligibility criteria prescribed in the RFRP; placing a plan submitted by an applicant with unverified or misrepresented credentials violates the Code and cannot be sustained even if approved by the CoC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) of the Code mandates that a resolution plan must confirm all regulatory requirements specified by the Board, including Regulation 39(1)(c) of the CIRP Regulations. The RP's submission of a plan lacking proper OC/CC documentation and genuine committed funds fails statutory scrutiny. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of objective records; the RP cannot rely on superficial assertions of 'deemed approval' when public development authorities confirm that applications for completion remain unapproved due to irregularities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority did not commit any error in rejecting the resolution plan and directing the RP to conduct a fresh process with an amended Form-G.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 963-965 of 2024 is dismissed; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 02.05.2024 rejecting the resolution plan is affirmed; all pending IAs are closed.
summary: Resolution Professional Gaurav Katiyar appealed against the NCLT New Delhi Bench's order dated 02.05.2024 rejecting his application for approval of the resolution plan submitted by the DS Infraheights and Anand Buildtech consortium for Earthcon Universal Infra Tech Pvt. Ltd. The NCLT found that the SRA failed to satisfy the EOI criteria of delivering 10 lakh sq. ft. of super area and providing proof of Rs. 20 Crores in committed funds. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the RP overlooked significant discrepancies, including the SRA's reliance on projects developed by third parties without authorization, the absence of completion certificates from the Lucknow Development Authority, and reliance on an uncommitted HDFC Bank comfort letter. The Tribunal affirmed the direction to issue a fresh Form-G.

case_title: Pancham Studios Pvt. Ltd. vs. Konark Aquatics & Exports Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pancham Studios Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent is Konark Aquatics & Exports Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), an entity in the seafood processing and export business; common promoter/family ties exist between directors Debasis Mahapatra and Devprakash Mahapatra. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Interest-free inter-corporate loan disbursed through banking channels to enable the Corporate Debtor to discharge liabilities towards secured financial creditors under a One-Time Settlement (OTS) arrangement. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 4,43,50,000/- recalled via demand notice dated 20.08.2019 to be repaid within 15 days; reflected continuously as unsecured loan in balance sheets from FY 2016-17 to FY 2020-21. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disbursement made through banking channels; five demand notices served between 02.08.2019 and 30.05.2022; Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 37/CB/2022 filed before NCLT Cuttack Bench; NCLT dismissed petition on 29.11.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank disbursement records; audited balance sheets of the Corporate Debtor for FY 2016-17, 2017-18, and 2020-21 recording Rs. 4,43,50,000/- as 'unsecured loans' from Pancham Studios without caveats; letter dated 28.10.2017 admitting utilization of funds to repay debt. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Cuttack Bench dismissed the Section 7 application on 29.11.2023 holding that an interest-free loan stemming from family property arrangements does not constitute financial debt, violated Section 186 of the Companies Act, and lacked an Information Utility record of default; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether an interest-free inter-corporate loan advanced to clear liabilities of a corporate debtor and acknowledged as an unsecured loan in its audited balance sheets constitutes a 'financial debt' under Section 5(8) of the IBC; whether non-compliance with Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013 renders the loan void and unenforceable by the corporate debtor; and whether an Information Utility record of default is mandatory under Section 7(3)(a).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An interest-free loan advanced to improve the financial health of a corporate debtor to settle creditor liabilities possesses the commercial effect of borrowing and constitutes a financial debt. A corporate borrower cannot evade repayment by asserting its or the lender's non-compliance with internal corporate approval mechanisms under Section 186 of the Companies Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8) encompasses interest-free loans when deployed for commercial borrowing effects, as established in Orator Marketing. Section 186 of the Companies Act provides internal penalties for corporate non-compliance but does not render the borrowing void or unrecoverable against a third-party debtor. Regulation 20(1A) of the IU Regulations does not override Section 7(3)(a) IBC, and default may be proved by financial statements under Regulation 2A of the CIRP Regulations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unqualified balance sheet entries constitute binding admission and acknowledgment of debt; written financial contracts are not mandatory where banking disbursements and financial statements prove the debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Debt and default were conclusively established; the NCLT erred in dismissing the Section 7 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 406 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 29.11.2023 passed by NCLT Cuttack Bench is set aside, and the Section 7 petition is admitted.
summary: Pancham Studios appealed NCLT Cuttack's dismissal of its Section 7 petition filed against Konark Aquatics & Exports for default of an interest-free loan of Rs. 4,43,50,000/-. The NCLT had held that the loan was an internal family arrangement lacking time value of money, was void for violating Section 186 of the Companies Act, 2013, and lacked an Information Utility record of default. The NCLAT reversed the order and admitted the petition, ruling that interest-free loans given to discharge corporate liabilities carry the commercial effect of borrowing under Section 5(8) IBC. The Tribunal held that unqualified balance sheet entries establish debt admission, that Section 186 non-compliance cannot be used by a debtor to deny repayment, and that an IU certificate is not the sole mandatory proof of default under Section 7(3)(a).

case_title: Joint Commissioner of State Taxes & Excise (SEZ), Parwanoo vs. M/s Radiant Castings Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Joint Commissioner of State Taxes & Excise (SEZ), Parwanoo, Himachal Pradesh (Operational/Tax Creditor); Respondent No. 1 is M/s Radiant Castings Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Vasudeo Agarwal (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory tax assessments and tax arrears under HPGST/CGST Act, 2017 during the CIRP of the Corporate Debtor. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted initial Form-C claim of Rs. 2,61,39,552/-; resolution plan allocated Rs. 50,309/- towards this claim (out of total Rs. 6,45,373/- government dues); Appellant asserted additional unfiled tax arrears of Rs. 13.60 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CoC approved Resolution Plan with 70.02% majority on 30.05.2023; NCLT approved plan on 30.08.2023; Appellant received Rs. 50,309/- under plan on 09.09.2023; Appellant filed IA No. 5488 of 2023 seeking recall of the plan approval order; NCLT dismissed recall IA on 20.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Communications dated 24.09.2022 and 28.10.2022 sent to RP alleging Rs. 13.60 Crores in arrears without filing formal claim forms; approved resolution plan providing liquidation value distribution under Section 53. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III dismissed IA No. 5488 of 2023 on 20.02.2025 holding that recall cannot be used as a disguise for review to admit belated claims after plan approval; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to recall an order approving a resolution plan to entertain belated statutory tax claims not formally filed during CIRP, and whether state tax debts under the CGST/HPGST Act constitute secured debts entitled to top-priority payment under the doctrine of Rainbow Papers.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Approval of a resolution plan imparts statutory finality under the clean slate doctrine, extinguishing all undecided and belated claims; an adjudicating authority cannot exercise recall powers to review an approved plan or permit reopening of claims absent fraud or lack of jurisdiction. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 82 of the CGST/HPGST Act expressly subordinates its charge to the provisions of the IBC, distinguishing it from the Gujarat VAT statute evaluated in Rainbow Papers. Operational tax claims fall under the waterfall mechanism of Section 53(1)(e) as government dues and cannot claim secured status to disrupt approved allocations. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Established criteria for recall; an applicant must establish absence of jurisdiction, fraud, or lack of notice, none of which were demonstrated where the creditor participated and accepted plan payouts. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The tax department's additional claim of Rs. 13.60 Crores was unfiled and belated; the approved plan complied with Section 30(2) and Section 53, and the recall application was an impermissible review in disguise.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 684 of 2025 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 20.02.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-III is affirmed without costs.
summary: The Joint Commissioner of State Taxes & Excise, Himachal Pradesh appealed against NCLT New Delhi's rejection of its application seeking to recall the approval order of the resolution plan for Radiant Castings Pvt. Ltd. The department argued that the plan provided only Rs. 50,309/- against its admitted claim of Rs. 2.61 Crores and ignored additional tax arrears of Rs. 13.60 Crores, claiming secured status under Rainbow Papers. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that Section 82 of the CGST/HPGST Act is subject to the IBC, placing tax claims under the Section 53 waterfall. Applying the clean slate doctrine, the Tribunal affirmed that belated claims cannot be entertained post-approval and that recall cannot serve as a review in disguise.

case_title: Puneet Resutra vs. Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Puneet Resutra is the erstwhile Director and Shareholder of M/s Ace Engineering (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent is Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Siddharth Bhatia and Munish Bhatia were Personal Guarantors/Co-Directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by Corporate Debtor comprising a Cash Credit facility of Rs. 9 Crores and a Secured Overdraft facility of Rs. 4 Crores, secured by personal guarantees and mortgages over commercial/factory properties. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 10,11,23,983.19 with interest at 12.15% and 12.65% p.a. as on 31.10.2018; accounts classified as NPA on 31.03.2016. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Accounts declared NPA on 31.03.2016; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued on 10.04.2017; Bank entered OTS with personal guarantors on 15.06.2017 for Rs. 10 Crores; guarantors paid Rs. 11.30 Crores by 05.01.2018 and secured personal release; Bank filed Section 7 petition on 07.01.2019; NCLT admitted Section 7 application on 06.03.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank letter dated 05.01.2018 expressly reserving the right to recover remaining balances from the Corporate Debtor; audited balance sheet of Corporate Debtor for FY 2017-18 acknowledging bank debt under Note C; internal Agreement to Sell dated 20.04.2016 between CD and guarantors (to which Bank was not a party). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench admitted the Bank's Section 7 application and initiated CIRP against Ace Engineering on 06.03.2023; Appellant appealed contending the debt was fully settled via the guarantors' OTS.
legal_issues: Whether a One-Time Settlement entered into between a lender and personal guarantors discharges the principal borrower from its debt liabilities when the bank expressly reserves recovery rights against the corporate debtor, and whether the Section 7 petition was filed within limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 128 of the Indian Contract Act, the liability of a guarantor is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor, but an independent settlement releasing a guarantor does not automatically discharge the principal borrower unless the creditor executes an express waiver or issues a No Dues Certificate to the borrower. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) mandates admission once debt and default are established; the discretion recognized in Vidarbha Industries does not apply to a going concern absent crystallized, realizable receivables sufficient to satisfy debts. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Section 18 Limitation Act acknowledgment test; balance sheet entries executed within three years of default renew the limitation clock, making an application filed within three years of the NPA date legally timely. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Bank preserved its rights against the Corporate Debtor; balance debt remained unpaid, default was established, and the Section 7 admission was proper.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 752 of 2023 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 06.03.2023 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench admitting the Section 7 petition is affirmed; all pending IAs closed.
summary: The erstwhile Director of Ace Engineering (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed NCLT Chandigarh's admission of a Section 7 CIRP petition filed by Jammu & Kashmir Bank Ltd. for an unpaid debt exceeding Rs. 10 Crores. The Appellant argued that the loan was fully satisfied through an OTS wherein the personal guarantors paid over Rs. 11.30 Crores, and that the company was a viable going concern handling defense contracts. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that the OTS and release were confined strictly to the guarantors, while the bank expressly reserved recovery rights against the Corporate Debtor. The Tribunal held that the debt was acknowledged in audited balance sheets, the petition was timely under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, and the Vidarbha exception did not apply.

case_title: Imbulle Realtors Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sanjeev Kumar & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Imbulle Realtors Pvt. Ltd. (unadmitted claimant/alleged financial creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Sanjeev Kumar (Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Realanchor Developers Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional (IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Claim of over Rs. 5 Crores lodged by Appellant in the CIRP of Realanchor Developers Pvt. Ltd. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor under Section 7 on 16.10.2023 by financial creditors in a class. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 16.10.2023; Appellant filed claim on 31.10.2023; NCLAT granted interim order on 22.10.2023 staying CoC constitution; NCLAT disposed of CA 1404/2023 on 12.11.2024 permitting Section 12A withdrawal application; NCLT Court-V heard 12A and other applications on 25.02.2025 directing written submissions; Bench reconstituted due to new appointments; Respondent No. 1 filed Transfer Application TA (IBC)-16(PB)/2025; President NCLT allowed transfer on 09.05.2025 to the bench that originally heard the matter on 25.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order sheets dated 25.02.2025 and 18.03.2025 showing conclusion of hearing and listing before newly constituted benches; Transfer Application TA 16(PB)/2025 impleading only the IRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Single Principal Bench (President, NCLT) allowed Transfer Application TA (IBC)-16(PB)/2025 on 09.05.2025 transferring the company petition and Section 12A application back to the erstwhile bench consisting of Member (Judicial) and Member (Technical) who heard arguments on 25.02.2025; Appellant appealed against this administrative transfer order.
legal_issues: Whether an appeal against an administrative transfer order passed by the President of NCLT under Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 is maintainable under Section 61 of the IBC or Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, and whether an unadmitted claimant has a legal right of hearing under natural justice in a transfer application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order of the President of the NCLT transferring proceedings from one bench to another is an administrative exercise of master-of-the-roster powers under Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 read with Section 419 of the Companies Act, 2013, and does not constitute an order under Part II of the IBC appealable under Section 61 IBC, though it is appealable under Section 421 of the Companies Act. A claimant whose claim has not yet been admitted has no vested locus to demand a personal hearing prior to an administrative transfer of proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 61 of the IBC is restricted to substantive quasi-judicial orders passed under Part II of the Code. The President's power under Rule 16(d) is an administrative prerogative to manage rosters and assign part-heard matters to benches that heard arguments to ensure continuity and prevent wastage of judicial time. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Natural justice and locus criteria; a party seeking to challenge an administrative roster assignment must establish legal injury and party status in the transfer proceedings. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transfer order was within the administrative jurisdiction of the President to ensure an effective decision on merits by the bench that concluded oral hearings; the Appellant, whose claim remains unadmitted, suffered no legal prejudice.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 934 of 2025 is dismissed without expressing any opinion on the merits of the Section 12A application or the Appellant's underlying claim.
summary: Imbulle Realtors Pvt. Ltd., an unadmitted claimant in the CIRP of Realanchor Developers Pvt. Ltd., challenged an order dated 09.05.2025 passed by the President of the NCLT allowing a transfer application to send the Section 12A withdrawal application back to the division bench that had fully heard the matter on 25.02.2025 before a bench reconstitution. The Appellant alleged violation of natural justice for not being heard. The NCLAT held that while the appeal was not maintainable under Section 61 IBC (as the order was passed under Rule 16(d) of NCLT Rules, 2016), it was maintainable under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013. On the merits, the Tribunal ruled that the President is the master of the roster and possesses administrative power to assign matters to the bench that heard the case, and that a third-party claimant whose debt is unadmitted has no right to participate in administrative transfer proceedings.

case_title: Vistra ITCL (India) Limited & Ors. vs. Satra Properties (India) Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1043 of 2024 & I.A. No. 3794 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Financial Creditors holding 32.19% voting share in the CoC of Satra Properties (India) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Respondent No. 1); Respondents No. 2 to 6 are Suspended Directors; Respondent No. 7 is Dev Land & Housing Pvt. Ltd. (third-party entity); Respondent No. 8 is C. Bhansali Developers Pvt. Ltd. (related-party entity). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Siphoning of funds under the garb of an unregistered MoU dated 18.08.2015 for purchase of land worth Rs. 75 Crores, and inter-corporate loans/deposits involving common directors. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fraudulent write-offs amounting to Rs. 29.35 Crores in favour of Respondent No. 7 and Rs. 3.24 Crores in favour of Respondent No. 8, aggregating to Rs. 32.59 Crores plus interest at 18% p.a. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 application filed on 11.05.2019; Corporate Debtor admitted to CIRP on 03.08.2020; Forensic Audit Report submitted on 15.11.2021; RP filed IA 1626/2023 under Section 66 on 12.04.2023; NCLT passed impugned order on 02.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic Audit Report by BDO India LLP identifying transactions as fraudulent; unregistered and unnotarized MoU dated 18.08.2015 on Rs. 100 stamp paper lacking payment schedules and unsigned by the suspended director; Deed of Cancellation dated 20.03.2020 executed on 2019 stamp paper citing unelaborated 'extraneous reasons' to forfeit 40% EMD (Rs. 29.35 Crores); ledger accounts showing Rs. 3.24 Crores written off as 'excess provision for interest' to related party Respondent No. 8 without supporting board approval or documentation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I partly allowed IA 1626/2023 on 02.04.2024, holding two minor transactions fraudulent, but rejected claims under Section 66 regarding Transaction No. 1 (Rs. 29.35 Crores) and Transaction No. 3 (Rs. 3.24 Crores) as ordinary commercial dealings; Financial Creditors appealed against this refusal.
legal_issues: Whether the forfeiture and write-off of an advance of Rs. 29.35 Crores under an unregistered MoU and an unelaborated cancellation deed, as well as an undocumented write-off of Rs. 3.24 Crores in favour of a related party, constitute fraudulent transactions under Section 66(1) of the IBC; and whether Section 66 prescribes any statutory look-back period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 66 of the IBC is not governed by any statutory look-back period; where a corporate debtor enters into one-sided agreements lacking commercial rationale, surrenders substantial earnest money advances without protest or legal action, or writes off debts owed by related parties without documentation while approaching insolvency, fraudulent intent to defraud creditors under Section 66(1) is firmly established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66(1) imposes personal liability on persons who knowingly carry on the business of the corporate debtor with intent to defraud creditors or for fraudulent purposes. Unlike Sections 43 and 46, Section 66 does not prescribe a two-year or one-year look-back period. Directors have a fiduciary obligation to preserve assets and exercise prudent business diligence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Fraudulent intent test; reckless indifference to corporate assets, complete surrender of 40% purchase consideration via arbitrary forfeiture clauses, common directorships, and sham cancellation deeds executed during impending CIRP establish fraudulent trading. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Transactions No. 1 and No. 3 were orchestrated sham arrangements intended to siphon Rs. 32.59 Crores to defraud creditors; the NCLT erred in treating them as bona fide commercial dealings.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1043 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 02.04.2024 to the extent of disallowing Transaction Nos. 1 and 3 against Respondents No. 7 and 8 is set aside; the petition in CP (IB) No. 534/MB/2023 is restored, and parties are directed to appear before the NCLT on 16.07.2025 for appropriate consequential directions under Section 66.
summary: Financial Creditors holding 32.19% of the CoC of Satra Properties (India) Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order refusing to declare two transactions aggregating Rs. 32.59 Crores as fraudulent under Section 66 IBC. The first transaction involved the complete forfeiture and write-off of a Rs. 29.35 Crore advance paid under an unregistered MoU to Dev Land & Housing Pvt. Ltd. based on a sham cancellation deed citing vague 'extraneous reasons.' The second involved a sudden write-off of Rs. 3.24 Crores owed by related party C. Bhansali Developers Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and reversed the NCLT's findings, holding that Section 66 contains no look-back period and that both transactions exhibited blatant fraudulent intent, collusion, and reckless surrender of corporate funds to defraud creditors.

case_title: Shri Rakesh Jolly vs. Indian Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Shri Rakesh Jolly (Personal Guarantor and Director of Principal Borrower M/s Aravali Infrapower Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 Indian Bank (Financial Creditor/Consortium Member); Respondent No. 2 Rakesh Mishra (Resolution Professional). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facility of Rs. 58.35 Crores sanctioned on 31.10.2012 under a Corporate Debt Restructuring (CDR) scheme, secured by a Deed of Guarantee executed by the Appellant on 13.02.2013 in favour of the consortium led by State Bank of India. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 200,90,24,194.19 demanded in Rule 7 notice dated 10.05.2022; initial SARFAESI demand of Rs. 109,43,77,905.11; borrower account classified as NPA on 29.10.2012. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 29.10.2012; Master Debt Restructuring Agreement on 27.12.2012; guarantee executed on 13.02.2013; acknowledgment of debt on 04.12.2014 and revival letter on 21.01.2015; SARFAESI Section 13(2) notice issued on 13.06.2016 granting 60 days (default maturing 12.08.2016); Appellant signed and submitted OTS proposal to lead bank on 19.03.2018; Supreme Court Covid limitation exclusion applied from 15.03.2020 to 31.05.2022; Demand Notice under Rule 7(2) served on 10.05.2022; Section 95 petition filed on 19.07.2022; NCLT admitted Section 95 petition on 24.07.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Deed of Guarantee dated 13.02.2013 (Clauses 12 and 19 establishing that borrower acknowledgments bind the guarantor); OTS proposal letter dated 19.03.2018 signed by Appellant acknowledging debt and CDR failure; Section 13(2) demand notices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench accepted the RP's Section 99 report (IA No. 4675/ND/2022) and admitted Indian Bank's Section 95 application vide order dated 24.07.2023; Personal Guarantor appealed on limitation grounds.
legal_issues: Whether an insolvency application under Section 95 of the IBC filed against a personal guarantor is barred by limitation when the original NPA occurred in 2012, but the borrower acknowledged the debt in an unaccepted OTS proposal in 2018 and the limitation period was protected by Supreme Court Covid-19 extension orders; and whether a single consortium member bank can maintain a Section 95 petition independently.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An acknowledgment of debt made in writing by a principal borrower before the expiry of the prescribed limitation period renews the limitation clock under Section 18 of the Limitation Act, 1963. Where guarantee covenants explicitly stipulate that admissions of liability by the principal borrower bind the guarantor as an authorized agent, such acknowledgment extends the limitation period for enforcing the guarantee against the personal guarantor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Article 137 of the Limitation Act governs Section 95 IBC petitions, giving a three-year period from the date the right to apply accrues. In computing limitation, periods falling within the Supreme Court's suo motu Covid-19 exclusion orders (15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022/31.05.2022) stand excluded. A member bank of a lending consortium maintains independent standing as a financial creditor under Section 95. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admission of liability in commercial correspondence; an OTS proposal letter signed by a director/guarantor detailing unpaid debt and debt restructuring failure constitutes a valid, binding acknowledgment under Section 18 even if the creditor eventually rejects the settlement terms. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 13(2) notice matured on 12.08.2016, the OTS proposal dated 19.03.2018 extended limitation to 18.03.2021, and the Supreme Court Covid exclusion preserved the limitation period up to 31.05.2022; hence, the Rule 7 notice of 10.05.2022 and Section 95 petition filed in July 2022 were timely.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1267 of 2023 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 24.07.2023 passed by NCLT New Delhi admitting the Section 95 application is affirmed without costs.
summary: Personal guarantor Rakesh Jolly challenged NCLT New Delhi's admission of Indian Bank's Section 95 IBC application, asserting that the proceedings were barred by limitation since the principal borrower Aravali Infrapower Ltd.'s account became an NPA in 2012 and the SARFAESI notice was issued in 2016. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the petition was timely. The Tribunal found that the Appellant, as director, had submitted an OTS proposal on 19.03.2018 acknowledging the debt, which bound him as guarantor under Clauses 12 and 19 of the guarantee deed and extended limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. Applying the Supreme Court's Covid-19 exclusion orders, the Tribunal held that limitation was preserved and the Section 95 petition filed in July 2022 was well within limitation.

case_title: The Authorised Representative for Granite Gate Properties Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Devendra Singh & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Authorised Representative of Homebuyers/CoC (CA 1479/2024) and New Okhla Industrial Development Authority [NOIDA] (CA 1713/2024); Respondents are Devendra Singh (Resolution Professional), M/s Granite Gate Properties Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), and M/s SMV Agencies Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Long-term lease deeds dated 30.12.2008 (Sector 100, Lotus Boulevard) and 29.12.2009 (Sector 110, Lotus Panache) executed by NOIDA in favour of Corporate Debtor for group housing projects. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in payment of land lease premium instalments; NOIDA claimed the 19th instalment (Rs. 23,26,12,405/- due 09.06.2019) and 20th instalment (Rs. 22,10,86,565/- due 09.12.2019), along with water/sewer charges and time extension penalties, as CIRP costs. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Lease deeds executed in 2008 and 2009; Corporate Debtor admitted to CIRP under Section 7 in CP(IB)-1248(PB)/2018; 19th and 20th instalments matured post-CIRP commencement; CoC approved SMV Agencies' plan on 22.07.2020; RP filed approval IA 3255/2020; NOIDA filed IA 2298/2021; NCLT passed common order on 24.07.2024 remitting plan to CoC and holding two instalments, water charges, and time extension penalties as CIRP costs. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Lease agreements stipulating a 7-to-8 year construction period with an extendable grace period of up to three years subject to 4%, 5%, and 6% penalties; Information Memorandum disclosing liquidation values; NeSL/banking statements of claim. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II vide order dated 24.07.2024 remitted the resolution plan back to CoC, replaced the RP, declared NOIDA a secured creditor, and directed under Para 79(h) that two lease premium instalments, water/sewer charges, and time extension charges be paid as CIRP costs; both the AR of Homebuyers and NOIDA appealed against distinct parts of the order.
legal_issues: Whether land lease premium instalments falling due after the commencement of CIRP constitute CIRP costs under Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31(b) of the CIRP Regulations; whether time extension penalties under lease deeds can be claimed as CIRP costs beyond the three-year contractual maximum; and whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in leaving the stage of CIRP resumption to the CoC's discretion rather than prescribing a binding timeline.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Capital land lease premium instalments falling due post-insolvency commencement are not costs incurred to keep the corporate debtor as a going concern and do not constitute CIRP costs, subject to the final outcome of pending Supreme Court proceedings. Unpaid water and sewage charges incurred during CIRP constitute essential operational CIRP costs. Contractual time extension charges are recognized as going-concern CIRP costs only up to the maximum three-year limit permitted under the underlying lease deed. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(13) read with Regulation 31(b) of the CIRP Regulations and the explanation to Section 14(1)(d) applies to government grants, licences, and operational services, but does not encompass capital land lease premiums, as held in Sunil Kumar Agrawal v. NOIDA. To preserve parity, resolution applicants must provide an undertaking to pay the instalments if the Supreme Court rules them to be CIRP costs in Civil Appeal No. 901/2023. Regulation 35 mandates confidentiality of fresh valuations, and long-delayed CIRPs should resume by issuing fresh RFRPs to final prospective bidders within strict timelines rather than restarting from the Information Memorandum stage. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual clause limitation; penalty clauses explicitly providing that extension cannot exceed three years prevent the statutory authority from claiming perpetual extension penalties as CIRP costs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Para 79(h) modified to hold lease premium instalments contingent on the Supreme Court ruling, water/sewer charges as CIRP costs, and time extension penalties capped at three years; Para 79(a) modified to direct issuance of RFRP within 30 days and CIRP conclusion within 90 days.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1479 & 1713 of 2024 are disposed of with modifications: (i) Para 79(a) modified directing the CoC to issue RFRP to final PRA list members within 30 days and conclude CIRP within 90 days; (ii) Para 79(h) modified making the 19th and 20th instalments payable as CIRP costs only if the Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 901/2023 holds lease premium to be CIRP cost (with RFRP requiring an undertaking), confirming water/sewer charges as CIRP costs, and capping time extension charges as CIRP costs to a maximum period of three years.
summary: The Authorised Representative of Homebuyers and NOIDA appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 24.07.2024 remitting the resolution plan of Granite Gate Properties Pvt. Ltd. back to the CoC. The NCLT had left the stage of CIRP resumption open to CoC discretion and directed payment of two post-commencement lease premium instalments, water/sewer charges, and time extension charges as CIRP costs under Para 79(h). The NCLAT modified the order, ruling that under its precedent in Sunil Kumar Agrawal v. NOIDA, lease premiums are not CIRP costs under Section 14(1)(d) explanation or Regulation 31(b); however, to protect NOIDA pending Civil Appeal No. 901/2023 in the Supreme Court, resolution applicants must provide an undertaking to pay them if held to be CIRP costs. The Tribunal upheld water/sewer charges as CIRP costs, capped time extension charges to the contractual maximum of three years, and ordered the CoC to issue fresh RFRPs within 30 days and conclude the CIRP within 90 days.

case_title: Atul Paper Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Rakesh Kumar Jain, Liquidator for RG Infra Build Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant/Occupant is M/s Atul Paper Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent/Liquidator is Rakesh Kumar Jain, Liquidator for Corporate Debtor M/s RG Infra Build Pvt. Ltd.; Appellant in connected appeal is Punjab National Bank (Secured Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Unregistered Agreement to Sell dated 24.04.2018 entered into between the Corporate Debtor and Atul Paper Pvt. Ltd. for commercial unit B-101, First Floor, RG City Centre, for total consideration of Rs. 2.70 Crores; Corporate Debtor had previously mortgaged the unit on 11.12.2015 to Punjab National Bank to secure a Rs. 4.5 Crore facility. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Atul Paper Pvt. Ltd. paid Rs. 2.01 Crores part consideration and took possession on 25.04.2018, leaving balance consideration unpaid; Corporate Debtor entered CIRP on 25.09.2019 and Liquidation on 16.03.2023; Atul Paper filed claim of Rs. 2,51,85,025/- before the Liquidator. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mortgage created on 11.12.2015; Agreement to Sell executed on 24.04.2018 with payment deadline 30.06.2018; CIRP commenced 25.09.2019; RP rejected claim on 27.08.2021; Liquidation commenced 16.03.2023; claim filed before Liquidator on 27.04.2023 and rejected for delay on 30.04.2023; Section 42 appeal CA No. 26/2023 filed; NCLT passed common order on 06.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unregistered Agreement to Sell dated 24.04.2018 (Clause 14.1 stipulating no right accrues until registered sale deed is executed); registered Mortgage Deed dated 11.12.2015 in favour of PNB; proof of partial payment of Rs. 2.01 Crores; deposit of balance Rs. 69 Lakhs pursuant to NCLAT interim order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Court-II disposed of RP/Liquidator's IA No. 355/2021 on 06.05.2024 directing Atul Paper to vacate the unit, but directed the Liquidator to pay Rs. 2.01 Crores to Atul Paper upon sale, and dismissed Atul Paper's Section 42 appeal (CA No. 26/2023) as infructuous; all parties appealed distinct parts of the order.
legal_issues: Whether a purchaser under an unregistered agreement to sell who took possession can protect possession against the Liquidator under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act read with Section 17(1-A) of the Registration Act, and whether the Adjudicating Authority can direct direct refund of part sale consideration outside the priority waterfall of Section 53 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unregistered agreement to sell conveys no title, interest, or statutory protection of part performance under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act, and properties belonging to a corporate debtor remain part of the liquidation estate. Further, adjudicating authorities cannot order out-of-turn preferential monetary refunds to claimants outside the statutory waterfall mechanism of Section 53 IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 17(1-A) of the Registration Act, 1908 mandates that contracts transferring immovable property for consideration have no effect for Section 53A Transfer of Property Act unless registered; Section 54 Transfer of Property Act establishes that a contract for sale creates no interest in the property. Section 53 of the IBC provides an exhaustive, mandatory code for distribution of liquidation proceeds that cannot be bypassed. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Document registration threshold; absence of registered conveyance leaves ownership with the corporate debtor, rendering possession unlawful against the liquidator. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Atul Paper must vacate the unit; the direction to refund Rs. 2.01 Crores is quashed; the Liquidator is directed to admit Atul Paper's claim of Rs. 2,51,85,025/- for distribution strictly under Section 53 IBC, and refund the interim deposit of Rs. 69 Lakhs.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1100 of 2024 is dismissed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1101 of 2024 is allowed, setting aside the dismissal of CA No. 26/2023 and directing the Liquidator to admit the claim of Rs. 2,51,85,025/- under Section 53; Company Appeals Nos. 1311 and 2137 of 2024 are allowed, setting aside the direction to pay Rs. 2.01 Crores to Atul Paper; interim deposit of Rs. 69 Lakhs with accrued interest to be refunded to Atul Paper within 30 days.
summary: NCLAT addressed cross-appeals arising from NCLT New Delhi's order directing Atul Paper Pvt. Ltd. to vacate a commercial unit belonging to Corporate Debtor RG Infra Build Pvt. Ltd., while ordering the Liquidator to refund Rs. 2.01 Crores from sale proceeds and dismissing Atul Paper's Section 42 claim appeal as infructuous[cite: 41]. The NCLAT held that because the Agreement to Sell was unregistered, Atul Paper could not claim protection under Section 53A of the Transfer of Property Act due to Section 17(1-A) of the Registration Act[cite: 41]. Affirming the eviction order, the Tribunal set aside the direction for a direct refund of Rs. 2.01 Crores, holding that all distributions must strictly follow the Section 53 waterfall[cite: 41]. It ordered the Liquidator to admit Atul Paper's claim and refund its separate Rs. 69 Lakh interim deposit[cite: 41].

case_title: Sandeep D. Maheshwari, RP of Setubandhan Infrastructure Ltd. & Anr. vs. State Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sandeep D. Maheshwari is the Resolution Professional of Setubandhan Infrastructure Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Appellant in CA 613/2025); Univastu India Ltd. is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA/Appellant in CA 612/2025); State Bank of India is the lead Financial Creditor (CoC majority); other CoC members are IL&FS Financial Services, Union Bank of India, and Kotak Mahindra Prime Ltd. (Dissenting Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Setubandhan Infrastructure Ltd. culminating in a Resolution Plan submitted by Univastu India Ltd. providing upfront cash, deferred consideration, optionally convertible debentures, and equity buy-back. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to CIRP admission on 28.11.2022; SRA proposed total plan outlay of Rs. 27.50 Crores (with potential upside up to Rs. 67.21 Crores), against liquidation value of Rs. 7.48 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 28.11.2022; Form-G published twice (last on 26.08.2023); CoC approved SRA plan on 16.01.2024 with 98.57% voting share; RP filed approval IA No. 07/2024 in January 2024; NCLT reserved orders on 21.08.2024, sought clarifications on 17.12.2024 and 19.12.2024; 18th CoC meeting held on 03.01.2025; RP filed Additional Affidavit on 15.01.2025; NCLT rejected plan on 24.03.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approved Resolution Plan; 15th and 18th CoC minutes explaining plan value calculations; Title documents for disputed assets (Pinnacle Mall, Raipur shops, Bhakti Sankul); EPFO revised claim of Rs. 4,520/-; proof of Rs. 48 Lakhs allocated for Dissenting Financial Creditor. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V dismissed IA No. 07 of 2024 on 24.03.2025, rejecting the resolution plan for alleged discrepancies in plan value, unequal treatment of operational creditors, omission of three assets, failure to provide for claims, and referred RP's conduct to IBBI; RP and SRA appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its limited jurisdiction under Section 31(1) of the IBC by rejecting a resolution plan approved by 98.57% of the CoC on grounds of commercial valuation, asset inclusion, treatment of operational creditors, and minor unverified claims, and whether convening a CoC meeting to address judicial queries warrants adverse reference to IBBI.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in evaluating the feasibility, viability, and financial distribution of a resolution plan is non-justiciable and paramount; an adjudicating authority exercising judicial review under Section 31(1) cannot substitute its own commercial assessment or reject a plan absent explicit statutory contraventions under Section 30(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2) and Section 31(1) circumscribe the scope of judicial inquiry; differential commercial treatment between categories of operational creditors is permissible within CoC discretion. Assets with disputed titles or lack of ownership documentation need not be forcibly included in the resolution pool. Convening a CoC meeting to obtain clarifications sought by the Tribunal is lawful and protected under IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ultra vires standard of review; where the CoC has evaluated contingent recoveries and approved financial parameters by overwhelming majority, the tribunal cannot reject the plan on perceived numerical discrepancies. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan satisfied all statutory requirements under Section 30(2) and Regulations 38 and 39; the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction in rejecting the plan and censuring the RP.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 612 & 613 of 2025 are allowed; the impugned order dated 24.03.2025 is set aside; the matter is remitted to the CoC to consider clarifications in light of NCLT queries; CIRP period extended by 90 days; adverse observations against the RP are expunged and reference to IBBI is set aside.
summary: The Resolution Professional and Successful Resolution Applicant (Univastu India Ltd.) challenged NCLT Mumbai's rejection of a resolution plan approved by 98.57% of the CoC for Setubandhan Infrastructure Ltd.[cite: 42]. The NCLT rejected the plan citing inconsistencies in plan valuation, unequal treatment of operational creditors, exclusion of three disputed immovable assets, and pending small claims, while referring the RP to IBBI[cite: 42]. The NCLAT set aside the order and remitted the matter, ruling that the NCLT exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 31 by interfering with the CoC's commercial wisdom[cite: 42]. The Tribunal held that differential payment terms are permissible, disputed assets were properly addressed, trivial claims do not vitiate a plan, and the RP acted lawfully in consulting the CoC[cite: 42].

case_title: Pravin Electricals Private Ltd. vs. Akshaya Engineering Works Private Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Pravin Electricals Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Main Contractor); Respondent is Akshaya Engineering Works Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor/Sub-contractor); MSEDCL is the Principal Employer. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Two sub-contracts dated 07.07.2018 for supply and installation/services awarded by Corporate Debtor to Operational Creditor for executing electrical infrastructure projects awarded by MSEDCL, providing for back-to-back payment terms tied to MSEDCL milestones and HOTO certificates. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt of Rs. 1.54 Crores (including interest) claimed under 17 unpaid invoices totalling Rs. 4.43 Crores, against which Rs. 3.28 Crores had been paid. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Contracts executed on 07.07.2018; 17 invoices raised between 31.10.2018 and 18.10.2019; MSEDCL issued partial termination on 09.01.2019; emails disputing accounts exchanged on 08.08.2021 and 04.09.2021; Demand Notice under Section 8 issued on 14.12.2021; Notice of Dispute issued on 25.02.2022; Section 9 petition filed on 16.03.2022; NCLT admitted Section 9 petition on 17.10.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Contract LoAs containing back-to-back payment clauses under Appendix-1; correspondence from MSEDCL dated 09.01.2019 and 28.06.2019 partially terminating the contract and imposing Rs. 3.10 Crores risk and cost and Rs. 1.88 Crores material penalties; pre-demand emails dated 08.08.2021 and 04.09.2021 where Corporate Debtor explicitly refused ledger confirmation pending final MSEDCL reconciliation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V admitted the Operational Creditor's Section 9 petition on 17.10.2023, holding debt and default established and finding no pre-existing dispute; Corporate Debtor appealed.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application under the IBC is maintainable where pre-demand communications and back-to-back contractual terms establish the existence of a genuine, plausible pre-existing dispute regarding incomplete project works, lack of reconciliation, and penal deductions imposed by the principal employer.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9(5)(ii)(d) of the IBC, an application for corporate insolvency resolution must be rejected if there is a plausible, genuine pre-existing dispute between the parties that is not a patently feeble legal argument or an assertion of fact unsupported by evidence; the adjudicating authority cannot delve into the merits of contractual breaches or resolve unliquidated claims. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Applying the test laid down in Mobilox Innovations v. Kirusa Software, a dispute exists when communications preceding the Section 8 demand notice reveal contestation over the crystallization of debt, contractual performance, or pending financial reconciliation under back-to-back payment terms. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Plausibility threshold; contemporaneous pre-notice emails refusing ledger confirmation coupled with employer notices imposing penalties and partial contract terminations constitute sufficient objective evidence of a genuine pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because genuine disputes over incomplete works, back-to-back milestone payments, and employer penalties were raised prior to the Section 8 notice, the debt was not undisputed and the Section 9 petition should have been dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1457 of 2023 is allowed; the impugned order dated 17.10.2023 admitting the Section 9 application is set aside; the Corporate Debtor is released from CIRP and restored to independent board management forthwith without costs.
summary: Pravin Electricals Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order admitting a Section 9 application filed by sub-contractor Akshaya Engineering Works for alleged default of Rs. 1.54 Crores[cite: 43]. The Appellant contended that payment was on a back-to-back basis under the contract with MSEDCL and that pre-notice emails of August and September 2021 demonstrated that accounts remained un-reconciled due to project deficiencies and penalties imposed by MSEDCL[cite: 43]. The NCLAT reversed the admission, holding that under Mobilox Innovations v. Kirusa Software, the Adjudicating Authority erred in ignoring pre-existing correspondence[cite: 43]. The record demonstrated genuine, plausible pre-existing disputes regarding work quality, project delay, and back-to-back payment terms, precluding the initiation of CIRP[cite: 43].

case_title: Univastu India Limited vs. Setubandhan Infrastructure Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Univastu India Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Setubandhan Infrastructure Limited (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 2 is Sandeep D. Maheshwari (Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 3 is State Bank of India (Lead CoC member). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of resolution plan for insolvency resolution of Setubandhan Infrastructure Limited proposing an initial infusion of Rs. 27.50 Crores with potential upside recoveries up to Rs. 67.21 Crores. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to admission into CIRP on 28.11.2022; total plan value exceeded liquidation value of Rs. 7.48 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 28.11.2022; CoC approved resolution plan with 98.57% voting share on 16.01.2024; RP filed approval IA No. 07/2024; NCLT reserved orders on 21.08.2024 and re-listed for clarifications on 17.12.2024; RP filed additional affidavit on 15.01.2025; NCLT dismissed IA No. 07/2024 on 24.03.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CoC minutes of 15th and 18th meetings detailing the commercial justification of the plan values; Addendum to Resolution Plan; title reports showing that excluded assets (Pinnacle Mall, Raipur shops, Bhakti Sankul) suffered from defective or un-transferred titles; EPFO revised claim letter for Rs. 4,520/-. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V dismissed IA No. 07/2024 on 24.03.2025, refusing to approve the resolution plan on grounds of value discrepancy, exclusion of assets, and alleged discrimination between operational creditors; SRA appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to reject a resolution plan approved by 98.57% of the CoC by questioning its financial valuation, asset composition, and commercial viability where no violation of Section 30(2) of the IBC is established.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors is non-justiciable and cannot be superseded by an adjudicating authority; judicial review of an approved resolution plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC is strictly confined to determining whether the plan satisfies the statutory requirements set forth in Section 30(2). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) read with Section 30(2) leaves no room for the adjudicating authority to evaluate whether the best possible financial offer has been accepted; the CoC has the authority to assess commercial feasibility, negotiate terms, classify operational creditors, and exclude assets with disputed titles. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Strict compliance with Section 30(2); absence of any statutory contravention makes approval mandatory once the CoC has approved the plan with the requisite majority. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan conformed to all requirements of Section 30(2) and CIRP Regulations; the NCLT's rejection of the plan was contrary to established law.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 612 of 2025 is allowed; the impugned order dated 24.03.2025 is set aside, and the resolution plan is remitted to the CoC for consideration of the NCLT queries within an extended CIRP period of 90 days; adverse remarks against the RP are expunged.
summary: Univastu India Ltd., Successful Resolution Applicant for Setubandhan Infrastructure Ltd., appealed NCLT Mumbai's rejection of its CoC-approved resolution plan[cite: 44]. The NCLT had rejected the plan alleging discrepancies in plan values, unfair treatment of operational creditors, and failure to include certain immovable properties in the asset pool[cite: 44]. The NCLAT allowed the appeal and set aside the rejection, ruling that the NCLT impermissibly interfered with the commercial wisdom of the CoC, which had approved the plan with 98.57% voting[cite: 44]. Reaffirming the Supreme Court's decisions in K. Sashidhar and Essar Steel, the Tribunal held that Section 30(2) compliance was fully met, valuation discrepancies were properly explained in CoC minutes, and title defects justified the asset treatment[cite: 44].

case_title: Mr. Gopal Kalra vs. Mr. Akhilesh Kumar Gupta, Liquidator for Easytech Global Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mr. Gopal Kalra is the erstwhile Director of Easytech Global Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent Mr. Akhilesh Kumar Gupta is the Liquidator of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported trading business of LED bulbs conducted during FY 2016-17 involving gross purchases of Rs. 9.33 Crores and gross sales of Rs. 9.88 Crores with entities such as Satyam Traders, Garg Sales Corporation, B.S. Enterprise, and SP Trading & Co. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Actual cash loss of Rs. 3,18,00,000/- caused to the Corporate Debtor through unrecovered sales balances (Rs. 0.52 Crores) and excess payouts to non-existent suppliers (Rs. 2.67 Crores). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Corporate Debtor admitted into CIRP under Section 9 on 04.10.2018; liquidation ordered on 03.04.2019; Forensic Audit Report submitted on 12.09.2019 for the period 10.10.2016 to 15.10.2018; Liquidator filed IA No. 5545/ND/2021 under Section 66; NCLT passed impugned order on 11.01.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic Audit Report by M/s Ravi Ranjan & Co. dated 12.09.2019; on-ground physical investigation reports revealing that supplier/customer addresses housed bicycle repair shops (Rehman Cycle Works) or different businesses operating since 2004; backdated debit notes (Rs. 6.28 Crores) and credit notes (Rs. 10.06 Crores) erasing trade on paper while actual cash exited corporate bank accounts; absence of physical LED stock. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II allowed Liquidator's IA No. 5545/ND/2021 on 11.01.2024, holding the transactions fraudulent under Section 66(1) and directing Appellant to contribute Rs. 3.18 Crores to the CD's assets; Appellant appealed.
legal_issues: Whether circular LED bulb trading transactions conducted with non-existent entities, paper-cancelled via debit/credit notes but resulting in actual bank fund outflows, constitute fraudulent trading under Section 66(1) of the IBC, and whether a direction ordering the director to personally contribute Rs. 3.18 Crores to the liquidation estate is legally sustainable.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 66(1) of the IBC, where a director knowingly carries on the business of the corporate debtor through sham transactions with fictitious entities resulting in actual depletion of company funds, such conduct constitutes fraudulent trading, and the adjudicating authority is fully empowered to order personal contribution equal to the demonstrated loss. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 66(1) is remedial and restitutionary in nature; fraudulent intent does not require direct criminal conviction and can be inferred from a compelling pattern of fictitious transactions, non-existent counterparties, and deliberate book adjustments designed to siphon corporate funds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Objective forensic verification; field audit reports establishing that counterparty vendors were fictitious, combined with ledger records showing irrecoverable cash outflows, conclusively establish actual loss rather than mere notional loss. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transactions were deliberately structured to project inflated revenues and siphon Rs. 3.18 Crores from the company; the order directing personal contribution of Rs. 3.18 Crores was lawful, proportionate, and fully justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 567 of 2024 is dismissed; the impugned order dated 11.01.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench-II directing the Appellant to contribute Rs. 3.18 Crores to the Corporate Debtor's assets is affirmed; all pending IAs closed.
summary: Erstwhile director Gopal Kalra appealed against NCLT New Delhi's order directing him to contribute Rs. 3.18 Crores to the assets of Easytech Global Pvt. Ltd. under Section 66(1) of the IBC for carrying on fraudulent trading[cite: 45]. The Liquidator's forensic audit revealed that the Appellant conducted bogus LED bulb trading transactions with fictitious entities, which were cancelled on paper through backdated debit and credit notes while actual cash was paid out[cite: 45]. Physical verification showed the vendor addresses housed unrelated businesses, such as a bicycle repair shop[cite: 45]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the transactions caused a real, quantifiable cash loss to the company and that the director was personally liable to make restitution under Section 66(1)[cite: 45].

case_title: Anil Syal vs. Ajay Gupta & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 523 of 2025 & I.A. No. 1993 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Anil Syal (Bankrupt/Personal Guarantor); Respondent No. 1 is Ajay Gupta (Bankruptcy Trustee); Respondent No. 2 is Union Bank of India (UBI/Major Creditor holding 97.27% voting share). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Personal guarantee extended by Appellant to secure financial facilities availed from Union Bank of India; UBI filed a claim for Rs. 71.90 Crores in the bankruptcy process, relinquishing security interest over Appellant's 50% undivided share in a residential flat at Uday Park, New Delhi. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to initiation of Personal Insolvency Resolution Process under Section 94 on 28.10.2020; failure of repayment plan led to Bankruptcy Order on 30.09.2022 (effective 23.12.2022). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Bankruptcy commencement date fixed as 23.12.2022; one-year period under Section 138(1)(a) expired on 22.12.2023; first auction held on 27.06.2023 set aside by NCLT on 04.07.2024; NCLAT granted liberty on 30.07.2024 to apply for discharge; 5th CoC meeting held on 30.07.2024; Appellant filed IA No. 3964/2024 on 06.08.2024 seeking discharge; NCLT rejected application on 11.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order of Adjudicating Authority dated 23.12.2022 fixing bankruptcy commencement; Minutes of 5th CoC meeting dated 30.07.2024 recording that one year had elapsed and UBI deferred the discharge agenda; order dated 04.07.2024 setting aside the first e-auction for lack of 30 days notice. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-III rejected Bankrupt's IA No. 3964/2024 on 11.02.2025, holding that the Bankrupt had no locus to seek discharge under Section 138(1)(a) and that granting discharge would obstruct the pending re-auction of the property; Bankrupt appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the statutory duty of the Bankruptcy Trustee to apply for a discharge order on the expiry of one year from the bankruptcy commencement date under Section 138(1)(a) of the IBC is mandatory, and whether a Bankrupt has the locus standi to petition the Adjudicating Authority to compel discharge when the Bankruptcy Trustee and creditors fail to perform this statutory obligation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory mandate under Section 138(1)(a) of the IBC requiring the filing of an application for discharge upon the expiry of one year from the bankruptcy commencement date is obligatory and not dependent on the consent or convenience of creditors; where the trustee defaults on this duty, the bankrupt has full locus standi to bring the non-compliance before the adjudicating authority. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Use of the word 'shall' in Section 138(1) creates a mandatory statutory obligation on the Bankruptcy Trustee to apply for discharge upon the lapse of one year; under Section 139, discharge releases the individual from bankruptcy debts without discharging the estate or divesting the trustee's power to liquidate assets. Delays in selling estate assets cannot justify deferring statutory discharge. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory timeline test; upon unrefuted proof that more than one year has elapsed from the commencement date, the statutory trigger is complete. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT abdicated its jurisdiction by refusing to enforce the mandatory one-year discharge timeline; the Bankruptcy Trustee cannot evade statutory obligations on the pretext of awaiting creditor concurrence.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 523 of 2025 is allowed; the impugned order dated 11.02.2025 is set aside; the Bankruptcy Trustee is directed to file an application for discharge under Section 138(1)(a) within 15 days, and the Adjudicating Authority is directed to decide the application within three months thereafter.
summary: Bankrupt individual Anil Syal appealed against NCLT New Delhi's dismissal of his application under Section 138(1)(a) IBC seeking discharge from bankruptcy following the expiration of more than two years from the commencement date[cite: 46]. The NCLT had rejected the plea on grounds that only the Bankruptcy Trustee could apply and that discharge would hinder the sale of the Bankrupt's 50% property share[cite: 46]. The NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that Section 138(1)(a) imposes a mandatory statutory duty on the trustee to apply for discharge after one year, which cannot be deferred at the whim of creditors[cite: 46]. Under Section 139, discharge releases personal liability while preserving the trustee's power to administer the estate, and the bankrupt has clear locus to seek enforcement of this statutory timeline[cite: 46].

case_title: M/s. K Computers vs. Mr. Pesaladinne Madhusudhan Reddy, IRP of M/s. Pi Data Centers Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant M/s K Computers is an Operational Creditor; Respondent No. 1 is Mr. Pesaladinne Madhusudhan Reddy, Interim Resolution Professional (IRP); Respondent No. 2 is Mr. Kalyan Muppaneni, Erstwhile Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Pi Data Centers Private Limited[cite: 47]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operational supplies/services provided to the Corporate Debtor resulting in unpaid invoices and initiation of Section 9 proceedings[cite: 47]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose under Section 9 proceedings in CP(IB)71/9/AMR/2020; exact debt quantum not specified in the appellate order[cite: 47]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on Section 9 admission; NCLAT dismissed appeals on 18.12.2024; Supreme Court in Civil Appeal Nos. 857-858/2025 on 22.01.2025 disposed of the appeal noting a settlement agreement and Form FA dated 02.01.2025 and leaving it open for IRP to file a Section 12A application; Appellant filed a police complaint alleging coercion on 21.01.2025; NCLT Amaravati allowed withdrawal IA (IBC)/32/2025 on 28.03.2025[cite: 47]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Settlement Agreement dated 02.01.2025 and statutory Form-FA withdrawal application signed on behalf of M/s K Computers; police complaint dated 21.01.2025; complaint letter to Prime Minister's Office dated 12.12.2024[cite: 47]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Amaravati Bench vide order dated 28.03.2025 allowed IA (IBC)/32/2025 under Section 12A read with Regulation 30A and dismissed the Section 9 petition as withdrawn; Operational Creditor appealed alleging that the settlement and Form FA were obtained through threat and coercion[cite: 47].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 12A withdrawal of CIRP based on a signed settlement agreement and Form-FA can be invalidated on bare allegations of threat and coercion when the applicant failed to initiate formal criminal proceedings or substantiate the allegations before a competent court[cite: 47].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An assertion that a settlement agreement or statutory withdrawal form under Section 12A of the IBC was executed under threat, duress, or coercion cannot be accepted on mere averments in insolvency proceedings; it must be established by credible evidence through due process of law or criminal investigation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A read with Regulation 30A of the CIRP Regulations empowers the Adjudicating Authority to allow withdrawal upon receipt of Form-FA submitted through the IRP; where the execution of the settlement agreement and Form-FA is admitted and was considered by the Supreme Court, unsubstantiated claims of coercion cannot derail withdrawal[cite: 47]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantive proof standard for coercion; filing an uninvestigated police complaint or representation without invoking Magistrate remedies under Section 156(3) CrPC / Section 173(4) BNS fails to establish prima facie coercion[cite: 47]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The settlement agreement and Form-FA dated 02.01.2025 were validly placed on record, and the Appellant failed to substantiate allegations of threat through appropriate legal recourse; the withdrawal under Section 12A was properly granted[cite: 47].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 227/2025 is dismissed for lack of merit; the NCLT order dated 28.03.2025 allowing withdrawal under Section 12A is affirmed; all pending IAs closed[cite: 47].
summary: Operational Creditor M/s K Computers challenged NCLT Amaravati's order allowing an application under Section 12A IBC read with Regulation 30A to dismiss its Section 9 CIRP petition against Pi Data Centers Pvt. Ltd. as withdrawn[cite: 47]. The Appellant argued that the settlement agreement and Form-FA dated 02.01.2025 were obtained through threat and coercion by the suspended director, citing a police complaint dated 21.01.2025[cite: 47]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Supreme Court had already noted the existence of the settlement and Form-FA, and that bare averments of coercion without any substantiated criminal trial or investigation under Section 156(3) CrPC cannot invalidate an admitted settlement agreement[cite: 47].

case_title: Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. vs. Kew Precision Parts Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. is the Financial Creditor; Respondent Kew Precision Parts Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor[cite: 48]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple financial credit facilities sanctioned between 21.11.2012 and 05.03.2014 totalling Rs. 22.46 Crores governed by a Master Facility Agreement dated 05.03.2014[cite: 48]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default commenced in June 2015; loan recall notice dated 07.10.2015 demanded Rs. 18,19,40,434/-; total outstanding claimed in Section 7 petition as of 18.11.2019 was Rs. 62,47,43,978/-[cite: 48]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account classified as NPA on 30.09.2015; Section 13(2) SARFAESI notice issued on 13.12.2017 for Rs. 34.79 Crores; CD proposed an OTS on 20.12.2018 for Rs. 24.55 Crores payable before 31.12.2018, which was accepted by Bank; CD defaulted on OTS; Bank filed Section 7 petition on 02.01.2019; NCLT admitted petition on 06.09.2019; NCLAT set aside admission on limitation; Supreme Court remanded on 05.08.2022 (CA No. 2176 of 2020) to consider Section 25(3) Contract Act; on remand NCLT dismissed Section 7 petition on 29.08.2023[cite: 48]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Master Facility Agreement; loan recall notice; 10 dishonoured cheques worth Rs. 19.34 Crores; OTS letter dated 20.12.2018 admitting outstanding liability; Bank acceptance letter dated 20.12.2018 containing Clause 6(i) revoking concessions and reviving full original liability upon default[cite: 48]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: On remand, NCLT dismissed the Section 7 application on 29.08.2023, holding that while the OTS constituted a fresh contract under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, the petition was unmaintainable because Part IV claimed the full original debt of Rs. 62.47 Crores instead of the settled OTS figure of Rs. 24.55 Crores; Bank appealed[cite: 48].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 application under the IBC is maintainable for the full original outstanding debt following default of an OTS agreement, where the OTS terms explicitly provide that upon failure of payment, all concessions stand revoked and original contractual loan terms are revived[cite: 48].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An OTS proposal made after the expiry of limitation constitutes a promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, 1872; where the creditor's acceptance expressly reserves the right to revoke concessions and revive the original debt upon default, the debtor cannot evade Section 7 insolvency on hyper-technical discrepancies between the OTS sum and the full claim amount in Part IV[cite: 48]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7 of the IBC read with Section 25(3) of the Contract Act permits a financial creditor to enforce the underlying loan liability upon default of a settlement promise; Clause 6(i) of the OTS terms legally reinstates the original loan balance, negating the need to restrict Part IV claims to the compromised OTS figure[cite: 48]. 3.
