EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual clause enforcement; express revocation clauses in settlement acceptance letters govern the consequences of breach, reviving pre-settlement liabilities[cite: 48]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor committed a continuous default by failing to honour the OTS, triggering the revival of its full original liabilities; the NCLT committed a patent error in dismissing the Section 7 petition[cite: 48].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1405 of 2023 is allowed; the impugned order dated 29.08.2023 passed by the NCLT is set aside; all pending IAs closed[cite: 48].
summary: Kotak Mahindra Bank appealed against the NCLT's dismissal of its Section 7 petition against Kew Precision Parts Pvt. Ltd. for default of Rs. 62.47 Crores[cite: 48]. Following a remand from the Supreme Court to evaluate an OTS dated 20.12.2018 under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, the NCLT held that while limitation was saved, the petition was defective because Part IV claimed the full original debt rather than the agreed OTS sum of Rs. 24.55 Crores[cite: 48]. The NCLAT reversed the decision, holding that Clause 6(i) of the OTS acceptance letter explicitly provided that upon default, all concessions were withdrawn and the original loan agreements were revived[cite: 48]. Because the debtor failed to pay the OTS amount by 31.12.2018, the Bank was fully entitled to pursue Section 7 for the entire restored debt[cite: 48].

case_title: Vishwas Lakras & Anr. vs. Dharmendra Pal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Vishwas Lakras and Deepti Lakras (50% shareholders and erstwhile managing directors); Respondents No. 1 and 2 Dharmendra Pal and Hansraj Pal (50% shareholders/Petitioners); Respondent No. 3 M/s Lakras Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. (Company); Respondent No. 6 Madhya Pradesh Financial Corporation (MPFC/Lender)[cite: 49]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint infrastructure development of a 28-flat residential multi-storied project named 'Nilaya Avenue' on a 12,600 sq. ft. plot financed by a term loan of Rs. 1,09,65,000/- from MPFC secured by mortgage and personal guarantees[cite: 49]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in loan repayments to MPFC resulting in default notice dated 24.10.2017; unauthorized collection of advances of Rs. 83.35 Lakhs from 6 investor-allottees for 27 flats without construction progress; projected net operational loss of Rs. 1.83 Crores[cite: 49]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company incorporated on 06.05.2009; MPFC loan sanctioned on 05.02.2015; statutory compliances discontinued post-2015; MPFC default notice issued on 24.10.2017; ROC Section 206 inspection notice issued on 17.07.2019; NCLT passed interim status quo on 31.01.2020; NCLT final order removing directors passed on 10.03.2023[cite: 49]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Secret removal and appointment of statutory auditors without notice to 50% shareholders; filing of financial returns without Respondent No. 1's signature; CA scrutiny report dated 27.08.2022 confirming discrepancies in creditor payments; failure to complete construction despite raising Rs. 4.43 Crores[cite: 49]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench allowed CP No. 91/2019 (TP No. 195/2019) under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013 on 10.03.2023, finding gross oppression and mismanagement, removing Appellants from the Board for three years, and handing management control to Respondents; Appellants appealed[cite: 49].
legal_issues: Whether the exclusion of 50% equal shareholders from management, diversion of secured loan funds, unauthorized replacement of statutory auditors, and stalling of project construction constitute continuous oppression and mismanagement justifying the removal of directors and transfer of management control under Section 242(2)(h) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 49].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Sections 241 and 242 of the Companies Act, 2013, where managing directors conduct the affairs of a quasi-partnership company in a manner prejudicial to its interests by diverting loan proceeds, excluding equal shareholders, and stalling core commercial projects while accumulating losses, the tribunal possesses wide remedial powers to remove such directors and vest control in the aggrieved faction to ensure corporate survival[cite: 49]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 242(2)(h) expressly empowers the Tribunal to order the removal of a managing director or directors where continuous acts of mismanagement are demonstrated; continuing defaults and statutory non-compliances defeat pleas of limitation under Section 241[cite: 49]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Fiduciary dereliction test; failure to maintain proper accounting records under Section 128(3), refusal of inspection, and stalling construction despite collection of funds establish a prima facie case of mismanagement[cite: 49]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants mismanaged company assets, siphoned funds, and brought the company to financial ruin; NCLT's exercise of power under Section 242 removing the Appellants for three years was proper and lawful[cite: 49].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 61 of 2023 is disposed of by upholding the NCLT order removing Appellants from the Board for three years and transferring management control to Respondents; a Local Commissioner is appointed to ensure handover of unsupplied company records within two weeks; all pending applications closed[cite: 49].
summary: Appellants Vishwas Lakras and Deepti Lakras appealed NCLT Indore's order under Sections 241-242 of the Companies Act, 2013 removing them from the board of Lakras Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. for three years and transferring corporate control to 50% shareholders Dharmendra and Hansraj Pal[cite: 49]. The Respondents alleged that the Appellants diverted an MPFC loan of Rs. 1.09 Crores, collected advances for 27 flats without completing construction, replaced auditors secretly, and failed to file statutory annual returns[cite: 49]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal on the merits, holding that continuous financial irregularities, total exclusion of equal shareholders, and failure to complete the project despite collecting sufficient capital constituted clear oppression and mismanagement, justifying removal under Section 242(2)(h)[cite: 49].

case_title: Mr. Rajendra Prasad Tak, Liquidator of M/s. KVK Nilachal Power Pvt. Ltd. vs. Mahanadi Coalfield Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Mr. Rajendra Prasad Tak is the Liquidator of M/s KVK Nilachal Power Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Mahanadi Coalfield Limited (Beneficiary); Respondent No. 2 is UCO Bank (Issuing Bank)[cite: 50]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Fuel Supply Agreement entered into between the Corporate Debtor and Respondent No. 1 for setting up a 300 MW coal-based power plant, secured by four Bank Guarantees issued by UCO Bank against margin money deposited by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 50]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 1 invoked the Bank Guarantees for failure of contractual performance; Liquidator claimed refund of the underlying margin money deposit[cite: 50]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 17.09.2019; liquidation ordered on 17.12.2020; Bank Guarantees invoked by Respondent No. 1 during liquidation; Liquidator filed IA No. 553/2023 seeking return of bank guarantees and margin money; NCLT dismissed IA on 13.04.2023[cite: 50]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Four Bank Guarantees issued by UCO Bank, margin money fixed deposits/deposits maintained by Corporate Debtor, contractual invocation notices issued by Mahanadi Coalfield Limited[cite: 50]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissed Liquidator's IA No. 553/2023 on 13.04.2023, holding that margin money is part of the invoked guarantee and cannot be refunded; Liquidator appealed[cite: 50].
legal_issues: Whether margin money deposited by a corporate debtor with an issuing bank to secure a performance bank guarantee constitutes an asset of the corporate debtor or a security interest under Section 3(31) of the IBC, and whether a liquidator can claim refund of such margin money upon invocation of the bank guarantee during liquidation[cite: 50].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Margin money deposited by a borrower to obtain a Performance Bank Guarantee is held in trust for the beneficiary to ensure execution of the contract; upon invocation of the guarantee, the margin money is appropriated toward payment to the beneficiary and does not form part of the assets of the corporate debtor or its liquidation estate under Sections 18 and 36(4) of the IBC[cite: 50]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 3(31) proviso of the IBC, a performance guarantee is expressly excluded from the definition of 'security interest'; consequently, the moratorium under Section 14(1)(c) does not prohibit the invocation of performance bank guarantees or the adjustment of underlying margin money[cite: 50]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Trust and appropriation principle; margin money retains the character of an impressed trust fund dedicated to satisfy the guarantee, which ceases to be the corporate debtor's property once invoked[cite: 50]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Bank Guarantees were validly invoked by the beneficiary, the margin money was absorbed into the guarantee payout; the Liquidator has no right to demand its refund[cite: 50].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (INS) No. 60 of 2024 is dismissed for lack of merit; the NCLT order dated 13.04.2023 is affirmed; all pending IAs closed[cite: 50].
summary: The Liquidator of KVK Nilachal Power Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Hyderabad's refusal to direct UCO Bank and Mahanadi Coalfield Ltd. to refund margin money deposited for four Bank Guarantees issued under a Fuel Supply Agreement and invoked during liquidation[cite: 50]. The Liquidator argued that the margin money constituted an asset of the Corporate Debtor under Section 35 and that the invocation violated moratorium[cite: 50]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under Section 3(31) of the IBC, performance bank guarantees are excluded from the scope of security interest and Section 14 moratorium[cite: 50]. Following its precedents in Punjab National Bank v. Supriyo Kumar Chaudhuri and Indian Overseas Bank v. Arvind Kumar, the Tribunal affirmed that margin money is held in trust for the beneficiary, and once the guarantee is invoked, it is absorbed towards the payout and cannot be pulled into the liquidation estate[cite: 50].

case_title: Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. & Anr. vs. Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1480 of 2023 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 10 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. (successor/lender) and Marine Solutions Distributions and Services Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Auction Purchaser); Respondent No. 1 is Suraksha Asset Reconstruction Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Sapphire Land Development Pvt. Ltd. is the Corporate Debtor (part of HDIL group); PMC Bank is the original lender[cite: 51, 52]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Moveable asset (Luxury Yacht 'Ferreti 881 HT') owned by Corporate Debtor attached by Economic Offences Wing (EOW) in criminal proceedings against HDIL group, auctioned by PMC Bank administrator pursuant to an order of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate (ACMM) dated 25.11.2019[cite: 51, 52]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to Section 7 CIRP admission against Corporate Debtor on 30.04.2021; Yacht auctioned for Rs. 3,50,00,000/- on 22.03.2021[cite: 51, 52]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ACMM granted permission to sell attached Yacht on 25.11.2019; auction held and 25% deposit paid on 22.03.2021 and 26.03.2021; Section 7 petition CP(IB) No. 987/IB/MB/2020 admitted on 30.04.2021; Suraksha ARC filed IA No. 2303/2021 before NCLT; NCLT set aside auction on 17.10.2023[cite: 51, 52]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Order of the ACMM dated 25.11.2019 permitting auction sale and directing proceeds to loan credit; auction bidding records and deposit receipts dated 22.03.2021 and 26.03.2021 pre-dating CIRP admission[cite: 51, 52]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V allowed IA No. 2303/2021 on 17.10.2023, setting aside the pre-CIRP auction sale of the Yacht and directing handover of the asset to the RP under Section 14 moratorium; Auction Purchaser and Lender appealed[cite: 51, 52].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction under Section 60(5) and Section 14 of the IBC to set aside an auction sale of a moveable asset conducted prior to the commencement of CIRP pursuant to lawful orders passed by a criminal court (Chief Metropolitan Magistrate) in public law proceedings[cite: 51, 52].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An auction sale conducted and concluded prior to the commencement of the Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process under the lawful direction of a competent criminal court is not hit by the moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, and company tribunals have no jurisdiction under public law to interfere with or cancel such prior judicial sales[cite: 51, 52]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14 operates prospectively from the insolvency commencement date to prohibit fresh pecuniary attacks or executions; it cannot invalidate an auction conducted on 22.03.2021 prior to admission on 30.04.2021[cite: 51, 52]. Under Embassy Property Developments and Kalyani Transco, the NCLT's jurisdiction under Section 60(5) does not extend to reviewing or quashing orders of criminal courts or statutory authorities operating in the realm of public law[cite: 51, 52]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Temporal jurisdiction test; where auction procedures and payments were effected prior to the CIRP admission date, Section 14 has no retrospective application[cite: 51, 52]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT lacked jurisdiction to set aside the pre-CIRP auction ordered by the ACMM, and its reliance on Section 14 moratorium was entirely misplaced[cite: 51, 52].
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1480 of 2023 and Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 10 of 2024 are allowed; the impugned order dated 17.10.2023 setting aside the auction is quashed; parties are left free to take appropriate steps regarding the deposited amounts in accordance with law[cite: 51, 52].
summary: Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. and auction purchaser Marine Solutions Distributions and Services Pvt. Ltd. appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order setting aside the auction sale of a luxury Yacht belonging to Corporate Debtor Sapphire Land Development Pvt. Ltd. and ordering its return to the RP[cite: 51, 52]. The Yacht had been attached in criminal proceedings against HDIL and auctioned on 22.03.2021 under an order of the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate, whereas CIRP commenced only on 30.04.2021[cite: 51, 52]. The NCLAT set aside the NCLT's order, holding that Section 14 moratorium cannot apply retrospectively to auctions concluded prior to CIRP admission[cite: 51, 52]. Citing Supreme Court precedents in Embassy Property and Kalyani Transco, the Tribunal held that NCLT lacks jurisdiction under public law to quash judicial sales executed under the orders of a criminal court[cite: 51, 52].

case_title: Indian Bank vs. Anshul Gupta, Liquidator of Topsgroup Services & Solutions Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Indian Bank is a Secured Financial Creditor; Respondent Anshul Gupta is the Resolution Professional and subsequent Liquidator of Corporate Debtor Topsgroup Services and Solutions Limited[cite: 53]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities availed by Corporate Debtor secured by hypothecation of current assets and receivables; Income Tax Department credited an Income Tax Refund into the CD's current account maintained with Appellant Bank[cite: 53]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to CIRP initiation on 19.02.2021; Income Tax Refund of Rs. 4,65,58,425.87/- received during moratorium on 08.06.2021 and detained by the Bank[cite: 53]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 19.02.2021; refund credited on 08.06.2021; RP sent multiple demand emails between October and December 2021; RP filed IA No. 2967/2021 on 16.12.2021; liquidation ordered on 21.09.2022; NCLT directed refund transfer to liquidation account on 20.12.2022; Liquidator filed contempt IA No. 2074/2023 on 15.05.2023; Bank filed recall IA No. 2481/2023 on 19.05.2023; NCLT dismissed recall and allowed contempt directions on 19.12.2024[cite: 53]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements proving receipt of Rs. 4,65,58,425.87/- on 08.06.2021; hypothecation agreement; emails dated 31.12.2021 where Bank refused transfer to Yes Bank citing it was a private bank[cite: 53]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-II vide order dated 19.12.2024 dismissed Bank's recall application IA No. 2481/2023 and allowed Liquidator's IA No. 2074/2023 directing the Bank to remit the refund amount to the Corporate Debtor's liquidation account; Bank appealed[cite: 53].
legal_issues: Whether an income tax refund received in a corporate debtor's bank account during the currency of a Section 14 moratorium belongs to the corporate debtor's insolvency/liquidation estate under the custody of the RP/Liquidator, or whether the depository bank can retain and set off such funds against its outstanding financial claims under a hypothecation charge on receivables[cite: 53].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Monies received in a corporate debtor's account during the currency of a statutory moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC constitute property of the corporate debtor; a creditor bank has no legal right to detain, set off, or unilaterally appropriate such post-commencement receipts, but must transfer them to the designated CIRP or liquidation account under the control of the resolution professional or liquidator[cite: 53]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1) prohibits any action to recover or enforce a security interest; under Section 17, management and custody of all assets and bank accounts vest exclusively in the RP/Liquidator[cite: 53]. Even if tax refunds constitute receivables under a hypothecation deed, realization of security interest during liquidation must be conducted strictly in accordance with statutory procedures and cannot justify self-help retention[cite: 53]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Temporal asset vesting rule; funds entering corporate accounts post-insolvency commencement are subject to the statutory custody of the tribunal-appointed professional[cite: 53]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Income Tax Refund belonged to the Corporate Debtor and was received during moratorium; the Bank was legally obligated to transfer the entire amount of Rs. 4,65,58,425.87/- into the liquidation account[cite: 53].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 85 & 96 of 2025 are dismissed; the impugned orders dated 19.12.2024 directing Indian Bank to remit Rs. 4,65,58,425.87/- to the liquidation bank account are affirmed[cite: 53].
summary: Indian Bank challenged two orders of NCLT Mumbai directing it to remit an Income Tax Refund of Rs. 4.65 Crores received in the Corporate Debtor's account on 08.06.2021 into the liquidation account of Topsgroup Services and Solutions Ltd.[cite: 53]. The Bank argued that under its hypothecation agreement, tax refunds constituted government receivables over which it held an un-relinquished security interest[cite: 53]. The NCLAT dismissed both appeals, holding that because the refund was received during the currency of the Section 14 moratorium, the funds belonged exclusively to the Corporate Debtor and vested in the RP/Liquidator under Section 17[cite: 53]. The Bank had no right to unilaterally detain or set off the funds against its claims, which must instead be adjudicated in accordance with the liquidation distribution framework under Section 53[cite: 53].

case_title: Gangadhar A. Kotian vs. Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Gangadhar A. Kotian is the Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor/Corporate Guarantor Bombay Rayon Clothing Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. is the Debenture Trustee/Financial Creditor; Respondent No. 2 Ram Singh Setia is the IRP; Principal Borrower is Reynold Shirting Ltd.[cite: 54] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Issuance of 1700 Non-Convertible Debentures (NCDs) aggregating to Rs. 170 Crores by Principal Borrower to ECL Finance Ltd. under Debenture Trustee Agreement dated 12.10.2017 and Debenture Trust Deed dated 14.10.2017, secured by a continuing Corporate Guarantee executed by the Corporate Debtor on 14.10.2017[cite: 54]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal Borrower defaulted, and NCDs were classified as NPA on 16.06.2020; initial recall notice issued on 16.09.2020 demanding Rs. 206.15 Crores; pursuant to Restructuring Agreement dated 27.12.2022 restructuring debt to Rs. 162.50 Crores, Principal Borrower paid Rs. 5 Crores upfront but defaulted on the second instalment of Rs. 20 Crores on 25.03.2023; total outstanding default claimed under the second Section 7 petition was Rs. 293,26,51,822/- as of 30.04.2024[cite: 54]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee executed on 14.10.2017; NPA classified on 16.06.2020; first guarantee recall on 16.09.2020; First Petition CP (IB) No. 629/MB/2022 filed against Principal Borrower on 15.03.2022; debt restructured on 27.12.2022 and First Petition withdrawn on 11.01.2023; second instalment default on 25.03.2023; cure notice on 20.06.2023; fresh recall-cum-guarantee invocation on 23.01.2024; Second Petition filed under Section 7 against Corporate Guarantor on 10.06.2024; NCLT admitted petition on 24.04.2025[cite: 54]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Continuing Guarantee Agreement (Clauses 5.3, 26, 31, 33); Restructuring Agreement dated 27.12.2022 superseding earlier communications; default cure notice dated 20.06.2023; recall-cum-guarantee invocation letter dated 23.01.2024[cite: 54]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-II admitted the Financial Creditor's Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 646(MB)/2024 on 24.04.2025, holding that the default occurred on 25.03.2023 post-Section 10A period; Suspended Director appealed contending the petition was barred under Section 10A[cite: 54].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 insolvency petition filed against a corporate guarantor is barred by Section 10A of the IBC where an initial guarantee invocation occurred during the Section 10A period, but the parties subsequently executed a voluntary restructuring agreement post-Section 10A period that was breached and gave rise to a fresh default date[cite: 54].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 10A of the IBC provides temporary immunity for defaults occurring during the prescribed suspension period but does not bar parties from voluntarily entering into debt restructuring arrangements thereafter; upon breach of post-suspension restructuring obligations, a fresh cause of action and date of default accrue outside the statutory embargo of Section 10A under a continuing guarantee[cite: 54]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 10A does not invalidate underlying debt or extinguish continuing guarantee obligations; where a restructuring agreement expressly supersedes prior notices and provides that default in restructured instalments constitutes an independent event of default, the date of default is determined by the breach of restructured terms rather than the original suspended notice[cite: 54]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Contractual novation and continuing guarantee construction; explicit terms defining independent events of default and establishing that the guarantee remains alive until full discharge govern the cause of action[cite: 54]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The default in payment of the restructured second instalment occurred on 25.03.2023, outside the Section 10A window; hence, the Section 7 petition was not hit by Section 10A and was rightly admitted[cite: 54].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 698 of 2025 is dismissed without costs; the impugned order dated 24.04.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-II admitting the Section 7 petition is affirmed[cite: 54].
summary: The Suspended Director of Bombay Rayon Clothing Ltd. appealed NCLT Mumbai's admission of a Section 7 application filed by debenture trustee Catalyst Trusteeship Ltd. for an outstanding default exceeding Rs. 293 Crores[cite: 54]. The Appellant contended that the debt was barred under Section 10A of the IBC because the initial guarantee invocation notice was issued on 16.09.2020 within the protected period[cite: 54]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the corporate debtor had voluntarily executed a fresh Restructuring Agreement on 27.12.2022 that superseded earlier communications[cite: 54]. Since the corporate debtor committed a fresh default under the restructured terms on 25.03.2023 (well after the expiry of Section 10A), and the corporate guarantee was of a continuing nature, the petition was not barred by Section 10A[cite: 54].

case_title: M/s Greenfield Overseas & Ors. vs. Anil Goel, Liquidator of Loha Ispaat Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are M/s Greenfield Overseas (Proprietor Pradeep Joshi, CA 1088/2024), M/s Arihant International (Proprietor Shripal Jain, CA 1089/2024), and M/s Marque Global (Proprietor Rahul Singh, CA 1090/2024), third-party trading entities; Respondent is Anil Goel, Liquidator of Loha Ispaat Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 55]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale/return of steel products (Hot Rolled Coils/scraps) between Corporate Debtor and Appellants during FY 2015-16 and FY 2016-17[cite: 55]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidator alleged undervalued purchase returns resulting in total losses of Rs. 53,26,35,721/- across all transferees; NCLT originally ordered recoveries of Rs. 5,49,23,112/- against Greenfield, Rs. 2,37,81,057/- against Arihant, and Rs. 26,76,91,364/- against Marque Global[cite: 55]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 28.04.2017; one-year look-back period under Section 46(1) for unrelated parties spanned 28.04.2016 to 28.04.2017; Liquidator filed avoidance application MA 1265/2018; NCLT passed impugned order on 30.04.2024[cite: 55]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Forensic Audit Report by Khandelwal Jain & Co. dated 13.01.2018; Tally database and stock item registers showing purchase returns of non-perishable HR Coils at deep discounts rather than fresh scrap sales; revised calculations showing loss during the statutory look-back period of 28.04.2016 to 28.04.2017[cite: 55]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed the Liquidator's avoidance application under Section 45 on 30.04.2024 and directed Appellants to refund the full financial year losses; Appellants appealed on grounds of ordinary course of business, third-party exemption, and miscalculation beyond the statutory look-back period[cite: 55].
legal_issues: Whether purchase returns of non-perishable steel coils at heavily discounted prices to unrelated third parties fall within the ordinary course of business exemption under Section 45(2) of the IBC; whether third-party transferees are subject to avoidance orders under Section 45; and whether the look-back period under Section 46(1) must be strictly computed from the insolvency commencement date rather than by full financial years[cite: 55].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In avoidance proceedings under Section 45 of the IBC, the look-back period for unrelated parties is strictly one year preceding the insolvency commencement date, and transactions falling outside this exact window cannot be subjected to avoidance or recovery; however, third-party beneficiaries of undervalued transfers remain fully amenable to Section 45 orders[cite: 55]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 46(1) prescribes the look-back period as one year preceding the insolvency commencement date (28.04.2016 to 28.04.2017); reckoning the period on a full financial year basis (from 01.04.2016) is contrary to the statute[cite: 55]. Under Section 45(2), heavy discounts on purchase returns of non-perishable commodities do not constitute transactions in the 'ordinary course of business'[cite: 55]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Rigorous statutory time-computation and accounting reconciliation; recovery liabilities must be adjusted to exclude transactions that occurred outside the 365-day statutory look-back window[cite: 55]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The transactions were undervalued and not in the ordinary course of business, but the recoverable quantum must be restricted strictly to transactions within the one-year look-back period (28.04.2016 to 28.04.2017), reducing the Appellants' liabilities[cite: 55].
operative_order: Appeals are allowed in part; the impugned order dated 30.04.2024 is modified to reduce the recoverable amounts to: Rs. 2,70,87,587/- for M/s Greenfield Overseas, Rs. 77,43,946/- for M/s Arihant International, and Rs. 20,66,33,868/- for M/s Marque Global based on revised look-back calculations; on all other grounds, the appeals are dismissed without costs[cite: 55].
summary: Three proprietorship firms appealed against NCLT Mumbai's order under Section 45 IBC directing them to refund substantial sums to the Liquidator of Loha Ispaat Ltd. for undervalued purchase returns of HR Coils[cite: 55]. The Appellants claimed the dealings were routine scrap purchases in the ordinary course of business, that third parties could not be roped into Section 45, and that the Liquidator improperly calculated losses across full financial years[cite: 55]. The NCLAT held that returning non-perishable steel at huge discounts was not in the ordinary course of business and that third-party beneficiaries are covered under Section 45[cite: 55]. However, the Tribunal held that Section 46(1) strictly limits the look-back period for unrelated parties to one year prior to CIRP (28.04.2016 to 28.04.2017), and accordingly modified the order to reduce the Appellants' liabilities to the re-computed look-back amounts[cite: 55].

case_title: Dicksons Overseas Private Limited vs. Mr. Prasad Dharap, Liquidator of Jejani Pulp & Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Dicksons Overseas Pvt. Ltd. is the Successful Auction Purchaser (SAP); Respondent Prasad Dharap is the Liquidator of Jejani Pulp & Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 56, 57]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: E-auction sale of Subject Land of the Corporate Debtor in liquidation conducted on 28.09.2020 with a reserve price of Rs. 9.30 Crores, wherein Appellant emerged as successful bidder for Rs. 9.23 Crores[cite: 56, 57]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total sale consideration was Rs. 9.23 Crores (including EMD of Rs. 90.30 Lakhs); Letter of Intent required balance payment within 90 days (by 29.12.2020); balance consideration of Rs. 13.52 Crores (inclusive of 12% p.a. interest) was eventually deposited following tribunal orders[cite: 56, 57]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Auction conducted 28.09.2020; LoI issued 01.10.2020; 90-day period expired 29.12.2020; SAP filed IA No. 12/2021 on 29.12.2020 seeking time stoppage under force majeure; SAP filed IA No. 560/2022 on 28.02.2022 seeking to acquire CD as going concern; NCLT dismissed IA 12/2021 and IA 560/2022 on 21.01.2025 while directing balance payment with 12% interest within 30 days[cite: 56, 57]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Government of Maharashtra notifications staying and resuming land conversion; high court writ orders restraining coercive steps; correspondence establishing SAP had available funds in SBI and repeatedly offered to deposit balance in escrow[cite: 56, 57]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench on 21.01.2025 rejected SAP's prayers to declare force majeure and treat the sale as an acquisition of a going concern, but directed SAP to remit balance consideration with 12% interest within 30 days; SAP appealed against the rejection of force majeure and interest stoppage[cite: 56, 57].
legal_issues: Whether the Successful Auction Purchaser is entitled to invoke force majeure to stop the running of the 90-day liquidation payment timeline and interest liabilities under Schedule I Clause 12 of the Liquidation Regulations due to land conversion delays, and whether appeals become infructuous once the full balance consideration with interest is paid and sale certificate issued[cite: 56, 57].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An auction purchaser who participates in a liquidation sale on an 'as is where is' basis cannot claim relief from interest obligations or convert an asset purchase into a going-concern acquisition under force majeure when extenuating delays are balanced out by interest payments. Where the purchaser subsequently tenders full payment with interest pursuant to tribunal orders and obtains a sale certificate, appeals challenging the underlying payment conditions become infructuous[cite: 56, 57]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Schedule I Clause 12 under Regulation 33 of the Liquidation Regulations allows 90 days for payment, with interest at 12% after 30 days; under Section 35 IBC read with Rule 11 of NCLT Rules, the tribunal may extend time in exceptional circumstances by balancing equities through interest payment, but cannot extinguish interest liability completely[cite: 56, 57]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Consummation of contract doctrine; full payment, execution of the sale certificate, handover of possession, and distribution of proceeds render appeals seeking alteration of sale terms infructuous[cite: 56, 57]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SAP having deposited the complete amount of Rs. 13.52 Crores with interest and having obtained possession and a sale certificate, its appeals challenging the rejection of force majeure and going-concern prayers are rendered infructuous[cite: 56, 57].
operative_order: Company Appeals (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 473, 485 & 463 of 2025 are dismissed as infructuous following the complete payment of balance consideration along with interest and execution of the sale certificate[cite: 56, 57].
summary: Successful Auction Purchaser Dicksons Overseas Pvt. Ltd. challenged NCLT Mumbai's order dated 21.01.2025 dismissing its applications (IA 12/2021 and IA 560/2022) which sought to declare a stoppage of the 90-day payment timeline and waiver of interest on grounds of force majeure (due to a state stay on land conversion) and sought acquisition of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern[cite: 56, 57]. The NCLT had rejected the force majeure plea but granted 30 days to pay the balance with 12% interest[cite: 56, 57]. The NCLAT held that while the NCLT properly exercised inherent powers under Rule 11 to grant extension subject to 12% interest to balance equities, the SAP had already complied by depositing Rs. 13.52 Crores, received possession, and obtained a sale certificate, rendering its appeals infructuous[cite: 56, 57].

case_title: Sushil Jejani vs. Mr. Prasad Dharap, Liquidator of Jejani Pulp & Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sushil Jejani is the Promoter/Ex-Management of Corporate Debtor Jejani Pulp & Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Prasad Dharap, Liquidator; Respondent No. 2 is Dicksons Overseas Pvt. Ltd., Successful Auction Purchaser (SAP)[cite: 56, 57]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Liquidation sale of Subject Land of the Corporate Debtor conducted by public auction on 28.09.2020 for a total consideration of Rs. 9.23 Crores[cite: 56, 57]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure to pay balance sale consideration within 90 days from the Letter of Intent dated 01.10.2020; Appellant sought cancellation of auction sale and forfeiture of EMD of Rs. 90.30 Lakhs[cite: 56, 57]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation initiated on 18.10.2019; auction held on 28.09.2020; LoI issued 01.10.2020; 90-day window expired 29.12.2020; state government imposed stay on Class II land conversion on 10.12.2020; Bombay High Court granted interim protection on 28.12.2020; Appellant filed IA No. 1365/2023 on 23.03.2023 (after 905 days); NCLT dismissed IA 1365/2023 on 21.01.2025 and granted 30 days to SAP to deposit balance with 12% interest[cite: 56, 57]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements showing SAP maintained sufficient funds in State Bank of India to pay the balance consideration; repeated correspondence from SAP to Liquidator offering to deposit money in escrow; revenue department rejection orders for land conversion[cite: 56, 57]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed Promoter's IA No. 1365/2023 on 21.01.2025, refusing to cancel the auction and allowing the SAP 30 days to pay the balance with 12% interest; Promoter appealed[cite: 56, 57].
legal_issues: Whether an auction sale in liquidation must be mandatorily cancelled upon the expiry of the 90-day period stipulated in Schedule I Clause 12 of the Liquidation Regulations when the delay was caused by third-party regulatory obstacles (land conversion freeze) and court restraint orders, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the inherent power under Rule 11 of NCLT Rules read with Section 35 IBC to extend time for payment[cite: 56, 57].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the 90-day timeline in Schedule I Clause 12 of the Liquidation Regulations is ordinarily mandatory, the Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 read with Section 35(1) of the IBC to extend the payment timeline in extraordinary and extenuating circumstances where non-payment was not a wilful default, subject to the payment of interest to balance equities[cite: 56, 57]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The statutory consequence of cancellation under Clause 12 is intended to penalize defaulting bidders; it does not divest the tribunal of discretionary authority under V.S. Palanivel v. P. Sriram to grant an extension when judicial orders, revenue freezes, and legal disputes over land tenure prevent timely execution of the conveyance[cite: 56, 57]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Readiness and willingness test; where contemporaneous bank certificates prove the bidder had sufficient liquidity and made repeated bona fide attempts to place funds in escrow, the default cannot be categorized as deliberate or strategic[cite: 56, 57]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The delay was occasioned by complex external legal impediments, and the SAP paid the full balance of Rs. 13.52 Crores along with 12% interest; the NCLT's refusal to cancel the auction was lawful and protected the liquidation estate[cite: 56, 57].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 449 of 2025 and Contempt Case No. 16 of 2025 are dismissed; the NCLT order dated 21.01.2025 is affirmed without costs[cite: 56, 57].
summary: Promoter Sushil Jejani appealed against NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of his application (IA 1365/2023) seeking the cancellation of an auction sale of land belonging to Jejani Pulp & Paper Mills Pvt. Ltd. to Dicksons Overseas Pvt. Ltd. for failure to pay the balance consideration within the 90-day statutory period under Schedule I Clause 12 of the Liquidation Regulations[cite: 56, 57]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under V.S. Palanivel v. P. Sriram and Rajabhau Shinde v. S.M. Electric Works, the Adjudicating Authority has inherent power under Rule 11 of the NCLT Rules to grant time extensions in extraordinary circumstances[cite: 56, 57]. Finding that the delay was caused by a state stay on land conversion and high court interim orders, that the SAP always had funds ready, and that the SAP ultimately paid the full consideration of Rs. 13.52 Crores with 12% interest, the Tribunal held the sale valid[cite: 56, 57].

case_title: Daksha Atul Desai vs. Registrar of Companies, Mumbai
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Daksha Atul Desai is a Shareholder/Director of the struck-off company; Respondent is Registrar of Companies (RoC), Mumbai[cite: 58]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Statutory company registration and compliance under the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 58]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Non-filing of statutory financial statements and annual returns, leading RoC to initiate suo motu striking off[cite: 58]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: RoC struck off the name of the company under Section 248(1) vide order dated 19.07.2017; Appellant filed appeal/application under Section 252(3) on 08.08.2023 (within the 20-year window); NCLT dismissed application as time-barred on 23.07.2024; Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 58]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RoC gazette strike-off notification dated 19.07.2017; shareholding records showing Appellant is a member/shareholder of the company[cite: 58]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench dismissed the Appellant's application on 23.07.2024 holding that because RoC struck off the company under Section 248(1), the appeal had to be filed under Section 252(1) within 3 years, rendering an application filed in 2023 hopelessly barred by limitation; Appellant appealed[cite: 58].
legal_issues: Whether an application filed by a member/shareholder for restoration of a struck-off company's name is governed by the 3-year limitation under Section 252(1) or the 20-year limitation under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013, where the striking off was initiated suo motu by the RoC under Section 248(1)[cite: 58].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013, the statutory limitation of 20 years under subsection (3) applies to applications for company restoration preferred by a company, member, creditor, or workman, irrespective of whether the strike-off was initiated suo motu by the Registrar under Section 248(1) or voluntarily by the company under Section 248(2)[cite: 58]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 252 creates no statutory dichotomy restricting Section 252(1) (3-year period) to Section 248(1) strike-offs and Section 252(3) (20-year period) to Section 248(2) strike-offs; Section 252(3) explicitly grants a company, member, creditor, or workman an independent right to apply for restoration within 20 years from the official gazette publication[cite: 58]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Standing and statutory classification test; proof of status as a member/shareholder automatically entitles the applicant to the benefit of the 20-year limitation period under Section 252(3)[cite: 58]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in reclassifying the application under Section 252(1) and dismissing it as time-barred; the application was filed by a member within 20 years and must be heard on merits[cite: 58].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 370 of 2024 is allowed; the impugned order dated 23.07.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai is set aside, and the matter is remitted to NCLT to hear the restoration appeal on merits; all pending applications closed[cite: 58].
summary: Daksha Atul Desai, a shareholder/director of a struck-off company, appealed against NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of her restoration application filed under Section 252(3) of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 58]. The company was struck off by the RoC on 19.07.2017, and the application was filed on 08.08.2023[cite: 58]. The NCLT held that because the strike-off was initiated by the RoC under Section 248(1), the 3-year limitation under Section 252(1) applied, making the application time-barred[cite: 58]. The NCLAT reversed the order, holding that Section 252 makes no distinction between voluntary and RoC-initiated strike-offs, and that any application filed by a member, creditor, or workman is governed by the 20-year limitation under Section 252(3)[cite: 58]. The NCLT was directed to hear the matter on merits[cite: 58].

case_title: Harish Kumar & Ors. vs. Jalesh Kumar Grover, Interim Resolution Professional & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 935 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 876 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Financial Creditors in a class comprise 75 allottees/homebuyers of residential units (Respondents No. 4 and 5 to 79); Corporate Debtor is M/s Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. (landowning subsidiary company); developer entity is M/s Premia Projects Ltd. (holding company undergoing CIRP); Appellants in CA No. 935/2025 are Harish Kumar and 3 other homebuyers of Premia Projects Ltd., and Appellant in CA No. 876/2025 is Radha Buildtech (India) Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant of Premia); Respondent No. 1 is Jalesh Kumar Grover (Interim Resolution Professional of Solitaire). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 11.03.2009, GNIDA allotted 45,398.50 sqm of land at Plot No. 201, Sector KP-V, Greater Noida West to Solitaire. On 01.10.2012, Solitaire entered into a collaboration agreement with Premia Projects Ltd. granting Premia possession and exclusive sales/marketing rights for 90% of the constructed area in exchange for Rs. 4.5 Crores consideration and 10% constructed area. Promoters common to both companies siphoned funds collected from 566 allottees who booked units in the project 'Premia Corporate City' without completing construction or handing over possession. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from failure to deliver possession of residential units to 566 homebuyers as promised under allotment letters and MoUs, triggering widespread debt defaults exceeding statutory thresholds. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Premia Projects Ltd. was admitted to CIRP under Section 7 on 30.05.2018 in CP (IB) No. 104 of 2018. On 18.11.2021, NCLAT in CA (AT) (Ins) No. 1069 of 2020 directed consideration of Section 7 initiation against Solitaire followed by joint consolidation. CP No. 740 of 2021 filed by Harish Kumar against Solitaire was dismissed on 22.12.2022 for lack of threshold. 75 homebuyers filed Section 7 CP (IB) No. 644 of 2023 against Solitaire on 20.07.2023. Radha Buildtech's resolution plan for Premia was approved by Premia's CoC on 27.12.2023 and submitted to NCLT on 15.01.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Collaboration agreement and MoU dated 01.10.2012; shareholding records proving Premia acquired near 100% equity in Solitaire; transaction audit report demonstrating extensive fund siphoning by common director Tarun Sheinh; minutes of Premia's CoC meetings dated 18.02.2020 and 20.12.2023 acknowledging that resolution of Premia was impossible without Solitaire's land. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: 75 homebuyers filed Section 7 petition CP (IB) (IBC) No. 644 of 2023 before NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-V; on 03.06.2025, NCLT admitted the petition and commenced CIRP against Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. based on established default and satisfaction of the minimum homebuyer threshold. Appellants appealed this admission order.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority was justified in initiating CIRP under Section 7 against a subsidiary landowning company on an application by homebuyers when a separate CIRP and a CoC-approved resolution plan proposing merger was already pending in respect of the holding developer company, and whether simultaneous or consolidated CIRP of both companies is permissible under the Code.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The pendency of corporate insolvency resolution proceedings or the approval of a conditional merger in a resolution plan concerning a holding developer company does not legally preclude financial creditors from triggering an independent Section 7 CIRP against an interconnected subsidiary landowning entity where a legally enforceable debt and default exist. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5) mandates that once the Adjudicating Authority is satisfied regarding the occurrence of a default in respect of a financial debt due and payable, admission must follow as a matter of course without equitable dilution. Furthermore, by virtue of Sections 18 and 36(4)(d), assets of a subsidiary cannot be unilaterally included in the resolution plan or liquidation estate of the holding company without subjecting the subsidiary to CIRP in accordance with law. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The strict test laid down in Innoventive Industries and M. Suresh Kumar Reddy requires the tribunal solely to verify the existence of a debt, default under Section 3(12), and completeness of the petition meeting the statutory numerical threshold of allottees, irrespective of collateral commercial arrangements. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Solitaire and Premia shared common control, commingled assets, and interwoven liabilities, and since the NCLAT's prior binding judgment of 18.11.2021 mandated initiation of CIRP against Solitaire as a condition precedent for joint consolidation to bring the project land into the resolution pool, the NCLT committed no error in admitting the Section 7 petition against Solitaire.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 876 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 935 of 2025 are dismissed. The impugned admission order dated 03.06.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed. There is no order as to costs, and all pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: NCLAT dismissed two connected appeals filed by the Successful Resolution Applicant of Premia Projects Ltd. and a faction of homebuyers challenging the NCLT New Delhi order dated 03.06.2025, which admitted a Section 7 petition initiated by 75 homebuyers against landowning subsidiary Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. The Appellants argued that the separate CIRP would disrupt Premia's resolution plan, which contemplated a merger of the two companies. Rejecting these contentions, NCLAT held that under Section 7 and Supreme Court precedents, admission is mandatory once debt and default are established. Following its prior binding decision dated 18.11.2021, NCLAT held that bringing Solitaire into CIRP was legally necessary to pool the essential land asset with Premia for an effective, consolidated resolution.

case_title: Radha Buildtech (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 876 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 935 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Radha Buildtech (India) Pvt. Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) of corporate debtor Premia Projects Ltd.; Respondent No. 1 is Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. (landowning subsidiary and Corporate Debtor) represented by IRP Jalesh Kumar Grover; Respondent No. 4 and Respondents No. 5-79 are 75 homebuyers/financial creditors in a class; co-appellants in connected appeal are Harish Kumar & Ors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA) allotted a 45,398.50 sqm land parcel at Plot No. 201, Sector KP-V, Greater Noida West to Solitaire on 11.03.2009. Solitaire and Premia executed a collaboration agreement on 01.10.2012 transferring land possession and 90% sales/marketing rights of 'Premia Corporate City' to Premia for Rs. 4.5 Crores and 10% constructed area. Through share transfers, Premia acquired 100% effective ownership of Solitaire, making it a wholly owned subsidiary under common promoter Tarun Sheinh, who siphoned funds collected from 566 allottees without delivering the flats. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from failure to construct and deliver residential units to 566 homebuyers; claimed default in CP (IB) No. 644 of 2023 was filed by 75 homebuyers whose collective debt and default met the statutory threshold under Section 7 IBC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Premia entered CIRP on 30.05.2018 in CP (IB) No. 104 of 2018. On 18.11.2021, NCLAT remanded the matter with directions to consider CIRP against Solitaire and subsequent consolidation. Section 7 petition CP No. 644 of 2023 was filed by 75 allottees on 20.07.2023. Radha Buildtech's resolution plan was approved by Premia's CoC on 27.12.2023 and submitted for NCLT approval via IA No. 06 of 2024 on 15.01.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Collaboration agreement and MoUs dated 01.10.2012; transaction audit report revealing diversion of funds; Information Memorandum issued by Premia's RP explicitly referencing NCLAT's remand order dated 18.11.2021; minutes of Premia's CoC meetings of 18.02.2020 and 20.12.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: 75 homebuyers filed Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 644 of 2023 before NCLT New Delhi (Court-V). By order dated 03.06.2025, NCLT admitted Solitaire into CIRP. Radha Buildtech appealed contending that admission of Solitaire would defeat its approved resolution plan proposing merger.
legal_issues: Whether the approval of a resolution plan by the CoC of a parent developer company proposing a merger with its landowning subsidiary deprives the Adjudicating Authority of jurisdiction to admit an independent Section 7 petition against the subsidiary filed by allottees, and whether the SRA has locus standi to oppose statutory CIRP admission of the subsidiary.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan in the CIRP of a parent company cannot extinguish or stay the statutory rights of financial creditors to seek initiation of CIRP against an interconnected subsidiary entity where debt and default are independently established. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 7(5) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction is strictly bounded by the inquiry into debt and default; once both are established, admission is mandatory. Further, under Section 18(1) explanation (b) and Section 36(4)(d), assets of a subsidiary company cannot be treated as assets of the parent debtor or included in its resolution plan without legally subjecting the subsidiary to CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying M. Suresh Kumar Reddy and Innoventive Industries, the adjudicating authority is not permitted to exercise equitable discretion to reject an otherwise complete Section 7 application where default is evident from the records. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA submitted its resolution plan with full knowledge of NCLAT's binding order of 18.11.2021 mandating CIRP against Solitaire prior to joint consolidation; hence, the SRA cannot challenge the lawful initiation of Solitaire's CIRP, and the admission order passed by NCLT was entirely justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 876 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 935 of 2025 are dismissed. The impugned order dated 03.06.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority is affirmed. All pending interlocutory applications are closed without any order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Radha Buildtech (India) Pvt. Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant of Premia Projects Ltd., challenging NCLT New Delhi's order dated 03.06.2025 which admitted landowning subsidiary Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. into CIRP under Section 7 on an application filed by 75 homebuyers. The SRA contended that its CoC-approved resolution plan for Premia incorporated a merger of Solitaire and that a parallel CIRP would derail resolution. NCLAT rejected this, holding that under Section 18 and 36(4)(d) of the IBC, subsidiary assets cannot be resolved without Solitaire undergoing CIRP. Upholding its binding 2021 remand order, NCLAT ruled that admission was mandatory upon proof of debt and default.

case_title: M/s. Prakash Oil Depot vs. G. Madhusudhan Rao, Liquidator for M/s Sarda Agro Oils Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 304/2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 306/2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in CA No. 304/2025 is M/s. Prakash Oil Depot (a partnership firm and Scheme Proponent); Appellant in CA No. 306/2025 and Respondent No. 1 is G. Madhusudhan Rao (Liquidator for Corporate Debtor M/s Sarda Agro Oils Limited); Respondent No. 2 is Indian Bank (erstwhile Allahabad Bank, Secured Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor M/s Sarda Agro Oils Limited was placed into liquidation; Appellant M/s. Prakash Oil Depot proposed a scheme of compromise/arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Regulation 2B of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 to revive the Corporate Debtor by settling creditors at a value substantially exceeding liquidation value. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in loan facilities leading to Section 7 proceedings in CP(IB)/102/7/HDB/2019; liquidation was ordered on 09.01.2023 in IA No. 1323/2022; the Scheme Proponent deposited an Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) cheque of Rs. 4,30,00,000/- (Rs. 4.30 Crores) dated 31.05.2024 to support the compromise scheme. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation was ordered on 09.01.2023. NCLT granted exclusions of time: 09.01.2023 to 29.08.2023 (order dated 29.08.2023), 29.08.2023 to 08.03.2024 (order dated 08.03.2024), and 08.03.2024 to 31.07.2024 (order dated 31.07.2024). Scheme submitted to liquidator on 25.01.2024; EMD paid on 31.05.2024; Indian Bank approved scheme on 21.11.2024; Bank of Baroda approved on 22.04.2025; IA(IBC)/833/2025 filed on 26.04.2025 seeking 90 days extension from date of order. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submission of compromise scheme on 25.01.2024; deposit of EMD cheque of Rs. 4.30 Crores on 31.05.2024; approval and formal consent letters from 100% of secured creditors within the Stakeholders Consultation Committee (Indian Bank and Bank of Baroda). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The Liquidator filed IA(IBC)/833/2025 in CP(IB)/102/7/HDB/2019 before NCLT Hyderabad seeking a 90-day extension to operationalize the Section 230 scheme. On 26.05.2025, NCLT rejected the application holding that granting a further extension contravened the 90-day outer limit under Regulation 2B(1). Both the Scheme Proponent and Liquidator appealed.
legal_issues: Whether the 90-day timeline prescribed under Regulation 2B(1) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 for completing a compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 is directory or mandatory, and whether the Adjudicating Authority has the jurisdiction to grant extensions beyond 90 days where 100% of secured creditors have approved the scheme.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Statutory timelines prescribed in subordinate liquidation regulations for completing a scheme of compromise or arrangement under company law are directory in nature, and adjudicating tribunals retain discretion to grant extensions where creditors have exercised their commercial wisdom to favor corporate revival over corporate death. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 contains no maximum outer time limit for completing a scheme of compromise or arrangement, and a subordinate regulation framed under Section 240 of the IBC (Regulation 2B) cannot be interpreted rigidly to curtail the substantive power of revival under the parent Act; Regulation 2B serves primarily to exclude time spent on compromise from the total liquidation period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Relying on Swiss Ribbons, Arun Kumar Jagatramka, and Y. Shivram Prasad, the governing standard is whether the scheme represents a realistic, bona fide alternative offering value maximization superior to liquidation, and whether it has secured the requisite approval of the Stakeholders Consultation Committee. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the scheme was approved by 100% of secured financial creditors and delay was caused by internal bank approval processes rather than bad faith, the NCLT erred in rigidly refusing an extension; a further 90-day period was warranted to achieve corporate revival.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 26.05.2025 passed by NCLT Hyderabad is quashed. A further period of 90 days from the date of uploading of the order is granted to complete the scheme of arrangement subject to compliance with Section 230(5) of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 8 of the Companies (Compromises, Arrangements and Amalgamations) Rules, 2016. Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 304/2025 and No. 306/2025 are allowed. All pending interlocutory applications stand closed.
summary: NCLAT Chennai allowed the appeals filed by scheme proponent M/s Prakash Oil Depot and the Liquidator of M/s Sarda Agro Oils Limited, setting aside NCLT Hyderabad's rejection of an extension of time to finalize a scheme of arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act read with Regulation 2B of the IBBI Liquidation Process Regulations. NCLT had rejected the extension on grounds that the 90-day limit in Regulation 2B had expired. Overruling the decision, NCLAT held that Regulation 2B is directory and cannot override substantive powers under Section 230. Respecting the commercial wisdom of 100% of secured creditors who approved the higher-value revival scheme, NCLAT granted a 90-day extension to complete the arrangement.

case_title: M/s. Nirmal Ujjwal Credit Co-Operative Society Ltd. vs. Ravi Sethia, Resolution Professional for Morarjee Textile Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s. Nirmal Ujjwal Credit Co-Operative Society Ltd. (a multi-state cooperative credit society and prospective resolution applicant); Respondent No. 1 is Ravi Sethia (Resolution Professional for Morarjee Textiles Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Shriniwas Spintex Industries Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant); Respondent No. 3 is the Committee of Creditors (CoC) of Morarjee Textiles Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process of Corporate Debtor Morarjee Textiles Limited, an industrial manufacturer of cotton and synthetic/man-made fabrics. Appellant, citing its net worth of Rs. 123.29 Crores and an agro-textile vertical 'Nirmal Textiles', submitted an EoI and a Resolution Plan offering Rs. 170 Crores to acquire the Corporate Debtor as a subsidiary. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on financial debts owed by Morarjee Textiles Limited leading to CIRP initiation on 09.02.2024 in C.P. (IB) No. 1318(MB)/2022; Appellant offered Rs. 170 Crores in its plan against competing offer of Rs. 156 Crores by Respondent No. 2. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 09.02.2024. Form G published on 01.05.2024 and amended on 23.05.2024. EoI submitted on 18.05.2024; provisional PRA list on 23.06.2024; final PRA list on 02.07.2024. Initial resolution plan submitted on 27.08.2024. Appellant passed an AGM resolution on 23.09.2024. Revised plan submitted on 02.01.2025. CoC resolved Appellant was ineligible in 22nd meeting on 04-05.02.2025; RP issued rejection letter on 10.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audited Profit and Loss Account of Appellant for the year ended 31.03.2024 showing interest income from banking business of Rs. 194.27 Crores versus a loss of Rs. 3.37 Crores from 'Nirmal Textiles'; Appellant's Bye-law Clause 5(s) restricting activities to agro products; Bye-law Clause 52 restricting investment avenues; absence of any prior General Body resolution under Section 19(1) of the 2002 Act; absence of amended bye-laws on plan submission date. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 880 of 2025 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-I challenging the RP's rejection communication dated 10.02.2025. On 09.04.2025, NCLT dismissed the application, holding Appellant statutorily and byelaw-wise ineligible to invest in the Corporate Debtor. Appellant appealed to NCLAT under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a multi-state credit cooperative society is legally eligible under Section 64(d) of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 and its own bye-laws to submit a resolution plan for an industrial textile company; whether eligibility must exist in praesenti at the date of plan submission or can be cured through post-facto bye-law amendments under Section 31(4) of the IBC; and whether the CoC can evaluate PRA eligibility within its commercial wisdom.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The legal eligibility and capacity of a prospective resolution applicant must exist in praesenti at the date of submission of the resolution plan, and an applicant disqualified by its governing statutory framework or corporate charter cannot cure foundational ineligibility through speculative post-approval amendments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 64(d) of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 restricts investment of cooperative funds strictly to subsidiary institutions or institutions operating in the 'same line of business'; a credit cooperative society whose bye-laws confine operations to agro-products cannot treat an industrial synthetic textile manufacturer as being in the same line of business. Furthermore, Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC prohibits submission of plans contravening applicable law, while Section 31(4) applies solely to statutory approvals and cannot validate antecedent ineligibility. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the strict in praesenti standard of ArcelorMittal and Phoenix ARC, the court examines whether the resolution applicant possessed actual legal capacity and requisite authority under its constitutive documents on the date of plan submission. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Morarjee Textiles was not an existing subsidiary and operated outside the Appellant's primary line of credit business and agro-scope under Bye-law Clause 5(s), the resolution plan contravened Section 30(2)(e) of the Code; the CoC and NCLT rightly disqualified the Appellant within their statutory domain and commercial wisdom.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 09.04.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 880 of 2025 in CP (IB) No. 1318(MB)/2022 is affirmed. Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 790 of 2025 is dismissed without costs. All pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Nirmal Ujjwal Credit Co-Operative Society Ltd. against NCLT Mumbai's order upholding its disqualification as a resolution applicant for Morarjee Textiles Ltd. Despite offering a higher bid of Rs. 170 Crores, the Appellant was disqualified because Section 64(d) of the Multi-State Co-operative Societies Act, 2002 and its bye-laws restricted investments to existing subsidiaries or entities in the same line of business. NCLAT held that the Appellant's business was credit and agro-processing, which did not encompass the Corporate Debtor's industrial synthetic textile operations. Affirming that eligibility must exist in praesenti at plan submission and cannot be retroactively cured by amending bye-laws, NCLAT held the plan non-compliant under Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC.

case_title: The Calcutta Cricket & Football Club vs. Karan Singh Grewal & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is The Calcutta Cricket & Football Club (a historic sporting club established in 1876 and registered as a Section 8 non-profit company with 1880 members); Respondents No. 1 to 3 are individual members of the Club (including Karan Singh Grewal). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Internal corporate governance and election of office bearers and general committee of the Section 8 company for the year 2024-2025 convened under a notice dated 07.09.2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Does not involve debt or financial default; disputes involve alleged electoral manipulation, irregularities, and mismanagement in the election held on 30.09.2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In October 2023, four members filed Company Petition C.P. No. 287 of 2023 under Sections 241-242 with a waiver application under Section 244(1), which NCLT allowed on 17.01.2024 (affirmed by NCLAT, subject to interim directions by Supreme Court in Civil Appeal No. 6604 of 2025). Notice for Club elections issued on 07.09.2024; voting held and results declared on 30.09.2024 with elected members assuming charge; on 03.12.2024, Respondents No. 1-3 filed IA No. 225 of 2024 seeking scrutiny and recounting; listed on 09.12.2024 where NCLT reserved orders while granting one week to file a reply; impugned order passed on 03.01.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Election notice dated 07.09.2024 appointing Election Officer and team of Scrutinizers; physical voting Scrutinizer's report dated 01.10.2024; participation of Respondents No. 1 and 2 in the election process and nomination of observers; absence of recorded reasons or evidence of fraud in NCLT's order. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In pending C.P. No. 287 of 2023 before NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-I, Respondents filed IA No. 225 of 2024; NCLT heard the IA on its first listing date (09.12.2024), simultaneously reserved the order, and on 03.01.2025 appointed an independent scrutinizer to recount manual and CDSL votes. Appellant appealed under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether an order passed by the Adjudicating Authority granting substantive interim reliefs without assigning reasons or recording prima facie findings violates principles of natural justice and is vitiated in law; and whether reserving orders on the very first day of listing while granting time to file a reply affidavit violates Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules, 2016.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An adjudicatory or quasi-judicial order that grants substantive interim reliefs altering settled corporate outcomes without recording reasons or independent objective satisfaction is void, as the requirement to state reasons is an indispensable component of natural justice and the lifeblood of judicial decision-making. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 mandates that an opposite party be afforded reasonable and effective opportunity to show cause and contest an application by filing a reply; reserving an order on the first day of listing while ostensibly allowing time to file a reply reduces statutory natural justice to an empty formality. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the rule of law laid down in Kranti Associates, Capoor, and Zee Entertainment, recording of reasons is the indispensable link between the evidence on record and the final conclusion; a mere recitation of an applicant's subjective 'reasons to believe' cannot substitute judicial findings of prima facie wrongdoing. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT completely failed to provide reasons or adjudicate the preliminary objections raised by the Club, rendering the order dated 03.01.2025 legally unsustainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 10 of 2025 is allowed. The impugned order dated 03.01.2025 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in IA No. 225/2024 in C.P. No. 287 of 2023 is set aside. The interim order dated 13.01.2025 is discharged, and the Appellant is directed to take custody of the election materials deposited in the NCLT. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by The Calcutta Cricket & Football Club against the NCLT Kolkata order dated 03.01.2025, which appointed an independent scrutinizer to recount and re-scrutinize votes of the Club's elections conducted on 30.09.2024. Setting aside the order, NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority passed an unreasoned order that merely recited the applicant's subjective suspicions without recording any independent judicial findings. Furthermore, reserving the order on the very first date of listing while granting one week to file a reply violated Rule 37 of the NCLT Rules, 2016 and principles of natural justice.

case_title: Mr. Ram Ratan Modi vs. Sumangal Dealmark Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ram Ratan Modi, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor Citystar Infrastructures Ltd. (developer); Respondents No. 1 to 4 are Financial Creditors (Sumangal Dealmark Pvt. Ltd., S.M. Carriers Pvt. Ltd., Samriddhi Metals Pvt. Ltd., and S.M. Niryat Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 5 is Corporate Debtor represented by IRP Aditya Kumar Tibrewal. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor held development rights under a 12.10.2007 agreement with Bengal Secretariat Cooperative Land Mortgage Bank & Housing Society Ltd. for redeveloping premises at 530/1, Jodhpur Park, Kolkata. On 18.02.2014, Corporate Debtor and Respondent No. 1 executed an agreement wherein Respondents agreed to extend financial assistance comprising a refundable 'interest-free security deposit' of Rs. 20 Crores and construction finance, in consideration for a 50% profit share in lieu of interest. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondents disbursed Rs. 13.20 Crores between 2014 and 2018. Total amount claimed in default under Section 7 petition was Rs. 78.73 Crores (principal of Rs. 13.20 Crores plus accrued interest/profits) with default crystallising upon unilateral contract termination on 24.12.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Formal refund demand issued by FCs on 23.11.2022 demanding Rs. 46.08 Crores; CD denied on 25.11.2022; fresh demand on 07.12.2022; CD unilaterally terminated the agreement and invoked arbitration under Section 21 of the 1996 Act on 24.12.2022; FCs replied demanding refund on 15.03.2023; arbitration statement of claim filed July 2023 and defence/counterclaim filed October 2023; Section 7 petition C.P. (IB) No. 78/KB/2024 filed on 18.04.2024; NCLT admitted CIRP on 24.10.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Agreement dated 18.02.2014 (Clauses 6-9); Board Resolutions of CD (28.01.2014) and FC-1 (13.02.2014) explicitly describing funds as 'financial assistance'; CD's termination letter dated 24.12.2022 admitting receipt of Rs. 13.20 Crores; CD's ledger accounts (2019-2022) reflecting interest credited on loans; Form 16A/26AS evidencing TDS deducted on interest under Section 194A; pleadings in arbitral Statement of Claim admitting financial assistance. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondents No. 1-4 filed Section 7 application CP(IB)/78(KB)/2024 before NCLT Kolkata Court-II. By order dated 24.10.2024, NCLT admitted the petition, holding the disbursement to be a financial debt having the commercial effect of a borrowing with default upon termination. Suspended Director appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether funds disbursed under the nomenclature of an 'interest-free security deposit' linked with a 50% profit-sharing entitlement under a real estate development financing agreement constitute a 'financial debt' having the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC; whether non-refund following unilateral termination of the agreement constitutes a default under Section 3(12); and whether the pendency of arbitral proceedings bars the admission of a Section 7 petition.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For a debt to qualify as a financial debt under Section 5(8), the nomenclature given by the parties is not determinative; an advance of funds intended to finance business operations repayable with an entitlement to profit share satisfies the requirement of time value of money and has the commercial effect of a borrowing under Section 5(8)(f). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 5(8)(f) is an expansive residuary catch-all provision; an interest-free financial disbursement is not excluded from the definition of financial debt (as held in Orator Marketing). Furthermore, once an agreement is unilaterally terminated, the debtor cannot enforce conditional clauses postponing refund until project completion, and retention of funds constitutes an immediate default. Under Section 7, the existence of pending arbitration is irrelevant to admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Pioneer Urban Land, Global Credit Capital, and Indus Biotech, the adjudicating authority must look behind the contractual nomenclature at the true nature of the transaction and admissions in contemporaneous board resolutions, ledgers, and tax deduction certificates. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the Corporate Debtor admitted receipt and utilisation of Rs. 13.20 Crores as financial assistance with profit share and failed to refund the amount upon unilaterally terminating the contract, debt and default were conclusively established, and NCLT's admission order was legally unimpeachable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2018 of 2024 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 24.10.2024 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench admitting the Section 7 petition and initiating CIRP against Citystar Infrastructures Ltd. is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by the Suspended Director of Citystar Infrastructures Ltd. against the NCLT Kolkata order dated 24.10.2024 admitting a Section 7 application filed by four financial creditors. The Corporate Debtor argued that the Rs. 13.20 Crores received was an interest-free security deposit refundable only upon project completion and that pending arbitration barred Section 7 proceedings. Rejecting these contentions, NCLAT held that under Section 5(8)(f) and Supreme Court rulings in Orator Marketing and Global Credit Capital, the advance had the commercial effect of a borrowing where the 50% profit share constituted time value of money. Upon the debtor's unilateral contract termination, the amount became immediately repayable, and pending arbitration was no bar to CIRP admission.

case_title: S. Vasudevan vs. IDBI Trusteeship Services Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is S. Vasudevan, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s Tuscan Consultants and Developers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Guarantor, registered in Bengaluru); Respondent No. 1 is IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. (Financial Creditor/Debenture Trustee); Respondent No. 2 is Ashok Mittal (Interim Resolution Professional); Principal Borrower is Ozone Projects Pvt. Ltd. (registered in Chennai). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Debenture Trust Deed (DTD) dated 29.06.2016, debenture holders extended financial assistance of Rs. 1,26,30,00,000/- (Rs. 126.30 Crores) to Ozone Projects. Repayment was secured by an unconditional, irrevocable Corporate Guarantee Agreement dated 29.06.2016 executed by Tuscan Consultants. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default of Rs. 126.30 Crores plus redemption premium occurred upon expiry of the revised debenture redemption date of 30.09.2021. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand Notice issued on 13.12.2021 giving 10 days; Final Demand Notice issued on 06.01.2022; Demand Certificate issued on 12.08.2022. Section 7 petition CP/IB/49/CHE/2023 filed against Principal Borrower Ozone Projects before NCLT Chennai on 05.08.2022 (registered 27.02.2023, admitted 01.05.2023). Section 7 petition CP/IB/81/CHE/2023 filed against Tuscan Consultants before NCLT Chennai on 19.09.2022 (registered 02.05.2023, admitted 09.10.2023). 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Debenture Trust Deed and Corporate Guarantee Agreement dated 29.06.2016; Demand Notices dated 13.12.2021 and 06.01.2022; Demand Certificate dated 12.08.2022; judicial order dated 17.04.2023 of NCLT Chennai overruling the Registry's territorial jurisdiction defect under Section 60(2). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Financial Creditor filed Section 7 CP/IB/81/CHE/2023 before NCLT Chennai against Tuscan Consultants. NCLT overruled Registry's territorial objection on 17.04.2023. Tuscan failed to file a counter on merits despite costs; NCLT closed right to reply on 04.09.2023 and admitted Tuscan to CIRP on 09.10.2023. Appellant appealed challenging NCLT Chennai's territorial jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether the filing of a Section 7 petition against a principal borrower constitutes 'pendency' of a corporate insolvency resolution process under Section 60(2) of the IBC so as to confer concurrent territorial jurisdiction on the same NCLT Bench over a corporate guarantor whose registered office is in another state; and whether a territorial jurisdiction objection can be raised for the first time in appeal after participating without challenging an adverse preliminary judicial order.
ratio_decidendi: 1.
