ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: For the purpose of invoking Section 60(2) of the IBC to institute proceedings against a corporate guarantor before the same bench where the principal borrower's case is situated, 'pendency' is reckoned from the date of initiation (filing) under Section 5(11) read with Section 7(1), and does not require prior admission or commencement under Section 5(12) and Section 7(6). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'pending' in Section 60(2) means a proceeding that has been instituted and remains undecided. The legislative intent behind Section 60(2) is an exception to Section 60(1) to avoid multiplicity of forums and conflicting rulings across different tribunals arising out of common financing and guarantee documents. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Section 21 CPC and the Supreme Court ruling in Pathumma, an objection as to the place of suing must be taken at the earliest opportunity in the court of first instance and accompanied by proof of consequent failure of justice; failure to challenge a formal order deciding jurisdiction constitutes waiver and submission to concurrent jurisdiction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Section 7 proceedings against the Principal Borrower were already instituted and pending before NCLT Chennai on 19.09.2022, NCLT Chennai had full jurisdiction under Section 60(2) to entertain and admit the Section 7 petition against the Corporate Guarantor.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 362/2023 is dismissed. The impugned admission order dated 09.10.2023 passed by NCLT Chennai is affirmed. All pending interlocutory applications are closed.
summary: NCLAT Chennai dismissed the appeal filed by the Suspended Director of Tuscan Consultants and Developers Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT Chennai's order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by IDBI Trusteeship Services Ltd. The Appellant contended that NCLT Chennai lacked territorial jurisdiction under Section 60(1) because Tuscan's registered office was in Bengaluru, arguing that Section 60(2) did not apply as CIRP had not yet 'commenced' against the principal borrower when the petition was filed. NCLAT rejected this, holding that 'pendency' under Section 60(2) commences from the date of filing (initiation) under Section 5(11) to prevent multiplicity of forums. NCLAT further held that having failed to challenge the NCLT's jurisdiction order dated 17.04.2023, the Appellant was estopped from raising territorial objections.

case_title: Paresh K. Mehta Investment Pvt. Ltd. vs. State Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Paresh K. Mehta Investment Pvt. Ltd., representing the Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s MKM Diamonds Pvt. Ltd. (formerly Eurostar Diamonds India Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Antwerp Branch, Belgium, claiming as Operational Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is IRP Ms. Dipti Amit Thite; sister company is Eurostar Diamond Traders NV (Belgium). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Bill discounting facility granted by SBI Antwerp to Eurostar Diamond Traders NV. Eurostar Belgium drew two commercial invoices for supply of polished natural diamonds on Corporate Debtor: Invoice No. 9001602957 dated 03.10.2016 for USD 1,394,214.56 (due 31.01.2017) and Invoice No. 9001602984 dated 05.10.2016 for USD 1,419,140.70 (due 02.02.2017). SBI Antwerp discounted the invoices and made payments to Eurostar Belgium; Corporate Debtor accepted and endorsed the bills. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational default in Section 9 application was Rs. 21,28,72,302.48 (principal of Rs. 16,77,17,732.21 plus interest) as of 15.02.2017. Corporate Debtor had made part payments of USD 174,214.56 on 15.05.2017 and USD 400,000 on 26.09.2017. Entire principal of Rs. 16,77,17,732.21 was paid by demand draft on 26.09.2023 during appellate proceedings. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invoices matured on 31.01.2017 and 02.02.2017. Demand Notice under Section 8 issued on 09.10.2020; reply issued by CD on 05.11.2020. Section 9 petition C.P.(IB) No. 877/IBC/MB/2022 filed by SBI on 12.07.2022; admitted by NCLT on 01.09.2023. Appeal filed on 06.09.2023; interim order staying CIRP passed on 27.09.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Endorsed Invoices dated 03.10.2016 and 05.10.2016 containing no interest clause; reply to Demand Notice dated 05.11.2020 admitting part payments to SBI on 15.05.2017 and 26.09.2017; bank draft dated 26.09.2023 evidencing payment of full principal sum of Rs. 16,77,17,732.21. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SBI filed Section 9 application before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-II. On 01.09.2023, NCLT admitted the petition, holding the claim was not time-barred due to Section 19 part payments and Covid-19 limitation exclusion orders. Suspended Director appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application filed on 12.07.2022 based on invoices falling due in February 2017 is saved from limitation under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 by virtue of part payments and Covid-19 exclusion orders; and whether an Operational Creditor is legally entitled to claim interest and continue CIRP where neither the contract nor invoices provide for interest and the entire principal debt has been paid.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Part payments made on a debt within the statutory period of limitation coupled with written acknowledgement extend the limitation period under Section 19 of the Limitation Act; however, an operational creditor cannot levy interest or continue CIRP solely for the recovery of disputed interest in the absence of an express contractual agreement or invoice stipulation consented to by the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 9 of the IBC, an operational debt includes interest only if interest is payable in terms of an underlying commercial agreement. Pursuing CIRP exclusively for the realization of unagreed interest after full liquidation of the principal debt constitutes an abuse of process contrary to Section 65 and the core objective of the Code, which is resolution and not debt collection. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where invoices contain no interest clause and no independent agreement for interest is proved, the evidentiary test under Krishna Enterprises, SS Polymers, and SNJ Synthetics mandates treating only the principal amount as actionable debt under Section 9. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 9 petition was timely filed by virtue of Section 19 part payments and Covid-19 exclusion periods, but SBI had no legal entitlement to interest; because the entire principal operational debt was fully discharged by the CD, the CIRP could not be sustained.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1197 of 2023 is allowed. The CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor M/s MKM Diamonds Pvt. Ltd. under the impugned order dated 01.09.2023 is closed, and the Corporate Debtor is freed from the rigors of CIRP. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed on behalf of MKM Diamonds Pvt. Ltd., closing the CIRP initiated under Section 9 by State Bank of India Antwerp. While NCLAT affirmed that the Section 9 application was filed within limitation by virtue of part payments made in 2017 under Section 19 of the Limitation Act read with Supreme Court Covid-19 exclusion orders, it held that SBI was not entitled to charge interest because neither the contract nor the discounted diamond invoices contained an interest clause. Since the Corporate Debtor had fully paid the entire principal operational debt of Rs. 16.77 Crores, NCLAT held that CIRP cannot be continued as a recovery forum for interest and terminated the insolvency process.

case_title: HDFC Bank Ltd. vs. M/s Hema Engineering Industries Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is HDFC Bank Ltd. (Secured Financial Creditor); Respondent is Corporate Debtor M/s Hema Engineering Industries Ltd., represented by Liquidator Vikas Garg. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by HDFC Bank secured by exclusive charges over specific movable and immovable assets of the Corporate Debtor. CIRP was initiated against CD under Section 9 on 05.04.2021; liquidation ordered on 17.05.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant submitted Form D on 01.06.2022 claiming Rs. 87,61,99,358.13 and opted to realize its security interest outside the liquidation estate under Section 52 of the IBC; Liquidator demanded Rs. 1,07,50,291/- towards liquidation costs/workmen dues and Rs. 89,63,788/- towards PF/gratuity dues. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation commenced 17.05.2022. Form D submitted 01.06.2022; Liquidator identified assets on 30.07.2022 and communicated approval on 09.08.2022. 90-day period under Regulation 21A(2)(a) expired on 15.08.2022. Liquidator issued notice on 08.09.2022 intimating assets fell back into common liquidation pool due to non-payment. Appellant replied on 14.09.2022; Liquidator reaffirmed on 16.09.2022. Appellant filed IA No. 4610 of 2022 before NCLT. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Liquidator's decision dated 30.07.2022 and email dated 09.08.2022; Liquidator's letters dated 08.09.2022 and 16.09.2022; Bank's reply dated 14.09.2022 refusing to deposit estimated sums prior to asset sale and disputing liability for workmen provident fund/gratuity; fact that Bank successfully realized movable assets but failed to make statutory deposits. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed IA No. 4610 of 2022 in CP No. IB-900/(ND)/2020 before NCLT New Delhi Court-III praying to sell secured assets first and deposit Section 53 dues only post-realization. NCLT dismissed the IA on 04.02.2025. HDFC Bank appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a secured creditor opting to realize its security interest outside the liquidation estate under Section 52 of the IBC has a legal right to withhold payment of its mandatory share of liquidation costs and priority workmen dues under Section 53(1)(a) and (b)(i) until after the actual realization of its secured assets; and whether failure to pay estimated costs within 90 days results in automatic vesting of the secured assets into the liquidation estate under Regulation 21A(3).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory obligation of a secured creditor realizing security interest outside liquidation to contribute towards liquidation costs and priority workmen dues under Section 53 within 90 days from the liquidation commencement date is mandatory and independent of the actual realization of the secured asset. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 21A(2)(a) of the IBBI Liquidation Regulations requires payment of estimated Section 53 dues within 90 days from the liquidation commencement date; failure to comply triggers the statutory consequence under Regulation 21A(3) whereby the asset automatically reverts to and becomes part of the liquidation estate. The statute confers no right on a creditor to defer payment until post-sale proceeds are in hand. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Moser Baer, Sunil Kumar Jain, and Shikshak Sahakari Bank, priority workmen dues under Section 36(4) and Section 53 are sacrosanct; an applicant seeking to bypass Regulation 21A must show timely compliance or seek formal extensions based on rare exceptional circumstances before default occurs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because HDFC Bank failed to deposit the estimated liquidation costs and workmen dues within the statutory 90-day window and only sought permission to pay after realization while refusing to contribute to PF/gratuity funds, the secured assets automatically vested in the liquidation estate, and NCLT properly dismissed the Bank's application.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 346 of 2025 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 04.02.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi in IA No. 4610 of 2022 is affirmed. No order as to costs. Pending interlocutory applications stand disposed of.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by HDFC Bank Ltd. against the NCLT New Delhi order dated 04.02.2025 which rejected the Bank's application seeking to realize its security interest outside liquidation without upfront payment of Section 53 dues. HDFC Bank claimed exclusive charge over certain assets of M/s Hema Engineering Industries Ltd. and argued that it should be permitted to sell the assets first and deposit liquidation costs and workmen dues from the sale proceeds. Rejecting the plea, NCLAT held that Regulation 21A(2)(a) mandatorily obligates a secured creditor to pay its estimated share within 90 days of liquidation commencement, independent of realization. Non-compliance resulted in automatic vesting of the assets into the common liquidation estate under Regulation 21A(3).

case_title: CA Santanu Brahma vs. Indian Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is CA Santanu Brahma (Liquidator of Corporate Debtor M/s Maheswary Ispat Limited); Respondent No. 1 is Indian Bank and Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (Secured Financial Creditors holding pari passu first charge). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: High Court winding-up proceedings transferred to NCLT Kolkata; liquidation initiated on 19.12.2023. Respondents submitted claims in Form D on 17.01.2024 and 09.02.2024 opting not to relinquish security interest over the Panagarh Factory under Section 52 IBC and proceeded to sell it under the SARFAESI Act. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidator calculated total estimated liquidation cost at Rs. 2,41,01,225/-, with Respondents' share at Rs. 2,14,71,839/-; Respondents made part-payment of Rs. 26,95,706/- (Rs. 21,55,706/- by R-1 and Rs. 5,40,000/- by R-2), leaving an unpaid balance of Rs. 1,87,76,133/- towards Liquidator's fee and costs. Panagarh Factory was sold under SARFAESI for Rs. 55.10 Crores (against banks' initial estimate of Rs. 15.79-20 Crores). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation initiated on 19.12.2023. Notice to contribute costs sent on 15.03.2024; Respondents gave written undertakings on 12.04.2024 and executed handover document on 30.04.2024 agreeing to pay liquidator's fees under Regulation 4(2)(b) on sale completion. Asset sold on 21.10.2024; demand for balance fees sent on 28.10.2024; reminder emails sent through December 2024; Liquidator filed IA No. 1 of 2025 before NCLT; NCLT rejected fees on 05.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Emails dated 12.04.2024 from both banks undertaking to pay Liquidator's fees under Regulation 4(2)(b) upon asset sale; physical Handover Document dated 30.04.2024 explicitly incorporating the undertaking to pay Regulation 4(2)(b) fees plus 5% clerkage; records showing Liquidator retrieved physical possession from the Official Liquidator, deployed armed security, resolved inter-bank priority disputes, and liaised with prospective buyers; Certificate of Sale dated 25.10.2024 confirming sale for Rs. 55.10 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant Liquidator filed IA (Companies Act) No. 1 of 2025 in T.P. No. 20 of 2022 before NCLT Kolkata seeking payment of Rs. 1,87,76,133/-. On 05.02.2025, NCLT disposed of the IA holding that since the sale was conducted by secured creditors under Section 52, the Liquidator was entitled to NIL fees. Liquidator appealed under Section 61(1).
legal_issues: Whether a Liquidator is entitled to fees computed under Regulation 4(2)(b) read with Regulation 21A(2) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 on the sale proceeds of an asset realized directly by secured financial creditors outside the liquidation estate under Section 52 IBC and the SARFAESI Act; and whether secured creditors are estopped from resiling from written undertakings given to pay the Liquidator's fees upon taking possession of the secured asset.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A secured creditor who exercises its right to realize security interest outside the liquidation estate under Section 52 is statutorily obligated to pay its proportionate share of liquidation costs, including the Liquidator's fee calculated as if the asset had been relinquished to the liquidation estate, and cannot deny fees merely because the physical sale was conducted under SARFAESI. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 21A(2) mandatorily binds secured creditors realizing security outside liquidation to contribute towards liquidation costs under Section 53(1)(a) read with Regulation 2(ea); the computation of such costs and fees must follow the formula in Regulation 4(2)(b). The clarification to Regulation 4(2)(b) applies only where different liquidators realize and distribute assets, and does not extinguish a liquidator's statutory fee entitlement under Regulation 21A(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Shikshak Sahakari Bank and SIDBI, the liquidator's entitlement is sustained where the liquidator took custody, protected and preserved the asset, mediated disputes, and facilitated value maximization, coupled with binding contractual and statutory undertakings given by the lenders. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Respondent Banks gave unambiguous written undertakings to pay the Liquidator's fee under Regulation 4(2)(b) to secure handover of possession and achieved a sale of Rs. 55.10 Crores; they are estopped from denying payment, and the NCLT's finding that the Liquidator was entitled to NIL fees was contrary to law.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 461 of 2025 is allowed. The impugned order dated 05.02.2025 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench in IA No. 1 of 2025 in T.P. No. 20 of 2022 is set aside. Appellant-Liquidator is held entitled to fees under Regulation 4(2)(b) arising from the sale of the Panagarh Factory. Respondent Banks (Indian Bank and SBI) are directed to jointly pay the balance amount of Rs. 1,87,76,133/- together with 5% clerkage within six weeks. No costs.
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by CA Santanu Brahma, Liquidator of Maheswary Ispat Limited, setting aside NCLT Kolkata's order dated 05.02.2025 which had denied the Liquidator fees on the sale of the Panagarh Factory. Indian Bank and SBI had realized the factory under Section 52 IBC and the SARFAESI Act for Rs. 55.10 Crores, refusing to pay balance liquidator fees on the pretext that the sale was conducted outside liquidation. Overruling NCLT, NCLAT held that under Regulation 21A(2) read with Regulation 2(ea) and 4(2)(b), secured creditors realizing assets outside liquidation are legally obligated to contribute towards liquidation costs, including liquidator's fees. Having provided written undertakings to obtain physical handover, the banks were directed to pay Rs. 1.87 Crores plus clerkage within six weeks.

case_title: Mrs. Latha Balasubramanian vs. IGP Engineers Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 70/2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 72/2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Mrs. Latha Balasubramanian, a minority shareholder holding 5.98% equity shares in Respondent No. 1 Company; Respondent No. 1 is IGP Engineers Private Limited; Respondents No. 2 to 14 are individual directors/shareholders; Respondents No. 15 and 16 are corporate entities (Karaikal Marketing Pvt. Ltd. and Pathakudi Trading Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate shareholding dispute wherein Appellant acquired 6,390 shares (5.98% paid-up capital) on 15.11.2019 following testamentary disposition from her late father, Late Mr. V. Krishnaswamy (original 30% shareholder since 1979), alleging oppression and mismanagement under Section 241. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: No financial loan or debt default; matter involves minority shareholder oppression, valuation of equity shares, and non-compliance with the statutory 10% shareholding threshold under Section 244(1)(a). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition CP/CA/96(CHE)/2023 along with Section 244(1) waiver application filed in 2023; parties agreed on 20.12.2023 to explore share valuation for exit; NCLT appointed Deloitte India on 31.01.2024; valuer report submitted on 20.09.2024; Appellant objected on 10.12.2024 while Respondent No. 1 accepted on 21.01.2025; impugned orders passed on 05.03.2025 and 16.04.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Testament of Late Mr. V. Krishnaswamy; share transfer records dated 15.11.2019; Deloitte India independent valuation report dated 20.09.2024; objection affidavit of Appellant dated 10.12.2024; affidavit of Respondent No. 1 dated 28.02.2025 agreeing to abide by the valuation. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP/CA/96(CHE)/2023 before NCLT Chennai, an application under proviso to Section 244(1) was filed. On 05.03.2025, NCLT abandoned the exit route due to disagreement on valuation and directed that the Section 244 waiver application be heard on merits; on 16.04.2025, NCLT rectified a clerical error in IA No. 68/2025. Appellant appealed both orders under Section 421.
legal_issues: Whether the consensual appointment of an independent valuer to explore an exit option amounts to an implied or deemed waiver of the statutory threshold under Section 244(1) of the Companies Act, 2013, and whether an interlocutory order directing that a pending Section 244 waiver application be decided on merits is appealable under Section 421.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Consensual or discretionary interlocutory mechanisms explored by a company court to achieve an amicable settlement cannot bypass, waive, or substitute the mandatory statutory requirement of obtaining an express judicial order of waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) where a petitioner lacks statutory shareholding thresholds. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The satisfaction of conditions under Section 244(1)(a) or obtaining a specific waiver under the proviso to Section 244(1) is an indispensable statutory condition precedent for conferring locus standi to institute and sustain an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Interlocutory orders that merely regulate procedure, direct valuation by consent, or schedule maintainability hearings without conclusively deciding substantive rights or a lis between parties do not qualify as appealable determinations under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the valuation was not mutually accepted and no order granting waiver under Section 244 had been passed, the Company Petition had not legally matured for trial on merits under Section 241; NCLT correctly directed that the Section 244 waiver application be adjudicated first.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 70/2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 72/2025 are dismissed as premature and lacking merit. The Adjudicating Authority is to decide the Section 244 waiver application on its own merits. All pending interlocutory applications stand closed.
summary: NCLAT Chennai dismissed two connected company appeals filed by Mrs. Latha Balasubramanian, a 5.98% minority shareholder in IGP Engineers Pvt. Ltd., against NCLT Chennai orders dated 05.03.2025 and 16.04.2025. During the pendency of Appellant's Section 244 waiver application, NCLT had consensually appointed Deloitte India to value her shares for an amicable buyout; however, when Appellant objected to the valuation report, NCLT abandoned the exit route and listed the Section 244 waiver application for adjudication on maintainability. Affirming NCLT's view, NCLAT held that consensual valuation does not constitute an implied waiver of Section 244(1)(a) thresholds and that deciding the statutory waiver application on merits is a mandatory prerequisite before proceedings under Section 241 can legally proceed.

case_title: Indian Overseas Bank vs. Consortium of GSEC Limited and Rakesh Shah & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Indian Overseas Bank (Secured Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Consortium of GSEC Limited and Rakesh Shah (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA); Respondent No. 2 is Bhuvan Madan (Erstwhile Resolution Professional); Corporate Debtor is Diamond Power and Infrastructure Ltd. (DPIL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities including Bank Guarantee (BG) facility granted by Appellant Bank to DPIL. Under the sanction terms and loan agreements, DPIL maintained cash margin in the form of Term Deposits with Appellant to secure BGs issued in favour of third-party beneficiaries. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Prior to CIRP, between 21.04.2018 and 23.05.2018, third-party beneficiaries invoked multiple BGs; Appellant honoured the BGs and adjusted Term Deposits towards Margin Money totaling Rs. 1,58,59,294/-, subsequently filing a revised claim reducing its dues to Rs. 51,54,93,366/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: BGs invoked between 21.04.2018 and 23.05.2018. Section 7 petition admitted against DPIL on 24.08.2018. Appellant submitted initial claim on 05.09.2018; adjusted margin money on 27.09.2018; submitted revised claim in Form C reflecting adjustment on 09.11.2018. Resolution plan approved by CoC on 06.01.2022 and by NCLT on 20.06.2022. SRA took over on 17.09.2022; issued legal notice on 13.02.2023; filed IA No. 440 of 2023; NCLT ordered refund on 24.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sanction letters and BG loan agreements; third-party BG invocation notices dated April-May 2018; revised Form C claim dated 09.11.2018 reflecting adjusted margin money of Rs. 1,58,59,294/-; Information Memorandum incorporating the reduced net claim; approved Resolution Plan dated 20.06.2022. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SRA filed IA No. 440 (AHM) 2023 in CP (IB)/137 (AHM) 2018 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench Court-I seeking refund of Rs. 1,58,59,294/- alleging post-CIRP adjustment violated Section 14 moratorium. On 24.04.2024, NCLT allowed the IA and directed the Bank to reverse the amount to the SRA. Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether Margin Money deposited in the form of Term Deposits to secure Bank Guarantees invoked prior to the commencement of CIRP constitutes an asset of the Corporate Debtor or a 'security interest' under Section 3(31) of the IBC; whether book adjustment of such margin money after CIRP initiation violates the Section 14 moratorium; and whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction to order clawback/reversal of an adjusted claim already incorporated into an approved, binding resolution plan under the clean slate doctrine.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Margin money deposited by a borrower for the issuance of bank guarantees creates a trust in favour of the beneficiary and the issuing bank; once the bank guarantees are invoked prior to CIRP initiation, the margin money ceases to be an asset of the corporate debtor and cannot be subjected to the statutory moratorium under Section 14. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Margin money does not constitute a 'security interest' under Section 3(31) of the IBC as performance guarantees are expressly excluded by the proviso thereto. Under the Explanation to Section 18(1) and Section 36(4), assets held under trust are excluded from the debtor's estate, and Section 14(3)(b) expressly exempts sureties in a contract of guarantee. Furthermore, ordering clawback of an adjusted claim validated in the Information Memorandum and approved resolution plan violates Section 31(1) and the clean slate doctrine established in Ghanashyam Mishra. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Ansal Engineering, Arvind Kumar, and Supriyo Kumar Chaudhuri, the decisive evidentiary test is whether the underlying bank guarantee was invoked before CIRP admission, extinguishing the corporate debtor's proprietary title to the margin money. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the bank guarantees were invoked prior to CIRP initiation, the margin money was impressed with a trust and belonged to the bank; its subsequent book adjustment did not violate Section 14, and NCLT lacked jurisdiction to modify the approved resolution plan by ordering its refund.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 943 of 2024 is allowed. The impugned order dated 24.04.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 440 (AHM) 2023 is set aside, and the direction for reversal of Rs. 1,58,59,294/- by Appellant Bank is struck down. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by Indian Overseas Bank against the NCLT Ahmedabad order dated 24.04.2024, which had directed the Bank to reverse Rs. 1,58,59,294/- appropriated from Diamond Power and Infrastructure Ltd.'s margin money term deposits after CIRP commencement. Setting aside the order, NCLAT held that margin money deposited for bank guarantees carries the character of a trust for third-party beneficiaries and does not constitute 'security interest' under Section 3(31) or an asset of the debtor under Section 18 of the IBC. Because the bank guarantees were invoked prior to CIRP admission, the margin money ceased to be the debtor's property, making its subsequent book adjustment immune to the Section 14 moratorium and an impermissible modification of the approved resolution plan under Ghanashyam Mishra.

case_title: Masyc Projects Pvt. Ltd. vs. Pulkit Gupta, RP of Vadraj Cement Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 831 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 855 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 856 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Operational Creditors (Masyc Projects Pvt. Ltd. claiming under an arbitral award; Chhotubhai Ramubhai Patel and Tushar Engineering claiming equipment hire charges); Respondent No. 1 is Pulkit Gupta (Resolution Professional of Vadraj Cement Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Corporate Debtor Vadraj Cement Ltd.; Respondent No. 3 is Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Vadraj Cement Ltd. initiated on Section 7 application by Oriental Bank of Commerce (now PNB) on 02.02.2024. Appellants supplied equipment and execution services; their admitted operational claims stood at Rs. 16.72 Crores (Masyc), Rs. 2.99 Crores (Chhotubhai), and Rs. 1.09 Crores (Tushar Engineering), forming part of total admitted operational claims of Rs. 77,65,00,755/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose on commercial dues. Corporate Debtor had admitted secured financial debt of Rs. 8,232.53 Crores and admitted operational debts of Rs. 79.83 Crores; average liquidation value was Rs. 1,080 Crores against average fair value of Rs. 1,606.8 Crores. SRA offered Rs. 1,693.07 Crores to secured financial creditors and NIL to other operational creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 02.02.2024. Form G issued, and Nuvoco Vistas submitted resolution plan approved by 100% CoC voting share on 01.04.2025. RP filed IA No. 11/2025; NCLT approved plan on 01.04.2025. Appellants filed appeals challenging NIL payout. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Claims admitted by RP reflected in list of creditors; consent arbitral award dated 10.09.2013 (Masyc); service orders and equipment supply records; Clause F of Section 20 of approved resolution plan stating operational creditors' liquidation entitlement is NIL; CoC voting records showing 100% approval. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 11 of 2025 in CP(IB) No. 3528 (MB) of 2018 before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I. By order dated 01.04.2025, NCLT approved the resolution plan submitted by Nuvoco Vistas proposing NIL payout to operational creditors (other than workmen/employees and government dues). Appellants appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan proposing NIL payment to operational creditors whose liquidation entitlement under Section 53 is NIL violates Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC or Regulation 38(1A) of the CIRP Regulations, 2016, and whether the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal can interfere with the commercial wisdom of a 100% CoC approval on grounds of equitable distribution.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan allocating NIL payment to operational creditors is valid and legally compliant where the liquidation value attributable to such operational creditors under the waterfall mechanism of Section 53 is NIL, as the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in distributing funds is non-justiciable absent an express statutory breach. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(b) guarantees operational creditors a minimum payment not less than their liquidation value under Section 53; it does not mandate parity or equality of recovery percentage with financial creditors. Regulation 38(1A) requires only a statement in the plan demonstrating how stakeholders' interests were dealt with, which is satisfied by addressing operational creditors in a specific classification even if the resulting financial entitlement is NIL. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Essar Steel, K. Sashidhar, Swiss Ribbons, and Rajat Metaal Polychem, judicial review is circumscribed to confirming compliance with Section 30(2); because admitted secured financial debts far exceeded the liquidation value of Rs. 1,080 Crores, the operational creditors' legal entitlement was demonstrably zero. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The resolution plan satisfied Section 30(2)(b) and Regulation 38; the CoC approved it with 100% voting share, and the tribunal cannot alter the legislative scheme or interfere with the CoC's commercial wisdom.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 831 of 2025, No. 855 of 2025, and No. 856 of 2025 are dismissed. The impugned order dated 01.04.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench approving the resolution plan of Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Ltd. is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed three connected appeals filed by operational creditors challenging NCLT Mumbai's approval of Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Limited's resolution plan for Vadraj Cement Ltd., which allocated NIL payment to operational creditors other than workmen and statutory authorities. Appellants contended that NIL payment violated Regulation 38(1A) and failed to balance stakeholders' interests under Essar Steel. Rejecting the appeals, NCLAT held that under Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC, operational creditors are entitled only to the minimum amount they would receive in liquidation under Section 53. Because secured debt exceeded the liquidation value of Rs. 1,080 Crores, their liquidation entitlement was NIL. Upholding K. Sashidhar, NCLAT ruled that the commercial wisdom of a 100% CoC vote cannot be disturbed.

case_title: Chhotubhai Ramubhai Patel vs. Vadraj Cement Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 855 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 831 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 856 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Chhotubhai Ramubhai Patel (Operational Creditor who supplied equipment on hire); Respondent No. 1 is Corporate Debtor Vadraj Cement Ltd. through RP Pulkit Gupta; Respondent No. 3 is Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Limited; connected appellants are Masyc Projects Pvt. Ltd. and Tushar Engineering. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Equipment hire services supplied to Corporate Debtor Vadraj Cement Ltd. under service orders. In the Section 7 CIRP initiated on 02.02.2024 by Punjab National Bank, Appellant filed an operational claim of Rs. 2,99,87,605/-, which was admitted in full by the RP and categorized under operational creditors (other than workmen, employees, and government dues). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid operational hire charges of Rs. 2,99,87,605/-. The Corporate Debtor had admitted secured financial debt of Rs. 8,232.53 Crores and admitted operational claims of Rs. 77.65 Crores against average liquidation value of Rs. 1,080 Crores. Approved plan provided Rs. 1,693.07 Crores to secured lenders and NIL payment to other operational creditors. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated 02.02.2024; public announcement 03.02.2024; Form G published; Nuvoco Vistas' resolution plan approved by CoC with 100% vote share on 01.04.2025; IA No. 11/2025 filed by RP; NCLT approved plan on 01.04.2025. Appeals filed under Section 61. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Service orders and equipment hire invoices; list of admitted creditors published by RP admitting Rs. 2,99,87,605/-; Clause F of summary of approved resolution plan stating operational creditors' liquidation entitlement is NIL; CoC voting sheet showing 100% affirmative vote. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA Plan No. 11/2025 in CP(IB) No. 3528 (MB) of 2018 before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I. On 01.04.2025, NCLT approved the plan submitted by Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Limited. Appellant appealed against the NIL distribution.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan proposing NIL payment to operational creditors whose liquidation value under Section 53 is zero violates Section 30(2)(b) of the IBC and Regulation 38(1A) of the CIRP Regulations; and whether the commercial wisdom of a 100% CoC approval can be subjected to judicial review regarding inter-class allocation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An approved resolution plan proposing NIL payout to operational creditors does not violate Section 30(2)(b) where the liquidation value of such creditors under Section 53 is NIL, and the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in negotiating and approving such distribution is immune from judicial review. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 30(2)(b), operational creditors are entitled only to the minimum statutory baseline of what they would receive in liquidation under Section 53; the Code does not require pro-rata or equitable parity in percentage payout between financial and operational creditors. Regulation 38(1A) is satisfied where the resolution plan expressly deals with and categorizes operational creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the binding principles of Essar Steel and K. Sashidhar, the adjudicating authority's scrutiny is confined to verifying whether the plan contravenes Section 30(2); since the liquidation value of Rs. 1,080 Crores was entirely exhausted by secured financial creditors, the liquidation payout to operational creditors was mathematically zero. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because no statutory non-compliance under Section 30(2) or CIRP Regulations was demonstrated, the NCLT committed no legal error in approving the resolution plan.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 855 of 2025 is dismissed along with connected appeals No. 831 and No. 856 of 2025. The impugned order dated 01.04.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench is affirmed without costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Chhotubhai Ramubhai Patel, an operational creditor with an admitted claim of Rs. 2.99 Crores, against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 01.04.2025 approving Nuvoco Vistas Corporation Ltd.'s resolution plan for Vadraj Cement Ltd. The plan proposed NIL payment to operational creditors (other than workmen and government dues). NCLAT affirmed that under Section 30(2)(b) and Essar Steel, operational creditors are legally entitled only to the amount receivable under liquidation pursuant to Section 53. Because secured financial debt far exceeded the liquidation value of Rs. 1,080 Crores, the operational creditors' entitlement was NIL, and the commercial wisdom of the CoC's 100% vote could not be disturbed.

case_title: Saariga Construction Pvt. Ltd. vs. Arvind Kumar, RP of Richa Industries Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 887 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 888 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Saariga Construction Pvt. Ltd. (Resolution Applicant and Financial Creditor holding 8.94% voting share in CoC); Respondent No. 1 is Arvind Kumar (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Richa Industries Ltd.); Mohit Chawla (Liquidator); Respondent No. 2 comprises CoC members Indian Overseas Bank (35.22% vote share) and Union Bank of India/Corporation Bank (12.15% vote share). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP of Corporate Debtor Richa Industries Ltd., wherein Appellant submitted a resolution plan after re-publication of Form G pursuant to NCLT order dated 01.02.2023. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities leading to CIRP initiation on 21.12.2018. In the e-voting on Appellant's resolution plan, 52.02% voted in favour, 0.08% voted against, and 47.90% abstained (Indian Overseas Bank 35.22%, Corporation Bank 12.15%, HDB Financial 0.53%). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 21.12.2018. Original plan rejected on 03.09.2019; RP filed liquidation CA No. 786 of 2019. Fresh Form G ordered on 01.02.2023. Plan discussed in 37th CoC on 28.08.2023 and 38th CoC on 02.09.2023. E-voting open from 04.09.2023 to 22.09.2023. Plan failed for lack of 66% majority. Appellant filed IA No. 483 of 2024. NCLT dismissed IA No. 483 and ordered liquidation on 11.06.2025. Appeals filed under Section 61. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes of 38th CoC meeting dated 02.09.2023; official e-voting portal results dated 22.09.2023 certifying 52.02% affirmative votes, 0.08% negative votes, and 47.90% abstentions; Form G publications. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 786 of 2019 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench Court-1, Appellant filed IA No. 483 of 2024 seeking a declaration that its plan was approved based on 'present and voting' votes. On 11.06.2025, NCLT dismissed IA No. 483 and allowed CA No. 786 of 2019 ordering liquidation and appointing Mohit Chawla as liquidator. Appellant appealed both orders.
legal_issues: Whether the statutory requirement of approving a resolution plan by a vote of not less than 66% of voting share of the Financial Creditors under Section 30(4) of the IBC is to be computed out of the total voting share of all financial creditors in the CoC or restricted solely to those 'present and voting', and whether the votes of members who abstained must be counted in the total denominator.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The statutory threshold of 66% voting share required for CoC approval of a resolution plan under Section 30(4) of the IBC must be computed against the entire voting share of all financial creditors constituting the CoC, and members who abstain from voting cannot be excluded from the denominator. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(4) explicitly prescribes 66% of the 'voting share of the financial creditors' and does not incorporate the phrase 'present and voting' found in other provisions (such as Section 25A(3A)). Principles of statutory interpretation prohibit courts from reading words into an unambiguous statute. Regulations 25 and 26 mandate electronic voting for absent members, refuting the contention that feasibility evaluation requires physical presence in the meeting. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying K. Sashidhar v. Indian Overseas Bank, approving votes must strictly fulfill the threshold percentage of the aggregate voting share of the CoC; abstentions operate as non-approval and cannot be subtracted to artificially inflate the majority percentage. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Appellant secured only 52.02% affirmative votes against the mandatory 66% of total CoC voting share, the resolution plan was legally rejected, and NCLT's liquidation order was entirely justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 887 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 888 of 2025 are dismissed. The orders dated 11.06.2025 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench rejecting IA No. 483 of 2024 and ordering liquidation in CA No. 786 of 2019 are affirmed. Mohit Chawla's appointment as liquidator stands confirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed two connected appeals filed by Saariga Construction Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT Chandigarh's orders dated 11.06.2025 which rejected its resolution plan and ordered the liquidation of Richa Industries Ltd. In the CoC e-voting, Appellant garnered 52.02% votes in favor, 0.08% against, while major lenders holding 47.90% abstained. Appellant argued that abstaining votes should be excluded and that its plan secured over 97% of votes 'present and voting'. Rejecting this interpretation, NCLAT held that under Section 30(4) and Supreme Court precedent in K. Sashidhar, the 66% threshold is computed against the entire voting share of the CoC. Abstaining votes cannot be excluded, and failing the 66% statutory benchmark warranted liquidation.

case_title: Sayam Shares & Securities (P) Ltd. vs. KSS Petron (P) Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1001 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1014 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sayam Shares & Securities (P) Ltd. (applicant for transfer and party seeking recall of admission); Respondent No. 1 is KSS Petron (P) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor in liquidation, represented by its Liquidator acting as Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Interim Resolution Professional; connected party is Kohinoor Crane Services. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Inter-corporate financial disputes involving Section 7 CIRP proceedings against Bhubaneshwar Expressways Pvt. Ltd. admitted by NCLT New Delhi (Court-II) on 09.12.2024, and insolvency petitions against KSS Petron pending before NCLT Mumbai Bench. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in underlying Section 7 proceedings; the instant appeals involve procedural transfer petitions and deferral orders rather than adjudication of debt metrics. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 09.07.2025, KSS Petron filed TA (IBC) No. 37(PB)/2025 seeking transfer of CP (IB) No. 526/ND/2024 from Delhi Court-II to Mumbai. Simultaneously, Appellant filed TA No. 38(PB)/2025 and Kohinoor Crane Services filed TA No. 39(PB)/2025 seeking reverse transfer from Mumbai to Delhi Court-II. TAs listed on 10.07.2025 in Supplementary List-2 before the President, NCLT. President heard parties, directed curing of defects and filing hard copies by 18.07.2025, and requested Delhi and Mumbai benches to defer hearings. On 11.07.2025, Delhi Bench Court-II deferred proceedings till 23.07.2025. Appeals filed challenging orders dated 10.07.2025 and 11.07.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Transfer applications TA Nos. 37, 38, and 39 of 2025; Supplementary Cause List-2 dated 10.07.2025; transcript/order sheets of President NCLT dated 10.07.2025; order sheet of NCLT Delhi Court-II dated 11.07.2025; Appellant's 14-point objection note. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: President NCLT passed order dated 10.07.2025 issuing notice on TAs, fixing 18.07.2025, and requesting respective benches to defer hearings. On 11.07.2025, NCLT New Delhi Court-II deferred proceedings in CP(IB)-526/ND/2024 till 23.07.2025. Appellant appealed both orders before NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether an order passed by the President, NCLT on a transfer application under Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules, 2016 is an administrative or judicial order appealable under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013; whether the President has jurisdiction to request coordinate benches to defer proceedings pending transfer determination; whether hearing an urgent transfer matter during lunch hours violates Rule 9 of the NCLT Rules; and whether a bench commits error in deferring proceedings pending disposal of cross-transfer applications.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When the President of the NCLT hears and decides a contested application for transfer of proceedings under Rule 16(d) of the NCLT Rules listed in a judicial cause list, the power exercised is judicial in nature, and orders passed therein (including interim requests to defer proceedings) are appealable under Section 421 of the Companies Act, 2013, though not under Section 61 of the IBC. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 419(3) proviso of the Companies Act empowers the President sitting singly to exercise the powers of the Tribunal. Rule 16(d) empowers the President to transfer cases when circumstances warrant, which inherently includes the incidental jurisdiction to request coordinate benches to defer hearings to prevent conflicting proceedings. Rule 9's sitting hours are directory ('ordinarily') and do not invalidate urgent hearings held during lunch hours upon notice. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Supreme Court decisions in Jitendra Singh and Manju Verma, judicial propriety requires that when cross-transfer petitions are pending between benches, a court acts prudently in deferring hearings to protect judicial impartiality and prevent parallel adjudication. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The President committed no jurisdictional illegality in requesting deferral of hearings pending transfer adjudication, and NCLT Delhi Court-II properly deferred proceedings awaiting the President's decision.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1001 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1014 of 2025 are dismissed. The orders dated 10.07.2025 and 11.07.2025 are upheld without expressing any opinion on the merits of the pending Transfer Applications. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed two appeals filed by Sayam Shares & Securities (P) Ltd. challenging an order dated 10.07.2025 passed by the President of NCLT in cross-transfer applications requesting NCLT Delhi and Mumbai Benches to defer hearings, and a consequential order dated 11.07.2025 by NCLT Delhi Court-II deferring proceedings. Clarifying the law on NCLT administration, NCLAT held that while an appeal against an order under Rule 16(d) is not maintainable under Section 61 IBC, it is maintainable as a judicial order under Section 421 of the Companies Act. On merits, NCLAT held that the President possesses full jurisdiction to request deferral to prevent conflicting proceedings and that hearing urgent transfer mentions during lunch hours does not violate Rule 9.

case_title: Ravindra N. Athavale & Anr. vs. Calyx Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Review Application No. 4 & 5 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 522 & 523 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Applicants are Ravindra N. Athavale and Dnyanaba Namdeo Karande (ex-employees representing themselves and other former employees of Corporate Debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Calyx Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA); Respondent No. 2 is Charu S. Desai (Resolution Professional of Calyx Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Implementation of the approved Resolution Plan in the CIRP of Corporate Debtor Calyx Chemicals and Pharmaceuticals Limited, specifically concerning statutory payouts and gratuity dues to former employees under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP on 06.02.2018 with total employee/workmen claims admitted at Rs. 6.29 Crores; SRA provided Rs. 4.83 Crores (including Rs. 2.56 Crores for gratuity on accrual basis to active employees). Applicants sought payment of unpaid admitted individual gratuity dues (including Rs. 1,00,000 for Ravindra Athavale) forming part of Rs. 54,44,849 claimed by 39 employees not on payroll. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 06.02.2018; RP prepared list of creditors on 13.03.2018; NCLT approved Resolution Plan on 16.04.2019 (affirmed by NCLAT on 30.08.2019 and by Supreme Court on 20.02.2020). Applicants filed IA before NCLT in 2022; NCLT allowed gratuity claims on 19.01.2024; NCLAT reversed on 18.12.2024; Supreme Court remitted via Civil Appeal Nos. 5052-5053 of 2025 on 07.03.2025; NCLAT heard review on 07.08.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: RP's List of Creditors dated 13.03.2018 under Regulation 13(2)(d); Resolution Plan Clauses 3.1 to 3.5; Annexure 7 of the Resolution Plan (specifically Table 3, Category 3) explicitly providing 'Nil' payments to 39 employees not on payroll as on 06.02.2018; proof of payment of Rs. 4.83 Crores by SRA to on-payroll employees. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai allowed Applicants' 2022 IA on 19.01.2024 directing payment of gratuity. NCLAT set aside NCLT's order on 18.12.2024. The Supreme Court remanded the matter on 07.03.2025 for NCLAT to examine whether gratuity claims formed part of the approved plan. Applicants filed Review Applications No. 4 & 5 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether the approved Resolution Plan provided for payment of gratuity dues to former employees who were not on the payroll of the Corporate Debtor as of the Insolvency Commencement Date, and whether an approved resolution plan that has attained finality up to the Supreme Court can be modified post-implementation to accommodate omitted employee claims under the Payment of Gratuity Act, 1972.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Once a corporate resolution plan is approved by the Committee of Creditors in its commercial wisdom and sanctioned by the Adjudicating Authority, all claims not expressly incorporated for payment within the plan stand extinguished under the clean slate doctrine, and finality cannot be disrupted post-implementation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Annexures to a resolution plan form an integral and non-severable part of the resolution framework under Section 31(1) of the IBC; where the text of a plan is qualified by a specific annexure allocating 'NIL' payment to a sub-category of former employees not on the payroll on the insolvency commencement date, such creditors have no enforceable legal entitlement against the Successful Resolution Applicant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Ghanshyam Mishra and Ebix Singapore, the court must construe the resolution plan and its annexures harmoniously to ascertain the exact payouts approved; mere inclusion of an admitted claim in the Information Memorandum or creditor list does not override an explicit 'NIL' allocation in the approved plan. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because Annexure 7 of the approved plan expressly allocated 'NIL' payout to the 39 former employees not on payroll as of 06.02.2018, and the plan had attained judicial finality and was fully implemented, no grounds existed under Rule 11 to review or recall the order dated 18.12.2024.
operative_order: Review Applications Nos. 4 & 5 of 2025 in Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 522 & 523 of 2024 are rejected. The findings in the judgment dated 18.12.2024 are affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT rejected the review applications filed by ex-employees of Calyx Chemicals & Pharmaceuticals Ltd. seeking payment of gratuity dues. Following a remand from the Supreme Court to verify whether the approved resolution plan included these gratuity claims, NCLAT examined the complete plan alongside Annexure 7. The Tribunal found that while employees on the payroll as of the insolvency commencement date were paid, Annexure 7 explicitly designated 'NIL' payments for the 39 former employees who were not on the payroll on 06.02.2018. Holding that the plan had attained finality up to the Supreme Court and was fully implemented, NCLAT applied the clean slate doctrine to rule that claims not factored into the plan cannot be enforced against the Successful Resolution Applicant.

case_title: Chintan Jhunjhunwala vs. Avani Towers Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Chintan Jhunjhunwala (Suspended Director and shareholder of Energy Properties Pvt. Ltd. and shareholder of Corporate Debtor Avani Towers Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Avani Towers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) through RP Jitendra Lohia; Respondent No. 2 is Committee of Creditors of Avani; Respondent No. 3 is Cheminare Tradecomm Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA); Respondent No. 4 is Mahesh Chand Gupta (RP of Energy Properties Pvt. Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Acquisition and development of 10.19 acres of land in Howrah under MoU dated 24.01.2008, Shareholders' Agreement dated 24.01.2008 (transferring 40% equity of Energy to Avani), and Joint Development Agreement (JDA) dated 16.06.2008 appointing Avani as exclusive developer with 60% developer's allocation and 40% owner's allocation, backed by Rs. 12 Crores security deposit. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in loan facilities leading to Section 7 CIRP against Avani on 15.10.2019; under JDA, Avani advanced security deposit of Rs. 12 Crores plus additional Rs. 3.50 Crores; SRA's approved resolution plan proposed infusion of Rs. 25,11,70,194/- (including Rs. 17,94,27,647/- for project execution). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP against Avani initiated on 15.10.2019. Supreme Court affirmed Avani's development rights on 14.03.2023. SRA's resolution plan approved by 100% CoC on 31.10.2023; RP filed approval IA No. 1892/KB/2023. CIRP against Energy initiated on 20.03.2024; RP of Energy withdrew objections on 25.06.2024. Appellant filed objection IA No. 1332/KB/2024 on 27.06.2024; NCLT rejected objection and approved plan on 03.01.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MoU and Shareholders' Agreement dated 24.01.2008; registered JDA dated 16.06.2008 (Clauses 6.1, 7.1, 8.1, 8.3, 10.1, 15.3, 20.8); Supreme Court judgment dated 14.03.2023 in Civil Appeal No. 1782/2021; audited financial statements of SRA demonstrating net worth of Rs. 4.74 Crores and deployed funds of over Rs. 11 Crores; Resolution Plan Clauses 5(c), 5(h), 5(i), 5(j), 5(l), and 5(m). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP(IB) No. 372/KB/2019 before NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-II, Appellant filed IA No. 1332/KB/2024 challenging the SRA's resolution plan. On 03.01.2025, NCLT dismissed IA No. 1332/KB/2024 for lack of locus and merit, and allowed IA No. 1892/KB/2023 approving the resolution plan. Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether clauses in a corporate debtor's approved resolution plan implementing development rights under a pre-existing Joint Development Agreement illegally extinguish the underlying land ownership rights of a third-party landowner or violate Section 30(2)(e) of the IBC; whether the plan is rendered invalid as contingent; and whether the SRA satisfied mandatory net worth/AUM eligibility criteria.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Development rights acquired by a corporate debtor under a valid joint development agreement constitute 'property' and an 'asset' of the corporate debtor under Sections 3(27) and 18(f) of the IBC, and an approved resolution plan that operationalizes those development rights in conformity with the underlying contract without transferring title does not usurp or extinguish the third-party landowner's title. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30(2)(e) requires a plan to comply with prevailing laws; provisions in a plan authorizing project financing, nominee directors, or substitution of developer power-of-attorney holders in alignment with JDA covenants and Regulation 37 are lawful. Furthermore, milestones tied to statutory sanctions do not render a resolution plan 'conditional' or 'contingent' under Regulation 38. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Following Victory Iron Works and Dharmesh Jain, the tribunal determines whether the plan adheres to the bundle of development rights vested in the corporate debtor; where Clause 5(m) explicitly mandates adherence to the MoU and JDA, allegations of contract violation are baseless. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The challenged clauses strictly conformed to the JDA; Energy's ownership was not alienated; the SRA met all financial eligibility criteria; and NCLT's approval was fully justified.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 326 of 2025 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 03.01.2025 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench Court-II rejecting IA (IB) No. 1332/KB/2024 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Chintan Jhunjhunwala, Suspended Director of Energy Properties Pvt. Ltd., challenging NCLT Kolkata's order dated 03.01.2025 which approved Cheminare Tradecomm Pvt. Ltd.'s resolution plan for Avani Towers Pvt. Ltd. Appellant contended that the plan altered terms of the 2008 Joint Development Agreement and usurped Energy's 10.19-acre land ownership. Rejecting this, NCLAT held that the Supreme Court had already established Avani's development rights as an 'asset' under the IBC. The plan's clauses regarding security deposit adjustment, project finance, and substitution of powers of attorney strictly mirrored the JDA and Clause 5(m) expressly pledged full adherence to underlying agreements. Finding the SRA eligible and the plan non-contingent, NCLAT upheld the approval.

case_title: Bharti Goyal & Anr. vs. Hector Realty Venture Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Bharti Goyal (Appellant No. 1) and Swati Srivastava (Appellant No. 2, representing 19 other homebuyers of 'Marvella City' project); Respondent No. 1 is Corporate Debtor Hector Realty Venture Pvt. Ltd.; Respondent No. 2 is Piyush Garg (Erstwhile Interim Resolution Professional); Respondent No. 3 is Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India (IBBI). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking and allotment of residential flats in 'Marvella City', Haridwar, launched in 2015 by Corporate Debtor; homebuyers executed Builder Buyer Agreements and paid substantial consideration, but construction never commenced. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose from failure to construct and deliver possession; Section 7 CIRP was initiated by 7 homebuyers in CP (IB) No. 1051/ND/2019; Corporate Debtor illegally alienated project land to Divya Yog Trust on 03.01.2020 during the Section 14 moratorium. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 09.12.2019; IRP appointed 06.01.2020; public announcement on 09.01.2020; 2nd CoC meeting held on 07.09.2020; after 943 days, on 05.09.2022, IRP filed IA No. 4281/2022 claiming pre-CoC stage settlement; NCLT permitted withdrawal on 07.09.2022; NCLAT granted liberty on 31.08.2023; Appellant filed recall IA No. 5659/2023 on 29.09.2023; NCLT rejected recall on 14.05.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Builder Buyer Agreements and payment receipts of 20 excluded homebuyers; signed minutes of 2nd CoC meeting dated 07.09.2020 proving CoC was constituted and active; fraudulent application IA No. 4281/2022 falsely affirming under oath that no CoC had ever been constituted; sale deed dated 03.01.2020 evidencing illegal transfer of project land during moratorium. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed IA No. 5659 of 2023 before NCLT New Delhi Bench-V under Rule 11 seeking recall of the withdrawal order dated 07.09.2022 on grounds of fraud. On 14.05.2024, NCLT dismissed the recall application, holding no documents were filed proving CoC constitution. Appellants appealed under Section 61(1).
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses inherent jurisdiction under Rule 11 to recall an order allowing withdrawal of CIRP under Section 12A of the IBC when such order was procured through fraud and false representations that no Committee of Creditors was constituted; and whether the IRP is legally obligated to collate claims of allottees reflected in the Corporate Debtor's financial records.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order of an adjudicating authority procured by fraud and active suppression of material jurisdictional facts is a nullity in law, and tribunals retain inherent powers under Rule 11 to recall such fraudulent orders to prevent abuse of process and miscarriage of justice. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 12A of the IBC read with Regulation 30A mandatorily requires the approval of 90% voting share of the Committee of Creditors once constituted; post-admission insolvency proceedings are proceedings in rem, and parties cannot privately settle and withdraw CIRP without CoC consent. Further, under Regulation 6A, an IRP has an affirmative statutory obligation to reach out to and collate claims of known allottees whose details appear in company records. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the five-judge bench rule in Union Bank of India v. Dinkar Venkatasubramanian and Satyam Fibres, fraud vitiates all judicial acts; signed minutes of a CoC meeting constitute conclusive official evidence that the CIRP has passed the pre-CoC stage. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the IRP falsely affirmed that no CoC had been formed despite holding recorded CoC meetings, and deliberately excluded known homebuyers from the settlement to circumvent Section 12A, the withdrawal order dated 07.09.2022 was vitiated by fraud, requiring immediate recall and CIRP restoration.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1545 of 2024 is allowed. The impugned order dated 14.05.2024 in I.A. No. 5659/2023 is set aside, and the order dated 07.09.2022 allowing withdrawal of CIRP is recalled. Company Petition CP (IB) No. 1051/ND/2019 is restored to the file of NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-V, with directions for parties to appear on 26.08.2025. No costs.
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeal filed by homebuyers of the 'Marvella City' project, setting aside NCLT New Delhi's order dated 14.05.2024 and recalling the fraudulent CIRP withdrawal order dated 07.09.2022 in respect of Hector Realty Venture Pvt. Ltd. The IRP had procured the withdrawal after 943 days by falsely stating under oath that no CoC had been formed, thereby bypassing the mandatory 90% CoC approval required under Section 12A of the IBC. Overruling NCLT, NCLAT held that the signed minutes of the 2nd CoC meeting of September 2020 conclusively proved the CoC was active and that known homebuyers were deliberately excluded. Affirming that fraud vitiates all proceedings and invoking Rule 11 recall powers under Dinkar Venkatasubramanian and GLAS Trust, NCLAT restored the CIRP.

case_title: EBPL Ventures Pvt. Ltd. vs. Sarguja Rail Corridor Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is EBPL Ventures Pvt. Ltd. (Sub-contractor and Operational Creditor); Respondent is Sarguja Rail Corridor Pvt. Ltd. (now Adani Track Management Services Pvt. Ltd. - Principal Employer and Corporate Debtor); primary contractors are Gannon Dunkerley & Co. Ltd. (GDCL) and Vijay Nirman Co. Pvt. Ltd. (VNCPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: SRCPL was awarded a contract by South East Central Railway to construct a private railway corridor. SRCPL awarded EPC contracts to GDCL and VNCPL. GDCL and VNCPL sub-contracted OHE and P-Way track works to EBPL under work orders dated 01.08.2015. When execution stalled due to payment disputes between EBPL and contractors, SRCPL intervened as facilitator. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational default under Section 9 was Rs. 22,12,90,900/- based on proforma invoice No. EBPL/P.I/272; Appellant subsequently confined its appellate claim to balance 50% dues of approximately Rs. 1.95 Crores under the GDCL sub-contract based on an undated Indemnity Bond. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Minutes of Meeting (MoM) and Indemnity Bond executed on 09.04.2018; SRCPL released initial 50% payment on behalf of GDCL on 17.04.2018; follow-up MoM held on 14.10.2019; Demand Notice under Section 8 issued on 01.12.2020; Section 9 petition CP(IB) No. 11/AHM/2021 filed in 2021; NCLT dismissed petition on 23.08.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Clauses 11.4 and 11.11 of General Conditions of Contract explicitly providing no privity of contract between employer and sub-contractor; MoM dated 09.04.2018; MoM dated 14.10.2019 signed by EBPL recording payments were made by SRCPL 'on behalf of GDCL'; independent Chartered Accountant reconciliation report concluding NIL amount payable to EBPL; letter dated 21.01.2019 from GDCL claiming Rs. 10.6 Crores excess payment from EBPL. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: EBPL filed Section 9 application CP(IB) No. 11/AHM/2021 before NCLT Ahmedabad Bench. On 23.08.2022, NCLT dismissed the application holding that SRCPL was not a debtor of EBPL and that serious pre-existing disputes existed. EBPL appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a principal employer acts as an operational debtor to a sub-contractor by stepping in as a facilitator to settle execution disputes and making payments on behalf of the main contractor; and whether an unresolved reconciliation of accounts and counterclaims of excess payment constitute a pre-existing dispute under Section 8 and 9 of the IBC.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In the absence of direct contractual privity between a principal employer and a sub-contractor, payments or facilitation assurances made by the employer on behalf of the primary contractor to prevent project disruption do not create an operational debt or novate the underlying contract. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Operational debt under Section 5(21) requires the direct provision of goods or services to the corporate debtor; contractual clauses stipulating that sub-contractor usage shall not create employer obligations negate debtor-creditor relationships. Furthermore, pending reconciliation of accounts and mutual financial claims constitute a bona fide pre-existing dispute barring Section 9 admission. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Essar Oil v. Hindustan Shipyard and Mobilox Innovations, direct payments made for convenience do not establish contractual privity; documentary evidence showing conflicting invoices and un-reconciled ledgers establishes a plausible, non-spurious pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: There was no privity of contract between EBPL and SRCPL, and substantial pre-existing disputes existed regarding reconciliation and excess payments; NCLT properly rejected the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1305 of 2022 is dismissed as devoid of merit. The order dated 23.08.2022 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in CP(IB) No. 11/AHM/2021 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by sub-contractor EBPL Ventures Pvt. Ltd. against NCLT Ahmedabad's order rejecting its Section 9 petition against principal employer Sarguja Rail Corridor Pvt. Ltd. (Adani Track Management Services). EBPL claimed over Rs. 1.95 Crores for railway siding works, arguing that SRCPL had substituted itself for main contractor GDCL by signing facilitation minutes and paying an initial 50% instalment. Affirming NCLT's dismissal, NCLAT held that under the Supreme Court's ruling in Essar Oil, third-party payments made by a project employer to ensure smooth execution do not establish contractual privity or operational debt. Furthermore, pending account reconciliation and GDCL's counterclaim of Rs. 10.6 Crores constituted a genuine pre-existing dispute under Mobilox Innovations.

case_title: IDBI Bank Ltd. vs. Hemangi Patel
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 991 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 992 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is IDBI Bank Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondents are Hemangi Patel (Appeal No. 991/2025) and Noopur Patel (Appeal No. 992/2025), Personal Guarantors of Corporate Debtor Great Logistic and Parking Services Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Cash credit facilities extended by IDBI Bank to Great Logistic and Parking Services Pvt. Ltd. secured by personal guarantees executed by the Respondents on 28.10.2010. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor defaulted on cash credit facility on 31.03.2016 leading to NPA classification; IDBI Bank obtained a DRT Recovery Certificate on 25.01.2019 for the adjudicated debt. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account classified as NPA on 31.03.2016; Guarantee invocation notice issued on 24.10.2016; Original Application filed before DRT on 31.03.2017; DRT Recovery Certificate issued on 25.01.2019. Demand Notice under Rule 7(1) of the 2019 Personal Guarantors Rules issued on 19.03.2024; Section 95 applications C.P. (IB) No. 55/MP/2024 and C.P. (IB) No. 54/MP/2024 filed before NCLT on 02.09.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Personal Guarantee deeds dated 28.10.2010; Guarantee invocation notice dated 24.10.2016; DRT Recovery Certificate dated 25.01.2019; Demand Notice dated 19.03.2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IDBI Bank filed Section 95 petitions before NCLT Indore Special Bench Court-I. By identical orders dated 05.05.2025, NCLT dismissed the petitions as barred by limitation, holding that the 3-year limitation from the recovery certificate expired on 25.01.2022 (extended to 11.01.2024 under Covid-19 exclusion orders) whereas the petitions were filed on 02.09.2024. IDBI Bank appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the period of limitation for filing an insolvency application against a personal guarantor under Section 95 of the IBC founded upon a DRT Recovery Certificate is 12 years under Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963 or 3 years under Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Applications for initiating insolvency proceedings under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (including proceedings against personal guarantors under Section 95) are governed by the 3-year limitation period prescribed under residuary Article 137 of the Limitation Act, 1963, and not the 12-year period under Article 136 applicable to decree executions. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While a recovery certificate issued by a Debt Recovery Tribunal under Section 19(22-A) of the 1993 Act creates a fresh cause of action and qualifies as a financial debt, it does not transform an IBC application into a decree execution proceeding; the creditor must initiate insolvency proceedings within three years from the date of issuance of the recovery certificate under Article 137. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Kotak Mahindra Bank v. A. Balakrishnan, Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave, and BK Educational Services, time begins to run from the date of the recovery certificate; the 12-year window in Article 136 is restricted to civil court executions and cannot extend the limitation for an IBC petition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The 3-year limitation period from the recovery certificate dated 25.01.2019, even after factoring in Supreme Court Covid-19 exclusion extensions up to 11.01.2024, expired well before the filing date of 02.09.2024, rendering the Section 95 applications hopelessly time-barred.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 991 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 992 of 2025 are dismissed. The impugned orders dated 05.05.2025 passed by NCLT Indore Special Bench rejecting the Section 95 applications as barred by limitation are affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed two connected appeals filed by IDBI Bank Ltd. against NCLT Indore's orders dated 05.05.2025 which rejected Section 95 insolvency applications filed against personal guarantors Hemangi Patel and Noopur Patel as time-barred. The Bank argued that under the Supreme Court's ruling in Tottempudi Salalith, a DRT Recovery Certificate is treated as a decree carrying a 12-year limitation period under Article 136 of the Limitation Act. Rejecting this contention, NCLAT clarified that under Kotak Mahindra Bank v. A. Balakrishnan and Gaurav Hargovindbhai Dave, insolvency applications under the IBC are governed strictly by the 3-year limitation period under Article 137. Since the recovery certificate was issued on 25.01.2019 and the applications were filed on 02.09.2024 (beyond the Covid-extended deadline of 11.01.2024), the petitions were barred by time.

case_title: Jindal Lifestyle Limited vs. Satyendra Sharma, RP of Arkin Creations Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Jindal Lifestyle Limited (erstwhile JSL Architecture Limited, corporate third-party debtor); Respondent No. 1 is Satyendra Sharma (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor Arkin Creations Pvt. Ltd.); Respondents No. 2 to 6 are directors of the Appellant. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Pre-CIRP supply of goods by Corporate Debtor to Appellant resulting in non-payment, for which Corporate Debtor initiated statutory arbitration under the MSMED Act, 2006 before the Haryana Micro and Small Enterprises Facilitation Council (HMSEFC), which referred the matter to Sole Arbitrator Shri P.P. Chhabra on 17.06.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal default of Rs. 21,50,332/- which, with accrued statutory interest, culminated in an ex-parte Arbitral Award dated 23.01.2017 for Rs. 44,99,365/- (Rs. 21,50,332 principal plus Rs. 23,49,033 interest). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Reference to arbitration on 17.06.2016; Arbitral Award passed on 23.01.2017. CIRP against Corporate Debtor Arkin Creations initiated on 07.10.2022 in CP (IB) No. 94/Chd/Hry/2020. RP issued demand notice under Section 60(5) on 18.01.2023; Appellant replied on 23.01.2023; RP filed IA No. 792 of 2023 before NCLT; NCLT allowed IA on 30.04.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MSME registration certificate of Corporate Debtor; referral order dated 17.06.2016; Arbitral Award dated 23.01.2017; RP's demand notice dated 18.01.2023; Appellant's reply dated 23.01.2023. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (IB) No. 94/Chd/Hry/2020 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench, the RP filed IA No. 792 of 2023 under Section 60(5) seeking direction against Appellant to pay Rs. 44,99,365/- under the Arbitral Award. On 30.04.2024, NCLT allowed the IA and directed payment. Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority possesses jurisdiction under Section 60(5) read with Section 238 of the IBC to enforce an un-challenged, final arbitral award in favour of a Corporate Debtor undergoing CIRP without requiring the RP to institute execution proceedings before a civil court under Section 36 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996; whether the 90-day timeline in Section 18(5) of the MSMED Act is mandatory; and whether insufficient stamping invalidates the award.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority possesses plenary jurisdiction under the non-obstante provisions of Section 60(5) and Section 238 of the IBC to adjudicate and enforce monetary recoveries and assets arising under an un-challenged arbitral award in favour of a corporate debtor undergoing CIRP, overriding the requirement to seek execution before civil courts. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60(5) confers expansive jurisdiction over 'any claim made by or against the corporate debtor' and any question of law or fact arising out of or in relation to CIRP. By virtue of Section 238, the summary, time-bound recovery mechanisms of the Code prevail over Section 36 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Furthermore, the 90-day timeline in Section 18(5) of the MSMED Act, 2006 is directory, and insufficient stamping is a curable defect that does not render a final award void. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying KS Oils and NN Global, where an arbitral award has attained finality without any statutory challenge under Section 34 of the Arbitration Act, it represents an undisputed liquidated debt that the Resolution Professional is duty-bound to collect for asset maximization. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Arbitral Award was final, legally valid, and executable; NCLT acted squarely within its jurisdiction under Section 60(5) in directing the Appellant to pay the award amount to the RP.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 1180 of 2024 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 30.04.2024 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench in I.A. No. 792 of 2023 is affirmed. No order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Jindal Lifestyle Limited challenging NCLT Chandigarh's order dated 30.04.2024 which directed the Appellant to pay Rs. 44,99,365/- to the Resolution Professional of Arkin Creations Pvt. Ltd. pursuant to an ex-parte MSME arbitral award dated 23.01.2017. The Appellant contended that NCLT lacked jurisdiction and that the RP was required to file execution proceedings before a civil court under Section 36 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. Rejecting this, NCLAT held that under Section 60(5) and Section 238 of the IBC, the Code overrides civil execution provisions, empowering NCLT to enforce debts and un-challenged awards to facilitate timely corporate revival. It also held that the 90-day disposal period under Section 18(5) of the MSMED Act is directory and that insufficient stamping is a curable defect.
