case_title: Sh. Sumeet Juneja vs. Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sh. Sumeet Juneja, Personal Guarantor of Corporate Debtor M/s Krishna Engineering Works Limited; Respondent No. 1 is Stressed Assets Stabilisation Fund (SASF, Financial Creditor/Assignor to Omkara Asset Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is Rajender Kumar Jain, Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial credit facilities availed by borrower M/s Krishna Engineering Works Ltd. from SASF, secured by a personal guarantee agreement executed by Appellant on 28.10.1994 (with a subsequent agreement dated 30.12.1996). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Borrower account was classified as NPA on 31.10.1998; OA No. 2777 of 2017 was allowed by DRT-I Chandigarh and a Recovery Certificate was issued on 23.01.2019; total default claimed under Section 95 was Rs. 780,21,90,384/- (Rs. 780.22 Crores) as on 23.01.2019 plus interest, which was also recorded with the Information Utility (NeSL). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee executed on 28.10.1994/30.12.1996; NPA declared on 31.10.1998; DRT Recovery Certificate issued on 23.01.2019; demand notice under SARFAESI issued on 28.07.2021; Form B demand notice issued on 29.03.2022; Section 95 petition CP (IB) No. 104/CHD/PB/2023 filed on 31.01.2023; RP appointed on 06.02.2024; Section 99 Report submitted on 17.02.2024; newspaper publication effected on 12.04.2024; debt assigned to Omkara ARC on 31.08.2024; NCLT admitted Section 95 petition on 12.09.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Personal guarantee agreement; DRT Recovery Certificate dated 23.01.2019; NeSL Form C record of default; emails and WhatsApp messages dated 10.02.2024/20.02.2024 exchanged between RP and Appellant confirming knowledge; substituted service by publication in Financial Express and Punjab Jagran on 12.04.2024; Assignment Deed dated 31.08.2024 in favour of Omkara ARC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SASF filed Section 95 application CP (IB) No. 104/CHD/PB/2023 before NCLT Chandigarh Bench Court-II. Following report submission under Section 99 and substituted service, Appellant was proceeded ex-parte on 30.07.2024. On 12.09.2024, NCLT admitted the petition under Section 100 initiating insolvency resolution against the Personal Guarantor. Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the Section 95 petition was maintainable without formal guarantee invocation; whether service of the demand notice and Section 99 report was legally valid through substituted service and electronic messaging when the guarantor changed addresses without notifying the creditor; and whether assignment of debt by the financial creditor during the pendency of proceedings (after orders were reserved) deprives the creditor of locus standi.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A personal guarantor cannot evade insolvency proceedings under Section 95 of the IBC by shifting addresses without notifying the creditor, and service effected via registered emails, phone/messaging, and substituted newspaper publication constitutes valid service; furthermore, assignment of debt after orders are reserved does not abate the proceedings as the assignee automatically steps into the shoes of the assignor under Section 5(3) of the SARFAESI Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Issuance of a DRT Recovery Certificate coupled with statutory demand notices under Rule 7(1) of the Personal Guarantors Rules, 2019 satisfies the requirement of guarantee invocation under Rule 3(e) of the 2019 Rules and Section 95(4)(b) of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where electronic records, NeSL certificates, and WhatsApp communications prove the guarantor's actual awareness of the insolvency proceedings, the guarantor is estopped from alleging non-service or procedural violations, and parallel pursuit of appeal and recall constitutes abusive forum shopping. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The debt of Rs. 780.22 Crores and default were established by the DRT Recovery Certificate; service was duly executed; and the assignment did not vitiate proceedings, rendering NCLT's admission order unimpeachable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 2169 of 2024 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 12.09.2024 passed by NCLT Chandigarh Bench admitting the Section 95 petition is affirmed. In view of suppression of facts, false pleas of non-service, and forum shopping, exemplary costs of Rs. 5,00,000/- are imposed on the Appellant to be deposited in the Prime Minister's Relief Fund within four weeks. All pending IAs stand disposed of.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Sh. Sumeet Juneja, Personal Guarantor of M/s Krishna Engineering Works Ltd., against NCLT Chandigarh's order dated 12.09.2024 admitting SASF's Section 95 insolvency petition for an outstanding debt of Rs. 780.22 Crores. The Guarantor claimed non-invocation of guarantee, lack of notice, and loss of creditor locus following debt assignment to Omkara ARC. Rejecting these contentions, NCLAT held that the DRT Recovery Certificate and statutory notices constituted valid guarantee invocation, and that the guarantor was bound to notify changes of address. Electronic records and WhatsApp messages proved actual service and notice. Holding that debt assignment after orders were reserved did not abate proceedings under Section 5(3) of the SARFAESI Act, NCLAT affirmed admission and imposed Rs. 5,00,000/- exemplary costs for evasive conduct.

case_title: M/S Propertree Real Estate Solutions Private Limited vs. Mr. A. Viswanadha Sarma, Resolution Professional of M/S Unibera Developers Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1659 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1660 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant in CA No. 1659/2024 is M/s Propertree Real Estate Solutions Pvt. Ltd. (real estate broker); Appellants in CA No. 1660/2024 are Vandana Gupta and Arun Gupta (Directors of Propertree); Respondent is A. Viswanadha Sarma, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Unibera Developers Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate brokerage services provided by Appellants for CD's project 'Unibera Towers' (later 'Unibera Heights') under brokerage agreements dated 10.04.2012 and 17.01.2013; CD allotted residential flats to Appellants, adjusting accrued brokerage commission against flat sale consideration through credit notes and MoUs dated 25.11.2021 and 03.02.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants claimed Rs. 81,05,211/- (IA 4354/2023) and Rs. 49,96,236/- (IA 4356/2023) as financial debts in Form CA; only Rs. 2,00,000/- was actually disbursed in cash towards an initial flat booking cancelled in 2017, while the remainder comprised adjusted brokerage commission on sales of approximately 101 flats. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Initial flat booked in 2012-2013; cancelled on 07.06.2017; Appellant issued Section 8 demand notice on 21.05.2018 for Rs. 1.96 Crores; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 868 of 2018 admitted on 12.11.2021; settled via MoUs dated 25.11.2021 and 03.02.2022, leading to withdrawal of CIRP on 08.02.2022; fresh CIRP initiated against CD under Section 9 on 13.01.2023 in CP (IB) No. 505/ND/2022; Appellants filed Form CA on 23.01.2023; RP reclassified claims as operational debt on 14.07.2023; NCLT rejected reclassification applications on 05.06.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Brokerage agreements dated 10.04.2012 and 17.01.2013; brokerage invoice dated 01.10.2016 for Rs. 99,77,449/-; credit notes dated 10.03.2015 and 02.07.2015; MoUs dated 25.11.2021 and 03.02.2022 showing consideration paid via adjustment of unpaid commission; record of prior Section 9 petition filed by Appellants as operational creditors. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed IA Nos. 4354/2023 and 4356/2023 before NCLT New Delhi Court-II seeking directions to the RP to admit their claims as financial debt under Section 5(8)(f). On 05.06.2024, NCLT rejected both applications holding the underlying liability was operational debt for services rendered. Appellants appealed under Section 61(1).
legal_issues: Whether unpaid real estate brokerage commission adjusted towards the purchase consideration of flats under MoUs and Builder Buyer Agreements qualifies as a 'financial debt' disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC; and whether a creditor who previously initiated CIRP as an operational creditor is estopped from reclassifying the same claim as a financial debt.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The allotment of real estate units in lieu of or via adjustment of outstanding service or commission fees without actual disbursement of money does not satisfy the foundational requirement of Section 5(8)(f) of raising funds having the commercial effect of a borrowing. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 5(8)(f) and the Explanation thereto read with Section 2(d) of the RERA Act, 2016, an 'allottee' acquires the status of a financial creditor only when money is disbursed as advance consideration to finance project construction; claims arising from the provision of services (such as brokerage) retain the intrinsic character of operational debt under Section 5(21). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Pioneer Urban Land, Anuj Jain (Jaypee Infratech), and Namdeo Ramchandra Patil, the adjudicating authority must examine the true substance and genesis of the underlying transaction; a creditor who previously triggered Section 9 proceedings for unpaid commission is legally estopped from asserting that adjusted barter allotments convert operational debt into financial debt. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The consideration for the allotted flats was merely an adjustment of unpaid brokerage without any actual infusion of funds for the time value of money; RP and NCLT rightly categorized the claim as operational debt.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1659 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1660 of 2024 are dismissed. The impugned common order dated 05.06.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Court-II is affirmed. No order as to costs. All pending IAs are disposed of.
summary: NCLAT dismissed two connected appeals filed by real estate broker M/s Propertree Real Estate Solutions Pvt. Ltd. and its directors against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 05.06.2024, which upheld the Resolution Professional's reclassification of their claims from financial debt to operational debt in the CIRP of Unibera Developers Pvt. Ltd. The Appellants argued that because unpaid brokerage commission was adjusted towards the purchase consideration of two flats under settlement MoUs, they were 'allottees' and financial creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC. Rejecting this, NCLAT held that under Pioneer Urban Land and Anuj Jain, financial debt requires actual disbursement of money for time value of money. Converting unpaid service commission into flat allotments without fresh funding does not constitute borrowing. Having previously initiated Section 9 proceedings as operational creditors, Appellants were also estopped from changing their stance.

case_title: Sendoz Commercial Pvt. Ltd. vs. IREL (India) Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Sendoz Commercial Pvt. Ltd. (Operational Creditor/Coal Supplier); Respondent is IREL (India) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor, a Central Public Sector Undertaking under the Department of Atomic Energy). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purchase Order No. 36/P/02171/PT/P.O.36-01060 dated 28.01.2020 for the supply of 8,000 MT (+/-10%) imported coal with Gross Calorific Value (GCV) between 2,800 to 3,400 Kcal/Kg and ash content below 50% for Respondent's mineral processing facility. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Operational debt claimed in Section 9 application was Rs. 1,83,57,886/- under Invoice No. SCPL/2019-20/055 dated 22.02.2020 for a consignment of 4,044.52 MT of coal. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Purchase order issued on 28.01.2020; consignment delivered and invoice raised on 22.02.2020; prompt rejection email issued by Respondent on 25.02.2020; Appellant requested re-sampling under Clause 3.0 on 29.02.2020; joint meeting held on 11.06.2020; arbitration notice issued by Appellant on 31.05.2020; joint sampling conducted on 14.08.2020; CSIR-NML report dated 11.09.2020; CSIR-IMMT report dated 06.11.2020; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 20.11.2020/25.01.2021; Section 9 petition CP(IB)-552/MB/2021 dismissed by NCLT on 24.02.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Rejection email dated 25.02.2020 showing supplied coal had GCV of 2,429 Kcal/Kg and ash content of 56.6%; minutes of joint meeting dated 11.06.2020 discussing blending options; conflicting test reports from CSIR-NML (GCV 3,580 Kcal/Kg) and CSIR-IMMT (GCV 2,053 Kcal/Kg, ash 60.21%); appointment of Sole Arbitrator by Orissa High Court on 15.07.2025 in Arbitration Petition No. 40 of 2024. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant filed Section 9 application CP(IB)-552/MB/2021 before NCLT Mumbai Bench. On 24.02.2023, NCLT dismissed the application on grounds of a pre-existing dispute and default falling within the Section 10A exclusion window. Appellant appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether a genuine pre-existing dispute regarding goods quality raised prior to the issuance of a Section 8 demand notice bars the admission of a Section 9 application; and whether an operational creditor can utilize the summary insolvency mechanism against a solvent public sector undertaking when the underlying dispute is pending before an arbitral tribunal.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 9 read with Section 8(2)(a) of the IBC, an application for initiating corporate insolvency resolution must be rejected if there is a plausible, pre-existing dispute supported by contemporaneous documentary evidence, and the summary insolvency jurisdiction cannot be invoked as a coercive debt-recovery forum. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A dispute under Section 8(2)(a) does not require that the corporate debtor establish a foolproof or ultimately successful defence, but merely that the contest is not spurious, hypothetical, or an illusory afterthought. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying Mobilox Innovations Pvt. Ltd. v. Kirusa Software Pvt. Ltd., prompt email rejections, recorded minutes of quality negotiation meetings, and sharply divergent lab test reports issued prior to the statutory demand notice establish the existence of a bona fide pre-existing dispute. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor promptly and consistently rejected the coal consignment for failure to satisfy contractual GCV and ash parameters months before the demand notice was served, and an arbitrator had already been appointed to resolve the contractual claims; NCLT correctly dismissed the Section 9 petition.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 533 of 2023 is dismissed. The impugned order dated 24.02.2023 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench rejecting CP(IB)-552/MB/2021 is affirmed. No order as to costs. Pending IAs are closed.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by coal supplier Sendoz Commercial Pvt. Ltd. against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 24.02.2023 which rejected its Section 9 application seeking to initiate CIRP against public sector undertaking IREL (India) Ltd. for alleged unpaid dues of Rs. 1.83 Crores. The Respondent had rejected the coal consignment within three days of delivery in February 2020 due to substandard calorific value (GCV) and excessive ash content, leading to subsequent conflicting CSIR lab reports and the invocation of arbitration. Affirming the dismissal, NCLAT held that under Section 8(2)(a) and the Supreme Court precedent in Mobilox Innovations, the prompt contractual rejection and ongoing arbitration conclusively established a genuine pre-existing dispute, barring insolvency proceedings against a solvent government enterprise.

case_title: Growfitter Private Limited vs. Gajesh Labhchand Jain, Liquidator of Talwalkars Healthclubs Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Growfitter Private Limited (fintech service provider); Respondent is Gajesh Labhchand Jain, Liquidator of Talwalkars Healthclubs Limited (THL / Corporate Debtor in liquidation, formerly Talwalkars Lifestyles Ltd.); sister company is Talwalkars Better Value Fitness Limited (TBVFL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: On 27.12.2016, Appellant entered into a Share Subscription and Shareholders Agreement (SHA) with TBVFL, under which TBVFL invested Rs. 5 Crores on 31.03.2017 in exchange for 9,598 equity shares (representing ~19% equity). On 21.12.2017, NCLT approved a scheme of demerger transferring TBVFL's gym business and investments automatically to the Corporate Debtor (Resulting Company). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dispute concerns the ownership and custody of 9,598 equity shares worth Rs. 5 Crores forming part of the liquidation estate under Section 36 IBC; Appellant refused to recognize Corporate Debtor's title, alleging shares were extinguished/bought back. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demerger scheme approved on 21.12.2017 in CSP No. 405/2017; TBVFL entered CIRP on 11.01.2021 and liquidation on 28.04.2022; Corporate Debtor entered CIRP on 09.03.2021; Liquidator issued demand letter on 27.09.2022 and legal notice on 02.11.2022; Liquidator filed IA No. 1579/MB/2023 on 05.01.2023; NCLT allowed IA on 07.02.2024; NCLAT directed compliance on 09.07.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: NCLT Scheme Approval Order dated 21.12.2017 (Clauses 2.1.5 and 5.1); audited balance sheets and Transaction Audit Report dated 24.12.2021 showing CD owned 19% equity in Appellant; RoC e-form MGT-7 for FY 2020-21 confirming shares were held by TBVFL; unverified board resolution dated 01.06.2020 and insufficiently stamped Form SH-4 relied upon by Appellant; absence of any bank entries showing repayment of Rs. 5 Crores by Appellant. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator filed IA No. 1579/MB/2023 in CP(IB) No. 923(MB)/2020 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV under Sections 35(1) and 60(5). On 07.02.2024, NCLT allowed the IA and directed Growfitter to issue fresh share certificates for the 9,598 equity shares in favour of THL within 7 days. Growfitter appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether equity shares transferred to a resulting corporate debtor pursuant to a court-approved demerger scheme constitute assets of the corporate debtor forming part of its liquidation estate under Section 36 of the IBC; and whether the issuing company can claim extinguishment or buy-back of shares without demonstrating compliance with Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013 and proof of repayment of consideration.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An asset or investment transferred and vested in a corporate entity under a sanctioned and binding scheme of arrangement cannot be unilaterally extinguished, transferred, or bought back by third parties on dubious, post-facto assertions of contract default without rigorous statutory compliance and documented consideration. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: By virtue of Section 35(1)(d) read with Section 36 of the IBC, a liquidator is statutorily mandated to identify, recover, and take custody of all movable assets and share investments belonging to the corporate debtor. A court-sanctioned scheme under company law operates in rem, automatically vesting title under Section 5.1 of the scheme without requiring separate deeds. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Shifting and contradictory stands (extinguishment vs. buy-back vs. third-party transfer) unsupported by entries in audited company balance sheets or bank records destroy credibility; a party alleging buy-back must prove actual financial outflow and compliance with Section 68 of the Companies Act, 2013. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The 9,598 shares vested in the Corporate Debtor by virtue of the approved demerger scheme and were confirmed by transaction audits; Appellant failed to prove any lawful buy-back or repayment of Rs. 5 Crores, and NCLT's direction to issue fresh certificates was entirely justified.
operative_order: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins.) No. 605 of 2024 is dismissed as devoid of merit. The impugned order dated 07.02.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV in I.A. No. 1579 of 2023 is affirmed. No order as to costs. All pending IAs are closed.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Growfitter Private Limited against NCLT Mumbai's order dated 07.02.2024 directing it to issue fresh share certificates for 9,598 equity shares in favour of Corporate Debtor Talwalkars Healthclubs Limited (THL) in liquidation. TBVFL had invested Rs. 5 Crores in Growfitter in 2017, and upon a court-sanctioned demerger, its gym business investments automatically vested in THL. Growfitter resisted handing over the shares, taking shifting positions that the shares were extinguished, bought back, or transferred to an ex-promoter. Rejecting these pleas, NCLAT held that the court-sanctioned demerger scheme conclusively vested ownership in the Corporate Debtor. Growfitter failed to prove any statutory buy-back under Section 68 of the Companies Act or produce proof of refunding the Rs. 5 Crores consideration, making the shares part of THL's liquidation estate under Section 36 IBC.

case_title: Hemant Sharma, Resolution Professional of Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. vs. Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Hemant Sharma (Resolution Professional of Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd., Corporate Debtor / Corporate Guarantor); Respondent is Indian Renewable Energy Development Agency Ltd. (IREDA, Financial Creditor); Principal Borrowers are Today Clean Energy Pvt. Ltd., Photon Suryakiran Pvt. Ltd., and Photon Sunbeam Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by IREDA to the three principal borrower companies: Rs. 68 Crores on 21.09.2015, Rs. 200 Crores on 19.08.2016, and Rs. 210 Crores on 07.11.2016, secured by corporate deeds of guarantee executed by the Corporate Debtor on 21.09.2015, 03.03.2016, and 29.12.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP on 31.10.2019. Respondent submitted a financial claim in Form C for Rs. 360,95,17,540/- (Rs. 360.95 Crores) based on the corporate guarantees; the guarantees had not been invoked prior to the insolvency commencement date of the Corporate Debtor. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 31.10.2019; public announcement 14.11.2019; claim filing deadline was 30.01.2020; Respondent emailed Form C claim on 31.01.2020 (1-day delay condoned); RP rejected claim on 13.07.2020 and 23.01.2021; Respondent filed IA No. 2504 of 2021 before NCLT; NCLT allowed IA on 09.04.2024 directing reconsideration; RP appealed under Section 61. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Facility sanction letters and loan agreements; Deeds of Guarantee dated 21.09.2015, 03.03.2016, and 29.12.2016; Form C claim submission dated 31.01.2020 for Rs. 360.95 Crores; RP's rejection emails dated 13.07.2020 and 23.01.2021. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: IREDA filed IA No. 2504 of 2021 in CP (IB)-2130(ND)/2019 before NCLT New Delhi Court-III challenging the RP's rejection. On 09.04.2024, NCLT set aside the RP's decision, held that RP had unlawfully adjudicated the claim, made adverse remarks against the RP, directed copy to be sent to IBBI, and ordered reconsideration. RP appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a claim submitted by a financial creditor based on an uninvoked corporate deed of guarantee must be collated and verified by the Resolution Professional in the CIRP of the corporate guarantor under Section 18 read with Section 3(6) and Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC; and whether an RP's refusal to verify a claim constitutes an 'adjudication' and 'abuse of power' justifying referral to the IBBI.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A corporate guarantee creates an enforceable financial obligation under Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC, and the creditor holds a valid 'claim' under Section 3(6) that must be collated and verified by the Resolution Professional in the CIRP of the corporate guarantor, irrespective of whether the guarantee was invoked or matured prior to the insolvency commencement date. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 3(6), a 'claim' includes a right to payment whether matured, unmatured, disputed, or undisputed; maturity of debt or guarantee invocation is required to establish 'default' under Section 7/9, but is not a prerequisite for filing and collating a claim under Section 18(1)(b) and Regulation 13. Furthermore, verification of claims under Regulation 13 is a statutory duty, and an erroneous verification decision does not per se constitute quasi-judicial adjudication or an abuse of office. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the Supreme Court rulings in China Development Bank v. Doha Bank and Swiss Ribbons, the existence of a valid guarantee deed establishes a subsisting claim; the RP is obligated to verify its factual basis from corporate records rather than rejecting it outright for lack of prior invocation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: IREDA's claim based on the guarantee deeds was a valid financial claim entitled to verification, and NCLT properly directed reconsideration; however, the RP acted in good faith, and the adverse remarks and referral to IBBI were unwarranted and deleted.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1039 of 2024 is dismissed, subject to the deletion of adverse observations against the RP in paragraph 5(viii) and the direction to forward the order to IBBI in paragraph 6(ii). The direction to the RP to reconsider IREDA's claim in accordance with law is affirmed. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: NCLAT affirmed the NCLT New Delhi order directing the Resolution Professional of Today Homes and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. to reconsider the Rs. 360.95 Crore financial claim submitted by IREDA based on corporate guarantees extended for three borrower companies. The RP had rejected the claim on grounds that the corporate guarantee was not invoked prior to the insolvency commencement date. Relying on the Supreme Court's ruling in China Development Bank v. Doha Bank, NCLAT held that under Section 3(6) and Section 5(8)(i) of the IBC, a claim based on an uninvoked guarantee remains a valid claim that must be collated and verified. However, NCLAT expunged the adverse remarks made by NCLT against the RP and set aside the directive referring the RP to the IBBI, clarifying that claim verification is a statutory duty and not an abuse of process.

case_title: Deepak Raheja & Anr. vs. Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1040 of 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1039 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Deepak Raheja and Anita Raheja, Suspended Directors of Corporate Debtors Gstaad Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (owner of JW Marriott Hotel, Bengaluru) and Neo Capricorn Plaza Pvt. Ltd. (owner of Crowne Plaza Hotel, Pune); Respondent No. 1 is Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Assignee of Piramal Finance Ltd.); Respondent No. 2 is IRP. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan Agreement dated 26.12.2017 sanctioned Term Loan of Rs. 450 Crores and Rs. 50 Crores revolving facility to Gstaad, and Rs. 100 Crores term loan to Neo Capricorn. Cash Management Agreement (CMA) executed on 17.01.2018 establishing Escrow: 66% hotel revenue to Expense Account and 34% to Retention Account for debt service. Additional loans availed under Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS-1 of Rs. 98 Crores to Gstaad and Rs. 19.5 Crores to Neo Capricorn on 29-30.12.2020; ECLGS-2 of Rs. 65 Crores to Gstaad on 11.03.2022). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default on 15.11.2022 under ECLGS-1, ECLGS-2, and Term Loan accounts; loan recall notices dated 15.02.2023 demanded Rs. 666,53,26,968/- from Gstaad and Rs. 119,99,23,320/- from Neo Capricorn; total default established as Rs. 17.16 Crores for Gstaad and Rs. 2.64 Crores for Neo Capricorn as on 15.11.2022. Debt was admitted in OTS proposal offering Rs. 743.71 Crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Default occurred on 15.11.2022; loans recalled under Clause 7.2.6 on 15.02.2023; Section 7 petitions CP(IB) Nos. 290 and 291 of 2023 filed on 09.03.2023; initially admitted on 09.01.2024; NCLAT remanded for fresh consideration on 08.01.2025; Karnataka High Court upheld debt assignment on 19.05.2024 (SLP dismissed 02.06.2025); NCLT re-admitted Section 7 petitions on 08.07.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements dated 26.12.2017, 30.12.2020, and 11.03.2022; Cash Management Agreement dated 17.01.2018; Loan recall notices dated 15.02.2023; certified Statements of Account establishing unpaid instalments and overdue interest as on 15.11.2022; written One Time Settlement (OTS) proposal dated 30.04.2025 offering Rs. 743.71 Crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Omkara Asset Reconstruction filed Section 7 petitions before NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I. Following remand by NCLAT on 08.01.2025, NCLT examined Statements of Accounts, the CMA, and DSRA reserves, and on 08.07.2025 admitted both petitions initiating CIRP against Gstaad Hotels and Neo Capricorn. Suspended Directors appealed under Section 61.
legal_issues: Whether the existence of a Cash Management Agreement providing for debt servicing through hotel revenue retention accounts absolves corporate debtors of their independent repayment obligations under the main Loan Agreements; whether alleged excess withdrawals and undisbursed Debt Service Reserve Account (DSRA) amounts negate the occurrence of default under Section 3(12) of the IBC; and whether running profitable hotels with positive EBITDA precludes CIRP admission.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Escrow, retention, or cash management agreements are mere structured mechanisms for servicing debt and do not override the borrower's primary, absolute contractual obligation to ensure repayment from independent sources when retention balances are insufficient; once non-payment of an undisputed financial debt is established, positive operational cash flows or EBITDA do not preclude CIRP admission under Section 7. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 3(12) of the IBC, default occurs the moment whole or any part of an instalment of debt becomes due and payable and is unpaid. Under Section 7(5), the adjudicating authority's jurisdiction is strictly bounded by the inquiry into debt and default, leaving no discretion to reject admission where default exceeds the statutory threshold. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying M. Suresh Kumar Reddy, Innoventive Industries, and Vidarbha Industries, the existence of overdue interest and unpaid instalments demonstrated by certified loan statements and acknowledged in an OTS proposal provides conclusive proof of default that cannot be erased by speculative adjustments against DSRA reserves. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Both Corporate Debtors committed substantial defaults under ECLGS facilities and the main Term Loan on 15.11.2022 and failed to satisfy the lawful recall notices; NCLT properly admitted the Section 7 petitions.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1039 of 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1040 of 2025 are dismissed. The impugned orders dated 08.07.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-I admitting CP (IB) Nos. 290 and 291 of 2023 are affirmed. Parties shall bear their own costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed two connected appeals filed by the Suspended Directors of Gstaad Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (JW Marriott Bengaluru) and Neo Capricorn Plaza Pvt. Ltd. (Crowne Plaza Pune) challenging NCLT Mumbai's orders dated 08.07.2025 which admitted Section 7 petitions filed by Omkara Assets Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. for defaults exceeding Rs. 786 Crores. Following a previous remand, Appellants argued that the debts were not in default on 15.11.2022 because debt servicing was governed by a Cash Management Agreement, excess funds had been drawn, and undisbursed DSRA amounts should have been adjusted. Rejecting these defenses, NCLAT held that under Clause 18.39 of the loan agreement and the rule in M. Suresh Kumar Reddy, borrowers bear an absolute obligation to repay debts if escrow balances fall short. Even after accounting for possible DSRA adjustments, substantial default existed, and positive EBITDA did not shield the debtors from statutory insolvency resolution.

case_title: Protech Impex Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. vs. Uttar Pradesh Rajkiya Nirman Nigam Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Protech Impex Pvt. Ltd. & Anr. (Operational Creditor/Contractor); Respondent is Uttar Pradesh Rajkiya Nirman Nigam Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/Government Entity)[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor issued 23 distinct work orders starting from 19.10.2012 to Appellant for civil works at the National Institute of Occupational Health (NIOH), Ahmedabad[cite: 30]. Work was completed, and a work completion certificate was granted to the Appellant on 15.01.2016[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claimed operational default was Rs. 3,65,75,820/- as principal and Rs. 3,45,83,690/- as simple interest at 24% p.a. till 23.12.2019, with the date of default stated as 15.01.2016[cite: 30]. Corporate Debtor admitted in ledger that only a security amount of Rs. 36,14,500/- remained withheld pending receipt from client NIOH, while an entry dated 16.10.2017 showed release of a Rs. 10,00,000/- security deposit cheque[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Completion certificate issued and default occurred on 15.01.2016[cite: 30]; security deposit cheque released on 16.10.2017[cite: 30]; Section 8 Demand Notice issued on 23.12.2019[cite: 30]; Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 19/ALD/2021 filed before NCLT on 20.02.2020[cite: 30]; NCLT dismissed petition on 17.05.2023[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Work orders from 2012[cite: 30]; work completion certificate dated 15.01.2016[cite: 30]; Section 9 application Part-IV and Part-V pleadings stating that 'no payment has been received from the corporate debtor till date'[cite: 30]; Corporate Debtor's counter-affidavit and ledger Annexure CA-1 showing release of security cheques dated 20.11.2016, 28.08.2017, and 16.10.2017 (Cheque No. 000488 for Rs. 10,00,000/-)[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Operational Creditor filed Section 9 application CP (IB) No. 19/ALD/2021 before NCLT Allahabad Bench[cite: 30]. On 17.05.2023, NCLT dismissed the application as barred by limitation, having been filed more than 3 years after the default date of 15.01.2016[cite: 30]. Operational Creditor appealed under Section 61[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether the refund/release of a security deposit cheque by a corporate debtor constitutes an acknowledgement of debt or payment towards operational debt under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 so as to reset the 3-year limitation period, especially in the absence of any specific pleading in the Section 9 application or any written acknowledgement signed by the debtor[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To claim the benefit of Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 to reset limitation, the payment must be made on account of the debt before the expiration of the prescribed period and accompanied by an acknowledgment of payment in writing signed by the payer; furthermore, the facts founding such extension must be specifically pleaded[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963 read with Order 7 Rule 6 CPC obliges the applicant to set out in the pleadings the specific exemption facts extending limitation; a bald statement in Part V of Form 5 that no payment was ever received precludes the applicant from taking advantage of Section 19 based on isolated ledger entries[cite: 30]. Furthermore, the refund of a contractual security deposit cannot be equated with an acknowledgement of liability or part-payment towards unpaid operational invoices for work done[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Applying the test of Shanti Conductors Pvt. Ltd. v. Assam State Electricity Board, oral evidence cannot substitute the requirement of a written or signed acknowledgment of payment, and subsequent disclosures in a respondent's counter cannot revive a claim dead at the date of presentation[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because the default occurred on 15.01.2016 and the refund of security on 16.10.2017 neither represented part-payment towards the work bills nor bore written acknowledgment of debt, Section 9 filed on 20.02.2020 was barred by limitation[cite: 30].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1054 of 2023 is dismissed[cite: 30]. The impugned order dated 17.05.2023 passed by NCLT Allahabad Bench rejecting the Section 9 application is affirmed[cite: 30].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Protech Impex Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT Allahabad's dismissal of its Section 9 application against Uttar Pradesh Rajkiya Nirman Nigam Ltd. on the ground of limitation[cite: 30]. The Appellant contended that a cheque refunding Rs. 10 Lakhs towards security deposit on 16.10.2017 extended the limitation period under Section 19 of the Limitation Act, 1963[cite: 30]. Rejecting the plea, NCLAT held that under the Supreme Court's ruling in Shanti Conductors, Section 19 requires specific pleadings and a signed written acknowledgment of part-payment towards the debt[cite: 30]. Since the Appellant had pleaded that no payment was ever received and the release of a security deposit does not constitute part-payment of operational dues for work done, the petition filed on 20.02.2020 for a 15.01.2016 default was barred by time[cite: 30].

case_title: Tahir Vasanali Isani vs. Registrar of Companies, Goa, Daman and Diu
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Tahir Vasanali Isani (Director and Shareholder/Member of M/s Elegance Property Developers Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent is Registrar of Companies (RoC), Goa, Daman and Diu[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Real estate development company incorporated on 19.08.2008 owning a 36,022 sq. meters unencumbered land parcel in South Goa purchased on 24.11.2008 for INR 6,05,00,000/- for developing real estate projects[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Statutory filing default under the Companies Act due to non-filing of annual returns and financial statements with the RoC and Income Tax Department from FY 2011-12 onwards, resulting in strike-off[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company incorporated 19.08.2008; financial statements filed till FY 2010-11[cite: 31]; RoC issued Form STK-5 notice on 04.07.2018; RoC struck off name via Form STK-7 on 05.09.2018[cite: 31]; Appellant filed restoration petition under Section 252(3) on 08.09.2023[cite: 31]; NCLT dismissed petition on 15.10.2024[cite: 31]; appeal heard by NCLAT in August 2025[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered sale deed dated 24.11.2008 showing acquisition of 36,022 sq. meters land parcel for Rs. 6.05 Crores[cite: 31]; balance sheets recording Rs. 6.42 Crores under inventories[cite: 31]; CA certificate and bank extracts proving no cash deposits during demonetisation[cite: 31]; affidavit stating no pending prosecutions[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Shareholder/Director filed Company Appeal No. 140(MB)/2023 under Section 252(3) before NCLT Mumbai Bench[cite: 31]. On 15.10.2024, NCLT dismissed the appeal as time-barred under the 3-year limitation of Section 252(1) and held that holding land without active operational revenue does not constitute carrying on business[cite: 31]. Appellant appealed to NCLAT[cite: 31].
legal_issues: Whether an application/appeal for company restoration filed by a shareholder/member against a compulsory strike-off under Section 248(1) is governed by the 20-year limitation period under Section 252(3) or the 3-year limitation period under Section 252(1) of the Companies Act, 2013; and whether owning valuable unencumbered immovable property intended for development makes it 'just and equitable' to restore the company to the Register of Companies[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 252 of the Companies Act, 2013 creates no statutory bifurcation confining Section 252(3) exclusively to voluntary strike-offs under Section 248(2); any application filed by a company, member, creditor, or workman seeking restoration is entitled to the 20-year limitation period under Section 252(3) regardless of whether the strike-off was initiated suo motu by the Registrar under Section 248(1)[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The expression 'otherwise it is just' in Section 252(3) is an expansive equitable ground empowering tribunals to restore a company to prevent the deadlocking or destruction of valuable unencumbered commercial assets, which would otherwise operate contrary to public policy[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where title deeds and balance sheets establish ownership of substantial immovable property and bank records confirm the company is not a sham shell entity or involved in dubious cash movements, the 'just and equitable' standard for restoration is satisfied[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in treating the application as time-barred under Section 252(1); since the company holds substantial unencumbered land and is not a shell entity, its restoration is just and equitable[cite: 31].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 56/2025 is allowed[cite: 31]. The impugned order dated 15.10.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai is set aside, and the RoC is directed to restore M/s Elegance Property Developers Pvt. Ltd. to the Register of Companies subject to payment of Rs. 2,00,000/- costs within eight weeks and filing of all pending annual returns and balance sheets within four weeks with applicable fees[cite: 31]. RoC remains free to initiate statutory penal actions for filing delays[cite: 31]. Pending applications are disposed of[cite: 31].
summary: NCLAT allowed the company appeal filed by a director-shareholder of M/s Elegance Property Developers Pvt. Ltd., setting aside NCLT Mumbai's dismissal of a restoration petition[cite: 31]. NCLT had held that a strike-off by the RoC under Section 248(1) must be appealed within 3 years under Section 252(1) and that holding idle land does not constitute active business[cite: 31]. Overruling this, NCLAT held that an application by a member is governed by the 20-year limitation under Section 252(3) irrespective of whether the strike-off was suo motu or voluntary[cite: 31]. Furthermore, because the company owned a 36,022 sq. meter unencumbered land parcel in Goa worth over Rs. 6 Crores and was not a shell entity, it was 'just and equitable' under Section 252(3) to restore the company, subject to Rs. 2 Lakhs costs and statutory filing compliances[cite: 31].

case_title: Ras Al Khaimah Investment Authority vs. Matrix Pharmacorp Private Limited & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 47 / 2025 with Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 46 / 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Ras Al Khaimah Investment Authority (RAKIA, a UAE decree-holder/judgment creditor); Respondent No. 1 is Tianish Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. (Transferor Company); Respondent No. 2 is Matrix Pharmacorp Pvt. Ltd. (Transferee Company); connected third-party judgment debtor is Mr. Nimmagadda Prasad and affiliated entity IQuest Enterprises Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 32] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate merger under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 between Tianish Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. and Matrix Pharmacorp Pvt. Ltd. sanctioned by NCLT Hyderabad, following an underlying corporate acquisition of active pharmaceutical ingredient (API) business from Viatris Inc.[cite: 32] 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant obtained an offshore money decree dated 02.02.2022 from Ras Al Khaimah Court (UAE) against Mr. Nimmagadda Prasad and sought execution for recovery of outstanding decretal dues through Commercial Execution Petition CEP No. 19 of 2023 in Hyderabad[cite: 32]. Neither Tianish nor Matrix were debtors or judgment debtors under the decree[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: UAE decree passed 02.02.2022; CEP No. 19/2023 filed 05.09.2023; Commercial Court recorded undertaking on 01.05.2024; Viatris acquisition completed 03.06.2024; Contempt Case No. 1378/2024 filed before Telangana High Court on 11.07.2024; status quo order passed by High Court on 19.07.2024; Amalgamation approved by boards on 04.07.2024; NCLT sanctioned amalgamation and dismissed RAKIA's intervention on 10.03.2025[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Offshore decree dated 02.02.2022; interim status quo order dated 19.07.2024 passed in Contempt Case No. 1378 of 2024 against IQuest, Swathi, and Nimmagadda Prasad; Scheme of Amalgamation between Tianish and Matrix; CRISIL credit reports; absence of any shareholding or creditor status of RAKIA in Tianish or Matrix[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In CP (CAA) No. 34/230/HDB/2024 before NCLT Hyderabad, RAKIA filed Intervention Petition No. 4/2024 seeking to halt amalgamation alleging violation of the High Court's status quo order[cite: 32]. On 10.03.2025, NCLT dismissed the intervention petition for lack of standing under Section 230(4) and sanctioned the amalgamation[cite: 32]. RAKIA appealed both orders under Section 421[cite: 32].
legal_issues: Whether a foreign judgment creditor executing a money decree against an individual promoter/affiliate has locus standi under the proviso to Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013 to intervene and object to a scheme of amalgamation between separate corporate entities; and whether non-disclosure of an interim status quo order passed against third parties in contempt proceedings violates Section 230(2)(a)[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An objection to a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 can strictly be maintained only by persons satisfying the statutory thresholds under the proviso to Section 230(4), and an external decree-holder of an individual promoter possessing neither shares nor debt in the amalgamating companies has no locus standi to intervene[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The proviso to Section 230(4) expressly restricts objections to persons holding not less than 10% of shareholding or not less than 5% of total outstanding debt; third-party creditors cannot bypass this statutory filter[cite: 32]. Furthermore, Section 230(2)(a) requires disclosure of material facts and proceedings against the amalgamating companies themselves, and does not mandate disclosure of personal contempt or execution proceedings against third parties where the merging companies were not parties[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Order XXXIX CPC and Section 10 of the Contempt of Courts Act, an interim status quo order operates in personam against named contemnors; it does not constitute an order in rem restraining independent corporate amalgamations under company law[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Because RAKIA held zero shares and zero debt in either Tianish or Matrix, its intervention was statutorily barred under Section 230(4), and the non-disclosure of unrelated contempt orders did not vitiate the sanctioned merger[cite: 32].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 46 / 2025 and Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 47 / 2025 are dismissed for lack of merit[cite: 32]. The orders dated 10.03.2025 passed by NCLT Hyderabad Bench dismissing the Intervention Petition and sanctioning the Scheme of Amalgamation are affirmed[cite: 32]. All pending IAs stand closed[cite: 32].
summary: NCLAT Chennai dismissed two connected appeals filed by Ras Al Khaimah Investment Authority (RAKIA) challenging NCLT Hyderabad's orders dated 10.03.2025 which rejected its intervention and sanctioned the amalgamation of Tianish Laboratories Pvt. Ltd. and Matrix Pharmacorp Pvt. Ltd[cite: 32]. RAKIA, holding a foreign decree against Mr. Nimmagadda Prasad, claimed that the merger was a fraudulent attempt to violate a status quo order issued by the Telangana High Court in contempt proceedings[cite: 32]. Affirming NCLT's decision, NCLAT held that under the proviso to Section 230(4) of the Companies Act, 2013, only shareholders with at least 10% equity or creditors holding at least 5% of total debt have locus standi to object to a scheme[cite: 32]. Since RAKIA was neither a shareholder nor a creditor of either company, and the merging entities were not parties to the contempt proceedings, RAKIA had no standing to intervene[cite: 32].

case_title: Rahul Kumawat vs. Bank of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Rahul Kumawat, Suspended Director of Corporate Debtor M/s MP Agro BRK Energy Foods Private Limited; Respondent No. 1 is Bank of India (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is IRP[cite: 33]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Multiple credit facilities sanctioned in 2014 by Bank of India, including a term loan facility of Rs. 1.90 Crores and two working capital cash credit facilities totaling Rs. 8 Crores (reviewed and renewed on 13.09.2017)[cite: 33]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in loan accounts resulting in NPA classification on 30.09.2017[cite: 33]; Section 13(2) notice demanded Rs. 1,066.21 Lakhs (Rs. 10.66 Crores)[cite: 33]; Section 7 application claimed total outstanding financial default of Rs. 11,57,89,697/- (principal Rs. 10.43 Crores + interest Rs. 1.14 Crores) as on 30.09.2017[cite: 33]; Corporate Debtor acknowledged defaults in an OTS proposal for Rs. 8.41 Crores (sanctioned 06.08.2019, revoked 07.10.2019) and subsequent OTS dated 08.01.2020 for Rs. 5.25 Crores[cite: 33]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30.09.2017[cite: 33]; Section 13(2) notice issued on 06.11.2017[cite: 33]; CD requested restructuring acknowledging dues on 10.01.2018[cite: 33]; Section 7 petition filed on 22.10.2018[cite: 33]; admitted on 05.03.2020; remanded by NCLAT on 14.11.2022; re-admitted on 04.04.2024; remanded again by NCLAT on 26.04.2024; NCLT re-admitted Section 7 on 02.05.2025[cite: 33]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Term loan and cash credit sanction agreements[cite: 33]; ZLCC minutes dated 13.09.2017 noting cash credit overdues of Rs. 79.22 Lakhs and term loan overdues of Rs. 10.54 Lakhs[cite: 33]; Section 13(2) notice dated 06.11.2017[cite: 33]; Corporate Debtor's letter dated 10.01.2018 admitting overdues of Rs. 1.80 Crores[cite: 33]; bank statements, CIBIL report, and failed OTS proposals dated 06.08.2019 and 08.01.2020[cite: 33]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Bank of India filed Section 7 CP (IB) No. 55/MP/2024 before NCLT Indore Special Bench[cite: 33]. Following two rounds of appellate remand, NCLT heard the parties on five specific framed issues and, on 02.05.2025, admitted the Section 7 application establishing debt and default exceeding Rs. 1 Crore[cite: 33]. Suspended Director appealed under Section 61[cite: 33].
legal_issues: Whether the classification of a borrower's account as an NPA or compliance with RBI's MSME circular dated 07.02.2018 is a relevant condition precedent for maintaining a Section 7 petition under the IBC; and whether the availability of cash deposits in a cash credit account negates default in a term loan account when unutilized limits are insufficient[cite: 33].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The foundation of an application under Section 7 of the IBC is the existence of a financial debt and the occurrence of a default under Section 3(12); NPA classification under RBI prudential norms is entirely extraneous and immaterial to the maintainability and admission of a Section 7 petition[cite: 33]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 3(12) defines default as non-payment of debt when whole or any part has become due and payable[cite: 33]. Under Laxmi Pat Surana and M. Suresh Kumar Reddy, the trigger for Section 7 is default in fact, not NPA notification[cite: 33]. RBI circulars granting relief to MSMEs operate prospectively and cannot retrospectively cure or extinguish a financial default that occurred prior to their issuance[cite: 33]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where certified account statements, bank records, CIBIL reports, and the corporate debtor's own restructuring requests and OTS proposals prove unpaid overdue installments exceeding the statutory threshold, default stands conclusively established[cite: 33]. A bank is not legally obligated to debit irregular cash credit accounts to service term loans in the absence of sufficient unutilized margins[cite: 33]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor committed substantial defaults in repayment of its term loan and cash credit facilities as on 30.09.2017, which were continuously acknowledged; NCLT correctly admitted the Section 7 application[cite: 33].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 753 of 2025 is dismissed[cite: 33]. The impugned order dated 02.05.2025 passed by NCLT Indore Special Bench Court No. 1 admitting the Section 7 application and initiating CIRP against MP Agro BRK Energy Foods Pvt. Ltd. is affirmed[cite: 33]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 33].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by the Suspended Director of MP Agro BRK Energy Foods Pvt. Ltd. against NCLT Indore's order dated 02.05.2025 admitting a Section 7 application filed by Bank of India for a default of Rs. 11.57 Crores[cite: 33]. The Appellant contended that its NPA classification on 30.09.2017 was flawed under the RBI's MSME circular of 07.02.2018 and that funds in its cash credit account should have been adjusted to service the term loan[cite: 33]. Rejecting the challenge, NCLAT held that under Laxmi Pat Surana, Section 7 requires only proof of debt and default, rendering NPA disputes immaterial[cite: 33]. The RBI circular was prospective, and certified statements along with the debtor's written restructuring and OTS admissions conclusively proved continuous default, justifying admission[cite: 33].

case_title: Byju Raveendran vs. Aditya Birla Finance Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Byju Raveendran (Suspended Director and Promoter of Corporate Debtor M/s Think and Learn Pvt. Ltd.); Respondent No. 1 is Aditya Birla Finance Ltd. (Financial Creditor); Respondent No. 2 is Pankaj Srivastava (Interim Resolution Professional - IRP); Respondent No. 3 is Glas Trust Company LLC (Financial Creditor holding 99.41% voting share); Respondent No. 4 is BCCI (Original Operational Creditor)[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: CIRP initiated against Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd. on 16.07.2024 under Section 9 on a petition by BCCI[cite: 34]. Respondent No. 1 filed a claim of Rs. 47.12 Crores in Form C arising out of customer financing and business agreements dated 28.10.2020; Respondent No. 3 filed a financial claim of Rs. 11,432.98 Crores[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in credit facilities and financing agreements leading to admitted claims of Rs. 47,12,00,000/- for Respondent No. 1 and Rs. 11,432,98,87,753/- for Respondent No. 3[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 16.07.2024; public announcement on 17.07.2024[cite: 34]; NCLAT stayed CIRP on settlement on 02.08.2024, which Supreme Court stayed on 14.08.2024 restoring CIRP[cite: 34]; IRP verified claims and constituted CoC on 21.08.2024 (Glas Trust 99.41%, ABFL 0.41%, Incred 0.18%, ICICI Bank) and filed IA No. 942/2024 on 22.08.2024[cite: 34]; on 31.08.2024, IRP unilaterally reconstituted CoC by reclassifying ABFL as operational creditor and Glas Trust as contingent, leaving Incred with 100% voting share, and passing resolutions on 03.09.2024 appointing himself as RP[cite: 34]; NCLT set aside reconstitution on 29.01.2025[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email dated 21.08.2024 and notice of 1st CoC meeting confirming valid constitution of initial CoC[cite: 34]; application IA No. 942 of 2024 certifying initial CoC[cite: 34]; IRP's subsequent letter dated 31.08.2024 and IA No. 671 of 2024 attempting to substitute a reconstituted CoC[cite: 34]; Business Agreement dated 28.10.2020[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Respondent No. 1 and Respondent No. 3 filed IA Nos. 660/2024 and 820/2024 before NCLT Bengaluru Bench under Section 60(5) challenging their exclusion and reclassification[cite: 34]. On 29.01.2025, NCLT allowed the applications, set aside the reconstitution dated 31.08.2024, restored the 21.08.2024 CoC, set aside the appointment of the RP, restored ABFL as Financial Creditor, and referred IRP to IBBI for disciplinary action[cite: 34]. Suspended Director appealed under Section 61[cite: 34].
legal_issues: Whether an Interim Resolution Professional (IRP) has statutory authority under the IBC to unilaterally review, reclassify, or alter the status of a creditor from financial to operational and exclude verified financial creditors from an already constituted Committee of Creditors without the approval of the Adjudicating Authority; and whether a CoC can be 'provisionally' constituted[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Interim Resolution Professional or Resolution Professional performs purely administrative and facilitation functions and possesses no adjudicatory powers under the IBC; once a Committee of Creditors is legally constituted, the IRP/RP has no power to unilaterally alter, review, or reclassify the status of a creditor or reconstitute the CoC without prior approval of the Adjudicating Authority[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 21(1) of the IBC read with CIRP Regulations 12, 13, and 17 mandates that once claims are collated and the CoC is constituted, subsequent updating under Regulation 14 is confined strictly to recalculating the quantum of claims and does not empower reviewing or changing the legal status of a creditor[cite: 34]. The IBC contains no statutory concept of 'provisional' constitution of a CoC[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Swiss Ribbons, Rajnish Jain, and Union Bank of India v. Rajdeep Clothing, claim categorization by the IRP/RP cannot be reviewed under the guise of claim updation; arbitrary exclusion of major financial creditors (holding over 99.8% voting share) to vest 100% control in a 0.18% claimant constitutes manifest administrative misconduct[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The IRP acted ultra vires and unlawfully in stripping Aditya Birla Finance and Glas Trust of their financial creditor status and reconstituting the CoC on 31.08.2024; NCLT's order restoring the 21.08.2024 CoC was fully justified[cite: 34].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 120/2025 is dismissed[cite: 34]. The impugned order dated 29.01.2025 passed by NCLT Bengaluru Bench setting aside the reconstitution of the CoC, restoring the CoC constituted on 21.08.2024, setting aside the resolutions of 03.09.2024, and restoring Aditya Birla Finance Limited as a Financial Creditor is affirmed[cite: 34]. Parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 34]. All pending IAs are closed[cite: 34].
summary: NCLAT Chennai dismissed the appeal filed by Byju Raveendran, Suspended Director of Think & Learn Pvt. Ltd., upholding NCLT Bengaluru's order dated 29.01.2025 which nullified the illegal reconstitution of the Committee of Creditors (CoC) by the IRP[cite: 34]. The IRP had initially constituted the CoC on 21.08.2024 with Glas Trust (99.41%) and Aditya Birla Finance (0.41%), but on 31.08.2024 unilaterally ousted them by reclassifying Glas Trust as contingent and ABFL as an operational creditor, leaving Incred with 100% voting power to confirm him as RP[cite: 34]. Affirming NCLT's ruling, NCLAT held that an IRP possesses purely administrative powers and cannot 'provisionally' form a CoC or reclassify a creditor's status under the guise of claim updation[cite: 34]. The original 21.08.2024 CoC was restored and disciplinary investigation against the IRP was upheld[cite: 34].

case_title: Mrs. Vandana Gupta & Anr. vs. Mr. A. Viswanadha Sarma, Resolution Professional of M/S Unibera Developers Private Limited
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1660 of 2024 with Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1659 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Mrs. Vandana Gupta and Mr. Arun Gupta (Directors of M/s Propertree Real Estate Solutions Pvt. Ltd., real estate broker); Respondent is Mr. A. Viswanadha Sarma, Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s Unibera Developers Private Limited[cite: 35]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants' company acted as authorized real estate broker for Corporate Debtor's residential projects 'Unibera Towers'/'Unibera Heights' under agreements dated 10.04.2012 and 17.01.2013[cite: 35]. Unpaid brokerage commissions earned by Appellants were adjusted towards the purchase price of residential flats in the project, formalized through credit notes and settlement MoUs dated 25.11.2021 and 03.02.2022[cite: 35]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellants filed Form CA claiming Rs. 81,05,211/- as financial debt in a class of homebuyers in respect of Flat No. T-V 2301; Appellants only paid Rs. 2,00,000/- in cash back in 2012-2013 towards a booking that was subsequently cancelled in 2017, whereas the entire balance consideration was adjusted against commission liabilities owed by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 35]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Unit 1204 booked 10.09.2013 and cancelled by CD on 07.06.2017[cite: 35]; Appellants filed Section 9 petition CP (IB) No. 868 of 2018 claiming unpaid commission[cite: 35]; CIRP stayed/withdrawn following settlement MoUs dated 25.11.2021 and 03.02.2022[cite: 35]; fresh CIRP initiated against CD under Section 9 on 13.01.2023[cite: 35]; Appellants submitted Form CA on 23.01.2023[cite: 35]; RP reclassified claim as operational debt on 14.07.2023[cite: 35]; NCLT rejected Appellants' IA No. 4354/2023 on 05.06.2024[cite: 35]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Brokerage agreements from 2012 and 2013[cite: 35]; brokerage commission invoice dated 01.10.2016 for Rs. 99,77,449/-[cite: 35]; credit notes dated 10.03.2015 and 02.07.2015[cite: 35]; cancellation letter dated 07.06.2017[cite: 35]; Section 9 petition filed by Appellants as operational creditors in 2018[cite: 35]; settlement MoUs dated 25.11.2021 and 03.02.2022[cite: 35]; Builder Buyer Agreement dated 16.02.2022 for Flat T-V 2301 showing consideration paid by adjusting outstanding brokerage fees[cite: 35]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellants filed IA No. 4354 of 2023 in CP (IB) No. 505/ND/2022 before NCLT New Delhi Court-II praying for their claim of Rs. 81,05,211/- to be admitted as financial debt[cite: 35]. On 05.06.2024, NCLT rejected the application holding that the underlying debt arose from brokerage services[cite: 35]. Appellants appealed under Section 61(1)[cite: 35].
legal_issues: Whether an individual who is allotted residential flats by a corporate debtor through adjustment and credit notes against unpaid real estate brokerage commissions (without monetary disbursement) qualifies as an 'allottee' and 'financial creditor' under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC; and whether the creditor is estopped from altering the nature of the claim from operational to financial debt[cite: 35].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: To qualify as an allottee/financial creditor under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC, there must be an actual disbursal of money by the claimant to the corporate debtor as an advance against the consideration for the time value of money to fund project construction; a barter or book adjustment of accrued service commission does not have the commercial effect of a borrowing[cite: 35]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The Explanation to Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC deems amounts raised from allottees under real estate projects to have the commercial effect of borrowing only where money was raised from such allottee; unpaid service fees and commissions remain operational debt under Section 5(21)[cite: 35]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under Pioneer Urban Land and Anuj Jain, courts must look to the genesis of the transaction; where the claimant previously issued Section 8 demand notices and filed Section 9 insolvency petitions for the exact same commission debt, they are legally estopped from asserting that subsequent settlement MoUs converting unpaid commission into flat allotments transformed the operational debt into a financial debt[cite: 35]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellants parted with no money for the time value of money, and their claims arose exclusively from brokerage services; NCLT correctly dismissed the application to treat the claim as financial debt[cite: 35].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1660 of 2024 is dismissed along with connected appeal No. 1659 of 2024[cite: 35]. The impugned common order dated 05.06.2024 passed by NCLT New Delhi Court-II is affirmed[cite: 35]. No costs[cite: 35]. All pending IAs are disposed of[cite: 35].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Mrs. Vandana Gupta and Mr. Arun Gupta, Directors of broker firm Propertree Real Estate Solutions Pvt. Ltd., against NCLT New Delhi's order dated 05.06.2024 which rejected their claim to be classified as financial creditors in the CIRP of Unibera Developers Pvt. Ltd[cite: 35]. The Appellants contended that because their unpaid brokerage commission had been adjusted under settlement MoUs towards the purchase of a residential flat (Flat T-V 2301) for Rs. 74.98 Lakhs, they were allottees and financial creditors under Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC[cite: 35]. Affirming the RP and NCLT's classification of the claim as operational debt, NCLAT held that under Pioneer Urban Land and Anuj Jain, financial debt requires actual disbursement of funds for the time value of money[cite: 35]. Adjusting unpaid service commissions does not constitute commercial borrowing, and having previously triggered Section 9 as operational creditors, Appellants were estopped from altering the debt's character[cite: 35].

case_title: Kolkata Municipal Corporation vs. Gajesh Labhchand Jain (Liquidator of Talwalkars Better Value Fitness Ltd.)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Kolkata Municipal Corporation (Appellant) and Gajesh Labhchand Jain, Liquidator of Talwalkars Better Value Fitness Ltd. (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Property tax assessed on corporate debtor's asset situated within Kolkata Municipal Corporation; warrant of distress issued in 2018 for unpaid dues amounting to Rs. 30,28,233/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Outstanding property tax claims totaling Rs. 51,72,258/- (later adjudicated as Rs. 34,23,403/-). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 11.01.2021; demand notice issued on 22.03.2022; liquidation commenced on 28.04.2022; property sealed on 24.09.2022 and de-sealed on 02.05.2023; Form-C claim filed on 12.05.2023; NCLT order passed on 19.07.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Statutory levy of property tax and distress warrant issued under the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Liquidator rejected the appellant's status as a secured creditor via letter dated 21.07.2023; NCLT partly allowed Appeal No. 03/2024 on 19.07.2024, admitting the claim but rejecting secured creditor status, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether Kolkata Municipal Corporation is a secured creditor in respect of its property tax dues by virtue of Section 232 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, and whether its dues constitute government/crown debts.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A statutory charge created by plenary legislation over lands and buildings for municipal taxes constitutes the municipal authority as a secured creditor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 232 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980 creates a first charge upon land and buildings for property taxes, subject only to prior payment of land revenue due to the government. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Statutory provisions explicitly establishing a first charge over premises create a security interest by operation of law, bringing the municipal corporation within the definition of a secured creditor under the IBC. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in categorizing the municipal dues as ordinary government/crown debts and denying secured creditor status.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; impugned order dated 19.07.2024 modified to declare Kolkata Municipal Corporation as a secured creditor; claim to be dealt with accordingly by the liquidator.
summary: Kolkata Municipal Corporation filed an appeal against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 19.07.2024 which admitted its property tax claim against the corporate debtor but rejected its status as a secured creditor, classifying the dues as crown debts. The NCLAT held that by virtue of Section 232 of the Kolkata Municipal Corporation Act, 1980, property taxes are a first charge upon the premises, thereby creating a statutory security interest. Relying on Supreme Court precedents regarding statutory charges, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's finding on this point and declared Kolkata Municipal Corporation to be a secured creditor in the liquidation process.

case_title: M/s Fimo Infosolutions Private Limited vs. Competition Commission of India
appeal_number: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 36 of 2022 with No. 48 of 2022 & No. 40 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants include Austere Systems Pvt. Ltd., Rahul Gajanan Teni (Director), Fimo Infosolutions Pvt. Ltd., and Jai Kumar Gupta (Director), opposing the Competition Commission of India (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tenders invited by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh for soil sample testing in 2017 and 2018 (specifically in Moradabad, Bareilly, Meerut, Saharanpur, and Jhansi divisions). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary penalties imposed ranging from Rs. 21,447/- to Rs. 44,25,569/- calculated at 5% of the average turnover. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Complaint filed on 07.08.2018; CCI prima facie order under Section 26(1) on 30.01.2020; DG report submitted on 08.04.2021; CCI final order passed on 04.04.2022; NCLAT judgment pronounced on 23.09.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Overlapping familial and business relationships, sharing of common addresses, submission of Earnest Money Deposits (EMDs) through bank accounts of rival directors, preparation of cover bids, and execution of false MoUs. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI found appellants guilty of bid-rigging and cartelization under Section 3 of the Act vide order dated 04.04.2022, which was challenged before NCLAT in Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 36, 48, and 40 of 2022.
legal_issues: Whether the appellants engaged in bid-rigging, collusive bidding, and market allocation in public procurement tenders for soil testing in contravention of Sections 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, and whether penalties were correctly computed.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In cartelization and bid-rigging cases, direct evidence of formal agreements is unnecessary; anticompetitive conduct and practical cooperation can be inferred from circumstantial evidence, shared business operations, and parallel conduct. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Related or family-owned corporate entities operating as independent legal personalities cannot claim immunity from antitrust scrutiny under the guise of being a 'single economic entity' when participating as separate bidders in public tenders. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Submission of bids by entities lacking technical qualifications, cross-financing of EMDs, and common address registrations establish a concerted effort to create a façade of competition. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Commission rightly held the appellants liable for bid-rigging and correctly computed penalties based on total turnover under the peculiar circumstances where relevant turnover from the illegal tender was nil.
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 36, 48, and 40 of 2022 are dismissed; the CCI impugned order dated 04.04.2022 imposing cease-and-desist directions and penalties is upheld.
summary: Appellants Austere Systems Pvt. Ltd., Fimo Infosolutions Pvt. Ltd., and their respective directors challenged the CCI order dated 04.04.2022 holding them guilty of bid-rigging and cartelization in soil testing tenders issued by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh. The NCLAT observed that the appellants—despite being related entities through family and business ties—submitted separate bids, paid EMDs from each other's accounts, and created a false façade of competition to secure tenders for Austere Systems, while geographically allocating bids with Yash Solutions. Finding no merit in the contentions regarding 'single economic entity' exemptions or relevant turnover limitations in first-time default cases, the NCLAT dismissed all appeals and upheld the penalties imposed by the CCI[cite: 7].
