case_title: Mrs. C. Valli Narayan vs. C. Krishniah Chetty & Sons Private Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) No. 65 of 2019 with Transfer Application (TA) No. 1 of 2023 in CA (AT) (CH) No. 70 of 2023
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants include Mrs. C. Valli Narayan and Mr. C. Ganesh Narayan (Narayan/CVN Group), opposing C. Krishniah Chetty & Sons Private Limited and Mr. C. Vinod Hayagriv and others (Hayagriv/CVH Group), along with statutory auditor Mr. Shyam Ramadhyani[cite: 10]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Family-run jewellery business structured under C. Krishniah Chetty & Sons Private Limited (R1 Company) with equal 50:50 shareholding distribution between the Narayan and Hayagriv groups, alongside various group entities and a Family Settlement Agreement (FSA) dated 09.01.2014[cite: 10]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Allegations of mutual oppression, mismanagement, exclusion from management, and breach of fiduciary duties under Section 166 of the Companies Act[cite: 10]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition No. 54 of 2014 filed before NCLT Bengaluru; NCLT dismissed CP 54/2014 on 24.01.2019 (challenged in CA No. 65 of 2019); subsequent CP No. 04/BB/2020 filed by Hayagriv group leading to ex-parte status quo orders on 12.07.2021 and final impugned order on 24.08.2023[cite: 10]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Execution of a binding Family Settlement Agreement (FSA) on 09.01.2014 (kept with an expert custodian), operational history of pre-existing group entity Deepali Co. Pvt. Ltd. (A-4), and board-level deadlock[cite: 10]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Bengaluru dismissed the Narayan group's oppression petition on 24.01.2019 and later allowed interim applications and dismissed recall applications in favor of the Hayagriv group on 24.08.2023, resulting in cross appeals tagged and transferred to the Principal Bench[cite: 10].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the oppression and mismanagement petition (CP 54 of 2014) and in confirming interim ex-parte status quo orders against the Narayan group while ignoring board deadlocks, quasi-partnership principles, and the operation of the Family Settlement Agreement[cite: 10].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In closely held family-run private companies operating on quasi-partnership lines with equal shareholding distribution, an irretrievable breakdown in trust and confidence resulting in a management deadlock warrants regulatory intervention under Section 242 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 10]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Equal 50:50 shareholders who are also directors are entitled to maintain a petition under Section 241/242 when systematically excluded from corporate affairs, and technical objections regarding family settlement enforceability cannot override equitable remedies[cite: 10]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Ex-parte interim injunctions granting final-stage reliefs without satisfying the triple test of a prima facie case, balance of convenience, and irreparable injury are legally unsustainable[cite: 10]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT orders dismissing the appellant's petition and confirming sweeping ex-parte restrictions are erroneous; to break the management deadlock, a professional Chairman and Managing Director must be appointed to oversee the company[cite: 10].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) No. 65 of 2019 and Transfer Application TA No. 1 of 2023 are allowed; NCLT orders dated 24.01.2019 and 24.08.2023 are set aside; Mr. Shyam Ramadhyani, CA, is appointed as Chairman and Managing Director of Respondent No. 1 Company for a period of one year to regulate its affairs[cite: 10].
summary: Appellants belonging to the Narayan group challenged two separate NCLT Bengaluru orders: one dismissing their petition alleging oppression and mismanagement (CP 54 of 2014), and another confirming ex-parte status quo orders against them in a subsequent petition filed by the Hayagriv group[cite: 10]. The NCLAT noted that the 50:50 family-run private company was suffering from an irretrievable management deadlock, mutual exclusion, and breakdown of trust[cite: 10]. Highlighting that sweeping interim injunctions had been improperly issued without satisfying the triple test, the NCLAT set aside the impugned NCLT orders and exercised powers under Section 242 of the Companies Act to appoint a professional Chartered Accountant, Mr. Shyam Ramadhyani, as Chairman and Managing Director for one year to break the deadlock and regulate the company's affairs[cite: 10].

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. vs. Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Committee of Creditors (CoC) through ICICI Bank, Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. & Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant Consortium), Resolution Professional Rohit Mehra, Sankalp Recreation Pvt. Ltd. (Unsuccessful RA), and suspended directors (Rajesh Patel & Ors.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) under Section 7 of IBC; resolution plan submitted by Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. in consortium with Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd. approved by 100% CoC voting share. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fair Value of CD determined at INR 429.09 crores and Liquidation Value at INR 277.09 crores. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 20.04.2022; RFRP issued on 17.08.2022; Challenge process held on 09.02.2023; Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 10.03.2023; NCLT rejected approval and partly allowed objections on 10.07.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consortium agreement dated 17.02.2023 introducing Check-Inn Hotels as a strategic investor to handle equity requirements mandated by RBI guidelines for ARCs, alongside 100% CoC approval and evaluation matrix scores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-II dismissed RP's application for plan approval (IA No. 1085 of 2023) and partly allowed objections by Sankalp Recreation and ex-promoters on 10.07.2024, leading to the present appeals by CoC, SRA, and RP.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the resolution plan approved unanimously by the CoC on grounds of alleged non-compliance with Regulation 39(1B) regarding consortium induction and material irregularities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is paramount and non-justiciable, and the Adjudicating Authority's review is strictly confined to checking compliance under Section 30(2) of the Code. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 15(1)(xi) of the RFRP empowering the CoC to permit changes or additions in consortium structure operates harmoniously to facilitate implementation, and a wholly-owned subsidiary of an eligible PRA cannot be treated as an unvetted third-party entrant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unanimous approval by 100% voting share, highest evaluation matrix scores, and compliance with statutory minimums for operational and financial creditors establish plan viability and commercial soundness. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 31 by substituting its own assessment for the commercial wisdom of the CoC and entertaining objections from an unsuccessful resolution applicant who had accepted refund of its bid bond.
operative_order: Appeals allowed; impugned order dated 10.07.2024 set aside; CP (IB) 1171/MB/2021 restored to its original position with directions for parties to appear before the Adjudicating Authority for plan approval on 15.10.2025.
summary: Appeals were filed by the Committee of Creditors, the Successful Resolution Applicant (Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. and Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd.), and the Resolution Professional challenging the NCLT Mumbai order dated 10.07.2024 which rejected the approved resolution plan for Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that the induction of Check-Inn Hotels as a strategic investor violated Regulation 39(1B), noting that the RFRP explicitly permitted consortium modifications, eligibility checks were duly conducted, and the plan received 100% CoC approval. Furthermore, unsuccessful applicant Sankalp lacked grounds for challenge after accepting its bid bond refund. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the impugned order and restored the matter for formal plan approval[cite: 11].

case_title: Bijendra Prasad Mishra vs. M/s. HS Mercantile Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Bijendra Prasad Mishra (Appellant/Suspended Director), M/s. HS Mercantile Private Limited (Corporate Debtor / Respondent No. 1), and M/s. Drolia Agencies Pvt. Ltd. / Subh Chintak Commotrade Pvt. Ltd. (Financial Creditor / Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Inter-corporate loan of Rs. 50,00,000/- disbursed by Subh Chintak to the Corporate Debtor on 07.11.2009 at an agreed 9% interest rate. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total debt claimed of Rs. 90,39,250/- including principal of Rs. 50,00,000/- and unpaid interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Loan disbursed on 07.11.2009; account classified as NPA; loan recall notice issued on 04.04.2016; amalgamation order passed on 28.03.2019; Section 7 application filed on 01.10.2019; NCLAT remand on 07.12.2023; NCLT admitted CIRP on 13.12.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank account statements reflecting disbursal, TDS deductions under Section 194A from 2010 to 2015 on interest, and written acknowledgment of debt in the audited financial statements of the Corporate Debtor for the financial year ending 31.03.2017. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT initially dismissed the Section 7 petition on 29.04.2022; NCLAT remanded the matter on 07.12.2023 to re-examine limitation; NCLT admitted the petition via impugned order dated 13.12.2024, which was challenged in the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the debt qualified as a financial debt under Section 5(8) of the IBC, whether a written financial contract is a mandatory prerequisite, and whether the application was barred by limitation.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A written financial contract is not a mandatory prerequisite or exclusive requirement for proving the existence of a financial debt under the IBC; financial debt can be established through alternative records including bank statements, TDS certificates, and balance sheet acknowledgments. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to extend the limitation period for filing a Section 7 application when the corporate debtor explicitly acknowledges the debt in its audited financial statements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Deduction of tax at source (TDS) on interest payments and recording of borrowings under long-term liabilities in balance sheets conclusively establish the commercial effect of a borrowing and time value of money. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in determining that the debt was a financial debt, default had occurred, and the application was within the extended limitation period.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 13.12.2024 initiating CIRP affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Bijendra Prasad Mishra, suspended director of HS Mercantile Limited, appealed against the NCLT Kolkata order dated 13.12.2024 admitting a Section 7 application filed by Drolia Agencies Pvt. Ltd. The appellant argued that the Rs. 50 lakhs was an advance for supply of goods rather than a financial debt, that no written agreement existed, and that the claim was time-barred. The NCLAT held that a written financial contract is not a sine qua non under the IBC, and the disbursal was adequately proved by bank statements, TDS deductions on interest, and debt acknowledgments in the corporate debtor's financial statements for 2016-2017. Finding that the debt, default, and limitation requirements were fully satisfied, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 12].

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. vs. Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Committee of Creditors (CoC) through ICICI Bank, Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. & Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant Consortium), Resolution Professional Rohit Mehra, Sankalp Recreation Pvt. Ltd. (Unsuccessful RA), and suspended directors (Rajesh Patel & Ors.)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) under Section 7 of IBC; resolution plan submitted by Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. in consortium with Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd. approved by 100% CoC voting share[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fair Value of CD determined at INR 429.09 crores and Liquidation Value at INR 277.09 crores[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 20.04.2022; RFRP issued on 17.08.2022; Challenge process held on 09.02.2023; Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 10.03.2023; NCLT rejected approval and partly allowed objections on 10.07.2024[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consortium agreement dated 17.02.2023 introducing Check-Inn Hotels as a strategic investor to handle equity requirements mandated by RBI guidelines for ARCs, alongside 100% CoC approval and evaluation matrix scores[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-II dismissed RP's application for plan approval (IA No. 1085 of 2023) and partly allowed objections by Sankalp Recreation and ex-promoters on 10.07.2024, leading to the present appeals by CoC, SRA, and RP[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the resolution plan approved unanimously by the CoC on grounds of alleged non-compliance with Regulation 39(1B) regarding consortium induction and material irregularities[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is paramount and non-justiciable, and the Adjudicating Authority's review is strictly confined to checking compliance under Section 30(2) of the Code[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 15(1)(xi) of the RFRP empowering the CoC to permit changes or additions in consortium structure operates harmoniously to facilitate implementation, and a wholly-owned subsidiary of an eligible PRA cannot be treated as an unvetted third-party entrant[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unanimous approval by 100% voting share, highest evaluation matrix scores, and compliance with statutory minimums for operational and financial creditors establish plan viability and commercial soundness[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 31 by substituting its own assessment for the commercial wisdom of the CoC and entertaining objections from an unsuccessful resolution applicant who had accepted refund of its bid bond[cite: 13].
operative_order: Appeals allowed; impugned order dated 10.07.2024 set aside; CP (IB) 1171/MB/2021 restored to its original position with directions for parties to appear before the Adjudicating Authority for plan approval on 15.10.2025[cite: 13].
summary: Appeals were filed by the Committee of Creditors, the Successful Resolution Applicant (Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. and Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd.), and the Resolution Professional challenging the NCLT Mumbai order dated 10.07.2024 which rejected the approved resolution plan for Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd[cite: 13]. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that the induction of Check-Inn Hotels as a strategic investor violated Regulation 39(1B), noting that the RFRP explicitly permitted consortium modifications, eligibility checks were duly conducted, and the plan received 100% CoC approval[cite: 13]. Furthermore, unsuccessful applicant Sankalp lacked grounds for challenge after accepting its bid bond refund[cite: 13]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the impugned order and restored the matter for formal plan approval[cite: 13].

case_title: Rajender Kumar Pahwa (Suspended Director of Goodluck Carbon Pvt. Ltd.) vs. Canara Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajender Kumar Pahwa (Appellant / Suspended Director of Goodluck Carbon Pvt. Ltd.), Canara Bank (Respondent No. 1 / Financial Creditor), Ashok Kumar Gulla (Respondent No. 2 / IRP), and Punjab National Bank (Respondent No. 3 / Lead Bank). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Project loan of Rs. 57.74 crores sanctioned under a consortium agreement dated 10.03.2014 by a consortium of banks led by Punjab National Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial debt default claimed of Rs. 90,43,74,091.45/- as on 31.08.2023, with date of default / NPA classified as 30.09.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30.09.2015; SARFAESI notice issued on 20.06.2017; working capital consortium agreement executed on 01.03.2017; multiple One-Time Settlement (OTS) proposals submitted by CD up to 2023; Section 7 petition filed on 02.09.2023; NCLT admitted CIRP on 18.10.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Execution of loan documents, consortium agreements, acknowledgment of debt through continuous submission of written OTS proposals, and deposit of 5% of OTS amount into an escrow account. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Court-IV) admitted Canara Bank's Section 7 petition and initiated CIRP via order dated 18.10.2024, which was challenged in the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a single financial creditor belonging to a consortium can maintain a petition under Section 7 of the IBC without the concurrence of other members, and whether pending consideration of an OTS proposal bars the initiation of CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The independent statutory right of a financial creditor to trigger CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC cannot be curtailed, restricted, or made subservient to any inter-se consortium agreement or pending One-Time Settlement (OTS) negotiations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC grants an overriding effect to the Code over any other instrument, and a debtor cannot claim a vested right to halt insolvency proceedings indefinitely under the guise of an unapproved OTS proposal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Continuous submission of written settlement proposals by the corporate debtor acts as a written acknowledgment of debt extending the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 petition upon proof of a valid financial debt and established default.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 18.10.2024 admitting the Section 7 application and initiating CIRP affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Rajender Kumar Pahwa, suspended director of Goodluck Carbon Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT order dated 18.10.2024 admitting Canara Bank's petition under Section 7 of the IBC. The appellant contended that Canara Bank could not initiate insolvency proceedings independently without the lead bank's consent while an OTS proposal was under active consideration by the consortium. The NCLAT held that an individual financial creditor possesses an independent statutory right under Section 7 to enforce its debt, which cannot be subordinated to inter-se consortium agreements or pending settlement talks. Finding that debt, default, and limitation were duly established, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 14].

case_title: Archernar Brand Technologies Private Limited & Ors. vs. Registrar of Companies
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Archernar Brand Technologies Pvt. Ltd. and 7 other transferor/transferee companies (Mensa Brand Technologies group) as Appellants, opposing the Registrar of Companies. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Composite Scheme of Arrangement involving the merger of 7 subsidiary transferor companies into the transferee company (Mensa Brand Technologies Pvt. Ltd.), all being subsidiaries of the parent Singapore entity (Mensa Brand Technologies Pte. Ltd.). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Projected post-merger net worth of the Transferee Company increasing from INR 551.29 crores to INR 913.37 crores, with remaining unsecured debt standing at a negligible amount (approx. INR 13.52 lacs across two companies). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board approvals obtained on 28.03.2025 and 01.04.2025; first motion application filed on 16.04.2025; NCLT Chandigarh passed impugned order on 10.06.2025; appeal filed on 22.07.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent affidavits obtained from unsecured creditors representing over 90% in value across the appellant companies, statutory auditor certificates, and positive net-worth statements. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh dispensed with meetings of shareholders and secured creditors but refused dispensation for unsecured creditors, directing a physical/virtual meeting of non-consenting unsecured creditors, which prompted the present appeal under Section 421 of the Act.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in refusing to dispense with meetings of unsecured creditors under Section 230(9) of the Companies Act, 2013 despite the applicant companies obtaining valid consent affidavits from unsecured creditors representing over 90% in value.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a proposed scheme of arrangement or merger does not involve any compromise or arrangement with creditors that adversely affects their rights and liabilities, and the transferee company possesses a robust positive net worth exceeding liabilities, the requirement of convening creditor meetings ought to be dispensed with under Section 230(9). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230(9) of the Companies Act empowers the Tribunal to dispense with meetings of creditors when creditors holding at least 90% in value agree and confirm by affidavit, without introducing artificial distinctions among creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Submission of valid consent affidavits exceeding the 90% statutory threshold, coupled with a significantly enhanced post-merger net worth, establishes that creditors' financial interests are fully safeguarded. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted contrary to the statutory scheme by declining dispensation and ordering meetings for remaining unsecured creditors representing less than 10% in value.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; directions contained in Paragraphs 24(f) to 24(s) of the impugned order dated 10.06.2025 requiring unsecured creditor meetings are set aside; the requirement of holding meetings of unsecured creditors is dispensed with[cite: 15].
summary: Archernar Brand Technologies Pvt. Ltd. and other group subsidiaries appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order dated 10.06.2025 which refused to dispense with meetings of unsecured creditors in a first motion amalgamation application, despite the appellants producing consent affidavits from unsecured creditors representing over 90% in value[cite: 15]. The NCLAT held that since the scheme was a corporate restructuring of parent-subsidiary entities that did not compromise creditor rights and where post-merger net worth substantially exceeded liabilities (reaching over INR 913 crores), the NCLAT was bound to dispense with creditor meetings under Section 230(9)[cite: 15]. Accordingly, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's directions ordering creditor meetings[cite: 15].

case_title: Rahul Gajanan Teni vs. Competition Commission of India
appeal_number: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 36 of 2022 with No. 48 of 2022 & No. 40 of 2022
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants include Austere Systems Pvt. Ltd., Rahul Gajanan Teni (Director), Fimo Infosolutions Pvt. Ltd., and Jai Kumar Gupta (Director), opposing the Competition Commission of India (Respondent)[cite: 16]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Tenders invited by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh for soil sample testing in 2017 and 2018 (specifically in Moradabad, Bareilly, Meerut, Saharanpur, and Jhansi divisions)[cite: 16]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary penalties imposed ranging from Rs. 21,447/- to Rs. 44,25,569/- calculated at 5% of the average turnover[cite: 16]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Complaint filed on 07.08.2018; CCI prima facie order under Section 26(1) on 30.01.2020; DG report submitted on 08.04.2021; CCI final order passed on 04.04.2022; NCLAT judgment pronounced on 23.09.2025[cite: 16]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Overlapping familial and business relationships, sharing of common addresses, submission of Earnest Money Deposits (EMDs) through bank accounts of rival directors, preparation of cover bids, and execution of false MoUs[cite: 16]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI found appellants guilty of bid-rigging and cartelization under Section 3 of the Act vide order dated 04.04.2022, which was challenged before NCLAT in Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 36, 48, and 40 of 2022[cite: 16].
legal_issues: Whether the appellants engaged in bid-rigging, collusive bidding, and market allocation in public procurement tenders for soil testing in contravention of Sections 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Competition Act, 2002, and whether penalties were correctly computed[cite: 16].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: In cartelization and bid-rigging cases, direct evidence of formal agreements is unnecessary; anticompetitive conduct and practical cooperation can be inferred from circumstantial evidence, shared business operations, and parallel conduct[cite: 16]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Related or family-owned corporate entities operating as independent legal personalities cannot claim immunity from antitrust scrutiny under the guise of being a 'single economic entity' when participating as separate bidders in public tenders[cite: 16]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Submission of bids by entities lacking technical qualifications, cross-financing of EMDs, and common address registrations establish a concerted effort to create a façade of competition[cite: 16]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Commission rightly held the appellants liable for bid-rigging and correctly computed penalties based on total turnover under the peculiar circumstances where relevant turnover from the illegal tender was nil[cite: 16].
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) Nos. 36, 48, and 40 of 2022 are dismissed; the CCI impugned order dated 04.04.2022 imposing cease-and-desist directions and penalties is upheld[cite: 16].
summary: Appellants Austere Systems Pvt. Ltd., Fimo Infosolutions Pvt. Ltd., and their respective directors challenged the CCI order dated 04.04.2022 holding them guilty of bid-rigging and cartelization in soil testing tenders issued by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh[cite: 16]. The NCLAT observed that the appellants—despite being related entities through family and business ties—submitted separate bids, paid EMDs from each other's accounts, and created a false façade of competition to secure tenders for Austere Systems, while geographically allocating bids with Yash Solutions[cite: 16]. Finding no merit in the contentions regarding 'single economic entity' exemptions or relevant turnover limitations in first-time default cases, the NCLAT dismissed all appeals and upheld the penalties imposed by the CCI[cite: 16].
