case_title: Unitech Machines Karamchari Sangh vs. Vivek Raheja (Resolution Professional of Unitech Machines Limited) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Unitech Machines Karamchari Sangh (Appellant / Workmen Union), Vivek Raheja (Respondent No. 1 / Resolution Professional of Unitech Machines Limited), and Ankit International (Respondent No. 2 / Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against Unitech Machines Limited (Corporate Debtor) on 01.03.2019 under Section 7 of the IBC. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Unpaid salaries, provident fund dues, and gratuity of workmen during the CIRP period following a layoff notice. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 01.03.2019; application under Section 60(5) filed by union on 21.07.2019; layoff notice issued by RP on 01.02.2020; resolution plan approved on 17.09.2021; NCLT dismissed union's IA No. 3780/2021 on 06.10.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Circular and layoff notice dated 01.02.2020 issued by the RP due to financial distress and lack of ongoing factory operations, and records showing non-attendance of workers post-layoff. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Court-VI, New Delhi dismissed the appellant's IA No. 3780/2021 via order dated 06.10.2023, upholding the validity of the layoff notice, which led to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Resolution Professional had the authority to issue a layoff notice under the IBC overriding the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and whether workmen who did not actually work during the CIRP are entitled to wages as CIRP costs.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 238 of the IBC, the provisions of the Code override any inconsistent laws, including the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and a Resolution Professional is empowered under Sections 20 and 25 to take necessary steps to protect corporate assets and manage operations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Wages and salaries of workmen can be included in CIRP costs under Section 5(13) only if it is established and proved that the corporate debtor was a going concern and the workmen actually worked during that period. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a factory is non-operational and a valid layoff notice has been issued due to severe financial constraints, workmen who do not perform duties cannot claim wages for the non-working period as CIRP costs. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in dismissing the challenge to the layoff notice, as the RP acted within statutory powers and the approved resolution plan binds all stakeholders under the clean slate theory.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 06.10.2023 passed by the Adjudicating Authority affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Unitech Machines Karamchari Sangh appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated 06.10.2023 which dismissed their application challenging a layoff notice issued by the Resolution Professional on 01.02.2020. The NCLAT held that the Resolution Professional acted within his statutory duties under Sections 20 and 25 of the IBC to protect corporate assets amidst severe fund crunches, and Section 238 gives the IBC overriding effect over the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. Furthermore, relying on Supreme Court precedents, the NCLAT reiterated that workmen are not entitled to wages as CIRP costs for periods they did not actually work when the corporate debtor was non-operational. Consequently, the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Sylvan Commercial Private Limited vs. Nitin Daga (Resolution Professional of Rishra Steel Limited) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sylvan Commercial Private Limited (Appellant / Promoter-Investor), Nitin Daga (Resolution Professional of Rishra Steel Limited), Official Liquidator, and Geepee Softech Services Pvt. Ltd. & JK Urbanscapes Developers Limited (Successful Resolution Applicant). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Winding-up orders issued against Rishra Steel Ltd. on 04.06.1990; revival scheme approved on 02.05.1997 inducting Sylvan as promoter and investing Rs. 2.15 crores under a court-appointed administrator; revival scheme set aside by Division Bench on 03.10.1997; subsequent Supreme Court directions for claim adjudication; CIRP initiated against Rishra Steel Ltd. on 18.07.2022. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Claim of Rs. 245 crores (including principal of Rs. 2.15 crores and interest of Rs. 213 crores) filed by Sylvan. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Winding-up initiated in 1990; Supreme Court remand on 06.08.2021 transferring proceedings to NCLT; CIRP commenced on 18.07.2022; Adjudicating Authority directed Sylvan to file claim before RP on 05.10.2023; RP rejected claim on 19.12.2023; Adjudicating Authority upheld rejection and approved resolution plan on 22.03.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Administrator's report and auditor certificates certifying expenses incurred by Sylvan, and partial admission of claim (Rs. 57.68 lakhs) by the Official Liquidator during winding-up proceedings. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench-II dismissed Sylvan's challenge to claim rejection (IA No. 15 of 2024) and approved the SRA's resolution plan (IA No. 2 of 2024) via orders dated 22.03.2024, leading to the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in upholding the rejection of the appellant's claim by the Resolution Professional and approving the resolution plan without providing for the appellant's historical investment made during the revival scheme.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Expenses genuinely incurred by an investor-promoter in pursuance of a court-mandated revival scheme prior to its setting aside constitute legitimate claims that deserve recognition during liquidation or resolution, to the extent substantiated by records. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Operational and financial claims must be evaluated under the IBC framework, superseding prior winding-up assessments, but verified expenditure admitted by the Official Liquidator must be accommodated in accordance with statutory priorities and voluntary settlement offers. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unsupported interest calculations without contractual agreement cannot be awarded, but verified principal expenditure certified by court administrators warrants equitable reimbursement. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority correctly approved the resolution plan since operational creditors were allocated zero under the liquidation waterfall, but the impugned order is modified to allow reimbursement of the Rs. 57.68 lakhs voluntarily offered by the SRA.
operative_order: Appeals allowed in part; impugned order approving the resolution plan affirmed, while the order dismissing IA No. 15 of 2024 is modified to direct the SRA to pay Rs. 57.68 lakhs to the Appellant within 30 days.
summary: Sylvan Commercial Private Limited appealed against two NCLT Kolkata orders dated 22.03.2024 which upheld the Resolution Professional's rejection of its claim of Rs. 245 crores and approved the resolution plan for Rishra Steel Limited. Sylvan had invested funds to revive the company in 1997 under a court-approved scheme that was later set aside. The NCLAT held that while exorbitant and uncontracted interest claims were rightly rejected and operational creditors received nil under the liquidation waterfall, the principal expenditure of Rs. 57.68 lakhs previously admitted by the Official Liquidator should be reimbursed. Noting the SRA's voluntary offer to pay this specific amount, the NCLAT affirmed the resolution plan's approval while modifying the claim rejection order to direct payment of Rs. 57.68 lakhs to the appellant.

case_title: Siddharth Satish Katariya (Ex-Director) vs. Central Bank of India Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Siddharth Satish Katariya (Appellant / Suspended Director of Superfine Extrusions Private Limited), Central Bank of India Limited (Respondent No. 1 / Financial Creditor), and Jitendra Palande (Respondent No. 2 / IRP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by a consortium of banks (Central Bank of India, Indian Bank, PNB, and Bank of Maharashtra) to Superfine Metal Pvt. Ltd. (Principal Borrower), secured by corporate guarantees executed by Superfine Extrusions Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor / Guarantor) on 22.08.2015 and 18.11.2016 for Rs. 73.61 crores and Rs. 92.47 crores respectively. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default amount claimed of Rs. 94,71,23,119.18/- as of 06.03.2023; Principal Borrower's account classified as NPA on 29.11.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee deeds executed in 2015 and 2016; working capital consortium agreement executed on 06.11.2020; NPA declared on 29.11.2020; SARFAESI notice issued on 29.06.2022; loan recall notice issued on 02.01.2023; guarantee invoked and demand notice issued on 06.03.2023; Section 7 petition admitted by NCLT on 07.01.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Execution of multiple guarantee deeds, sanction letters, and possession of valid Stamp Duty Exemption Certificates by both the Principal Borrower and Corporate Guarantor covering the mortgaged properties. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-III admitted Central Bank of India's Section 7 application against the corporate guarantor on 07.01.2025, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition is maintainable based on corporate guarantee deeds that are allegedly insufficiently stamped, and whether execution of subsequent loan documents constitutes a novation that extinguishes prior guarantees.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Insufficient stamping of a guarantee deed is a curable technical defect, and in the absence of any demand or failure by the obligor who holds a valid stamp duty exemption certificate, such technical objections cannot defeat insolvency proceedings. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Execution of subsequent credit sanction letters and working capital agreements containing clauses expressly preserving existing securities does not amount to a novation of contract extinguishing prior corporate guarantees. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Possession of valid stamp duty exemption certificates covering the exact mortgaged properties precludes the guarantor from raising belated pleas of insufficient stamping. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 application upon proof of a valid debt and established default by the corporate guarantor.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 07.01.2025 admitting Section 7 application and initiating CIRP affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Siddharth Satish Katariya, suspended director of Superfine Extrusions Pvt. Ltd. (corporate guarantor), appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 07.01.2025 admitting Central Bank of India's Section 7 petition. The appellant argued that the guarantee deeds executed in 2015 and 2016 were insufficiently stamped and thus inadmissible in evidence, and that subsequent loan documents in 2020 novated and extinguished the earlier guarantees. The NCLAT held that insufficient stamping is a curable defect and both companies held valid stamp duty exemption certificates covering the mortgaged properties. Furthermore, the subsequent agreements explicitly preserved existing securities, negating any novation. Finding debt, default, and valid invocation established, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Madras Race Club vs. R.D. Ramasamy & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Madras Race Club (Appellant / Section 8 non-profit company), R.D. Ramasamy (Respondent No. 1), and M. Magesh Kumar (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Dispute regarding membership validity and induction of members into the Madras Race Club, resulting in a special audit by M/s. Brahmayya & Co. and an inquiry report by former Judge Hon'ble Justice Mr. K.P. Sivasubramaniam (Retd.) which identified 635 non-compliant members. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Removal of 635 non-compliant members from the Register of Members pursuant to NCLT and NCLAT orders dated 24.09.2019 and 29.05.2020 respectively. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CP/31/2017 initiated; NCLT order passed on 24.09.2019; NCLAT appellate judgment rendered on 29.05.2020; waiver application CP (CA) / 64 (CHE) / 2022 filed under Section 244; NCLT granted waiver on 09.01.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Audit reports and judicial findings confirming that the respondents failed to satisfy mandatory membership procedures and pay entrance fees, leading to their removal as members. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai granted waiver under Section 244(1)(b) to the respondents on 09.01.2024 to pursue an oppression and mismanagement petition, which order was challenged by the club in Company Appeal (AT) (CH) No. 17 of 2024.
legal_issues: Whether individuals who have been judicially determined to be non-compliant members and whose names were ordered to be removed from the Register of Members can maintain an application for a waiver under Section 244(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 to file an oppression and mismanagement petition under Section 241.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An applicant seeking a waiver under Section 244 of the Companies Act, 2013 must satisfy the pre-condition of being an existing member of the company as defined under Section 2(55). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The exception carved out by the proviso to Section 244 for granting waivers applies exclusively to existing members who fall short of statutory shareholding or numerical thresholds, and cannot be invoked by former or removed members. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where judicial reports and binding appellate orders confirm that individuals were unlawfully inducted and failed to pay entrance fees, their status as non-members deprives them of the locus standi to maintain an application under Section 244. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in granting a waiver under Section 244 on hypothetical grounds and self-perceived exceptional circumstances to respondents who had ceased to be members.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT impugned order dated 09.01.2024 granting waiver in CP (CA) / 64 (CHE) / 2022 is quashed and set aside; pending interlocutory applications closed.
summary: Madras Race Club filed an appeal against the NCLT Chennai order dated 09.01.2024 which granted a waiver under Section 244(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 to R.D. Ramasamy and M. Magesh Kumar to pursue an oppression and mismanagement petition. The NCLAT noted that the respondents had been conclusively determined to be non-compliant members who failed to follow Articles of Association procedures or pay entrance fees, resulting in the lawful removal of their names from the Register of Members under prior binding judicial orders. Holding that only an existing member can invoke Section 244 for a waiver, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's waiver order and allowed the club's appeal.

case_title: Successful Resolution Applicant Mr. Harry Dhaul vs. Regional Provident Fund Commissioner II & Anr. (with Regional Provident Fund Commissioner vs. Harry Dhaul)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1691 of 2024 & No. 1752 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Harry Dhaul (Successful Resolution Applicant / Appellant in 1691) and Regional Provident Fund Commissioner II, Delhi Central (EPFO / Appellant in 1752). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against Global Energy Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) on 02.12.2019; resolution plan approved by CoC on 23.03.2023. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO claim submitted on 06.03.2023 for Rs. 1,33,19,135/- based on an Area Enforcement Officer's Report (AEOR), comprising principal dues of Rs. 77,67,128/- and tentative damages/interest under Sections 14B and 7Q amounting to Rs. 55,52,007/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced and moratorium imposed on 02.12.2019; public announcement made on 09.06.2022 (last date 22.06.2022); EPFO claim filed on 06.03.2023; CoC approval on 23.03.2023; NCLT approved resolution plan on 03.07.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: AEOR inspection report and assessment initiated on 06.02.2023 and finalized on 01.03.2023 during the subsistence of the moratorium, alongside affidavits furnished by the SRA undertaking payment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai approved the resolution plan on 03.07.2024 while incorporating directions for the SRA to pay EPFO dues, leading to cross-appeals by both the SRA and the EPFO.
legal_issues: Whether assessment proceedings and demands initiated by the EPFO under Sections 7A, 7Q, and 14B of the EPF Act after the imposition of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC are legally enforceable, and whether an SRA's undertaking on affidavit can validate such claims.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: After the initiation of the CIRP and imposition of moratorium under Section 14(1) of the IBC, assessment proceedings cannot be initiated or continued by the EPFO so as to impose pecuniary liabilities on the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Claims arising from assessment proceedings carried out during the prohibited moratorium period are unenforceable and cannot be pressed or admitted in the CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Demands based on inspection reports and assessments conducted post-moratorium are void ab initio, and an SRA's undertakings given under a misconception of law cannot validate unenforceable statutory claims. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in directing payment of EPFO claims arising from post-moratorium assessment proceedings, requiring the SRA's appeal to be allowed and the EPFO's appeal to be dismissed.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1691 of 2024 filed by the SRA is allowed and the direction in the impugned order dated 03.07.2024 for paying Rs. 1,33,19,135/- to the EPFO is set aside; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1752 of 2024 filed by the EPFO is dismissed.
summary: Cross-appeals were filed by Successful Resolution Applicant Harry Dhaul and the Regional Provident Fund Commissioner against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 03.07.2024 approving the resolution plan for Global Energy Pvt. Ltd. while directing payment of EPFO claims. The NCLAT held that the EPFO's claims—stemming from an inspection and assessment initiated in early 2023—were entirely barred and unenforceable because Section 14(1) of the IBC imposes a statutory freeze preventing the initiation or continuation of assessment proceedings after the commencement of CIRP. The NCLAT ruled that the SRA's affidavit undertakings could not validate an otherwise illegal and statutorily barred claim. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the SRA's appeal and dismissed the EPFO's appeal.

case_title: Rupinder Singh Gill vs. Three C Universal Developers Private Limited (Through Resolution Professional Rakesh Kumar Gupta)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rupinder Singh Gill (Appellant / Director of Challengerz Web Solutions Pvt. Ltd. and Hacienda Infosoftech Pvt. Ltd.), and Three C Universal Developers Private Limited (Corporate Debtor through RP Rakesh Kumar Gupta). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor entered into two Agreements to Sell (ATS) dated 08.10.2018 with the appellant for transferring 100% equity shareholding in subsidiary companies Challengerz Web Solutions Pvt. Ltd. and Hacienda Infosoftech Pvt. Ltd. for Rs. 10 crores and Rs. 30,93,75,000/- respectively, with an 11-month execution timeline expiring on 07.09.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Failure of the appellant to pay the balance consideration within the stipulated 11-month timeframe, leading to termination notices served on 16.01.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: ATS executed on 08.10.2018; CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 17.12.2019; RP filed IA Nos. 2102/2020 and 2276/2020 in 2020; NCLT passed impugned order on 07.08.2020. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Original share certificates and title deeds of subsidiaries temporarily handed over to the appellant, and claims by the appellant that documents were lost in August 2019 at City Centre, Khanna, supported by an unverified police complaint dated 26.10.2019. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II allowed the RP's interlocutory applications via order dated 07.08.2020, directing the appellant to return the original share certificates and title documents of the subsidiaries to the Resolution Professional, which led to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority and Resolution Professional are empowered under Sections 18 and 25 of the IBC to take custody and control of share certificates and title documents of corporate debtor's 100% subsidiaries held under a terminated Agreement to Sell.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Sections 18(1)(f)(v) and 25(2)(a) of the IBC, a Resolution Professional is statutorily mandated to take immediate custody and control of all assets of the corporate debtor, including business records, title documents, and shares held in any subsidiary of the corporate debtor. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 60(5), 63, 231, and 238 of the IBC vest exclusive jurisdiction in the NCLT and NCLAT over all matters relating to corporate insolvency, overriding civil courts and invalidating unperformed agreements affected by efflux of time or moratorium. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an Agreement to Sell stands determined by efflux of time and default in payment of consideration, the purported custodian cannot retain original share certificates and title deeds of corporate debtor's subsidiaries under unverified claims of document loss. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in directing the appellant to hand over the original share certificates and subsidiary documents to the Resolution Professional.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 07.08.2020 passed by the Adjudicating Authority affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Rupinder Singh Gill appealed against the NCLT New Delhi order dated 07.08.2020 which directed him to hand over original share certificates and title documents of the corporate debtor's 100% subsidiaries, Challengerz and Hacienda, to the Resolution Professional. The NCLAT held that under Sections 18(1)(f)(v) and 25(2)(a) of the IBC, the Resolution Professional is duty-bound to secure all assets and securities, including shares held in subsidiaries. Noting that the Agreements to Sell had expired by efflux of time and the appellant failed to prove payment of consideration or substantiate claims of document loss, the NCLAT affirmed the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction and orders, dismissing the appeal.

case_title: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. vs. Ajit Gyanchand Jain (RP) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. (Appellant / Assignee of Bajaj Finance Ltd.), Ajit Gyanchand Jain (Respondent No. 1 / RP of Sare Gurugram Pvt. Ltd.), and Successful Resolution Applicant (Respondent No. 3). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Financial facilities advanced by Bajaj Finance Ltd. to Sun Agrifresh Industries Pvt. Ltd. (Borrower) for purchasing 7 flats developed by Sare Gurugram Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor), secured by equitable mortgage and governed by a tripartite agreement entered into in July 2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Principal claim of Rs. 6,65,08,737/- and total claim of Rs. 9,62,02,610/- submitted by Phoenix ARC. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Assignment taken on 04.04.2018; CIRP initiated against Corporate Debtor on 09.03.2021; public announcement on 24.03.2021; Phoenix ARC filed claim in Form-F as 'other creditors' on 24.03.2021; list of creditors issued on 11.11.2021; CoC approved resolution plan on 26.12.2021; NCLT approved resolution plan on 24.04.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Tripartite agreement showing mortgage on 7 units, claim submission in Form-F (other creditors), and non-inclusion of Phoenix ARC in the list of financial creditors in a class. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Principal Bench, New Delhi approved the resolution plan via order dated 24.04.2023, which was challenged by Phoenix ARC in Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 800 of 2023.
legal_issues: Whether an assignee holding a tripartite agreement and mortgage over specific flats for a loan advanced to a third-party borrower is entitled to be treated as a financial creditor in the corporate debtor's CIRP, and whether the resolution plan's treatment of the claim under 'other creditors' violates Section 30(2).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A creditor who files its claim in Form-F as an 'other creditor' and fails to challenge its categorization during the CIRP cannot belatedly seek reclassification as a financial creditor after the CoC has approved the resolution plan. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31 of the IBC limits the Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal's scrutiny of an approved resolution plan to verifying compliance with the mandatory requirements of Section 30(2). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Approval of a resolution plan by the CoC in its commercial wisdom cannot be interfered with on belated classification disputes when the plan duly provides for the admitted claim category. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in approving the resolution plan, and the appellant's recourse for executing debt recovery lies against the principal borrower through competent courts.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 24.04.2023 approving the resolution plan affirmed, clarifying that plan approval does not preclude the appellant from executing debt recovery decrees against the principal borrower; no order as to costs.
summary: Phoenix ARC Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Principal Bench order dated 24.04.2023 approving the resolution plan for Sare Gurugram Pvt. Ltd. The appellant, an assignee of Bajaj Finance, argued that it should have been treated as a financial creditor rather than an 'other creditor' on the strength of a tripartite agreement and mortgage over 7 flats for a loan given to a third-party borrower. The NCLAT held that since Phoenix ARC filed its claim in Form-F as an 'other creditor' and never challenged its categorization during the CIRP before plan approval, it could not belatedly contest the plan's validity. Noting that the resolution plan complied with Section 30(2) and was approved by the CoC in its commercial wisdom, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal while clarifying that plan approval does not bar the appellant from executing recovery decrees against the principal borrower.

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Rakesh Hariram Agarwal & Anr. (with State Bank of India vs. Sarvesh Hariram Agarwal & Anr.)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 246 of 2025 & No. 282 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: State Bank of India (Appellant / Financial Creditor), Rakesh Hariram Agarwal & Sarvesh Hariram Agarwal (Respondent No. 1 / Personal Guarantors), and Birendra Kumar Agrawal (Respondent No. 2). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Loan of Rs. 10.50 crores (enhanced to Rs. 18.0 crores and Rs. 20.0 crores) advanced by SBI on 23.09.2009 to Asis Global Limited (Principal Borrower), backed by personal guarantees and supplementary personal guarantee agreements dated 30.07.2010 and 28.06.2012. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default in loan repayment leading to NPA classification, SARFAESI notice on 31.12.2013, O.A. No. 1819/2016 before DRT Mumbai, and an approved OTS proposal on 31.10.2017 fixing liability at Rs. 9.10 crores, followed by a DRT consent decree / recovery certificate on 22.03.2018. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA; DRT recovery certificate issued on 22.03.2018; principal borrower filed Section 10 IBC petition (C.P. No. 4442/2018) on 20.11.2018 acknowledging debt; balance sheet for FY 2018-2019 signed on 05.09.2019; Rule 7 demand notice issued on 30.05.2022; Section 95 petitions filed on 30.11.2022 and 28.12.2022; NCLT dismissed petitions on 09.12.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Loan agreements, guarantee deeds, OTS acceptance letter, DRT recovery certificate, principal borrower's Section 10 IBC petition, audited balance sheets, and COVID-19 lockdown exclusion periods. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissed SBI's Section 95 petitions against personal guarantors on 09.12.2024 solely on limitation grounds, leading to the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether a petition filed under Section 95 of the IBC against personal guarantors is barred by limitation when computed from the date of default mentioned in Part III versus subsequent acknowledgments of debt under Section 18 of the Limitation Act and COVID-19 exclusion periods under Supreme Court's Suo Motu orders.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The limitation period for initiating insolvency proceedings under Section 95 of the IBC against personal guarantors does not run strictly from the initial date of default if subsequent acknowledgments of debt (such as a debtor-initiated Section 10 petition or audited balance sheets) extend the limitation under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238A of the IBC makes the Limitation Act applicable to tribunal proceedings, and tribunals are statutorily bound to compute limitation based on all facts on record, irrespective of the default date stated in pleadings. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The COVID-19 exclusion period mandated by the Supreme Court's Suo Motu orders (15.03.2020 to 28.02.2022) must be fully excluded when calculating the unexpired limitation period for initiating insolvency actions. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed a patent error in restricting limitation computation to the OTS acceptance date and ignoring subsequent debt acknowledgments and COVID-19 exclusions, thereby rendering the Section 95 petitions well within time.
operative_order: Appeals allowed; impugned orders dated 09.12.2024 passed by the Adjudicating Authority in C.P. (I.B) No. 15 of 2023 and C.P. (I.B) No. 62 of 2023 are set aside; the Adjudicating Authority is directed to admit both petitions and proceed in accordance with law.
summary: State Bank of India appealed against two NCLT Mumbai orders dated 09.12.2024 which dismissed its petitions under Section 95 of the IBC against personal guarantors, Rakesh Hariram Agarwal and Sarvesh Hariram Agarwal, on grounds of limitation. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred by restricting the limitation start date to the OTS acceptance in 2017 while ignoring subsequent written acknowledgments of debt, such as the principal borrower's Section 10 IBC petition filed on 20.11.2018 and its audited balance sheet signed on 05.09.2019. Furthermore, incorporating the COVID-19 limitation exclusion period mandated by the Supreme Court's Suo Motu orders, the NCLAT concluded that SBI's petitions filed in late 2022 were well within time. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT orders and directed the admission of both Section 95 petitions.

case_title: Committee of Creditors of Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. vs. Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Committee of Creditors (CoC) through ICICI Bank, Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. & Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant Consortium), Resolution Professional Rohit Mehra, Sankalp Recreation Pvt. Ltd. (Unsuccessful RA), and suspended directors (Rajesh Patel & Ors.)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) initiated against Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) under Section 7 of IBC; resolution plan submitted by Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. in consortium with Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd. approved by 100% CoC voting share[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Fair Value of CD determined at INR 429.09 crores and Liquidation Value at INR 277.09 crores[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP admitted on 20.04.2022; RFRP issued on 17.08.2022; Challenge process held on 09.02.2023; Resolution Plan approved by CoC on 10.03.2023; NCLT rejected approval and partly allowed objections on 10.07.2024[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consortium agreement dated 17.02.2023 introducing Check-Inn Hotels as a strategic investor to handle equity requirements mandated by RBI guidelines for ARCs, alongside 100% CoC approval and evaluation matrix scores[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-II dismissed RP's application for plan approval (IA No. 1085 of 2023) and partly allowed objections by Sankalp Recreation and ex-promoters on 10.07.2024, leading to the present appeals by CoC, SRA, and RP[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority erred in rejecting the resolution plan approved unanimously by the CoC on grounds of alleged non-compliance with Regulation 39(1B) regarding consortium induction and material irregularities[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors in approving a resolution plan is paramount and non-justiciable, and the Adjudicating Authority's review is strictly confined to checking compliance under Section 30(2) of the Code[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 15(1)(xi) of the RFRP empowering the CoC to permit changes or additions in consortium structure operates harmoniously to facilitate implementation, and a wholly-owned subsidiary of an eligible PRA cannot be treated as an unvetted third-party entrant[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unanimous approval by 100% voting share, highest evaluation matrix scores, and compliance with statutory minimums for operational and financial creditors establish plan viability and commercial soundness[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction under Section 31 by substituting its own assessment for the commercial wisdom of the CoC and entertaining objections from an unsuccessful resolution applicant who had accepted refund of its bid bond[cite: 13].
operative_order: Appeals allowed; impugned order dated 10.07.2024 set aside; CP (IB) 1171/MB/2021 restored to its original position with directions for parties to appear before the Adjudicating Authority for plan approval on 15.10.2025[cite: 13].
summary: Appeals were filed by the Committee of Creditors, the Successful Resolution Applicant (Rare Asset Reconstruction Ltd. and Check-Inn Hotels Pvt. Ltd.), and the Resolution Professional challenging the NCLT Mumbai order dated 10.07.2024 which rejected the approved resolution plan for Rajesh Business and Leisure Hotels Pvt. Ltd[cite: 13]. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that the induction of Check-Inn Hotels as a strategic investor violated Regulation 39(1B), noting that the RFRP explicitly permitted consortium modifications, eligibility checks were duly conducted, and the plan received 100% CoC approval[cite: 13]. Furthermore, unsuccessful applicant Sankalp lacked grounds for challenge after accepting its bid bond refund[cite: 13]. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the impugned order and restored the matter for formal plan approval[cite: 13].

case_title: Rajender Kumar Pahwa (Suspended Director of Goodluck Carbon Pvt. Ltd.) vs. Canara Bank & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Rajender Kumar Pahwa (Appellant / Suspended Director of Goodluck Carbon Pvt. Ltd.), Canara Bank (Respondent No. 1 / Financial Creditor), Ashok Kumar Gulla (Respondent No. 2 / IRP), and Punjab National Bank (Respondent No. 3 / Lead Bank). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Project loan of Rs. 57.74 crores sanctioned under a consortium agreement dated 10.03.2014 by a consortium of banks led by Punjab National Bank. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Financial debt default claimed of Rs. 90,43,74,091.45/- as on 31.08.2023, with date of default / NPA classified as 30.09.2015. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Account declared NPA on 30.09.2015; SARFAESI notice issued on 20.06.2017; working capital consortium agreement executed on 01.03.2017; multiple One-Time Settlement (OTS) proposals submitted by CD up to 2023; Section 7 petition filed on 02.09.2023; NCLT admitted CIRP on 18.10.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Execution of loan documents, consortium agreements, acknowledgment of debt through continuous submission of written OTS proposals, and deposit of 5% of OTS amount into an escrow account. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi (Court-IV) admitted Canara Bank's Section 7 petition and initiated CIRP via order dated 18.10.2024, which was challenged in the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a single financial creditor belonging to a consortium can maintain a petition under Section 7 of the IBC without the concurrence of other members, and whether pending consideration of an OTS proposal bars the initiation of CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The independent statutory right of a financial creditor to trigger CIRP under Section 7 of the IBC cannot be curtailed, restricted, or made subservient to any inter-se consortium agreement or pending One-Time Settlement (OTS) negotiations. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC grants an overriding effect to the Code over any other instrument, and a debtor cannot claim a vested right to halt insolvency proceedings indefinitely under the guise of an unapproved OTS proposal. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Continuous submission of written settlement proposals by the corporate debtor acts as a written acknowledgment of debt extending the limitation period under Section 18 of the Limitation Act. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 petition upon proof of a valid financial debt and established default.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; impugned order dated 18.10.2024 admitting the Section 7 application and initiating CIRP affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Rajender Kumar Pahwa, suspended director of Goodluck Carbon Pvt. Ltd., appealed against the NCLT order dated 18.10.2024 admitting Canara Bank's petition under Section 7 of the IBC. The appellant contended that Canara Bank could not initiate insolvency proceedings independently without the lead bank's consent while an OTS proposal was under active consideration by the consortium. The NCLAT held that an individual financial creditor possesses an independent statutory right under Section 7 to enforce its debt, which cannot be subordinated to inter-se consortium agreements or pending settlement talks. Finding that debt, default, and limitation were duly established, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal.

case_title: Archernar Brand Technologies Private Limited & Ors. vs. Registrar of Companies
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Archernar Brand Technologies Pvt. Ltd. and 7 other transferor/transferee companies (Mensa Brand Technologies group) as Appellants, opposing the Registrar of Companies. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Composite Scheme of Arrangement involving the merger of 7 subsidiary transferor companies into the transferee company (Mensa Brand Technologies Pvt. Ltd.), all being subsidiaries of the parent Singapore entity (Mensa Brand Technologies Pte. Ltd.). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Projected post-merger net worth of the Transferee Company increasing from INR 551.29 crores to INR 913.37 crores, with remaining unsecured debt standing at a negligible amount (approx. INR 13.52 lacs across two companies). 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Board approvals obtained on 28.03.2025 and 01.04.2025; first motion application filed on 16.04.2025; NCLT Chandigarh passed impugned order on 10.06.2025; appeal filed on 22.07.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Consent affidavits obtained from unsecured creditors representing over 90% in value across the appellant companies, statutory auditor certificates, and positive net-worth statements. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh dispensed with meetings of shareholders and secured creditors but refused dispensation for unsecured creditors, directing a physical/virtual meeting of non-consenting unsecured creditors, which prompted the present appeal under Section 421 of the Act.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT erred in refusing to dispense with meetings of unsecured creditors under Section 230(9) of the Companies Act, 2013 despite the applicant companies obtaining valid consent affidavits from unsecured creditors representing over 90% in value.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a proposed scheme of arrangement or merger does not involve any compromise or arrangement with creditors that adversely affects their rights and liabilities, and the transferee company possesses a robust positive net worth exceeding liabilities, the requirement of convening creditor meetings ought to be dispensed with under Section 230(9). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 230(9) of the Companies Act empowers the Tribunal to dispense with meetings of creditors when creditors holding at least 90% in value agree and confirm by affidavit, without introducing artificial distinctions among creditors. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Submission of valid consent affidavits exceeding the 90% statutory threshold, coupled with a significantly enhanced post-merger net worth, establishes that creditors' financial interests are fully safeguarded. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority acted contrary to the statutory scheme by declining dispensation and ordering meetings for remaining unsecured creditors representing less than 10% in value.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; directions contained in Paragraphs 24(f) to 24(s) of the impugned order dated 10.06.2025 requiring unsecured creditor meetings are set aside; the requirement of holding meetings of unsecured creditors is dispensed with.
summary: Archernar Brand Technologies Pvt. Ltd. and other group subsidiaries appealed against the NCLT Chandigarh order dated 10.06.2025 which refused to dispense with meetings of unsecured creditors in a first motion amalgamation application, despite the appellants producing consent affidavits from unsecured creditors representing over 90% in value. The NCLAT held that since the scheme was a corporate restructuring of parent-subsidiary entities that did not compromise creditor rights and where post-merger net worth substantially exceeded liabilities (reaching over INR 913 crores), the NCLAT was bound to dispense with creditor meetings under Section 230(9). Accordingly, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT's directions ordering creditor meetings.

case_title: Satish Kumar Agarwal & Anr. vs. Competition Commission of India
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants include M/s Satish Kumar Agarwal (Sole Proprietor) and M/s Siddhi Vinayak & Sons (Sole Proprietor), opposing the Competition Commission of India (Respondent)[cite: 31]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Soil testing tenders issued by the Department of Agriculture, Government of Uttar Pradesh in 2017 and 2018 (specifically Moradabad and Bareilly divisions)[cite: 31]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Monetary penalties imposed of Rs. 15,59,451/- on M/s Satish Kumar Agarwal and Rs. 12,62,007/- on M/s Siddhi Vinayak and Sons, calculated at 5% of average turnover[cite: 31]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Complaint filed on 07.08.2018; CCI order under Section 26(1) on 30.01.2020; DG report on 08.04.2021; CCI final order on 04.04.2022; NCLAT judgment on 16.09.2025[cite: 31]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Submission of fake experience certificates and fabricated work orders issued by Yash Solutions, identical serial numbers on machine purchase invoices, and use of common e-bidding IP addresses and login IDs[cite: 31]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI found appellants guilty of cartelization and bid-rigging under Section 3 of the Act on 04.04.2022; appellants challenged the order in Competition Appeal (AT) No. 39 of 2022[cite: 31].
legal_issues: Whether the appellants engaged in bid-rigging and collusive bidding in public tenders for soil testing in contravention of Sections 3(3)(c) and 3(3)(d) read with Section 3(1) of the Act, and whether the monetary penalty was proportionate[cite: 31].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Participation in public tenders by submitting cover bids and using fabricated experience documents to support a primary cartel winner constitutes illegal bid-rigging under Section 3 of the Competition Act[cite: 31]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While total turnover is appropriately used to compute penalties in first-time default cases where relevant turnover from illegal tenders is nil, the quantum of penalty must reflect the supportive or secondary role of a cover bidder rather than a primary ringleader[cite: 31]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Admission of lack of technical infrastructure combined with identical invoice serial numbers and shared e-bidding IP addresses conclusively proves concerted collusive practices[cite: 31]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Commission rightly held the appellants liable for bid-rigging, but the penalty percentage should be reduced from 5% to 3% to align with coordinate bench rulings for supporting cover bidders[cite: 31].
operative_order: Competition Appeal (AT) No. 39 of 2022 allowed in part; CCI order holding appellants guilty under Section 3 and issuing cease-and-desist directions is upheld, while the monetary penalty under Section 27(b) is reduced from 5% to 3% of the average annual turnover[cite: 31].
summary: M/s Satish Kumar Agarwal and M/s Siddhi Vinayak & Sons appealed against the CCI order dated 04.04.2022 which found them guilty of cartelization and bid-rigging in Uttar Pradesh agricultural soil testing tenders[cite: 31]. The NCLAT observed that the appellants—who were primarily traders in food articles with no soil testing experience—admitted to submitting cover bids and using fake experience certificates supplied by Yash Solutions to create a false appearance of competition[cite: 31]. Following the precedent set in the Toyfort case for secondary participants, the NCLAT upheld the guilt and cease-and-desist orders of the CCI but reduced the penalty from 5% to 3% of average annual turnover[cite: 31].

case_title: Sahara Export vs. About U Fashions Private Limited
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Sahara Export (Appellant) and About U Fashions Pvt. Ltd. (Respondent). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appeal filed against the impugned order dated 11.08.2023 under the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Refiling delay of 91 days. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Appeal e-filed on 25.09.2023; defects notified on 04.10.2023; refiled on 10.01.2024; delay condonation application decided on 20.08.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Online filing records, registry defect notifications, and refiling logs showing a 91-day gap without detailed factual explanations in the affidavit. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Appellant sought condonation of a 91-day refiling delay in CA (AT) (Ins.) No. 304 of 2024, which NCLAT Principal Bench dismissed on 20.08.2025 due to a total lack of factual explanation for the delay.
legal_issues: Whether a delay of 91 days in refiling an appeal can be condoned under Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules, 2016 in the absence of any factual explanation or cause shown in the condonation application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While the timeline for curing defects and refiling under Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules is directory and not governed by the strict confines of Section 5 of the Limitation Act, an applicant seeking condonation remains under an obligation to state minimum facts that can prima facie explain the delay. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Time is the essence of the IBC, and procedural discipline must be maintained to prevent indefinite delays that erode asset value. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Blanket assertions attributing delay to generic 'logistical constraints' without narrating concrete facts or circumstances fail to discharge the applicant's burden of showing sufficient cause. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The application for condonation of delay in refiling must be rejected when the applicant provides zero factual justification or explanation for the massive delay.
operative_order: Delay condonation application (I.A. No. 825 of 2024) dismissed; memo of appeal rejected.
summary: Sahara Export filed an appeal against About U Fashions Pvt. Ltd. along with an application to condone a 91-day delay in refiling the appeal after curing defects notified by the registry. The NCLAT Principal Bench held that although the 7-day window for curing defects under Rule 26 of the NCLAT Rules is directory, an appellant must still plead concrete facts explaining the cause of delay. Because the appellant's application merely cited vague 'logistical constraints' without providing any factual basis, the NCLAT dismissed the delay condonation application and rejected the appeal.

case_title: M/s. Prakash Oil Depot vs. G. Madhusudan Rao (Liquidator of Sarda Agro Oils Limited) & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 304 of 2025 & No. 306 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Prakash Oil Depot (Scheme Proponent), G. Madhusudan Rao (Liquidator of Sarda Agro Oils Limited), and Indian Bank (Financial Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Debtor Sarda Agro Oils Limited was placed under liquidation on 09.01.2023; scheme proponent Prakash Oil Depot submitted a scheme of compromise/arrangement under Section 230 of Companies Act read with Regulation 2B of Liquidation Regulations, along with a cheque of Rs. 4.30 crores towards EMD on 31.05.2024. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Liquidation of Corporate Debtor following failed insolvency resolution. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation ordered on 09.01.2023; scheme proposed on 25.01.2024 / EMD submitted on 31.05.2024; NCLT rejected extension application on 26.05.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Approval of the scheme by 100% of secured creditors within the Stakeholders Consultation Committee (SCC), and consent obtained from Indian Bank and Bank of Baroda. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed IA No. 833 of 2025 on 26.05.2025 refusing extension of time under Regulation 2B, leading to appeals by the scheme proponent and liquidator.
legal_issues: Whether the 90-day timeline prescribed under Regulation 2B of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016 for completing a scheme of compromise or arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 is mandatory or directory, and whether time can be extended by the Adjudicating Authority.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The 90-day time period prescribed under Regulation 2B of the Liquidation Process Regulations for completing a scheme of arrangement under Section 230 of the Companies Act is directory and not mandatory. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Provisions facilitating revival and preventing corporate death through compromise or arrangement must be interpreted flexibly to fulfill the primary objective of the IBC. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where a scheme is backed by the commercial wisdom and 100% approval of secured creditors in the SCC and offers value maximization, procedural delays should not defeat revival. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority has the discretion to extend time beyond the initial 90 days if there is a realistic chance of approval and revival of the corporate debtor.
operative_order: Company Appeals allowed; NCLT order dated 26.05.2025 set aside; further period of 90 days granted from uploading of order for completion of the scheme of arrangement.
summary: Appeals were filed against the NCLT Hyderabad order dated 26.05.2025 rejecting the liquidator's application for extension of time to complete a scheme of compromise and arrangement proposed under Section 230 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Regulation 2B of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016. The NCLAT held that the 90-day timeline under Regulation 2B is directory, not mandatory, and the Adjudicating Authority erred in refusing an extension when the scheme had received 100% approval from secured creditors in the SCC and promised value maximization and revival of the corporate debtor. Accordingly, the NCLAT set aside the impugned order and granted an additional 90 days to complete the scheme.

case_title: Radha Buildtech (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 876 of 2025 & No. 935 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Radha Buildtech (SRA of developer company Premia Projects Ltd.), Harish Kumar (Homebuyer/Appellant), Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd. (Land-owning Corporate Debtor), and homebuyer respondents. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: GNIDA allotted land to Solitaire Infomedia on 11.03.2009; Solitaire entered into a collaboration agreement with Premia Projects Ltd. on 01.10.2012 for developing a housing project ('Premia Corporate City') while collecting funds from homebuyers. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by developer Premia Projects Ltd. and land-owning company Solitaire Infomedia in delivering possession of residential units to 566 allottees. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP of Premia commenced on 30.05.2018; NCLAT remand order passed on 18.11.2021; Section 7 petition against Solitaire filed on 20.07.2023; NCLT admitted CIRP of Solitaire on 03.06.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Transaction audit reports showing siphoning of funds by common promoter Tarun Sheinh through interlocking corporate structures and back-to-back agreements. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT admitted Section 7 application against Solitaire Infomedia on 03.06.2025, which was challenged by SRA Radha Buildtech and homebuyers in Company Appeals No. 876 and 935 of 2025.
legal_issues: Whether initiation of CIRP against the land-owning subsidiary company (Solitaire Infomedia) is permissible and legally sustainable when the holding company (Premia Projects Ltd.) is already undergoing CIRP and has an approved resolution plan proposing merger.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where a developer company and a land-owning subsidiary company are intertwined, commonly controlled, and share interwoven assets essential for a real estate project, piercing the corporate veil and initiating separate CIRP against the land-owning entity followed by consolidation is legally permissible and necessary. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 60 of IBC permits simultaneous proceedings against interconnected corporate entities, and land owned by a subsidiary cannot be subsumed into the holding company's resolution plan without the subsidiary undergoing its own CIRP. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The 14-point test for group insolvency and corporate consolidation established in Videocon Industries applies when companies share common control, directors, and inter-laced assets. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in admitting the Section 7 petition against Solitaire Infomedia to enable subsequent consolidation and fair resolution for homebuyers.
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 876 of 2025 and No. 935 of 2025 are dismissed; the impugned order dated 03.06.2025 commencing CIRP of Solitaire Infomedia is affirmed.
summary: Radha Buildtech (Successful Resolution Applicant of Premia Projects Ltd.) and certain homebuyers appealed against the NCLT order dated 03.06.2025 which commenced CIRP of the land-owning subsidiary company, Solitaire Infomedia Pvt. Ltd., under Section 7 of the IBC. The appellants contended that initiation of parallel CIRP would derail Premia's resolution plan, which already provided for merger. The NCLAT dismissed the appeals, holding that in accordance with its earlier remand order dated 18.11.2021 and established principles of group insolvency and corporate veil piercing, the land-owning company must be subjected to CIRP before its assets can be consolidated with the developer company. Since Solitaire committed default and met statutory thresholds, its CIRP admission was valid and necessary to protect homebuyers.

case_title: CA Santanu Brahma vs. Indian Bank & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is CA Santanu Brahma (Liquidator of Maheswary Ispat Limited), Respondent No. 1 is Indian Bank, and Respondent No. 2 is State Bank of India (Secured Creditors). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Winding up proceedings initiated before the High Court at Calcutta under Companies Act 1956 were transferred to NCLT, where liquidation commenced under IBC and the Panagarh Factory of the Corporate Debtor was sold by the secured creditors under Section 52. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Estimated liquidation cost of Rs. 1,34,55,000/- claimed from secured creditors, with additional contribution of Rs. 1,87,76,133/- sought post-sale. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Liquidation commenced on 19.12.2023; claims submitted in January-February 2024; Panagarh Factory sold on 21.10.2024; NCLT impugned order passed on 05.02.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Email communications and handover documents dated 30.04.2024 wherein respondent banks provided undertakings to pay liquidator fees under Regulation 4(2)(b). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Original winding up C.P. 560 of 2011 filed in High Court at Calcutta, transferred to NCLT, liquidation commenced on 19.12.2023, and NCLT disposed of IA No. 1 of 2025 on 05.02.2025 denying liquidator fees.
legal_issues: Whether the liquidator can be denied entitlement to fees under Regulation 4(2)(b) read with Regulation 21A(2) of the Liquidation Process Regulations, 2016 when secured creditors directly realise security interest under Section 52 / SARFAESI Act.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Secured creditors choosing to realise security interest outside liquidation under Section 52 of IBC are statutorily mandated under Regulation 21A(2) to bear their proportionate share of liquidation costs, which include the liquidator's fees under Regulation 2(ea) and Regulation 4. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 21A(2) and Regulation 4(2)(b) must be read conjointly; the liquidator's fee is an essential component of liquidation costs irrespective of direct asset realization or distribution by the liquidator. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Written undertakings given by nationalized banks in handover documents create a binding contractual and statutory estoppel preventing them from resiling from fee payment obligations. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator is entitled to fees under Regulation 4(2)(b) and secured creditors must contribute their share of liquidation costs.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; NCLT order dated 05.02.2025 set aside; Liquidator held entitled to fees under Regulation 4(2)(b); Respondent banks directed to jointly contribute balance Rs. 1,87,76,133/- plus 5% clerkage within six weeks.
summary: CA Santanu Brahma, liquidator of Maheswary Ispat Limited, filed an appeal against the NCLT Kolkata order denying him liquidator fees after respondent secured creditors (Indian Bank and State Bank of India) realized the Panagarh Factory asset under Section 52 of the IBC without relinquishing security interest. The NCLAT held that under Regulation 21A(2) read with Regulation 4(2)(b) and Regulation 2(ea) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, secured creditors are strictly obligated to pay liquidation costs including liquidator fees, regardless of direct realization. Furthermore, the respondent banks had provided explicit written undertakings in handover documents to pay such fees. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the NCLT order and directed the respondent banks to pay the balance liquidation costs within six weeks.

case_title: Shanti International (Through Mr. Amol) vs. Ram Singh Setia (Liquidator of Gajanan Solvex Ltd.)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Shanti International through Amol Mittal (Appellant / Successful Bidder) and Ram Singh Setia (Respondent / Liquidator of Gajanan Solvex Ltd.). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Sale of corporate debtor Gajanan Solvex Ltd. as a going concern on an 'as is where is', 'as is what is', 'whatever there is', and 'no recourse basis' pursuant to an e-auction under liquidation. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Winning bid sale consideration paid in full by the appellant amounting to Rs. 8,91,00,000/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 20.07.2022; liquidation ordered on 01.03.2023; 12th e-auction held on 26.07.2024; Sale Certificate issued on 24.09.2024; NCLT passed order on 09.05.2025 on IA No. 1368 of 2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Sale Certificate dated 24.09.2024 and 40 extensive tax and administrative concessions prayed for in IA No. 1368 of 2025. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-V disposed of IA No. 1368 of 2025 on 09.05.2025, granting 22 essential reliefs and concessions while declining or conditioning others, leading to the present appeal challenging the partial refusal.
legal_issues: Whether a successful auction purchaser acquiring a corporate debtor as a going concern under liquidation is entitled as a matter of right to all broad, omnibus tax exemptions, waivers of past litigations, and carry-forward of unabsorbed depreciation without approaching the concerned statutory authorities.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A bidder who purchases a corporate debtor as a going concern in liquidation on an 'as is where is' basis is entitled to operational reliefs necessary to run the business, but cannot claim automatic, blanket waivers from all past tax liabilities, penalties, and custom litigations without applying to the competent statutory authorities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The liquidator's auction sale in liquidation does not automatically attract provisions designed for resolution plans under the corporate insolvency resolution process unless expressly sanctioned by the code or the terms of the e-auction process document. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where the Adjudicating Authority grants core operational reliefs enabling continuance of business but relegates omnibus tax and regulatory waivers to the respective competent authorities, no legal infirmity arises. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed no error in declining excessive and unmerited tax concessions while securing the smooth operational takeover of the corporate debtor.
operative_order: Appeal dismissed; the impugned order dated 09.05.2025 is affirmed; no order as to costs.
summary: Shanti International, the successful auction purchaser of Gajanan Solvex Ltd. in liquidation, appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 09.05.2025 to the extent it refused or conditioned certain tax and regulatory reliefs sought in IA No. 1368 of 2025. The NCLAT held that purchasing a company as a going concern in liquidation on an 'as is where is' basis does not entitle the buyer to blanket, omnibus exemptions from tax liabilities, past litigations, and statutory compliances. Noting that the Adjudicating Authority had already granted 22 essential reliefs necessary for running the business and rightly relegated complex tax matters to the concerned authorities, the NCLAT dismissed the appeal[cite: 40].

case_title: ICICI Bank Limited vs. Seeta Neeraj Shah & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: ICICI Bank Limited (Appellant / Financial Creditor), Seeta Neeraj Shah (Respondent No. 1 / Ex-Director of Ushdev Engitech Limited), and Trupalkumar Patel (Respondent No. 2 / RP of Ushdev Engitech Limited). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facility extended by ICICI Bank to Ushdev International Ltd. (UIL) on 24.12.2014, backed by a Corporate Guarantee executed by Ushdev Engitech Ltd. (UEL) on 10.08.2016. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default by principal borrower UIL; guarantee invoked by ICICI Bank on 16.10.2017; total revised claim admitted by RP for Rs. 67.98 crores, comprising Rs. 25 crores principal guarantee amount and Rs. 42.98 crores default interest. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Guarantee executed on 10.08.2016; invoked on 16.10.2017; CIRP admitted against UEL on 26.04.2023; claim filed on 10.05.2023 and revised on 24.06.2024; RP admitted Rs. 67.98 crores on 02.07.2024; NCLT passed impugned order capping liability at Rs. 25 crores on 29.04.2025. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Guarantee Deed dated 10.08.2016 containing Clause 3 (default interest obligation) and Clause 33 (liability capping non-obstante clause). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Following Delhi High Court directions, ex-director Seeta Neeraj Shah filed I.A. No. 4194 of 2024 before NCLT Mumbai Bench-V, which capped UEL's liability at Rs. 25 crores via order dated 29.04.2025, leading to the present appeal by ICICI Bank.
legal_issues: Whether a non-obstante liability-capping clause in a corporate guarantee deed overrides a separate contractual obligation requiring the guarantor to pay default interest in the event of failure to discharge guarantee obligations within the cure period.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A guarantee agreement must be read holistically and harmoniously to give full legal effect to all distinct obligations, and a liability-capping clause does not automatically extinguish separate default interest liabilities arising from the guarantor's own failure to pay upon invocation. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Clause 3 (default interest on guarantor's delay) and Clause 33 (overall liability cap of Rs. 25 crores) operate in independent spheres without direct conflict, rendering the application of an overriding non-obstante effect unjustified. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear contractual provisions providing for default interest upon delayed payment by a guarantor remain enforceable alongside principal guarantee limits unless an explicit conflict exists. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority committed an error in holding that default interest over and above the Rs. 25 crores principal cap violated the guarantee contract.
operative_order: Appeal allowed; the impugned order dated 29.04.2025 passed by the Adjudicating Authority capping the guarantor's liability at Rs. 25 crores is set aside; no order as to costs.
summary: ICICI Bank appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order dated 29.04.2025 which capped Ushdev Engitech Limited's corporate guarantee liability at Rs. 25 crores. The bank argued that while the principal guarantee obligation was capped at Rs. 25 crores under Clause 33, Clause 3 independently obligated the guarantor to pay default interest in case of delayed payment upon invocation. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority erred in applying the non-obstante capping clause to override the default interest provision, as both clauses operate harmoniously in distinct spheres. Consequently, the NCLAT set aside the impugned order and upheld the RP's admission of the revised claim inclusive of default interest[cite: 42].

case_title: Employees Provident Fund Organisation vs. CA Pankaj Shah (with related appeals by EPFO)
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 17 of 2025 with No. 102 of 2025 & No. 103 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: CA Pankaj Shah (Resolution Professional / Appellant in 17), and Employees Provident Fund Organisation (EPFO / Appellant in 102 and 103). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) commenced against Premshree Prime Properties Private Limited (Corporate Debtor) on 17.02.2023. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: EPFO assessment order dated 25.09.2023 determining Provident Fund dues of Rs. 50,90,793/-, damages of Rs. 50,66,686/-, and interest of Rs. 35,60,358/-, totaling a revised claim of Rs. 1,37,17,837/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 17.02.2023; EPFO inspection notice issued on 11.05.2023; Section 7A assessment order passed on 25.09.2023; revised claim filed on 26.09.2023; NCLT passed common disposal order on 13.11.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Inspection report dated 10.05.2023 and Section 7A assessment order dated 25.09.2023 issued post-commencement of CIRP. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Indore Bench disposed of RP's IA No. 5 of 2024 and EPFO's IA No. 409 of 2024 via order dated 13.11.2024, holding that assessment proceedings are permissible during moratorium but directing EPFO to furnish employee-wise computation details, leading to cross-appeals by both parties.
legal_issues: Whether the EPFO can initiate or continue assessment proceedings under Sections 7A, 7Q, and 14B of the EPF & MP Act after the imposition of moratorium under Section 14 of the IBC, and whether claims based on such post-moratorium assessments are enforceable in CIRP.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Following the initiation of CIRP and imposition of moratorium under Section 14(1) of the IBC, no assessment proceedings can be initiated or continued by the EPFO against the corporate debtor to fasten pecuniary liabilities. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 14(1) creates a broad statutory freeze covering all proceedings that impact the corporate debtor's assets, distinguishing CIRP moratorium from post-liquidation provisions under Section 33(5). 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Assessment orders and inspection demands finalized after the commencement of CIRP are void ab initio and cannot form the basis of an admissible claim in insolvency. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in holding that assessment proceedings could continue during moratorium; hence, the RP's appeal must be allowed and the EPFO's claims based on post-moratorium assessments declared unenforceable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 17 of 2025 filed by the RP is allowed; the Adjudicating Authority's order in IA No. 5 of 2024 and IA No. 409 of 2024 is set aside; EPFO's claims based on post-moratorium assessments are declared unenforceable; Company Appeal Nos. 102 and 103 of 2025 are disposed of.
summary: Cross-appeals were filed by Resolution Professional CA Pankaj Shah and the EPFO against the NCLT Indore order dated 13.11.2024 concerning PF dues of Premshree Prime Properties Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT held that the Adjudicating Authority committed an error in ruling that assessment proceedings under the EPF Act could continue during the moratorium period. Reiterating settled jurisprudence, the NCLAT ruled that Section 14(1) of the IBC imposes a strict statutory freeze prohibiting the initiation or continuation of assessment proceedings post-CIRP commencement, rendering any assessment orders and claims derived therefrom during moratorium entirely void and unenforceable. Consequently, the NCLAT allowed the RP's appeal and set aside the directions favoring EPFO[cite: 39].

case_title: Yashveer Singh vs. Rabindra Kumar Mintri & Anr.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 170 of 2025 & Connected Appeals
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are homebuyers/allottees as Financial Creditors in a Class, Respondent No. 1 is the Resolution Professional, and Respondent No. 2 is the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) for Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allottees booked residential units in the housing project 'Ridge Residency' and paid substantial considerations under allotment letters issued in 2011 and thereafter. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor underwent CIRP initiated on 20.08.2019; claims were filed by Appellants belatedly beyond 90 days after CoC approval of the resolution plan on 04.03.2020. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Public announcement was made on 24.08.2019 with a last date of 03.09.2019; claims were rejected by RP upon submission in 2023/2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Payments made by Appellants were duly reflected in the books of accounts and records of the Corporate Debtor, and documented in an affidavit filed by the Resolution Professional. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT dismissed applications for condonation of delay and admission of claims on 22.01.2025, prompting the present appeals.
legal_issues: Whether belated claims of homebuyers whose payments are duly reflected in the records and books of the Corporate Debtor can be rejected and excluded from consideration inեց the resolution plan after the remittal of the plan by the Adjudicating Authority?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Bona fide homebuyers whose payments and allotments are duly reflected in the records of the Corporate Debtor cannot be relegated to mere refund claimants or excluded from resolution plans merely due to delayed filing of claims when the plan is still pending approval. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 30 and CIRP regulations must be interpreted to ensure equitable and fair resolution, aligning with the principle that extinguishment of claims occurs only upon final plan approval. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of payments through the Corporate Debtor's books of accounts and records constitutes sufficient recognition of liability requiring appropriate consideration by the resolution applicant. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority's order rejecting the belated claims of homebuyers whose payments are reflected in the RP's records is set aside, and the SRA is directed to incorporate their claims via an addendum.
operative_order: The impugned order dated 22.01.2025 is set aside; the appeals are allowed directing the SRA to prepare a second addendum to include the Appellants' claims as reflected in the RP's affidavit and treat them as Financial Creditors in a Class without applying the 50% refund cap.
summary: Multiple appeals were filed by homebuyers against the NCLT order dismissing their applications for admission of belated claims in the CIRP of Today Homes Noida Pvt. Ltd. The NCLAT held that since the payments made by the Appellants were duly reflected in the books of accounts and records of the Corporate Debtor, their claims could not be ignored or relegated to the 50% refund clause. Citing precedents like Puneet Kaur and Amit Nehra, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the NCLT order and directed the Successful Resolution Applicant to prepare an addendum to include the Appellants as Financial Creditors in a Class for fair treatment.

case_title: Sarang Kumar Wadhawan vs. Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is the shareholder of the Corporate Debtor (Privilege Power and Infrastructure Private Limited - PPIL), Respondent No. 1 is Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. (erstwhile PMC Bank), and Respondent No. 2 is the Interim Resolution Professional. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: PMC Bank advanced financial assistance by way of an overdraft facility (Account No. 002140700001790) sanctioned initially in 2007 with a limit of Rs. 40 crores, later enhanced and secured by mortgage deeds and promissory notes up to Rs. 81.50 crores in 2017-2018. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was declared an NPA w.e.f. 31.08.2012 due to unpaid interest, and the total debt claimed under Section 7 was Rs. 138,48,08,867/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 petition was filed in 2020 following the discovery of fraud and re-auditing of PMC Bank accounts concluded on 27.12.2019. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Balance confirmation letters signed by the Appellant up to 2019, part payments made by vendors, mortgage deeds, and demand promissory notes executed in 2017-2018. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: The NCLT Mumbai Bench admitted the Section 7 petition vide order dated 15.02.2023, which was challenged by the shareholder in this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether a Section 7 petition filed in 2020 for a debt defaulted in 2012 is barred by limitation, and whether subsequent execution of security documents and balance confirmations constitute a valid promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act or extend limitation under Sections 17, 18, and 19 of the Limitation Act?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Execution of balance confirmations, mortgage deeds, and promissory notes for a time-barred debt constitutes an express promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, creating a fresh cause of action and limitation period. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 17 of the Limitation Act extends limitation periods when default and key documents are fraudulently concealed until discovery through re-audits. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Signed balance confirmations and renewal documents serve as clear acknowledgments and unconditional promises to pay. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 7 petition is well within limitation under Sections 17, 18, 19 of the Limitation Act and Section 25(3) of the Contract Act, and the NCLT order admitting the petition is upheld.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with no orders as to costs, upholding the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 15.02.2023 admitting the Section 7 petition.
summary: The appellant, a shareholder of Privilege Power and Infrastructure Private Limited, challenged the NCLT order admitting a Section 7 application filed by Unity Small Finance Bank Ltd. (erstwhile PMC Bank). The appellant contended that the petition was barred by limitation since the default occurred on 31.08.2012 and the petition was filed in 2020. The NCLAT held that the petition was well within limitation, as the limitation period was extended under Section 17 due to fraudulent concealment discovered during PMC Bank's re-audit in December 2019, and revived through multiple balance confirmations and security documents executed in 2017–2019, which constituted a valid promise to pay under Section 25(3) of the Contract Act. The appeal was accordingly dismissed.
