case_title: West Bengal Housing Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. vs. Kshitiz Chhawchharia (Liquidator of Concast Steel and Power Ltd.)
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is West Bengal Housing Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. (WBHIDCO), and Respondent is Kshitiz Chhawchharia, Liquidator of Concast Steel and Power Ltd. (CSPL). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A 99-year lease of land measuring 3608.87 sq. meters in New Town, Kolkata was granted to Concast Ispat Ltd. (CIL) on 17.09.2012, which subsequently amalgamated with CSPL in November 2015. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CSPL went into liquidation on 26.09.2018, and the liquidator included the leasehold rights in the liquidation estate and advertised the property for auction. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The appellant issued a notice on 30.05.2019 attempting to terminate the lease after the liquidation commencement date and moratorium. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Correspondence between the parties showed that WBHIDCO had knowledge of the amalgamation and its counsel had advised getting the amalgamation order rectified to include the leasehold property. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench dismissed WBHIDCO's IA No. 1763 of 2019 seeking exclusion of the land from the liquidation estate, leading to the present appeal.
legal_issues: Whether leasehold rights transferred via an amalgamation/merger scheme approved by the High Court constitute assets of the corporate debtor forming part of the liquidation estate under Section 36 of the IBC, and whether the lessor can contest inclusion without prior lawful termination of lease?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Leasehold rights acquired through a valid amalgamation scheme constitute intangible assets of the corporate debtor under Section 3(27) and Section 36 of the IBC and can be included in the liquidation estate. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Inclusion of leasehold rights does not transfer ownership of the underlying land, but protects the bundle of rights and interests acquired for consideration. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Implied consent of the lessor to the amalgamation, evidenced by active participation and correspondence facilitating rectification of the merger scheme, bars subsequent revocation. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The liquidator acted lawfully in including the leasehold rights in the liquidation estate, and the NCLT order rejecting the lessor's application is upheld.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed with parties bearing their own costs, confirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 30.08.2024.
summary: West Bengal Housing Infrastructure Development Corporation Ltd. (WBHIDCO) appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order dismissing its application to exclude a leased plot of land from the liquidation estate of Concast Steel and Power Ltd. (CSPL). WBHIDCO contended that the leasehold rights were transferred without express consent through an amalgamation scheme and reverted to the state. The NCLAT held that leasehold rights constitute intangible assets of the corporate debtor under Section 3(27) and Section 36 of the IBC, and WBHIDCO had given implied consent through correspondence and facilitating the rectification of the amalgamation order. Consequently, the liquidator was legally empowered to include the leasehold rights in the liquidation estate, and the appeal was dismissed.

case_title: Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd. vs. Gaurav Misra (Resolution Professional of Alchemist Infra Reality Ltd.) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant - SRA), Respondent No. 1 is Gaurav Misra (Resolution Professional of Alchemist Infra Reality Ltd.), and Respondent No. 2 is the Directorate of Enforcement (ED). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Alchemist Infra Reality Ltd. (Corporate Debtor) faced a provisional attachment order issued by the ED on 24.01.2019 under Section 5 of the PMLA following a SEBI complaint. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP was initiated against the Corporate Debtor on 23.03.2022, and the SRA's resolution plan was approved by the CoC and subsequently by the Adjudicating Authority on 04.07.2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Provisional attachment was made in January 2019; NCLT approved the resolution plan on 04.07.2024 while refusing to lift the ED's attachment in paragraphs 60-61. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Records confirmed that the SRA was an unrelated party fulfilling all criteria under Section 32A of the IBC. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: SRA filed the appeal challenging paragraphs 60 and 61 of the NCLT order which directed the SRA to approach PMLA authorities for release of attached properties.
legal_issues: Whether provisional attachment orders issued under the PMLA prior to the commencement of CIRP cease to operate upon the approval of a resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC granting immunity under Section 32A to an unrelated Successful Resolution Applicant?
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 32A of the IBC provides absolute immunity to the corporate debtor and its property from prior offences and attachments once a resolution plan involving a change in management to an unrelated party is approved. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Attachment under PMLA is an interim measure in aid of potential confiscation, which abates and ceases when criminal liability ceases under Section 32A. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Fulfillment of statutory conditions under Section 32A(1) and (2) automatically ring-fences the corporate debtor's assets from pre-CIRP attachments without requiring separate proceedings before PMLA authorities. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The NCLT erred in directing the SRA to approach PMLA authorities; the provisional attachment order ceases to have effect upon approval of the resolution plan under Section 32A.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the appellant is entitled to the benefit of Section 32A, and the provisional attachment order dated 24.01.2019 is treated to have ceased upon approval of the resolution plan, obviating any need for separate PMLA proceedings.
summary: Vantage Point Asset Management Pte. Ltd., the Successful Resolution Applicant (SRA) for Alchemist Infra Reality Ltd., appealed against the NCLT order approving the resolution plan while refusing to lift the Directorate of Enforcement's (ED) provisional attachment over the Corporate Debtor's properties made on 24.01.2019. The NCLAT held that under Section 32A of the IBC, upon approval of a resolution plan resulting in a change of management to an unrelated party, the corporate debtor's liabilities cease and its properties receive complete immunity from pre-CIRP attachments and confiscation. The Appellate Tribunal set aside the NCLT's directions requiring the SRA to approach PMLA authorities, ruling that the provisional attachment automatically ceases to operate upon plan approval.

case_title: C Ganesh vs. Ashok Seshadri & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant C Ganesh is the Successful Scheme Proponent, Respondent No. 1 is Ashok Seshadri (Liquidator/Erstwhile Liquidator), and Respondent No. 2 is the Monitoring Committee of M/s RA Samy Trading Private Limited (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Under a Scheme of Arrangement sanctioned under Sections 230-232 of the Companies Act during liquidation, the secured financial creditor (Punjab National Bank) was to receive Rs. 14,25,00,000/- as full and final settlement, alongside CIRP costs of Rs. 32,35,493/-, liquidation costs of Rs. 86,78,468/-, and EPFO dues of Rs. 11,98,819/-. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant paid the initial 10% to PNB along with interest, EPFO dues, and 10% liquidation costs, but defaulted on paying the remaining 90% balance within the stipulated timelines from the effective date of 22.03.2024. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Scheme was approved on 22.03.2024; Liquidator issued a default email on 16.09.2024 demanding payment by 21.09.2024; Appellant filed IA(IBC)/2232(CHE)/2024 on 19.09.2024 seeking extension. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Delay occurred due to the liquidator filing the sanction order with the ROC late (07.12.2024) and errors in Form INC-28, which prevented the CD's status from changing from 'in liquidation' to 'active', impairing the Appellant's ability to borrow funds; Appellant subsequently tendered demand drafts totaling over Rs. 18.5 crores. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai dismissed IA(IBC)/2232(CHE)/2024 on 02.06.2025 (followed by cancellation of the Scheme on 15.07.2025) due to non-compliance with payment timelines, prompting this appeal.
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT/NCLAT has the discretionary power under Section 231(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 to grant an extension of timeline for depositing the balance settlement amount under an approved Scheme of Arrangement during liquidation, to prevent corporate death.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The Adjudicating Authority and Appellate Tribunal possess supervisory jurisdiction under Section 231(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013 to modify timelines and grant extensions for implementing a sanctioned Scheme of Compromise or Arrangement to achieve corporate revival. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 231(1)(b) confers wide discretionary powers to give directions or modify schemes for proper implementation, and earlier extensions do not operate as an absolute legal bar against further extension if the proponent demonstrates bona fides. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Production and tender of substantial demand drafts covering the principal settlement and willingness to clear accrued interest/costs sufficiently prove bona fide intent and financial capability. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Considering contributing administrative delays by the liquidator and the primary statutory objective of reviving the corporate debtor from liquidation, the refusal of extension was unsustainable, justifying an extension of 60 days.
operative_order: The appeal is allowed; the impugned order dated 02.06.2025 is quashed, IA(IBC)/2232(CHE)/2024 is allowed granting 60 days to make full and final payment with accrued interest and costs, and demand drafts in IA No. 1085/2025 are ordered to be handed over within 3 days.
summary: C Ganesh, Successful Scheme Proponent for M/s RA Samy Trading Pvt. Ltd., appealed the NCLT Chennai order dismissing his application for extension of time to deposit the balance settlement amount under an approved Section 230 Scheme of Arrangement. The NCLAT held that under Section 231(1)(b) of the Companies Act, 2013, the Tribunal holds wide discretionary powers to supervise and modify timelines to prevent corporate death. Finding that delays were partly due to ROC status rectification issues and noting that the Appellant demonstrated bona fides by preparing substantial demand drafts, the NCLAT set aside the impugned order and granted 60 days for full settlement.

case_title: Reliance Realty Limited vs. Mr. Anup Kumar (Liquidator of Independent TV Limited) & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Reliance Realty Limited is the lessor of commercial premises (DAKC), Respondent No. 1 is Anup Kumar (Liquidator of Independent TV Limited - Corporate Debtor), and Respondent No. 2 is M/s Shree Sai Baba Ship Breaking Co. (Successful Auction Purchaser - SAP). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Premises were leased on 27.11.2017 to the CD for its DTH business along with pre-packaged infrastructure facilities pursuant to a Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) and an unexecuted Draft Agreement for Premise Use. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CD stopped paying service/rental charges after October 2018; CD was admitted to CIRP on 26.02.2020 and liquidation on 17.03.2023; assets consisting of 1874 inventory items were auctioned to SAP for Rs. 4,18,54,500/-. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 26.02.2020; public e-auctions were held in 2023-2024; Sale Certificate and Possession Memo issued on 10.12.2024; Appellant first raised ownership objections on 24.12.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP/Liquidator prepared inventory lists in 2020, 2022, and 2023 with ex-management confirmation; Appellant was not a signatory to the SPA; Appellant relied on internal SAP software records without producing purchase memos, asset registers, or supporting invoices. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench allowed the Liquidator's IA No. 660 of 2025 on 06.06.2025 permitting removal of assets and restraining Appellant from obstructing access, which was appealed herein.
legal_issues: Whether the burden of proving ownership over movable assets lying within leased premises in the legal custody of the Liquidator rests on the third-party landlord claiming ownership, and whether failure to object during CIRP and liquidation amounts to acquiescence barring obstruction to an auction purchaser.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: When movable assets are found in the lawful custody and possession of the Corporate Debtor during CIRP and liquidation, a third party claiming ownership bears the burden under evidence law to prove title through cogent documentary evidence like invoices, books of accounts, and purchase memos. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Sections 18(1)(f), 35, and 36 of the IBC empower the RP/Liquidator to take custody of assets appearing in the debtor's books and premises; mere unexecuted draft agreements or uncorroborated internal accounting software entries do not rebut the statutory presumption of ownership. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Prolonged inaction, silence during multiple public auction notices, and failure to present purchase invoices or assert title prior to auction conclusion constitute acquiescence. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to discharge the burden of proving ownership over the auctioned assets, and the NCLT correctly permitted the Liquidator and auction purchaser to remove the goods without obstruction.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 06.06.2025 permitting the Liquidator and SAP to access the premises and remove the assets.
summary: Reliance Realty Limited appealed an NCLT Mumbai order directing it to grant access to the Liquidator of Independent TV Limited and the successful auction purchaser to remove 1874 units of movable assets lying at its leased premises. The Appellant contended it owned the infrastructure assets under a draft agreement and internal SAP records. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the Liquidator held lawful custody since CIRP commencement and that the burden of proving ownership rested entirely on the Appellant. Because the Appellant remained silent through four auction rounds and failed to produce invoices or title documents, the NCLT's direction allowing removal of the assets was upheld.

case_title: Mr. Subhash Aggarwal vs. State Bank Of India & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Subhash Aggarwal is the Personal Guarantor (former Executive Director), Respondent No. 1 is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor), and Respondent No. 2 is Vijender Sharma (Resolution Professional) for M/s J.V. Strips Ltd. (Corporate Debtor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant executed a personal guarantee on 25.08.2009 for a credit facility of Rs. 41.25 Cr. extended to the CD, with his liability specifically capped at Rs. 3.84 Cr. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: The account was declared NPA on 25.07.2018; Loan Recall Notice issued on 29.07.2019 claiming Rs. 68.86 Cr.; Section 95 petition filed on 26.05.2022. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice in Form-B issued on 23.08.2021; Appellant replied on 16.09.2021; Section 95 application filed on 26.05.2022. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant resigned on 13.02.2012 (Form 32 filed on ROC); subsequent facility enhancements up to Rs. 70 Cr. and a 2014 guarantee deed bore alleged forged signatures supported by a private handwriting expert report; however, the 2009 deed contained continuing and irrevocable guarantee clauses. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench-II admitted SBI's Section 95 petition on 01.02.2024, which was appealed by the Personal Guarantor.
legal_issues: Whether a personal guarantee deed executed prior to a director's resignation continues to bind the guarantor for subsequent credit facility enhancements without express revocation, and whether the guarantor's liability in insolvency resolution under Section 95 can be restricted to the original guaranteed amount.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Resignation from directorship does not automatically revoke an express continuing and irrevocable personal guarantee; however, under Section 133 of the Contract Act, variance in the contract discharges the surety regarding subsequent transactions, leaving pre-existing liabilities intact. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 3(12) and Section 95 of the IBC, default occurs upon non-payment following demand under the continuing guarantee, and the limitation period runs from the demand/default date, not the NPA classification date. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear, undisputed execution of the original continuing guarantee deed establishes debt and default, even where subsequent supplemental deeds are disputed for forgery. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 95 insolvency process was rightly initiated, but the guarantor's liability must be restricted strictly to the amount agreed upon in the validly executed 2009 guarantee deed (Rs. 3.84 Cr.).
operative_order: The appeal is disposed of modifying the impugned order dated 01.02.2024 to the extent that the initiation of insolvency resolution of the Appellant is upheld, but his personal liability is strictly restricted to Rs 3.84 Cr.
summary: Subhash Aggarwal, erstwhile Director and Personal Guarantor of M/s J.V. Strips Ltd., appealed against the NCLT order admitting SBI's Section 95 application against him. He argued that he resigned in 2012, that subsequent loan enhancements and guarantee deeds were forged, and that the 2009 guarantee was never invoked. The NCLAT held that the 2009 Guarantee Deed was continuing and irrevocable, and mere resignation without written revocation did not discharge his liability for pre-resignation transactions. However, applying Section 133 of the Contract Act regarding subsequent alterations, the NCLAT modified the order by restricting his liability to Rs. 3.84 Cr. as per the 2009 deed.

case_title: Mr. V. Jaisankar vs. Mr. Mahalingam Suresh Kumar (Liquidator of Ganga Foundations Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant V. Jaisankar claims to be a purchaser/creditor, Respondent No. 1 is Mahalingam Suresh Kumar (Liquidator of Ganga Foundations Pvt. Ltd. - Corporate Debtor), and Respondents 2 and 3 are suspended directors. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant entered into a registered Agreement for Sale dated 30.11.2020 for purchase of a 11,400 sq. ft. plot for Rs. 45,60,000/- (paid Rs. 34 lakhs), and subsequently claimed to have advanced a loan of Rs. 50 lakhs to the CD against deposit of title deeds under an unregistered MoDT dated 30.12.2020. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP was initiated against the CD on 10.01.2022; liquidation order was passed on 15.03.2023; Liquidator demanded return of original title deeds on 23.08.2023. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Invitation of claims closed on 14.04.2023; Appellant did not submit any claim to the liquidator; Liquidator filed IA/1701/2023 under Section 19(2) r/w Section 35 of the IBC. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor's books of accounts reflected receipt of Rs. 34 lakhs under the agreement to sell, but showed no record of the alleged Rs. 50 lakh loan; the MoDT was unregistered, and no charge was registered under Section 77 of the Companies Act. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chennai allowed IA/1701/2023 directing the Appellant to handover original title deeds to the Liquidator, which was appealed herein.
legal_issues: Whether an unregistered Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds (MoDT) without registration of charge under Section 77 of the Companies Act or compliance with Section 17 of the Registration Act entitles a person to retain original title deeds of a Corporate Debtor's property against the Liquidator.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An agreement for sale does not convey title, and an unregistered Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds purporting to create an equitable mortgage cannot create a valid security interest or charge enforceable against a liquidator in the absence of mandatory statutory registration. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Section 77(3) of the Companies Act, no charge shall be taken into account by a liquidator unless duly registered; under Section 17 of the Registration Act (Tamil Nadu Amendment) and Section 49, an unregistered MoDT cannot be received in evidence. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Absence of financial transactions in the corporate debtor's books of accounts and failure to file a timely claim with the liquidator vitiates claims of secured creditor status. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant had no legal right or title to retain the original title deeds, and the NCLT's direction under Sections 19(2) and 35 to surrender them to the Liquidator was entirely lawful.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order directing the Appellant to handover the original title deeds to the Liquidator.
summary: V. Jaisankar appealed an NCLT Chennai order directing him under Sections 19(2) and 35 of the IBC to surrender original title deeds of a property belonging to Ganga Foundations Pvt. Ltd. (in liquidation). The Appellant claimed ownership and secured creditor status via a registered agreement for sale and an unregistered Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds (MoDT) for an alleged Rs. 50 lakh loan. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that an agreement for sale confers no ownership, the unregistered MoDT was inadmissible under Section 17 of the Registration Act, and no charge was registered under Section 77 of the Companies Act. The Liquidator was thus legally entitled to custody of the title deeds.

case_title: Satinder Singh Bhasin vs. Col Gautam Mullick & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1593 of 2023 & Connected Appeal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are erstwhile directors of Bhasin Infotech and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and Grand Venezia Commercial Towers Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtors); Respondents are allottees/Financial Creditors in a Class led by Col. Gautam Mullick. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Allottees booked commercial office spaces, luxury shops, and units in the integrated project 'The Grand Venice' at Greater Noida, developed jointly by both Corporate Debtors on land allotted by UPSIDC/UPSIDA. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default claimed under Section 7 was Rs. 30,70,68,335/-; CD failed to complete construction, failed to execute tripartite lease deeds as mandated by UPSIDC since 2006, and stopped paying assured returns in 2014. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: The Section 7 petition was filed on 03.06.2021 by 103 allottees; NCLT New Delhi admitted the petition on 04.12.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Both CDs shared common management, family control, and common directors, and issued unified booking/allotment letters and receipts; inspection reports by an independent Observer (retired High Court Judge), the IRP, and UPSIDA proved the project was dilapidated, unbuilt on upper floors, and lacked occupancy/fire safety clearances. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi admitted the Section 7 joint petition on 04.12.2023, leading to the present appeals by the directors.
legal_issues: Whether a single joint Section 7 petition is maintainable against two interconnected group companies collaborating on a single real estate project, and whether subsequent settlements reduce the mandatory threshold of 100 allottees.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: A single Section 7 application can be maintained jointly against two corporate entities where their operations, control, and shareholding are interwoven and intertwined in executing a single real estate project. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under the second proviso to Section 7(1) of the IBC, the threshold of 100 allottees is evaluated strictly as on the date of presentation/filing; subsequent settlements or withdrawals do not affect maintainability. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Physical site inspection reports conclusively demonstrating incomplete, uninhabitable structures and lack of statutory NOCs establish default in delivering possession. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The joint petition satisfied the statutory threshold on filing, debt and default were conclusively established, and the NCLT order admitting CIRP is affirmed.
operative_order: The appeals are dismissed, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 04.12.2023 admitting the Section 7 petition against both Corporate Debtors.
summary: Erstwhile directors of Bhasin Infotech and Infrastructure Pvt. Ltd. and Grand Venezia Commercial Towers Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT order admitting a Section 7 petition filed by 103 homebuyers of 'The Grand Venice' project. The Appellants argued that a single joint petition against two distinct entities was impermissible and that the threshold was lost due to pre- and post-filing settlements. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that joint CIRP is maintainable where group entities operate with intertwined control and common projects. Following the Supreme Court ruling in Manish Kumar, the Tribunal affirmed that the threshold must be assessed on the date of filing, and physical inspection reports conclusively proved default in project completion.

case_title: Rakesh Bhailalbhai Patel vs. Vasundhara Seamless Stainless Tubes Private Limited & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Rakesh Bhailalbhai Patel is the suspended director of the Corporate Debtor (Vasundhara Seamless Stainless Tubes Pvt. Ltd.), Respondent No. 1 is the CD through its IRP, and Respondent No. 2 is Hiralal Bhimjibhai Kumavat, Proprietor of B.N. Enterprises (Operational Creditor). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: A Sale Agreement was executed on 31.01.2019 for the sale of machinery and scrap lying at the CD's premises for a total consideration of Rs. 1 Crore, which was fully paid in advance by Respondent No. 2 between 29.01.2019 and 27.02.2019. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose when the Corporate Debtor failed to deliver the scrap/machinery or refund the advance of Rs. 1 Crore. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 01.05.2023 (unreplied); Section 9 petition filed on 23.06.2023. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Four demand letters sent between 2019 and 2023 bore the Corporate Debtor's official stamp; audited balance sheets of the CD up to FY 2021-22 explicitly listed Rs. 1 Crore under 'Advance from Others - B.N. Enterprises' without qualification; Appellant's police complaint alleging forgery was lodged belatedly on 20.07.2024 after orders were reserved. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench admitted the Section 9 petition on 22.08.2024, which was appealed by the suspended director.
legal_issues: Whether an advance payment made for the supply of goods constitutes an operational debt when goods are not delivered and no refund is made, and whether a criminal complaint lodged after hearing can substantiate a pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox standard.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Advance payments made by a buyer for the procurement of goods or services constitute an 'operational debt' under Section 5(21) of the IBC if the seller fails to deliver the goods or refund the consideration. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 18 of the Limitation Act applies to unqualified acknowledgments in audited balance sheets, continuously extending the limitation period for insolvency applications. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: To constitute a valid pre-existing dispute under Mobilox Innovations, the dispute must be plausible and predating the Section 8 demand notice; post-facto police complaints filed as an afterthought are spurious. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Unqualified balance sheet entries and failure to rebut demand notices establish undisputed debt and default, justifying admission under Section 9.
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 22.08.2024 initiating CIRP against the Corporate Debtor.
summary: The suspended director of Vasundhara Seamless Stainless Tubes Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Ahmedabad Bench order admitting an operational creditor's Section 9 application. The Appellant contended that advance payments for scrap did not constitute operational debt, that the claim was time-barred, and that correspondence was forged, pointing to a police complaint. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that under the Supreme Court's ruling in Consolidated Construction Consortium, unreturned advance payments for goods constitute operational debt. Furthermore, balance sheet entries up to FY 2021-22 extended limitation, and the belated police complaint filed after orders were reserved was an afterthought that failed to establish a pre-existing dispute under Mobilox.

case_title: CNH Industrial (India) Pvt. Ltd. vs. SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant CNH Industrial (India) Pvt. Ltd. is an Operational Creditor, Respondent No. 1 is SREI Equipment Finance Ltd. (Corporate Debtor through Administrator Rajneesh Sharma), and Respondent No. 2 is National Asset Reconstruction Company Limited (SRA)[cite: 23]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Parties executed a Cooperation Agreement dated 01.07.2016 for retail vendor equipment financing (with origination fees payable to Appellant) and an MoU dated 12.01.2018 for a loss-sharing risk pool arrangement[cite: 23]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant claimed Rs. 8,97,05,608/- against unpaid sourcing invoices, sought set-off of Rs. 5,56,59,526/- payable to CD towards the risk pool, and filed a net claim of Rs. 3,40,46,082/-[cite: 23]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated against CD on 10.10.2021; initial Form-B claim filed on 22.10.2021; Administrator demanded gross payment on 24.11.2022 and rejected set-off on 27.01.2023 citing Section 14; Appellant re-filed for Rs. 8,97,05,608/- under protest on 03.02.2023[cite: 23]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Both parties admitted the exact mutual dues under the 2016 and 2018 agreements; the RP admitted Rs. 8,66,89,866/- of the gross claim[cite: 23]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench approved the resolution plan with Nil payout to operational creditors on 11.08.2023 while the Administrator pursued the unadjusted demand against Appellant, leading to this appeal[cite: 23].
legal_issues: Whether an Operational Creditor during CIRP can invoke contractual and transactional/equitable set-off under Column 8 of Form-B and whether Section 14 moratorium bars setting off admitted mutual pre-CIRP claims arising from connected transactions[cite: 23].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: While statutory insolvency set-off does not automatically apply in CIRP, genuine contractual and transactional/equitable set-offs arising from closely connected pre-CIRP mutual dealings are fully permissible and not eclipsed by Section 14 moratorium[cite: 23]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Column 8 of Form-B under Regulation 7 of the CIRP Regulations specifically contemplates setting off admitted mutual credits, mutual debts, and mutual dealings between the CD and the creditor[cite: 23]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where mutual financial claims are ascertainable, admitted by both sides, and flow from integrated commercial arrangements, bifurcating them to enforce the CD's claim while denying set-off is manifestly unjust and legally unsustainable[cite: 23]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Operational Creditor was legally entitled to set off the mutual debt of Rs. 5,56,59,526/- against its admitted claim in Form-B, and the Administrator's refusal to recognize the set-off is overturned[cite: 23].
operative_order: The approval of the resolution plan is not interfered with; the Appellant's claim in Form-B dated 22.10.2021 for Rs. 3,40,46,082/- after set-off of Rs. 5,56,59,526/- is treated as accepted in CIRP, and the Appellant is declared entitled to set off the amount due to the CD[cite: 23].
summary: CNH Industrial (India) Pvt. Ltd. appealed against the NCLT Kolkata Bench order approving the resolution plan of SREI Equipment Finance Ltd., challenging the Administrator's refusal to permit contractual set-off of mutual pre-CIRP dues[cite: 23]. The Appellant had filed a claim under Form-B adjusting Rs. 5.56 Cr. payable to the CD against Rs. 8.97 Cr. receivable from the CD[cite: 23]. Following the Supreme Court ruling in Bharti Airtel Ltd. v. Vijaykumar V. Iyer, the NCLAT held that transactional and contractual set-off of admitted mutual debts is legally permissible under Regulation 7 (Form-B) and is not barred by Section 14 moratorium[cite: 23]. The appeal was allowed to the extent of recognizing the set-off[cite: 23].

case_title: Sonali Prashant Shinde vs. Vikram Vilasrao Salunke & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sonali Prashant Shinde is a family shareholder/director, and Respondent Vikram Vilasrao Salunke is a brother/shareholder in Accurate Engineering Company Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 24] 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: In an oppression and mismanagement petition (CP No. 56/2014), the NCLT appointed a mediator to achieve a family settlement regarding the transfer of manufacturing and service business assets[cite: 24]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Consent terms were executed on 07.01.2023, under which the Appellant agreed to transfer her shareholding in exchange for a monetary settlement[cite: 24]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Consent terms signed on 07.01.2023; Appellant sent objection emails on 09.01.2023; mediator submitted reports on 27.11.2022, 24.01.2023, and 18.03.2023[cite: 24]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Appellant received the full monetary settlement contemplated under the agreement, but sought to invalidate the consent terms alleging duress, coercion, lack of free consent, and absence of finalized machinery schedules (Annexures 1 & 2), requesting that the payment be reclassified as a gift[cite: 24]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed Appellant's IA No. 143/2023 on 03.10.2023 holding the consent terms valid, which was challenged in this appeal[cite: 24].
legal_issues: Whether consent terms executed before a mediator can be avoided on allegations of duress, coercion, or undue influence under the Contract Act without specific evidence, and whether subsequent signing of technical plant and machinery annexures renders the agreement incomplete[cite: 24].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: General allegations of pressure, family emotional outbreaks, or duress without precise particulars do not establish coercion under Section 15 or undue influence under Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act to invalidate signed consent terms[cite: 24]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Under Companies (Mediation and Conciliation) Rules, 2016, Rule 26's timeline for recording settlement is directory, serving the primary objective of expeditious dispute resolution[cite: 24]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: A party who has received full financial consideration under a settlement cannot challenge its validity merely to obtain tax advantages or over technical machinery distribution schedules signed by the remaining contesting parties[cite: 24]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The consent terms executed on 07.01.2023 were a binding and enforceable contract, and the Adjudicating Authority committed no error in rejecting the application to set them aside[cite: 24].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT order dated 03.10.2023 enforcing the consent terms[cite: 24].
summary: Sonali Prashant Shinde appealed against the NCLT Mumbai order rejecting her application to set aside mediation consent terms dated 07.01.2023 in an oppression and mismanagement dispute involving Accurate Engineering Company Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 24] The Appellant claimed the settlement was vitiated by coercion, duress, and missing technical schedules[cite: 24]. The NCLAT held that vague assertions of family pressure do not satisfy Sections 15–16 of the Contract Act, especially since the Appellant had already accepted the full monetary settlement[cite: 24]. Finding that the technical annexures were duly executed by the brothers who divided the business, the Tribunal affirmed the NCLT's dismissal[cite: 24].

case_title: Accurate Engineering Company Pvt. Ltd. & Ors. vs. Vikram Vilasrao Salunke & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Accurate Engineering Company Pvt. Ltd. and Aditya Salunke (Managing Director), and Respondents are Vikram Vilasrao Salunke and family members[cite: 25]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Mediated family settlement dividing the manufacturing and service businesses and distributing corporate assets and companies between two factions[cite: 25]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Consent terms were signed on 07.01.2023; Managing Director Aditya Salunke later attempted to retract by terming the agreement a non-binding draft pending execution of plant and machinery asset lists[cite: 25]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Mediation sessions conducted between October 2022 and March 2023; final mediation report submitted to NCLT on 18.03.2023[cite: 25]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The mediator held a final session on 16.03.2023 where both brothers finalized and signed Annexures 1 and 2 relating to plant and machinery; consent terms were fully supported by mediator reports[cite: 25]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai dismissed IA No. 147/2023 on 03.10.2023 enforcing the consent terms, which was appealed herein[cite: 25].
legal_issues: Whether an executed mediation agreement can be unilaterally rescinded by characterizing it as a draft due to subsequent finalization of plant and machinery annexures, and whether technical non-compliance with Rule 26 of the Mediation Rules invalidates the order[cite: 25].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Where parties arrive at a comprehensive settlement and sign consent terms, subsequent attempts to disown the contract on the pretext of pending technical attachments will not vitiate the agreement if the attachments are eventually finalized[cite: 25]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Procedural timelines in the Mediation Rules, 2016 (Rules 25 and 26) are directory and intended to assist quick disposal, not to defeat a genuine settlement[cite: 25]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Execution of final schedules by authorized parties before the mediator establishes completion and enforceability of the settlement[cite: 25]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The consent terms dated 07.01.2023 and completed on 16.03.2023 constitute a binding contract, rendering the challenge devoid of merit[cite: 25].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed, upholding the NCLT Mumbai Bench order dated 03.10.2023[cite: 25].
summary: Accurate Engineering Company Pvt. Ltd. and its Managing Director Aditya Salunke appealed an NCLT Mumbai order rejecting their plea to declare mediation consent terms dated 07.01.2023 unenforceable[cite: 25]. The Appellants claimed the terms were merely a tentative draft as the plant and machinery annexures were signed subsequently[cite: 25]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, holding that the consent terms constituted a completed, binding family arrangement once the annexures were finalized before the mediator on 16.03.2023, and that procedural timelines under the Mediation Rules are directory[cite: 25].

case_title: Mr. Babu Lal (Through LR Mr. Sunder Lal) vs. Jasrati Education Solutions Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Sunder Lal is the legal heir of Late Babu Lal (landowner/seller), Respondent No. 1 is Jasrati Education Solutions Ltd. (SRA), Respondent No. 2 is OSN Infrastructure and Projects Pvt. Ltd., Respondent No. 3 is Shonu Chandra (POA holder), and Respondent No. 6 is Educomp Infrastructure & School Management Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 26]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Babu Lal and his sons executed an MoU in 2010, unregistered Agreements to Sell (A2S) on 16.03.2011, and registered General Power of Attorneys (POAs) on 08.04.2011 appointing Shonu Chandra to execute sale deeds for agricultural land in Alwar, Rajasthan, subsequently assigned by OSN to Educomp[cite: 26]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Full consideration was paid and unfettered possession delivered via a registered Deed of Possession dated 24.04.2011; Educomp underwent CIRP with SRA taking over, but formal sale deed execution remained pending[cite: 26]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Educomp entered CIRP on 25.04.2018; resolution plan approved by CoC on 23.09.2019; SRA filed IA No. 1620 of 2024 to perfect title[cite: 26]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Registered POAs and Possession Deeds explicitly acknowledged receipt of full sale consideration; the land was reflected as an asset in Educomp's balance sheets and Information Memorandum[cite: 26]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Chandigarh Bench allowed IA No. 1620 of 2024 on 01.07.2025 directing the POA holder and legal heirs to execute the sale deed, which was challenged in this appeal[cite: 26].
legal_issues: Whether the NCLT possesses jurisdiction under Section 60(5) of the IBC to direct a Power of Attorney holder and legal heirs of a deceased seller to execute a conveyance deed to perfect title for the SRA over property fully paid for and possessed by the Corporate Debtor pre-CIRP[cite: 26].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 60(5)(c) of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority has broad jurisdiction to adjudicate questions of fact or law necessary to implement an approved resolution plan and perfect title to property in the Corporate Debtor's lawful possession[cite: 26]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A Power of Attorney coupled with an interest and full consideration is not automatically revoked under Section 201 of the Contract Act upon the death of the principal, and transactions concluded prior to Suraj Lamp (2011) remain protected[cite: 26]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Clear recitals in registered POAs and Deeds of Possession admitting receipt of full consideration and delivery of possession extinguish the seller's beneficial title[cite: 26]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The sellers having received full payment and parted with possession, the legal heirs have no subsisting beneficial interest, and the direction to execute the formal sale deed to implement the resolution plan is lawful[cite: 26].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the NCLT order and directing the POA holder and legal heir to execute the Sale Deed in favour of the Corporate Debtor within 30 days[cite: 26].
summary: Sunder Lal, legal heir of deceased landowner Babu Lal, appealed against an NCLT Chandigarh order directing the execution of a registered sale deed in favour of Jasrati Education Solutions Ltd., the SRA of Educomp Infrastructure & School Management Ltd.[cite: 26] The Appellant contended that the POA expired upon the principal's death, consideration was unpaid, and the NCLT lacked jurisdiction over specific performance[cite: 26]. The NCLAT held that under Section 60(5) of the IBC, the NCLT is competent to pass directions to perfect title for assets held by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 26]. Since registered documents confirmed receipt of full consideration and transfer of possession in 2011, the POA was irrevocable and the direction to execute the deed was affirmed[cite: 26].

case_title: Ms. Gorinka Pratyusha vs. Mr. Birendra Kumar Agarwal (RP of M/s Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant Gorinka Pratyusha is an unexecuted sale agreement purchaser of commercial mall units, Respondent No. 1 is Birendra Kumar Agarwal (RP of Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd.), Respondent No. 2 is the Monitoring Committee, and Respondent No. 3 is Lulu International Shopping Malls Pvt. Ltd. (SRA)[cite: 27]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant claimed purchase of commercial units on the second floor of Manjeera Mall under unregistered/incomplete sale agreements with the Corporate Debtor[cite: 27]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Sale deeds were never executed due to title disputes with the Telangana State Housing Board[cite: 27]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: On 17.09.2024, NCLT directed the RP to reflect liabilities toward the Appellant in the Information Memorandum; Appellant filed Contempt Petition No. 6/2025 alleging non-compliance[cite: 27]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP disclosed the Appellant's customer advance in the Trial Balance Report and Annexures to the Information Memorandum; Appellant alleged the disclosure was partial and insufficient[cite: 27]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed Contempt Petition No. 6/2025 on 26.03.2025 finding no wilful or deliberate disobedience, leading to the present appeal under Section 61 r/w Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act[cite: 27].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 lies against an order of the NCLT dismissing a contempt petition, and whether insufficient disclosure of liabilities amounts to civil contempt[cite: 27].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 lies strictly as of right only against an order imposing punishment for contempt, and no appeal is maintainable against an order dismissing a contempt petition[cite: 27]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act is an appellate mechanism created by statute solely for punitive decisions under Section 12, not against orders refusing to exercise contempt jurisdiction[cite: 27]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Substantial disclosure in trial balances and financial annexures rebuts the allegation of deliberate and contumacious disobedience[cite: 27]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order dismissing the contempt petition is not an appealable order under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, rendering the company appeal non-maintainable[cite: 27].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971[cite: 27].
summary: Gorinka Pratyusha appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing her contempt petition against the RP of Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd., alleging failure to fully update the Information Memorandum with liabilities arising from an unexecuted sale agreement[cite: 27]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal as non-maintainable, holding that pursuant to Supreme Court precedents in Midnapore Peoples' Coop Bank and Ajay Kumar Bhalla, an appeal under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act lies strictly against orders imposing punishment, not against orders dismissing contempt petitions[cite: 27].

case_title: Mr. Srinivas Kalluri & Anr. vs. Mr. Birendra Kumar Agarwal (RP of M/s Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd.) & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants Srinivas Kalluri and Rajani Kalluri are purchasers under an agreement to sell, Respondent No. 1 is Birendra Kumar Agarwal (RP of Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd.), Respondent No. 2 is the Monitoring Committee, and Respondent No. 3 is Lulu International Shopping Malls Pvt. Ltd. (SRA)[cite: 28]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellants claimed rights over units 26, 27, and 36 at Manjeera Mall under agreements for sale and lease agreements executed by the Corporate Debtor[cite: 28]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Full conveyance was never executed due to title litigation with the State Housing Board[cite: 28]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: NCLT directed the RP on 11.06.2024 to disclose liabilities towards the buyers in the Information Memorandum; Appellants filed Contempt Petition No. 8/2025 alleging wilful disobedience[cite: 28]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: The RP had incorporated customer advance amounts in the Trial Balance annexed to the Information Memorandum; Appellants claimed this disclosure was inadequate[cite: 28]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Hyderabad dismissed Contempt Petition No. 8/2025 on 26.03.2025 finding no intentional disregard, which was appealed under Section 61 r/w Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act[cite: 28].
legal_issues: Whether an appeal under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 read with Section 425 of the Companies Act is maintainable against an order dismissing a contempt petition[cite: 28].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An appeal under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 lies exclusively against an order of punishment and cannot be maintained against an order declining to exercise contempt jurisdiction or dismissing a contempt petition[cite: 28]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Contempt proceedings are strictly between the Court and the contemnor to protect the majesty of justice, where the complainant acts merely as an informer and has no right of appeal against dismissal[cite: 28]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Mere allegations of incomplete information do not satisfy the legal threshold of deliberate, intentional contumacy required for civil contempt[cite: 28]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The order under challenge is not an appealable order under Section 19, necessitating dismissal of the appeal[cite: 28].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed as not maintainable under Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971[cite: 28].
summary: Srinivas Kalluri and another purchaser appealed an NCLT Hyderabad order dismissing their contempt application against the RP of Manjeera Retail Holdings Pvt. Ltd. for allegedly providing incomplete liability disclosures in the Information Memorandum[cite: 28]. The NCLAT dismissed the appeal, ruling that Section 19 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 provides a right of appeal only against orders imposing punishment, and does not permit an appeal against an order of dismissal[cite: 28].

case_title: Dorni Vinimoy Private Limited vs. Rachna Anchalia (Resolution Professional of Imperial Tubes Private Limited) & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 411 of 2025 & Connected Appeals
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellants are Dorni Vinimoy Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant) and Rachna Anchalia (Resolution Professional of Imperial Tubes Pvt. Ltd. - Corporate Debtor); Respondents include unsuccessful prospective resolution applicants M/s Yaana Apparels Pvt. Ltd. and Krishna Wax[cite: 29]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Resolution process of Imperial Tubes Pvt. Ltd. wherein Form-G was issued on 22.08.2022 specifying 21.10.2022 as the deadline for Expression of Interest (EoI)[cite: 29]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dorni submitted a delayed EoI 47 days past the deadline, which the RP initially rejected[cite: 29]; NCLT allowed IA 86/2023 condoning the delay to submit its EoI and plan by 22.01.2023[cite: 29]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Resolution plan submitted by Dorni on 22.01.2023; EMD of Rs. 50 lakhs deposited on 25.01.2023 due to intervening public holidays[cite: 29]; CoC approved Dorni's plan on 11.05.2023 with 99.87% votes[cite: 29]; RP filed IA 1003/2023 for plan approval on 19.05.2023[cite: 29]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Unsuccessful applicants alleged procedural breaches of Regulations 36A and 39(1B)(b) for non-inclusion of Dorni in the provisional/final PRA lists, but were present during plan openings, countersigned sealed envelopes, and submitted modified offers on request[cite: 29]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench allowed intervening applications (IA 20/2023 & IA 1/2024) on 20.12.2024 setting aside CoC approval of Dorni's plan on grounds of material irregularity, prompting the present appeals[cite: 29].
legal_issues: Whether the admission and consideration of a resolution plan submitted by a resolution applicant whose delayed EoI was condoned by the Adjudicating Authority constitutes a 'material irregularity' under the CIRP Regulations sufficient to invalidate the approval of the Committee of Creditors[cite: 29].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Not every procedural deviation or breach of CIRP Regulations amounts to a 'material irregularity'; it must be determined by an objective impact assessment of whether the violation caused palpable unfairness, plain illegality, or compromised the integrity of the resolution process[cite: 29]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: CIRP Regulations are facilitatory and directory adjective rules designed to aid value maximization; they cannot be interpreted inflexibly to defeat the core statutory objective of corporate revival[cite: 29]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Where an applicant submitted a closed bid before the common deadline pursuant to an unreversed judicial order and other applicants were given equal opportunities to improve their proposals, no unmerited advantage or material irregularity is established[cite: 29]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC lawfully exercised its commercial wisdom in approving the resolution plan, and the Adjudicating Authority erred in setting aside the plan approval[cite: 29].
operative_order: The appeals are allowed; the impugned order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 20.12.2024 is set aside, and IA No. 1003 of 2023 filed by the RP for approval of the resolution plan under Section 31 of the IBC is revived for decision[cite: 29].
summary: Appeals were filed by the Successful Resolution Applicant (Dorni Vinimoy Pvt. Ltd.) and the Resolution Professional against an NCLT Kolkata order that set aside the CoC's approval of Dorni's resolution plan for Imperial Tubes Pvt. Ltd. upon challenge by unsuccessful bidders[cite: 29]. The NCLAT held that procedural deviations under CIRP Regulations 36A and 39 do not automatically constitute material irregularity unless they prejudice process integrity or introduce palpable unfairness[cite: 29]. Finding that Dorni submitted its plan within the general deadline pursuant to an unchallenged NCLT condonation order and that competing bidders had an equal chance to submit improved offers, the Appellate Tribunal reversed the NCLT decision and revived the plan approval application[cite: 29].

case_title: Korea Trade Insurance Corporation vs. Amrit Polychem Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is Korea Trade Insurance Corporation (insurer and assignee of supplier JT Corporation - JTC), and Respondent is Amrit Polychem Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/buyer)[cite: 30]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondent placed three Purchase Orders and Proforma Invoices (PIs) with JTC for chemical supplies (Toluene Diisocyanate and Polymeric MDI) with 90-day credit from Bill of Lading[cite: 30]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: JTC failed to supply goods under the first PI (USD 124,000) forcing Respondent to buy locally at higher costs; Respondent withheld payment under the third PI (USD 171,000) claiming adjustment/set-off for losses[cite: 30]; Appellant reimbursed JTC and took an assignment of debt on 20.12.2017[cite: 30]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Section 8 issued on 03.10.2019; Corporate Debtor responded on 01.12.2019 disputing the claim; Section 9 application filed on 21.07.2020[cite: 30]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Corporate Debtor sent emails to JTC and an email dated 26.09.2017 to the Appellant detailing losses, price differences, and claims of set-off prior to the execution of the Letter of Assignment[cite: 30]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-IV dismissed the Section 9 application on 02.08.2023 due to a pre-existing dispute, which was appealed herein[cite: 30].
legal_issues: Whether a Section 9 application is maintainable by an assignee-insurer when the Corporate Debtor had raised bona fide counter-claims and disputes regarding non-delivery under connected purchase orders prior to the assignment and demand notice[cite: 30].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An application under Section 9 of the IBC must be rejected if there is a plausible, bona fide pre-existing dispute that is not spurious, hypothetical, or an illusory afterthought, as IBC proceedings cannot be converted into debt recovery actions[cite: 30]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: A notice of dispute issued beyond the ten-day period under Section 8(2) does not lose its validity to demonstrate a pre-existing dispute if the record shows disputes existed prior to the demand notice[cite: 30]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Under the Mobilox standard, contemporaneous pre-demand correspondence establishing unadjudicated cross-demands and adjustments demonstrates a real dispute[cite: 30]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Corporate Debtor communicated its counter-claims to the Appellant before the assignment deed, establishing a genuine pre-existing dispute that bars Section 9 admission[cite: 30].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's dismissal of the Section 9 petition, with liberty to seek alternative remedies in civil law[cite: 30].
summary: Korea Trade Insurance Corporation, assignee of South Korean supplier JT Corporation, appealed against an NCLT Mumbai order dismissing its Section 9 application against Amrit Polychem Pvt. Ltd.[cite: 30] The Corporate Debtor had withheld payment on a third invoice to set off losses incurred from non-supply of goods under a prior contract[cite: 30]. The NCLAT held that contemporaneous emails sent in 2017, well before the assignment of debt and the Section 8 demand notice, established a genuine, plausible pre-existing dispute under the Mobilox doctrine[cite: 30]. Consequently, the Section 9 petition was rightly rejected as IBC cannot be used for recovery of disputed claims[cite: 30].

case_title: M/s Meck Pharmaceuticals and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. vs. M/s Accurate Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is M/s Meck Pharmaceuticals and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. (alleged Financial Creditor), and Respondent is M/s Accurate Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor/developer)[cite: 32]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Appellant advanced an unsecured sum of Rs. 1 Crore by cheque on 19.02.2010 to the Corporate Debtor for construction of a project named 'Madina Heights', allegedly under an oral understanding for repayment upon project completion with 18% p.a. interest and a 15% share in project profits[cite: 32]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Appellant claimed default of Rs. 6,30,07,982/- (Rs. 1 Cr. principal plus Rs. 5.30 Cr. interest at 18%) allegedly occurring on 01.09.2019 upon project completion[cite: 32]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Disbursal in February 2010; legal notice issued on 03.11.2020; demand notice issued on 01.07.2021; Section 7 petition filed on 13.04.2022[cite: 32]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: No written loan contract existed; TDS certificates on interest were produced only for FY 2009-10 and 2010-11 with no interest demanded or deducted thereafter; balance sheets for 2010 and 2011 showed 'Loan from Directors and Shareholders' of Rs. 1.01 Cr., but subsequent balance sheets were not produced before the NCLT; the project was still undergoing regulatory compliances and was incomplete[cite: 32]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Ahmedabad Bench-II dismissed the Section 7 petition on 17.01.2024 holding that the transaction did not qualify as a financial debt and no default occurred, which was appealed herein[cite: 32].
legal_issues: Whether an advance given without a written agreement, with no fixed tenure and with interest/profit-sharing linked indefinitely to real estate project completion, constitutes a 'financial debt' disbursed against consideration for the time value of money under Section 5(8) of the IBC[cite: 32].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 5(8) of the IBC, a debt qualifies as a financial debt only if the foundational element of disbursal against consideration for the time value of money is clearly established by credible evidence[cite: 32]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: While a formal written contract is not mandatory, sporadic TDS deductions on interest for only two years without consistent accrual or subsequent demand do not establish that the transaction possessed the commercial effect of borrowing[cite: 32]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Unsubstantiated oral understandings where funds are advanced indefinitely and tied to uncertain speculative project profits do not establish an enforceable right to immediate payment or default[cite: 32]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Appellant failed to establish the existence of a financial debt and occurrence of default, and the dismissal of the Section 7 petition is upheld[cite: 32].
operative_order: The appeal is dismissed without costs, affirming the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 17.01.2024 rejecting the Section 7 application[cite: 32].
summary: Meck Pharmaceuticals and Chemicals Pvt. Ltd. appealed against an NCLT Ahmedabad order dismissing its Section 7 petition against Accurate Infrabuild Pvt. Ltd. for an alleged default on an advance of Rs. 1 Crore made in 2010[cite: 32]. The Appellant claimed the advance was an interest-bearing loan repayable upon completion of the 'Madina Heights' project with a profit share[cite: 32]. The NCLAT held that absent a written agreement, consistent interest servicing, or balance sheet acknowledgments after 2011, the transaction resembled a speculative investment rather than a financial debt disbursed for the time value of money[cite: 32]. As the project remained incomplete and default was not proved, the appeal was dismissed[cite: 32].

case_title: State Bank of India vs. Dr. Jitendra Das Maganti & Anr.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (CH) (Ins) No. 360 of 2024 & Connected Appeal
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant is State Bank of India (Financial Creditor through RP Chillale Rajesh), and Respondents are Personal Guarantors Dr. Jitendra Das Maganti and Dr. Renuka Rani Maganti for M/s Seven Hills Health Care Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 34]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Respondents executed personal guarantee agreements securing credit facilities extended by SBI to the Corporate Debtor[cite: 34]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Personal guarantors defaulted on payment of the outstanding debt amounting to Rs. 129,58,95,550.79[cite: 34]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Demand notice under Rule 7(1) in Form-B issued on 17.08.2021 and dispatched via post on 03.09.2021; Section 95 application in Form-C filed on 07.04.2022[cite: 34]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: While the NCLT found the demand notice address differed from the guarantee deed address, the Personal Guarantors had explicitly admitted in their own pleadings before the Supreme Court (Writ Petition (C) Nos. 843 & 941 of 2022 filed in September 2022) that SBI had issued and served the demand notice dated 17.08.2021 upon them[cite: 34]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Amaravati Bench rejected SBI's Section 95 petitions on 22.07.2024 solely for want of due service of the demand notice, which was appealed by SBI[cite: 34].
legal_issues: Whether service of a demand notice under Section 95(4)(b) of the IBC read with Rule 7(1) of the Personal Guarantor Rules is mandatory, and whether the respondent's explicit admission of receipt in writ pleadings before the Supreme Court cures defects in postal delivery to satisfy statutory service[cite: 34].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Admission of receipt of a statutory notice in judicial pleadings before a superior court constitutes the best evidence of service, rendering technical objections regarding postal dispatch or address variance redundant[cite: 34]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Service of a demand notice in Form-B under Rule 7(1) read with Section 95(4)(b) of the IBC is a mandatory condition precedent to filing an application under Section 95(1)[cite: 34]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: The purpose of service is to impart knowledge of default; where clear knowledge and receipt are acknowledged under oath in constitutional writ proceedings, service stands legally perfected[cite: 34]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Adjudicating Authority erred in dismissing the Section 95 petitions on hyper-technical grounds of non-service despite clear admissions of receipt, warranting remand for decision on merits[cite: 34].
operative_order: The impugned orders dated 22.07.2024 are quashed, and the proceedings under Section 95 are remanded back to the Adjudicating Authority to be decided on merits in accordance with law[cite: 34].
summary: State Bank of India appealed against the NCLT Amaravati Bench orders rejecting its Section 95 insolvency applications against personal guarantors of Seven Hills Health Care Pvt. Ltd. for default on over Rs. 129 Crores, on the ground that demand notices were not served at the addresses specified in the guarantee deed[cite: 34]. The NCLAT held that while serving a demand notice under Section 95(4)(b) read with Rule 7(1) is mandatory, the personal guarantors had explicitly admitted receipt of the notices in their writ petitions before the Supreme Court[cite: 34]. Holding that judicial admission is the best evidence of service, the NCLAT set aside the orders and remanded the applications to the NCLT for adjudication on merits[cite: 34].

case_title: Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit & Anr. vs. Amrapali Fincap Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. (registered MSME developing real estate). Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit, Ms. Rita Dixit, and Ms. Vasudha Gaur Dixit are ex-promoters and Successful Resolution Applicants (SRA). Amrapali Fincap Limited is an unsuccessful Resolution Applicant and objector. The sole Committee of Creditors (CoC) consists 100% of Financial Creditors in Class (allottees/commercial space buyers) represented by an Authorized Representative. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development of a commercial space real estate project wherein 286 allottees filed claims for commercial space units, leading to initiation of CIRP. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in the real estate project leading to admission under Section 7 on 13.12.2019 upon application by Financial Creditors in Class. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 13.12.2019. SRA submitted revised resolution plan on 13.10.2021. Re-voting directed by NCLT on 28.10.2021 took place on 10-11 November 2021. SRA issued Letter of Intent on 13.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SRA produced net worth certificates totaling Rs. 51.02 Crores (Rita Dixit: Rs. 36.59 Cr, Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit: Rs. 10.74 Cr, Vasudha Gaur Dixit: Rs. 3.69 Cr), satisfying the RFRP criteria of Rs. 50 Crores. MCA portal records confirmed active DIN status, reinforced by MCA confirmation email dated 07.03.2025 showing removal of director disqualification under Section 164(2) in 2018 following Delhi High Court and NCLT restoration orders. Performance Bank Guarantee of Rs. 5 Crores was furnished by investor/co-developer Rishikesh Hire Purchase and Leasing Pvt. Ltd. on behalf of SRA. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 256/ND/2019 was admitted on 13.12.2019. In the 18th CoC meeting, AR voted 100% in favour of SRA and Amrapali plans following majority voting under Section 25A(3A); SRA scored higher on the tie-breaker formula. RP filed IA No. 5752 of 2021 for plan approval. Amrapali filed IA No. 850 of 2022 objecting under Section 29A. NCLT New Delhi Court-IV on 22.07.2025 erroneously declared SRA ineligible under Section 29A(c),(e),(g),(i),(j), quashed the approved resolution plan, and dismissed IA No. 5752 of 2021.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan is validly approved under Section 30(4) via Section 25A(3A) where the Authorized Representative casts 100% vote share based on a majority vote of allottees; whether ex-promoters of an MSME are disqualified under Section 29A(c), (e), (g), (i), and (j); and whether furnishing Performance Bank Guarantee through an identified investor/co-developer violates Regulation 36B(4A) of the CIRP Regulations.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Authorized Representative representing a class of financial creditors is statutorily mandated to cast 100% of the voting share in accordance with the decision taken by more than 50% of the creditors who voted, satisfying the statutory 66% threshold under Section 30(4). Ex-promoters of MSME corporate debtors enjoy statutory exemption under Section 240A from disqualification under Section 29A(c) and (h). A director whose DIN is active on the MCA portal with prior disqualification cured pursuant to judicial orders cannot be deemed disqualified under Section 29A(e) read with Section 164(2) of the Companies Act. A third-party investor specifically designated in the resolution plan to provide funding and co-development may deposit performance security on behalf of the resolution applicant without breaching Regulation 36B(4A). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25A(3A) overrides Section 25A(3), operating as a sail-along/drag-along mechanism binding all class creditors once a 50% threshold of voting participants is crossed. Section 240A(1) creates a non-obstante exception removing the direct bar of Section 29A(c) and (h) for MSMEs. Section 29A(e) requires an existing, uncured disqualification under the Companies Act as on the submission date. Regulation 36B(4A) requires performance security to be provided pursuant to the RFRP, which encompasses security tendered through an identified consortium investor on behalf of the resolution applicant. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary verification of MCA portal records and formal regulatory confirmation showing 'active' DIN status, certified net worth certificates combining all applicant family members named in the plan, and explicit clauses of the resolution plan mapping financial obligations of third-party investors. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA fulfilled the net worth requirement, suffered no disqualification under any sub-clause of Section 29A, and complied with performance security regulations; therefore, the rejection of the resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority was legally untenable and perverse.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1149-1151 of 2025 are allowed; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 22.07.2025 is set aside; IA No. 850 of 2022 filed by Amrapali Fincap Ltd. is rejected; IA No. 5752 of 2021 filed by the Resolution Professional for approval of the SRA's plan is revived before the Adjudicating Authority with directions to dispose of it within three months; Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1172 of 2025 and 1552 of 2025 are dismissed; no orders as to costs.
summary: NCLAT set aside NCLT New Delhi's order that had disqualified the ex-promoters of MSME Corporate Debtor M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. under Section 29A of the IBC and quashed their CoC-approved resolution plan. NCLAT held that the plan was lawfully approved with 100% vote share under Section 25A(3A) as the Authorized Representative correctly voted pursuant to majority allottee assent. The bench ruled that MSME promoters are protected under Section 240A from Section 29A(c) bars, their active DIN status removed disqualification under Section 29A(e), combined net worth satisfied RFRP criteria, and deposit of PBG by an investor on behalf of the SRA complied with Regulation 36B(4A), directing NCLT to consider plan approval within three months.

case_title: Vishal Arora vs. Union Bank of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Financial Creditor is Union Bank of India (lead lender). The Corporate Debtor is Solapur Tollways Private Limited (STPL), a Special Purpose Vehicle (SPV) incorporated by Coastal Projects Limited and SREI Infrastructure Finance Limited. Respondent No. 3 is the National Highway Authority of India (NHAI). Appellant Vishal Arora is a suspended director of the Corporate Debtor. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Common Loan Agreement dated 03.08.2013 (amended up to 2016) extending a rupee term loan facility of Rs. 588.42 Crores (UBI commitment: Rs. 200 Crores; Rs. 174 Crores disbursed in 43 instalments) for executing a Concession Agreement dated 29.02.2012 with NHAI for the Solapur-Maharashtra/Karnataka border stretch of NH-9, accompanied by a tripartite Substitution Agreement dated 04.09.2013. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Total claimed default of Rs. 195,55,65,022.45 (Principal: Rs. 184,23,86,839.03; Interest: Rs. 11,31,78,183.42) as of petition filing; loan account classified as NPA on 29.10.2023 following continuous interest service default since 31.07.2019. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Financial default notice issued on 25.09.2019; default cum recall notice demanding Rs. 186.10 Cr principal and Rs. 2.10 Cr interest issued on 04.02.2023; event of default and substitution notice issued on 10.05.2023; Section 7 petition CP (IB)/33/KB/2024 filed on 01.02.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Authenticated NeSL Information Utility record of default; Balance Sheets and Auditor's Reports for FY 2022-23 admitting default in debt repayment to financial institutions alongside severe losses; Debit Balance Confirmation letters dated 28.03.2018, 06.04.2022, and 31.03.2023; and bank statements showing non-payment. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench admitted UBI's Section 7 petition on 20.12.2024, holding that debt and default were conclusively established and the adjudicating authority cannot probe into contractual disputes between STPL and NHAI or pending arbitral claims.
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority under Section 7(5) of the IBC is required to investigate the 'causation of default' or allegations of an 'induced/contrived default' resulting from NHAI's takeover of project escrow accounts and termination of a concession agreement; and whether pending arbitral claims for termination payments bar or defer the admission of a Section 7 insolvency application.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 7 of the IBC, the Adjudicating Authority's jurisdiction is strictly confined to verifying the existence of a financial debt and an occurrence of default. Once satisfied that a debt is due, payable, and defaulted upon, the Adjudicating Authority has no discretion or equitable jurisdiction to investigate the underlying causes, contractual breaches of third parties, or whether the default was contrived or induced. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 7(5)(a) mandates admission once default under Section 3(12) is established. The phrase 'default' entails non-payment of whole or any part/instalment of debt that has become due and payable in law or fact. Contractual rights to termination payments or claims under arbitration are external contingencies that do not discharge the corporate debtor's primary repayment obligations under independent financing agreements. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Authenticated Information Utility (NeSL) records, financial balance sheet acknowledgments, and bank account statements serve as prima facie and unrebutted proof of default; summary Section 7 proceedings cannot be stalled by invoking Section 8 or 9 of the Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: STPL committed prolonged, uncured defaults under the Common Loan Agreement independent of its disputes with NHAI, and lenders are not obligated to await uncertain arbitration outcomes before triggering CIRP.
operative_order: The order dated 20.12.2024 passed by NCLT Kolkata Bench admitting the Corporate Debtor into CIRP is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 44 of 2025 is dismissed; Resolution Professional directed to proceed with CIRP; no order as to costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by a suspended director of Solapur Tollways Private Limited against the NCLT Kolkata Bench's order admitting Union Bank of India's Section 7 petition for a default of over Rs. 195 Crores. The appellant argued that the default was contrived due to NHAI's suspension of its concession agreement and takeover of the project escrow account, and that pending arbitration for termination payments exceeded the debt. NCLAT held that under Section 7 of the IBC, the tribunal is only required to verify the existence of debt and default and cannot examine the causation of default, third-party contractual breaches, or await arbitral awards, reaffirming the admission of CIRP.

case_title: Abishek Nath Sarvaria vs. JC World Hospitality Private Limited & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Abishek Nath Sarvaria, an individual allottee (commercial space buyer) and Financial Creditor in Class. The Corporate Debtor is M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. (under CIRP). Respondents include the Resolution Professional (Mr. Krit Narayan Mishra) and Resolution Applicants Amrapali Fincap Ltd. and ex-promoters Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit & Anr. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Booking of commercial space in the real estate project of the Corporate Debtor, where the entire Committee of Creditors consists 100% of commercial space allottees as Financial Creditors in Class represented by an Authorized Representative (AR). 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Admission into CIRP on 13.12.2019 upon application under Section 7 of IBC initiated by Financial Creditors in Class. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 13.12.2019; re-voting on all submitted resolution plans conducted in the 17th CoC meeting on 10-11 November 2021 pursuant to NCLT directions dated 28.10.2021; voting results tabulated in the 18th CoC meeting on 13.11.2021. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Minutes and e-voting results of the 18th CoC meeting showing Amrapali Fincap Ltd.'s plan received 43.27% 'Yes' votes and 42.60% 'No' votes (50.39% of votes cast), while the Promoters' plan received 44.01% 'Yes' votes and 41.34% 'No' votes (51.56% of votes cast). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: In the 18th CoC meeting, the AR cast 100% voting share for both plans under Section 25A(3A) as both secured over 50% majority of voting participants; Promoters' plan was approved via the tie-breaker formula. NCLT on 22.07.2025 in IA No. 850 of 2022 disqualified the promoters and directed reconsideration of Amrapali's plan or issuance of fresh Form G. Appellant filed appeal challenging the direction to consider Amrapali's plan and sought exclusive issuance of a fresh Form G.
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan voted upon by a class of financial creditors fails for lack of the mandatory 66% threshold under Section 30(4) when the individual 'Yes' votes do not cross 66% of the total class voting share, or whether it stands approved with 100% vote share when the Authorized Representative casts the entire vote based on a majority (>50%) of the voting allottees pursuant to Section 25A(3A).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 25A(3A) of the IBC, the Authorized Representative is mandated to cast the vote on behalf of all financial creditors in a class in accordance with the decision taken by a vote of more than 50% of the voting share of the creditors who have cast their votes. Once that majority threshold is met, the AR's vote represents 100% of the voting share of the entire class, fully satisfying the 66% requirement under Section 30(4) and binding all dissenting or non-voting creditors under the statutory drag-along mechanism. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The 50% calculation in Section 25A(3A) is computed strictly with reference to the voting share of those creditors in the class who choose to exercise their franchise, and not out of the total potential voting share of the entire class. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Verification of the CoC meeting minutes and e-voting records confirming that the assenting vote of cast votes exceeded 50% (51.56% for Promoters and 50.39% for Amrapali), triggering the AR's obligation to cast 100% affirmative vote share. 4.
