DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Both resolution plans validly achieved the statutory voting threshold; therefore, the appellant's claim that neither plan garnered 66% was legally incorrect, and his prayer for an order directing only a fresh Form G was unsustainable.
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1552 of 2025 is dismissed; the resolution plan approval process is governed by the common judgment in Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1149-1151 of 2025 reviving the plan approval application (IA No. 5752 of 2021) before the Adjudicating Authority; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by an individual commercial space buyer challenging the CoC's voting process in the CIRP of J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. The appellant contended that neither the promoters' nor Amrapali Fincap's resolution plan obtained the mandatory 66% voting share under Section 30(4) and sought fresh bidding under Form G. Rejecting this contention, NCLAT held that under Section 25A(3A) of the IBC, once more than 50% of the allottees present and voting in a class vote in favour of a plan, the Authorized Representative must cast 100% of the vote share of that class. Hence, both plans met the statutory threshold, and the promoter's plan prevailed on the tie-breaker formula.

case_title: WhatsApp LLC vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: WhatsApp LLC (wholly owned subsidiary of Meta Platforms, Inc.) is the provider of WhatsApp OTT messaging services. The Competition Commission of India (CCI) is the statutory regulator (Respondent No. 1). Informants are Prachi Kohli (Respondent No. 2) and Internet Freedom Foundation (Respondent No. 3). Meta Platforms, Inc. is the parent holding corporation (Respondent No. 4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Provision of zero-priced smartphone OTT communication services to over 500 million Indian users, funded indirectly through user data aggregation utilized in cross-platform digital display advertising. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Imposition of a monetary penalty of Rs. 213.14 Crores jointly/severely based on 4% of average relevant turnover in India (post 60% mitigation discount) for abusing dominant position. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: 2021 Terms of Service and Privacy Policy announced on 04.01.2021; mandatory rollout notifications issued on 05.01.2021; initial deadline 08.02.2021 deferred on 15.01.2021 to 15.05.2021; suo motu Section 26(1) probe initiated by CCI on 24.03.2021; WhatsApp statement deferring account deletions on 07.05.2021; DG Report submitted on 12.01.2023; CCI final order passed on 18.11.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Contractual comparison demonstrating removal of the 2016 30-day opt-out mechanism; expanded metadata harvesting covering usage logs, hardware details, location, and business interaction data; records showing 264.5 million users (61% DAUs) accepted under threat of service cutoff by 07.05.2021, rising to 84% by March 2024; and third-party advertising competitor depositions (Snap, InMobi, Affle, Taboola). 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI initiated suo motu Case No. 01 of 2021 and clubbed Cases 05 and 30 of 2021. On 18.11.2024, CCI found contravention of Section 4(2)(a)(i), 4(2)(c), and 4(2)(e), levied Rs. 213.14 Cr penalty, and directed behavioral remedies including a 5-year ban on data sharing for advertising purposes under Para 247.1. WhatsApp appealed under Section 53B.
legal_issues: Whether CCI has jurisdiction to assess user data collection and privacy policies under Section 4 of the Competition Act in view of data privacy frameworks; whether WhatsApp's 'take-it-or-leave-it' 2021 Policy constitutes an unfair condition under Section 4(2)(a)(i); whether data sharing violates Section 4(2)(c) and 4(2)(e); and whether the 5-year data sharing ban under Para 247.1 was justified.
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Competition law and data privacy legislation are complementary regimes; user privacy is a vital non-price parameter of competition, and excessive or coercive collection and sharing of data by a dominant platform amounts to service quality degradation and the imposition of an unfair condition under Section 4(2)(a)(i). Section 4(2)(e) requires an enterprise to be legally dominant in the first market to leverage into another, which cannot be applied where the entities in the respective markets are distinct legal persons; however, cross-platform data integration by a corporate group resulting in foreclosure and entry barriers violates Section 4(2)(c). 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4(2)(a)(i) encompasses non-price conditions forced upon consumers without meaningful choice. Section 4(2)(c) prohibits practices resulting in denial of market access 'in any manner' by an enterprise or group, without requiring dominance in the affected market. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Qualitative effects analysis based on market structure, insurmountable network effects, switching barriers, and industry testimonials demonstrating market distortion, without requiring quantitative user referendums or surveys. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: WhatsApp abused its dominance in the OTT messaging market under Section 4(2)(a)(i) and contributed to group denial of market access under Section 4(2)(c), but Section 4(2)(e) was inapplicable due to separate corporate personalities. Restoring user autonomy via opt-out remedies makes an absolute 5-year ban arbitrary and redundant.
operative_order: Competition Appeal No. 1 of 2025 is partly allowed: the finding of contravention of Section 4(2)(e) is set aside; the 5-year advertising data sharing ban under Para 247.1 is set aside; the findings of violation under Sections 4(2)(a)(i) and 4(2)(c), the opt-out behavioral remedies under Paras 247.2.1 through 247.2.4, and the monetary penalty of Rs. 213.14 Crores are upheld; no costs.
summary: NCLAT partly allowed WhatsApp LLC's appeal against CCI's order finding abuse of dominance regarding its 2021 Privacy Policy update. The tribunal affirmed that privacy is a non-price competition parameter within CCI's jurisdiction, holding that WhatsApp abused its dominant position in the Indian OTT messaging market under Section 4(2)(a)(i) by coercively imposing a 'take-it-or-leave-it' policy without opt-out rights. It further sustained the finding of group denial of market access in online display advertising under Section 4(2)(c) and the Rs. 213.14 Crore penalty. However, NCLAT set aside the Section 4(2)(e) leveraging finding due to Meta and WhatsApp being separate legal entities, and quashed the 5-year blanket data sharing ban under Para 247.1 as redundant in light of user opt-out remedies.

case_title: Meta Platforms Inc. vs. Competition Commission of India & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Meta Platforms, Inc. (parent corporation incorporated in Delaware, USA, operating Facebook and Instagram) is the Appellant. Respondents are the Competition Commission of India (R1), Prachi Kohli (R2), Internet Freedom Foundation (R3), and WhatsApp LLC (wholly owned subsidiary, R4). 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Operating a multi-sided ecosystem offering social media, messaging, and online display advertising services in India, utilizing cross-platform data pooling to enhance advertiser targeting and ad impressions. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Imposition of Rs. 213.14 Crores monetary penalty calculated at 4% of average combined relevant turnover of WhatsApp and Meta in India for CY 2020-2022 (Rs. 13,321.52 Cr), discounted by 60% for mitigating circumstances. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: WhatsApp 2021 Policy introduced on 04.01.2021; CCI suo motu order passed on 24.03.2021; DG Report completed 12.01.2023; CCI final penalty and cease-and-desist order issued on 18.11.2024. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SEC Form 10-Q filing for Q1 2021 admitting data-sharing between WhatsApp and Facebook aids service delivery and targeted ads; market share data showing Meta sold 3,013.2 billion ad impressions in 2021 (over 95% of competitors combined) and generated USD 1,887.43 million in display ad revenue in India; absence of standalone financial statements for WhatsApp; and shared management executives between Meta and WhatsApp. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: CCI held Meta liable under Section 4(2)(a)(i) through WhatsApp, found denial of market access under Section 4(2)(c), and found leveraging of dominance under Section 4(2)(e), imposing a Rs. 213.14 Cr penalty and behavioral directions including a 5-year advertising data-sharing ban. Meta appealed to NCLAT.
legal_issues: Whether a parent corporation can be held liable under Section 4(2)(e) for leveraging dominance from a market where its subsidiary operates into a market where it holds a leading position; whether group data integration causing entry barriers constitutes denial of market access under Section 4(2)(c); and whether computing monetary penalty on the combined Indian relevant turnover of parent and subsidiary is lawful under Section 27(b).
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An enterprise cannot be held liable for leveraging under Section 4(2)(e) of the Competition Act across separate markets where the entity dominant in the first market and the entity operating in the second market maintain distinct legal personalities. However, where a parent group exercises complete operational control over a dominant subsidiary and absorbs its user data into its core business to foreclose competitors, liability for denial of market access under Section 4(2)(c) is sustained against the group. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 4(2)(c) applies to an 'enterprise or a group' indulging in practices resulting in denial of market access in any manner, and does not require pre-existing dominance in the market where access is denied. Penalty under Section 27(b) may be computed on the relevant turnover linked directly or indirectly to the contravention, encompassing both entities where financial consolidation and operational unity exist. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Qualitative assessment of market foreclosure and entry barriers supported by comparative market metrics (ad impressions and ad revenue) establishing unmatched scale, alongside corporate records demonstrating total ownership, integrated products, and common executive direction. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The Section 4(2)(e) leveraging finding against Meta fails due to separate legal entity status, but Section 4(2)(c) liability stands established; the penalty calculation on combined relevant turnover in India is legally valid, while the 5-year data sharing prohibition under Para 247.1 is set aside as excessive and redundant.
operative_order: Competition Appeal No. 2 of 2025 is partly allowed: the finding of contravention of Section 4(2)(e) is set aside; the 5-year ban on data sharing for advertising under Para 247.1 is set aside; the finding of violation of Section 4(2)(c), behavioral remedies under Paras 247.2.1 through 247.2.4, and the penalty of Rs. 213.14 Crores imposed on Meta are confirmed; parties to bear their own costs.
summary: NCLAT partly allowed the appeal by Meta Platforms, Inc. against the CCI's order penalizing it for data-sharing practices under WhatsApp's 2021 Privacy Policy. NCLAT set aside the finding that Meta breached Section 4(2)(e) by leveraging dominance from OTT messaging to online display advertising, holding that Meta and WhatsApp are distinct legal entities and Meta itself was not dominant in the messaging market. However, the tribunal upheld the finding under Section 4(2)(c) that Meta's group data aggregation created entry barriers and denied market access to rival display advertisers. The penalty of Rs. 213.14 Crores based on combined relevant turnover in India was affirmed, while the 5-year blanket ban on advertising data sharing was vacated in favor of user opt-out mechanisms.

case_title: Praful Satra & Ors. vs. Ms. Vaishali Patrikar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (Praful Satra, Vishal R. Karia, Kamlesh B. Limbachiya, Rubina K. Kalyani, and Sahara A. Murad) are erstwhile/suspended directors of Satra Properties (India) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 6]. The Respondent is Ms. Vaishali Patrikar, Chairman of the Implementation and Monitoring Committee (former Resolution Professional) of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint Venture Agreement dated 11.08.2005 and Supplementary Agreement dated 03.04.2010 between the Corporate Debtor and M/s Shreeniwas Developers for the Borbhat SRA slum redevelopment project in Mumbai[cite: 6]. An MOU dated 17.12.2019 was executed under which the CD was to extend financial assistance up to Rs. 20 Crores to Shreeniwas Developers[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dissipation of Rs. 91,00,000/- via two cheques dated 31.07.2020 (RBL Bank Cheque No. 791037 for Rs. 50,00,000/- and IndusInd Bank Cheque No. 791035 for Rs. 41,00,000/-) drawn in favour of M/s Darshan Developers (a firm run by Praful Satra's first cousin Pravin Viram Satra)[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 1632/MB/2019 reserved for orders on 19.02.2020; cheques issued on 31.07.2020; CIRP initiated and Section 14 moratorium imposed on 03.08.2020; funds credited post-CIRP on 04.08.2020; cheques encashed on 06.08.2020[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements showing that on the date of cheque issuance (31.07.2020), CD's accounts had negligible balances of Rs. 8,398/- and Rs. 9,151.56/-; fresh post-CIRP credits of Rs. 50,00,000/- and Rs. 41,00,000/- were received on 04.08.2020 and utilized to clear the cheques on 06.08.2020 in violation of Section 14[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 3921 of 2022 under Section 60(5); on 02.01.2024 NCLT directed Darshan Developers to refund the amount with liberty to file under Section 66 against directors[cite: 6]. RP/IMC Chairperson filed IA No. 1099 of 2024 under Section 66[cite: 6]. On 23.01.2025, NCLT Mumbai Bench-I directed Appellants to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 91,00,000/- with 12% p.a. interest under Section 66(2)[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether Section 66(1) and Section 66(2) of the IBC are independent provisions requiring different legal thresholds; whether suspended directors are liable under Section 66(2) for issuing cheques two days prior to CIRP admission without funds that were subsequently encashed during moratorium; whether Section 96 interim moratorium bars Section 66 proceedings; and whether NCLT has power to award interest under Section 66[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 66(1) and Section 66(2) of the IBC are disjunctive, self-contained, and independent provisions[cite: 6]. Section 66(2) does not require proof of mens rea or fraudulent intent; it operates on objective criteria where a director knew or ought to have known that CIRP was unavoidable and failed to exercise due diligence to minimize potential creditor loss[cite: 6]. Encashed cheques during Section 14 moratorium violate the statutory stay[cite: 6]. Section 96 interim moratorium applies strictly to existing debts and does not shield directors from statutory avoidance or wrongful trading liability under Section 66[cite: 6]. Adjudicating Authority has discretion under Section 66 to order restitution inclusive of interest reflecting the time value of money[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Use of the disjunctive 'or' in Section 67(1) confirms Section 66(1) and 66(2) operate independently[cite: 6]. The phrase 'make such contributions to the assets of the corporate debtor as it may deem fit' under Section 66 empowers the tribunal to award interest to restore the asset's value[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Temporal proximity of cheque issuance to the CIRP admission order after judgment was reserved, negligible bank balances on issuance date, post-moratorium encashment, and absence of bona fide commercial consideration or underlying liability towards the recipient[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The directors were fully aware of imminent CIRP and dissipated company funds to a relative's entity without due diligence, squarely attracting joint and several liability under Section 66(2) with interest[cite: 6].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 23.01.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 1099 of 2024 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 348 of 2025 is dismissed; all pending IAs disposed of; no orders as to costs[cite: 6].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by suspended directors of Satra Properties (India) Ltd. challenging NCLT Mumbai's order directing them to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 91,00,000/- with 12% interest under Section 66(2) of the IBC[cite: 6]. The directors had issued two cheques two days before CIRP admission with negligible bank balances, which were subsequently encashed post-admission using fresh funds in breach of the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 6]. NCLAT held that Section 66(1) and 66(2) operate independently, that Section 66(2) wrongful trading requires lack of due diligence rather than proof of mens rea, that personal insolvency moratorium under Section 96 does not stay Section 66 proceedings, and that the award of interest to restore asset value is within the tribunal's jurisdiction[cite: 6].

case_title: The Cosmos Co. Op. Bank Ltd. vs. Mr. Kailash T. Shah & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is The Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd., sole Financial Creditor and sole CoC member of Sterling Lam Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 1 is Kailash T. Shah (Resolution Professional), Respondent No. 2 is Naresh Tradelink Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant), and Respondent No. 3 is the Gujarat State Tax Department[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by the Appellant Bank; Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP under Section 9 on 10.11.2020[cite: 7]. SRA submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 7.85 Crores to Financial Creditors against admitted claims of Rs. 17,00,42,520/-[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 3 filed an operational claim of Rs. 38,58,19,833/- on 01.12.2020, admitted by RP to the extent of Rs. 3,37,65,975/-[cite: 7]. Disputed distribution amount is Rs. 1,31,19,769.08 withheld by RP[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Pre-CIRP attachment on CD's factory land at Village Mahiyal, Talod was executed on 09.07.2019 under GVAT assessment orders; CIRP commenced 10.11.2020; RP filed IA No. 522/2021 on 24.07.2021 to lift encumbrances; CoC approved resolution plan on 13.10.2021; NCLT approved plan on 29.06.2022[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-B filed on 01.12.2020 expressly listing attachment of factory land dated 09.07.2019; RP's statements in IA No. 522/2021 orders dated 13.12.2022 and 22.09.2023 recording that Rs. 1,31,19,769.08 was kept aside pending Supreme Court ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After Supreme Court decided Rainbow Papers (06.09.2022), Appellant filed IA No. 195/2024 to release the retained Rs. 1.31 Cr[cite: 7]. On 22.02.2024, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed IA No. 195/2024 and directed RP to release Rs. 1,31,19,769.08 to Respondent No. 3 as a secured creditor under Section 48 GVAT Act and Section 53 IBC[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction to direct the release of retained resolution plan proceeds to a State Tax Department as a secured creditor after plan approval under Section 31(1), where an application regarding the statutory charge was sub judice prior to plan approval[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 48 of the GVAT Act, 2003, a statutory first charge created by operation of law constitutes a security interest under Section 3(31) of the IBC, elevating the State Tax Department to a secured creditor under Section 53(1)(b)(ii)[cite: 7]. Where the issue of statutory charge and classification is pending before the Adjudicating Authority via an undecided application (and funds are expressly set aside by the RP), directing disbursement of the reserved funds pursuant to binding Supreme Court precedent does not constitute an impermissible modification or review of an approved resolution plan, but is an implementation of law on a sub judice dispute[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC overrides other statutes only in case of inconsistency; there is no conflict between Section 48 of the GVAT Act and Section 53 of the IBC as statutory charges fall squarely within 'security interest' under Section 3(31)[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented pre-CIRP tax assessment and land attachment orders in Form-B, alongside court-recorded reserving of funds prior to disbursement[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The State Tax Department was a secured creditor whose rights were preserved by the pending IA No. 522/2021 and retained funds; NCLT rightly directed release of the funds[cite: 7].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 22.02.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 195(AHC)/2024 and IA No. 522/2021 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 774 of 2024 is dismissed; pending IAs closed; no order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd. challenging NCLT Ahmedabad's post-resolution-plan direction ordering the RP to release Rs. 1.31 Crores to the Gujarat State Tax Department as a secured creditor under Section 48 of the GVAT Act[cite: 7]. The bank argued that the plan had attained finality under Section 31 and could not be modified[cite: 7]. NCLAT held that the tax department had attached the CD's factory land prior to CIRP and the RP's application to remove the encumbrance was sub judice when the plan was approved, with the funds kept aside[cite: 7]. Applying the Supreme Court's ruling in Rainbow Papers, NCLAT held that releasing the reserved funds to the statutory secured creditor did not amount to altering the plan but constituted valid implementation of settled law on a pending issue[cite: 7].

case_title: Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit & Anr. vs. Amrapali Fincap Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. (registered MSME developing real estate)[cite: 8]. Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit, Ms. Rita Dixit, and Ms. Vasudha Gaur Dixit are ex-promoters and Successful Resolution Applicants (SRA)[cite: 8]. Amrapali Fincap Limited is an unsuccessful Resolution Applicant and objector[cite: 8]. The sole Committee of Creditors (CoC) consists 100% of Financial Creditors in Class (allottees/commercial space buyers) represented by an Authorized Representative[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development of a commercial space real estate project wherein 286 allottees filed claims for commercial space units, leading to initiation of CIRP[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in the real estate project leading to admission under Section 7 on 13.12.2019 upon application by Financial Creditors in Class[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 13.12.2019[cite: 8]. SRA submitted revised resolution plan on 13.10.2021[cite: 8]. Re-voting directed by NCLT on 28.10.2021 took place on 10-11 November 2021[cite: 8]. SRA issued Letter of Intent on 13.11.2021[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SRA produced net worth certificates totaling Rs. 51.02 Crores (Rita Dixit: Rs. 36.59 Cr, Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit: Rs. 10.74 Cr, Vasudha Gaur Dixit: Rs. 3.69 Cr), satisfying the RFRP criteria of Rs. 50 Crores[cite: 8]. MCA portal records confirmed active DIN status, reinforced by MCA confirmation email dated 07.03.2025 showing removal of director disqualification under Section 164(2) in 2018 following Delhi High Court and NCLT restoration orders[cite: 8]. Performance Bank Guarantee of Rs. 5 Crores was furnished by investor/co-developer Rishikesh Hire Purchase and Leasing Pvt. Ltd. on behalf of SRA[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 256/ND/2019 was admitted on 13.12.2019[cite: 8]. In the 18th CoC meeting, AR voted 100% in favour of SRA and Amrapali plans following majority voting under Section 25A(3A); SRA scored higher on the tie-breaker formula[cite: 8]. RP filed IA No. 5752 of 2021 for plan approval[cite: 8]. Amrapali filed IA No. 850 of 2022 objecting under Section 29A[cite: 8]. NCLT New Delhi Court-IV on 22.07.2025 erroneously declared SRA ineligible under Section 29A(c),(e),(g),(i),(j), quashed the approved resolution plan, and dismissed IA No. 5752 of 2021[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan is validly approved under Section 30(4) via Section 25A(3A) where the Authorized Representative casts 100% vote share based on a majority vote of allottees; whether ex-promoters of an MSME are disqualified under Section 29A(c), (e), (g), (i), and (j); and whether furnishing Performance Bank Guarantee through an identified investor/co-developer violates Regulation 36B(4A) of the CIRP Regulations[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Authorized Representative representing a class of financial creditors is statutorily mandated to cast 100% of the voting share in accordance with the decision taken by more than 50% of the creditors who voted, satisfying the statutory 66% threshold under Section 30(4)[cite: 8]. Ex-promoters of MSME corporate debtors enjoy statutory exemption under Section 240A from disqualification under Section 29A(c) and (h)[cite: 8]. A director whose DIN is active on the MCA portal with prior disqualification cured pursuant to judicial orders cannot be deemed disqualified under Section 29A(e) read with Section 164(2) of the Companies Act[cite: 8]. A third-party investor specifically designated in the resolution plan to provide funding and co-development may deposit performance security on behalf of the resolution applicant without breaching Regulation 36B(4A)[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25A(3A) overrides Section 25A(3), operating as a sail-along/drag-along mechanism binding all class creditors once a 50% threshold of voting participants is crossed[cite: 8]. Section 240A(1) creates a non-obstante exception removing the direct bar of Section 29A(c) and (h) for MSMEs[cite: 8]. Section 29A(e) requires an existing, uncured disqualification under the Companies Act as on the submission date[cite: 8]. Regulation 36B(4A) requires performance security to be provided pursuant to the RFRP, which encompasses security tendered through an identified consortium investor on behalf of the resolution applicant[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary verification of MCA portal records and formal regulatory confirmation showing 'active' DIN status, certified net worth certificates combining all applicant family members named in the plan, and explicit clauses of the resolution plan mapping financial obligations of third-party investors[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA fulfilled the net worth requirement, suffered no disqualification under any sub-clause of Section 29A, and complied with performance security regulations; therefore, the rejection of the resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority was legally untenable and perverse[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1149-1151 of 2025 are allowed; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 22.07.2025 is set aside; IA No. 850 of 2022 filed by Amrapali Fincap Ltd. is rejected; IA No. 5752 of 2021 filed by the Resolution Professional for approval of the SRA's plan is revived before the Adjudicating Authority with directions to dispose of it within three months; Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1172 of 2025 and 1552 of 2025 are dismissed; parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 8].
summary: NCLAT set aside NCLT New Delhi's order that had disqualified the ex-promoters of MSME Corporate Debtor M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. under Section 29A of the IBC and quashed their CoC-approved resolution plan[cite: 8]. NCLAT held that the plan was lawfully approved with 100% vote share under Section 25A(3A) as the Authorized Representative correctly voted pursuant to majority allottee assent[cite: 8]. The bench ruled that MSME promoters are protected under Section 240A from Section 29A(c) bars, their active DIN status removed disqualification under Section 29A(e), combined net worth satisfied RFRP criteria, and deposit of PBG by an investor on behalf of the SRA complied with Regulation 36B(4A), directing NCLT to consider plan approval within three months[cite: 8].

case_title: Exclusive Capital Limited & Ors. vs. Mrs. Kanta Agarwala & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Exclusive Capital Limited (NBFC), Appellant No. 2 is Satya Prakash Bagla (promoter/MD holding 90% equity), and Appellant No. 3 is Achal Kumar Jindal (Director)[cite: 9]. Respondents No. 1 and 2 (Mrs. Kanta Agarwala and Mr. Suresh Agarwala) are minority shareholders holding 1,17,325 equity shares each (aggregating 10% voting power)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management of NBFC affairs, including equity infusion, issuance of optionally convertible debentures (OCDs) to Teesta Retail Pvt. Ltd. to the tune of Rs. 315 Crores subsequently converted to compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS), and substantial lending operations[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive siphoning of company assets via related-party unsecured transactions, including Rs. 17 Crores loan to Sulojay Realty Pvt. Ltd. at sub-market interest (7-9%), Rs. 4.90 Crores undocumented loan to MD Satya Prakash Bagla, Rs. 2.05 Crores loan to Jayant S. Mirani for luxury car purchase without security/board approval, and purchase of three luxury cars (Bentley Bentayga, BMW X5, Bentley Mulsanne) worth over Rs. 16 Crores without verified company utilization[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition CP No. 48/PB/2024 filed 28.02.2024; NCLT passed interim order on 15.05.2024 appointing Administrator; NCLAT appointed Justice (Retd.) R.K. Gauba as Observer on 31.05.2024; Supreme Court passed interim order on 24.02.2025 granting liberty to move NCLT; Respondents filed IA No. 130 of 2025 under Section 213 on 29.04.2025; NCLT passed impugned investigation order on 16.07.2025[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Three comprehensive status reports dated 01.07.2024, 02.12.2024, and 18.03.2025 submitted by Observer Justice R.K. Gauba establishing non-cooperation, suppression of records, lack of loan documentation, fabrication of board minutes, evasion of IRAC norms, and RBI's affidavit before the Supreme Court dated 24.04.2025 affirming it is not the appropriate authority to investigate fraud/siphoning[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II in IA No. 130 of 2025 in CP No. 48/PB/2024 held that 'good reasons' and circumstances suggesting fraud under Section 213 were established, directing an investigation into the affairs of Exclusive Capital Ltd.[cite: 9] Appellants appealed under Section 421(1)[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether NCLT was functus officio after its order dated 15.05.2024 when considering an application under Section 213; whether Chapter III-B of the RBI Act (Section 45Q/45N) ousts NCLT's jurisdiction to order an investigation under Section 213 into an NBFC's affairs; and whether the reports of an Observer appointed by the tribunal can furnish sufficient subjective satisfaction and 'good reasons' to warrant a Central Government investigation under Section 213[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order directing an investigation under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the Tribunal to form a subjective satisfaction based on prima facie evidence that there are 'good reasons' and circumstances suggesting fraudulent conduct, siphoning, or misconduct[cite: 9]. Conclusive proof is not required at the threshold referral stage[cite: 9]. Regulatory supervision of NBFCs by the RBI under Chapter III-B does not oust or preempt the Tribunal's statutory jurisdiction under Section 213, as the two regimes operate in distinct spheres: RBI governs monetary and financial regulation, whereas Section 213 targets corporate fraud and prosecution under Section 447[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 213(a) requires applicants holding 10% voting power to show 'good reasons' supported by evidence, which must be read with the circumstances suggesting fraud under Section 213(b)(i)-(iii)[cite: 9]. Non-obstante clause in Section 45Q of the RBI Act applies to regulatory aspects and does not bar investigation into penal offences under Company Law[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Subjective evaluation of detailed, independent reports of a judicial Observer documenting undocumented unsecured loans to related parties, unaccounted luxury vehicles, and persistent defiance of document requisitions[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT had full jurisdiction pursuant to Supreme Court liberties, was not functus officio, and possessed abundant prima facie material to justify an investigation under Section 213[cite: 9].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 16.07.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench, Court-II in IA No. 130 of 2025 is upheld; Company Appeal (AT) No. 166 of 2025 is dismissed; all pending IAs closed; no orders as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by Exclusive Capital Limited and its directors challenging NCLT New Delhi's order directing an investigation into the NBFC's affairs under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9]. Minority shareholders holding 10% equity alleged extensive siphoning of funds through undocumented, low-interest loans to related entities and personal luxury car purchases[cite: 9]. NCLAT held that NCLT was not functus officio, that the RBI's regulatory oversight under Chapter III-B does not oust company court jurisdiction over fraud and siphoning, and that detailed reports submitted by the court-appointed Observer (a former High Court Judge) provided ample 'good reasons' and subjective satisfaction under Section 213 to refer the company's affairs for investigation[cite: 9].

case_title: Amrapali Fincap Limited vs. Krit Narayan Mishra, RP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amrapali Fincap Limited is the Appellant (unsuccessful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 1]. Respondents include Krit Narayan Mishra (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd.), the Committee of Creditors (100% allottees), and the SRA/ex-promoters (Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit, Rita Dixit, and Vasudha Gaur Dixit)[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of competing resolution plans in the CIRP of real estate corporate debtor J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd., whose CoC consists entirely of commercial space buyers/allottees[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor under Section 7 on 13.12.2019[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In the 17th CoC meeting re-voting on 10-11 November 2021, Appellant's plan obtained 43.27% affirmative votes (50.39% of votes cast) while SRA's plan obtained 44.01% affirmative votes (51.56% of votes cast)[cite: 1]. SRA plan was approved pursuant to the approved tie-breaker formula and Letter of Intent issued on 13.11.2021[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Objections raised by Amrapali under IA No. 850 of 2022 alleging SRA disqualification under Section 29A(c),(e),(g),(i),(j), shortfall in net worth (< Rs. 50 Cr), and improper PBG deposit under Regulation 36B(4A)[cite: 1]. Records confirmed SRA net worth was Rs. 51.02 Cr, DINs were active following high court orders and MCA clarification, and PBG was lawfully deposited by an investor on behalf of SRA[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT on 22.07.2025 partly allowed Amrapali's IA No. 850 of 2022, disqualified SRA under Section 29A, quashed the plan, and directed CoC to reconsider Amrapali's plan or issue fresh Form G[cite: 1]. Amrapali appealed seeking direct approval of its resolution plan under Section 31(1) without CoC reconsideration[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant is entitled to seek mandatory submission and approval of its resolution plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC upon alleged disqualification of the H1 bidder; and whether the CoC-approved plan of the promoters was invalid under Section 29A or CIRP Regulations[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsuccessful resolution applicant has no vested right to compel the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal to approve its resolution plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC, as plan approval lies exclusively within the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors[cite: 1]. Furthermore, where the highest-ranked successful resolution plan of the promoters is found legally compliant, eligible under Section 29A (read with Section 240A), and approved by the requisite statutory majority under Section 25A(3A), the claims and prayers of rival resolution applicants are legally untenable and must be rejected[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) requires prior approval of the resolution plan by the CoC under Section 30(4); an adjudicating forum cannot impose an unapproved or second-choice plan upon the CoC contrary to its commercial voting results[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of CoC minutes, voting matrices, and statutory eligibility documents of the SRA[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: SRA was fully eligible, its resolution plan was validly approved by the CoC, and Amrapali's challenge to the plan and its demand for approval of its own plan are devoid of merit[cite: 1].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1172 of 2025 is dismissed; IA No. 850 of 2022 filed by Amrapali Fincap Ltd. is rejected; the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 22.07.2025 is set aside; parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 1].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Amrapali Fincap Ltd., an unsuccessful resolution applicant in the CIRP of J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd., seeking direction for its resolution plan to be submitted for approval under Section 31(1) of the IBC[cite: 1]. NCLAT reversed the NCLT order that had disqualified the ex-promoters, holding that the promoters fulfilled the net worth criteria, were exempt under Section 240A from Section 29A(c), and held valid active DIN status[cite: 1]. Because the promoters' plan was validly approved by the CoC via the tie-breaker formula with 100% vote share under Section 25A(3A), Amrapali had no legal entitlement to enforce approval of its alternative plan, and its appeal was dismissed[cite: 1].

case_title: Praful Satra & Ors. vs. Ms. Vaishali Patrikar
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (Praful Satra, Vishal R. Karia, Kamlesh B. Limbachiya, Rubina K. Kalyani, and Sahara A. Murad) are erstwhile/suspended directors of Satra Properties (India) Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 6]. The Respondent is Ms. Vaishali Patrikar, Chairman of the Implementation and Monitoring Committee (former Resolution Professional) of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 6]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Joint Venture Agreement dated 11.08.2005 and Supplementary Agreement dated 03.04.2010 between the Corporate Debtor and M/s Shreeniwas Developers for the Borbhat SRA slum redevelopment project in Mumbai[cite: 6]. An MOU dated 17.12.2019 was executed under which the CD was to extend financial assistance up to Rs. 20 Crores to Shreeniwas Developers[cite: 6]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Dissipation of Rs. 91,00,000/- via two cheques dated 31.07.2020 (RBL Bank Cheque No. 791037 for Rs. 50,00,000/- and IndusInd Bank Cheque No. 791035 for Rs. 41,00,000/-) drawn in favour of M/s Darshan Developers (a firm run by Praful Satra's first cousin Pravin Viram Satra)[cite: 6]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 1632/MB/2019 reserved for orders on 19.02.2020; cheques issued on 31.07.2020; CIRP initiated and Section 14 moratorium imposed on 03.08.2020; funds credited post-CIRP on 04.08.2020; cheques encashed on 06.08.2020[cite: 6]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Bank statements showing that on the date of cheque issuance (31.07.2020), CD's accounts had negligible balances of Rs. 8,398/- and Rs. 9,151.56/-; fresh post-CIRP credits of Rs. 50,00,000/- and Rs. 41,00,000/- were received on 04.08.2020 and utilized to clear the cheques on 06.08.2020 in violation of Section 14[cite: 6]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: RP filed IA No. 3921 of 2022 under Section 60(5); on 02.01.2024 NCLT directed Darshan Developers to refund the amount with liberty to file under Section 66 against directors[cite: 6]. RP/IMC Chairperson filed IA No. 1099 of 2024 under Section 66[cite: 6]. On 23.01.2025, NCLT Mumbai Bench-I directed Appellants to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 91,00,000/- with 12% p.a. interest under Section 66(2)[cite: 6].
legal_issues: Whether Section 66(1) and Section 66(2) of the IBC are independent provisions requiring different legal thresholds; whether suspended directors are liable under Section 66(2) for issuing cheques two days prior to CIRP admission without funds that were subsequently encashed during moratorium; whether Section 96 interim moratorium bars Section 66 proceedings; and whether NCLT has power to award interest under Section 66[cite: 6].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 66(1) and Section 66(2) of the IBC are disjunctive, self-contained, and independent provisions[cite: 6]. Section 66(2) does not require proof of mens rea or fraudulent intent; it operates on objective criteria where a director knew or ought to have known that CIRP was unavoidable and failed to exercise due diligence to minimize potential creditor loss[cite: 6]. Encashed cheques during Section 14 moratorium violate the statutory stay[cite: 6]. Section 96 interim moratorium applies strictly to existing debts and does not shield directors from statutory avoidance or wrongful trading liability under Section 66[cite: 6]. Adjudicating Authority has discretion under Section 66 to order restitution inclusive of interest reflecting the time value of money[cite: 6]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Use of the disjunctive 'or' in Section 67(1) confirms Section 66(1) and 66(2) operate independently[cite: 6]. The phrase 'make such contributions to the assets of the corporate debtor as it may deem fit' under Section 66 empowers the tribunal to award interest to restore the asset's value[cite: 6]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Temporal proximity of cheque issuance to the CIRP admission order after judgment was reserved, negligible bank balances on issuance date, post-moratorium encashment, and absence of bona fide commercial consideration or underlying liability towards the recipient[cite: 6]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The directors were fully aware of imminent CIRP and dissipated company funds to a relative's entity without due diligence, squarely attracting joint and several liability under Section 66(2) with interest[cite: 6].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 23.01.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 1099 of 2024 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 348 of 2025 is dismissed; all pending IAs disposed of; no orders as to costs[cite: 6].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by suspended directors of Satra Properties (India) Ltd. challenging NCLT Mumbai's order directing them to jointly and severally contribute Rs. 91,00,000/- with 12% interest under Section 66(2) of the IBC[cite: 6]. The directors had issued two cheques two days before CIRP admission with negligible bank balances, which were subsequently encashed post-admission using fresh funds in breach of the Section 14 moratorium[cite: 6]. NCLAT held that Section 66(1) and 66(2) operate independently, that Section 66(2) wrongful trading requires lack of due diligence rather than proof of mens rea, that personal insolvency moratorium under Section 96 does not stay Section 66 proceedings, and that the award of interest to restore asset value is within the tribunal's jurisdiction[cite: 6].

case_title: The Cosmos Co. Op. Bank Ltd. vs. Mr. Kailash T. Shah & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is The Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd., sole Financial Creditor and sole CoC member of Sterling Lam Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 7]. Respondent No. 1 is Kailash T. Shah (Resolution Professional), Respondent No. 2 is Naresh Tradelink Pvt. Ltd. (Successful Resolution Applicant), and Respondent No. 3 is the Gujarat State Tax Department[cite: 7]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by the Appellant Bank; Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP under Section 9 on 10.11.2020[cite: 7]. SRA submitted a resolution plan offering Rs. 7.85 Crores to Financial Creditors against admitted claims of Rs. 17,00,42,520/-[cite: 7]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Respondent No. 3 filed an operational claim of Rs. 38,58,19,833/- on 01.12.2020, admitted by RP to the extent of Rs. 3,37,65,975/-[cite: 7]. Disputed distribution amount is Rs. 1,31,19,769.08 withheld by RP[cite: 7]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Pre-CIRP attachment on CD's factory land at Village Mahiyal, Talod was executed on 09.07.2019 under GVAT assessment orders; CIRP commenced 10.11.2020; RP filed IA No. 522/2021 on 24.07.2021 to lift encumbrances; CoC approved resolution plan on 13.10.2021; NCLT approved plan on 29.06.2022[cite: 7]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Form-B filed on 01.12.2020 expressly listing attachment of factory land dated 09.07.2019; RP's statements in IA No. 522/2021 orders dated 13.12.2022 and 22.09.2023 recording that Rs. 1,31,19,769.08 was kept aside pending Supreme Court ruling in Rainbow Papers[cite: 7]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: After Supreme Court decided Rainbow Papers (06.09.2022), Appellant filed IA No. 195/2024 to release the retained Rs. 1.31 Cr[cite: 7]. On 22.02.2024, NCLT Ahmedabad Bench dismissed IA No. 195/2024 and directed RP to release Rs. 1,31,19,769.08 to Respondent No. 3 as a secured creditor under Section 48 GVAT Act and Section 53 IBC[cite: 7].
legal_issues: Whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction to direct the release of retained resolution plan proceeds to a State Tax Department as a secured creditor after plan approval under Section 31(1), where an application regarding the statutory charge was sub judice prior to plan approval[cite: 7].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Section 48 of the GVAT Act, 2003, a statutory first charge created by operation of law constitutes a security interest under Section 3(31) of the IBC, elevating the State Tax Department to a secured creditor under Section 53(1)(b)(ii)[cite: 7]. Where the issue of statutory charge and classification is pending before the Adjudicating Authority via an undecided application (and funds are expressly set aside by the RP), directing disbursement of the reserved funds pursuant to binding Supreme Court precedent does not constitute an impermissible modification or review of an approved resolution plan, but is an implementation of law on a sub judice dispute[cite: 7]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 238 of the IBC overrides other statutes only in case of inconsistency; there is no conflict between Section 48 of the GVAT Act and Section 53 of the IBC as statutory charges fall squarely within 'security interest' under Section 3(31)[cite: 7]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documented pre-CIRP tax assessment and land attachment orders in Form-B, alongside court-recorded reserving of funds prior to disbursement[cite: 7]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The State Tax Department was a secured creditor whose rights were preserved by the pending IA No. 522/2021 and retained funds; NCLT rightly directed release of the funds[cite: 7].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 22.02.2024 passed by NCLT Ahmedabad Bench in IA No. 195(AHC)/2024 and IA No. 522/2021 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 774 of 2024 is dismissed; pending IAs closed; no order as to costs[cite: 7].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by Cosmos Co-operative Bank Ltd. challenging NCLT Ahmedabad's post-resolution-plan direction ordering the RP to release Rs. 1.31 Crores to the Gujarat State Tax Department as a secured creditor under Section 48 of the GVAT Act[cite: 7]. The bank argued that the plan had attained finality under Section 31 and could not be modified[cite: 7]. NCLAT held that the tax department had attached the CD's factory land prior to CIRP and the RP's application to remove the encumbrance was sub judice when the plan was approved, with the funds kept aside[cite: 7]. Applying the Supreme Court's ruling in Rainbow Papers, NCLAT held that releasing the reserved funds to the statutory secured creditor did not amount to altering the plan but constituted valid implementation of settled law on a pending issue[cite: 7].

case_title: Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit & Anr. vs. Amrapali Fincap Ltd. & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. (registered MSME developing real estate)[cite: 8]. Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit, Ms. Rita Dixit, and Ms. Vasudha Gaur Dixit are ex-promoters and Successful Resolution Applicants (SRA)[cite: 8]. Amrapali Fincap Limited is an unsuccessful Resolution Applicant and objector[cite: 8]. The sole Committee of Creditors (CoC) consists 100% of Financial Creditors in Class (allottees/commercial space buyers) represented by an Authorized Representative[cite: 8]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Development of a commercial space real estate project wherein 286 allottees filed claims for commercial space units, leading to initiation of CIRP[cite: 8]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default arose in the real estate project leading to admission under Section 7 on 13.12.2019 upon application by Financial Creditors in Class[cite: 8]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced on 13.12.2019[cite: 8]. SRA submitted revised resolution plan on 13.10.2021[cite: 8]. Re-voting directed by NCLT on 28.10.2021 took place on 10-11 November 2021[cite: 8]. SRA issued Letter of Intent on 13.11.2021[cite: 8]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: SRA produced net worth certificates totaling Rs. 51.02 Crores (Rita Dixit: Rs. 36.59 Cr, Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit: Rs. 10.74 Cr, Vasudha Gaur Dixit: Rs. 3.69 Cr), satisfying the RFRP criteria of Rs. 50 Crores[cite: 8]. MCA portal records confirmed active DIN status, reinforced by MCA confirmation email dated 07.03.2025 showing removal of director disqualification under Section 164(2) in 2018 following Delhi High Court and NCLT restoration orders[cite: 8]. Performance Bank Guarantee of Rs. 5 Crores was furnished by investor/co-developer Rishikesh Hire Purchase and Leasing Pvt. Ltd. on behalf of SRA[cite: 8]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Section 7 petition CP (IB) No. 256/ND/2019 was admitted on 13.12.2019[cite: 8]. In the 18th CoC meeting, AR voted 100% in favour of SRA and Amrapali plans following majority voting under Section 25A(3A); SRA scored higher on the tie-breaker formula[cite: 8]. RP filed IA No. 5752 of 2021 for plan approval[cite: 8]. Amrapali filed IA No. 850 of 2022 objecting under Section 29A[cite: 8]. NCLT New Delhi Court-IV on 22.07.2025 erroneously declared SRA ineligible under Section 29A(c),(e),(g),(i),(j), quashed the approved resolution plan, and dismissed IA No. 5752 of 2021[cite: 8].
legal_issues: Whether a resolution plan is validly approved under Section 30(4) via Section 25A(3A) where the Authorized Representative casts 100% vote share based on a majority vote of allottees; whether ex-promoters of an MSME are disqualified under Section 29A(c), (e), (g), (i), and (j); and whether furnishing Performance Bank Guarantee through an identified investor/co-developer violates Regulation 36B(4A) of the CIRP Regulations[cite: 8].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An Authorized Representative representing a class of financial creditors is statutorily mandated to cast 100% of the voting share in accordance with the decision taken by more than 50% of the creditors who voted, satisfying the statutory 66% threshold under Section 30(4)[cite: 8]. Ex-promoters of MSME corporate debtors enjoy statutory exemption under Section 240A from disqualification under Section 29A(c) and (h)[cite: 8]. A director whose DIN is active on the MCA portal with prior disqualification cured pursuant to judicial orders cannot be deemed disqualified under Section 29A(e) read with Section 164(2) of the Companies Act[cite: 8]. A third-party investor specifically designated in the resolution plan to provide funding and co-development may deposit performance security on behalf of the resolution applicant without breaching Regulation 36B(4A)[cite: 8]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 25A(3A) overrides Section 25A(3), operating as a sail-along/drag-along mechanism binding all class creditors once a 50% threshold of voting participants is crossed[cite: 8]. Section 240A(1) creates a non-obstante exception removing the direct bar of Section 29A(c) and (h) for MSMEs[cite: 8]. Section 29A(e) requires an existing, uncured disqualification under the Companies Act as on the submission date[cite: 8]. Regulation 36B(4A) requires performance security to be provided pursuant to the RFRP, which encompasses security tendered through an identified consortium investor on behalf of the resolution applicant[cite: 8]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Documentary verification of MCA portal records and formal regulatory confirmation showing 'active' DIN status, certified net worth certificates combining all applicant family members named in the plan, and explicit clauses of the resolution plan mapping financial obligations of third-party investors[cite: 8]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The SRA fulfilled the net worth requirement, suffered no disqualification under any sub-clause of Section 29A, and complied with performance security regulations; therefore, the rejection of the resolution plan by the Adjudicating Authority was legally untenable and perverse[cite: 8].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1149-1151 of 2025 are allowed; the Adjudicating Authority's order dated 22.07.2025 is set aside; IA No. 850 of 2022 filed by Amrapali Fincap Ltd. is rejected; IA No. 5752 of 2021 filed by the Resolution Professional for approval of the SRA's plan is revived before the Adjudicating Authority with directions to dispose of it within three months; Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) Nos. 1172 of 2025 and 1552 of 2025 are dismissed; parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 8].
summary: NCLAT set aside NCLT New Delhi's order that had disqualified the ex-promoters of MSME Corporate Debtor M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd. under Section 29A of the IBC and quashed their CoC-approved resolution plan[cite: 8]. NCLAT held that the plan was lawfully approved with 100% vote share under Section 25A(3A) as the Authorized Representative correctly voted pursuant to majority allottee assent[cite: 8]. The bench ruled that MSME promoters are protected under Section 240A from Section 29A(c) bars, their active DIN status removed disqualification under Section 29A(e), combined net worth satisfied RFRP criteria, and deposit of PBG by an investor on behalf of the SRA complied with Regulation 36B(4A), directing NCLT to consider plan approval within three months[cite: 8].

case_title: Exclusive Capital Limited & Ors. vs. Mrs. Kanta Agarwala & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Appellant No. 1 is Exclusive Capital Limited (NBFC), Appellant No. 2 is Satya Prakash Bagla (promoter/MD holding 90% equity), and Appellant No. 3 is Achal Kumar Jindal (Director)[cite: 9]. Respondents No. 1 and 2 (Mrs. Kanta Agarwala and Mr. Suresh Agarwala) are minority shareholders holding 1,17,325 equity shares each (aggregating 10% voting power)[cite: 9]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Management of NBFC affairs, including equity infusion, issuance of optionally convertible debentures (OCDs) to Teesta Retail Pvt. Ltd. to the tune of Rs. 315 Crores subsequently converted to compulsorily convertible preference shares (CCPS), and substantial lending operations[cite: 9]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Massive siphoning of company assets via related-party unsecured transactions, including Rs. 17 Crores loan to Sulojay Realty Pvt. Ltd. at sub-market interest (7-9%), Rs. 4.90 Crores undocumented loan to MD Satya Prakash Bagla, Rs. 2.05 Crores loan to Jayant S. Mirani for luxury car purchase without security/board approval, and purchase of three luxury cars (Bentley Bentayga, BMW X5, Bentley Mulsanne) worth over Rs. 16 Crores without verified company utilization[cite: 9]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Company Petition CP No. 48/PB/2024 filed 28.02.2024; NCLT passed interim order on 15.05.2024 appointing Administrator; NCLAT appointed Justice (Retd.) R.K. Gauba as Observer on 31.05.2024; Supreme Court passed interim order on 24.02.2025 granting liberty to move NCLT; Respondents filed IA No. 130 of 2025 under Section 213 on 29.04.2025; NCLT passed impugned investigation order on 16.07.2025[cite: 9]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Three comprehensive status reports dated 01.07.2024, 02.12.2024, and 18.03.2025 submitted by Observer Justice R.K. Gauba establishing non-cooperation, suppression of records, lack of loan documentation, fabrication of board minutes, evasion of IRAC norms, and RBI's affidavit before the Supreme Court dated 24.04.2025 affirming it is not the appropriate authority to investigate fraud/siphoning[cite: 9]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT New Delhi Bench Court-II in IA No. 130 of 2025 in CP No. 48/PB/2024 held that 'good reasons' and circumstances suggesting fraud under Section 213 were established, directing an investigation into the affairs of Exclusive Capital Ltd.[cite: 9] Appellants appealed under Section 421(1)[cite: 9].
legal_issues: Whether NCLT was functus officio after its order dated 15.05.2024 when considering an application under Section 213; whether Chapter III-B of the RBI Act (Section 45Q/45N) ousts NCLT's jurisdiction to order an investigation under Section 213 into an NBFC's affairs; and whether the reports of an Observer appointed by the tribunal can furnish sufficient subjective satisfaction and 'good reasons' to warrant a Central Government investigation under Section 213[cite: 9].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An order directing an investigation under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013 requires the Tribunal to form a subjective satisfaction based on prima facie evidence that there are 'good reasons' and circumstances suggesting fraudulent conduct, siphoning, or misconduct[cite: 9]. Conclusive proof is not required at the threshold referral stage[cite: 9]. Regulatory supervision of NBFCs by the RBI under Chapter III-B does not oust or preempt the Tribunal's statutory jurisdiction under Section 213, as the two regimes operate in distinct spheres: RBI governs monetary and financial regulation, whereas Section 213 targets corporate fraud and prosecution under Section 447[cite: 9]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 213(a) requires applicants holding 10% voting power to show 'good reasons' supported by evidence, which must be read with the circumstances suggesting fraud under Section 213(b)(i)-(iii)[cite: 9]. Non-obstante clause in Section 45Q of the RBI Act applies to regulatory aspects and does not bar investigation into penal offences under Company Law[cite: 9]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Subjective evaluation of detailed, independent reports of a judicial Observer documenting undocumented unsecured loans to related parties, unaccounted luxury vehicles, and persistent defiance of document requisitions[cite: 9]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: NCLT had full jurisdiction pursuant to Supreme Court liberties, was not functus officio, and possessed abundant prima facie material to justify an investigation under Section 213[cite: 9].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 16.07.2025 passed by NCLT New Delhi Bench, Court-II in IA No. 130 of 2025 is upheld; Company Appeal (AT) No. 166 of 2025 is dismissed; all pending IAs closed; no orders as to costs[cite: 9].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal by Exclusive Capital Limited and its directors challenging NCLT New Delhi's order directing an investigation into the NBFC's affairs under Section 213 of the Companies Act, 2013[cite: 9]. Minority shareholders holding 10% equity alleged extensive siphoning of funds through undocumented, low-interest loans to related entities and personal luxury car purchases[cite: 9]. NCLAT held that NCLT was not functus officio, that the RBI's regulatory oversight under Chapter III-B does not oust company court jurisdiction over fraud and siphoning, and that detailed reports submitted by the court-appointed Observer (a former High Court Judge) provided ample 'good reasons' and subjective satisfaction under Section 213 to refer the company's affairs for investigation[cite: 9].

case_title: Amrapali Fincap Limited vs. Krit Narayan Mishra, RP & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: Amrapali Fincap Limited is the Appellant (unsuccessful Resolution Applicant)[cite: 1]. Respondents include Krit Narayan Mishra (Resolution Professional of Corporate Debtor M/s J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd.), the Committee of Creditors (100% allottees), and the SRA/ex-promoters (Dr. Vijay Kant Dixit, Rita Dixit, and Vasudha Gaur Dixit)[cite: 1]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Submission of competing resolution plans in the CIRP of real estate corporate debtor J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd., whose CoC consists entirely of commercial space buyers/allottees[cite: 1]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: CIRP initiated against the Corporate Debtor under Section 7 on 13.12.2019[cite: 1]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: In the 17th CoC meeting re-voting on 10-11 November 2021, Appellant's plan obtained 43.27% affirmative votes (50.39% of votes cast) while SRA's plan obtained 44.01% affirmative votes (51.56% of votes cast)[cite: 1]. SRA plan was approved pursuant to the approved tie-breaker formula and Letter of Intent issued on 13.11.2021[cite: 1]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Objections raised by Amrapali under IA No. 850 of 2022 alleging SRA disqualification under Section 29A(c),(e),(g),(i),(j), shortfall in net worth (< Rs. 50 Cr), and improper PBG deposit under Regulation 36B(4A)[cite: 1]. Records confirmed SRA net worth was Rs. 51.02 Cr, DINs were active following high court orders and MCA clarification, and PBG was lawfully deposited by an investor on behalf of SRA[cite: 1]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT on 22.07.2025 partly allowed Amrapali's IA No. 850 of 2022, disqualified SRA under Section 29A, quashed the plan, and directed CoC to reconsider Amrapali's plan or issue fresh Form G[cite: 1]. Amrapali appealed seeking direct approval of its resolution plan under Section 31(1) without CoC reconsideration[cite: 1].
legal_issues: Whether an unsuccessful resolution applicant is entitled to seek mandatory submission and approval of its resolution plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC upon alleged disqualification of the H1 bidder; and whether the CoC-approved plan of the promoters was invalid under Section 29A or CIRP Regulations[cite: 1].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: An unsuccessful resolution applicant has no vested right to compel the Adjudicating Authority or Appellate Tribunal to approve its resolution plan under Section 31(1) of the IBC, as plan approval lies exclusively within the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors[cite: 1]. Furthermore, where the highest-ranked successful resolution plan of the promoters is found legally compliant, eligible under Section 29A (read with Section 240A), and approved by the requisite statutory majority under Section 25A(3A), the claims and prayers of rival resolution applicants are legally untenable and must be rejected[cite: 1]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 31(1) requires prior approval of the resolution plan by the CoC under Section 30(4); an adjudicating forum cannot impose an unapproved or second-choice plan upon the CoC contrary to its commercial voting results[cite: 1]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Examination of CoC minutes, voting matrices, and statutory eligibility documents of the SRA[cite: 1]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: SRA was fully eligible, its resolution plan was validly approved by the CoC, and Amrapali's challenge to the plan and its demand for approval of its own plan are devoid of merit[cite: 1].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1172 of 2025 is dismissed; IA No. 850 of 2022 filed by Amrapali Fincap Ltd. is rejected; the order of the Adjudicating Authority dated 22.07.2025 is set aside; parties shall bear their own costs[cite: 1].
summary: NCLAT dismissed the appeal filed by Amrapali Fincap Ltd., an unsuccessful resolution applicant in the CIRP of J.C. World Hospitality Pvt. Ltd., seeking direction for its resolution plan to be submitted for approval under Section 31(1) of the IBC[cite: 1]. NCLAT reversed the NCLT order that had disqualified the ex-promoters, holding that the promoters fulfilled the net worth criteria, were exempt under Section 240A from Section 29A(c), and held valid active DIN status[cite: 1]. Because the promoters' plan was validly approved by the CoC via the tie-breaker formula with 100% vote share under Section 25A(3A), Amrapali had no legal entitlement to enforce approval of its alternative plan, and its appeal was dismissed[cite: 1].

case_title: Pankaj Mahajan, RP of Arshiya Limited vs. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company & Ors.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellant is Pankaj Mahajan, Resolution Professional of Arshiya Limited (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 12]. Respondents No. 1 to 8, 11, and 12 are financial creditors comprising the Committee of Creditors (CoC), led by Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Company (79.00% voting share)[cite: 12]. Respondents No. 9 and 10 are wholly owned subsidiaries undergoing independent CIRP: NCR Rail Infrastructure Limited and Arshiya Northern FTWZ Limited (ANFL)[cite: 12]. Intervenor Ajay Shankarlal Mittal is the suspended director and personal guarantor of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 12]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Proposed private sale under Regulation 29 of the CIRP Regulations of non-core land parcels admeasuring 42.08 acres located at the Free Trade Warehousing Zone (FTWZ) in Khurja, Uttar Pradesh (39.56 acres situated on the site of NCR Rail and 2.52 acres forming part of the spine road on the site of ANFL)[cite: 12]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was admitted to CIRP under Section 7 on 23.04.2024 with total outstanding debt exceeding Rs. 6,600 Crores; the valuation of the subject land parcels was determined at approximately Rs. 32 Crores by two independent registered valuers[cite: 12]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP initiated on 23.04.2024; CoC approved the two-part sale by 85.46% majority vote in the 7th and 8th CoC meetings (concluded 18.03.2025); RP filed IA No. 1927 of 2025 before NCLT Mumbai Bench seeking approval for the sale under Regulation 29[cite: 12]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Valuation reports of two independent registered valuers fixing fair market value; CoC meeting minutes establishing that the 39.56 acres are landlocked and non-contiguous within NCR Rail's railway tracks and the 2.52 acres form part of a 6.31-acre spine road vital for FTWZ connectivity; and written consents to the sale by sole charge-holders/mortgagees Edelweiss ARC and SREI Equipment Finance[cite: 12]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench on 16.07.2025 partly allowed IA No. 1927 of 2025, permitting the sale in principle but erroneously directing the RPs of NCR Rail and ANFL to invite independent bids from their respective Prospective Resolution Applicants (PRAs) under Regulation 36A(1A)[cite: 12]. The RP of the CD, along with RPs of ANFL and NCR Rail, appealed to NCLAT[cite: 12].
legal_issues: Whether the manner and mode of sale of non-core encumbered assets of a Corporate Debtor under Regulation 29 of the CIRP Regulations is a commercial decision within the exclusive domain of the CoC; whether the Adjudicating Authority exceeded its jurisdiction by directing parallel CIRPs of distinct corporate entities to invite bids from their PRAs; and whether Regulation 36A(1A) applies retrospectively to sales approved by the CoC prior to its notification[cite: 12].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: The mode and manner of disposing of a corporate debtor's non-core assets to achieve value maximization under Regulation 29 of the CIRP Regulations lies within the commercial wisdom of the Committee of Creditors and is non-justiciable absent statutory non-compliance[cite: 12]. Encumbered assets may be validly sold under Regulation 29 where the secured charge-holders expressly consent to the sale, constituting an effective waiver of prejudice[cite: 12]. An Adjudicating Authority supervising the CIRP of one corporate entity lacks jurisdiction to issue directions that make its process contingent upon or interfere with the independent CIRP proceedings of distinct subsidiary companies pending before different benches[cite: 12]. Regulation 36A(1A) is substantive and prospective, having no application to asset sales approved by the CoC prior to its enactment[cite: 12]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Regulation 29 permits sale of assets outside the ordinary course of business; while the text refers to unencumbered assets, consensual disposal with mortgagee consent is legally valid[cite: 12]. Regulation 36A(1A) cannot be invoked to compel bidding across separate corporate debtors[cite: 12]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Commercial rationality demonstrated by independent valuation reports, unviability of third-party acquisitions due to landlocked geographic layout in a notified FTWZ, and 85.46% affirmative CoC voting[cite: 12]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The CoC lawfully exercised its commercial wisdom to maximize value by selling the land parcels to the SRAs of the respective subsidiaries; the NCLT's directions mandating competitive bidding among PRAs of other entities were legally unsustainable and quashed[cite: 12].
operative_order: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 1450, 1451, and 1452 of 2025 are allowed; the impugned directions in the order dated 16.07.2025 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench are set aside; the sale of the subject land parcels as approved by the CoC in IA No. 1927 of 2025 is allowed as prayed; Intervention Application IA No. 5807 of 2025 is dismissed; no orders as to costs[cite: 12].
summary: NCLAT allowed the appeals filed by the Resolution Professionals of Arshiya Limited, Arshiya Northern FTWZ Limited, and NCR Rail Infrastructure Limited against NCLT Mumbai's order modifying a CoC-approved asset sale[cite: 12]. The CoC of Arshiya Limited had approved with 85.46% majority the private sale of 42.08 acres of non-core, landlocked parcels within the Khurja FTWZ to the Successful Resolution Applicants of its subsidiaries to maximize value[cite: 12]. NCLAT held that the mode of sale of assets under Regulation 29 lies within the non-justiciable commercial wisdom of the CoC, that encumbered assets can be sold with mortgagee consent, that NCLT cannot make a CIRP contingent on parallel CIRPs of separate companies, and that newly inserted Regulation 36A(1A) does not apply retrospectively[cite: 12].

case_title: Ankit Suresh Wadhwa vs. Bank of India & Ors.
appeal_number: Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 828 of 2024 & Comp. App. (AT) (Ins) No. 1298 of 2024
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants are Ankit Suresh Wadhwa (suspended partner of Corporate Debtor Wadhwa Buildcon LLP and proposed Resolution Applicant) and Ramkumar Pal (alleged Power of Attorney holder of certain homebuyers)[cite: 13]. Respondent No. 1 is Bank of India (dissenting secured financial creditor)[cite: 13]. Respondent No. 2 is Manish Lalji Dawda (Resolution Professional, replacing erstwhile RP Vishal Ghisulal Jain)[cite: 13]. Respondent No. 3 is Prabhat Jain (duly appointed Authorised Representative of the class of homebuyers)[cite: 13]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Credit facilities extended by Bank of India to the Corporate Debtor for real estate development across projects including Wadhwa Rhodesia, Wadhwa Florence Pearl, and Wadhwa Regalia[cite: 13]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Default leading to CIRP admission on 28.07.2020 upon Section 7 application filed by Bank of India, with admitted financial claims of Rs. 32,57,14,026/-[cite: 13]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CIRP commenced 28.07.2020; initial resolution plan submitted on 21.01.2021 (accompanied by a stale Section 29A affidavit dated 30.11.2020); Appellant declared a wilful defaulter by Indiabulls Housing Finance on 30.10.2022; revised resolution plan submitted on 11.11.2022 and final plan submitted on 20.01.2023; CoC voted to approve the plan by 66.64% on 20.01.2023[cite: 13]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: CIBIL and RBI records establishing that Indiabulls Housing Finance declared Ankit Suresh Wadhwa a wilful defaulter on 30.10.2022; Clause 1.15 of the RFRP requiring eligibility under Section 29A at three distinct stages (submission, consideration, and sanction); failure of the applicant to submit an updated Section 29A eligibility affidavit with the revised plan of 11.11.2022; and subsequent participation of the Appellant under a fresh Form G issued in October 2024 after curing default[cite: 13]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: Erstwhile RP filed IA No. 402 of 2023 for plan approval under Section 30(6); Bank of India filed IA No. 828 of 2023 challenging SRA's eligibility under Section 29A(b)[cite: 13]. NCLT Mumbai Bench Court-V on 20.03.2024 allowed IA No. 828 of 2023, rejected the resolution plan, extended CIRP by 180 days, and directed issuance of fresh Form G[cite: 13]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 13].
legal_issues: Whether a resolution applicant declared as a wilful defaulter prior to the submission of a revised resolution plan is disqualified under Section 29A(b) of the IBC; whether eligibility under Section 29A must exist at all stages specified in the RFRP (submission, consideration, and sanction); and whether an individual homebuyer acting through a Power of Attorney has locus to challenge a CIRP order when the class is represented by a statutory Authorised Representative[cite: 13].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 29A(b) of the IBC statutorily bars any person who is a wilful defaulter under RBI guidelines from submitting or having a resolution plan considered or approved[cite: 13]. Where the terms of the Request for Resolution Plan (RFRP) and the applicant's own solemn undertaking stipulate that eligibility must be maintained across three crucial stages—submission, CoC consideration, and Adjudicating Authority sanction—incurring a statutory disqualification prior to the submission of a revised/updated plan or during CoC consideration invalidates the plan, rendering any CoC approval void ab initio[cite: 13]. Regulation 39(1)(a) requires a contemporaneous affidavit of eligibility, and failure to furnish an updated affidavit alongside a revised plan violates mandatory CIRP framework[cite: 13]. Individual allottees represented by an Authorised Representative under Section 21(6A) have no independent locus to litigate via power of attorney[cite: 13]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: Section 29A(b) read with Regulation 39(1)(a) admits of no exceptions for wilful defaulters, even for MSMEs under Section 240A (which only exempts clauses (c) and (h))[cite: 13]. Clause 1.15 of the RFRP binds participants to continuous eligibility[cite: 13]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Undisputed declaration of wilful default on record as of 30.10.2022 and absence of an updated Section 29A affidavit[cite: 13]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: Ankit Suresh Wadhwa was ineligible under Section 29A(b) when his revised plan was submitted and considered; NCLT rightly rejected the plan and directed fresh bidding[cite: 13].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 20.03.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench in IA No. 828 of 2023 in CP (IB)-2946/MB/2019 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 828 of 2024 and Company Appeal (AT) (Ins) No. 1298 of 2024 are dismissed; pending IAs closed; no orders as to costs[cite: 13].
summary: NCLAT dismissed two appeals challenging NCLT Mumbai's rejection of a resolution plan submitted by Ankit Suresh Wadhwa (suspended partner of Wadhwa Buildcon LLP)[cite: 13].
