Since the applicant incurred disqualification before submitting his revised plan and failed to provide a valid contemporaneous affidavit under Regulation 39(1)(a), the plan was statutorily barred, and NCLT's direction for a fresh Form G was upheld[cite: 13].

case_title: Anubhav Anilkumar Aggarwal & Anr. vs. Rajendra Kumar Girdhar & Anr.
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Appellants (Anubhav Anilkumar Aggarwal and Gokul Anilkumar Aggarwal) are erstwhile directors of Chamber Construction Pvt. Ltd. (Corporate Debtor)[cite: 14]. Respondent No. 1 is Rajendra Kumar Girdhar (Resolution Professional/Liquidator)[cite: 14]. Respondent No. 2 is Invent Assets Securitization and Reconstruction Pvt. Ltd. (ARC)[cite: 14]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Purported assignment of a debt receivable from Mafatlal Engineering Industries Ltd. (a company in liquidation since 1999, with claim admitted at only Rs. 16.68 Crores by its Liquidator)[cite: 14]. Kotak Mahindra Bank assigned the debt to Respondent No. 2 on 29.11.2011; Respondent No. 2 and the CD executed an MOU on 17.12.2011 to assign the debt to CD for an inflated consideration of Rs. 36.90 Crores[cite: 14]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor was siphoned of Rs. 38,19,05,000/- paid to Respondent No. 2 between 11.10.2011 and 07.01.2014, including Rs. 36,53,00,000/- paid prior to 28.11.2011[cite: 14]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: CD admitted to CIRP on 16.07.2019; RP filed IA No. 2853 of 2021 under Section 66 of the IBC in CP No. 3962 of 2018; NCLT passed the contribution order on 07.05.2024[cite: 14]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: MOU terms requiring 99% payment by 28.11.2011—a date prior to Respondent No. 2's own acquisition from Kotak (29.11.2011) and prior to MOU execution (17.12.2011); deliberate payment of only 98.997% to create an automatic artificial default triggering a built-in 'no recourse and forfeiture' clause; failure to execute any assignment deed; and retention by Respondent No. 2 of both the forfeited sums and recoveries from Mafatlal's Liquidator[cite: 14]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 2853 of 2021 held the transaction to be fraudulent, declared the MOU sham and void ab initio, and directed the Appellants under Section 66(1) to contribute Rs. 36.53 Crores to the assets of the Corporate Debtor[cite: 14]. Appellants appealed to NCLAT[cite: 14].
legal_issues: Whether Section 66(1) of the IBC contains a look-back period limiting the investigation of fraudulent business transactions; whether the Adjudicating Authority has jurisdiction under Section 66 to examine and treat a fraudulent contract as void ab initio; and whether erstwhile directors are liable to contribute assets for carrying on business with intent to defraud creditors under Section 66(1)[cite: 14].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Section 66(1) of the IBC prescribes no statutory look-back period; fraudulent trading carried on with intent to defraud creditors or for any fraudulent purpose can be examined irrespective of the time elapsed prior to CIRP commencement[cite: 14]. Section 66(1) and Section 66(2) operate independently in distinct spheres[cite: 14]. While Section 66 does not confer general powers of contractual avoidance as under Sections 43-51, where a contract is per se fraudulent, collusive, and engineered to siphoning assets, it is void ab initio and non est in the eyes of law, and the Tribunal possesses incidental jurisdiction to disregard it and direct restitution[cite: 14]. Directors who knowingly orchestrate transactions designed to forfeit corporate funds under sham arrangements are personally liable to contribute to the corporate debtor's estate[cite: 14]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The legislature deliberately omitted a look-back period in Section 66, unlike Sections 43 and 46[cite: 14]. Fraud vitiates all solemn acts and nullifies contracts ab initio[cite: 14]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Circumstantial proof establishing pre-arranged dates of payment preceding asset acquisition by the assignor, grossly inflated price exceeding admitted liquidation debt, deliberate default of tiny fraction to invite contractual forfeiture, and complete inaction to enforce rights over a decade[cite: 14]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The acquisition and forfeiture arrangement was a fraudulent device to extract corporate funds; NCLT rightly directed the directors to contribute Rs. 36.53 Crores[cite: 14].
operative_order: The impugned order dated 07.05.2024 passed by NCLT Mumbai Bench-I in IA No. 2853 of 2021 is affirmed; Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 1277 of 2024 is dismissed; pending IAs closed; interim orders vacated; no order as to costs[cite: 14].
summary: NCLAT dismissed an appeal filed by erstwhile directors of Chamber Construction Pvt. Ltd. challenging NCLT Mumbai's order directing them to contribute Rs. 36.53 Crores under Section 66 of the IBC[cite: 14]. The directors had caused the company to pay over Rs. 38 Crores to an ARC for assigning a debt of a company in liquidation worth only Rs. 16.68 Crores, under an MOU structured so that 99% consideration was due before the ARC even acquired the debt, with an artificial default engineered to trigger forfeiture[cite: 14]. NCLAT held that Section 66(1) has no look-back limitation period, that fraud vitiates transactions ab initio allowing the tribunal to treat such sham contracts as non est, and affirmed the personal contribution order against the directors[cite: 14].

case_title: Orissa Alloy Steel Private Limited vs. S M Steels And Power Limited & Ors.
appeal_number: Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 255-257 of 2025 & Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 214-216 of 2025
material_facts: 1. PARTY IDENTITIES: The Corporate Debtor is Corporate Power Limited (in liquidation)[cite: 17]. Pankaj Dhanuka is the Liquidator[cite: 17]. Orissa Alloy Steel Pvt. Ltd. (OASPL, part of Rashmi Group) is an anchor bidder/purchaser[cite: 17]. S M Steels and Power Limited (SMSPL) is a prospective bidder and applicant[cite: 17]. Assets Care and Reconstruction Enterprise Limited (ACRE) is a majority SCC member holding 60.65% voting share[cite: 17]. 2. COMMERCIAL TRANSACTION: Private sale of the Corporate Debtor as a going concern adopting a Swiss Challenge Mechanism under Regulation 33(2)(d) of the Liquidation Process Regulations following nine failed public e-auctions[cite: 17]. 3. DEFAULT METRICS: Corporate Debtor admitted to CIRP on 19.03.2020 and ordered into liquidation on 08.10.2021; reserve price started at Rs. 770 Crores in the 1st auction and fell to Rs. 292.91 Crores in the 9th failed auction; OASPL proposed private sale anchor bid of Rs. 265 Crores[cite: 17]. 4. STATUTORY TIMELINES: Public announcement issued on 22.02.2024 fixing last date for eligibility documents as 27.02.2024, last date for EMD as 29.02.2024 (12:00 PM), and bidding on 05.03.2024; Liquidator filed IA No. 447/KB/2024 on 24.02.2024; LOI issued to OASPL on 06.03.2024; SMSPL intervened on 16.03.2024 offering Rs. 300.20 Crores and filed IA No. 586/KB/2024 on 18.03.2024 and IA No. 995/KB/2024 on 09.05.2024[cite: 17]. 5. FACTUAL EVIDENCE: Process Document dated 29.02.2024 published two days after the deadline for submitting eligibility documents (27.02.2024); disproportionately high EMD of Rs. 150 Crores (exceeding 50% of the reserve price) required within hours of document publication; absence of prior permission from NCLT before initiating the private sale; and common beneficial ownership between OASPL and security receipt holders of ACRE[cite: 17]. 6. PROCEDURAL HISTORY: NCLT Kolkata Bench on 20.12.2024 dismissed the Liquidator's IA No. 447/KB/2024 for failure to obtain prior permission under Regulation 33(2)(d), set aside the public notice, and ordered a fresh Swiss Challenge with OASPL as anchor bidder and standard EMD[cite: 17]. OASPL and SMSPL both appealed[cite: 17].
legal_issues: Whether a non-participating entity has locus to challenge a private sale process prior to confirmation of sale by the Adjudicating Authority; whether the requirement of 'prior permission' under Regulation 33(2)(d) of the Liquidation Process Regulations mandates obtaining approval before initiating the terms of a private sale; whether abridged timelines and post-dated release of the Process Document vitiate the sale process; and whether commonality of beneficial interest between a creditor trust and a bidder establishes collusion under Regulation 33(3)[cite: 17].
ratio_decidendi: 1. ABSTRACT LEGAL RULE: Under Regulation 33(2)(d) of the IBBI (Liquidation Process) Regulations, 2016, 'prior permission' of the Adjudicating Authority is mandatory before initiating and setting the terms for a private sale of non-perishable corporate assets, and seeking post-facto or contemporaneous sanction presents a fait accompli that invalidates the sale[cite: 17]. A private sale process that curtails statutory timelines, withholds the governing Process Document until after eligibility deadlines pass, and imposes an exorbitant Earnest Money Deposit (EMD) is opaque and fatally flawed as it prevents competitive price discovery and asset value maximization[cite: 17]. Allegations of collusion under Regulation 33(3) require tangible proof and 'reason to believe' based on facts, which cannot be inferred merely from shared group affiliations when the concerned creditor lacked the 66% voting threshold to dictate SCC decisions unilaterally[cite: 17]. 2. STATUTORY INTERPRETATION: The term 'prior' prefixed to 'permission' in Regulation 33(2)(d) is strict and mandatory, precluding retrospective regularisation[cite: 17]. Schedule I auction timelines do not automatically apply to private sales, but private sales must afford reasonable opportunities to bidders[cite: 17]. 3. EVIDENTIARY TEST APPLIED: Concrete documentary proof demonstrating that the Process Document was dated and circulated after the deadline for eligibility submissions had expired, and absence of independent collusive acts beyond lawful voting by a multi-member SCC[cite: 17]. 4. DEFINITIVE CONCLUSION: The initial private sale was rightly set aside due to lack of prior permission, opaque process management, and prohibitive EMD terms; a fresh private sale with a reasonable EMD of 10% was ordered to ensure true price discovery and value maximization[cite: 17].
operative_order: Both Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) Nos. 255-257 of 2025 and 214-216 of 2025 are disposed of by modifying the impugned order; the setting aside of the public notice dated 22.02.2024 is affirmed; the Liquidator is directed to restart and conclude a fresh private sale within 60 days open to all eligible bidders (including OASPL and SMSPL) with the reserve price maintained at Rs. 265 Crores and EMD fixed at 10% of reserve price; no orders as to costs[cite: 17].
summary: NCLAT disposed of cross-appeals by Orissa Alloy Steel Pvt. Ltd. (OASPL) and S M Steels and Power Ltd. (SMSPL) against NCLT Kolkata's order setting aside a Swiss Challenge private sale of Corporate Power Limited[cite: 17]. NCLT had rejected the sale because the Liquidator failed to seek mandatory 'prior permission' under Regulation 33(2)(d) of the Liquidation Process Regulations before launching the sale[cite: 17]. NCLAT affirmed that prior permission cannot mean post-facto ratification and held that the process was fatally compromised by issuing the Process Document after the eligibility deadline had expired and imposing an exorbitant Rs. 150 Crore EMD[cite: 17]. NCLAT directed the Liquidator to conduct a fresh, open private sale within 60 days with reserve price at Rs. 265 Crores and standard 10% EMD[cite: 17].
